"The Shadow Reader" was one of the best debut last year. That's why I am sad to announce that the sequel let me down. 
 "The Shattered Dark" starts almost immediately after events of the first book. The rebels are now in the Silver Palace trying to hold their positions and catch remnants. 
 The reason I was displeased with this book, was because it was very erratic. Whole book consisted of running, ambushes and fights. And that left no time for character growth, for deepening the world-building, or just for simple dialogs (which there were so few). There wasn't enough of Kyol. And McKenzy's relationship with Aren seemed stuck. 
 I think that the plot lacked purpose, a mission. In the first book rebels were on the offence with the goal to overthrow the king which meant they were always planning, scheming, truing to think of some ways to do it. But in this book rebels are on the defense. They don't have a goal beside to hold their position one fight at a time. Which left this book with a lot of disconnected fights and no mission to bound them into thrilling quest. 
 A lot of reviews said that this book ends with a cliffhanger. I actually disagree. Of course some story lines were left open for the future installments, but main problems were solved. 
 I really hope that now when the worst of the war is out of the way the third book will be more paced and will manage to claim the glory of "The Shadow Reader".

There's a young man interested in her daughter who turns out to be Guilas Duncan's ancestor . So Clair recounts to her daughter and the young man the story from where the first book left off through her trip back through the stone.

Johnathan Randal also makes an appearance, and the relationship between himself, his brother, Claire and Jamie I think is one of the best parts of the book. It adds a layer of complexity to the bad guy  As always Gabaldon's strength is in her character development and historical research. For me her weakness is in the density of the story. It's dense but it moves so quick that if you zone out for a few pages you're completely out of the story. 
 I finished the book because I read the back of a future novel and realized Jamie and Claire make it to the American Revelation and I'm excited to read that... but I'm also glad I finished the book for it's own sake. I learned a lot and the next book I read felt somewhat dull to the people and places I'd been in Dragonfly in Amber. Give it a read but don't skip the first book.

I guess the end to Little Women doesn't bother me as much as it bothers others, but I thought that was drastic and annoying and I wasn't too impressed with the other twist either. For book meta, I will take Jasper Fforde and Thursday Next any day. At least they like their books.

 There are not enough words in the universe to describe how much I love this book! 
 I'll admit I was skeptical at first. Contemporary books are normally not my thing. But Pushing the Limits got such rave reviews and I thought the plot sounded intriguing, so I figured I'd give it a whirl. I fell completely in love. I felt like I was Echo.. and Noah. Pushing the Limits yanked my heart out as I suffered through Echo and Noah's pains, and then put it back together as they healed. I was living every moment with them, my emotions rising and falling with theirs. 
 I laughed, I cried, I giggled insanely.. god, I'm ready to read it all over again! 
 Okay, Ashley, focus. 
 Pushing the Limits is riddled with raw emotion. It deals with some really intense issues that you wouldn't usually expect in a romance novel, but that's what makes it feel so genuine and so powerful. 
 Throughout the entire book, it was so much fun watching Noah and Echo's chemistry evolve. It's the furthest you could get from insta-love. It starts out as sort of a "hate" relationship. Echo has this preconception of Noah as a troubled, bad boy, girl-using druggie. And Noah has a preconception of Echo being the pathetic, loner, possibly suicidal outcast. When their relationship evolves, you see both of these characters wondering why they're falling for the other person. They don't understand it; it's weird; it doesn't make sense. But somehow these two people are drawn together and attracted to each other because they manage to find common grounds in the darkest parts of their lives. 
 Even if you don't have a dark and terrible past like Noah and Echo do, this book makes you sympathize; it makes you understand. Every word on every page is so genuine and filled with raw emotion that you feel like you're living the story. Pushing the Limits deals with topics like abuse, foster care, psychological disorders, and divorce. But don't worry, it's not all heavy, intense subjects. 
 Echo and Noah both have 'lesser' problems as well -- ones that most teenagers face and thus, might be easier to relate to for some people. They both just want to have normal lives. Echo struggles between two guys: the ex boyfriend who constantly tries to pressure her into having sex, and the bad boy who she thinks is probably no good for her. She worries about not having a date to the social dance, about never finding a guy who will love her, getting the courage to ask her parents for birth control, and so on. These are problems that most teenage girls think about at one time or another. 
 My one grip? So much sexual tension and no climax! Katie, why must you taunt me so??? 
 This is definitely one of the best books -- if not the best -- I have read this year! I've already preordered my own copy of this book and I'm recommending Pushing the Limits to every single person I know!

Uggh. I really wanted to like this. I was really in the mood for a good contemporary YA but this just did not make the cut. I didn't find the protagonist, Andie, particularly interesting. (So much that for a second just now, I thought her name was Addie.) She was fine, but there was nothing that interesting about her. I didn't particularly care about her problems which were, basically, that her summer plans were ruined and that - the classic YA girl problem - her life was too planned and perfect. I've seen this "too perfect" problem SO many times (it's the plot of like at least half of Sarah Dessen novels), and that is a real issue for girls - the pressure to be perfect - but it was just not that interesting here. The twist that her dad was a Senator was sort of interesting, but, again, we've seen that before (My Life Next Door), and his scandal wasn't even that interesting. (Unless it got more interesting later? Maybe?) And also her whole thing about not wanting to get too attached to anyone - seen it before, and it doesn't feel real. Basically, the stakes here weren't high enough, and the narrator wasn't particularly compelling. She wasn't shy and quirky like Cath in Fangirl, or sassy and funny like Laura Jean in To All The Boys I've Loved Before. She was just blah...In fact, all of the characters (at least as far as I read) seemed very boring and one-dimensional. Andie had three friends that basically seemed like copies of each other except one was like..kind of sassy? And one was...kind of shy? They all liked texting? I don't know. 
 Also, as a Goodreads friend of mine said about another Morgan Matson book, this book was so white. White and upper middle class. The kids playing "beruit" at their house parties and drinking Starbucks. Not that there's something wrong with being white, or writing what you know, but it felt a bit tone deaf I guess? A lack of self-awareness? I don't know. It didn't feel very modern, like the direction that YA is (and should be) going in. Like, it really irked me when the "cool" friend is described as being blonde, skinny, and yet somehow able to eat anything she wants. Come on, Morgan Matson. Do better.

ACTUAL RATING: 0.5. I only wish I could go that low. 
 *Some spoilers, although I don't think these could ruin the book any further. 
 There are many things wrong with this book. 
 First off, I graciously tolerated it for a full 176 pages. I continued to read, because I wanted to see it better itself. I waited and read, waited and read. Eventually, I was skimming over the pages, waiting to see if anything even changes. 
 It didn't. 
 I was aware of a few things when I was reading. One, was that it was the classic "dark mysterious Edward going after the not-so-known- Bella, with a happy go lucky but distant Jacob" thing going on. I mean this in the most serious way: The first half of the book was really all about how two guys are trying to go for her. How convenient they both just moved to the school, huh? In the course of 150 pages, she already had 2 near death experience, and it just so happens that she doesn't even remember either of them clearly, doubting herself. 
 Oh. 
 And what was THAT about. Patch in her head or something? He just appears to be everywhere she is. He's known the girl personally for what 5 days, then he's a stalker in denial? No one DOES that. NO ONE. I know this book is suppose to be about the supernatural world, it is based off of some sort of reality, and no one in reality gets that intimate that quickly. He even goes and wipes lip-gloss off of her. Creep. 
 At first, the beginning drew me in, then it was all over as soon as it started. 
 And what was up with that sex ed thing in the beginning? I didn't understand how that was relevant to the novel what so ever. I kept on having to remind myself it wasn't written in third person, although I constantly felt like it was. 
 I found it entirely amusing that she let him into her house after going on the Archangel, after she told herself multiple times he's "bad and dark". 
 Oh. And that bomb threat. They were that desperate to look up a guy on student records to call in a BOMB THREAT? They hardly know Patch, but they broke into the office, issued a bomb threat, and looked through the file folder? I get that they think he's a stalker, but a bomb threat? Really? 
 I can't believe I used up my precious time on this book when I could be reading something a lot better. I thought it would get better. The best thing this book did to me was make me smile. Not laugh - just smile. 
 Horribly written book, and I have no idea how it even got published.

 Out of the blue Webber invites Tristan on a working holiday. They have a few weeks to sort out their feelings for each other and redefine their relationship.

Good in that it was a sweet read with likeable characters and a pretty angst light storyline, bad in that the characters and storyline felt a bit artifical to me. Can a story be too romantic? I sound like such a scrooge but while this was a cute, gentle read it just wasn't really to my taste. 
 If you're in the mood for a super sweetly romantic M/M then this would be an excellent choice.

This book taught me what horror is. I read it first in translation (and it was such a beautiful translation!) at the tender age of eight - and learnt the meaning of "delicious nightmare". I read it again in the original English in my twenties, and found that the story had not lost any of its power, for me. 
 I know many people do not find the Count frightening nowadays: I daresay I wouldn't either, if I read it for the first time now. Our palate has been jaded by heavy dosages of horror since this book came into existence. 
 But Bram Stoker did not just create a story - he created a whole new myth. Count Dracula took off on his bat wings from the pages of this book and has been fluttering around the literary and movie establishment ever since (even infiltrating the world of animated movies). 
 Hotel Transylvania 
 Even one of the famous pulp writers in my native language, Malayalam, has written a series of popular novels featuring Dracula. 
 ("Dracula's Castle" by Kottayam Pushpanath) 
 This is no mean achievement! 
 -------------------------------------- 
 Now coming to the novel - the book is brilliantly written. The epistolary format with its lack of atmosphere building enhances the terror, rather than ameliorating it. The story begins at a high point - Jonathan Harker's nightmare stay in Dracula's Carpathian castle - then drops into a trough, to slowly mount back again to the peak of terror in a rising crescendo. The final chase across the snow-capped Carpathian mountains is worthy of any modern thriller. 
 I think it's time for another read.

I was really disappointed with this book. Not because it is bad or even that I didn't like the characters; but it was so normal. Too normal. Lost Lake is a book that Kate Morton or Jane Green would write, which again, is not bad; I read Kate Morton or Jane Green. When I'm in the mood for Kate Morton or Jane Green. But I was in the mood for Sarah Addison Allen, and this was not a Sarah Addison Allen book. 
 I get veering from your course as an author because you're on to better things (I've done it) or even Sarah Addison Allen's heartbreaking and unique case, writing a book post-cancer-diagnosis-and-treatment. So I feel bad about being disappointed, but I am, and it's either because cancer changes perceptions (this was the first book Allen wrote after her public battle with cancer) or Sarah Addison Allen decided to stop writing magical books (which can't really be true because First Frost came after this and I loved it). I know I'm not supposed to review the author. I'm sorry. I'm just bummed that my favorite author and inspiration--the author whose new book you buy even before you know what it is about--has written this. She's better than this. I know; I've read all of her books. 
 Anyway. Lost Lake. Kate's husband Matt dies and she takes her daughter Devin to her great aunt's property where there is an alligator who used to be a little boy and where Kate's first love Wes is waiting for her. It sounds like a Sarah Addison Allen book, but I assure you it is not. The magic in all of Allen's stories is missing; there are no mood-altering flowers or person-chasing books. It's a mundane child's imagination and Wes's character is underdeveloped, so much that I really didn't care about him at all. I was happy it was over when it was and just kind of shrugged at the end. It took me a really a long time to get through this--like, months. I make it sound awful, but it's really not, for someone who is not expecting that Sarah Addison Allen flair. But for someone who is, you will probably be sorely disappointed. Luckily, life gets better. Like I said First Frost was released after Lost Lake and it is so much better (especially if you've read Garden Spells). 
 If you want a random cute love story you might like it. True Sarah Addison Allen fans, though, would be better off skipping this one.

The Masked Truth has its faults, just as every book does. Even those five star books have something that could have been improved, despite what your heart-that is fully infatuated with the book-says. The things that were impressive about this book are pretty even with the aspects that could have been improved. However, the impressive parts outweigh the not-so-impressive parts in how they're not in YA books enough. 
 I have never, ever read a book solely about a hostage situation. I'm really glad this was my first one. Although slow at times, there are so many twists, and I was genuinely scared for these characters. A lot of people are saying the situation isn't realistic, but who is going to think that there is three psychopaths in masks holding a therapy group hostage? Especially considering it's just a normal warehouse in a kind of...barren town. It makes even more sense once you get to the end, and all the plot holes are explained almost perfectly. 
 My favorite thing about the whole book is the phenomenal representation. There's a gay character, a Hispanic character, and a schizophrenic character. Even better, all are handled super well. I have no complaints. Then we have the slight theme that those in authority (the police, mainly) can't always be trusted. This theme resonated with what has been going on with the police and people of color. Really hit home. 
 I remember, too, overhearing a couple of guys a police BBQ saying Dad was soft on the gangbangers because he'd grown up with guys like that. Which was presumptuous and racist bullshit. Dad was raised in the suburbs. He didn't shoot that kid because he wouldn't shoot any kid. 
 Then we have the creepiness of this book. Imagine: going to the bathroom at your therapy session. Getting pulled aside by a man in an alien mask. With a gun. Fast forward. Running for your life in a warehouse, hearing gunshots occasionally and seeing the bodies strewn in the hallways. Terrifying. Yeah, there were things that seemed too easy for these characters, but I didn't think it was that implausible. 
 The romance didn't even annoy me as much as I was expecting. It's apparent at the beginning of the book that Max is kind of infatuated with Riley, and he doesn't turn that off even when they're running for their life. There were a couple times when I wanted to scream "less flirting, more hiding!" but it was outweighed by how these two complemented one another. I wouldn't go as far as saying they're an OTP of mine, but they weren't a negative in the novel. 
 My only minor complaint is that Max's "inside voice" got a little annoying/confusing at times. I understand why it was included, but I didn't think it added that much to his character. Plus, it was slow at parts, but I excuse that for the most part considering there's not much you can do when you're trapped in a warehouse, and all you can do is run and hide. 
 Definitely pick this one up if you haven't. It's way better than I was expecting.

"There are some things I have to tell you," Betonie began softly. "The people nowadays have an idea about the ceremonies. They think the ceremonies must be performed exactly as they have always been done, maybe because one slip-up or mistake and the whole ceremony must be stopped and the sand painting destroyed. That much is true. They think that if a singer tampers with any part of the ritual, great harm can be done, great power unleashed." He was quiet for a while, looking up at the sky through the smoke hole. "That much can be true also. But long ago when the people were given these ceremonies, the changing began, if only in the aging of the yellow gourd rattle or the shrinking of the skin around the eagle's claw, if only in the different voices from generation to generation, singing the chants... At one time, the ceremonies as they had been performed were enough for the way the world was then. But after the white people came, elements in this world began to shift; and it became necessary to create new ceremonies. I have made changes in the rituals. The people mistrust this greatly, but only this growth keeps the ceremonies strong. She taught me this above all else: things which don't grow are dead things. They are the things the witchery people want. Witchery works to scare people, to make them fear growth. But it has always been necessary, and more than ever now, it is. Otherwise we won't make it. We won't survive. That's what the witchery is counting on: that we will cling to the ceremonies the way they were, and then their power will triumph, and the people will be no more."I found myself in the book, in the story about witch* people and how white settlers were created in a contest to show off the scariest thing possble. I'd already heard Thomas King's version of this story, but it meant something else to me then, it had a different emphasis. In this story I myself come into being, a destroyer's vampire ghost. From the backs of my thighs to the base of my spine to my stomach's underside I felt a chill crawling up to my chest, I felt myself blur into the world, fibres of my being knitting into the half-poisoned London air. I am not outside this story. It has no borders. Its materials, its hero, Tayo, are only one cycle of the sun, one fold of the skein. 
 They live, these materials of the story, these people and lands, written with the clarity of morning light and changing rhythm of a dance that made me read slow, slow, fast, slow. Written with ferocity and calm. Some of what is real is what I know, and some I am not ready to know and have to pass over as mystery, magic shaken out of a story like sand from a shawl. The teachers with their books of science trying to shout over everyone sound so reedy, weak and distant. They are inside too, not encircling nature but encircled. Outside Plato's cave is the cave of the sky. But as usual I am getting carried away, let me stay earthbound, let me stay with our storyteller who is making the dry land of the southwest so sonorous with its mesas and arroyos, cousins so distant from the drizzle-rinsed and misty hills that I know... 
 It took me until the end to realise that Silko made her healing ceremony a book. And there I was again, coming through the ceremony, and I can see the healing is for me too (it isn't easy, though, it's never been easy for anyone, to travel from rage and loss and pain into love, to mend things that have been broken). I had to rethink how race is read when the circle closed and Tayo's connection with the Japanese turned out to be nothing to do with ethnic links - resemblance was a misleading sign. The people of Nagasaki and Hiroshima were the ones Silko's ceremony came too late to save.  
 *in my culture many of the stories about witches are lies spread to prevent women from disrupting white male power as propagated through the church and state (the divine right of kings). As a feminist, and since in Britain 'witches' were often what Silko might call medicine people, those in touch with and learned in ways of healing that involved herb lore, an ethics of care and community, and practical wisdom derived from an oral tradition and personal experience of observing the cycles of nature, I myself am very fond of the word witch, and I appreciate the literature that seeks to rehabilitate it. This literature includes Phillip Pullman's

Basic plot: When the story begins, the king, queen, and crown prince of Carthya have been murdered. With no one in line for the throne, it looks like Carthya will fall to war. 
 Sage is an orphan. One night he is bought by Connor, a noble, along with three other orphans. Connor's plan is to train the boys and pass one of them off as the missing (assumed dead) Prince Jaron, who would be next in line for the throne. Connor tells the boys to compete with each other to see who can pass themselves off as the most convincing prince, and implies that whoever is not chosen will be killed for security reasons. 
 My thoughts: There were a lot of things about this book that I liked, including Sage himself. I'm a huge fan of books where characters switch identities. Sage is a fun narrator with a sharp tongue and amusing antics. Watching the boys compete with each other was exciting, even though it was obvious that Sage would win from the beginning. The part I was looking forward to the most was seeing how Sage would rule, and how he would manage to deceive the court, once he (inevitably) won the throne. Unfortunately, that never came to pass; the book ends shortly after Sage takes the throne. 
 The main thing I disliked was the plot twist near the end: Sage truly is the missing prince, and has been passing himself off as an orphan for the past few years for reasons of his own . Everything that made the book interesting to me is thrown out the window. It ties everything up nicely with a tidy bow... which is competent storytelling, I suppose, but not very interesting or unique. I think I would be more forgiving if this was a standalone book, but it's not. Thanks to that plot twist, the sequels have exactly one direction they can go, and I have no desire to read them. The only good thing I can say about the plot twist is that I didn't predict it (because I never imagined the author would intentionally limit herself like that). 
 My smaller complaint has to do with the secondary characters. Connor, who at first seems like a man who uses questionable means to ensure the lasting peace of his country, is slowly revealed to be an unsympathetic villain. Towards the beginning of the book it looked like he had potential to be a nuanced, morally gray character. Unfortunately, the author decided to go with the "he was evil all along" route. The other minor characters were under-developed at best and one-dimensional at worst. 
 Overall, it's a good book if you're looking for something quick and light to pass the time. If you're looking for a novel with more depth, you should look elsewhere.

So...I really wanted to dislike this book. I was determined not to allow myself to be one of "those girls." You know...the ones who plan ladies night out to watch Sex and the City. I've never had a desire to read Bridget Jones' Diary or The Devil Wears Prada (although I do hate to admit that I actually liked Devil as a movie) I mean, it's Chick Lit. Fluff without the smut. What fun is that? 
 Turns out, it's more fun than I was expecting. The book started out in such a way that I was expecting to give up before making it past a few chapters. I practically sighed with exasperation over the flighty, bumbling, office girl who embarrasses herself in front of her boss without knowing who he is. The thoughts in my head were practically burning a hole in the Nook. No, I don't care about what crappy fashion you're wearing to the office. No, I don't care that you're really a size 12 but tell people you're an 8. No, I don't care that you have a lame ass boyfriend who listens to jazz and likes bad movies. 
 Just as I was about to hit "delete" and ditch the book from my ereader, something happened. I started laughing. A LOT. Not the polite little giggly "oh that's cute" type of laughter. The snorting, choking, oh-my-god I'm dying laughter. My husband even looked up from his zombie like trance mid-video-game to give me a wtf? look. 
 It took several chapters for me to warm up to the book and truth be told, if I hadn't promised myself that I wanted to finish at least one chick lit book just to say that I had given the genre a shot, I would have quit out before getting to the part where it started to get good. Once I got past the mediocre parts revolving around the main character's office and family life, and got into the part where she was spending most of her time trying to figure out how to make a relationship with her boss work, I was along for the ride. It was quite the fun ride, too. I was pleasantly surprised. 
 Will I continue to read chick lit after this? Hmmm...I don't know. This book was fun and I'm completely glad that I read it, but I still am not fond of the office girl/modern day girl formula that seems to be pretty big in this genre. Even with as funny as this book was, I've browsed some reviews for the author's books and it looks like she tends to stick with a similar subject matter for most of her books.

 3.5 stars. For a 700 and something page book, this read very quickly, and the writing is very good. The story was not at all what I was expecting. I knew how the book began but not at all where it was going. 
 There was a lot of hype surrounding this book. It got fantastic reviews and was likened to Dickens, which was a major appeal to me. Plus I was intrigued by tragedy tied to a painting. I immediately liked Theo and his mother. After the bombing, I was so distressed about what would happen with Theo and spent hundreds and hundreds of pages worrying about him, about this boy who had no one to care for him or be a proper caregiver to him (except Hobie, of course). 
 Thus Theo embarks on a life of utter sadness, and throughout the part where he lives in Las Vegas, I endured with him constant and extraordinary drug use, drinking, poor hygiene, and parental neglect. I worried about Theo and his friend Boris, but stressed as well by the allusions to an undercurrent of potential Mob violence. 
 When Theo finally leaves Las Vegas, I worried the whole bus ride home with him about his little dog, Popchik, and of course, about Theo, too. What would happen to Theo in New York City? What is going to happen to this poor kid and how on earth is anything good going to happen with the painting? 
 Well, to keep my review from being 700 and something pages, let me start to wrap up. Theo continues to have numerous serious problems, most of them caused by his own very poor choices. Somehow he still seems a likeable character. But this book takes you to the complete depths with him. In the back of my mind, I kept thinking, if this book is getting such great reviews and everyone loves it, then the author must swing the story back up, in the end. 
 It was the end that kept this book from being tossed across the room. After enduring such terrible neglect, constant and variable substance abuse, extremely poor choices, and tragedy way beyond the terrorist attack at the museum, I was not happy that I was reading this book (especially around New Year's Eve, which I find to be very depressing, anyway). The book doesn't end with justice, there is no happily ever after. But, in the last few pages, Theo philosophizes in a way that I wish I had glimpsed in the rest of the book. He looks hard at his life and realizes some truths. These were very powerful pages containing thoughts and ideas I'd like to ponder further. I also am intrigued by Boris, and some of his last lines questioning-- can't some good come from a life of bad? Not all good comes from good. 
 Again, very good writing. The characters of Hobie and Pippa created a such a warm familial sense that I longed for Theo to end up with those two. I also liked Mrs. Barbour and Boris, very much too, though Boris is a challenging character. 
 I am glad I read the book. It was very sad and depressing, ultimately and the story was completely unexpected. I wonder if I would enjoy reading it again in a few years, knowing the story and being able to enjoy the writing and characters without worrying quite so much about their welfare.

When a new Molly Harper "Jane Jameson" book comes out I am always a happy camper and she doesn't disappoint with the newest installment. Filled with Molly's Jane's Molly's Molly's and Jane's snarky repartee, this is the first book in the series that brought tears to my eyes for laughter and poignancy. Yes, there is a slightly sad bit, but it's appropriate to the story line. Romantically sexy but not too steamy. 
 If you know Jane's mother (think overwhelming) you understand why Jane would be reluctant to tell her she is engaged to her Sire, Gabriel. But, rare is the wedding where a family escapes unscathed. Molly certainly gets that! And, you have to love all the characters, except of course the characters trying to kill Jane or who are trying to steal her house, River Oaks. 
 You have to love Gabriel, Jane's sire and fiance. He is a romantic man and proposes quite divinely. 
 The story goes much the same way but for an immense twist I did not see coming really. Really! And, it appears this is the last novel Molly Harper plans featuring Jane's story, but she will appear, as will the Hollow in the spin off THE CARE AND FEEDING OF STRAY VAMPIRES (excerpt at the end of this book). 
 Harper brings such loving realism to her characters you will find yourself missing them when you turn the last page. You'll even miss the obnoxious mothers and aunts and the sketchy Vampire redneck, Dick Cheney. They're the characters you want to invite over for a Bloody Mary. 
 Though snarky and about vampires it could be snarky and about any group of people struggling against ignorance. Although in this instance, for once, it isn't stupid bigotry that is causing the biggest issue for the Jane and Gabriel. There is some bigotry, but it's at a personal level and speaks to love and family and acceptance. 
 In the end what I take from Harper's series is that whether we're werewolves, human or vampires we're all just people with flaws and strengths, we're lovers parents, sons and daughters, friends and neighbors. It's the simplest thing in the world, isn't it yet it's obviously something we need to hear over and over in life. 
 Harper make us laugh as we learn these truths and that's the best way to learn simple things; it is not at all pedantic and I doubt she sits down to write about "loving thy neighbor." 
 NICE GIRLS DON'T BITE THEIR NEIGHBORS is a must read if you've read the series and if you haven't read the series you are missing out and it's still a must read.

 Meet Hazel Grace. She's a survivor. Diagnosed at age 13 with Stage IV thyroid cancer, she was prepared to die. That was until at age 14, a medical miracle shrunk the tumours in her lungs, prolonging her life. 
 Now at age sixteen, Hazel lives tethered to an oxygen tank. And she's sick of living this way, not knowing when she could die, and that when she dies, all she'll leave behind is sorrow and heartache. 
 "I'm like. Like. I'm like a grenade, Mom. 
 I'm a grenade and at some point I'm going to 160/488 
 blow up and I would like to minimize the casualties, okay?" 
 And so she refuses to bring anyone else into her doomed life. Well, that is, until one day at Cancer support group she meets Augustus Waters; fun, happy and all around optimist. 
 Together, they re-examine the unfair and unpredictable journey called life and it's inevitable destination... 
 There will come a time when all of us are dead. All of us. There will come a time when there are no human beings remaining to remember that anyone ever existed or that our species ever did anything. There will be no one left to remember Aristotle or Cleopatra, let alone you. Everything that we did and built and wrote and thought and discovered will be forgotten and all of this will have been for naught. Maybe that time is coming soon and maybe it is millions of years away, but even if we survive the collapse of our sun, we will not survive forever. There was time before organisms experienced consciousness, and there will be time after. And if the inevitability of human oblivion worries you, I encourage you to ignore it. God knows that's what everyone else does." 
 "That's part of what I like about the book in some ways. It portrays death truthfully. You die in the middle of your life, in the middle of a sentence" 
 They try to make the best of their numbered days.... 
 "There are infinite numbers between 0 and 1. There's .1 and .12 and .112 and an infinite collection of others. Of course, there is a bigger infinite set of numbers between 0 and 2, or between 0 and a million. Some infinities are bigger than other infinities. A writer we used to like taught us that. There are days, many of them, when I resent the size of my unbounded set. I want more numbers than I'm likely to get, and God, I want more numbers for Augustus Waters than he got. But, Gus, my love, I cannot tell you how thankful I am for our little infinity. I wouldn't trade it for the world. You gave me a forever within the numbered days, and I'm grateful." 
 And they fall in love... 
 . 
 "I'm in love with you," he said quietly. 
 "Augustus," I said. 
 "I am," he said. He was staring at me, and I could see the corners of his eyes crinkling. "I'm in love with you, and I'm not in the business of denying myself the simple pleasure of saying true things. I'm in love with you, and I know that love is just a shout into the void, and that oblivion is inevitable, and that we're all doomed and that there will come a day when all our labor has been returned to dust, and I know the sun will swallow the only earth we'll ever have, and I am in love with you." 
 "I fell in love the way you fall asleep: slowly, then all at once." 
 "Some people don't understand the promises they're making when they make them," I said. 
 "Right, of course. But you keep the promise anyway. That's what love is. Love is keeping the promise anyway." 
 "But I believe in true love, you know? I don't believe that everybody gets to keep their eyes or not get sick or whatever, but everybody should have true love, and it should last at least as long as your life does." 
 But as their days become fewer, they must face the fact that all good things really do come to an end... 
 "You gave me a forever within the numbered days, and I'm grateful." 
 And so they grieve... 
 "Augustus Waters was a self-aggrandizing bastard. But we forgive him. We forgive him not because he had a heart as figuratively good as his literal one sucked, or because he knew more about how to hold a cigarette than any nonsmoker in history, or because he got eighteen years when he should've gotten more.' 
 'Seventeen,' Gus corrected. 
 'I'm assuming you've got some time, you interupting bastard. 
 'I'm telling you,' Isaac continued, 'Augustus Waters talked so much that he'd interupt you at his own funeral. And he was pretentious: Sweet Jesus Christ, that kid never took a piss without pondering the abundant metaphorical resonances of human waste production. And he was vain: I do not believe I have ever met a more physically attractive person who was more acutely aware of his own physical attractiveness. 
 'But I will say this: When the scientists of the future show up at my house with robot eyes and they tell me to try them on, I will tell the scientists to screw off, because I do not want to see a world without him.' 
 I was kind of crying by then." 
 "But it is the nature of stars to cross, and never was Shakespeare more wrong than when he has Cassius note, 'The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars / But in ourselves." 
 "That's the thing about pain...it demands to be felt." 
 ...and they learn... 
 "The real heroes anyway aren't the people doing things; the real heroes are the people NOTICING things, paying attention" 
 "We're as likely to hurt the universe as we are to help it, and we're not likely to do either." 
 ...and with the memories, they move on because what else can you really do at the end of the day? It always comes down to two choices: life or death. And they choose to live because death is inevitable. Life isn't. You don't get a repeat or have a chance to change the things that you did or did not do. You have one life and you make the most of it and when death comes knocking on your door, you won't have to be afraid or say that you regret your life because you've done all that you could have. You lived, you grieved, you had fun and you changed the world, even if it is just that of one person. But you can say that you made your life worthwhile. 
 "My name is Hazel. Augustus Waters was the great star-crossed love of my life. 
 Ours was an epic love story, and I won't be able to get more than a sentence into it without disappearing into a puddle of tears. 
 Gus knew. Gus knows. I will not tell you our love story, because--like all real love stories--it will die with us, as it should"

 I'm still crying. I'll probably never ever, ever recover from this book. Did I regret reading it though? Nope! Now I really know what book-depression is. I'm supposed to be packing my suitcase right now and cleaning up the house but instead, I am curled into a fetal position on my bed under the covers, hugging my brown bear which i renamed Bluie while writing a review to try to get over a book I'll probably never get over! The Fault in Our Stars is a very emotionally wrecking book. I cried for the last few chapters of the book continuously and cried after the book ended for a long while too. What shocked me even more though is that such an emotional book could be written by a man! I fell in love with Augustus to be honest. He was just such a happy-go-lucky person whom, despite his illness, was a humorous and happy person. 
 "I lit up like a Christmas tree, Hazel Grace." 
 From this phrase onwards, I was broken. 
 Needless to say, I read this book with tears streaming down my face all the way. I loved Hazel and Isaac and Augustus and there is no way I can ever tell anyone just how amazingly and beautifully this book was written and I don't think anyone can ever know unless they read it for themselves. I give this book 5 stars cuz it has everything I am looking for in a great book. 
 Augustus was just such a strong character and he was humorous even when he was in pain. He showed Hazel the brighter side of things and i loved that. He is just the type of gentle, funny, strong, caring, sweet and brave main male character that I can't get enough of. 
 I loved Isaac and I think he is one of my favourite supporting characters ever. I loved the way Augustus and him got along and how they were just the ideal best friends. Even though he was not mentioned a lot in the book, I think part of my heart belongs with him too. 
 Hazel is just one of the best realistic female characters ever. Unlike other books about cancer patients who wanted pity and enjoyed the attention they got, Hazel disliked all these things which made her seem more realistic. She didn't want to burden her parents with her death and didn't want to be a "grenade". In this way, I kind of understand her, having gone through what seemed like an unrecoverable situation(though not a fatal one). She was not delusional and did not hope for some sudden miracle to occur to rid her of her cancer. I really liked her and admired her character. 
 Overall, The Fault in Our Stars is a fantastic book. Will I be reading it again soon though? Definitely not! ( My eyes are still so sore and sensitive from all the crying and my stomach still aches.) But if anyone is looking for a great, emotional book, I will definitely suggest this one! No doubt about it. I could hardly breathe while reading this. Thank you so much John Green for gifting us with such a tear-jerking, eye-hurting, heart-breaking and yet incredible novel, The Fault in Our Stars. 
 John Green couldn't have explained my feelings about this book more perfectly. It's just that this book is so precious and close to my heart that telling everyone about it seems like an inappropriate thing to do but at the same time I want everyone to read it so that they can experience this amazing piece of work.

The Run-Down 
 Juliet Moreau used to be part of the rich society unil the scandal that pronounced her father as a madman. 
 But that was many years ago. Now Juliet's mother is dead, her father thought to be dead, and she works as a maid. 
 But after discovering that her father might not be dead after all, running into her an old friend, and basically getting fired from her job, she gets taken to the island where her father has lived all these years. 
 But strange things are going on at the island... 
 My Thoughts 
 Apparently, this is a retelling of The Island of Dr. Moreau Which I haven't even heard of until this book came out. 
 But I read this book anyway!! (YAY!) 
 I really did like this book. 
 I loved how it was written, I loved how it was put together... 
 To summarize, I basically loved it. 
 This book though is, well, creepy. 
 Strangely, I did not have a problem with that! 
 The Romance 
 There's this unspoken rule that every YA book must have romance! 
 So, of course, this book had it too. 
 I was not a fan of the romance. 
 It seemed to take away some of the focus. 
 The story is mainly supposed to focus on the island, the madman, the creatures, and all that other happy stuff! 
 But the romance got some unnecessary attention. 
 There was also a teensy little love triangle. 
 Okay, maybe not a teensy one but the love triangle added to my annoyance. 
 Juliet would act like she completely chose one guy and then she will start thinking about the other guy or start doubting herself. 
 I usually don't have a problem with romance but it just didn't do it for me in this book. 
 The Ending 
 OH 
 MY 
 CHEESE 
 THAT 
 ENDING 
 I did not see any of that coming. Believe me when I say that the ending is full of surprises. 
 And a cliffhanger... 
 In Conclusion 
 I believe the only problem I really had with this book was the romance. 
 There were some scenes that I didn't see the point of (Usually romance scenes) but everything else was AMAZING! 
 If it's not obvious by the 5 star rating, I really loved this book. 
 So do I recommend this book? Yes, yes I do. But if you're the type of person that avoids creepy/ horror stories? This book is not for you.

This is one of Dean Koontz's earlier novels and originally written in 1989. I was only 19 when I originally read it, boy, that makes me feel old! I'm reread it on unabridged audio recently. Despite its age it still holds up pretty well as a straight up horror novel where the citizens of a nice little town turn into horrifying blood-lusty creatures all thanks to a power-hungry geeky rich madman. Come to think of it, this is even scarier stuff in this day and age . . . 
 Anyway, I enjoyed it a lot and loved the back cover picture of Dean and his beautiful golden friend. Back to the contents, the computer technology is very dated. The fact that the hero has to search high and low for a public telephone to call headquarters really brought that fact home. It's amazing to see how far things have come since 1989. If only one could go back in time and be able to eat in a restaurant without hearing little musical ditties buzzing away in every corner. I know, I know, I sound more like a grandma everyday. 
 Like many a Koontz novel this one does go on (and on) a wee bit too long but it's a minor complaint as it kept me entertained without wanting to put it down never to be picked up again.
Great start to the series. I'm looking forward to seeing where this series is heading.

Okay...first let give a sort of introduction. I liked this book, and that's a relief as the last several YA books I've read have been, disappointing. Since I read the Harry Potter books (each as it came out) "with" my own children (though they were grown by the time the series completed) I've continued occasionally reading a YA book as some of them are excellent and not to be missed...even if "we" are old, grown-up, and decrepit. LOL 
 Now as to this book. I considered giving it a lower rating, and after this I'll say why. First I want to say I like the book. It's a good idea, it's handled well, and well told. I wanted to say all that as some might wonder why I'd rate a book 4 stars and then spend a lot of time on it's failings. Well, it's because a lot of what "I" found wanting here "may" be because I am an adult and have read literally thousands of books. What I find predictable or even a little trite may not be so to others, especially younger readers... 
 So, here goes. 
 Yes, this is a good book. BUT I would be sure that the "youth" reading it has a good "reality concept". In spite of my own local public library calling it or rating it "juvenile" I'd say the description "young adult" would be more apt. There are a lot of fairly "creepy" scenes including danger to children and reference to the death of children. 
 There is the slightly negative view of religion here that has become so prevalent of late, but it's mild and left open to later interpretation/reinterpretation in later books. The view seems to be based on the kind of negative impression that can be left by "religious" folk of an overly legalistic or judgmental mindset. 
 And some parents may share those views, so to them it may not seem as much of a problem. 
 I'd say these and any other "drawbacks" could be handled by a parent/guardian/responsible adult who loves the young person in question reading the book either with or before the youth and being ready to explain, discuss and otherwise guide the said youth. 
 ***Possible Spoiler Below *** 
 There are times in this book when I think anyone who has done any reading at all will see what's coming a proverbial mile away. Tom is told "whatever you do don't EVER do this". Of course we know that things will transpire so that Tom finds himself doing exactly that. This kind of thing happens several times in the book. But as I said, to younger readers this may not be as big a deal as it will be to adults. It's still a good read and enjoyable. 
 As to being sure that a young person is mature enough or has a good enough reality concept to read the book, remember the movie Hocus Pocus? While it cleared pretty good money world-wide it didn't do nearly as well as expected. Why? In my opinion it's because the movie opens with the murder of a little girl by the witches... no it's not graphic, we only see the witches "sucking" the life from a child who's back is turned to the camera, but it was something that parents weren't thrilled with. I always wondered who at Disney studios missed that little detail... oh well. Anyway, here in this novel, there is mention of "infant's blood cakes" and there is a child at one point being drained of life by an evil witch (we're told all witches aren't necessarily evil in the book's text lest this concern some)... so be aware. 
 There are a few of these scenes. Among the plot points are not only child endangering evils but also possession and of course, hauntings, etc. So, be aware. I don't think these reasons necessarily to avoid this book, just something to be considered in choosing who reads what. It's well written and well told just be aware and tailor the reading to the young person. 
 I have sent for the next 2 from the library and plan to see how they go...

"The truth is like bourbon - it'll burn going down." 
 Tiffany Reisz couldn't have picked a more perfect time to release her newest novel The Bourbon Thief. In a time of racial stress and a struggle for human empathy and understanding in America, this book of fiction contributes much needed perspective in my opinion. It shows examples of white privilege, the frustrations of persons of color who live a never-ending history of being viewed/treated differently, and it offers a necessary perspective of how slavery continues to impact an entire race. It's present in family trees, in the memories of precious elders, in coffee table photo albums, and at the core roots of some successful businesses that continue to thrive today. Slavery may already have found a place in the history books but it lingers still. 
 The Bourbon Thief is quality entertainment; it's complex as all get out with family, cultural, and historical dynamics, it has an engaging romance with one hell of a jaw-dropping revelation (just wait for it!), and the storytelling is superb as a present-day narrator takes us into the past. I hope every reader also gains some additional insight though. I loved this book and absolutely adore Ms. Reisz for writing it...whether she meant for it to have such an impact or not. Read it! 
 My favorite quote: 
 "How are you going to get revenge against dead people? Dig 'em up and stake 'em through the heart?" "I asked myself that same question, and I think I know the answer. You destroy what they loved, and you love what they destroyed." 
 Note: For readers who follow Ms. Reisz, it's important to note that The Bourbon Thief is more historical fiction with a touch of mystery and less of the erotica you may be accustomed to from her. I wouldn't want your expectations to be too disappointed, wink wink. However, she wouldn't be our fabulous Tiffany Reisz if she didn't push the envelope in some way. Just read it, you'll see what I mean ;)

I discovered Laini Taylor via an NPR best books of the year list. (Lips Touch Three Times was top 5). She is an excellent writer and I love the bonus of beautiful illustrations by her husband, Jim Di Bartolo. 
 It took awhile to be grabbed by this book, which I think was due to all the characters you get to know intimately before the pace picks up. Not to say it is slow in the beginning, but it gets faster. 
 From the jacket: 
 Magpie Windwitch, granddaughter of the West Wind, is not like other faeries. While most of her kind live in tranquil seclusion deep in their forests, escaped devils are creeping back into the world after millennia of imprisonment, and Magpie is all that stands in their way. 
 I'm not versed in the lore of faeries, but it wasn't a problem. Taylor drops you right in the midst of their world, but it unravels for newbies with important information embedded in the story. 
 Plot: Amazing. I can't love female protagonists who kick ass enough. And Magpie is one worthy of an entourage. Acknowledges her fear, but plunges into darkness willingly. The story is scary, exciting, fascinating, and hopeful. Hard to put down once you get in deeply. 
 Characters: Also incredibly loveable. The crows, the faeries, the imp (Batch Hangnail is disgustingly hilarious), did I mention the faeries? They are small and lovely, but fascinating and very human too. So believable in fact that you may start scanning the woods for signs of them. 
 Writing: Taylor does not disappoint- clear, concise, and lovely word choice. Truly a pleasure to read. Dramatic and fun and funny. Beautifully done. 
 There's a detail I just loved- the faeries have wings from different animals. This may be faerie lore that I didn't know existed, but it's awesome. Magpie has dragonfly wings, Poppy has butterfly, some have moth wings... I loved this. And the illustrations of them. 
 Despite the slow tread into the story, definitely a 5 star book. Looking forward to reading the second- Silksinger.

Hmmm, I really liked the writing-style, but Kitty annoyed me and I also didn't like Cat. 
 Edit: also on http://thedailyprophecy.blogspot.com 
 I consider myself a big fan of the Tudors era. Most of the historical fiction I read are about the queens and the court of Henry VIII. Last year I've read my first book about Catherine Howard: Alisa Libby - The king's rose. I was surprised by the voice of Cat, but this book is completely the opposite. The Cat we see here is the same as the queen we see in the television show. This made it hard for me to rate this book. While I was intrigued by her and Kitty's story, I had a hard time to connect to the characters. The writing-style was definitely pleasant and the atmosphere for the treacherous court was nicely done. That is why I settled down to a rating of 3. 
 This story is told from the POV of Kitty Tylney, best 'friend' of Catherine Howard. They live a boring and quiet life in Cat's grandmothers house. Except for the secret nights were Cat and Francis are having fun, not knowing that this will become Cat's downfall. 
 Cat always dreamt of living at court: dancing, flirting and gossiping. Kitty is her shadow and she follows Cat everywhere. That was one of the annoying things and I had a hard time to overlook this aspect of Kitty's personality. She has no spine. She is obedient and blind when it comes to her 'friendship' with the egoistic Cat and that results in many stupid decisions. 
 When the King marries his new queen - Anne of Cleves - he is looking for new maidens. Cat is one of the lucky girls and she is soon swept away in her new life. Kitty stays behind and as a true whiner, she feels rejected and jealous. But Cat is climbing on her social ladder and she caught the King's eyes. Soon, she is married with him and she brings Kitty to court. 
 From here on we encounter many facepalm situations. Or even better: 
 I can understand that Cat is still a young, naive girl and it's very clear that she isn't ready for such an important task, but the thing she does.. She should have known better and Kitty is just as stupid. Instead of seeing the truth (that Cat is a horrible friend who only uses her to feel better) she keeps bowing for Cat's fits. I wished that she would have grown throughout the book, but her character development is non-existent. 
 Despite my annoyance for most of the characters, I was hooked to the good writing-style. Longshore has a descriptive, flowy way of writing and it was fun to see the treachery among the court members. I'm definitely excited enough to read part 2, which will be about my favorite Queen from this era: Anne Boleyn.

There were some really well done parts of this book. The main characters are interesting and unique enough they feel real. Antonio feels like someone I would meet at a bar who tells all these stories and you're not sure if believe him or not. Mark and Brian have a real relationship, and the conflict and resolution felt, again, real. There wasn't more angst then necessary, no long drawn out fights, but the mutual understanding that adults have along with the mistakes and forgiveness that comes with understand people are imperfect. 
 The family is split between the 'God Squad' and the people who truly care and make a difference in the world. That was a lovely contrast. I just wonder how the 'God Squad' was made from same two parents Mark has. Though we don't see much of the mother, I adored Mark's father. 
 The reflection on loss, the parallels between Brian and Mark's mother, were so well done. I cried for Brian. Literal tears down me cheeks. I'll give it to Webb. He doesn't pull back from the emotional gut punch.  While this book is ultimately about love and forgiveness, the characters do have to fight for their happy ending. The loss in this novel is just painful and beautiful. It's that contrast that makes the relationships ache yet ultimately fulfilling. 
 While Antonio's gradual falling in love was beautifully done, I didn't quite believe the extent of the personality change he goes through in the latter part of the book. No spoilers, but, to me, the end seemed rushed or not quite as in line as the rest of the novel. A little too much HEA packed at the end of the story. However, Antonio and Mark's relationship and that slow, unrushed evolution, and the loyalty Mark has for the people he loves, really lifts the novel above simpler, cotton candy romances. 
 Though the main characters had a wonderful sense of individuality, I didn't get that same feeling from Robbie. Of all the characters, this was the only one who fell flat. The repercussions of the kind of abuse he went through are white washed, which bothers me. The author has worked with foster children, so I could be totally off and this is something based on his experiences. I hope so. I hope kids like Robbie can find happiness. 
 A surprising element in the novel was the dom sexual relationship Mark has with his partners. This is part of what makes me wonder about Antonio's later transformation. I suppose Mark is coaching him to be a sub, but Antonio never struck me as a man who would want that all that time.  What I do like about the dom/sub relationships that are established is that you can tell these are lovers who have talked and communicated their needs and who understand each other very well even if we aren't privy to the conversations that lead to their understanding. It's the background of a long relationship where we see the product rather than the lead to.

 Well, this was a most interesting book. A story about the war, different from any other story i read before and i really liked. 
 The War had just been declared, people were euphoric about it, certain about the victory and how fast the war would end. Mary was among them, as she hurried in London to volunteer, afraid that the war would end before she can accomplish something. 
 But war is never as it is expected. 
 This is a story about how war change people, those far away from the battle fields and yet see their lives chatter around them. The story of loss, despair and chattered lives. 
 It really touched me how the author painted the deprivation of soldiers, of bombed cities and lost persons. 
 The different characters were very interesting, each one of them with a different reaction towards the war, each of them changing after all those experiences and all relationships between them, Mary, Tom, Hilda, Alistair and many others, including Palmer, a very funny and interesting character. 
 I also enjoyed the introduction of the author with his grandfather's story, it made me feel closer to all these characters. 
 I would recommend it to my friends.

I hate to be a naysayer, but all I can say is: are you for real?! This book has crazy positive reviews. It has a 4.31 rating with over 3000 people reviewing it. That's serious praise. So I figured it was a no brainer. It'd love it. I hate to say it, but I was seriously disappointed. There are some serious flaws with this book. 
 For one thing, there's no back story to speak of. We're just plopped down in the middle of the action, which is fine. Lots of YA books start off that way. But then they take a minute to do some world building and described how our characters got here and why the world is the way it is. Ee does none of that. Here are just a few questions she never answered: Why are the angels evil and out to kill all humans? Where did they come from and why did they choose this moment to attack? How did they manage to defeat mankind? From what we see, angels fight with super sharp swords and their heightened speed, strength, and agility. So how is it that San Francisco is a heap of rubble after the angel attack? It's not like they're using the atom bomb. And for goodness sake, why are some of their wings red, blue, and tiger stripped?? 
 You could say that Ee doesn't explain this to us because Penryn doesn't know, but I think that's a cop out. Penryn is a smart girl. She would have been asking way more questions than she does throughout the book. Many times, Ee has Penryn swallow a question she's burning to ask, often so that she doesn't look like a fool in front of Raffe or confirm his opinions about her. That just didn't fit Penryn's general character. 
 Secondly, I thought that some of the writing - especially the dialogue - was rather awkward.  ECHO is a book that's hard for me to "rate" - there were certainly parts that I loved, as well as parts that I rather despised. Overall, however, ECHO was a quick, action-filled, and relatively enjoyable read!

I especially liked the idea of different timelines and the different types of Ethereals. Not only are there "Flooders" (water), "Breathers" (air), "Movers" (earth), and "Burners" (fire), but there's also Benders who control metal, Ethereals who control ether, and Seers, who, well, see the future. I also liked seeing them train and eventually fight off mages in different villages! At this time, I also liked Ashara as a heroine - she was strong, brave, selfless, and extremely loving towards her family. 
 It was around 70% or so into the book that I felt a little iffy, though. The pacing was still as quick, but Ashara, though brave, seemed to become really reckless. It seemed like she couldn't stand not fighting so much that she'd do almost anything to get out, even if it meant someone else would get hurt. And when someone else would get hurt, she would feel really bad and guilty. And then she would do something reckless. Without thinking. Again. She's also supposed to be this super bad-ass ether controller, but whenever she's actually in battle, she doesn't fight much either.

I have a certain amount of hillbilly blood myself. At least on one side, there's a family history of coal mining, moonshine-running, and disreputable behavior; my grandfather (like J. D. Vance, I always called him Papaw) is famous in family lore for having outright told the sheriff that he would shoot a man for coming on his property one more time. "Dammit, Richard," the sheriff sighed, "you can't just tell me that." So although I didn't grow up nearly as rooted in those traditions and settings as Vance, I know this culture at least a little, and enough to say that as far as I can tell, Vance's warm but not infatuated portrayal of it is on the money, and deserves the acclaim it's been getting. 
 Hillbilly Elegy is a powerful memoir qua memoir, in the vein of stories like The Glass Castle or Breaking Night: A Memoir of Forgiveness, Survival, and My Journey from Homeless to Harvard: how one kid from stifling, unpromising circumstances climbed the social ladder to success, Horatio Alger with less money and more Ivies. I have a soft spot for that kind of thing and Vance does it well. He doesn't surround himself with false modesty--he's clear on how his own intelligence and worldview helped him out, and in fact the helpfulness of individual drive and perspective is one of the angles he's pushing--but he also doesn't neglect to credit the substantial assistance he got along the way. His ascent out of the low-income hopelessness that surrounded him as a child was facilitated by a loving, supportive family (especially his grandparents and older sister) who encouraged his academic interests and did their best to provide him with islands of stability, and he doesn't stint on his praise of them. 
 In addition to the pleasures of the Alger format, there's the cultural tourism of Vance's particular milieu, where men force-feed cotton panties to other men in revenge for insults to their sisters, where mothers try to kill their own sons, and where fried bologna sandwiches are a lunchtime standard. (I've had them, they're pretty good.) That blend of hyperbolic honor and horror with mundane, kitschy, culturally-specific poverty is another selling point of the book: if you like a strong sense of place, this has it in spades. Vance points out similarities between hillbilly culture and inner city culture, but the specifics of this couldn't have played out anywhere but Appalachia. 
 The other angle the book takes is political, and it's in that light that it's been so widely recommended recently, for the obvious reason that there are a fair number of people over the last few months who want to know what the hell the Rust Belt is thinking. Vance, thoroughly rooted in his background but also endowed with perspective outside of it, conservative but thoughtfully attentive to the other sides of all possible issues, is a good guide to that question. Basically, he says, hillbilly culture is suffering because it has sickened: it's grown pessimistic, and while it might be right to think that the odds of success have gotten lower, its grim response has become a self-fulfilling prophecy. Motivation is down. People get good jobs and lose them because they're convinced that having a good job won't make a lick of difference in the end. And furthermore, Vance argues, there's nothing in particular anyone can do about this on a governmental level: there's no law that will restore a community's patriotism to provide necessary pride or make families stay together to provide necessary stability. This particular ailment can only really be treated by the people within the community changing their outlook and their response. 
 You can argue with that--I'm inclined to point out myself that all the chipper optimism in the world won't help you get a decent job when there simply aren't enough decent jobs to go around--but Vance is genuinely persuasive, and I'm inclined to think he's genuinely right about the limitations of top-down intervention in changing people's beliefs and behaviors, especially in a culture that's very resistant to being meddled with. So Hillbilly Elegy isn't a call to action, unless you happen to be a hillbilly yourself. It really is an elegy--an enticing, highly readable epitaph of a way of life that's becoming less and less functional and may, if things don't change, die out entirely. I'd like to say it's a call to empathy, because calls to empathy are very much my speed, but it's not, really, because while Vance is sympathetic, he's not especially empathetic. He feels for the people who don't make it out, but there's a decided distance there, an incomprehension: he notes that they're bitter about calls to feed their children less processed sugar not because they don't believe it but because they know it already and hate that they can't seem to stop, but why they can't seem to stop eludes him. He can see their hopelessness but not the reason for it; can connect with the child whose tempestuous childhood leaves him failing his classes but not with the adult who moves their kid from household to household. That's a fair line to draw in terms of who he'll pity, but it does mean that ultimately there's a gap there that can't be bridged, that we get close to the hillbillies but still run into a glass pane. That's ultimately why this loses a star for me. It's a great book, but there's a circularity to it; something paradoxical to the notion that the culture can only be saved if it learns to be ignorant of itself and be a group of losers--in Vance's own term--who crawl out of loserdom by losing the ability to recognize that they're losers. 
 This might be a failure on my part, to end the book thinking, Well, this is great, but what am I supposed to do about it?, but if the answer is "nothing, really," then I want the compensation of some fuller and even more tragic understanding, and we get right up to the line on that... and then stop. But this still comes tantalizingly close, and if it can't engender complete empathy, it at least engenders fondness and familiarity, which is helpful in its own right. 
 Also, it's funny. Another hillbilly strength, as I'm sure Vance would agree.

Tegan is sixteen and just like every other girl living in 2027. She's happiest when playing the guitar, she's falling in love for the first time, and she's joining her friends to protest the wrongs of the world: environmental collapse, social discrimination, and political injustice. But on what should have been the best day of her life, she dies, and wakes up a hundred years in the future, locked in a government facility with no idea what happened. Tegan is the first government guinea pig to be cryonically frozen and successfully revived, which makes her an instant celebrity, even though all she wants to do is try to rebuild some semblance of a normal life. But the future isn't all she hoped it would be, and she appalling secrets come to light, Tegan must make a choice: keep her head down and survive, or fight for a better future? 
 When We Wake is intriguing, incredibly thoughtful, and incredibly relevant. How much will the world change between now and 100 years from now? What will be our worth as people? What will the planet look like? How will visitors and refugees from different countries be treated? If a terrible truth is being hidden from the rest of the world, will anyone be brave enough to bring it to light? This is an exploration of a changing world, an exploration of faith, and a conformation that, sometimes, you have to speak out in order to save the world. 
 The best comment I can give Karen Healey about this book is that I hope I never experience a future like this. It's frightening realistic. I don't live in Australia, but I can recognize hints and pieces of what's happening then happening now. It's eerie, and scary, and serves in increase both my fear for the future and my hope that we won't ruin it. 
 Tegan brings a 21st century Aussie teen's attitude and knowledge of her world to a far different 22nd century Melbourne. And it's not just Melbourne, it's the whole world. She's so normal, she has friends and a boyfriend and she's passionate about changing the world, and suddenly she's a publicity stunt, a girl brought back to life, an instant celebrity. The culture shock is staggering at every turn but she still manages to fight her way through every roadblock, even when it looks like she might not make it out alive. 
 The future Tegan encounters is different from the present she knows. There's a notable loss of resources, the shrinking of the oceans and the disappearance of forested areas. The temperature is on the rise, inflation is on the rise, technology is on the rise. There are new diseases to fight, new battles to encounter. The social customs and norms aren't what she's used to, and neither is the technology, but Tegan is a fighter. Her guts and strength are what propel her into the unknown, into the journey she tells the reader all about. 
 I think the purpose of books like this is to show readers, teenagers and adults alike, that things need to change now in order to keep the future from looking similar to what's portrayed. Destruction, devastation, poverty, refugees. It all sounds pretty depressing. But we can hope that, if the future turns grey and dismal and if there's a secret as big as the one Tegan discovers, that there will be those fighting to tell the truth and help humanity remember its roots. The future doesn't have to be frightening, it can be better, but we're the ones who have to work hard to keep it bright.

The Lies of Locke Lamora is a adventure novel about the schemes and tribulations of Locke Lamora and his group of young conmen, set in a light fantasy world. The first chapter intrigued me by teasing interesting, developed side characters and a plot that would spool out non-linearly but with a narrative thread that made sense. It didn't hurt to see fantasy in a setting other than the typical swords and sorcery format. 
 Obviously my two-star rating means I was let down. It's a shame because I can see the person that would enjoy this as a piece of light, wish-fulfilment, fantasy-adventure. But whenever I tried to talk about the book with people I ended up doing long, angry rants. 
 The heroes abilities scale to just be above their opponents. It's like how in martial art movies the hero has an equally hard time fighting one ninja or seven ninjas. Like the Bondsmage are supposed to be scary powerful but then Locke takes him down incredibly easily. And we're told how much physical pain Locke is in, but it doesn't actually affect his actions or outcome in any real way.  
 Things come way too easily to Locke. He gets into crazy situations that he supposedly manoeuvres his way out of based on cunning. Really, it's a combination of deus ex machina, blind luck, and writing that stretched the plot to the point of impossibility. More than one antagonist's decision is on par with leaving James Bond alone with the laser sharks and just assuming he'll be killed off. 
 The writing is clunky. The story alternates between the present and flashbacks. At first this felt like a good way to slowly flesh out the character. But it quickly turned into transparently showcasing a character learning a skill or lesson that would immediately be put into use in the next chapter. Plot 'twists' are telegraphed and there aren't any surprises. Early on, the voice of a passage completely changes to dump in five completely out of place exposition paragraphs about a seemingly random topic. Geez, I wonder if that stuff will be crucial later on? 
 Ultimately, the conceit didn't appeal enough for me to overlook the flaws. It felt like reading a bad YA novel with the wish fulfilment, one-note characters, and obvious plot twists. But if you feel like cheering for the scrappy Mary Sue (is there a name for the male version of that? If so, it really is kind of fun.

The title is kinda generic for epic fantasy (shadows being about as ubiquitous as shattered things--I am waiting for one called "The Shattered Shadows") but hey, titles are like covers, meant to signal FANTASY HERE! to likely readers. 
 And this one delivers the goods. I devoured the first in this series, finding the female characters excellent, some nice gender-bending stuff going on, and the warfare first-rate. The magic, when it happened was creepy and fascinating. 
 In this second installment, Janus and Winter and Marcus have returned to their capital because the king is dying, and the teenage princess, heir to the throne, is in danger of being controlled by the Last Duke, Orlanko, Minister of Information. The king in one of his last acts makes Janus Minister of Justice in hopes that he can stop Orlanko, meanwhile both sides are trying to deal with the fact that magic really exists. 
 At the start, in an author's note, Wexler says that he was inspired by Simon Schama's Citizens, a people's eye view of the French Revolution from a modernist POV, the many horrors mitigated by a thread of dispassionate humor. Those glints of humor, and the modernist narrative drive, demonstrate Schama's influence as strongly as do certain familiar incidents. (And the tongue-in-cheek echoes of names, such as Danton, here an impassioned orator whose mind is . . . well, you have to read it. In fact, read both books!) 
 Winter's arc was probably the most satisfying, besides Princess Raesiena's. The women definitely get their innings in this book, as does some interesting gender expectation turnabout. The revolution unfolds with a slowly accelerating pace until a patented terrific Wexler military climax, setting things up for the next book. 
 I enjoyed it thoroughly, while not finding myself as glued to the pages as the first book. For about three quarters of the book I couldn't figure out why--though I always looked forward to reading the next chapter, it was easy to lay down again. Why, when we were in the middle of revolution? 
 I finally figured it out: because this is a second book, the main characters remain on a fairly even keel, unlike the first book with its dramatic character arcs. At the end of the first book, the main characters are not at all what they once were. In this book, they pretty much are the same people at the end that they were at the beginning--though there is one significant (and delightful) addition to Winter's life (leading me to think, hmmm . . .If the third book ends in tragedy for the lead lesbian couple, I am going to be really, really pissed. It's about time for the gays to get happily ever afters, too! ). 
 This doesn't mean one should skip this second book and go straight to the third. There is plenty to enjoy, and also to learn about the world.

Ever wonder what sort of neurological repercussions there are on your brain from being on the Internet every goddamn minute of your life? Ever wonder how clicking "send and receive" over and over again is utterly disturbing your neural networks? Have you not been able to complete either of the above sentences in one go? Do you see the irony here, since you're reading this on the Internet? Maybe not. But Nicholas Carr does. 
 Ever since Socrates hated on the written word because it'd destroy our memories, people have greeted new technologies with enthusiasm ranging from "the Internet is my God" to "I will smash my fist through the control machine raping my attention span". Carr looks into why the first group are out of their goddamn minds. Literally. There's a lot covered here. The most interesting bits are when neurologists and brain-studying people discuss how our neural plasticity will be our undoing because the wondrous "tool" of the Internet is basically teaching our brains to be stupid, curt, and unable to focus on anything for more than a few seconds. The science is light, as it should be, we're laypeople, but you get enough to let you know that this isn't mere alarmist rhetoric: this shit is for real. Attention span failure, inability to feel compassion and empathize with others, the growing monopoly of "amplifiers of popularity" like Google and Facebook, it's all in here. 
 I'd recommend this book to anyone who can't sit still and read for more than a minute or two. It's pretty enlightening stuff, and not shrill at all.
