Cool that she didn't make the bodyguard too young to be appropriate for the role. Cool, too, that she made them closer in age so that the attraction later will make sense. 
 Awesome that 5' 9" isn't considered short as it is, in fact, about average for the UK. I love that he's average height. That is so rare in these books. They're always either huge or tiny. 
 A 400 year old house is a normal house? Wow. 
 He has meds. Interesting. 
 Pasta is not "good for you." 
 It's weird that Max is hanging out at the swim team practice, listening in to what the coach says, when he's not on the team. I would think that wouldn't sit well. 
 Why didn't he have background checks done on the lifeguards? 
 They don't have a coach? Just a team captain? That makes no sense. 
 I like that they're not automatically first and best at every race. 
 Competitive guys on a collegiate swim team don't have long hair. 
 Every book I've read about bodyguards recently (and I've read several) mention the movie The Bodyguard and say life's not like that. Then they go on to do exactly that. 
 I can't picture this house that has four rooms plus four half baths upstairs but only a kitchen, living area and full bath down. The living room has only one couch so how big can it be? And the bedrooms aren't too tiny because they're the same size as Max's at home. Are these like those German chalet type things where the top overhangs the bottom? 
 Why am I not as enamored of Lucien as I am with Max? He's kind of wimpy. Maybe that's it. 
 Why doesn't Max look in the abandoned bag? 
 Do people with no fat like a competitive swimmer float automatically if they're not dead? 
 What a difference between the UK and US. It was "only a fifteen-minute walk and not worth using Max's car for." It's the middle of the night on January and freezing cold. There was ample parking (because, oddly, students don't generally have cars!) Here in the U.S., that is definitely time to drive the car, and students have cars unless they live in a huge city. 
 Excellent action, thrills, danger, but sadly no peril. Still, this is a five star read except I never really connected with the prince. I think it may be--and I'm ashamed to admit this--because I pictured him so much bigger than Max, I saw him as being weak and pathetic, whereas if he had been smaller, I would have loved him. 
 4.5 stars

5 freakin' HOH stars! 
 I LOVED this book! The only regret I had was reading the latter quarter of the book while at school because I really wanted to cry and I had to stop myself because that would be just embarrassing. I loved the concept of the story even though there was just minimum dialogue and it was purely in the hero's POV (except the epilogue). I had lots of unanswered questions at the beginning because, as I said, there was hardly any dialogue and the heroine had no thought input at all. We don't even know what she's talking about. 
 Ehd was plain adorable. He's a caveman and he was literally primitive and even though he barely ever talked at all except for asking his Beh for kisses and his occasional Hoh!'s, I found him wonderful. He was very sweet and he really cared about his mate and we know that because all he ever thought of was taking care of her, making her happy and putting a baby in her. Yup! Putting a baby in her! He didn't hurt his Beh and did everything to make her comfortable. I especially liked the scenes where Beh was combing his hair. 
 Despite not knowing any of Beh's thoughts at all, I also liked her because she was so easy to forgive Ehd when he made her angry and that she stayed with him even when she was given the chance to come back to her previous life. In spite of being thrown to a time and place that was very far from where she's from and what she's used to, she didn't take out her frustrations on Ehd, instead she did what she could to help Ehd. She was also able to show Ehd that she cared for him and that she loved him. 
 Transcendence was amazing! It was really worth all the time that I spent with Ehd and Beh and it made me happy inside. The story was heartwarming and the ending was bittersweet and would have made me cry happy and sad tears if not for the fact that I was surrounded by people and even just thinking about it now makes me teary-eyed. I actually told my classmate about the book and the ending and my voice was very shaky.

Actual rating is probably 3.5 stars. 
 This book is pure Dystopian fluff, which isn't necessarily a bad thing. It was a quick read and was over all enjoyable, but look to closely, and you'll come up with a few plot holes. The general concept of the story was still pretty good, and even though things were sometimes a bit too easy for the main characters  How is it that Sunny and Jack were able to escape so many times without almost any conflict at all? I kept waiting for things to get really hard on our main characters, but honestly, they didn't struggle much with the exception of Sunny having to endure near heat stroke every time she went to work.  , the book was fast paced. Sunny was invited (forced) upstairs to be presented to the powers that be at the dome, which resulted in her falling into Leisel's snare. 
 One small complaint, exclamation points were used often. That wasn't a deal breaker for me, and it won't be for most readers, but if someone was excited! mad! happy! or scared! you could be sure there was an exclamation point at the end of their dialogue. 
 I believe the rest of the trilogy is already published, which is a good thing because since they are readily available, I will check them out to see what happens to Sunny and Jack (and Leisel. She better get what is coming to her, haha), but I don't think I would have pursued the sequels (despite the bit of a cliffhanger at the end of this one) if I had to wait for them to be released. I would recommend this if you are a fan of the dystopian genre in general and are looking for a quick fun read.

 Lucas, I wanted a bit of honesty from him and I think if he had given to me, I mean Val, things would have gone very differently.  This book is made of lust, love, jelousy, betrayal, vampires, wolves, fey, witches & a little half empath. So much to love. I can not wait to find out what is going to happen next...If you haven't read this series, pick up book 1 - Love is Darkness!

Now this may not be the best of the series, but I think it was the most enjoyable read for me of the three. This is because I was now acclimated to the characters, the style, and so forth. Thus the technological info that I found a bit too much in the earlier books were intriguing this time around. I tried to figure out if I really needed to know that an IBook was used at a particular point, etc, etc. (I do have to say that I had to seriously suspend disbelief at Salander's zippy Palm --- it seemed to have a faster data speed than any current smartphone I know about! I mean she wrote pages and pages with a stylus to boot! She easily downloaded massive amounts of data. And so forth and so on.) 
 The NYTimes reviewer complained that Larsson seemed to be a coffee-addict. Now I remember thinking that the coffee drinking just seemed typical European --- at any rate, I've lived in Germany and people always serve coffee when you visit. So I figured it was the same in Sweden. Of greater interest was the way Larsson described what his characters (I think more the female characters) wore in colorful detail. He seems to particularly have liked red jackets for them. 
 As for the plot --- there seemed to be a good resolution to most of Lisbeth's dreadful history. One piece though that is left dangling is her sister. She is mentioned a few times and I have to wonder if Larsson had in mind to bring her into future stories. Can't imagine why else she'd even exist otherwise.

 The whole process was quite the emotional roller coaster. 
 I thought the pacing was good, it never made me bored, and it was never rushed. I hated Ty at first, but then slowly he clawed his way to my heart and I found space for compassion for him. 
 The ending was heartbreaking and blurry. I wish I could know what happened to Ty, and what happened to the shaky relationship built between Ty and Gemma. Throughout the whole book I could feel myself wanting them to get together, to just give in but at the same time I hated it, hated how far Ty took things, just to get Gemma.

 If you haven't read Joelle Charbonneau's The Testing series you have to! i absolutely loved it so I squealed when I had the chance to read Need. I will say it was addictive and I didn't want to put it down but there was just something about it that kept me from adoring it like I did The Testing. I think that it was so unbelievable and yet takes place in the present which makes it hard to accept some of what happens. 
 The story line was fascinating and it always comes to mind when my kids tell me they NEED something and I always have to ask do you really need it? Or do you just want it? Need builds off that question about how far people are willing to go for something they feel they "need". I think many people might find reading it jarring because there must have been maybe 7 or 8 different points of view. At first it was hard to keep track of what was what but it all comes together and you start to get why it jumps around so much. 
 The main character was an interesting blend of emotions and at times I really disliked her for being so dumb but then at times I just shook my head because I could totally see myself having done something like that at her age. So while she and a few other characters aren't the most endearing because of their behavior that makes them seem more real because in real life people don't always make the "right" choice. 
 All in all, an addictive story but little things like the many POVs, less than likeable characters and some story line pieces that were hard to believe made this a good but not amazing read for me.

I'm torn between liking Wolfsbane and wanting to really throw it against the wall. Don't get me wrong, I liked Nightshade, well, I liked pretty much everything about it except the love triangle but it seems that as much as Wolfsbane tries to add more to the plot, my mind keeps going back to the romance. 
 First things first, the covers. WTH? The original covers were so cool. The new versions are, one, so ugly, two, too sexualizing for its own good. I'm sorry but why does Calla's legs have to be so wide open? At least the original covers had some context from the books. 
 All right, plot-wise, Wolfsbane fares decently. I say this reluctantly because there's quite a few plot lines I don't agree with as well as some twists I guessed quite easily that it upset me. My biggest resentment would be the fact that this novel introduces many new characters but only few actually had any purpose. I really wished the novel could have been streamlined because seriously, after finishing the story, I felt like I had just finished a marathon. Oh, did I mention info dump as well? Annoying as crap. 
 Character development is a little iffy as well. A big point for me is this boy, a Searcher, named Ethan. He is portrayed as a boy who pretty much hates the Guardians, because, hey, they're sworn enemies. This is the result of years and years of his upbringing, beliefs, etc. What I don't understand is how in the matter of a few days, after rescuing a certain Guardian, Ethan suddenly has a change of heart and decides, well, I don't hate them so much anymore. NO NO NO NO NO NO! 
 I was going to rant a little about Calla but then looking back at my review for Nightshade, I realized I did that already. I also said that the boys were the "sane" ones in the love triangle. I WAS WRONG. 
 I cannot be more upset at Shay. As much as it pains me to say this, it almost feels like Shay has the beginnings of an abusive "boyfriend". In this love triangle, it is obvious that Calla still has feelings for Ren and that's understandable because they grew up together, they cared for each other and before Shay appeared, they were pretty sure they were going to spend the rest of their lives together. 
 But in Wolfsbane, every time Calla and Shay kiss or whatever and Calla stops because she's still affected by memories of Ren, Shay gets mad or worse, compares himself to Ren endlessly. 
 You love him. But you love me more. 
 It's like this all the time. Before Calla can even respond, she's always bombarded by Shay going, "it's okay as long as you love ME more". He keeps isolating her from her own feelings and that just doesn't sit right with me. 
 I will probably finish the series since I always have Bloodrose on my desk but if Shay doesn't clean up his act, I might just stop reading mid-way.

I was given a free copy of this book on it's blog tour for an honest review. 
 In book one of the Lilith Straight series; we are introduced to the main character. Narrated by Lil in a very candid no bars held funny sort of way. Here are two of my favorite lines: 
 * "The woman you always wanted to be." 
 * "Married to someone better looking than your husband, and his salary climbed into figures so high that you'd have to be married to six men before their incomes equaled his." 
 She goes on to talk about her cars, her home, her daughter's prestigious education, celebrity parties and socialite status. Yet all in the same breathe her tune changes because within the span of a year this snotty diva is brought down to Earth to live like less than a commoner. She lives on a substitute teacher's salary in a 2-BR shabby townhome with her unemployed step sister, unofficially adopted delinquent ex niece-in-law, and daughter. Just when she thinks things can't get worst, her free loading step sister moves in her psychic friend/love interest. And that's only covers 10% of chapter one. The real fun begins when Lilith takes an unfortunate trip to the hot zone. This story literally took me on a ride I will NEVER forget. The only complaint I couldn't get over was "ALIMONY"! This would have been so much more believable if she had something to show for the lost of her elaborate lifestyle of the rich and famous courtesy of her penny pinching ex. Instead, it was kind of painful to watch her struggles and not have that little common sense voice shouting it in my head. After Lil's conversion into the supernatural realm and the new characters that came with it were very entertaining as well. It was surprising to see the author incorporate morals along with depicting Lil's inner battle without being preachy. The only thing keeping me from rating this as a five or higher is the unfair divorce settlement and the ending. I really held out hope for a different ending.

ARC by NetGalley. 
 So, the story is a free interpretation of the early years of Sophie, who later becomes Catherine the Great. 
 She wants the throne of Russia but first she has to win the heart of the Grand Duke Peter. 
 You know what happens next, right? Of course, everyone fall in love with her. 
 I enjoyed the book but my main problem was that this felt as if someone put a whole season of a tv show in 262 pages. There was no room for development or really get to know anyone. 
 Sophie had all this crazy plans to win the crown, which hey, they sounded pretty awesome! But in less than 200 pages she falls in love within days with a guy, decides that Peter is an idiot and suddenly when she can't be with this guy she becomes a cold-hearted person. 
 It's funny, how I once swooned at the thought of being married to Peter, and then later was so horrified at the idea. Now, it seems somehow neutral. We are both so broken and damaged, perhaps we will find comfort in each other, perhaps our affection will grow. 
 She is broken because she can't be with this guy?? Cry me a river. 
 I'd love this if you like historical fiction and are patient enough with love triangles/squares/whatever.

This is an excellent example of why Mieville's signature style has been dubbed "New Weird." The story starts strange and gets stranger, as a routine(?) museum theft turns out to herald one of the many ends of the world. There's a whole sea of invention here - weird semi-magical powers, genuinely creepy villains, and, as usual, the sense that the city itself is one of the major characters. (Also a number of laudatory references to Amy Winehouse, which cracked me up.) 
 I won't say I didn't like it. But I found the pacing rather too slow to really keep me enthralled, and there was perhaps too many things that were given lavish detail simply because they were neat. I suspected the true villain at the very start, was successfully distracted from him for a while, and then, two thirds of the way in, remembered him because there were simply too many red herrings for it to be anyone more obvious. The actual end was well-played, but it just took too long to get there to really suit me. 
 That said, if you're willing to go with the flow for a long while, this is a neat book in a very similar vein as Gaiman's American Gods.

The final book in the Newsflesh trilogy played out like the last 45 minutes of an action packed thriller. Well... that is, an action packed thriller with an anti-climatic ending so disappointing, it had me shaking my head and mourning the unfulfilled potential. It wouldn't have been so bad had the first two books in the series not finished with such heart-stopping, epic conclusions! With the bar raised like that, one could only expect the final book, the book Grant promised would reveal all, would eclipse the other two in the shadow of its behemoth of a finale. 
 No. This was not the case at all. 
 While I enjoyed the majority of the book, the "endgame" as it was called, was left until the last 100 pages and didn't offer much more in explanation that readers didn't already know. Oh, and a very key plot point was almost completely skimmed over!. Please only read the following spoiler if you have finished this series in its entirety. 
 The evil doctor from the CDC tells them there can never be a cure for the virus without destroying peoples' immune systems and that individuals with reservoir conditions must be eliminated in order to prevent people dying needlessly from second-guessing themselves. I get that, I really do, but once the good old doc is dealt with and it is revealed to the actual fucking scientists that Shaun is immune from his prolonged exposure to Georgia and her reservoir condition, it is completely overlooked as far as future cure research is concerned. Sure they must immediately make a run for their lives and don't have time to really think it over, but in the epilogue, which is over nine months later, Mahir reiterates that there can never be a cure! Ummm... so the EIS decided to completely disregard immunity via sexy time with reservoir conditioned lovers? Not even gonna look into it? No? Too much of a hassle for you? Ok, sure! We're cool with Zombieland USA anyways.  
 After all the build-up, the fantastic world building, the endearing characters, the insane plot-twists, and the BALLS Grant had to posses to take the risks she did, this ending felt sloppy and rushed in comparison. Why bother putting in all that hard work? Why bother with the extensive research? Why bother developing the science when you are going to end it all like THAT? As you can see, I'm pissed, and for good reason too. I had so much invested in this series. I cried, laughed, and sweated bullets with these characters for nearly 2,000 pages total for all three books. I grieved at the losses, raged over the injustices, and rejoiced in their triumphs, only for it all to come down to such a baffling conclusion. 
 I am disillusioned 
 I am disheartened 
 I am utterly disappointed with a series that had begun to define me as a reader and shift my standards for what makes great fiction. 
 I bet you've gotten to this point in the review and are wondering, "What the hell, Jess? If you're so pissed, why give it 4 stars?" 
 Well my Wicked Darling, while I am obviously upset over the ending, I did mention earlier that I enjoyed the majority of this book. The shifting view points from chapter to chapter was a nice change from the usual stagnant single narrator POV from the previous two books. 
 Each new revelation presented on page made for perpetually increasing possibilities. I don't know how many times Wigs and I said to each other, "There are so many ways this could go horribly wrong! And we love it!" The level of excitement that was built up over 3/4 of the book had me frantic to get to the climax. Only to have it wind down rather than explode in a blaze of glory. (Yes that innuendo was intentional.) 
 Regardless of my sadness over how it all went down, this still remains a series I will keep close to my heart. I can't say the same for Wigs, who wasn't nearly as attached as I was in the first place and was still disappointed. Wigs, at least we'll always have THE FOX. 
 Adorable 
 Frightening 
 Bat-shit 
 I am The Fox

Lexi is a spoiled rich girl who, in the fashion of The Bling Ring, enjoys risky stunts with her equally spoiled friends and brother. When her father is arrested for illegal activities at a bank he worked at, Lexi will do anything to help his boss also receive justice. Christian is a teenage bank robber - he has to or else the gang that rules his hood will kill him and his family. The gang declares that one of the biggest jobs they have ever done is about to go down - with Christian and his friends a part of it all. How fateful that the two of them meet when they both want to take down the bank... 
 For what it was, I really enjoyed this book. I have read reviews about people being upset that it was not realistic, or that it made it seem too easy to rob a bank. I don't know about you, but I don't read these types of stories as a "how-to" as I am reading them for entertainment. And entertained I was. Amy Christine Parker knows how to weave a story together of 2 alternating viewpoints, keeping you engaged, and not getting lost in the story. I keep seeing "for fans of Heist Society" and I have those on my shelf, so I may be reading those next! 
 I received this e-book from the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review.
I cried, a lot.

Ehhh...it was ok. It seemed to alternate on what part of the story to focus on, her life as an inventor and then a somewhat shoe-horned in romance. One was definitely more interesting than the other. Also it felt like the romance was just there to tie in to the retelling and then went an unconventional route which just ended up confusing and threw off the pacing near the end. I'd definitely recommend Cinder over this book.

What an awesome surprise this one was to me. I could not believe how I was immediately connected to these characters. 
 This story is about Jared and Aly. Jared and Aly have been childhood friends since they were kids. A tragedy happened when Jared was 16 that drove him to leave his hometown. 6 years later he returns and meets with his childhood best friend and Aly's older brother, Christopher. Christopher offers Jared his place while he looks for his own. Aly is also Christopher's roommate, but what Christopher and Jared do not know that Aly has been love with Jared since they were kids. So Jared moves in Christopher and Aly and the story begins. 
 "Jared Holt was here." 
 It was such a beautiful story and told perfectly with the dual POVs. Lately, and I have mentioned this several times, authors can destroy a story by writing dual POVs and giving away too much. A.L. Jackson does an amazing job. I felt it all. I was engrossed. I started reading it while I was waiting for my daughter to finish her lesson. Usually my daughter's 2 hour lessons drag, but I found myself wishing I had more time since the book, this love story, was so beautiful. I could not stop reading. My heart broke for Jared and the guilt he suffered every day. He was worthy of love. Aly described him as beautiful. He was beautiful inside and out even though a mistake that took everything from him and drove him to some ugly behavior. He thought he was not worthy of love, but you will see when you read this that he was. He was worth taking the chance and saving. 
 "It isn't worth it if it doesn't hurt a little." 
 The story ended at the perfect spot. Not necessarily a cliffy, but wanting the reader to grab the next book to read about the next chapter in this couple's lives. 
 Now my question is if we are going to get Christopher's story. Christopher is a good person but it is obvious that he has something going on that he is always on the "hunt" for a new girl every night. I have a feeling it has to do with the love he lost. 
 Bottom line: Very well written. I felt the angst, I felt the tension. The switch in POVs and the flashbacks were perfectly paced. The intimate scenes...not redundant or overdone. They had meaning. Great characters, great story, and very well written. 
 "I see beauty an pain. Joy d sorrow. I see the good and I see the bad...and I love it all."

The Noise is a man unfiltered, and without a filter, a man is just chaos walking. 
 If there is a way to explain this book, I have yet to find it. 
 It's unique-- 
 It's fantastic-- 
 It's amazing-- 
 It's new-- 
 It's completely unheard of. 
 I had no idea what to expect from this book. With so many books on my list of to-read, the synopsis was lost in my head somewhere. All I knew was that it was sort of offsetting, perhaps a little difficult to understand at first, and that it really was a strange book. Off the wall, actually, not so much strange. But in the best way possible. The Knife Of Never Letting Go is not the best of best books I have ever read, but it's definitely one of the coolest ones I've had the pleasure of engrossing myself with. 
 Patrick Ness creates a world in which the Noise is in complete control. He takes a small concept, a small and very overused concept (mind reading) and amplified it in a way that both captured your attention and held absolutely no prisoners. The way the book was written was super trippy. It's first person, but it seems like though Todd may know something, you don't. It's like your hearing him like other people are hearing him. Difficult to explain and maybe difficult to understand, but the Noise was a crazy concept that made the easiest bit of sense. 
 This takes mind-reading to whole new level. This is no Edward Cullen dilemma, ladies and gentlemen. 
 Oh and the characters! The emotion behind them and the journey they go through. Todd may be the 'main' character but it feels like you're seeing everyone as a coherent whole. "If one of us falls, we all fall" right? Man, until the end you don't even begin to understand how absolutely critically it is to the storyline. And with that understand the whole book before the enlightenment becomes a finished puzzle. It's less that you're frequently questioning what's going on - as a majority of the time Ness does a fabulous job of conveying understanding - and more that suddenly it all just sort of makes sense. Everything they go through and stuff, all the hopes along the way were purposely filled. 
 Or at least most of them, as I believe. 
 It takes a while to get into and I won't say that I didn't drift a few times while reading, or that everything made perfect sense, because it didn't. But I don't think I've read one book where I haven't zoned more than once. Or one that made entire sense, especially if we're talking Young Adult, so it's a minor flaw. Aside from it being long and a pest to carry 'round sometimes, The Knife of Never Letting Go has achieved great potential rather than simply holding the flimsy idea. It's very well worth the read, up to the very last page.

Mystic River..I heard about this book so much. Highly rated and all. A successful movie that couldn't supersede the book. But, why it took me so long to grab this book I dont know. 
 So, anyways I started this book, hoping it wont be a pretentious read.And as I moved forward, I realized this book is different. For one, its not heavy on killer dialogues. You know, the kind usually laden in books on life and all. The book is actually a study on human behavior wrapped in a crime mystery. The 3 friends, Jimmy, Sean and Dave are all fucked up in their own way. They have their own survival strategies. Everyone is trying to defy their own nature of character, trying to mold himself into something more acceptable, trying hard to compensate for all their imperfections. So, I connect with them. Trying hard to be what the society requires us to be, to be capable of being loved. And then there's the loneliness of everyone. The wives, the parents, the children, the protagonists, hell, the city's. Almost everyone talks to him/her self. Almost everyone tries to fight his/her own devils. Rarely have I rooted for as well as hated all 3 characters equally. Rarely have I secretly wanted Sean to have his wife back. Secretly I wanted Dave to be normal again, to disabuse himself from the illusions he has. And very rarely, have I stopped to wonder the effects of a murder (Crime and Punishment, In True Blood, comes to my mind). And yet, as we unravel their world, know the murdered, the book gets over, I only let out a sigh and say to myself "What the fuck is wrong with this world ?". 
 I actually figured the perpetrator midway the novel. But, man, my interest didn't wane a bit. Probably because of the clever writing, the curiosity to see what emotions make us capable of. However, its a man's world out there. Everyone is strong. The weak are flushed out. Ballsy women are treated with respect. Weak ones are treated with derision. I could easily make out the limitations of Lehane to sketch out female characters without typecasting them. 
 Must read book. I recommend it to everybody. The movie however disappointed me. The characters werent as enticing as they are in my head.

I see a lot of people who rate this book so high. I think I'm just not into the writing style? 
 I have no idea why I couldn't finish this book. I can't say I was really bothered with any of the characters or the plot. I just read, and after some time the book became a little repetitive for me. So, I'm sorry, I decided to read the ending, find out what happens, and not touch this book ever again. 
 I REALLY tried. I just couldn't make myself read.

Sadly, this series feels like maybe it's starting to have run its course. Most of the tension between Ty and Zane feels manufactured at this point, and the new couple - or as I like to call them, the 'B team' - have taken the spotlight to try and pick up some of the slack. Nick and Kelly are fine, but not all that interesting to be honest. The Scottish castle was fun for about five minutes. 
 Oh well. I think there's only one left in the series, so being a completist I'll finish it up.

Quite an entertaining read. Love the second chance/ older woman younger man dynamic; it's so unique in a historical romance. Especially love the fact that Leo has loved her always. So Cute. Instead of going off in a rant, I'll just post some of my favorite quotes in this novel. Yes, I realized that they're all from Leo. 
 "You were the moon of my existence; your moods dictated the tides of my heart." 
 "Just that I have loved you, even when I was nothing and no one to you, when you didn't know my name and barely knew my face." 
 "It doesn't matter where I am; I'm yours." 
 "Why geometry? Of course geometry. How else will man discover the shape of the universe?" "What if we never discover the shape of the universe?" "It's still not wasted. There is nothing like higher mathematics to impress an overly serious woman," he said, grinning.

 I am a new reader to Stephen King [this is my eighth King book] having mostly began my love affair with his books just this year when I read several of his stories for my Goodreads yearly book challenge. I have read only a few of his books in past but for my challenge this year I ended up reading Under the Dome, Carrie and The Shining. I actually didn't know about this sequel when I chose to read the Shining so it turned out to be a rewarding coincidence that allowed the story to be fairly fresh in my mind as I approached this book. I was thrilled to discover Will O Patton was the narrator of the audio book, which certainly adds to my 5 star enjoyment as he is one of my most favorite actors and my #1 favorite audio book narrator!! 
 This book will always be memorable for me in two personal ways. First, as I say I haven't been reading King for that long so unlike many of his other loyal fans, this was the first time I had the experience of pre-ordering a King book, getting it the day it comes out and immediately starting to read it. Actually it is the first time I've done that with any book, beginning to read it on the day it was released! I was excited for this for a few weeks leading up to it so I can say my expectations were high going into it. And never at any point can I say did the story let me down. In fact, to my utter joy, it grabbed me from the opening chapter. So many of the elements of The Shining that I loved came back in such delightfully clever and fulfilling ways. Especially the character of Halloran, who is such a likeable character then and now more than ever. 
 The pop culture references made me smile as one in particular was to the television show Sons of Anarchy, which happens to be my favorite TV show right now. And come to think of it, I remembered that King himself had an exceptionally awesome cameo on an episode of that show a while back! I have a huge crush on "Jax Teller" the main character of the show, so it was neat that [spoiler] Abra mentions she believed adult Dan looked similar to Jax!! I hope when they go to make the movie version of this they end up casting him! 
 Now a word about the villain, Rose the Hat. Throughout the story I wouldn't say there were too many times I was "scared" but more "worried" for Abra's safety as I came to really like her and I could feel what a tremendous threat Rose was to her. I got a real sense that if Rose could get to Abra she could really do some very serious harm to her physically and mentally. Some of my favorite moments were when Abra flexed her own true power and I found myself breathlessly impressed with the strength of her "shining." One of my most favorite parts of the whole story was Abra doing her "Khaleesi Game of Thrones" style mental smack down of Rose. [ending spoiler!] I found myself actually quite relieved that Abra and Dan didn't get really hurt at the end. Also there were other close calls like with the Crow, so many times Abra could have seriously gotten tortured and that threat was always looming so close. That was where the suspense lay for me throughout the entire story up to the awesome finale. And to see the Overlook location return and play out was such a treat. "Life is like a wheel." 
 The theme of alcoholism was a strong underlying part of this story for Dan, and I have to say it was another part of this story I REALLY enjoyed. There was such a ring of truth and authenticity to the AA storyline. [spoiler, spoiler] By the end, the "Anniversary" chapter and the last time we see "Doc" using his comforting bedside assist, both chapters I could feel very emotional as if I could cry. 
 Which leads me to one last thing I'd like to share about this book and it is actually quite personal and the second reason why this book will be important to me forever. As I neared the end of the audio book with about 2 hours left, it was getting so good and then - in my personal life I was struck with some devastatingly painful news involving my family. It was pretty heavy stuff and I found the weight of it truly hard to bear. In that one moment of my life, hearing the news, I'll never forget that day. I had to take my mind off of it. Most people in this type of scenario, perhaps like our hero Dan would maybe grab a bottle or self medicate in some way. But as I happened to be at such a gripping part of this book, when I was able to take a breath, calm down and relax, I simply returned to the story. For those last two hours, this book helped me to safely escape real life sadness and perhaps that is why I responded so heavily to the story by the end. Having a story be there for me to lift my spirits, just like a friend would, makes this book have special significance that I know in my lifetime of reading I'll never ever forget. 
 This is the first time I've read 40 books in one year. This is book 39 out of 40. I have one more book to go to complete my challenge. But unless my next book is spectacular enough, I can already say this book when I rank what I read from #40 down to #1 of favorites I read this year, THIS BOOK is as of now, my number 1.

Once again, I'm in the minority for a book review. 
 I'm saying this as nicely as I can, but there was absolutely nothing special about this book. It's the same story line and was honestly very predictable. I'm sure the author, whom I've never read before, wasn't looking for twists and turns, but a little ambiguity would have been nice.

 "His voice is delicate, like a wind chime." 
 "She hisses like a cornered cat." 
 "He stares at my mouth like a starving man." 
 "Feeling like an alien surrounded by Martians." 
 If you haven't read the book yet, you'll catch the similes EVERYWHERE. Once it's pointed out, it's impossible to not not hear them.

Decent YA-fantasy-superhero-sci-fi novel. It is however similar to Sanderson's other YA stories and mistborn to some degree, so there is a bit of been there done that feeling, but I think the feeling exists with most YA books as they tend to be simpler. 
 However the world and ideas were quite good and sound, and I will read the next when it comes out for sure.

Anyway, At just under 400 pages and with a completed story arc, I was quite sad when it was over. I'm hoping Schwab will re-visit this world again.

Like many long trips, On the Road begins with a great deal of milling about and confusion - in this case an attempt to leave New York with a few bucks and pursue the growing legend of the maniacal traveler and monologist Dean Moriarty. 
 The narrator, Sal Paradise, has few other interests besides engaging Moriarty, and it is only incidentally that we learn it is 1947, and practically nothing about who these drifters are, or their plans for the future, although presumably most are war veterans. Clearly, Sal and Dean are too young for World War II: they have their sights set on a new agenda of restless travel that will, in some manner, open new doors to consciousness, although Sal/Kerouac has not yet encountered the language and discipline of Buddhism, and is only beginning to self-consciously label himself part of a new "beat" generation. 
 What they invariably find is more confusion and bumps on the road - whether New York, San Francisco, New Orleans, or Denver-- but there can be little doubt that Kerouac himself believed the open road as the way to transcendence and Dean Moriarty (Neal Cassidy in real life) as its avatar. Not that either one meets our contemporary image of a road warrior: Sal dislikes driving, and Dean, except for his "hell-bound" Hudson, seems relatively indifferent to the brand names and performances of his automobiles. It's the road that counts, after all, not the vehicle. 
 Whether drenched or broke, Sal is rarely daunted, especially when he can organize another trip with Dean. Even when scraping by for gas and bread and cheese - the basics - Sal and company never break faith in their fundamental optimism that the American roadway is going to deliver something new and wonderful. And every once in a way it does, such as in the San Francisco jazz nightclub Jamson's Nook. 
 Kerouac offers up a set of vivid personalities - Moriarty above all - including Marylou, Dean's one true love and one of the few women who can survive any length of time in their world, whether traveling with them or waiting patiently for their return to San Francisco or New York. 
 Exactly what Sal and Dean and their merry band actually discover about the world remains necessarily vague - there can be no writing challenge more difficult than depicting human beings in ecstatic states, or just plain drunk-- although Kerouac tackles it with varying degrees of success. What is clear is what Kerouac doesn't want to talk about: any look back on the war and the lessons it might offer. Instead, he and Dean are seeing a new, more authentic language of consciousness that will take more explicit form in later books exploring Zen Buddhism. 
 But the continued search for ecstatic in a material world can exact a high price. Dean loses much of his charisma in Sal's eyes as Dean finds himself burdened with divorces, ex-wives, and children - and still reduced to depending on the kindness of strangers. He also suffered a debilitating hand injury. By the end, Sal and Dean face only one frontier left for them to cross: Mexico. But here Dean begins to sound silly as he projects the label "sublime hepcats," onto a sympathetic yet essentially impoverished population - even Sal can see it. 
 They return to New York and Sal goes home. For now, the journey is ended, but as we all know, the destination was never the point of the trip in the first place.

 I'll be honest with you; I can't identify that one thing that made me love this book. Mainly since it was a mere 210 pages long (or less than a five-hour audio). Usually, this leaves a lot to be desired in the way of character development and story, but Nic Stone just might be a genius. She managed to pack one hell of a story in those few pages without sacrificing quality. This story can easily be compared to Angie Thomas's The Hate U Give, in fact, there is mention of the "thug life" in Stone's book and a shout out from her on the cover, but this can easily stand on its own two feet, no comparison needed. 
 Justyce McAllister is doing everything he's been told he needs to to be successful. He goes to a prestigious boarding prep school, killed his SATs, is on the debate team, has great friends, and has an Ivy league college acceptance letter. He's also black and from the wrong side of town. He's a scholarship kid, and boards there so he's not immersed in his neighborhood life where circumstances might have taken him on a different path in life. Justyce also lives in a bubble of safety. That bubble is unceremoniously popped when he's trying to be the good guy and help his very drunk ex-girlfriend, who is sitting on the ground next to her car attempting to drive. During his efforts to help her, a police officer drives by, and sirens start. The next thing he knows is he's on the ground, being cuffed, hit in the head, mother-effed, and not allowed to speak. A day later, still shaken for being arrested for carjacking, Justyce can't reconcile his secure life at school with what just happened to him. He finds inspiration in Martin Luther King and begins journaling to him to sort out his thoughts. He'd like to be like the pacifist MLK, social justice hero of his time, and handle things calmly and peacefully but it's hard when he wants to punch people in the face when he feels his anger raging. Justyce thinks things will go back to normal at his school, but he soon realizes that his bubble of safety might not be safe after all. His best friend is black but has never lived in anything less than a McMansion, so he doesn't get it either. Both boys have different ways of coping with the intentional and unintentional racism that their eyes are now open to. As Justyce starts to understand that just because he's going to an Ivy League college, it's his skin color that will matter the most. How he chooses to live his life with this knowledge is something he's going to struggle with for a long time and decide if it will define him or lead him. 
 Nic Stone doesn't shy away from some pretty awkward and unsettling conversations and situations in this story. She does manage to portray both sides- I never felt like I was being preached to or told how to feel. Highly recommend this short but perfect story. The audio was excellent- and fast!

 Former FBI Academy rivals Jessica Harlow and John Shepherd meet again when they're assigned to work on an undercover case as partners. They're both facing complicated situations in their personal lives, since John was cheated on and Jessica had recently gone through a divorce, but their careers couldn't be going any better. John, for example, is about to join FBI's elite Hostage Rescue Team: the place where all the toughest agents gather together to face the deadliest challenges and save people's lives. BTW, I'd love to read a series about men (and women) in the Hostage Rescue Team. Can Julie James start writing it, please? 
 Since John and Jessica had a past that was all that friendly, working together was a challenge. Working together when they realized their past rivalry was mostly fueled by their attraction to each other was even harder. 
 I loved the dynamic here, because although there was tension and rivalry, these two were really respectful of each other. It's so easy to fall into a trap when writing enemies to lovers, but Julie James never did. It could easily see how Jessica and John admired each other and recognized each other's strengths. That made me admire them a lot more. 
 John and Jessica were also great characters individually. They were strong, career-focused, but still found time for their families, intelligent and passionate. 
 Another thing I could easily relate to was the case they were working on. Unfortunately, corruption is a reality in my country. Finding a politician who isn't involved in a corruption scandal has become almost impossible, so I had no trouble understanding and following the case. 
 I've come to expect great things from Julie James' books, and after reading my fifth book by this author, I can safely say I'll read whatever she writes next.

Jesus Christ, could anything more horrible, more sinister, more depressing be written? I am distraught, bitter, saddened, feeling all kinds of things. The ending of this book is both brilliant and unexpected, and leaves me feeling utterly dejected. This entire book is an unnerving tease. To me it is incomprehensible to compare most modern dystopias to this novel. None of the ones I've read have come close to 1984 and the terror within it. I can think of only one recent novel, The Hunger Games, and maybe even parts of Unwind, but they both fall short in my eyes. I don't know what to think or what to even say. Two quotes stood out to me while reading this book, and I feel they summarize what 1984 is all about--at least for me--so I guess I'll start with those: 
 "The terrible thing that the Party had done was to persuade you that mere impulses, mere feelings, were of no account, while at the same time robbing you of all power over the material world. When once you were in the grip of the Party, what you felt or did not feel, what you did or refrained from doing, made literally no difference. Whatever happened to you vanished, and neither you nor your actions were ever heard of again." 
 "Already we know almost literally nothing about the Revolution and the years before the Revolution. Every record has been destroyed or falsified, every book has been rewritten, every picture has been repainted, every statue and street and building has been renamed, every date has been altered. And that process is continuing day by day and minute by minute. History has stopped. Nothing exists except an endless present in which the Party is always right." 
 This world that Orwell creates is horrifying on many levels. Not only are all citizens hateful to the core, uneducated, lack privacy, and live in poverty and surrounded by disease, but they are also divided, controlled, and constantly being put up against one another. The most vile of citizens are actual children, who are encouraged since birth to turn in their own families to government officials if they suspect them of conspiring or disobeying the Party, knowing full well that the punishment is most likely death. 
 Citizens are presumably being killed by their own government during random "enemy attacks" to reinforce the idea that there's a war going on against enemies that change at whim. The very core of humanity is stripped away from these citizens, they have no aspirations, values (unless the Party introduces them and holds them to it), or even fulfilling partnerships. Love is a joke, and so is marriage. They are nothing but empty shells. Is there anything more horrifying than that kind of world? Has anyone read anything as dreadful? 
 When Winston and Julia were caught by the Thought Police, I was hoping against hope that they would escape, that it was a trick... or I don't know, that they would start their own revolution. But in retrospect I was clearly naive. I was foolish to think this book would have a happy ending. When Winston starts being tortured I accepted it as part of the plot. But then the torture continued, on levels I couldn't imagine, and for several chapters. I almost wished Winston would die so I wouldn't have to witness his pain. After a while I couldn't bear it. 
 And then, just when I thought it couldn't get any worse, Room 101 is revealed to us. In Room 101 your worst fears become realized and for Winston this is rats. The goal of Room 101 is to confront the victims with their worst fear so that they in turn will finally betray the people they love the most, and wish that their own worst fears are forced on those same people. That's right, it's torture to the third degree. Simple torture and brainwashing is not enough in this world.  
 I think this is where the genius of 1984 lies. There is nothing like it. As a reader you recognize that it's a horrible world in the beginning, a clear dystopia, but you are not prepared. Citizens are controlled, yes. The past and the future don't matter, true. Winston is captured. He is tortured. But he doesn't just suffer physical pain, humiliation, paralyzing fear, and degradation--he is reconstructed, broken down, and then rebuilt completely.  
 "We shall crush you down to the point from which there is no coming back. [...] Never again will you be capable of ordinary human feeling. Everything will be dead inside of you. [...] You will be hollow. We shall squeeze you empty, and then we shall fill you with ourselves." 
 He is not a person, he is a zombie. Nothing more than a dispensable pawn in a game controlled by slavery of the mind and the spirit. All the convictions and hatred that Winston had for the Party at the beginning of the book were erased, his initial courage is forgotten, his inner rebellion never existed, and this new Winston is presented to us, an oblivious stranger. He doesn't recognize the past or cares for it. His love affair with Julia was a dream he was all too ready to give up. It washed away with this new Winston and I could do nothing but witness his slow and deliberate demise right until the very end of the book.  
 I don't think I'll be re-reading this one anytime soon, but somethings tells me I'll have to re-visit this book eventually. It's just too good to forget.

 The opening and premises are indeed, in short, amazing. A down on his luck detective. A mysterious meeting at a bar. It was all so secretive, seductive, smoky and noir, but sweeter and more romantic rather than the traditional femme fatale. 
 The Amazon preview had been enough to convince me that I really wanted to read this book. And at $1, I thought, why not? 
 But perhaps the incredible opening and positive reviews left me with expectations that couldn't possibly be reached. 
 Connor wakes up and the woman is gone, thus setting up the title and most of the rest of the book. Little did I know, or enjoy, that the book took the "finding" quite literally. 
 Because the opening had such an enjoyable sense of noir, I had supposed the "finding" would involve a lot of Connor discovering what Claire had done in the past ten years. Instead, the "finding" is taken in a far more literal sense, and Finding Claire Fletcher becomes a tedious police procedural, reminiscent of a cross between Without a Trace and Criminal Minds. There's nothing particularly bad about Without a Trace or Criminal Minds (I've probably seen tons of their reruns whenever I veg out in front of the TV), but they strain the logic/credibility of their cases. Everything seems to have a habit of just working out in the end. When watching a TV drama, you just roll your eyes and roll with it. However, in a book, you want cases to be tougher, and tougher not as in a more brutal crime, but tougher with more dead ends, frustrating days in front of a desk with cups of coffee. 
 Another way Without a Trace, Criminal Minds, and now, Finding Clair Fletcher fails is in the characterization. TV shows get away with it because it's often hard to juggle the case of the week and astounding character development. Connor, however, goes from "the cop with a bad day at the bar", to a total Prince Charming off to rescue his Damsel in Distress. 
 When there are multiple narrators, you expect them to be on equal footing, but while Connor is off on his TV procedural routine, Claire holds all the cards and does...basically nothing. She made a phone call to Connor and then that was it until the climax and the ending  Instead, for the Claire scenes, we get flashbacks. The old adage, "show not tell" springs to mind, but since it was in the first person, and it was a flashback, I guess it was acceptable. It would have been more interesting if she had been telling some of this to Connor, or Connor discovering some of it, instead of Claire just telling the readers what happened. 
 And of course, the ending. Endings can make or break a book. However, in this case, it did neither. In this case, the book closed with the resounding satisfaction of an episode of a "case of the week" procedural. There was never any sense of real urgency or tragedy because the book was clearly leading up to a happy ending. 
 Suspense doesn't necessarily stem from keeping the readers completely in the dark and having no expectations. In fact, if a seemingly cliche book can make the reader doubt the next scene or ending, even for a moment, suspense is heightened. If Not Quite a Husband, a mostly stereotypical historical romance, could make me doubt the happy ending for a couple moments, than something with the premises of Finding Claire Fletcher should have been far more tense, especially at the climax, than it was. 
 And in fact, there were two happy endings. First, Claire gets reunited with everyone, but the author apparently decided this wasn't enough. The book needs MoRe DRaMa! *cue eye roll* So Claire sets off on a revenge mission, like Katniss at the end of Mockingjay, except Claire had even less in book buildup and rationale than Katniss did. And at the end, Claire doesn't come to a recognition and choose to commit revenge or quit, instead, she's saved with a deux ex machina from the author and a side character kills the bad guy instead. *cue another eye roll*  
 So in conclusion, Finding Claire Fletcher isn't a bad book, but here's what it doesn't have: 
 1. It doesn't have an original plot, outside of the opening. The rest of the book reads almost exactly like a crime drama on CBS 
 2. It doesn't have extremely complex and in-depth characters. The characters are likeable, they just don't scratch very far beneath surface tropes. 
 3. It doesn't have an explosive ending that leaves you thinking. It's drama filled in a sort of contrived, overly-flaky short of drama. 
 If you like TV crime dramas with just a dash more character development, then this is the book for you.

 Why I Read It: Anna Dressed in Blood was far from being a favourite of mine, but I enjoyed it enough to pick up the ARC of the sequel I had received from a manager at work. This review will have inevitable spoilers for Anna Dressed in Blood, though none for Girl of Nightmares. 
 Some of the few less-than stellar reviews I saw for Anna Dressed in Blood came back for second offerings with Girl of Nightmares and ended up LOVING it. I was really hoping that I would experience this as well, but alas, it was not meant to be. I still liked this book well enough, but I'll never love this series with the same fervor as everyone else. 
 First off, to be at all invested in the story in this second book, you have to be invested in the doomed romance of Anna and Cas. If you read my review for Anna Dressed in Blood, you'll already know that I wasn't. I liked both characters just fine on their own, but together? I couldn't see it. With that said, this entire book is about Cas finding out if Anna is okay since sacrificing herself to save the others from the Obeahman, and then subsequently attempting to rescue her from whatever dimension she's been sent to. I was all for saving Anna; I liked Anna! But reading about Cas's near obsessiveness with discovering how to help her didn't illicit much sympathy. Sure, I felt bad because I felt bad for ANNA, but I didn't feel bad for the heartache that Cas was experiencing. 
 The origins of that knife that Cas carries around everywhere is explained more, but I seriously found the whole Order thingie weird and didn't make much sense to me. For one, Cas has always seemed to be working solo. Yeah, he's got his British father figure helping him out all the time, but he was definitely never under the direction of some higher-ups or anything. Yet, when Cas eventually goes to Britain seeking answers, it's discovered that the Order is in fact hoping to "replace" him. Uh, what? Why would they even need to replace him? Why not just send in his replacement (some girl who's name I can't remember) out in the field and get her killing some ghosts in the UK? Why can there only be one? I know it had something to do with him owning the knife and it being imbued with the blood of his ancestors or something, but I honestly found the explanations so muddled and riddled with holes that I can't make heads or tails of it anymore. 
 But again, despite having these rather large complaints, I can't say that I didn't enjoy this book at all, because I did. They're fun, they're mindless, and they're a great way to pass the time when you want something a little different. Cas also continued to be a great narrator; despite having made friends and settled down a little, he's still Cas. His awkwardness in certain situations was amusing, but you can tell that he really does care about his friends, even when he doesn't show it in the same ways as other people might. 
 Final Verdict: Me and this duology are obviously just not a very good match. I like them okay but I doubt I'll be pressing them into the hands of others. While Cas was still a great narrator in this installment, I just wasn't invested enough in the relationship he established with Anna in the previous book to care about this storyline as much I maybe should have. Also, there were some world-building issues and inconsistencies in internal logic that threw me off. They're still fun books, but they ultimately ended up being a mildly fun distraction for me and not much more.

 Caelen, the last McCabe brother, offered to marry his brother's jilted bride Rionna to keep their alliances in check. He is to be Laird of her clan but knows he doesn't want a wife. Although he owned up to his commitments, he desperately tried to bring Rionna to heel. A warrior princess at heart, Rionna wants to fight with her clan and her husband. When she is attacked Rionna and Caelen come to an agreement and they move to face the biggest battle either of their clans have dealt with in the past. 
 I was really excited to get to Caelen's story. Caelen had been the gruff, nearly rude brother throughout the entire series so far. He was against the earlier marriages but after reading the first two books it was clear he was a genuinely nice guy. He protected his sister-in-laws and other members of his clan. He knew he was destined for virtually nothing as the youngest brother of a Laird but he made something of himself through his marriage to Rionna. I was so excited to get to his story because he had been this dark knight throughout the books and I couldn't wait to see what happened when he fell in love.

 My Soul to Steal is the fourth book in this series and, as I said after I read the last book, it just keeps getting better. And annoying me more and more. 
 The book picks up shortly after the last one, and Kaylee is still trying to decide if she can forgive, if not forget, the way Nash not only lied to her and allowed Avari, a hellion, to possess her but how he was able to trade his memories of her for his fix of Demon's Breath. 
 Within the first few pages of the book, Kaylee finds out that attempting to forgive Nash is only part of what she'll have to deal with, as his ex-girlfriend, Sabine, from his previous hometown has transferred to their school and has set her sights on Nash again. 
 I absolutely hate Sabine. She's an evil troll (okay, technically she's a mara, but I think she's got some troll in there somewhere) who does everything she can to get Nash, despite him constantly telling her he wants to be with Kaylee, not her. She treats Kaylee like crap, never missing a chance to attack her verbally but also to use her own powers to mess with her in more serious ways. 
 One thing she harped on when telling Kaylee why she was no good for Nash was that she, Sabine, accepted him the way he was, faults and all, and that Kaylee refused to do so. She kept saying that Kaylee couldn't look past his previous addiction to Frost and would be unable to ever forgive him for what he did to her. Sabine also told Kaylee that they'd never last because she didn't need Nash anymore, even though he needed her, and it seems like Kaylee, at least to a certain extent, is starting to believe this. What I kept screaming in my head was, who cares if you don't need someone?! If you like, love and want somebody, what does it matter if you don't need them? 
 ***SOAPBOX ALERT*** 
 Okay, so it seems that every time a character in a book rags on veg food, I'm going to be commenting on it. At one point, Sabine compares eating the fears of an old person to eating tofu, while chowing down on the fears of a teenager is more like eating a sirloin.  On top of all of this Kaylee, Nash, Alec (who's staying with Kaylee and her dad and working at the Cinemark) and Emma have to figure out how and why some people at their school are dying while others are hopping on the first train to crazy town.

Quick-Fire Review: Ugh. Pretty Little Liars meets Gossip Girl. Rich people problems. Deception and blackmail. Pettiness. Opulence. Bleh. 
 Full Review: 
 I read books because I enjoy reading (obviously), but it's always a bonus when you feel like the book has taught you something new, made you feel something inside, or caused you to rethink your opinion and thoughts. I think it's possible to find value in any book on any level and surpass mere enjoyment. This is not one of those books. 
 Set in the future, The Thousandth Floor is about a enormous skyscraper that has a thousand floors. The wealthier people live on the higher floors while the poor are scrunched into the lower levels. The building is immense in area and girth and personally very hard to wrap my head around the world-building and logistical details of the building. There are museums, parks, clubs, restaurants, and neighborhoods, all of which I just couldn't fathom or imagine in my mind. Katherine McGee created some fascinating technological advances and neat trinkets in her book, but ultimately I was unimpressed with the world-building. Why was this skyscraper built? What is the rest of the country like? What has happened from modern day to 100 years later at the time of this book? 
 The Thousandth Floor alternates among five different points of view. At first it was more than slightly disorienting and annoying, but as the lives of all the people overlap the switches felt more natural and fluid. I just wish I liked any of the people in this book. They all are ambitious, some to a cutthroat level. And their problems are so darn petty. They are worried about people liking them, being popular, maintaining their elite status, and although it was guiltily entertaining at first, it got old fast. The characters were not likable or understandable in their actions. I am tired of reading descriptions of these characters presented in such a revering way, like the reader and everyone else should worship the ground these "perfect" people walk on. I didn't feel like these characters were guiding the story, I felt like the plot pulled the strings of these people like marionettes. 
 Some romances are interspersed in this book, and I really like one of the couples and really detest the other. There is a romance that feels so gross and incest-like that I can't get on board with it. It's cheesy and feels like a weak plot device just to cause more drama and tension and set up the ending. 
 I'll admit the ending is crazy and has *unfortunately* hooked me to read the next book. Blackmail, drama, and secrets abound in this book, so if that's your thing then check out this book!

Wow, it almost pains me to say anything is darker than the first (in which babies were boiled alive in a cauldron) but I think this was. This is a very personal reaction, and it has to do with something which is a big spoiler - and part of that is my ending up angry because someone had done something which is an absolute deal-breaker for me and yet it was the 'right thing' to do because everything was LITERALLY going to HELL. What I didn't mind - which puts me in a small minority, I think - was the role Neil Gaiman played as a fairly significant character in the book. Possibly if I liked Neil Gaiman I might have cared more, but don't and didn't. 
 What stopped the grimness of the first from being overwhelming was the way Quill and his team gradually started working together as a team, despite severe lack of trust and even disgust in some cases, and they went up against extremely powerful, probably undefeatable supernatural forces, as "coppers". And Quill kept bringing it back to that, while struggling with what had been done to him personally, and with his own need and inability to trust the others. I loved Lofthouse's tentative, very partial joining their group at the end too - hope we'll get her story some point soon. 
 I still love the way the real London is mixed with the supernatural one, with odd and unexpected twists and turns (the Blue Peter garden as a site of ancient horror, for example!). I'm less happy with the nature of magic - or perhaps that's specifically with magic in London - as it involves the kind of 'sacrifice' that's all about taking on pain and how much you're willing to harm yourself to get something you want in return. That has already become very clear, even before there's an auction of London stuff at the Tate Modern - only for those who are sighted, of course.  I was already thinking that Ross and Costain were way out of their league when they went to the auction hoping to get the Bridge of Spikes - with what to offer? But when Ross gave up all her happiness, forever, in order to get just a look at the ledger book, it was unbearably grim. Worse than when Quill was killed, because I *knew* he was going to be rescued somehow, but NO BACKSIES ON THE AUCTION. Presumably. Maybe eventually something will change, but there's a ring of finality to it (and to Ross's saying that she'll *never* forgive Costain) that there wasn't about Quill's death. 
 Then it got worse, because Costain stole the thing in order to rescue Quill, and it was both the worst thing he could have done and the ONLY thing that could have made Ross's sacrifice even close to worthwhile, as we learn at the end. I mean, really - Hell contains EVERYONE WHO EVER LIVED IN LONDON. Had Ross rescued her dad he'd have been super-happy, have died eventually and GONE TO HELL. Forever this time, too. Ross herself, Costain, Sarah and Jessica (yup, young children in Hell too) - everyone. And yet I loathe the "make his/her choice for him/her because you love them" thing as much as anyone. Even Quill, though, who knew how things were 'wrong' and how Hell had nothing to do with how you'd lived and only whether you'd lived in London, even HE blamed Costain for stealing the BoS and saving him. I have to believe that "healing his unit" includes forgiveness for Costain, whose act was selfless if not good in other ways.  
 The "racist newspaper mogul", the riots in London - a few things like that seemed a bit *too* on the nose, but I loved Quill's final return to form. When he tells the Smiling Man he's not going to do what he's expected to do tell everyone who'd believe it what the sign at the gate to Hell says , but instead is going to "find a way to heal my unit. I'm going to wait until I'm sure they're able to cope with what I know. Then we're going to find some way to change it" I was - warily - back on board. I might wait just a while after book 3 comes out, and if I see a lot of people saying it's darker than the first two, it's bailing time.

Fraternize is book one in a brand new series, Players Game, by Rachel Van Dyken. When I decided to read this book, first, it was because I love this author. So that alone assured that I would enjoy the book. But I wasn't prepared for how this book made me feel. It is a love triangle so you need to know that right up front. But not your usual love triangle. This is a woman that just achieved her life long dream. But as soon as she got there, she was faced with both someone from her past re-entering her life, and someone new coming into her life. She is faced with choosing between her past and her present. Between an old love or a new love. 
 Emerson Rodner is not your typical skinny girl. She has curves. Her lifelong dream was to be an NFL Cheerleader. She has tried out before but never made it. But this year was the one. She was accepted into the cheerleading squad of the Bellevue Bucks. Their manual pretty much rules their life. Diet restrictions, surprise weigh ins, and most importantly, no fraternizing with the football players. 
 It's her first day of practice and Emerson meets Grant Sanchez, one of the captains of the team. Grant is gorgeous and is known for his playboy ways. Grant has set his sights on Emerson. He slowly wears her down. And to her surprise, he is not the man she thought he was at all. He is sweet, considerate, kind, and boy does this man had the ability to sweet talk. I heard myself sigh out loud while I was reading this. This man made me swoon, made my heart miss a few beats. He was adorable. 
 But with all these things going on in Emerson's life, she is forced to face someone from her past at the same time. Miller Quinton was her childhood best friend. And in their last year together, he became her first love. She gave him her virginity. But then his dad moved them away and all connections were broken. She blames Miller but Miller thinks it's her fault. Neither of them really know the truth, what caused them to lose contact. Miller was the love of her life and the source of her greatest pain. One look at him and she knows she still loves him. But he is her past. Could he be a part of her future? Or was there too much history? 
 "No matter how damaged your heart may be, it never loses its ability to choose again, to try again, to want love even after loss. How could something so wrong feel so right?" 
 I think I lived this book right along with Emerson! I was completely emotionally invested. And I completely ended up feeling exactly the opposite as I thought I would. Both of these men loved Emerson. Both wanted nothing but her happiness for her. One of them would have to make the sacrifice. Would have to decide that they weren't the right man for her. That she would be better off with the other one. 
 What I also loved about this book was that it showed the closeness of the football players, the brotherhood. How they had each other's backs. What they would do for each other. Was there a bad seed in the group? Yes. But aside from him, these men couldn't be any closer. There was nothing they wouldn't do for each other. And it showed in their games, in their abilities as a team. 
 "I was still afraid, afraid that this was a dream, that this feeling - this thing we had between us - wasn't real. And I needed it so badly to be real. For something this good to stay this good." 
 My rating for this book started out as a four. Then it quickly went to a five. I fell in love. I fell for all three of these characters. One in particular will stay with me. Which one? I don't want to say. I want to see who you chose. Then I'll tell you. So if you want a book about real people, real emotions, real issues, while still being fun, sexy and sweet, this one is for you. I loved it. I hope you do too.

 "No! I like you because you make me want to fix them."

Well wow, this was heartbreaking and just oh so good, a totally unique and beautiful story that will be hard to forget. 
 17yr old Mia's life is pretty great when we join her on a snowy morning in Oregon. A gifted cellist with a bright future at Julliard on the horizon, she has good friends, a family she doesn't mind spending time with and a gorgeous boyfriend on his way to becoming a rock star who loves her even though she's kinda straight laced and not into the whole club scene. 
 At 7:09 A.M school has been cancelled so her family decides to take advantage of the day by going for a drive. They will be back in time for her to attend Adam's concert that night in Portland and a bonus day looms ahead. The reader immediately gets a feel for this loving and happy family that laughs, teases and gets along. Yes, unlike most girls her age Mia actually thinks her parents are cool and likes her little brother. I liked her parents too; kinda hipster and her brother... well I can't think too much about him now without wanting to cry. 
 Sometime between 8 and 9 that morning, as her family laughs and fights over which radio station to listen to Mia's life changes forever. In an instant almost everything is taken from her. 
 "You wouldn't expect the radio to work afterward. But it does. The car is eviscerated. The impact of a four-ton pickup truck going sixty miles an hour plowing straight into the passenger side had the force of an atom bomb." 
 Now Mia is caught between life and death, her body comatose but her spirit watching as the paramedics scramble to keep her alive. She goes with herself to the hospital and roams the corridors when the ICU becomes too much. Her grandparents are there, friends and family in a waiting room. Is this real? Am I dead? Finally Adam rushes in, his eyes red and swollen and Mia is forced to make a decision. 
 If I Stay is only about 200 pages long but wow what an impact. As Mia hovers between life and death, she reflects on her life and we learn all aspects of it, her dreams for the future and her relationship with Adam. And we're with her when she realizes she has to make a choice because to live is going to hurt and take more courage than she may have. Will she stay and face the pain of an unknown future or will she simply let go... 
 I just loved this story, but I'm such a sucker for a good tragedy, this tore me to pieces in the best of ways. Cheers

A GIRL LIKE ME went in a few directions I didn't expect or didn't like or.. wasn't sure about. 
 I found the beginning kind of confusing. I was left uncertain as to where Scott was going with everything. But then.. some of that went away. Things were getting better. Events were calming down; until they weren't. 
 Yes, this is all going to be the vaguest of vague, because there's so little I can say that won't ruin this duet for new readers. 
 I don't want to totally rehash my rant to a book buddy (hi Rebecca!) but one of my big pet peeves with contemporary novels that try and push the thriller/drama elements is that when you already those on the go.. why push it further? I definitely feel a line was crossed into escalating things after they should've been resolved. There's just a lot happening, basically from the beginning, and all wrapped around Joss and.. like, I get it, but c'mon. Give me a break. Sometimes it's just way too much and I cannot suspend my disbelief. But. Having said that, the scene in question that really got me going.. it served a purpose and I suppose it was necessary for how everything needed to wrap up. I'm still not really happy about it, though, because it could've gone a hundred other ways to get to that same point. But I digress. 
 Personally, despite some of the interpersonal dynamics between characters and groundbreaking repair to some damaged relationships, I honestly could've done without this one. A BOY LIKE YOU could almost stand on it's own and I kind of like that idea better. Take book one and replace those final two chapters with those of A GIRL LIKE ME.. and we have a standalone book that I'm on board with. 
 Despite the unexpected turn of this final installment, I enjoyed a lot of this story and these damaged, broken, hopeful, characters. I did find some of Scott's word choice to be a little repetitive (she was pretty hung up on certain facial expressions and eye contact, but, hey, YAish romance, whatever) but I'm looking forward to reading more from this author.

 Hysteria, simply, blew me away. Just when I thought it was heading in one direction, Miranda would make a u-turn and head in a completely different direction. Sometimes this was confusing as hell, but on the whole, it just added to the suspense and thrill of the ride, emulating Mallory's thought process. There were some things that I saw coming, but that wasn't a disappointment. Actually it was a nice change of pace, to know what was going on for a change, in addition to upping the tension. You know what's about to happen, and are willing the characters to figure it out too before it's too late. 
 There are two storylines running almost simultaneously in Hysteria, which compliment as opposed to distract from each other, and the ending does a great job of tying all those loose ends together. I know the ending will please some readers but may disappoint others. I was in the former category. There are several unnerving scenes of bloody handprints which definitely upped the tension throughout, and those combined with a series of flashbacks to the events before Mallory came to boarding school give us just enough to keep questioning what the heck is goings on. 
 The characters were engaging and believable, and their reactions to specific events were very realistic. Mallory herself is a contradiction in terms. Brave but shattered, she has been through something traumatic, and as intended, she sometimes comes across as slightly unhinged. Like Mallory, we are kept guessing as to what is real, and Miranda does a fantastic job of keeping us guessing. 
 There is romance there, it was sweet and just what you'd expect from the characters, but it was more in the background than upfront, which I think in this case was the way to go, leaving the main focus to be Mallory's struggle with right and wrong, real and not real. 
 I'm not sure what else I can say without giving any of the story away, but if you're looking for a creepy, Soul Survivors type of psychological thriller, then this is the book for you.
