I had to leave it a couple of weeks before I wrote this review. My emotions were too tangled up to be objective. 
 I'm a Kitty Thomas fan. I know she writes a very specific type of dark erotica and I had a good idea what to expect. I knew she would mess with my head and play with my emotions and I was not disappointed in that respect. 
 Grace longs for total 24/7 submission and becomes obsessed with the idea of becoming a slave on a remote and unusual island - one where normal civil rules no longer apply. Against the advice of her best friend, she abandons her life to become the slave of a Dom she has been Skypeing with for over a year. Her dreams are shattered when, slightly predictably, he turns out to be a monster. 
 She endures months of abuse before he sells her on to another Dom, one who is reputed to have killed his previous slave. This all happens in the first 24%. The rest of the book is her developing relationship and dependence on her new Dom, Asher. 
 She is confused by his initial, gentle treatment of her, but slowly learns to trust him. To love him - even when he hardens his stance and begins to treat her like a pet. This was, after all, what she'd been looking for. 
 I know I struggle with animal-play, it's a kink that I dislike, but even without that I failed to like Asher. Lots of reviewers have slated Grace's actions but I could go along with them, with her confusion and longing to be something that she wasn't. I bought into that, but I didn't feel the love for Asher. Sorry, Kitty. 
 Asher seemed as though he was playing a part, I didn't get the sense that his heart was in it, and maybe that was the point of the whole story? Grace wants something, Asher wants to provide it, but neither of them are honest enough to talk about it? I don't know * shrugs *. 
 Books are very personal things and while I didn't 'get' Asher, plenty of other readers did. It won't stop me from reading Kitty Thomas. I enjoy her style too much :-)

I've only read one other book by Yann Martel (the one everyone knows, The Life of Pi) but judging from these two I don't need to read any more. The same themes in Pi are once more present here - animals, religion, science, and magical realism - and those last three work together about as well gratingly as they did then. 
 The High Mountains of Portugal consists of really three loosely interconnected short stories, all in the 20th century, though spaced several decades apart. In each, we are shown people processing the grief they experience as a result of losing a loved one, learning to move on the only way they can. 
 Stylistically, Martel's writing is wonderful. His characters are deeply emotional and complex, and still easily empathized with. The reader is given no special treatment or introductions: we start in the middle and are expected to construct pasts and motivations ourselves based on whatever information is given. This device is especially effective here because Martel is also a master at the sleight of hand, able to somehow divert our attention from the obvious plot until he wants it revealed. 
 But why oh WHY decide that you want to bring in science, religion, and magical realism? Science and religion obviously are oil and vinegar, a push and pull that could probably balance each other if they were the only two subjects discussed. Adding magical realism in the form of that super weird autopsy when a body contained: a wooden flute, vomit, a chimpanzee and hammer, among other things  only succeeded in reducing a moving scene to something that was borderline absurd. It made what could have been a legitimate faith-based experience impossible to take seriously. In The Life of Pi, essentially the same thing happens and Martel attempts to rationalize this ridiculousness by saying, in effect, "but don't you prefer the better story?" 
 I guess in his mind "better" equates to more dramatic and more sensational, but.. no. The High Mountains of Portugal had some raw emotional scenes that would have been so profound and nuanced if Martel had simply left the weird out of it. I love magical realism when it's done well, but I have to grudgingly admit that it just wasn't here. Sadly disappointing.

Her father is desperate to know what happened in the years she was gone. Her mother, a born again Christian, simply wants to reconnect with her daughter. This is a good plot, but the author weighs it down with side stories that end with no resolution. The mother is in love with the preacher at her church, but we don't find out the nature of their relationship. The father struggles with some childhood trauma that isn't fully confirmed or denied and certainly isn't developed enough to take up as much space as it does. The fathers half brother is sinister in a shadowy kind of way- never enough to cast him as the kidnapper, but merely as some sort of ex alcoholic, ex gambling, former abused child who may or may not have an inappropriate relationship with his niece. The idea of him selling her to her eventual kidnapper is tossed around a bit, but the narrator doesn't seem too concerned with this prospect so... Neither are we. 
 What is truly missing here is the viewpoint of the daughter herself. Caitlin, the character who the entire book is about, is barely a ghost on the page. When she speaks it's only to profess how much she loves her kidnapper and wants to go back. We see a completely one dimensional view of her, not as a victim of a serious trauma, but as a lovesick silly teenager. In fact, the ordeal she undergoes seems to be less about her but more for forcing character development in her parents and uncle. Why is her suffering pushed aside like this? I feel bad for her. She needs some time away with qualified therapists and parents who care more about her than they do their own petty relationship drama.

Calamity had sparks of brilliance which made me love Books 1 and 1.5 (Steelheart & Mitosis respectively). A few inspired action scenes were palpable in their execution, so much so that my current reality fell away and I was fully enveloped in Sanderson's dystopian Calamity universe. Sad to say, but I did not experience a similar feeling reading Firefight (Book 2). Overall, Calamity was much more refined, and even David's horrible metaphors started making some bit of sense. 
 In Calamity, the last book in the trilogy, the surviving members of the Reckoners are without much needed resources, are experiencing a serious chasm in leadership on top of which are fighting for their very existence against an enemy possessing of almost godlike powers. This High Epic of High Epics is also vastly experienced and most of all, intimately understands the Reckoners like no other. We have to admit that David isn't much of a leader, and more a half-cocked gun, jumping into volatile confrontations and naturally improvising as he does best. 
 The explosion blew above, and it somehow seemed louder because I'd been expecting it. The chunks of metal fell exactly where they had before, slamming to the ground inches from where I crouched - but I was left unharmed, as was Megan. 
 The robots, on the hand, acted like a bunch of youthful dreams and got thoroughly crushed. 
 I have mixed feeling about the climax and ending. Spoiler time! I will take pity on those who haven't read Calamity and I won't spoil the surprise. So here goes:  WTF did I just read! He streaked toward us, cape fluttering behind. An outfit I knew all too well...For in that world, my father's shirt had borne a symbol. A symbol I recognized -a stylized S shape. A symbol that meant something... Does that ring a bell? And then my mind went back to those hints related to David's High Epic powers. Invulnerability, man of steel, flight, issues with flight. To say I was surprised is an understatement. Well played Sanderson. Well played.

THIS BOOK WAS UNBEARABLY FRUSTRATING, OH MY GOSH. It's longer than Sabriel, with less enjoyable characters, a more epic sweep (ugh), and a lot of muddly "why did we need to see this" scenes. While the worldbuilding is interesting, the ending is so obscenely infuriating that I'm actively angry about it. 
 Look, here's the big problem. Lirael tries to take on international politics, xenophobia, and the matter of what to do about massive numbers of refugees--and I was incredibly excited by all this when I started, because these are subjects that are as relevant now as in 2001. Unfortunately, while all of this is roiling in the background, the foreground story moves like molasses in January, and by the end of the book, not a single bit of it has actually been dealt with. The book ends at what feels like a midpoint, even though it's a slog just to get there. When I hit the epilogue, I wanted to scream BUT YOU DIDN'T TELL ME THE STORY YET. It felt like a total letdown. 
 I also spent large portions of the book wanting to drown Lirael in a well. She's sad that she's not a Clayr, and that's mildly interesting, but she's sad about it for hundreds of pages. Sameth was much more sympathetic to me; while he's a whiny baby as well, he's got trauma issues he has no real way to deal with. Besides, his discovery that going on an adventure is actually really unfun at times is genuinely charming and a gentle rebuke to gee-whiz sword and sorcery stories. Lirael's depression is comparatively dull and irritating, though that's in part because I have enough real-life experience with depression that sitting through a long secondary-world fantasy novel featuring a heroine like her is like being stabbed in the face with shards of pure boredom. 
 What makes me sad is that I can see how this could be a good idea. If the focus had remained strongly on Lirael and imply that all the geopolitical stuff was actually going to be engaged with during this book, it wouldn't have felt like the book didn't just stop. Her character arc is a clear and complete one, but all the clutter around it takes away from it. With a little more focus (and please, please, a little more movement in Lirael's world), this would have been a good story. 
 Alternately, drop this next-generation business and write me the story of two nerds in love who 1. are incredibly inexperienced in love and 2. have to try to rebuild a country that's been chaos for two centuries. Those early chapters of Sabriel and Touchstone's story are what genuinely interest me, and the possibility for conflict both within their relationship and outside it is off the charts. 
 I listened to this as an audiobook, and Tim Curry's performance is marvelous. I only wish the material he was reading was up to his acting.

This is a book that is easy to read and discount for its violent content, but if one is willing to look deeper there are important themes that we can learn from, as exist in all great dystopian novels. 
 "Does God want goodness or the choice of goodness?" 
 That is the central question asked in A Clockwork Orange. Alex is a violent, yet intellectual teenager. He doesn't easily fit into any stereotypes of criminals who are too ignorant to know better. The truth may be even worse, he simply enjoys it. 
 While Alex's actions are abhorrent, there are also hints about his youth and the poor state of the communist society that cause him to be the way he is. When he is incarcerated, we learn that the 'good guys' who make it their goal to rehabilitate him are no better. 
 This is a book that could be read quickly, but you will miss out on the way it can provoke you to think differently about deeply held beliefs and the role of government in society. The use of Burgess' own cockney/Russian language for Alex give it an otherworldly atmosphere that assures the reader that this isn't the world we live in . . . . but could it be?
Not as good as Touchstone.

Rosie and Don are enjoying their HEA in the wake of 'The Rosie Project', that is until Rosie reveals she's pregnant. Don tries to figure out what to do with the upcoming new addition to his life - and hilarity ensues. 
 And like I said in the review of The Rosie Project: and I mean hilarity. 
 This book is every bit as funny as funny as its predecessor, but with the added surprise of being more moving. In the previous book I knew what the outcome would be so the tension was not so high for me. In this book - even though I thought I knew what the outcome would be I still found myself growing increasingly tense and at several points genuinely uncertain as to the ultimate outcome. 
 Not only is Don struggling, trying his best to understand, adapt, and learn what to do while facing pressure from other forces as well, but Rosie is struggling too. Rosie wants to continue to be the strong 'do it all herself' woman she always has been until now. She wants to keep on with her degree, contribute financially to the family, and raise the child. And then there's the hormones, and Don's odd behaviour and reactions. as someone who was recently pregnant I empathised intensely. 
 I liked the new characters, George, Dave, and Sonia, but mostly wanted to slap Lydia every time she graced the page. 
 My two issues with the book (one small, one large) were SMALL: the lame 'turn-about' where Gene - kicked out by Claudia for his continued philandering after the agreement they no longer had an open marriage - convenient turned out to not actually have slept with as many women as he claimed. Instead he had merely dated most up to a point where he felt that sex was a sure thing then bailed on them. Except I find that extremely hard to believe. It also just didn't seem to fit with his character. For me it seemed like an attempt to make Gene sympathetic since he was kicked out, then rejected by his new possible love interest. I neither liked nor believed it. In my own personal head-cannon this is a lie he told everyone to attempt to keep their friendships. 
 LARGE: The manner in which Rosie becomes pregnant. She stops taking her birth control, WITHOUT properly discussing it with Don. I can understand all her behaviours once she's knocked up because I know what a terrible mindflip pregnancy is and how crazy it makes you, but I just can't figure out why she would do such a low thing. It's not too dissimilar to the woman who doesn't want to lose her man so gets pregnant to trap him - except she was not in danger of being dumped. I know, I know she thought it would take her longer to fall pregnant because their friends had taken years to, but surely she, as a medical student, would be aware that they were younger and more physically fit than that couple, not to mention their friends had other complications barring the way. Surely she wasn't so stupid as to honestly believe it would take years as well. And certainly not stupid enough to BET on that fact. This just seemed out of character for her, and a bit of a dick move in regards to their relationship since she didn't keep Don informed of her actions. My own personal head-cannon is that she simply forgot to take her birth control for a few days while stressing over her thesis so became pregnant inadvertantly  
 A lot of the problems and reactions/solutions to those problems are sitcom-esque in their ludicrousness, but it just made for even more of a laugh in my opinion, though I did quirk an eyebrow on several occasions when certain characters made certain decisions. 
 Overall a magnificent sequel which I utterly adored.

4.5 Another surprise. I nearly didn't pick this one up because of overly coy marketing -- I ended up reading it because I was visiting my mum and she had it out from the library, so an opportunistic read. I was expecting it to be just the sort of literary fiction I hate -- where boring people talk about their boring lives and love affairs, someone's past trauma and present sex life intersect, and everyone is damaged but has a really erudite narrative voice. 
 Well, this one has some of that. I'm going to spoil it, but as I wouldn't have picked it up unspoiled, maybe it's better to be spoiled. In this one, the past trauma and family issue is that the narrator was brought up twinned with a chimpanzee, her sister Fern. It's definitely a book with an agenda around the use of animals for human purposes, but there was a lot more to it than that. The thing that I found most interesting was the narrator, Rosemary -- it took me far too long to work out that she was an unreliable narrator, and that she was seemingly unaware of her own unreliability. It is literary fiction, so at times it's like slogging through a dictionary, but in Rosemary's voice, it also helps to draw the comparison between the non-verbal Fern (who is very present in the novel despite being physically absent for the vast majority of it) and the allegedly garrulous Rosemary. There's a lot of neat stuff going on with mirrors, twinning, even the title -- being beside ourselves as an image for the human/chimp relationship as well as evoking the cliche. There's a lot of allusions, some of which don't always come off -- I thought Mdm Defarge as a puppet and representative of the human ignoring the horrors of what is in front of them, then "vanishing" when both Harlow and Rose cease to ignore the plight of animals in their different ways. 
 I'm not sure why people have been so coy about Fern being a chimp. I can see Rosemary's reasoning -- she is, after all, fired by her agenda -- but I don't think that we should necessarily take account of the motivations of the narrator in the marketing and spoiling of the book. I worked it out early on, and I think you're supposed to work it out early on, and see the deliberate withholding of the information as symptomatic of Rosemary's manipulation and guarded jealousy. If I'd known this was about the 1990s (excellent sense of era evoked, btw), animal research, and Rosemary as a "monkey girl", I'd have wanted to read it right away, rather than picking it up idly because I'd heard good things but wasn't sure what it was about.

Jenny Morton was born with a disease that kills. On the day she was born her mother and all the hospital staff died from touching her. As a result, her father raised her to avoid all direct contact with people, and as Jenny learned early on, with just about everything living. She spends her whole life not knowing the touch of another, and desires only to be normal, to have normal things like simple human contact that others take for granted. 
 From an early age Jenny is tormented for being different. She wears gloves, long sleeves, and jeans, even when it's hot, to diminish any possibility of passing on her plague. After a freak encounter with what would become her arch nemesis, Ashleigh, she quickly earns the name Jenny Pox. Now in her last year of high school, Jenny's former nickname is but a distant memory for most everyone in her class. Except Ashleigh who will never forget the scars of that one fateful day years ago. She lives to torment Jenny, giving her the new nickname of Jenny Mittens, which is quickly adopted by the whole school. 
 Everyone is wrapped around Ashleigh's finger, her boyfriend, friends, school staff, and everyone is town, and it seems Jenny is the only one who can see the evil that lurks behind the angelic demeanor and Christian do-gooder charm that exudes from Ashleigh's pores. When Seth, Ashleigh's boyfriend, stops along the side of the road and helps her to save her dying dog one day, Jenny finds that maybe she isn't alone after all. It seems she and Seth share a common thread, and they strike up a quick friendship, much to Ashleigh's horror. The girl's rivalry escalates far beyond high school drama and eventually turns deadly. 
 Definitely a page turner! This book was filled with fantastic detail. I loved the characters that I was meant to love, and loathed the characters I was meant to loath. Ashleigh is the kind of girl you hate to your core, and much of the townspeople left a sour taste in my mouth. A few were so disgusting I had to put the book down for a bit before I could stomach any more. I was on the edge of my seat from the very beginning. I simply had to know what was in store for Jenny next! Some people compared this to Carrie and I would have to agree. I had the same thought at a particular moment in the book, but as with Carrie, I understood why she did what she did. This is one of the best stories I have read in a while, so I fully plan to pick up the next one and see where this author takes me.

8 out of 10 
 Genre: High Fantasy, Young Adult 
 Series: Six of Crows 
 Fav. Character: Nina 
 Writing: Pretty good 
 Recommended for: Anyone who likes gritty, dark settings, misfit/criminal characters; Fans of the Grisha Trilogy 
 !There is a spoiler in this review hat is hidden by a spoiler tag! Do NOT click it, if you haven't finished the book yet and don't want to massively spoiled! 
 I had a somewhat hard time going into this book. I wasn't such a massive fan of the first one as everyone else on my update feed, and while I myself hate those people that rate a book down because they think that it doesn't 'deserve the hype' (after all, it's not the book's fault that it got popular after people read it), I felt myself sliding into a similiar mindset. I was just tired of seeing all the - for me - unjustified hype around this series, because, honestly, I never really connected with the main characters as everyone else seemed to do. Still, I over all enjoyed the first book and would pretty much read anything that Leigh Bardugo writes anyway, so it was clear that I wouldn't skip this one. Even if only to see what all the fuss was about. 
 Like with the first book, this book struck me as one of the good sort, strong plot, entertaining characters, good writing, but still, I didn't really feel myself getting all hyped-up about it. I tried to rid myself of any expectations that reviews and status updates had built up, and since I tried to stay mostly clear of Crooked Kingdom-reviews beforehand (didn't want to get spoiled after all), I mostly succeeded. 
 The best thing about this book for me was the setting. I loved Ketterdam in the first book, how Bardugo described it so beautifully, with its narrow and crooked alleys, dubious characters, all the grit and darkness that she worked into her world. Therefore, I was excited to douse deeper into the city, see more of its districts, get a more detailed image of how the city works. Since this is a follow-up series to the Grisha series, Bardugo now had five books to expand her world and it really shows in this book. There are so many different (sometimes familiar) nationalities that come together in Ketterdam, it's a blast to read. 
 In the first book, my main problem was that I didn't connect to the characters as much as many other readers did. I'd say that they grew closer to me in this book, and I certainly have my favorites (*cough* Nina *cough* Matthias), but I still don't really feel a strong connection to any of them. When Matthias died at the end, I wasn't expecting it, and I was sad that he out of all of them had to die, but it didn't shock me like many other character deaths have . I'd say I like Kaz the least out of all the characters, despite him being a somewhat fan-favorite from what I can tell. He just feels so unorganic and constructed to me. Whenever he appeared, I had a hard time actually feeling the character as a vivid, organic person. I know that no fictional character is real, but there are those that feel real, that I don't experience as the work of an author, but as an independent, lively (if fictional) person. And Kaz just doesn't give me that feeling. 
 I was super excited to see some familiar faces from the Grisha series reappear, and their appearance just fortified the feeling, that I connected to the Grisha characters better. I wish they'd been a bigger part of this series, but then again, this is a new series, so I understand that Bardugo wants the spotlight on the new characters. 
 Another thing that bothers me is how strong the YA element is despite the gritty atmosphere. Now, don't get me wrong, I like Young Adult books, but in a series that tries so hard to establish the character's ruthlessness and callousness, has them dealing with (international) politics, repeats over and over again what they've all experienced in their lives/professions in the Barrel, it just feels wrong and a bit imature to be reminded that the characters are only seventeen years old. And we have six characters, and they all perfectly match up into 3 love couples. Come on? I thought we were trying to get a gritty gangster vibe across here? It just doesn't fit with the whole YA thing. 
 Regardless of those complaints, the book was very entertaining, the plot unpredictable and the writing as good as always in Bardugo's work, and the book therefore earns a well-deserved four star rating from me.

One thing about EH's books is that there is always a bit of fairy-tale or snippet that is related to each chapter. Like an opening act to a concert. 
 So for this book the opening act would be the title of the book - The Raven Prince. I guess it draws parallel to the main story as both involve a hero that is not quite perfect or "normal" and the one thing that saves them is the heroines true love. 
 Here we have a hero that does not fit the conventional Historical Romance of being handsome, dashing with beautiful eyes, etc etc. The hero, Earl of Swartingham (ok...even the title does not roll off the tongue well) is someone who is not handsome and scarred by pox (i googled some images of pock-marked faces) therefore considered "ugly". This makes him self-conscious about his looks and he has a mean temper to boot. Sounds very anti-hero. But he writes about agriculture and he gets his hands dirty working side by side with his tenants (intelligent and a man of action?). The heroine, Anna, is a woman who has just come into her own. She has been living by the rules all her life, is kind and virtuous, but was unfortunately cheated on by her husband (boo!) who died of some ailment (yes!). 
 The story is quite fast-paced albeit a bit choppy (wondering if this is Ms Hoyt's first novel). I've read the Maiden Lane series and those had a smoother style of story-telling. Nonetheless, the story is unconventional (scarred hero + good girl gone bad heroine), it has colourful supporting characters that i'm sure would appear in the next installation and the HEA is worth it. So I'd recommend it.

This was my first Kristen Ashley book. This may upset some people to say, since I know that she has a big fanbase, but I don't think that KA is that good of a writer. Some of her sentences in this book were worded in such way that it made my brain hurt. I often had to re-read sentences to try to figure out what she was even trying to convey. I also found a lot of typos, and personally, I hate when an author has to consistently use curses to convey strong emotions. But, while KA may not be a strong 
 writer 
 , she is definitely a strong 
 story teller 
 , which makes up for a lot of weaknesses in the prose itself. 
 Wildest Dreams is a fantasy/adventuremance, centering around Seoafin "Finnie" Wilde (from our world), and Frey Drakkar (from a parallel world with fantasy elements). Finnie trades places with Princess Sjofn, her "twin" (so to speak, even though there's no actual relation) from the parallel world. What Sjofn didn't tell Finnie before the switch, however, was that she was slated to wed The Drakkar, who is a pretty intimidating dude. Once the switch takes place, that becomes Finnie's fate. But, once The Drakker (Frey) figures out that Finnie isn't Sjofn (whom he really dislikes), he warms up to her pretty quickly, and adventuremance ensues. 
 While I really enjoyed the story, I had a few issues with this set up. For one, I find Frey's reason for hating Sjofn so intensely (prior to finding out about the switch) a bit unfair. While I understand the situation (basically being that Sjofn is a lesbian ) would cause a lot of frustration and maybe even a bit of anger, the outright hatred he seems to have toward her (or Finnie, thinking that Finnie is Sjofn) seems unfair and unwarranted. If anything, I think a bit of sympathy might be warranted toward Sjofn, and I really hated that Frey was such a dick about it. It was kind of hard for me to reconcile the jerk that he was in the beginning versus the amazingly sweet guy he was with Finnie throughout the book, making his behavior the beginning seem more like a plot ploy than anything else. 
 As for Finnie, I really enjoyed her. It did get a little grating how everyone just couldn't help but love her (ugh), except of course for the most evil characters, and that this was often shoved down our throats. But, for the most part, she was a fun protagonist that's worth rooting for. 
 While the strength of the story and world-building made this book good, the writing and pacing kept it from being great. Some parts of the book made me impatient to find out what happened next in Finnie's adventures, while some parts seemed to just drag. Furthermore, there were constant time jumps in the book (two weeks later... one day later... one month later... etc.) that I found really jolting and distracting. 
 As for the romance, it was mostly sweet and enjoyable, with a lot of hot smut as well... but overall, there was nothing all too memorable about it. Frey just seemed to fall in love with Finnie so quickly, and I think it would have been more believable if he took a bit more time trying to discover and understand his feelings. 
 I think my overall takeaway from this book is that Kristen Ashley is the kind of writer who will deliver a book with a great and engaging story, a sweet romance, and fun adventures. I'm not sure if she can deliver a book with quality writing and layers of depth, though. With that said, sometimes you are just in the mood for these light, fluff reads (as I am now), so I definitely am going to go and check out more of KA's works, even as I finish writing this!

I had this at 5 stars after reading the sample. I'd like to give it 4.5, but can't. So 4 it is, simply because there are a few things that kept me from a 5. 
 From the first page, I was hooked. It's a page turner for sure, and the chapters in the beginning with Cassie wandering about alone and flashing back to the other waves, were vivid and emotional. I was engrossed in the story, and picturing myself in her shoes, watching the planes fall from the sky. Imagining loved ones bleeding to death. Wondering how, if I'd lived through that, I would make it or if I would even want to live. Her story was grim, and I was left with this impression of a badass chick who has managed to survive, even though there were times that she would have probably rather died. 
 Cassie is badass. And I love Zombie, even though he's not so badass. He's got likeable traits though. 
 Cue Evan Walker. I'm not so sure what to think of him. Well, not him so much as what he does to Cassie. Suddenly badass Cassie turns into googly-eyed teenage girl. Granted, if I were in a "safe" place with a gorgeous guy with who knows how much time to live, I'd probably sneak in a little bit of smoochy time too. But the effect on the story is a little jarring to me. Her shift in character throws off the momentum, and I didn't like it. For some of the middle of the book, I'm left asking, "where is Cassie the badass?" I was longing to read more of Zombie's chapters so Cassie would have time to snap out of it and get back into the unstoppable girl on a mission to save her brother. It was alluded to in her chapters in the middle, but in between kisses. 
 That was the thing that kept me from giving 5. Even though Evan's story, and her story, and their connection all made sense in regards to the plot, I couldn't help but feel emotionally detached a little bit. He was too clingy too fast, she became too soft at the wrong times. I've rewritten this review several times, simply because I cannot put it into words quite right. Something just didn't feel right during the middle, in their time together. And I'm not sure what it was, but their dialogue in discussing him being a Silencer was... well... just off. The way Evan and Cassie interacted, the way they spoke, and their weird little cross-brain communication was just... awkward. Parts of their "love" I would have a hard time believing, and other times it felt right. Again, hard to put into words. These strange moments in YA fiction are the ones that have me desperately seeking more "adult" novels.  It wasn't until she finally took off to the base when I felt like I had my badass Cassie back. 
 And when badass Cassie came back, I got my badass story back. I really enjoyed the first 1/3 of the book, and the last 1/3, but the middle sagged ever so slightly in a book that I had waited and waited for. I liked the last bit. I really liked it. Except one thing. 
 Why does YA feel compelled to throw in a love triangle???? Seriously, the last few paragraphs had me pissed. The only love connection between Ben and Cassie exists in her head. Her crush on him. There was no mention of him liking her, and that kiss at the end made me cringe. Why? Why? Not necessary. They can have a friendship, and Cassie can even have a crush still, but as far as I know, Ben's got the hots for Ringer, and there is no foundation for a kiss at the end. I want Evan back.  
 I will definitely read the next one. If you want a sci-fi twist on YA, this is a well-written and refreshing story in a sea of cookie cutter novels. For the most part, it feels more grown up than others, with more depth and critical thinking opportunities than some of its fellow YA books.

I almost gave up on this. I couldn't get a grip. A GR friend had said there was a great section at the end. I flipped there and discovered where SATIN in the title comes from, and noticed that in The Acknowledgements McCarthy talks about spending his grant time watching video loops of oil spills projected on his office walls. That was my entry point. I started again. 
 This profoundly disturbing novel is written in chapters that resemble memos to oneself while the main character, U, engages in a corporate job that requires much flight-time and international conferences. "Call me U" is an anthropologist, an in-house ethnographer for a consultancy. "The Company (let's continue to call it that) advised other companies how to contextualize and nuance their services and products. It advised cities how to brand and re-brand themselves; regions how to elaborate and frame regenerative strategies, governments how to narrate their policy agendas...What we essentially do is fiction."It can hardly be said U was happy in his work. U would dream at night, like many of us, but his sexual dreams might have pieces of his work or things he'd read in the news incorporated. If he read about an oil spill, for instance, his dreams would have some kind of female figure, sexy, arising out of the sea covered in oil blobs: "a sluttish Aphrodite frolicking in the blackened foam, her face adorned with the look that readers' wives and models have in dirty magazines." At least two things were happening to U while he was preparing a report for the corporation he worked for. One was that he'd read about a parachutist whose strings to his parachute were cut before he took a dive, and the other was that a business associate of his was dying of thyroid cancer. Both men "were dead before they hit the ground," as it were. The crime scene was "in the sky", in the very air we breathe. 
 This is a novel about our death, but before the "fall" as it were. The parachutist "had been murdered without realizing it." The man with thyroid cancer is already dead while he continues to relate the doctor's findings every day. The people on this planet are dead while we continue to document to infinitude the activities of humans past and present, including the oil spills and the waste dumps, one of which is Satin Island, formerly Staten Island, now covered over with golf courses and walkways and greeting visitors to the United States in the same general vicinity as the Statue of Liberty. You (that is, U) don't have "to go to Staten Island--actually go there--[that] would be profoundly meaningless....Not to go there was, of course, profoundly meaningless as well...the explosion's already taking place--it's always been taking place. You just didn't notice..."U has a sense, while he does his work as an anthropologist, of having come "too late." He knows there is more to the patterns he sees in the oil spills and the sudden deaths but he can't make them out until a coworker tells him of her experience as a demonstrator, a protester, against the G8 Summit in 2001. 
 The novel is disturbing because I also think there may be no way back to health on the planet, but I would never just give up. When some of our best scientists are thinking one way to save the human race is by sending representatives to colonize Mars, life as we know may be...let's say, limited.  
 Only after finishing the novel did I know what that earlier reviewer I linked to in the top of this review meant. When you get there, you will see it, too.

 I read these books almost six years ago, not long after Mockingjay was released, and I kind of forgot about them. I mean, I knew they were on my shelf. I remembered devouring them with the single-minded awe that I think all of us book lovers have known at least once in our lives. I remembered admiring Katniss and falling a little in love with Peeta and not wanting the series to end. But I also remembered how the movies ruined it for me. After the movies, I never really looked at them the same, but this summer, I got ahold of a matching set of the books. Yesterday, I was looking through my endless piles of books, hoping to find something that would make me feel... something. You can never really rely on a book that you've never read to give you that. I thought maybe I could recapture some of that childish wonder that I had at thirteen, even just a snag of that desperation that makes you forget you're reading a book. After all, I've changed a lot in six years. 
 Apparently, I haven't changed enough to forget the gripping magic of The Hunger Games trilogy and all of it's twisted, gruesome turns. It is truly a story about war and the depravity of humanity. Plenty of people have their complaints about Mockingjay in particular--all entirely valid complaints--but I disagree with most of them. The senseless deaths, the layers of conspiracy and distrust, the non-fatal casualties (such as Katniss and Gale's lost friendship and Peeta as he was in the first two books), the unanswered questions, these are all things that force us to experience the worst of us. The last book, to me, was the most realistic of them all. 
 It left me raw and crying, aching for the people who died and, more so, the people who didn't. These characters are the kind so real that you can't help but fall in love with them. They don't leap off the page, but rather, you fall into the book and land next to them. You have to watch them grow up too fast and cling to the last dregs of their youth in the form of defiance and naivety surrounding love. When Rue dies, you cry because she could be your little sister or your daughter or your cousin, and when Finnick dies, you weep because you could be his lover in Thirteen, waiting for him to come back to you. I'm so thankful that Collins chose to explore so many of the characters' stories because her loyalty to showing their depth is what makes them real. 
 I know I'm ages behind the rest of you, only posting my review now, but these books left me with as much feeling tonight as they did six years ago. Not sitting down and pouring out at least some of them would have driven me a little bit insane. I could talk about these books for ages and not touch on everything I could say--the theme of personal tragedy and my appreciation for the fact that there was a well-portrayed demiromantic main character among others. 
 I've also realized that I'm apparently incapable of writing actual book reviews and I usually stray towards something along the lines of discussing my experience reading the book as opposed to actually praising the merits and pointing out the flaws, so sorry about that.

This one has been driving me nuts, and I'm fairly certain that today I hit a turning point and am giving up. 
 First, I don't like the characters - Liv and Cam are ... well, they're okay, for the most part, but they're ... boring. And naive, yet there are lines about them being "six years older but a century wiser and more jaded." These characters are anything but jaded, in my opinion. I think I take a more cynical look at my job, and I'm only twenty-two. Sure, their world is dark and gritty and they have every reason to be full of angst, but these characters sound like teenagers who have had an admittedly difficult past (I guess? I can't say that I really know all that much about their histories...) but are just now beginning to pass on their own in the real world, ie: I feel like I've had as much real-world experience as them at times, and I only just graduated college. Maybe that's my own perspective bleeding through, or maybe they just don't feel real enough to me for me to understand them as they are supposed to be. Either way, it was a big turn-off for me, though not enough to get this to the DNF shelf all on its own. 
 Second, I'm really not a fan of alternating first-person. Generally, if you want to alternate POV, use third-person, either limited or omniscient and I'll be happy. I've only known the occassional author to successfully pull off alternating first-person POV, and they're on my favorites lists for more reasons than just that. Vincent is not one of them. (Maybe this is another reason I don't like her characters ...) 
 And the secrets drove me nuts. I love a good mystery - really, I do. There's nothing I like more than a book that keeps me guessing. It's one of the best ways to drive suspense and interest. But the secrets in this one weren't even good ones. They surprised me, and not in the way that they should. I was surprised at how lame they were at their revelation. And I don't know, maybe they develop more much further than they seem to have been, but somehow I just don't think so. 
 Oh, and this one touched on a big pet peeve of mine: don't make reference to intimate details about "most people" if they don't seem to be accurate. There are two passages about trying to figure out this guy's password. TWO! The first one has Cam comment that he couldn't get into this guy's account because there wasn't an obvious file with passwords in it. Then, later, Liv is apparently clever for thinking about how the passwords are saved in a notepad file on his phone. Initially, I figured it was a simple excuse to make it difficult for the main characters to learn their desired information. Then, when they didn't mention the password-protected accounts to the professional hacker, I figured it wasn't really important. Then we spent an awfully long time learning about notepad files on cell phones and how most people nowadays apparently keep a document of passwords on their phones. Frankly, if you're going to suddenly have an easy time finding that information, I'd sooner believe that the guy was stupid enough to save his passwords into his browser, which is what most of the folks my age tend to do in lieu of documenting their passwords - especially if it's on their personal computer. 
 Maybe it's a tiny detail and I'm nitpicking, but there are other silly little things that have been driving me nuts. That was just the most memorable one. 
 All of which I could live with. 
 But she's so torn about loving this guy and wanting to protect him - we don't find out until halfway through the book why she needs to protect him - and then she won't let him come near her until she makes sure that he understands the consequences of them being together. She even thinks about the fact that she'd blood bound to "the enemy" when she's fending him off and explaining things, but she doesn't say anything about it then. 
 Then they start to have sex and he sees her mark, that she conveniently didn't mention until she was naked. Seriously? You know things are going to get steamy, you think about the fact that you haven't told him your biggest secret, you know that he'll find out as soon as he sees the mark on your upper thigh, and you don't say anything before you two strip down? 
 ... And that's about where I gave up. 
 Maybe I'll give this another go at another time, but I've had a bad week. I need comfort books, not ones I'm nit-picking. 
 That said, I've heard very good things about Rachel Vincent's work, and I've also read a few other reviews implying that this is not one of her best. Maybe I'll hunt down another one of hers and circle back to this one after I've gotten to know her style a bit better. After all, the plot of this one really does have potential, which is why I'm giving it 2 stars even though I'm not willing to finish it right now. The overarching plot is a good one, and the world is fairly intriguing. So far it needs a stronger, or at least more present, antagonist, but I have high hopes that the potential villains will develop more later in the book. It's the sub-plots that have been getting to me.

 [Marco narrating:] "Rachel isn't here to cast her vote. So, on her behalf, I'll say what she would say: What we need to do is find a way to kick this Veleek's butt." 
 Cassie smiled. "And what would the real Marco say to that?"

 [Marco narrating:]I had a tiger in the back of a pickup truck I could barely drive, and I was being chased by the most powerful monster I had ever seen.

 /How do you know it wears out?/ [Rachel asked.] 
 "We don't." 
 /This isn't much of a plan,> I said. /Are you Animorphs always this hopeless?/

 6. Tricks the Dark Fae- she will make for a good book, and I think she is in fact in the next book.

I am a bit worried that all the books will be like this. Karen Rose's crime romances always do this and it has always made the book a bit harder for me to take seriously.

Last year I read Cracked Up To Be, Courtney's debut novel and I was blown away. It was an amazing novel and no words could describe just how much the book touched me so I was looking forward to reading her 2010 release Some Girls Are. 
 The thing about Some Girls Are is that Regina is evil and there's a part of me that hates her for what she did to other people. But on the other hand, just because she was a bully doesn't mean it's carte blanche for her to be bullied and have what Donnie did happen to her. Two wrongs don't make a right and all that. 
 Some Girls Are is entirely about bullying, showing the effects of what it is to bully, what it means to be bullied yourself and it shows just how much bullying effects people, mentally and physically. The things that happen in the novel make me sick to my stomach, especially that final scene just before the end of the book. Any person who has been bullied in their lives will resonate with this book and the debate will rage long and hard about whether or not Regina got her just desserts. Personally, I don't think Regina's bullying was 'worthy', I just thought it was wrong. Regina wasn't perfect, and although it took her until she herself was bullied to see the error of her ways, she did see them. Big time. And for me, that said a lot. 
 I loved the book and managed to finish it in about three hours. There was a part of me that didn't want to carry on reading, because as a person who was bullied herself, it was hard to read about what Anna and Kara did to Regina, and what Regina herself had done to others. It was a very raw novel, and it portrayed bullying at its very worse. I loved Michael, who Regina befriends once she's frozen out by her clique. I applaud Courtney Summers for tackling the subject, she did it with aplomb and it gives the very clear message that it doesn't matter who you are, bullying is not acceptable at all. This book should be read by all, it's brutal and it's honest and although it was hard to read at times, I'm glad I did read it.

This is the tale of Medusa. But it's not the one you're use too. No, this is a spin on Medusa's story that has heart and makes you feel for this poor ol Medusa and the struggle she went through. I will say I wasn't too familiar with her story, so as I started to read this I took a minute to read the original story. To say I was pleasantly surprised with this book would be an understatement, I was ecstatic with this retelling. 
 "It out to be noted I have some of the most wretched luck ever to be doled out." 
 Now, I'm not one to recap the story in my reviews, I feel like it takes away from reading the book so instead I'm going tell you all the wonderful things I loved about it. The first is Medusa herself. This is her story. Yes, there is a romance in it (swoon) but it's more than that. This is a story of redemption and finding you're way back to the living after being shunned for ages. Medusa has a lot to prove but underneath her worries and her fear, she is very strong. Yes, it's scary for her to try all these new things, to open herself up for these emotions she has had to keep hidden, but she does it. She takes the steps necessary to live a life worth living. And I loved watching her on this journey, finding the strength within herself. 
 "When I look up at him, all I can think is, he won't let me fall." 
 She has help along the way. Oh heeeyy there Hermes. Hermes was a character that surprised me. He was soft and kind and loving to Medusa. I was expecting that. And I guess since they have known each other for so long, their emotions made sense, how they were already kind of there. What did surprised me was how...alpha male he could get. That, I was not expecting. I mean, he is a God, I guess it makes sense. And I know he was doing it to protect Medusa. Because he does protect her, he does everything within his power for Medusa. 
 The other part that was real plus in this story is the talent of Heather Lyons to weave the mythology in this book so effortlessly. There is a lot to keep track of and she does so magically! I loved all the Gods and loved how they were portrayed. 
 "For the first time in two thousand plus years, time stands still. I pray it stays that way, because this moment here? Divine." 
 The ending. Again it was a way I was not suspecting the story to go but I did enjoy it! I was so proud of Medusa and all of the things she did. She truly become a strong independent female. And one of the last scenes, where everything is coming undone, secrets revealed, it was great. I couldn't put the book down until I found out everything!! 
 "Love makes every misery, every struggle, every moment of life worth it." 
 Medusa's journey in Heather Lyon's book is a tale of love, strength, family, and overcoming the cards that have been dealt to you. I loved this book. I was different and keep you on your toes and had total swoon worthy moments where you just melt into a puddle of awwww. This is a book to pick up!

I'm only just noticing that "Ysabel" has the lowest average Goodreads rating among Kay's books. My theory on why this might be? It tries too darned hard NOT to be a Kay book. 
 I have swooned over the Fionavar Tapestry, admired "Tigana", and enjoyed "A Song for Arbonne". If there's a standard criticism of Kay's works, it's that he has a tendency to overdo the epic mythical-ness of everything. I can agree with that assessment, but to me it's a mark in his favor. I adore the Fionavar Tapestry specifically *because* it sweeps me into the midst of a Epically Epic tale, full of deliberately archetypal characters and situations stolen from at least a half-dozen other writers and mythic traditions. 
 I do not, on the other hand, read Kay to think about Eminem. Therein lies the central failure of "Ysabel." The main character, Ned, is your basic North American teen, who is swept up in a millenia-old tale. This is a promising dust-jacket premise. Unfortunately, Kay doesn't seem to trust in his own characterization of Ned, and instead relies on CONSTANT reminders that Ned is a 21st-century teen. He likes Coldplay! And Led Zepplin! And chicks who wear Doc Martens and make jokes about blowjobs! He uses "google" as a verb! 
 Even worse, the plot doesn't even kick into gear until nearly halfway through the book. Until then, we have mostly read about how modern Ned is and endured pages and pages of banter between the various modern-day characters, which I *think* is intended to underline how modern they are, too. Once the plot does get going, it's entirely too clear how much more comfortable Kay is with his fantastic and historic details, rather than his clunky attempts at "witty" present-day dialog. 
 That said, I'm giving "Ysabel" 3 stars, because it did have a satisfying ending, and I did become rather fond of the characters -- even Ned, with his stupid iPod.

"My father took one hundred and thirty-two minutes to die. 
 I counted. 
 It happened on the Jellicoe Road. The prettiest road I'd ever seen, where trees made breezy canopies like a tunnel to Shangri-La. We were going to the ocean, hundreds of miles away, because I wanted to see the ocean and my father said that it was about time the four of us made that journey. I remember asking, 'What's the difference between a trip and a journey?' and my father said, 'Narnie, my love, when we get there, you'll understand,' and that was the last thing he ever said." 
 Aaah, this book really made me fall in love with Marchetta's writing. It was so touching and poetic in a non-overwhelming way. I really hate the 'look at me, I'm so deep and philosophical' type of writing and I was so glad I didn't find it here. No, in this book, the writing was, at times, subtle, at times poignant, in such a natural, realistic way. 
 This is definitely a character-driven book. It's not about the action, it's about experiences, it's about growing up, friendship, getting over life. Though a little confusing in the beginning, as one is not sure whose voice one is reading, everything falls into place later on and I was kept glued on to the pages. 
 I'm not really sure why this one is marked as YA and romance; it's really more literary fiction than anything else. The romance sub-plot is really secondary and always runs in the background of the characters' journey. 
 The only flaw I can find is the silliness of the so-called 'territory wars'. It really didn't make sense in the beginning, but later in the book, it becomes clearer that  they are just a game . 
 Overall, I really loved this book. Perhaps it's not perfect, but I give it 5 stars just because it came across as so honest and sincere. Taylor's musings really reminded me of some of my existential issues at around the same age. Would definitely re-read this.

 Title: Shadows: The Ashes Trilogy 
 Author: Ilsa J. Bick 
 Rating: 3 Stars 
 Amazon Summary: The Apocalypse does not end. The Changed will grow in numbers. The Spared may not survive. 
 Even before the EMPs brought down the world, Alex was on the run from the demons of her past and the monster living in her head. After the world was gone, she believed Rule could be a sanctuary for her and those she'd come to love. 
 But she was wrong. 
 Now Alex is in the fight of her life against the adults, who would use her, the survivors, who don't trust her, and the Changed, who would eat her alive. 
 Welcome to Shadows, the second book in the haunting apocalyptic Ashes Trilogy: where no one is safe and humans may be the worst of the monsters. 
 My Review 
 Wow there is a LOT going on here. It had been a while so I had to go back and re-read most of Ashes to figure out what was going on. And that's because in this title Bick uses many more characters and POVs than in Ashes. In fact, the overall cast is pretty darned huge. It's definitely a bridge book. You get the sense that she has all these pieces, people, and places that she's weaving together...but they are mostly so disjointed that the story jumping can be a little challenging to follow. 
 Also, it gets hard to hold onto your love for the original main characters because you don't get to hear from them as much. I did like that there was still plenty of Alex. Without that, I'm not even sure if I would have been interested in the rest of the story. The first book gets you very invested in Alex's character and well-being and you wouldn't care for anyone else at all, I think, if you didn't get a lot of her perspective in this book. 
 Ungodly disgusting things happen in this book. Unspeakable, horrifying, nauseating things. It adds to the terror, but for me it pushes it so far into the *yuk* category that it was sometimes hard to take. Alex is always smelling something rotten, or fetid, or putrid. I swear, I've never seen the word *snot* used more in a single book in my life. I know Bick's purposefully pushing the envelope and for real zombie lovers, that will probably go over well. For me it was a little too much phlegm, pus, blood, blowback, etc. in general and not enough love or triumph or peace to balance it. When nothing but bad things happen with no in-between, I get a little fatigued. 
 When I was trying to characterize what I felt overall about this book the thing that came to mind was this: too many, "Dear God, No!"s. It's like the end of each POV has to have that DUHN-DUHN-DUHN moment to it. That sounds great because she does give you tension, but when you do that EVERY time you leave a character POV and there are (Alex, Chris, Lena, Peter, Jed, and I can't remember who else) THAT many characters, you end up with about 30 "Dear God, No!"s and you end up with the boy who cried wolf scenario... I ignore it. I don't believe it. I think, "Whatever. Everything is horrifying," and it all blends into one. 
 What I Did Like 
 Again, she used enough Alex for me to like it. I was always rooting for her. Also, I love Tom. Tom is completely impossible not to love. Her action scenes, though too many and too long for my taste, were well-written and gave you a proper sense of how bad-ass Alex is. I like the whole concept of the CHANGE and what may cause it or affect it. You know I love it whenever people try to get all science-y. I like the mysteries surrounding Rule. There is something much older and deeper than the EMP going on there and you really want to know what it is. I like the mysteries surrounding the cause of the EMP. Was it the military? Are they rounding up children? I also like the way she portrays all the different ways that people might react in this vastly different world of children and seniors. Since nearly everyone else is gone, you have to remember while you read that everyone in her story is either very young or very old. So militias form, but some are run by older people and some are run by younger people. Bounty hunters seek children and the Changed. There are looters and raiders who are unaffiliated with anything or anyone. And there's bastions like Oren and Rule. All of that world-building stuff that she's done, I really liked. 
 First of all, Bick is a very capable writer. In fact, her vocabulary sometimes had me reaching for my dictionary, and that is quite a feat! Also, I did read this pretty quickly because I was dying for certain things to happen, that unfortunately didn't...in this book. (No spoilers since this is a new title.) Still, I'm not giving it 2 stars or saying don't read it. It was entertaining enough and my interest in finishing Alex's unique story is strong enough that I would recommend this to those who liked the first. That's why I'm giving it 3 stars, and that's why I plan to read the final installment. And if you really like zombie grossness and unending, teeth-chomping action, this one is probably a 4 or 5 star book for you.

I received this book through NetGalley and Lake Union Publishing in exchange for an honest review. 
 Dropped at 45% percent- I can't push myself to read any further, it's keeping me from other books. 
 To be completely fair and honest- I'm from North Carolina. I'm writing this review in North Carolina, not too far from where the book is based in (an analog Matthews). I can't bring myself to keep reading because, to be honest, if I wanted to hear a bunch of dissatisfied North Carolinians complain about trivial but nigh-immediately fixable problems, I'd go to a community barbecue. This book is half marital problems and half unresolved childhood frustration, and none of it is the dark intrigue I was promised in the summary. 
 Onto an actual review of the contents: 
 There are far too many characters to keep track of, especially since none of them are distinctly memorable. I constantly got Bryte and Jencey mixed up because, save for one Getting The Guy and one not, their personalities are so interchangeable that I couldn't differentiate between them. I think I speak for everyone when I say that a reader shouldn't have to take notes when reading casually to figure out who is doing what at all times, but I found myself having to highlight minute details like "Everett's wife" or "Jencey's friend". None of them are inherently decent people, either- which, honestly, reflects North Carolinians, but I find it hard to believe that only the 1 child in the narrative is the only one with a conscious. We have grown ass adults saying "cheating isn't cheating unless my wife/husband finds out about it" and the narrative completely allows for it, with no punishment. The narrative just lets these very minor (but still terrible) plot points to pass with absolutely zero conflict- the only thing that pushes the story forward collectively is Cutter's status in the hospital... which hasn't changed at all at 45%. 
 This is one of the major pitfalls of this book- nothing of substance actually happens, but the writing tries to compensate and fails. Purple prose is stretched far too thin over descriptions of just about anything, and I'm just stuck here, tapping my foot and trying to get through another page. Someone cheating on their still-living spouse?  Barely a footnote, they're not caught. Someone taking in an unrelated child whose mother doesn't know them, and keeping her in their house ? No one even questions this. There's nothing to drive the conflict forward, and nothing to hold my interest as a reader. The story drags its heels with half-baked nonexistent conflicts that are supposed to be titillating, but just come off as distracting from the main plot. 
 Also, there are also no people of color which, hoo-boy, am I calling bullshit on. A North Carolinian town without a single black person? I don't know what town Marybeth is living in, but it's gotta be a fantasy one for there to be not a single latinx or black neighbor. 
 Long story short? I bet this is a real novelty for white people that don't live in North Carolina, but, to me, it just read like the author had caught too much gossip on people she cared about and thought she could spin a story out of it.

I don't even know what to sat about this book besides that it was great. Though there were parts to make me bring it down a point, so my rating is at 4.5 stars. 
 This book is a fun read, adventurous and quick for the subject matter and it being a dystopian book. I read it in all of four days which sounds kind of slow but it's really not. It's good and fast paced and many other positive adjectives.

Otherwise, it was good book and kept me intrigued until the end of the book, throwing deaths and plot twists right and left. The cover is beautiful, too!

This book is going to be difficult to review. I don't know why; it's fairly straightforward, bordering on simple, but I'm having a tough time picking through my initial/final feelings regarding The Lightkeepers. It's the story of Miranda, a nature photographer, who travels to the Farallon Islands, far off the coast of San Francisco, to photographically document life there for a year. The islands themselves are as remote and dangerous as any on earth, but year-round is home to a varying bunch of biologists: our six other characters. The story is told through Miranda's letters to her dead mother, which is a touching addition, but the main plot revolves around a nasty incident on the island, and the inevitable unraveling and life on the Farallons. 
 Here's the thing: I treated this novel like a string of one night stands. I'd pick it up, enjoy it for a brief while, and subsequently forget about it over the course of the past week and a half. It took me longer than most to finish, which is just as odd seeing as how it's not a very large book. So, I'll chalk it up to two things: 
 1. Heretofore mentioned in my 'About Me', I come into modes of habitual interests at varying times throughout the year, where all I want to do is read -for months straight, rarely ceasing. Without preamble, that will change overnight into binge-watching TV or movies (or in this instance, getting back into video games after a four year hiatus. Skyrim will ruin you!), and neglecting altogether the books I was previously so invested in. 
 However, after catching sight of my piles of 'to-be-read' books amassed (and amassing, still) on my bed, I put down the controller/turned off the computer, and flew into action. I was determined to finish this book (and, in turn, reinvigorate my reading frenzy). 
 2. The other reason it took me so long to read The Lightkeepers is because I wasn't fully invested in the story (at least, not at the start). When I first read the synopsis, I was giddy with anticipation of owning it. I love mysteries. More specifically, I love mysteries involving a group of people isolated and alone (a la Agatha Christie's And Then There Were None). Also, sharks, as much as I fear them, and nature/biology in general, fascinate me. So, I went straight from the last words of the synopsis, to ordering it on Amazon. Much to my dismay, though, it was not in stock. Whatever. I ordered it anyways. But my mind reeled. I couldn't wait for it to become available; the uncertainty of "when" a cruel temptress. Something overcame me, and I had an overwhelming urge to have the book then and there. I went to the book store at the earliest convenience, found it, cancelled my online order still floating in the Void of Unavailability, and hauled it home, wherein I read maybe 14 pages, and thusly fell asleep. The same thing happened the next time I attempted its reading; so and and so forth. 
 I still don't understand why I could only take a few pages of this novel at a time. The writing was well done, the story building and fact of it being a sort of epistolary novel neat, the science and nature and biology absorbing and en pointe... I will surely have to blame my cousins for reintroducing me to Skyrim's existence for my then-burgeoning lack of engrossment. But in the beginning, it was an effort (and I realize I could've easily come out and said that right off the bat, and saved anyone reading this review my delirious rambling. Ah, well! What's done is done.). 
 I digress. 
 Finally, I cracked the spine with purpose and continued where I left off, somewhere around page 100. From there, I didn't stop reading until the moment I turned the last page. Thankfully, the story started falling into what I read in the synopsis, and it was a smooth progression from then-on-out. 
 (I can see this review is certainly not in any sort of coherent order, but I am determined to get some form of a point across) 
 The 3 star reasoning... 
 Here are my complaints: 
 -At the 3/4 mark, I was guessing the final rating was to be 4 stars (not 5, solely because I wasn't pulled in from the get-go). I was enjoying the sort of subtle, toneless mystery at the time. Then, of course, another tragedy struck our remaining characters. I understood the repeated dangers of the Farallon Islands. Miranda, our dutiful narrator, and the band of biologists express this multiple times. But four tragedies (three major) was just one too many for the amount of time they spent there. To explain, Miranda had been on the Farallons for about a year, which is not such a long span, considering the others had spent 5-10 years on the islands. In all that time, there were mentions of injuries (serious and otherwise), but never so many in a single year. Especially multiple deaths. The first one I get. I understand why it had to happen, plot-wise, following the sexual assault. The incident w/ Charlene a supposed "accident," obviously, but the final death, however, was a cheap shot. A lazy attempt to garner sympathy before the novel's conclusion . I'll be vague here for those not privy to the spoiler, but introducing an (to me) unnecessary tragedy at the end was a total "cheap ploy" to elicit sympathy/emotion/tears/whateveritmaybe. I get how accidents can happen, the unpredictability of nature coupled with a dangerous terrain, but three all while Miranda is there? I don't think so. It was, again, in my opinion, unnecessary for that last "tragedy" to occur. 
 I was so ready to give this book 4 stars... and then that happened. Really, though, that's my main complaint. Otherwise, I found Miranda an intriguing case study. The other characters were quite fleshed-out, as well, but I truly found Miranda a creature of vast interest. Galen, too, should get his own story. 
 *My brain is mush. My cue to take a break from this review, and my tiny phone screen. Maybe I'll come back to this review again and tighten it up, and maybe I won't. Frankly, I'll ready to move on.*

I love this book! Let me just say that all the hype for this one was true for once. I had my doubts about Forget Me because it had a really good plot and the synopsis on here was really intriguing so I was a little wary of authors that start the book good and go in a whole other direction and turns out to be horrible, most of them turn into DNF, but Forget Me was definitely not like that, it was better. 
 I was glad for the suspense and the whole mystery of the things happening in this book because I was left wondering what was going on, which had me turning the pages and I literally could not put the book down. As I was reading, I had all these theories going through my head- did it have to do with clones? or spies, with some sort of conspiracy going around Stell pharmaceuticals? And I wasn't expecting what actually happened! No spoilers but it had lots of twists and turns that quite literally had me reeling to know what was going to happen next. I especially liked how everything that happened in the story, even with secondary characters and to the secrecy of Morgan's parents, all tied in together with how the mystery was finally explained. And let me tell you, the suspense is worth the wait. 
 The romance wasn't cheesy or overly done, it was written pretty well considering that the love interest Evan has an uncanny resemblance to Morgan's dead boyfriend. Evan and Morgan get to know each other while also trying to figure out the mystery of the things that are happening- that one letter Evan received warning him away from Morgan- but even the relationships between the secondary characters was well done. 
 All in all, there was action present throughout the book, especially near the end, and there was also romance, suspense/mystery, and humor in this book- I especially loved Morgan as a main character, she's independent, smart, not afraid to speak her mind and takes the initiative to do things, not backing down, even if it meant breaking into houses to figure out the truth and not to mention she has a good sense of humor. I definitely loved this book as one of my favorites.

From Colossus we advance through a whole host of short stories, novels, movies and even TV programs that have been a mainstay of science fiction. many seem to take one side or the other of the debate. From the view that artificial intelligence (AI) will come to the conclusion that "we" should be wiped out or alternately controlled to Isaac Asimov's "3 laws" and the idea that "robots"(AIs)can live in harmony with humans. This in the end  seems to take a sort of middle ground. That the AI can come to the conclusion that humans have reached their "end" and then other AI may come to an alternate conclusion . 
 As I said I like pretty well. The idea that a sufficiently advanced artificial intelligence might come to a "logical" conclusion that humanity was a threat never seemed too far fetched to me. I think it's probably the logical outcome of the way things are going. Will things shake out as in this book? 
 I'll just say it wouldn't surprise me. While we don't have the variety of "humanoid robots" pictured in the novel (yet) many of the advancements pictured here are already in place or on their way. Logic, logic may turn around and bite us all in the.....

The first paragraph sets the tone for GWYS; tongue-in-cheek humor tied in a rather ugly sports coat murder mystery. Perry fleeing his apartment and crashing into Nick sucked the reader into the story. Not only are we interested in finding out what happened to the dead body in the bathtub, but also we want to know just what's going to happen between Perry and Nick. 
 Perry Foster is an ordinary man, nice and unassuming. A man people can identify with or at least recognize someone we know and sympathize in his attempts to do better, be more, succeed. Most all of us have been where Perry is in his search for love and romance, and the failure therein. He is the underdog sort we alternately encourage from the sidelines and duck and hide in embarrassment for him. 
 Nick Reno is the kind of man we all dream of either having in our life or being. Strong, competent, confident, a no-nonsense sort of man, he exudes a sensuality with unsuspected sensitivity. He is the perfect counterpart to Perry, and the two together fill the other's holes. 
 The third character in this story has to be the house. In contemporary 30s mystery fashion, this overly large, rambling house provides the backdrop to mysterious happenings, voyeurs, dames in trouble, and hidden treasures. From attic to basement and beyond, the house is a picture puzzle, revealing a little at a time until it's all uncovered. 
 This story strongly reminded me of a Raymond Chandler mystery - but with a good dose of humor. It has all the elements of a good mystery, a good murder/romance mystery - a romance that's alive and full-bodied, if seemingly doomed from the start, a mystery that has several twists and red herrings during its investigation, a cast of the usual, unusual suspects, and a dead body that disappears and winds up in unexpected places. 
 I greatly enjoyed reading this book and have recommended it to not only my like-minded friends, but also to those who love a good mystery with humor.

Solid thriller with a satisfying ending. Gripping enough that I tore through it in a matter of days. I appreciated that I was engaged enough that I didn't guess the mystery until it the story's third act, and that when the truth was revealed it was satisfying for both plot and character reasons. 
  I would have liked a little more resolution with the secondary characters in the denouement, especially Riley, the woman detective. I expected her to come to an understanding with Rachel, or to see and understand, but we weren't given that. That would have been too victorious for her, I suppose. Similarly Rachel's relationships with Anna and Scott were never resolved. Another gripe. I don't understand why she and Anna had to create a story that Tom came at her with a corkscrew. Tom's a big guy, and given he attacked her with a bottle I think she could be forgiven for responding with a weapon. At that point I think the truth would have been enough to claim self defense, as it certainly was. But then again I'm not sure if Tom was posthumously convicted of Megan's murder. Presumably that was part of what Anna and Rachel told police, otherwise Scott would still be under suspicion for Megan's murder. But they don't tell us if the police ever recover the damning cell phone, or check Tom's DNA against Megan's unborn child. Sure, you want to wrap things up quickly at the end of a book like this, and it's part of the book's aesthetic to leave loose ends. But I would have appreciated a little more detail on the technicalities of the resolution.  
 Overall I very much enjoyed the read, and found the plot more satisfying than Gone Girl (which, full disclosure, I have only seen not read). Definitely check it out.
