Stolen Songbird is an overall solid book. It has many positive and original traits, first of all its theme and its setting. It also has some flaws, but these are easily excusable given this is a debut. 
 Trolls are not very featured in fantasy books, and here they are re-invented in a convincing way. They are not ugly or stupid; they are flawed but sympathetic figures. From the gentle and brokenhearted Marc to the amusing twins Vincent and Victoria, I found the trolls to be all quite charming. I also liked Anais, a strong, badass female character - there is really no hope that she survived?  
 The setting is equally original. Trollus, the city under the mountain, is fascinating. It has a claustrophobic feeling to it, and yet there are many peculiar and magical things in it. The labyrinth with the terrible slaugs adds an even more menacing touch to the setting. 
 I liked the main characters, Celine and Tristan, even if they are not perfect and sometimes annoyed me. Celine is pretty great in the first half of the book: she is brave, intelligent and optimistic. She finds herself in a terrifying situation but struggles to make the best of it. After a while, she also wants to learn more about the trolls and their culture, and starts to genuinely care for them. Unfortunately, after she starts to realize her feelings for Tristan, she becomes reckless and even foolish. For example, when she gets jealous she runs away into the labyrinth where the slaugs are. Seriously?!  
 I felt the same way about Tristan. He is great in the beginning: he is terribly arrogant and rude, but also irresistibly witty and sarcastic. I liked him as soon as he started talking, because even if he was so unlikeable you could also see his inner goodness. However, he too starts to act foolishly as the book goes on. I also did not like his perpetual mistrust of Celine. I could see his point, but could he not feel that her feelings were authentic just like his own? And his many talks about what was best for her, without actually listening what she wanted for herself, reminded me of Edward Cullen. 
 As for the romance, you must surely be thinking that I did not appreciate it, given that I started to like Celine and Tristan less after they fell in love. But that's not true! I actually liked their slow building relationship. Well, it was not perfect: their chemistry and affinity was clear from the start, but then their feelings were a little rushed, given that they spent not much time together - and most of it fighting. But they were cute enough. 
 I also liked their bond. I don't think I've ever read about something like this, so it was very interesting. I just found it a little unbelievable that Celine and Tristan had such problems understanding each other when they could feel each other's emotions, but it was still a fascinating concept. 
 The major flaw that weakens the book, in my opinion, is its lenght. The plot is quite involving: there is plenty of politics and intrigue, as well as the romance parts. But there are several parts which felt pointless and quite boring. I also think the two narrators were unnecessary. Most of the story is told from Celine's point of view, while fewer chapters are told by Tristan. I don't think these added much to the story: they just gave some insight of his feelings, but these were quite clear from Celine's point of view already. Those parts would have been better as a short story. 
 In the end, Stolen Songbird is surely not perfect, but it is a promising debut and an enjoyable read. I will check the sequel out.

 Initially, I'm very iffy when it comes to books with multiple POVs. But for this story's case it suited. TIWIE is a novel that gripped me at every page, portraying an all too realistic scenario, one that no one can ever imagine occurring happening in their lifetime, but has already occurred 15 in the US alone this year (source: wikipedia). 
 In the span of 54 minutes, every student and teacher present in the auditorium of Opportunity High School, Alabama, is fighting for their lives against one boy, one of their own. What has frightening about this story is that it can happen everywhere. But there's a difference between hearing about that and being thrown into such situation. 
 This book follows a few different characters during the hour that the shooting takes place. Each character is so completely different and so important in their own ways. I think a main aspect which I really enjoyed was the diversity of the characters. There's a scene where Tomas is worried for Fareed and how, his faith and heritage, may portray him as a threat to the police officers was a touching moment for me because of how real it was. I really hope more authors begins to write about marginalised character because, honestly, I'm all for seeing more Muslim characters in novels. 
 However, I do believe the psychology behind the perpetrator's act was a bit foolish. It boils to the simple "He was evil," and that's it. We never really find out why Tyler did it-- he goes from being a supportive brother to someone who beats and abuses his sister. It's too simplistic, and I think that was a fatal flaw in this novel, along with missing out a chance of looking at the psychology of teen shooters and focusing more on the cheap thrills. I didn't like how dramatic the ending it, I wanted it to be real. 
 Overall, it was an interesting read. Though some scenes felt strange, but I don't want to judge because who on earth would know what they'd do in this situation when they don't know what else is going to happen?

This is one of those books that you "should read" because it will teach you something about history, and that is particularly the line on this book in Minnesota where I live, as it was where a big chunk of the story takes place. It's historical fiction, as the orphan trains did actually bring orphans from the East coast to the Midwest during this timeframe. Overall I liked the book, learned something, and it was enjoyable. However, it did suffer a little bit from an Oprah-esque tendency to put our poor protagonists through more misery than seemed realistic, fair, or even reasonable in fiction. This is the same main fault I found in The Light Between the Oceans and other books that I generally like, but think the author twists the knife with a little too much glee sometimes. 
 I liked the setting in Maine, and also Vivien's journey story. They were both well drawn, beautiful and tragic, and very believable. I really liked the parallel stories of Vivien and Molly. Their shared love of books, the people in their lives whom they hold dear, and their relationship with each other. I liked the story arc overall as well. This is not a complicated or burdensome read, and that is ok, as I think it would be good for young adult readers (if you could get them to pick it up). 
 Now here's my frustration, but it's spoilery, so I'll tag that part. Like so many other books, the author seems to pile on unnecessary layers of cruel near misses and bad luck, even on characters who have already suffered plenty. Examples Vivien has already lost her family, been treated horribly by the first two foster placements, and then finds Dutchy, only to lose him very soon after finding him again in WWII. Ok, I could accept that, but then we find out that her awful New York neighbors stole her baby sister, didn't bother to tell Vivien that she was alive, and she lived for DECADES not having the chance to know her, only for Molly to track her down a couple years after she died old. Seriously. After these two, I thought for sure the author was a complete sadist who would then allow Molly to track down the baby that Vivien had gave up for adoption 70 years ago only to have the daughter be murdered at the train station on her way to meet Vivien. Ok, so I'm glad that didn't happen, but seriously, it was unnecessarily cruel piling on the loss of Dutchy and the sister forever (and doesn't reach out to this sister's many children and grandchildren, etc.). I tried to forgive this book its many faults. I can be a nit-picky reader at times. When Annie describes watching Detroit fade away as she flies out of DTW and I thought, "I've flown in and out of that airport dozens of times heading to or coming from the west and have never seen the city from the airplane," I try to forget that. And when Annie is surprised to read "The Yellow Wallpaper" in the feminist literature section of her lit survey as though it is not the starter short story for reading feminist literature, I tried to forget that too. And again when the story really heavy-hands it with the yellow wallpaper parallel. But... 
 The Ruining had a shaky start, but it did have an interesting middle. By chapter thirteen, I had figured out what turned out to be the big reveal, but was still interested in Libby, the mom that Annie nannies for. She obviously is trying to control Annie, but to what end? If she is making her go crazy, how exactly is that? I thought she must be drugging her in someway. After Annie is poisoned by the nutmeg in the banana bread, I think the story goes off the deep end (PUN INTENDED). Annie has moments of lucidity as she spirals toward the crazy house, but none of it makes sense or is even emotionally believable. We are told that she works long hours, has to skip class, doesn't get enough sleep, but also that Libby is great and is the only person who cares about Annie. None of this is actually shown in the story's action. And how is Libby controlling Annie's phone? That part is never explained. 
 I also found the love interest compelling through the first half of the book, but after that he seems to exist for a kind deus ex machina. He will save you Annie! He doesn't have to move after all! He's rich and you can live with him! He loves you! He will talk to the shrink and the shrink will suddenly become not-a-villain! And he can computer hack away all your plot problems! 
 "'You're forgetting that I'm an expert when it comes to computers,' Owen said. 'I can hack into almost any system.'"

Oh man, how did this happen? 
 When i heard Infini would be about Luka, many can agree i was over the moon. I had fallen in love with him in Amour Amour and wasn't expecting the twins to tell his story before Timo's. I was so excited and thankful since i'm a defensor of the seemingly quiet and kind ones, but then some things started to go wrong for me. 
 Firstly, i feel like the synopsis didn't correctly set what the book is really about. It takes two aspects -the friendship to lovers aspect and the list that had us all so intrigued- that honestly didn't feel as important as others. Maybe a blurb about saving Infini, maybe something about working together but not being able to interact outside work or maybe the struggle of sharing a secret and the pain of hiding it from their loved ones. Honestly, there are many better options than the ones chosen, or even so, better ways to introduce them. 
 This left me with a rather small idea of what to expect from this book, so it's no surprise that all the sudden angst hit me in the face. It was so different from Amour Amour -which is not necessarily a bad thing, but unexpected and not my cup of tea-. 
 I was a little unsettled by Luka's narrative, and at the same time that i got used to it, i also got unattached to his character. I had a really hard time understanding him and Baylee, and an even harder time sympathizing for their relationship. What i love about Krista and Becca's books is that usually they make me believe that the characters are in love, but just saying it over and over again is not what makes it so real... -am i making any sense?-. What was missing were more scenes of backstory, not just mentions of the past. All i got from their friendship are some of their thoughts like "he was there when i was sad", "oh god he remembers this thing is my fave", "we would spend so much time together", and so on and so on -over simplified for the sake of spoilers-. Maybe some throwbacks of how they forged said friendship would have made it much more solid. 
 Likewise, being the first book with a Kotova narrating, we could have gotten a much better understanding of their past, we could have explored so much more about this family that let's be honest, we all love so much. But what we got were chapters of mixed emotions because of the many, oh so MANY, unfortunate events. (what happened to Thora and Nik... arguably used just as a plot devise and i'm so against it.  
 The reason they were set apart was... eh, then came the infamous list that honestly... okay, all i have to say about the list is: ???????okay????i guess?????. It didn't make too much sense to me. NOT what it said, that makes all the sense, but the situation and what it lead to. Just... okay. 
 I didn't see the circus' magic through Luka and Baylee's eyes, and i still am not sure if they got any character development. At the end of the book -which also felt like 50 pages of solving a list of things that had to be solved, but weren't developed throughout the book because they were so busy dealing with things that didn't make too much sense anyway-, what changes is their situation, not them. 
 On a side note, i think the twins need to ease a little on this thing they do, which is repeat over and over again a set of characteristics they set for the characters. I get it, it differentiates one from another, but how many times did they really have to mention that Baylee loves grilled cheese? It's just a little thing that has bugged me a little in the past, but now got too evident. 
 Krista and Becca Ritchie fans, PLEASE DON'T HATE ME. I really, really from the deep of my heart, wanted to love this book. But we just didn't click. For me it felt messy and just another fictional story -which is not what i ever expect from the twin's books. 
 What i can say positively is that again and as always, they did an amazing and respectful job when it comes to sexuality. And having a male character dealing with bulimia is so important. At least in my country, guys would laugh at the idea of a boy having bulimia, since they believe that's only for girls. -sad, i know-.  
 I love the Kotovas, and i still want to read about them -GIVE ME A KATYA BOOK-, so despite my difficult relationship with Infini, i'm looking forward to all future books in this series.

The Winner's Curse has been on my TBR for awhile. I vaguely remember the hype when it came out and then, more recently, the hype when the finale released. I am glad I waited to read it because I didn't have any expectations at this point and just wanted an entertaining story to engage me and not feel like work to trudge through. The Winner's Curse was exactly what I needed and I enjoyed it. 
 Kestrel was a likable character because she was different. She was not a rule follower and the fact that her father was a general allowed her a little more freedom to be more of herself. She played instruments and went around without an escort despite the society frowning upon it. She had great instincts and was good at strategizing, even giving her father tips when she felt so inclined. She ended up purchasing a slave at an auction without really understanding why. She wasn't the type to take advantage of her station and participate in the slave trade, but she couldn't help herself. 
 It could've been a love story and I suppose in some ways it was, but not in the way I expected. It was like she noticed the slave's defiance and craved that as someone who also considered herself defiant. She wanted someone who understood her, I think. And he did, but he had some motives of his own. I feel like they had a mutual respect that neither one wanted to acknowledge too much and I don't know if it's really love so much as respect and attraction, but I'm intrigued to see where the story will go after the events that took place in this first book. I don't want to give too much away about the plot, but I was glad that it wasn't centered completely on Kestrel and her feelings for a slave and dealt with outside plots and forces, too. 
 I don't think the book is without flaws, though. The romance, if you can call it that, seemed a bit rushed, but maybe that's because I don't really think they love each other and I think they have a respect and wariness about the other that creates a sort of push and pull. It was good tension, but I'm not completely sold on the relationship. I also think it rushed what takes years or even decades to happen in societies. I don't want to give too many details away, but the events, while plausible, would not happen overnight and literally do in the book. That's not how revolutions or wars work in short spans of time, though the things that happen would totally happen over a longer length of time. I don't understand why the events are so rushed, but it kind if makes the whole book seem a lot less plausible as a whole. I have to believe there's a reason for the rushed events because the author has some places she needs to put the characters in order to formulate her grand story, so since it's the first book, I'll cut it some slack and continue reading. 
 I am concerned about a triangle, though, but I haven't read the synopsis of book two, so I might be way off. 
 Overall, the book was entertaining and I finished it quickly, so it did exactly what I needed it to do. I'm back on my reading wagon where I don't spend days on the same paragraph of whatever book I'm trying to finish, and that's what I needed. I recommend the book, but only as long as you're not expecting it to be the next earth shattering YA novel. It's.. it's just not quite there yet.

Bleh! You ever bite into what looks like yummy piece of chocolate, all decorated with caramel icing, only for it to taste GROSS when you reach the center?

 And my god, it's HORRID! 
 Rapunzel is a terrible first person character, whose telling of the story is a constant repeat of three elements. One: The weather (seriously, she ALWAYS mentions THE FREAKING WEATHER AND SEASON), two: How she feels while having sex (these scenes are hysterically badly written, I might add, as well as redundant) and three: her/other people's angst as felt through her magic hair. 
 The romance (BOTH of them, Rapunzel and the prince and the Rapunzel/Gilles thing) was forced and made no sense. There was no SHOWN build up to Rapunzel and Gilles falling for each other; we just had to believe it cuz "the book says so". 
 I felt sorriest for Snow White, the ONLY halfway likable character in the entire book, who of course gets a houseful of rapist bandits instead of dwarfs. It's like a bad rip off of "Snow White: A tale of terror" except boring. 
 At first, reading this book even though I was already beginning to dislike it on its merits as a story, I could tell Turgeon wrote it because she had some simply beautiful prose. Then this petered out, and it was just the same drivel OVER AND OVER AND OVER. 
 Won't read it again, that's for sure. 
 Please just read Mermaid instead, it's a much better example of this author's work!

 My most recent read was The Night Circus by Erin Morgenstern. I have been looking forward to reading this book for quite some time for a few reasons. One, I was told that I would love it because it is an adult version of Harry Potter. Two, the cover of it is beautiful and mysterious. Lastly, it has wonderful reviews, not only by people who I trust to give good reviews, but also by multitudes of other people. 
 I had started reading it just after Christmas, however, I just wasn't in the mindset for the book, so I shelved it to finish it later. When I started it this time, I felt much more ready to enter this intricate world. I must say, I wasn't disappointed. Morgenstern has done a brilliant job of painting this circus of black and white and shades of grey. Her detailed description of the acts, tents, and people make you feel like you are there watching everything happen. She pulls you in from the very beginning. 
 I both liked it more than I thought I would, and less than I thought I would, if that makes any sense. I think the only people who will understand that is people who have read the book. I didn't want the magic to end. Every time I opened up the book again, it was like coming home to old friends. But I wanted it to be done with so that I could find out what the point of it all ways. I often found myself getting a headache trying to figure it out before it happened. All in all though, I did thoroughly enjoy the book, and I can see myself reading it again and learning more about Le Cirque des Reves and falling in love all over again.

I would have to say this book is the worst and the best of the trilogy. Somewhere along the way you find yourself too emotionally involved and engrossed that even when many horrible events occurs and you need to take a breath to take it all in, you can't stop and you need to read more. Reading about these characters to eventually let them go is really hard, especially when the writer doesn't give their deaths justice. I won't mention who I mean in case of any spoilers. But after 2 or 3 books getting familiar with them it is too painful to let them go. Some deaths at the end are justified and you come to terms with it but others you just find yourself screaming "WHY?". 
 As well as, the fact that the storyline at many points build up to these amazing magnificent events and then nothing, the writer falls short on describing them. We go from her magnificent ability to redraw day to day events that is performed by Katniss, to a patched up description of the battlefield. That completely baffles me. 
 Another thing, that bugs me the most, is the ending. How easily it was put with no great discovery of when Katniss had finally realized who she wanted, who she chose. It is just .... BLAH. I know if the book was the way I imagined it, full of detailed narrative of every single act performed by Katniss, it would be another hundred pages longer at the least. But isn't being consistent with the flow of events and satisfying the readers want of justification a normal thing ? I would have loved to read it as long as it would have been, if only it left me satisfied at the end. Not jump from event to event not really knowing what happened. 
 I would give this trilogy a hundred stars if I can; but this book was a little too harsh that I must give it a star less then the two before. I must sound so consumed by the book to have this much to rant about ..... but yes I was. It is an amazing book in spite of all the heartbreaking deaths. 
 I'd never read it ever again ...

Cassie doesn't feel like she fits in her large, Italian family. Her dad is gone most of the time, so she stays with her grandmother. She used to live with her mother, but that ended a few years ago when Cassie stumbled in on the gruesome scene of a struggle, lots of blood, but no body. Her mother posed as a psychic, working the room with Cassie, reading people and guessing their secrets. Cassie's a natural at this, profiling people. She's so good that a secret program with the FBI notices and recruits her to join their ranks. 
 Moving to DC, Cassie is rooming in a house with several kids just like her; kids with different abilities that allow them to see through cold cases and solve them. But then a murder hits a little too close to home; it is eerily similar to what happened to her mother. Is it a serial killer? And is he escalating? 
 So?: If you read Ms. Barnes' previous book, Every Other Day, you know you already like her style. Very interesting and different plots, coupled with a good mystery. The Naturals does not disappoint; the idea of a junior FBI squad (very hush-hush, of course) is fantastic. Each teen has their own specialties that are intriguing, and the issues that come with rooming with a group of strangers fleshes out the story. It doesn't hurt that there's a hint of hormones as well, coming in the form of two very opposite male characters. 
 The Bottom Line: If you enjoy mysteries and don't mind a little blood spatter talk, then go for it.

Okay. When I went into this book, the only thing that I knew about it was what the Goodreads summary said. Perhaps that was my first mistake. 
 This is not a spoiler, really, because you find out within the first few pages, so I'm not going to tag it (I will for all of the other plotty discussion), but this book deals with a school shooting. This is where my dislike of this book first started to show. School/mass shootings are one of my biggest anxiety points, to the point where I have nightmares about them and, before I graduated, I would sit in class on campus wondering where I would go if someone came in with a gun. Maybe I shouldn't have continued to read this book once I knew it would be dealing with a shooting but, I thought, maybe it would touch on some important topics about them in a way that shows how they affect the families of shooters. It didn't. I will talk about that more in spoiler tags down below. Moving on. 
 This book had entirely too much going on. If all of the subplots had been cut down, if there had only been focus on one or two things, this book would have been okay. But it had to be a thriller instead of just a contemporary romance and that changes things. Here is a list of plotty details that made me laugh, cringe, or just roll my eyes: 
 1. If a school shooter (a murderer) escapes from prison/hospital/whatever, it will not be kept quiet. A year ago (maybe? give or take), a school shooter escape from an Ohio prison. The news about it was everywhere. These things are not taken lightly. 
 2. The details surrounding why they wanted to keep Ryan's escape a secret just didn't make sense to me. Actually, I don't even know what the details are. They wanted to talk to him more? I don't know. I'm given no good reason as to why this is happening. 
 3. The parents are MIA. You would think, in a book partially about what it is like to live as a family of a school shooter after the fact, the parents would play a big role. Nope. The mom stays upstairs and cleans. The dad is some sort of lawyer? I don't know. It's just weird, man. 
 4. I can buy the whole "we are moving away and changing our name" thing. I guess. It's one thing that didn't bother me as much as everything else. I can even get why they would want to keep it a secret. Still. Meh. 
 5. I don't understand why the heck Michael and Alane would still be so ride or die for Julia/Lucy this whole book. They stick with her through everything! Alane has her mom cancel her dentist appointment so she can go do shady crap with Julia/Lucy! I can't!!! Michael sees her with a gun? No biggie. All good. BFF forever. 
 6. Do we see Julia/Lucy kill Dr. Spence? Did I just read that and forget about it? She did do that, right? By the point where she said she framed Ryan for it or whatever, I was just so done. 
 7. The incest. Okay. Here we go. I will admit, I didn't think that the book would go there. Despite all of the creepy descriptions of how close the twins were, how they were born holding hands, I didn't think they would actually be in love (or, I didn't think Julia would persuade her brother into being with her. Is that how it happened?). Regardless, it happened. It's not the worse thing in the book. 
 8. The description of the shooting itself. This is where I finally thought that the author went overboard with this plot line. The twins end up making out while drenched in blood surrounded by eleven dead bodies. That was just too much for me and it left me feeling nauseous. It felt like something that should be on this season of American Horror Story. Really unnecessary. 
 9. Wait! I forgot! This bitch got into a police station dressed as a cop she drugged! What EVEN?!?!? How did this happen? Why are police written so inadequately in books like this. 
 10. And then she made it to New York City all on her own with only an hour's lead. "I'm assuming the cops want to keep everything that happened...a secret." My God. No. That's not how this works. If her brother winds up dead in a jail cell and the sister goes missing, the cops are going to be looking for her?! I can't. I just honestly can't. How is she making it in NYC with a false identity as a teenager? The world will never know.  
 The romance in this book was laughable. From that very first cooking scene, I knew I wouldn't be buying it. A boy (described as a literal golden retriever) comes into your house to make you an omelet and the whole time he is there, your parent doesn't come down to notice? Too busy washing the bathroom or whatever, I guess. AN OMELET. In her house. I just. Be still my beating heart. 
 Okay, I laughed so hard when she was like freaking out and he got down to hug her and his head rested on her SHOULDER not her BOOBS. She was so impressed. Such high standards, Lucy/Julia. 
 And their love blooms so quickly. Towards the end of the book, she was like "Michael won't cheat on me," and I'm like... two pages ago you said you guys should be apart. When did this become official? Huh?! Instalove at its best. At least she didn't kill him, though.  
 You know the theme song for Full House? "Whatever happened to predictability?" It's here. In this book. I can only be told that something happened in the band room so many times before realizing that what everyone thinks happened is not what actually happened. 
 Lucy/Julia's personality changed in an instant. If you are going to do an "I'm not really traumatized, I am the mastermind behind it all" reveal, it needs to be subtle, with little things that make me wonder about the character's true intentions. That didn't happen here. One page, she was having panic attacks and mentioning that she used to pass out every time her father cracked his joints. The next, she was like "I'm going to kill you." Okay? 
 I just want to know this: did she really have all of those PTSD-like reactions before? Was she that traumatized from the shooting or was she just so good that she could fake it all? Everything shifted so fast, I got whiplash. Probably like she did when she hit a guy with her car. Or when her brother cut the brakes on her boyfriend's car. Wow. This story, you guys.  
 Her brother killed eleven people in the band room, but she can't tell anyone what happened because she can't remember those 22 minutes. How many times do you have to read that before you think that isn't what actually happened. Answer: like two times. 
 I think that about covers it. I can't believe I went this whole time without mentioning how completely ridiculous Spence's journal entries were. He needs to get his credentials taken away (I mean, he is dead, so. That's for the best for any future patients. ). 
 The writing was decent. There were some good moments, some good suspense, but I just had everything figured out that nothing really took me by surprise.

Based on the synopsis, I started reading Level 2 with high expectations of "gripping exploration", action and general awesomeness. Sadly, that was not the case. 
 I'll give the book points for originality, don't get me wrong. Level 2 had huge potential. A sci-fi afterlife, more reminiscent of hell rather than heaven, is definitely not an overused idea. However, the execution was subpar at best. 
 I didn't like the writing, it felt choppy, no flow whatsoever to the narrative. It fits the world of the novel, it is very clinical and fails to evoke any kind of emotion. 
 Also, I had this feeling like I was missing the beginning of my novel, like maybe my book was missing the first chapters because you're thrust into this weird world with no explanations, no exposition, nothing. That might work for the likes of Ilona Andrews, but the woman's a writing goddess. 
 It certainly didn't help that I disliked most of the characters, as well, starting with Felicia who's this holier than thou, bleeding heart of an MC. Not the best combo. 
 Add to that some dubious choices by Felicia, an epic love I'm supposed to be rooting for that takes place before the actions in the novel and we only get to see in memories (needless to say, didn't really make me root for it), and Level 2 suddenly doesn't have much to offer me. 
 Not picking up the sequel.

Comparisons to dystopian classics Brave New World and Nineteen Eighty-Four are apt, except that this time the boogeyman isn't Big Government or Big Industry -- it's Big Tech. 
 It is flawed, mind you. I got the feeling that Eggers was trying to be subtle about the moral of the story at first -- that allowing the encroachment of technology into private lives is perilous -- but I personally thought it got to be a bit tiresome pretty quick. And I have to admit that I bristled 2 or 3 times at the descriptions of the young, hip techies just blindly accepting whatever shiny new thing their company asked them to swallow. Maybe I'm just a little touchy about all the "Millennials blah blah this," and "Snake People blah blah that," swirling around in the media these days, but the assumption that pretty much everyone, but especially almost all young adults would just unquestioningly accept some of the shit that went down in this book really rubbed me the wrong way. 
 So... why 3 stars? Because despite all of that, I practically devoured the book. The plot pacing is addictive. Warts and all, it's still a well-written, provocative book.
Ended WAY better than it started. Looking forward to #5 :)

While their characters did improve somewhat toward the end of the story, they spent most of the first part thinking only of themselves. Both constantly disparage the positions they have been placed in (goose girl, servant, shepherd, ect.) as though these are jobs lowly and beneath them, making it clear that they think the same of those people who normally hold those positions. And yet they are described as being kind and caring people. 
 Maybe this wouldn't bother me so much if they didn't constantly daydream about how their enemies would receive their comeuppance. While I understand wanting to be avenged, it is frustrating to read characters who want vengeance... but not real vengeance. They want to see the expressions of horror on their enemies' faces when they are found out, but don't want the attempted murderers imprisoned or executed. Because somehow, only wanting the "Aha" moment makes the heroes good people. 
 There were a few moments between the couple that were cute to read, and I guess that in the end, they did help the people they were supposed to. But those moments were far fewer than I cared for.

Title: The Unwanted Wife 
 Series: Unwanted, #1 
 Author: Natasha Anders 
 Rating: 4.5 Stars 
 Cliffhanger: No  
 HEA: Yes  
 "The only thing that matters to me is you. You're the sun I revolve around..." 
 After reading the blurb, I knew I wanted to read this book, though the title, The Unwanted Wife, stopped me for a bit, because I could tell that the book would be heartbreaking and while I was excited to read it, it took me some time to pick it up. 
 But boy did I enjoy The Unwanted Wife, if the rating is any indication. From the first page, I was hooked. 
 First off, the main heroine, Theresa, was an insecure and broken version of herself, traumatized by a year and a half of an unhappy marriage, and a husband who treated her no better than a doormat. But throughout the book, Theresa became stronger and started to stand up for herself. 
 When, after finally gaining enough courage, Theresa asked for a divorce from her husband, Sandro, all she wanted was an out. Out of the marriage, and out of the horrible life with an unloving husband. But the only way she was getting it, was giving Sandro a son, he so desperately wanted. 
 "Chemistry was a terrible thing, sometimes it simply sparked between the wrong people" 
 But the thing she couldn't understand, was why he would want a child with her. With a woman he despised and couldn't stand. 
 And strangely, after she finally decided not to let him walk all over her, Sandro started showing her affection and treating her better. After so long, he started acting like a real husband, trying to make the marriage work. 
 But for Theresa, it was too late. She was done being pushed around and told what to do. And even though she still loved him, he hurt her too badly. 
 "I'm your husband..." 
 "No. You are not my husband," she interrupted in a voice thickened with hatred and tears. "You have never been my husband. A husband loves, honours and cherishes! A husband is a lover and a champion....Look into the next room if you want to see what a real husband is, because you are no such thing!" 
 And I perfectly understood her. Even though I sometimes wanted her to act nicer towards him because he tried, I also loved that she didn't give in to his charms. He deserved everything he got. 
 And even so, I loved them together. What can I say, I'm a hopeless romantic! After him suffering for some time for how he treated her, I wanted for them to end up together and get a HEA in the end. 
 All in all, 
 The Unwanted Wife 
 , told in the 3rd-person's POV is an emotional and unforgettable read. The writing was great, and the plot well thought out and original. Natasha did an amazing job with the book and I am glad I decided to read it! I will definitely be picking up her other works. 
 "Sandro, you gorgous idiot... I never stopped loving you. I just got much better at hiding it from you. I was too afraid of being hurt again."

To summarize, it seems even the best authors can fall victim to Middle Book Syndrome.

It was filled with incredible world-building and a well-paced journey with a complex and likable heroine. But whereas The Fifth Season was probably 70% backstory, I should really have known this installment would focus more on the present. 
 The first half of the book was (comparatively) dull as mud. Nothing of much interest happens to Essun, she appeared stagnant and incapable. We got more about Nassun, Essun's daughter, and her life-changing journey after the beginning of the latest apocalypse. Ultimately, she was interesting, but not for a long while. 
 By the time things really started happening, I had already given into my boredom. I really wasn't invested, and all I was really hoping for was more of Schaffa's backstory. He had quickly become the most intriguing character, as my love for Essun kind of waned. 
 I'm still going to read the final installment of this trilogy, but I hope the pacing improves in the next one.

 Odea's mother goes missing, she (Odea) ends up in the mental ward, and she starts to feel sick from not walking any dreams. She needs Connors help to escape, but when she does, she isn't prepared for what she will learn about her mother and herself. 
 I thoroughly enjoyed this book but the weird, mysterious aspects of the book moved too quickly for my taste. I wanted more of the dream world and less reality once we got to that point of the book which is why I only rated it 4 stars. I felt that we were introduced to characters and potential plot points that were later rushed over to tie up the last chapter. The Slaves, impending war, why her mother escaped in the first place, the boy she met in the dream world who ultimately turned her in....

"I am so sad it makes me heavier than the sum of my parts." 
 This book was so wonderful, it surprised me a lot. I picked up this book because I love good books involving zombies and this one has been getting decent review. I've actually wanted to read this book for about a year and a half now but I never got around to it. This morning I just decided to pick it up and 3 hours later I was finished with it. It was so good and intense and interesting and this is so much more than just a zombie apocalypse story, it's a coming-of-age story. This story follows Sloane, a 17 year old girl who has been thrown into a zombie apocalypse. Sloane is suicidal because her older sister Lily abandoned her 6 months ago (before the zombie apocalypse), and ran away leaving Sloane behind with their abusive Father. Now the story takes place a few days later where Sloane is surviving with five other teenagers in their old high school. 
 I think it was interesting to read about a zombie apocalypse through the eyes of someone who wants to die. This book is written so beautifully and at times it made me want to cry. I love how each of the five teenagers all had their own stories and their own things to contribute to the story. I liked the brother and sister relationship between Grace and Trace, and seeing how that affected their decisions. I also absolutely adore Rhys, and I totally ship him and Sloane so hard. They had some really cute scenes in this book that made me smile. 
 This book kind of felt like The Breakfast Club meets the zombie apocalypse. It focuses so much more on human relationships as opposed to the apocalypse itself, and it was refreshing. I love the way it implies that zombies aren't always the biggest threat (because Sloane's abusive Father is more scary than any zombie could ever be.) I feel like this is a very realistic take on how teenagers would handle themselves in a zombie apocalypse; all very frantic and unsure of what to do and afraid to kill zombies and people. It's not like you just suddenly become okay with killing zombies just because you're in an apocalypse, and those zombies were people once too. 
 The only complaint I have about this book is the ending. It didn't give me any closure and since I had become so attached to these characters it sucked not getting to see the rest. That was so sad though when Grace died in Trace's arms, and then later Trace and Sloane are talking and Trace just shoots himself in the head and kills himself like damn. That was so sad it made me want to cry. Also, that was sad to see that Sloane's sister in the end was already a zombie. I saw that coming but it was still sad to see Sloane react to seeing her sister as a zombie. I can't believe Sloane and Rhys are the only two that survived! I want to know if they make it to the military camp and what the hell happens after they leave Sloane's house.  Overall, this was a really great read and this is the first book I've read by Courtney Summers but it certainly won't be the last.

Um... Well... Okay... 
 This was the mermaid version of Twilight. Twilight did a lot of things for paranormal YA lit, but this is just a similar story, except with Royal Mermaids. The main character of Emma is quite fluid and never really seems to gain traction on any consistent character traits. She is a self aware version of Emma Swann. She even thinks to herself "Oh, this is going to look great that I let my ex BF bully me- I wonder what people will think. While self aware, she still lets him manipulate her. 
 Galen is a broody Edward Cullen who is trying to track down a mate for his brother and gets to play the emotionally manipulative boyfriend on land. Apart from his good looks and cool tattoo, I don't know what he has going for him. 
 Rayna and Toraf make it bearable when they are in the scenes with the characters. I also like some of the settings like the archive caves, but this story and novel really weren't great. Emma believed things too quickly, the plot was predictable, and the "surprise" ending wasn't a surprise at all. 
 I don't anticipate picking up the sequel.

This is proving to be one of the biggest books of the year when it comes to critical acclaim. I liked it, no more, no less. It didn't necessarily live up to my expectations but it is a humorous meditation on what it means to combine two families in marriage and remain true to yourself at the same time. The characters irked me a bit at times, but I think that might have been part of the point. This WAS the strangest/most unconventional/most offbeat thing I've read in a long while...that is until I started reading Amelia Gray's Gutshot at the same time. Now that's some crazy shit!

Surprisingly engaging and entertaining. It's also quite a poignant story. 
 The characters are interesting and fun, while moving the story on nicely. Really enjoyed this.

The Aether storms, the senses, the pods, the realms, it was a lot of science fiction. I'm not big on science fiction but I do get into it occasionally and this book worked for me. The concept of the realms is kind of cool, but scary at the same time. You're "living" your life without physically doing anything. Creepy. 
 I loved both Aria and Perry. I enjoyed Aria's self discovery of her real self, though there was one really weird moment that had me laughing and cringing at the same time. It was awkward. The things that Perry went through were just awful. I can't imagine making some of the choices he had to make. 
 I loved the ending. It reminded me of Hunger Games or the Harry Potter books where the story in the book had an end. It wasn't a happily ever after end (it's a trilogy so lets not get carried away) but it has an end, and then a little extra to give you a taste of what's coming. 
 My one complaint about the book is the lack of information. You're thrown into the story (which is ok) but as the book progresses there were a lot things that were never explained, or only given a partial explanation. The "reason" why everything happened was one of those partial explanations. 
 Overall I really enjoyed the book and I'm looking forward to the next book in the trilogy.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I go back and forth between one and two stars. I understand the high ratings. People are enjoying their fairy smut... however, I can't believe I'm the only one out there that doesn't believe this isn't a perfectly crafted world. 
 I liked some parts, particularly while they were on the hunt for the book. But then something would ruin it. 
 I hate this love story. Feyre complains that Tamlin keeps her under his control, that he doesn't tell her enough. Ok. Rhys literally bonded himself to you via a tattoo and has been listening to your mind... in addition to that he hides so much-- the mate, testing her to get her own wedding ring. That was ridiculous. 
 She confided in Lucien, not Tamlin, about her unhappiness. And she assured Tamlin that she wasn't happy with her Rhys deal/week... so consider when she was stolen from the alter, then sends a "don't come find me note" whilst holed up with a man who Tamlin knows can control minds-- consider how Tamlin perceives the situation. Of course he makes a shady deal to get her back! Also Tamlin was under the mountain as well. Why is there no consideration of his PTSD? And it seems like his whole story just dropped. Of course he had to show up at the end, but it seemed like they should've checked in w his POV at some point. They did a Rhys narration at the end. 
 Let her just move on. Let her be honest and tell Tamlin that she doesn't love him like she thought she did. Don't try to make it out like he's a terrible person, when his actions aren't really any different than Rhysland's or Feyre's. 
 I think her world building is terrible. The courts are well done, but she releases information when it comes up in the plot without enough foreshadowing. So many things are convenient-- like how Feyre realizes she has the power to do literally anything. I know she has the powers from all of the courts, but she was training one minute and becoming the wind the next. 
 Maas also borrows heavily from other stories. I don't know if she thinks it was an homage? The Rhysland-Mr. Darcy switch (whose family slaughtered whose!?!?), the "mate"... I mean basically imprinting. At least when Meyer did it w Jacob and a baby, there was comic relief. Here it was like Lucien looked up and BAM. She's my mate. And can we talk about the mate thing? There's all these rules that she somehow knew existed... and the feeding? Ew. "I'm a strong independent woman who just wants to be licked, forced into a physical and mental bond, do whatever Rhys tells me even though I hated it about Tamlin and still complain about that in my whiny inner monologue, I must paint you, and now I will present you with food..." It's just me!?!?!?!?!?!? 
 This is just not well written. If I never read the words snarl, hiss and mate again, I'll be fine. Or Clythia. An actual name she chose. And all of you Rhys fans... have fun when you hop in bed with him and touch his wings accidentally... eye roll. 
 G'day mate.

I was actually impressed with the worldbuilding and the map and then I started to have some doubts when I encounter this paragraph  To improve their kingdoms' economies, rulers use Royal Conduit magic to enhance certain areas of expertise that their kingdoms developed based on geography or the natural talents of their citizens. If a certain kingdom showed an interest in education, the ruler used magic to make their people excel at learning; if another kingdom showed an aptitude for fighting, the ruler used conduit magic to make their soldiers more lethal. Winter sat north of the richest part of the Klaryns, so our queens enhanced our ability to find minerals and granted us endurance and courage in the bottomless, dark places of the earth. 
 This is a really weird government and it has magic! Have you heard Ministry of Magic in HP bowing to the citizen's majority wish? Like, can't you have a normal, unapologetic propaganda instead of using something like magic to enhance everything? How stupid can the citizens be that magic helped them to learn something? I understand the main point the author wants us to believe but this entire nonsense didn't sit well with me.  
 What fuckery is this? 
 Its polished surface lets me watch my scared expression swing inward as it opens, and behind the door is, I hate to say it, exactly the bedchamber I'd design if I had endless resources and nothing more to worry about than room furnishings. 
 You were scared and you've never seen nice things (you're a nomad for god's sake) and you think that highly of yourself that you can design pretty things? How can I actually relate to this brat? You were so jealous of other people's wealth that you didn't even want to glance at the ballroom, and pointedly looking at your muddy boots. Oh my god the stupid is gaining on me. 
 Is this Where I had expected it to be as over-the-top as Noam's gate, it's nothing but a canopy bed (a really nice canopy bed), an armoire (a really nice armoire), and an intricate lavender rug stretched over a wood floor the kind of thing you would give 4 stars? What was the purpose of the brackets? Was it as a guide or just to give clueless readers like me a sense of ease, like, gosh, I accidentally imagined a common bed and reading the brackets I should have conjured a 'really nice' one instead. Is this the kind of YA stuff in demand nowadays? 
 Managed up to Chapter 10. DNF. Will not waste time being in a stupid world being a stupid girl.

The book is as pleasant and warm as the film it describes, with none of the memorable lines or humor. Elwes offers goodnatured reminiscences, which will warm the cockles of Princess Bride fans. There's nothing remakable here, except perhaps his unfailing ability to cast everyone in a fond glow. There is a fair amount of repetition, as contributions of various PB players echo Elwes' thoughts exactly. A few interesting bits, but not enough to make this essential for film buffs. Fans will appreciate this, but won't see it as essential.

Originally posted on my blog. Birds of a Writer 
 I was really looking forward to reading this book, so when my school library got it, I immediately jumped on renting it. It took me about a week to read through despite it not being that thick of a book. But then, I was reading it at night an hour before I went to bed. 
 Anyways, pacing wise the book wasn't the greatest. In the beginning, the book wasn't the most exciting but it was definitely exciting. There were bombs and And the middle dragged. The ending 
 finally picked up. 
 I liked the characters in the beginning. Nathaniel was a protagonist that I liked because I felt I could related to him personality wise. And I also liked Mori as well. He was an intriguing character because you weren't sure if he was behind the bombs or not. And I enjoyed Grace's character because she reminded me of Alana from Tamora Pierce's books but she was a scientist, which was cool to see a woman being portrayed in the 1800s. 
 And as much as I wanted to really love this book, I just can't. Even thinking about it a while later, I'm still with the same conclusions. There was a lot of plot points that to me, didn't really seem to make a lot of sense. And I felt that the pacing was either slow or it dragged a lot. So the characters didn't seem to make rational choices, and a lot of things went unexplained. At the end of the book, I was left with more questions than answers. Questions to things I felt there shouldn't have been questions to. 
 There was a marriage towards the end of the book that I felt came out of seemingly nowhere and it wasn't really explained well. I felt the characters involved kinda talked about it, but their reasons weren't strong enough and I felt the whole ordeal could have been avoid, Grace's parents certainly seemed to overreact to her going over to Mori's that it was a bit ridiculous. While I saw Grace's point in trying to get married so she could get her aunt's house, I wasn't completely sold on Thaniel's reason. I did not feel that Thaniel was torn between two opposing loyalties when Grace got involved. 
 Overall, I felt that the historical accuracy was pretty on point, and that nothing popped out at me of being out of time for the Victorian period. The book made a big deal about the Irish at the beginning and as the book went on, that was a detail that seemed forgotten at times. The description seems to say that its look at "Japan's civil war as its long standing traditions crumble" will be exciting, but it was not. I did not get a sense of a civil war and the way that it affected Japan's traditions. 
 I haven't studied too much yet into the Meiji period, but from what I do know, I can say this, the way the atmosphere of Japan was portrayed as seems correct though. Ignoring the part about the civil war, I was fine with that. I wish though that we would have seen more looks of Japan and how it affected Mori later on. 
 Another thing that bugged me about the book was the "dazzling flights of fancy". There is magic in this book, although you wouldn't realize it until about halfway in. No one in this book ever addressed this, where the magic came from, if Mori was the only one with it, and other things. The book was more alternative history/science fiction/light fantasy. And I wish that the fantasy elements would have been dealt with more. Thaniel never seemed to be bothered by any of it, except for the fact that Mori could have been creating clockwork bombs. The only person with a dash of common sense in this whole book was Grace and even then, I question her. 
 The biggest thing that brought me out of the story was in the end when we find out that Thaniel and Mori are in love and on their wedding night, Thaniel leaves Grace for him. And honestly, it was such a deal breaker for me. As Grace thankfully pointed out, it was ridiculous and rude of him and cruel. I get wanting to go through with it because you feel stuck, but once they had married...well there had to have been a better time to break things off. Like, I dunno, BEFORE the wedding or at least wait a while after you've been married. Or even just leave her at the alter. I just lost a lot of respect for Thaniel as a protagonist and it almost ruined the book for me. 
 Not only that, but the relationship between Mori and Thaniel seemed so sudden to me. It was as if it came out of no where. There were probably signs before hand, but they were so subtle I didn't catch them. I guess in a way, I give my complements for not being so obvious, but it was such a shock. In a way to me it seemed as if the author suddenly decided that she wanted to throw them together and then never went back to change anything about their friendship. 
 Overall, this book had a lot of potential, but it was lacking in a lot of places as well. I'm disappointed in this book and I definitely think it could have been better if it had been longer and the author had taken the time to flesh out parts of the book a little bit more. Its almost there, but not quite yet.
Wow -- that was really good. I think Sybella's story is still my very favorite, but this book did a great job of tying these three companion books together

It might not be saying much, but this is by far, the best book I've read all year. The writing was perfect (and I know people say that's not possible, but this book definitely achieves the impossible--wink, wink) and beautiful. I knew what was going to happen (I'm really bad at not spoiling books for myself), but I was shocked by nearly all of the plot twists and revelations. I loved the characters so so so much. 
 [minor spoilers ahead] 
 Cath is a great role model. If you know what this book is about (pssst, it's a story about the Queen of Hearts), you'll question my calling a her a wonderful role model, but I just loved her so much. She isn't afraid to dream and she tries fiercely to turn her dreams into reality. She's such a passionate character who strives to get what she wants even when everyone tells her no, her ambitions are stupid. She's determined and an unstoppable force of power. Jest, the love interest, was fabulous. There's no questioning that, but the story wasn't about him. It was about this fervent inspired girl who works so hard to escape what everyone tells her is her fate. Though the romance was swoon-worthy, it wasn't the focus of the book. Cath was. 
 [notably less minor spoilers ahead; translation: stop reading if you haven't read the book] 
 What I didn't like, however, was how Cath treated Mary Ann. In YA books, I hate how female main characters often abandon their best friends. They choose the guy over the friend over and over again. I can't say I would've treated Mary Ann differently had I been in Cath's shoes, but I wished she would've had a bit more sympathy. . . though it's hard to care about anyone's feelings when your own heart's been split in two. When Mary Ann betrayed Cath and told her secrets, however, Cath was blinded with her encompassing love for Jest. I've never been in love with anyone either than a fictional character, but I hope that love doesn't separate you from your friendships. 
 I really, really loved Jest and I wish that I'd gotten to know him better. I cried (on the inside) when he died. It was so quick and sudden. The sad part is, he and Cath were so close, in a way, to the future that they'd suffered through so much to have. They were absolutely beautiful together. And, unlike many other books, Cath wasn't rendered weak and helpless when she was around him. She could love Jest, the protector, and fend for her own when she needed to. 
 My favorite scene, the one part that I picture whenever I see the book's cover, is the tea party. The mad tea party. I read that scene wanting to be in Hatta's Marvelous Millinery, wondering what I would do if I was in the entertainer's seat. That's one of the scenes that will stick with me the most. Other than the almost every scene that Jest was in. . . 
 This book was impossibly perfect. The writing, I just have to say again, was amazing. I could picture everything and the words spoke to my heart. The whole novel was done in such a way that I can imagine this book being read and loved for a very long time. It needs to be read by more people. The characters were wonderful. Some gave me chills, like the Sisters and sometimes Hatta, and others made me want to live in Hearts despite the simple, simple King, like Cath and Jest and sometimes Hatta. Point being, I love Heartless. . .with all of my heart, you could say.

 Love, Your Concierge 
 By 
 Jessica Ingro 
 Hello. I'm Elizabeth Ward. Your Personal Concierge. 
 Elizabeth owns a small company as a personal assistant to different people. 
 Basically her job is to do random errands that rich people don't have time to do. Like cleaning, washing and etc. 
 While on the job, she meets Grant Morgan. 
 The oh-so-hot blue eyed hunky executive who was coincidentally one of her clients. 
 These eyes should never leak tears and these lips shouldn't do anything but smile. 
 But, mixing business with pleasure rarely turns out good. Will she risk her business for love? 
 This was a very emotional read filled with numerous ups and downs. Having a relationship with your boss and all that was very cliche but everything is cliche already. 
 The difference is how the book was written and the way it went. 
 Nevertheless, it was a good read though I can't classify it as a book that I would remember for a long time.

Just when me and my friends were complaining about the plateau plots of HR's lately, I come across an unread Julia Quinn and then, BAM, I take it back. I take it all back! There is hope as long as we have such books in our lives. 
 I enjoyed the first half of the Bridgertons series, I loved loved loved all the characters and how their stories were brilliantly written. I did not however enjoy the last few, as well as the SS Quartet so instead of tainting my thoughts on Ms. Quinn's writing I stopped reading her books. Then one day, I was digging through my friend's (Hi Riddhi!) favorite shelf and found this book and BAM, I took the cake and ate it and indulged in it and now I am a happy happy girl who is brimming with so much love from the book I just read. 
 I loved loved loved this one! This may probably be the funniest HR book I have ever read! The banters and quick witted dialogues were just all over the place. This, this is why I love Julia Quinn - now I remember. Humor aside, this book also oozed with sweet sweet unbridled romance that made me frantically flip through the pages! The H/h were amazing and I loved how their characters were 'stress-free' - meaning they didn't induce any anger (nor did they make me curse them. Their chemistry was just off the charts! 
 Also, we meet again the scheming and ever so funny Lady Danbury here! I love this woman, I love how she thinks and how integral she is to everybody's lives (even during the Bridgertons' time). So yes, if you're up to rekindle your faith in beautifully written HR then go pick this up! 
 Elizabeth planted her hands on her hips and glowered up at the handsome estate manager. "How dare you think I would blackmail this sweet old lady!" 
 "Sweet?" Mr. Siddons echoed. 
 "Old?" Lady Danbury hollered. 
 Go on, read the book.

2.5 stars maybe 3. Im not sure. 
 Retelling of Sleeping Beauty. What happens after Aurora wakes up? ... well nothing exciting really. There is no plot. I got so bored I almost DNF this but I hate doing. So I kept reading, waiting for something, anything. 
 What kind of princess let's people walk all over her? bruhh

WOW!!! This was tremendous! 
 As I was reading the first couple pages, I was so confused and hoping I wasn't going to be the one person who just didn't "get it", but WOW!!! I can't say WOW enough!

Grisham's second novel is probably his most famous thanks in no small part to the film starring a certain Tom Cruise and Gene Hackman. It's a far simpler story than his magnum opus "A Time To Kill", and in many ways the novel benefits from a more focused plot. 
 Mitch McDeere, a newly graduated law student, gets tempted to work for the titular firm with an over generous employment contract. He soon finds his new colleagues are frontmen for mafia gangsters. Can he help the FBI bring down his new employers and get away with his life? 
 Maybe not the greatest story ever told and certainly saved by great acting in the film, the central story shines through and that's what gives this famous outing 5 stars.
13 to life was a really good book, and I would recommend it for anyone who likes novels about werewolves and teen romance.

This is a great darker second book. This is Sybella's story and her battle with the blackness that she believe she has in her. It was great to see someone who was supposed to be dead not be (would know if read the first book),and watching her fall in love. There was also old characters, and my hate was still there for the older ones. The romance was a little more rushed in this book, but I still loved seeing Sybella come into herself and find her true purpose. 
 I really want the final Mortal Heart,because these books are addicting and I want to see what happen after that ending. However it may be a while and that makes me a little sad. If you haven't started this trilogy then you should because it's a really gripping story.

Ok, so I usually assume that books or series that go viral are overrated, but this was truly a great book. I think that the BDSM elements have been blown out of proportion by the media, but I read a lot of BDSM books, so maybe it is wild to the average housewife. I won't go into details about the book or what I loved because all the other reviewers will have already discussed it all, but I will say that I LOVED the book but was left really frustrated and angry at the end. I will definitely read the next two - I'm dying to know how it all works out for Christian and Ana.

This book was great. Just simply great. 
 I rarely give out 5 star reviews anymore. Some of my rock solid favorite authors are lucky to get 4's from me. While this book didn't earn the 5 stars for being insanely amazing, it did earn it for a few reasons. 
 1) I was in the mood for a good YA PNR. I like to pretend I'm too mature for them, but I secretly get a craving for them every so often. This one DELIVERED on sating my craving. 
 2) There was really nothing I didn't like about this book. That is to say, it didn't piss me off in any way! For example... You know how authors like to make popular girls evil and completely conniving? Well, in my experience, that's usually not the case. Sure there are some mean girls out there, but even they aren't completely without good qualities. Well, this author was smart enough not to throw the popular girl completely to the wolves. I love that! Not one character was a cardboard cut out of a bad cliche. It makes me trust this author to be an actual intelligent being. I will read her books because of things like this. 
 3) The heroine was rarely annoying.  She actually didn't cheat on her boyfriend, nor did she for a second entertain the thought of cheating on him. She's supposed to be an angel, so in that way she acted like one. So often the girls in these types of books are supposed to be above others for some supernatural reason, yet they make horrible choices. I can take all sorts of taboo subjects in books, however, I cannot abide infidelity. It makes me sick. I loved that Clara had the strength of character (as should befit an angel) to steer completely clear of betraying Tucker.  
 4) Tucker Tucker Tucker. Sigh... Love me some Tucker! 
 Mostly the reason this book got 5 stars is because it hit me in all the right spots. It was a perfect fit for me personally and what I needed at the time that I read it. Hopefully others have a similar experience.
Loved it. And I could do a thorough review, but I'm guessing there are already dozens of them out there, so just suffice it to say - Loved it.

Okay, so I got a little caught up in this story, which surprised me because I had no interest in Sed, AT ALL. I had some technical difficulties with my Kindle which caused me to need more time to finish this than it needed (resulting in Amazon sending me a replacement Kindle actually). And when I finally finished yesterday, my husband caught me saying, "That's it?? That's the end??" And he said, "I hate it when the ending leaves me feeling like that." 
 I've spent some time mulling over my review and honestly, when it comes right down to it, I didn't really like this book. 
 I mean, first of all, this relationship that has ruined Sed, only lasted 4 months to begin with. And it ruins them both, for two years. THEN, they get back together in totally whacked fashion and they play games and Sed is just an idiot. And Jess decides to quit law school, but Sed is a jerk and she goes back. Only to realize that he's right and she never should have decided to quit in the first place. It makes her whole argument that she should be allowed to make her own decision that much weaker. He admires her for being strong, but he doesn't treat her like she's strong. And then she proves that she isn't even honest with herself or know her own mind. That's disappointing. 
 Then there's this whole big blow up about the law school teacher and the dean and the lawsuit she's going to bring...which seems to just disappear (yea I'm sure it'll be continued in the next book, but from arm's length since it will be about another bandmate and his HEA). 
 And what about Trey's weird happening, the whole thing. Whatever. I'm a little less interested in him now than I was after Brian's story. 
 And what about the electric violin? 
 And what about Brian. Who seems to only be as good as the last thought that was planted in his head. Whatever. 
 At least Jace continues to be interesting. Looking forward to his story. So all in all, this wasn't enough to deter me from eagerly awaiting the next one.

Ms. Slaughter never disappoints.This tale was a little different to her others because of the back and forth aspect in time but it was materfully done, and gave a great insight into what policing was like at a time when racial and sexual discrimination were prevalent. The only snag was that the characters I love the most - Sara and Will - were almost backseat in this story. Sara is becoming more and more shadowy as there was more of a concentration on Evelyne and Amanda. I won't talk about the plot - it tied up loose ends and was satisfying! Good to know more about Will for a start! 
 I read it all at one go - a fast paced exciting criminal thriller and I look forward to the next.

This is my favourite Jojo Moyes book to date. This quirky family dramedy made me laugh, cry (as per usual with a Jojo Moyes book), and cheer for these characters. The perfect read for rainy afternoons, lounging on the beach, or just wanting to escape with a good book. For fans of the film "Little Miss Sunshine".

This was an interesting, original book and I enjoyed reading it, but honestly I'm not sure what all the fuss is about. I appreciate the historic relevance and moral message of the plot, but I felt the way it was presented was very in your face and not at all subtle. The bad guys and the escalation of their corruption just felt quite two-dimensional and lacking in depth for me. I knew where it was heading so really the story lacked any sense of conflict and it just felt like a story to teach you how horrible people (or in this case, animals) can get when put in power . That was fine and all but from such a well-loved modern classic I was expected something a little more complex. Like maybe if it was from the bad guy's perspective or if they had more development. As it was, it felt like they were pretty bad people (sorry, pigs) in the first place, so their decent into evilness wasn't so impactful to me.

 Suzanne Brockmann finally returns with another fast-paced and sexy adventure read. It feels like I've been waiting forever for this. Why? Because I HAVE BEEN WAITING FOREVER FOR THIS. 
 In Some Kind of Hero, Brockmann gives her readers what they love: a hot, brave, and sensitive Navy SEAL hero whose life is thrown all kinds of sideways. He meets a smart, real, and also brave woman (sometimes it's a man gY~S ) who ends up tangled in his crazy world and together they do crazy things to save the day. Sure, it's a formula, but it's one that is so well done. This is book #17 in the Troubleshooters series and it never feels stale. 
 (Side note: if any book in this world can be considered a standalone, then it's this one. There's no need to read the others before, though the author recommends reading the trio of novellas, 
 Free Fall 
 , 
 Home Fire Inferno 
 , and 
 Ready to Roll 
 that were published prior to SKoH--which I didn't read.) 
 As I said, it's been a while since I've read a new Brockmann, so I forgot that I pretty much inhale her reads. Some Kind of Hero starts with a car chase (An actual car chase. As in, Pete flags down Shayla and hops in her car, tells her he just saw his missing daughter jump in a strange car, and Shayla proceeds to rev the engine and followthatcar!). Sooo, you don't get any time to settle in. The rest of the novel follows the two, with alternating POVs from Maddie, the runaway, and Izzy, lovable SEAL featured in other TS books (which you still don't need to read). 
 The story is filled with energy, filled with humor and fun, and filled with emotions. Brockmann showcases her talent at creating engaging characters with real stories, complicated thoughts and feelings, and throws them in situations, that may seem over-the-top, but nevertheless gives us the opportunity to see their true selves quickly. She basically writes action movies with realistic chemistry and better dialogue. 
 I had loads of fun reading Some Kind of Hero

While the whole "friends with benefits" theme has been done many times before, I really liked Zanetti's spin on it. In Rising Assets we have Colton and Melanie, two best friends since childhood who both have feelings for each other, but are unwilling to cross that line. I really loved their friendship and how close they were. It's understandable how, despite their strong feelings, they didn't want to take the risk. I enjoyed the slow progression from friends to lovers, complete with all the highs and lows you'd expect when two people try to make it work. 
 I thought Colton and Mel has great chemistry together. Not only were they amazing in bed, or rather, lack thereof, but they also had great dialogue and a general ease between them. They understood each other like no one else and it was clear how great these two were together. What had me entertained the most was how much their town knew they belonged together. You'll see a running gag throughout the whole story in that regards, but I don't want to give it away. While Colton ticked me off at times with his hesitance and also a rather needless blowout, I still really liked him as a character and as a person. He was a great guy to his family, friends, and the town. Mel was a stellar character, too. I loved how she didn't put up with Colton's crap and she was a strong, independent character in her own right. 
 The steam factor was definitely there for these two and while I always enjoy that, you know I look for more in romance novels nowadays. I have to say that even though Rising Assets didn't amaze me or anything, it still had a decent plot going aside from the romance. I also loved seeing familiar characters from the previous books and catching up on their lives. If you're a fan of this series already, you'll want to give this a read. As far as romance reads go, this one is light and quick one so I'm sure romance readers will enjoy it.

A math nerd who gets visions when touching people or personal objects, touching their calculators & having visions of their math problems makes her a tutoring genius. But visions of peoples emotions (she calls them fractals) with everything else makes an already awkward Eva, the queen of awkward. Eva accidentally touches new cute boy Zenn's jacket and she gets a hurricane of a fractal. The title Zenn diagram is a clever play on Venn diagram (the one with the overlapping circles) and Zenn's name. 
 "I envy how touch is, for most people, as easy as breathing" This book is a sweet sad, with doses of intelligent humor & the smile worthy quads. Her quadruplet 3 year old siblings that are the epitome of cuteness & a breath of fresh air for Eva (she can touch them because children's fractals are innocent, pleasant). 
 Having this ability all her life has made personal relationships quite hard, something the author succeeds in conveying. It is torture to find out things about others & not really being able to help. And exhausting to this big secret by avoiding touch (people think she is a germophobe), and all the people's you have learned by accident too. 
 The best friend who likes the popular guy & starts pulling away is a bit of a eye rolling cliche & in my opinion takes away from the story but luckily is quickly rectified. But Zenn is worthy of his name in the title. Not only is he gorgeous, but smart, grounded, hardworking, nice & gets Eva's dry skeptic wit & is quite witty himself. 
 And just when you think this is going to be an unusual romance due to the fractals, "bam!" a kick in the gut revelations proves yet again that the universe loves to play cruel jokes & the story changes again, to a shared tragedy. 
 A heartfelt great ending & a tear in your eye epilogue
