Changed My Opinion 
 Any time I hear someone mention World War I, it makes me cringe because it seemed to be the only thing we ever discussed in my history classes. However, this book completely changed my opinion. Yes, it's fiction but it made me rethink the war, strangely enough. The idea of having two groups, the Darwinists (Allies) and Clankers (Central Powers), is interesting in that it makes science play such a huge role in the war. As a science nerd, it made me love the book even more. 
 Monsters, Machinery, and Boys. Oh my! 
 These seem to be the three focuses of the novel. First off, there are the Darwinists, who's biological monsters walk the streets of London or fly through the air, like the airship Leviathan, which resembles a whale. Then there are Clankers, who are all about the machines and using technology versus biology. Everything's completely mechanical for them and they hate the Darwinists. Last, but not least, the two main characters: Alek, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, who's a Clanker and Deryn, a girl masquerading as a boy so she can fly with the Darwinists, must work together to stay alive. The combination of these three groups, plus beautiful descriptions, gave Leviathan a life of its own and made it stand out against any other steampunk novel I've ever read. 
 More MG, less YA 
 I love to read YA novels, however I found this book to be written more for a MG level. It was a very easy read in general, and the illustrations, while adding to the descriptions, also made it seem more childish. The main characters, Deryn and Alek, who are supposed to be around 15-16 years old seem younger. I thought it would be more of a YA novel but it seemed aimed at a younger audience as well. 
 Despite the novel seeming to be written more for an MG audience, I loved it and readily give it 5 stars. It was so different from any other book I've read, and added to that is my love for Scott Westerfeld's books, so I thoroughly enjoyed Leviathan.

Oscar, the title character, is a hand, a step below an apprentice, to the most powerful magician in this fantasy setting. It is Oscar's job to collect and combine the herbs that his Master and apprentice sell. He is told he is worthless, doesn't know anything by many characters and he's come to internalize it. It is Oscar's hero's journey, and ours, to discover just how much he knows and is capable of. 
 What's fascinating and very well done about this novel to me is that Oscar is clearly on the autism spectrum, though that word is never used to describe him, since it was first used in 1942. Instead, his behaviors are described: he has difficulty looking people in the eye, he doesn't understand facial expressions, he is able to concentrate and remember which plants do which things, but doesn't know how to speak to his neighbors, he reads very well, but writing is difficult for him and many more. This is up there with The Speed of Dark, Mockingbird and a few others as exemplary novels describing an autistic person's thought processes. To this reader, mom and special education teacher, anyway. 
 "There are ways to do things, ways to act with people, and I do not understand them. I cannot understand what people mean when they talk. I do not do things right. I do not feel things right. I do not see things right. I am not ...I'm not made of the same thing as everyone else." (216)

 The Map of Time by Felix J. Palma 
 Translation by Nick Caistor 
 My Rating: 2 of 5 Stars on Goodreads **Ultimately this book was not for me** 
 Genre: Alternate History, Romance, Mystery, Fantasy, Science Fiction 
 Audiobook: Narrated by James Langton 
 Produced by: Recorded Books, licensed by Simon & Schuster Audio 
 Felix J. Palma: Goodreads | Official Site | Twitter 
 Spanish writer, Felix J. Palma is acclaimed by critics as one of the most brilliant and original storytellers of our time, this novel is an international best seller and the recipient of the Ateneo de Sevilla XL Prize. 
 Summary 
 "Welcome, Dear Reader, as you plunge into the thrilling pages of our melodrama where you will find adventure of which you never dreamt!" 
 Broken into three parts, this novel begins with the story of Andrew Harrington, a privileged young man who is contemplating suicide over the guilt and loss of his love. Eight years earlier Andrew had fallen in love with Marie Kelly, a Whitechapel tramp, who becomes the fifth and final victim of the infamous Jack the Ripper. Andrew is now absorbed in his depression and guilt over arriving too late that very same evening to save her. Andrew's cousin, Charles, in order to dissuade Andrew from suicide, suggests traveling back in time to kill Jack before he has a chance to do in the poor Marie. This idea of course coming naturally to Charles since time travel is the current rage of the elite ever since the publication of H.G. Wells' famous novel, The Time Machine. Charles suggests going to Murray's Time Travel, who offers the opportunity to travel into the future to see the year 2000 and witness the battle between Man and Automatons, to organize a trip into the past. 
 Wells is the central piece of the three parts of the novel, each part acting as a mini stand-alone story with new side characters such as Tom and Claire in Part 2, the actions and characters all intersecting on Wells or his novel. In the end Wells is forced into hunting down a mysterious killer before its too late for him. 
 General Thoughts: 
 When a story opens the author makes the reader a promise. Here we are promised adventure coupled with two full pages of praise from reputable reviewers (some duplicated on the back cover), and the enticing cover art, all ensuring our investment to be that of quality and substance. 
 I personally envisioned proper time travel, a steampunk adventure through history, thus I did not feel satisfied that the promise to me was an honest one. The one theme that stood out to me was betrayal, not only the characters betraying one another but the reader also. The story was not the one I had envisioned prior to cracking the cover, but there were things that I liked and other things that were a hindrance to my liking the novel. 
 Palma was reaching for the original with this and he succeeded, truly I have not read a novel quite like it before. Was it an adventure that I have never dreamt of before? No. Palma has created a Victorian world very thoroughly, he was descriptive enough with the ensemble cast (their characters and attire) as well as the surroundings that I could picture Wells walking through old London. The story arc and character arcs were well planned out, the overlapping and returning to Wells was done with proper timing as to not let too much foreshadowing ruin the ultimate reveals. 
 However, in creating his plot web Palma provided extensive background on characters that I don't believe to be entirely necessary. These long winded diatribes stole the momentum of the story, as did the narrator. It seemed that the narrator was constantly reasserting his superior knowledge, redirecting the story at his whim, and adding in his own opinions on the situations and society at hand that ultimately detracted from the story for me. Part 2, for example, starts with the following, incase you forgot who was ultimately in charge: 
 "As I have previously explained, I possess the faculty to see everything, including what no one else can see..." 
 I enjoyed the individual character arcs for what they were (with the exception of Tom and Claire's relationship), and in the end with the culmination of all intertwined arcs I had a bit of enjoyment for not only the completion of the story but the end result for H.G. Wells. 
 Audiobook Review: 
 James Langton does a good job with this, he fits quickly into the overseeing narrator role quiet well, giving vocal changes when necessary for the character voices. His intonations assist in giving the story an added edge of suspense. 
 His voice however may have contributed to my increasing distaste for the narrator since he did a good job with that embodiment. And at the end his voice gets breathy when he voices yet another baddy (technical term) which I tend to have issues with in narrators. I'm sorry but nasal and breathy voices are like fingers on a chalk board for me. 
 Done Well: 
 This was indeed an original inventive story, blending together multiple genres to pull off a well executed web of character plots that come to a close in a complete package. 
 The overall structure of the novel and non-linear story structure parallel the time travel theme quite well. 
 Palma's execution of concepts of time travel and the effects that choices can make on reality, whether there truly do exist parallel universes, or whether time is a concept that only exists if there is someone to witness it, were structured an positioned well. Having Wells think in the terms of time travel, learning at the same pace as the reader. 
 Didn't work for me: 
 Pompous know-it-all narrator that approached the reader as if we were an unintelligent bafoon providing excessive background killing momentum from the plot. 
 Excessive background - really slowed the momentum for me. 
 Claire and her utter gullibility that allowed for everything that came out of her mouth and subsequent actions. I really wanted to reach through the pages of the book and slap her silly. 
 Lack of Steampunk and Science Fiction; again I was expecting a different story. 
 One of the larger issues I have is in the spoiler section below regarding time travel and how Palma worked part 3 of the novel. 
 I personally wish that I had the power to unravel time, so that I can have the hours dedicated to this book back. 
 ***SPOILER***  
 One other thing that did not work for me and which was (in my opinion) only just another way to flip the story on its head was the method of time travel that finally arrived in Part3. After being lied to about time travel (having no legitimate time travel up to this point just the continual farce of men) finally Palma gets to it, but I feel that he wrote himself in a corner and this was his only way out. A Gene activated by the Brain allows for time travel but not necessarily controllable time travel. H.G. Wells himself the father of a new human species that has the ability many, many generations into the future to properly control their mutant power. I had to re-listen to that segment of the audiobook again to ensure that I heard it correctly. I understand why it was done to a point, Palma needed a way to get Wells into the future not only with one journey but multiple lending to a larger time gap, meeting the lady who he would create his super time travel race with, and then allowing a letter written by Future Wells to end up in the hands of Present Wells. It felt out of place but was the only other option since Palma had already discounted both magic and scientific time travel via machinery.

Dead to You, by Lisa McMann, was a fascinating look into the lives of those affected by an abduction. It was a quick fast read that had me on the edge of my seat unable to put the book down until I finished it. 
 Ethan De Wilde was abducted at age 7. At 16, he's found his way home. Only he doesn't remember his life before the abduction, his younger brother is filled with anger, and he has a little sister he sees as the "replacement" child. Ethan and his family begin to work through his reintroduction but are met with a number of problems along the way. 
 I loved this book. Once I cracked the cover, I couldn't put it down. McMann's writing is superb. She's done her homework. You see the situation from every angle, from every character's point of view. And you feel the turmoil and anguish. The story is told from Ethan's point of view, and McMann is triumphant in delivery of a sixteen-year-old male's voice. She doesn't waste time with superfluous environmental descriptions, which I admire so much. It's refreshing to read an author who just gets down to business painting the emotions and situations that are pertinent to the storyline. 
 I really loved Ethan and his flaws. His thoughts were deep and real and emotional. The reader really gets to see inside his head and I liked it there. I loved Gracie and all of her lisping, adorable glory. I loved Maria De Wilde, a fierce mama bear who loved her family and worked hard to take care of them. She was the opposite of her husband Paul, who was quiet and uncertain at times, but like his wife, always tried to do the right thing for everyone. I loved Cami and her open, hopeful heart. I even loved Blake, or at least felt for him and saw his side of things. 
 I thought about giving this book fewer stars because of the ending, but couldn't. I was riveted the whole book. And I had doubts from the scene in the train station, so the last few chapters weren't entirely a surprise.  
 Plain and simple, this was a great read. I'd like more of the story and its characters.

 To summarize: I did not enjoy this book, but that's just because I like books to be plot-driven. I'd still recommend it for others.

This is a book after my linguist heart. Why do we use the words we do to describe the things we want to describe? Nick Allen, a 5th grader, asks that very question. When his teacher, Mrs. Granger, tells him that things are in the dictionary because someone, at some point, made them up, Nick decides to take matters into his own hands and changes the name of a "pen" to a "frindle." The word soon catches on and spreads beyond Nick's control. Mrs. Granger treats this as an issue of respecting her authority and the battle is on. 
 Overall, this slim children's book says a lot about language, conformity, the pressures of society, and the bravery to be a catalyst for change. The characters are well-rounded, including the authority figures, who are often painted with a broad brush in children's fiction as being the enemy--in Frindle, we see that different adults react differently to new things, and that adult reactions often have good underlying reasons. Brian Selznick's great pencil illustrations complement the text.

I've never read anything like that. It that uses the life of a famous actor who dies in the first scene of the book  as a framework for the characters and some of the plot. And also Shakespeare, to a somewhat smaller degree. 
 -The Writing: This woman has the power of words. I was swept away in her prose. It's true omniscient storytelling which is interesting. How she weaves these strangers together (and apart) over the course of decades--like 50 years--both before and after the Collapse is amazing. I could never write this book. I always ask myself, could I have written this? Could I have done it better? (I know, what hubris...) And this story is not the one I would tell and this method of telling it is definitely not one I could even think of. It is incredibly well-done. All of this intricacy draws you back chapter after chapter because you never know where the story will shift next, to which character, to what time. She even changes mediums, included letters and interviews at several points. She switches to present tense at times. It's very fluid and beautiful. 
 -The Setting: If you have ever spent any time trying to think of how the world ends (as I have extensively, for writing research primarily), then this is a great book. The author really dove into what it would be like at hour 1, day 3, month 7, year 15... She makes you feel like you can see it. I can see the world struck down by a crazy flu pandemic. I can feel the desperation and wildness of it. I liked seeing it from different POVS--different ages, genders, life stages, nationalities, locations. And I felt like I could picture it. I don't have to write that book now. It's been written. 
 What made this story not great/less interesting: 
 -The Characters: This is complicated. I don't really know how to explain it. I didn't hate them. Not at all. But I didn't love them. This being literary fiction, you come to expect the seemingly senseless deaths and tragedies that the godlike author loves to bestow on her captive readers. Everything seems so futile in the omniscient POV. Can I love a character that's likely to be killed by a crazy flu or anarchists or something in just a few poignant but casual words? Seriously, whole plot points are blown up in just a line or two. I found myself having to skip back on the audiobook because missing a tiny bit of narrative could mean missing a huge piece of the puzzle. That's an interesting skill to have as a writer, but to read...I don't know. It's not my favorite thing to read. And it's not that the story isn't emotional either. It is. There are passages about longing and life and regret and whatever... and they get you. You feel that wonderful sense of YES! But you're not going to cry over these people. You won't feel their loves. You won't ache for them when tragedy strikes again and again. There's a disconnect between you and the story. And I don't like that. I want to feel IN it. I want to be drowning in tears over every plot twist because I am the characters now and they are real to me...So maybe it's not about characters. Maybe it's The Tone. Or The Style. Or The Genre--because this is how literary fiction ALWAYS feels to me. 
 -Not Enough Shakespeare: When I read Just One Day and Just One Year by Gayle Forman, I remember feeling like I was living and breathing Shakespeare. It wasn't just a backdrop on the story. It pumped life into it. I wanted to read every play and go to the theater. I wanted to be able to talk conversationally about the themes of A Midsummer Night's Dream and King Lear. I felt like Shakespeare was a vital part of the story and LOVED it all. I thought I'd feel the same about a Traveling Symphony that survives by performing Shakespeare after the world ended. But it feels like a backdrop of this story. Not essential. It could be replaced with almost anything else. The real driver of this story is Arthur Leander (great name, btw, I could say that all day long). It's this dead actor who makes everything have meaning, gives characters their history, and their quirks. It's a fascinating device. It reminds me of the Brad Pitt movie Babel. It's good. But I wanted more of the Bard. 
 -Station Eleven: It's strange to me that this is the title of the book. I'm quite intrigued by the story's fictional graphic novel by the name and would love to see a very meta Rainbow Rowell-esque incarnation of it. But I don't see it being the thing that drives the story. Again, it's all about Arthur. "Station Eleven" is just another one of his things that gets woven and spun into and out of the lives of several characters. It could be that I, like Arthur himself, don't quite get the story of "Station Eleven." Perhaps it's something critical I missed while listening to the audiobook, but it doesn't seem worthy of the title of the book. But I liked that plot line. Take that as you will. 
 -The Narrator: For the first few hours listening to the audiobook narrator, I kept thinking she's similar to Khristine Hvam (who read the Daughter of Smoke and Bone series by Laini Taylor), but not quite good enough. Her tone is so dramatic sometimes. So deep. She voices children too low. She annunciates strangely sometimes. Eventually I got lost in the story and stopped critiquing the reader. But still, it stuck out to me. I'd probably still recommend the audiobook. I've only become this particular about readers after years and years of obsessive audiobook listening.

When I first read the summary of this book I immediately thought of the film Shes all that for some reason, you know 'boy bets friend he can get the girl and all that' so I guess that was what made me read it. Of course it wasnt actually like the film Shes all that because Brittany was rich and Alex was in a gang. This book was amazing, it tells the tale of Brittany who lives on the south side of town. Which is the rich end. Blonde, beautiful. Who pretends be this perfect girl at school who has her life all planned out for her. She portrays a role model for her school. And then you have Alex who lives on the west side of town. The poor end. Hes a bad boy, whos in gang wars and everyone is scared of him at school. Brittany dosent like Alex and Alex thinks shes a rich snob. So when their paired up for chemistry with each other it can only cause trouble? Wrong! He is easy going and gets along with everyone in it. I quite liked the friendship between Brittany and Sierra because unlike most books she wasnt a bad friend to Brittany she was there when she needed her. I think one of the most important things of this book that made me really give it the top rates was how they dealt with disablities, because Brittanys sister is disabled and unlike alot of books we got to see how families dealt with stuff like this and her sister made such a wonderful character in this book too because some people dont understand how difficult it can be.The ending was cute aswell, it has a pretty shocking epilogue that made me think on it for ages for some reason.

The Summer Prince is not what I expected. To be truthful, I expected fairies or some odd witches who can control the seasons. Maybe it's a hopeful thought inspired by The Iron Fey (written by Julie Kagawa). The Summer Prince should be named The Summer King instead because there isn't a Summer Prince in the book. (Another random thought of mine). 
 The Summer Prince is narrated by June Costa. Remember the term "starving artist?" Well, that's what June Costa seems to be. Underrated. Underappreciated. Invisible. Silent. Hidden. Worthless until dead. The Summer Prince tells of June's adventure and times through Palmare Tres. The Summer Prince is an Young Adult, Dystopian, and Futuristic book. The Summer Prince is amazing, and stunning. Every moment is surprising yet also random, or at least in the beginning. 
 The Summer Prince's plot is entertaining. Every moment is a moment I don't want to miss. The Summer Prince isn't crying material, but it is close, like many good books. As I think about this book over and over again, The Summer Prince gets better and better. The writing is somewhat confusing and the author didn't do a really good job of explaining the futuristic words (dialects). I had to guess the meanings because the words are so odd, and replaces nouns. 
 WOW! What a beautiful ending! I never dream the ending was going to be like that. (MINOR SPOILER ALERT) I thought that Enki was going to defy his destiny and live with June forever or at least until death. But no. He isn't going to. (END MINOR SPOILER) I almost, almost cried at the end. 
 Characters: 
 June is unafraid of being on the wrong side of law. She sees things in a whole different perspective than normal people. We see a king, but she sees an artist. A possible friend and maybe even more than that. (Or at least she likes to think so). June struggles with her identity and roles in her life. She doesn't know what to do and is going in circles until she met Enki. All because of a boy, like always. 
 Enki is trapped within a pretty and rich cage. He's fearless, scandalous, and unafraid to do something totally outrageous, like upsetting the Queen and even boldly daring the Aunties. (I have no idea who are the Aunties, but they seem to be advisers to the Queen and hold some power). I can see why June is so smitten with Enki. 
 Rating: Four out of Five

This is a very particular kind of fantasy novel, as much a literary (filled with albeit imaginary books) novel as it is a deep travelogue between two richly imagined fantasy lands. 
 At first, I was put off by the oh so lengthy passages of works and legends and overlong paragraphs, but like a lot of great fiction, it takes a learning curve and it often takes a bit of patience. Once I fell into the actual story rather than the many allusions made of whole cloth from a new mythology both familiar to us and strange, it became much easier to read. 
 The fact is: there's an awful lot to love in this novel as long as you're a lover of myths, stories within stories within stories, and don't mind being thrown into the mind of a heavy reader and eventually the mind of a heavy writer that is literally spurned on to write by the demonic exhortations of a ghost he eventually learns to love. 
 And don't think this is an entirely dry novel, either, because it eventually has some startling surprises and import for the land he's visiting. It's hard being a holy man, especially if you're a tourist, but it shouldn't be any kind of surprise that tourists will eventually return home and bring along tales and change. 
 It's a very satisfying novel if you can get through it, but be forewarned, it's dense with words and myth. It's a true work of the imagination, drilling deep and deeper and deeper into the two worlds that had been written. 
 Take your time, too. You'll be glad you did. :)

This is a book that I delved in quite quickly. It's a feel-good romantic comedy that could be the alternative script in some parallel universe if The Big Bang Theory chose to rewrite the show so that Sheldon Cooper would have a romantic relationship with Penny (a smarter Penny perhaps). 
 Yes, this comparison's already been mentioned a couple of million times, but it's true. Don Tillman is what I would imagine to be a more handsome, older version of Sheldon with high functioning Autism - or Asperger's. Another good comparison would be Adam, from the film Adam, starring Hugh Dancy (a great film by the way). But enough with all the comparisons, and let's stick to the story. 
 I found Don to be really charming despite his lack of it, I found him to be really considerate despite his lack of consideration, and I found him to be really really sweet. When Don and Rosie meet and they start hanging out, I loved watching him slowly let go and allowing himself to sort of follow Rosie's lead for a change, and do things her way. I enjoyed their interactions, their conversations, how she seemed to bring out a side of him that's not been seen by any of his friends and family before. She was able to make him feel love, but she was also able to make him feel hurt, and I think that's important in this overall journey of emotions that Don was experiencing. We got to know him better through Rosie, we were able to understand him better, to delve into his life a little deeper, and find out things about him and his past that we probably wouldn't have known had it not been for Rosie's influence on him. 
 But the story was very funny too! In true RomCom style, their interactions varied from laugh out loud funny to cringe-worthy. Their trip to New York was very interesting for me, and I loved how Simsion made me actually feel like I was experiencing New York with them! The mystery to try and find out who Rosie's biological father was also a great storyline, even though I had it figured out long before they did. 
 Over all, a fun and charming story to read. I actually seem to be picking up a lot of books with autistic characters lately (mother mother, the curious incident of the dog, rosie project, and now reading Isla and the happily ever after), but I would say Don has been my favourite character out of the bunch so far.

[[5 STARS]] 
 It's not secret that Alpha Ze'ev Kesley owns a special place in my heart. I love him like most of the fandom love Thorne. Seriously, I live for any time the name "Wolf" is mentioned in the stories. And this gorgeous little novella was just what I needed in my life. A glimpse into Wolf before he was conscripted; his time after he was turned into a Lunar Special Operative - a story about how he became Alpha of his pack. I adored every single thing about this and seriously couldn't allow myself to give it any less that 5 stars, if I'm completely honest with myself haha.

There are certain things about this series that I absolutely loved. Each character has their own personality and reason for being involved with the story that I could actually get behind. 
 I was especially impressed with the monstrous humanoid characters of Achmed the Snake, and Grunthor, Child of the Stone. Achmed is an assassin who is freed early on from his enslavement to his brotherhood by the character of Rhapsody. He is unlikable and gruff and very driven, which of course makes me want to read about more of him all the time. Grunthor, with his booming character and jolly warrior mentality wormed his way into my heart very early on in the story. 
 I wanted to like Rhapsody as well. I have a soft spot for fantasy stories featuring a strong female lead...but the more I read about perfect Rhapsody and her obliviously beautiful nature the more I was like 'okay...that's nice...so when does she fall in love with one of the two monster brothers' 
 Spoiler alert, she doesn't. She falls into the 'destined romance' trope with a beautiful boy she had a moment of passion with that she barely remembers. A kindred love or whatever. 
 The writing is solid, the story is solid, and I may find myself reading the rest of the series at some point in the future, but I had really hoped that the author wouldn't fall for the same tired tropes that I have seen in so many fantasy stories recently.

This was a nice blend of fairy tales and sci-fi. I like how each book in incorporates a different fairy tale into the overall arc of the story. In the first one I would have never guessed how Wolf's character would come to blend into the story nor Scarlett's. There wasn't a part of the story that seemed easy to guess. Another late night finishing this since I just couldn't put it down.

And from there, in every reincarnation he has, the catalyst that causes his death is getting his memories back and having sex with Regin. 
 Now we have Declan. He has had a ROUGH life. Before we get to hear about any of that I thought he was the biggest ass. He treated all immortals in captivity with an iron fist. He abused them, tortured them, and had no respect for anyone. On top of that he was a bit of a junkie with the drug he was taking to suppress his berserker nature. And he didn't treat Regin any better. I will say that I was VERY glad he was not the one that left Regin in the state we saw a glimpse of in the last book. That was done behind his back and as soon as he found out he went on a rampage! Awwww And that Regin couldn't go through with getting his memories back so that he would die. 
 He just grew on me. He managed to really care for Regin and take care of her. And by the end of the book I was happy that she ended up with Declan instead of Aidan, even though I felt the other way around before. Or maybe you can say she has the best of both? 
 Lothaire... Lothaire... Lothaire... Sneaky little vampire! What is with him? Who is he rescuing? What is he doing? I can't wait for his book!

 Favorite Quotes: 
 "She feared that she might be a lot more than infatuated with this reincarnation. Like on her way to falling-off-a-skycraper-onto-your-face in love with him." 
 "Can you see me, see the man that I am? Accept me, Regin, because I'm holding to nothing but you."

 I have so many conflicting feelings about this book. First, it was my first Neal Stephenson book and also first cyber punk novel. I also listened to this book on Audible which probably wasn't the best idea since this book, for me anyway, required a lot of concentration. 
 There were large portions of the book that were basically big info dumps. Not that I necessarily minded that. Those parts of the book, where the idea of Snow crash, ancient religions and viruses, Sumeria, and binary code, were discussed in great depth were actually some of my favorite parts of the book. I thought the ideas in the book were highly original and practically genius. I was blown away by Stephenson's amount of research and creativity that went into this book. On this level I would have clearly given the book 5 stars. 
 But I could not get into the plot of this book. For me, the ideas were so exciting and original that the execution and main plot points of the book paled in comparison. Most of the book felt disjointed to me. There were many different plot points going on, which I usually enjoy very much, but they didn't weave together coherently enough for me. The character build up was ok, but I felt we didn't learn that much about the characters and their backstory until well into the last half of the book. I wish we could have gotten to know them earlier. Then I might have felt a greater connection to them. 
 As it was, I often found myself struggling to keep listening to the story and was glad when it ended. I might give another Stephenson novel a try in the future, but it's definitely not a priority.

For a long time the shack has been on my list of books to read. Church friends have raved about how amazing this book is. It's a NY times best seller. A couple of years ago at parachute music festival the author was one of the speakers and while i don't remember what exactly he spoke about I remember it being very engaging. And then the movie is coming out this year so of course i needed to read the book first beforehand. 
 So now that I have actually finished the book I have mixed feelings about it. Yes I liked it, but have to say it was waaaaay overhyped. 
 So lets break this down a bit. 
 Things I liked: 
 The characterisation of God. 
 I thought this was done so well, and how the author has portrayed the various facets of God just worked. I remember hearing the controversy about how one part of god was portrayed as a black woman, but you know what it made me smile and really wasn't too much of a stretch of the imagination. Actually the way that God was written was full of life and just felt real and relatable. 
 The explanations for common theological questions. 
 This I thought was also very well done. The explanations made a lot of sense and were pretty easy to follow. 
 Missy's story arc 
  Ok the resolution of Missy's story made me cry, that was just painful to read, but any book that makes me care that much about a character or storyline to make me cry instantly gets bonus points  
 Things I did not like: 
 The human characters ( except Missy ;) ) 
 I just didn't connect with them. To be fair I think because they, and when I say they i'm mostly talking about Mackenzie, was used to be more of a plot device to explain theology rather than a fully developed character in their own right. I could see the author was really trying to develop the characters and I mean the whole point of the book was  the reconciliation of Mackenzie with God, and that is major character development . But I just wasn't feeling it. I think it was because Mac was suppposed to be average human, who really could actually be you or me asking God all the questions we have about life, the world and God himself. And just because of the way it's portrayed Mac just felt flat. Plus the writing at the start and the end in the 'real world' was pretty average, it threw me out of the story and I just couldn't connect 
 The information dumps

 After We Fall is a beautiful and emotional second chance love story. It will make you cry and break your heart, but just as quickly, it will make you laugh out loud and feel giddy with hope. 
 I loved Jack and Margot - both individually and together. I also loved that the story was told from both of their points of views and that we got glimpses into the feelings and reasons they were acting the way they were. On paper, Margot and Jack couldn't be more different, but once the walls and masks fell away, they really complemented each other so well. I did want to scream at Jack a few times for the way he behaved, but in the end it was hard not to fall in love with him after everything he had experienced. Plus, there were plenty of swoony and steamy moments that left me blushing! Let's just say, that I have a new appreciation for farmers! ;) 
 The other characters in the book were just as great! I loved Jack's brothers, Pete and Brad, and his sister in law, Georgia, and how cute was his nephew, Cooper!? My heart melted every time they were together. I liked that his family pushed when they needed to, but also just supported Jack the way that they thought was most helpful (even if Jack didn't/couldn't see it that way). I especially enjoyed Margot's best friend, Jamie. She is the girlfriend we all need, who will tell you like it is, but still have your back 100%. One of my favorite parts of the book though, were all the scone puns! Seriously, they were so funny and helped lighten the mood when things got a little heavy. 
 I definitely enjoyed After We Fall a lot and the only reason it's not 5 stars for me is that I'm not really a fan of the dead spouse/lover storyline and I thought the ending chapters felt a little rushed. The epilogue was perfection though and Melanie's writing is so witty and relatable that this was still an amazing read! If you're really not a fan of the dead spouse trope though, you may not enjoy the book as much since it plays a big part in Jack's character arc.

 My first ever Chief Inspector Gamache novel was The Beautiful Mystery, which is #8 in the series.I fell in love with Louise Penny's writing and Chief Inspector Gamache and have started on the series from the beginning, recently finishing Still Life. How the Light Gets In does not disappoint. The storytelling is luminescent, the plotting taut and filled with suspense, the characters charming and emotional. I cried for Jean-Guy, I laughed at Ruth and her duck, I ached for Chief Inspector Gamache, and I hated Francouer for what he was doing to Jean-Guy and to Gamache. 
 How the Light Gets In is two mysteries in one. Constance Pineault visits Myrna, her friend and former therapist, in the little village of Three Pines, but before she returns for a second visit at Christmas, she is murdered in her home. With her untimely death comes the revelation that she was the last survivor of the famous Ouillet quintuplets. In the background of her death and Gamache's investigation is Francouer's campaign to destroy Gamache. 
 I couldn't put it down. Penny paces the story well, keeping key information hidden while artfully placing breadcrumbs along the trail, leading the reader through the maze. Following them is compulsive, and each one is a discovery, but the motives and the solution remain a mystery until they are disclosed with all the finesse of a master magician. 
 I told a friend that reading Louise Penny's writing is, for me, the literary equivalent of listening to the opera. And this is opera at it's finest, complete with comical characters, tragedy, depth of emotion and, finally, redemption. If you haven't read one of these books, this one is a good place to start. I enjoyed reconnecting with Three Pines and its residents, all introduced in Still Life, but I find that each of these books stands well on its own. Like me, you'll probably finish it and then run out to get and read the rest of the series. 
 At the time this review is posted, this book is available on pre-order. While you're waiting for the publication date, you'll have time to read The Beautiful Mystery - or any one of the other books in the series.

I'll try to keep this as brief as possible, because I could honestly write for the next four hours about precisely everything that I hated about this. 
 Firstly; the plot was unforgivable. This was literally a compilation of all the worst, most stupid, most common fanfic tropes. My first clue was the Trolley Witch T1000  moment. I mean... why? It wasn't funny, it wasn't scary. It didn't add to the Harry Potter world, or create an exciting new piece of wizarding world lore. It was just bad. Like, really cringey bad. And then things got worse when Albus and Scorpius break ALL THE RULES THAT WE KNOW ABOUT TIME-TURNERS for reasons we're only vaguely assured of (there's some half assed, unconvincing explanation in the last twenty pages, but it's hardly a fix . And worse  when they get back to the future and Biff is the president and strong, smart, girl-power Hermione is a miserable spinster because she never married Ron (? the fuck JK?) and we're wishing each other a Happy Voldemort's Day (? the fuck JK?), and of all the beloved characters we could have revisited we end up with Ludo Bagman (? the fuck JK?), Bane the centaur (? the fuck JK?) and an in-depth exploration of why kind, gentle, charming Cedric would *definitely have become a Death Eater if someone embarrassed him in front of his peers* . And finally, the Voldemort and Bella baby  thing. Again, why? It's inconceivable within everything we know of the characters. Mercedes from Mercy's Bookish Musings made the excellent point that instead of stubbornly remaining fixated on the one "bad guy" we're familiar with, why aren't there new ones? As Sirius so eloquently puts it, "the world isn't divided into good guys and Death Eaters". 
 And the beautiful, powerful themes from the original stories seemed to have gone out the window here. If poor Delphi, despite not ever meeting Voldemort or Bella, was doomed to be evil purely because of her parentage, doesn't that totally contradict "It is our choices not our qualities that determine who we are, Harry" ? And what about this awful, one-dimensional, Slytherin-bad, Gryffindor-good? Haven't we moved past this? What the hell point are you trying to make with this?  
 To be honest, this felt lazy and heartless. These didn't feel like the characters we grew up alongside.  Harry's an arrogant asswipe who speaks to McGonagall, one of his greatest mentors and adult influences, like a rude customer at the drive-thru speaks to the server. Ron's reduced to the weird-uncle character. And I've already touched on Hermione and Cedric's very confusing developments. The new characters suck as well. Sorry to the Scorpius lovers, but dialogue like "Zoinks, oh my Dumbledore, my geek-ness is off the charts!". Paraphrased but you get it. . 
 I'm not sure what I expected, but I'm more disappointed than even my worst expectations could have allowed for. If the Powers That Be were really, *really* determined to continued milking this particular cow, an homage to what we know and love would have more than sufficed. It didn't need to be a huge, fast paced adventure story. That's not what we were looking for. We wanted to catch up with our old friends from Hogwarts and see how they're doing and be reminded why we loved it so much in the first place.

 Gavin Brawley is star tight end of the New York Barons's American football team. And he's got himself a six month house arrest because he couldn't control his temper. This temper is well know both on and off the field and now, because of his house arrest, he needs a personal assistant who can stand up to his temper. 
 Enter Noah Monroe, a guy who needs a job - any job. With student debt, his father being sacked and leaving his last job under a cloud (thanks to his boss/ex), he thinks taking this job will be easy. It's only for six months. What's the worse that could happen? 
 I still whizzed through them both within four/five days (which, for me, is fast!) and it was a fun, addictive read. 
 Also, I liked that, even though the timeline was six months and the story jumped forward a few weeks every now and then (and sometimes, that did annoy me), I liked that it was a slow burn romance. It wasn't insta-love (a troupe I am slowly growing to dislike) and it did have a level of snark that I warm to. Plus, I liked reading from both Noah's and Gavin's points of view (though I do wish that, when this happens in books, each character has a different font so readers can go "Oh, am reading Character X or Character Y). 
 Just a tiny heads-up, there are sex scenes in here. No "Fade to Black". So, if you are not a fan of sex scenes but want to read this, you might want to fast forward these chapters. 
 There are one or two things I want to nitpick over. The first is that, at times, there was a few troupes and cliches that I saw and went "... really?" over. I know that this is going to happen with romance novels - I know this, I accept this - but am always a fan of a surprise twist or someone taking a troupe and turning it on its head. Plus, there was one or two moments I thought "I wonder if this is going to go Scandal and we have Noah doing the "If you want me, EARN ME!" scene [probably the best in Scandal from the little I have seen - plus, if anyone fancies writing a romance with a gay/bi/pan president or Prime Minster, please do and shout at me! I will read the heck out of it!) 
 The second nitpick is the pacing. Most of the time, I was on board with it. The romance is a slow burn and I like a nice slow burn. But then, with the last 20% of the book, things happened which felt a little fast. I get why, but there was a moment I went "If this had a extra few percent, this could be dragged out a little more". Maybe I like the angst and the heartbreak and I wanted to see the fallout. 
 I liked this (though adult romance is outside my comfort zone) and am tempted to see what happens in the next book in the series, Down by Contact, which follows another character who I really loved reading. As long as it's just as fun, sexy and addictive, this series and me should get on...

 The first Monster Haven book was a fun supernatural romp through a wacky urban fantasy world. It had some issues with plotting, not thoroughly mixing the storylines. Luckily, Pooka in My Pantry shows vast improvement in this area. The plotting was more consistent, and tension was sustained for a longer amount of time. I'm always glad to see an author improve, and Ms Naquin did overcome some issues that were prevalent in her debut novel. 
 Because of the happenings in Pooka in My Pantry, the tone of the novel is slightly more serious than the one in Monster in My Closet. Though it never gets truly dark, the atmosphere in this novel fits the subject matter. The stakes are raised for out main characters, as the people Zoey loves get in plenty of danger. It made for an engaging read, but for me the fun moments were too few and far in between. I was hoping for more laughs from this book, and less sadness. 
 That said, the Monster Haven world is still crazy, and I always enjoy seeing what kind of monsters the author comes up with now. The world is slowly expanding, more lore is being added, without it being overwhelming. I'm looking forward to see what comes next for Zoey, the reaper she's dating, and her closet monster.

After so much time, reading a Miranda Kenneally book feels like coming back home.

 I loved the overall story, the characters, the ending - which for me didn't read like a cliffhanger at all (like so many people kept saying)... It just felt like a beautiful, open ending, full of hope. 
 Annie is extremely easy to relate with... 
 She is so transparent, her emotions so open. I can't say that I cared much for her past relationship - you know, with it being 'past' I felt quite a bit detached, but I understood her pain, her commitment. 
 Her heart is filled with grief (as she's lost an entire future with the boy she loved) and she is struggling to heal, but there is so much more to this character and I loved to see her evolve through the story. 
 Don't get me wrong, this is not only a book about getting over a lost love, "Breathe, Annie, Breathe" is also about friendship, about working hard for the things you want so badly, and about getting there through all the pain that comes with the hard work. It is a book about devotion, about exceeding your limits, about pushing yourself over the edge when you feel like you can make it. 
 And it is also a love story... 
 The romance is sweet. It doesn't have the usual pacing at all, it feels more like a summer storm - unpredictable, unstable, still refreshing and most needed. 
 Friendship is another aspect that I loved... And if you've read the other books in the series, you will be pleased to see some of the main characters from back then. 
 I could say more about this book, but I won't. I will leave you discover it page by page and I hope that you will enjoy it just as much as I did. Just keep in mind that this is a wonderful contemporary story that has the power to steal your heart.

I love the Percy Jackson series. It's great for what it is (kid's literature). Rick Riordan isn't the world's best writer, but his books are entertaining and educating at the same time, and the PJ series in particular has an engaging plot and characters. Most of what he's written after that series has felt kind of redundant to me, not only in plot, but also in the way that he structures both individual books within a series and the series as a whole. The Heroes of Olympus is a continuation of the Percy Jackson universe with new characters mixed in, and besides a little bit of repetition, it's pretty great. The Kane Chronicles trilogy - of which The Serpent's Shadow is the third and final volume - has been much more problematic for me the whole way through. 
 The Kane Chronicles follows brother and sister Sadie and Carter Kane, who are descended on their father's side from the Egyptian pharoahs. They also happen to be magicians and hang out with Egyptian gods on a regular basis. The big villain of the trilogy is the god Apophis, the chaos serpent. The big quest in The Serpent's Shadow is for the kids and their team of fellow magicians to find a way to defeat Apophis's plan to swallow the sun and turn the forces of chaos loose on the universe. The plot is pretty standard, and I bet you can guess how it all turns out, but where The Serpent's Shadow fails (and I think where the whole trilogy fails) is in the way Riordan brings that story across. Book two show marked improvement over book one, The Red Pyramid, so I had high(ish) hopes for book three. But The Serpent's Shadow ended up being almost as disappointing as book one. 
 In addition to not really caring about any of the characters, I was completely turned off by the framing device, which involves Riordan pretending that Sadie and Carter would stop and take the time to painstakingly "record" their story conveniently in the style of children's novel on some battered audiocassettes or something. This was cheesy for the first two books, but at least it made some sort of sense, as purportedly Sadie and Carter were recording this in case something happened to them and they didn't make it out alive. Obviously, they made it out alive from The Serpent's Shadow, if they're making the recording, so what's the point? Nothing, except Riordan being cutesy and giving himself the excuse to have Sadie and Carter "adorably" interrupt one another whilst recording. I wish it had just been a straight up book-book, you know? Not to mention, hi! Spoiler! They make it out alive! Happy ending! And with the exception of a truly creepy solution to Sadie's love triangle problem (she's in love both with Anubis the god of death, who appears to her in the form a gorgeous leather-clad seventeen year old boy, and with her fellow wizard, Walt, who is dying of a King Tut's curse, King Tut being his ancestor), the book is just really kind of predictable. 
 In the case of the mythological gods universe that Riordan has created, I'm starting to think that more isn't more. The more "epic" stuff he shoves in to his universe, the less epic the stories actually feel. One of the reasons I loved the original Percy Jackson series so much is that it felt kind of intimate and cozy to be a part of that world, but each of his successive books have just had more and more stuff stuffed into them that there's barely any room for coziness at all. Hints that The Kane Chronicles actually exists in the same fictional universe as Percy Jackson and Company should get me excited, but really it just makes me nervous. The idea of combining the Egyptian gods with the Roman/Greek ones somewhere down the line is intriguing, but I'm not exactly sure Riordan could pull it off. He does his best work with a small cast of characters, with one or two major plot threads. I have a feeling that any Kane Chronicles/Percy Jackson crossover would end up just being another example of even more plot stuffed into even less space, with less room for all the stuff that I love about these universes he's created.

I selected The Underground Railroad because it was a group read choice and it had received so much acclaim that I considered it worth a shot. 
 To lay everything on the table before I get into why I'm giving such a highly regarded novel only three stars, I will say that while I absolutely love historical fiction, and the setting for this book is one I've studied at least a moderate amount, this period is not one that usually grips me in any way. As a result, I would never have selected this book if it hadn't been part of a group read. 
 Whitehead's work is fabulous, and I can absolutely see why The Underground Railroad became so popular. By creating characters with depth and interest, placing them into a well-known yet difficult time in history, and bending some elements of the truth in order to create a more fascinating narrative, Whitehead gives new consideration to runaway slaves (albeit fictional ones). 
 Thanks to the great writing and clever chapter divisions, the story carries the reader without any hesitation or lag. Knowing what happens to any of the characters, especially to Cora, feels important and necessary, rather than just like an interesting possibility. 
 One thing I really enjoyed was Cora's progression, especially involving her various jobs and the way in which her thoughts were clear and strong. This felt like a good decision to help readers follow along and better understand where Cora was coming from and what the difference really was between what she was being told and what she believed. 
 Despite all of these positives, I only just sort of liked The Underground Railroad. In short, it simply wasn't for me, as I originally predicted. I did really like Cora as a character, and I was curious to see how her story would unfold. Nevertheless, I wasn't drawn in by this story as much as I'm sure I was meant to be, if only because I knew of so many other time periods I would've preferred exploring. 
 Whitehead deserves great credit for the thought-provoking novel he wrote, and I recommend this for anyone who's interested, even though it wasn't my favorite by any means.

 I love reading book set in Regency England. I will literally read ANY fantasy book set in Regency England. Throw in good writing, an enjoyable practical Main Character, and a decent premise? I am there so hard! 
 So my favorite thing about this book: Helen is a young aristocratic girl out for her first season. She is also a "demon" fighter with super powers. How will she go out and about fighting demons when she also has to go to balls and other social events, be chaperoned everywhere and basically do what everyone tells her to. 
 The conflict in this book is so delicious. It's uncomfortable in the best ways. I love that Helen actually thinks about things and although she has reservations, it's not the "I just want to be a cheerleader" kind that other super girl types have. She legit is worried about the danger, not just to her person, but to her soul. BECAUSE THAT JUST MAKES SENSE, am I right? Helen doesn't rush into things head first and she isn't whiny and pathetic. She takes the time to think about things, but she's still an interesting character. 
 Goodreads reviewer, Emily May pointed out that Unwed girls of this time have VERY FEW choices in life and in a genre where super girl types usually have no choice but to accept the responsibility thrust upon them, Helen has a choice here. I love that. The juxtaposition of having few choices in her daily life vs. having a choice whether or not to join up with a demon fighting group. Really cool. And how it's handled in the end is really good. 
 I don't like Lord Carlston, Helen's magic mentor. And I don't think you as a reader are really supposed to. Helen barely even likes him. I don't really like the chemistry/attraction between them as barely there as it is. 
 I really didn't like Helen's brother, although he redeems himself a little in the end. 
 And I started out like the Duke of Selburn, but I don't really like him that much in the end. He seems too much like a plot foil and not enough like a real person. 
 I am Hella excited for Book 2 though. And I definitely recommend this book!

 All I need Is You is the first book I have read by Wendy S. Marcus, and the second book in the Loving You series. It was a quick, easy read, and grabbed me at the start with the letters between Neve and Rory being the introduction to the story, but it wasn't without its issues, and for me they detracted a bit from my overall enjoyment. 
 I liked Rory, back from a year serving in Afghanistan, he has returned with more than a few bad memories, and I liked the way he tried to work through the PTSD without involving Neve. And although I loved the way Neve helped Rory with his demons, and the bond that formed between them due to the mutual care taking, I really struggled to find much else about her that I liked for the rest of the book. 
 I have no issue with the fact that prior to Rory entering her life, she was happy to go out and take exactly what she wanted from a man, and then leave in the morning with no regrets, but the authors portrayal of this and the recurring incidences of her past 'one and dones' continually popping up just went a little too far for me. Her internal monologue and reactions to things at points just had me thinking 'bitch' and added to her overall up and down mood swings it just got a little tiresome. 
 There are a lot of secondary characters in this one too, Rory's family, Nate (Neve's brother) as well as many more, and to be honest at points everything that was going on felt a little too busy, and erroneous to the actual focus of the story. 
 This wasn't a bad book, and I would certainly think about reading more from the author in the future, it just didn't tick all of my boxes on this occasion. Although book two in the series, I believe it can absolutely be read as a standalone as I didn't feel I was missing out on anything having not read Loving You Is Easy.

Lately I find myself in the frustrating position (not uncommon among booksellers) of being surrounded by far more books than I can read. Not only are there books in the shop, but in my spare moments at work I browse Goodreads, Abebooks and my local library system, and so have a constant stream of books passing through my hands, many of which I can do no more than glance at before returning them or putting them away for later. Into this deluge has flowed this novella by Clarice Lispector, a book which I hear tell was scribbled on scraps of paper at intervals of months or years before coalescing into its current form, and which is - on one level - as evanescent and difficult to grasp as this technique suggests, even while being - on another - as direct as a bullet to the heart at ten paces. Imagine that famous Goya painting with the white shirt and the firing squad, but focus on the victim's face until you're so close the ridges in the paint are as important - as moving - as his expression. Ever read the Borges story 'The Secret Miracle'? When the raindrop which has hit Jaromir Hladik's face just as time stopped starts sliding again, that's maybe something like the little self-conscious 'explosions' with which Lispector riddles her narrative. Structurally, strip Beckett's Malone Dies to the bone - the fictional writer who tells the story as much the protagonist as s/he whose story he tells - and you've got a rough outline of The Hour of the Star. I say rough because either this is a book to read two or three times before knowing anything certain about it or my current white-water reading technique is just not up to the task. Whatever the case, this is a hard book to comprehend, coming as it does so directly from a place beyond comprehension, and I presume Lispector made a habit, like Beckett, of gazing intently on things beyond comprehension. Still, it's not a 'difficult' book - not on the level of language, anyway - and reports of the strangeness of its prose have, to my mind, been exaggerated. To me it reads quite naturally, especially in the new translation, and from what few pages I saw of the old translation I suggest forgetting that relic immediately and getting your hands on this one. It's modern, that's for damn sure - I doubt there is much else out there as sleek and arresting and asymmetrical as this. And it's haunting: Lispector speaks through her (male) narrator who speaks through his character Maccabea. I had just read (on the train to and from work, as perhaps readers of the Brazilian newspaper which published them might have read them) Lispector's Chronicas when I started the novella, and consequently had a vivid, if oblique, impression of her in mind as I read this. Unfortunately I don't have a copy of The Hour of the Star with me as I write, but perhaps these lines from one of her Chronicas ('Creating Brasilia') will help suggest the kind of writer she is or can be: 
 Brasilia is built on the line of the horizon. 
 When I died, I opened my eyes one day and there was Brasilia. 
 The two architects who planned Brasilia were not interested in creating something beautiful. That would be too simple; they created their own terror, and left that terror unexplained. 
 Besides the wind, there is another thing that blows. It can only be recognised in the supernatural rippling of the lake. - Wherever you stand, you have the impression of being on the edge of a dangerous precipice. 
 Its founders tried to ignore the importance of human beings. The dimensions of the city's buildings were calculated for the heavens. 
 It is a shore without any sea. 
 How I should love to set white horses free here in Brasilia. At night, they would become green under the light of the moon - I know what those two men wanted: that slowness and silence which are also my idea of eternity. 
 Fear has always guided me to the things I love; and because I love, I become afraid. 
 What kind of writer is Clarice Lispector? The rarest kind. The fact that her Chronicas ever made it into a newspaper at all - let alone week after week - is, to this Australian, astonishing. That The Hour of the Star is a bestseller and its author a household name in her own country is even moreso. Judging from what little I've read, Lispector's ruthless stripping away of everything but the visionary/intuitive/paradoxical is unmatched by any prose writer except Beckett, and when and if I ever have the time and resources to do so I will approach her ouevre as I once approached his: piece by piece, in a quiet room in the country with her biography close at hand. 
 This is a work so elemental it seems hewn from rock, or washed up on the shore in Brasilia from that non-existent sea. If I don't give it a perfect score it's only because I don't yet know if she speaks directly to my heart. But her example, her aesthetic determination, is unsurpassed. 
 Clarice Lispector: this woman, our contemporary, a Brazilian woman... it is not books that she gives us, but the act of living saved by books, narratives, constructions that make us step back. And then, through her window-writing, we enter into the frightening beauty of learning how to read: and we pass, through the body, to the other side of the I. To love the truth of what is alive,... to love the origin, to be personally interested in the impersonal, in the animal, in the thing. 
 (Helene Cixious)

Makani makes one jealous mistake and her life was over. She lost her boyfriend and her friends. Not even her parents look at her the same, not that she blames them. Her parents decide to ship her off to live with her grandma and enter a small town life where no knows who she is and what her secret is. However, small town life goes from normal to alarming when a terrifying killer appears without a clear pattern. 
 I really enjoyed the rotating perspectives with Makani being the central voice that we see. I love several of the characters, especially Makani's grandma. I would love to hang out with her grandma and put together puzzles and stuff. I loved Makini's friends and the high school gossip element as well. It reminded me of being back in school and the gossip that spread fast. 
 However, there were a few things that kept taking me out of the story. The first thing is Makani's big secret past. I wish we knew what it was a lot sooner than when she finally spilled the beans so that we knew what was weighing her down so much. I was finding myself more interested in what the big secret was than the murder plot. Finally, the romance plot overshadows the horror plot. I wish the creepy factor was a little more amped up and that the romance was scaled back a bit. 
 Several of my friends have been raving about this book, so I really wanted to love it. Sadly, it just isn't a match made in heaven. For me, this novel is far more YA romance than horror, which is not something that I was expecting. There are things that I like about this book, but the things that bothered me just made it fall flat. All in all, it's not a bad book. There are definitely some good things going on in it. I think it simply comes down to it just not being my cup of tea. That said, several of my friends love it and I already plan on recommending it to a few more because I know they'll love it too. I also think that it would make a great slasher movie that I would most likely enjoy.

Westerfeld's first book in three years might well be his most experimental. Split between two different narratives - the real-world trials and tribulations of Darcy Patel as she gets into writing, living on her own, finding her first love (with another girl - kind of a shocker, because like Willow Rosenberg, Darcy never really was into girls until she met that one that made her happy), mixed with the text of her novel-within-the-novel, also called Afterworlds. 
 I actually found myself relating to Darcy a lot. Like her, I write (not officially published yet, but hopefully someday it'll happen!) Like her, I take my parents' religion and alter it considerably so it could sell as a YA novel (but I don't feel quite so guilty about it, even though my parents' religion has a reputation for causing guilt). Like her, I'm finding myself falling for a girl who writes her own unique story (but Angel doesn't have the same kinds of issues as Imogen.) 
 The odd thing is, I found myself more interested in Darcy's story than in the story of her creation, Lizzie. Even though Lizzie had a great and unique story that felt like traditional Westerfeld material (Lizzie sure beats Tally and Jessica, and is on par with Hunter, but still falls short of equaling Westerfeld's best protagonists, Cal, Alek, and Deryn), it wasn't quite as engaging. 
 Still, though, I really hope there's a sequel to this one, because this book felt like it ended way too abruptly, especially with Darcy's story. We never even get to find out what "Untitled Patel" is gonna be called, for one thing.

It was a conclusion that didn't disappoint - we got that happily ever after we were all waiting for. 
 The last book carried just about the same action and suspense that is found throughout the whole series. It was just as entertaining and hard to put down. 
 However as much as I love this series and the characters, I felt as if the ending was incomplete. Namely regarding this new shocking revelation dhampir + dhampir can have baby dhampirs  that really had no impact to the characters, story and world because nothing really happened with this new knowledge. 
 There now needs to be a brand new series with another set of lead characters to expand on this new revelation and to also provide us with an update with all the incomplete spirit research like the anti-Strigoi vaccination etc. etc. 
 However, regardless of these loose ends, it was a satisfying conclusion and it will be very hard to let go of the characters I have grown to love.

 Will you learn anything from reading this book? No. Well, maybe some twenties' slang. 
 Is this book accurate to the period? No, there are some liberties, but it's good enough as wallpaper to the players and scenes. 
 Is this book entertaining beyond belief? A resounding YES! 
 VIXEN is very easy to read and captured my attention from the first page, and while it may not be the best book ever, I had a lot of fun reading it. While there's nothing glaringly obvious anachronism-wise, I did question some word choices, phrases, and actions, but overall they were easy to overlook and I likened it to watching A Knight's Tale starring Heath Ledger. Written in third-person, each chapter focuses on one the three girls' point-of-view, starting with Gloria and continuing with Clara and then Lorraine, throughout the book until the end. 
 As for the characters, Clara (named after Ms. Clara Bow?) was definitely my favorite to read about, she's recovering from the aftereffects of her life in New York City (which includes a boy, of course), and is trying her best to leave the past behind and move on with her life. Her story had a lot to offer and she felt like a real person who had made mistakes and was now left dealing with the repercussions. Lorraine was a trainwreck you can't take your eyes off of, and while I can't say I liked her, I felt sorry for her. She tries way too hard to stand out and ends up making herself look pathetic; if she keeps it up she'll turn into a very ugly person whom everyone hates. Forget Gloria, Lorraine is the "real" poor little rich girl of the book. She's in the middle of making all the wrong decisions and we're along for the journey, which made her multidimensional and interesting to read about as well. Gloria was my least favorite, mainly because I don't think the author knew quite how to write her. At one moment Gloria seemed like a good girl rebelling, but then there would be moments where she was a real bitch and those two aspects just didn't gel into a cohesive whole. Now if she was seemingly sweet on the outside and really was a conniving bitch underneath, then I'd be on board or at least would get it. But she wasn't that type of bitch and she wasn't Alexis Carrington-bitchy (or insert less-dated reference here) either. How she was written made her look more like Sybil and didn't render me to sympathize with her at all. It didn't help that I felt she was too close to a Mary-Sue for my liking. I don't like perfect or near-perfect characters, they're boring and so was she. What was her motivation for anything, such as singing? Was that always a dream or did it just now come about? Is her recent behavior only happening because she's unhappy? Sorry, but there's just not enough there to make me care about this character. Gloria needed to be more fleshed out to make her feel like a real human, with real thoughts in her head and real feelings, and not a cliched cardboard cut-out. 
 The love aspects of the novel were fairly glossed over, mainly Gloria and Jerome's story, and felt more like teenage hormones than actual real love. 
 "I don't know you but you're hot and I love you." 
 "Nothing will keep us apart!" 
 "We'll be together forever!" 
 Which is too bad because I like the idea of an interracial romance taking place in the 1920's, it could have been fantastic, but instead was tepid and generally unromantic. It didn't help that half the duo was boring old Gloria and the other half never developed beyond the fact that he's a black musician who's forbidden to her due to the color of his skin. I wished for more impact and still hope for that in the next installment of the series. Clara's budding relationship with Marcus was far more realistic because they actually had conversations *gasp* and was well-paced. The relationships between the girls were touch and go, sometimes they felt authentic, then at other times interactions appeared too advanced to where the relationship had last left off; it was like there were scenes edited out in chunks. The same could be said of the developing romance between Gloria and Jerome. 
 So a few things bothered me in the book, such as the issue I had with every girl who wasn't one of the main trio being cattily described, i.e. eyes are close together, that color makes her look sallow, etc. Can we get over doing that already? That's not encouraging good behavior. A little more positivity would be a refreshing change. Another thing that annoyed me was at one point, the crap hit the fan and *minor spoiler* Gloria's career as a torch singer, which she's naturally perfect at (of course), came out into the open. So who does she immediately blame? Her best friend, Lorraine of course, whom she slaps! And who to this point Gloria had no provocation to even think it'd be her who had spilled the beans. Lorraine had not done anything to deserve Gloria's wrath, or at least nothing she knew about yet, so I don't know if the author had forgotten that fact or what. It did not make any kind of sense because there were other people who knew what Gloria was up to and others who could have easily found out. To me it was sloppy writing. What kind of friend does that make Gloria anyway? Not one I'd like, who always thinks the worst of her best friend without any miniscule proof of guilt. Told ya she was a bitch . There were some minor editing inaccuracies, such as when Gloria's dress goes from gold sequined to red in less than a page (pages 74-5) but nothing too overt to jar me out of the book altogether. Lastly, perhaps there was a bit too much twenties' slang that wasn't always incorporated into the text as smoothly as possible. 
 Overall, the plots were well-done and moved along at a brisk enough pace that I never got bored. The ending unfolded so that it tied up the multiple plotlines while still keeping plenty of loose ends for the sequel. So, a lot of the book is superficial, in some cases there are caricatures instead of characters, and it is a shallow interpretation of the Roaring Twenties, I don't care, the book is just plain fun and sometimes that's all I need. And while I can't say I loved this book and it totally lived up to its beautiful cover (seriously that dress is gorgeous, though I could do without the pit shot), I was suitably entertained and will read the sequels to find out what happens next, while I keep up the hope that Gloria will turn into a real, live girl.

Emotions are running high on this one...let me start by saying I did not expect magic or Harry Potter or any of those elements folks have been criticized for expecting. What I had to go on was that it was by JK Rowling and it was about a small town's council. On the surface, it sounded like great grounds for a satire and that was mostly what I was expecting. Knowing a character dies, I thought it might also be a murder mystery. I think it was reasonable to expect, knowing Ms Rowling's work, : inventiveness, humor, and creativity. Not so much. What the book is instead is almost the anti-Harry Potter: very realistic. A grim portrait of a modern day British town, the have-nots vs the haves. The characters are well realized, and if you persist to the end you will be rewarded with some satisfying redemptive story telling. Unfortunately, I bet a lot of folks give up. This book is at least 100 pages too long, most of them at the beginning. It takes over 300 pages for the book to build a head of steam, and the real action is in the last 100 pages. I understand the author is trying to build up her characterization, but it just takes too long. Had any other name been on the cover, I may not have picked this up at all, or at least we're not have persisted. I'm glad I finished it, and I developed real sympathy for several of the characters. Ms. Rowling will never be accused of writing only non-sympathetic characters, to her credit (I hate that modern trend!). I will continue to anticipate her growth as an author of adult novels and I hope next time she allows herself to bring in her natural sense of humor. Nothing humanizes like humor, or gives more poignance to tragedy. For this effort, I'd give a B- to B rating. I trust the next book will be better.

I've been absolutely in love with these books since I read the first one when it was released three years ago. I love Lara Jean, and how her voice is always so poignant and real. I love her family, how close they are, and the bond between the three sisters. And of course, I love Peter Kavinsky! But most of all, I love the way these books seamlessly combine all of these elements in way that makes them so touching and full of depth. This final installment in Lara Jean's story was no different. I am so glad that Jenny Han decided to write it, because this series absolutely needed it. It felt like the closing of a full circle and it was an absolutely perfect conclusion. Lara Jean's family were just as well-written as ever, and many scenes between them had me tearing up. Margot's subplot was a favorite of mine, and I was glad that it was resolved so nicely. Kitty remained a favorite of course, but I love all three sisters equally for different reasons. 
 It was nice to see Lara Jean and Peter just together as a couple without any petty drama, and instead working through real issues. The issues they dealt with felt genuine and important, and not placed there just to create drama.  I really am happy that they ended up together! Peter's list in her yearbook was so sweet and a perfect way to bring the series full circle.  Peter is such a great love interest and their scenes were as cute as ever! 
 I was so proud of Lara Jean for making her college decision! I was crushed for her when  she didn't get into UVA, but I was so happy when she decided to go all in for UNC.  I loved the way her family supported her through it all, and how things ended up with her and Peter. Her decision process gave me flashbacks to my own, and I totally felt for her! 
 Overall, I absolutely adored this book, just as much as I did the other two, though it might be my favorite of the three! I am so grateful that Jenny Han decided to write a third book! This series will always have a special place in my heart and I am already planning on rereading all three soon!
