As a whole, I did like this book, but there were things that I loved about it and other things that I hated. If you like historical fiction and/or any of Aprilynne Pike's other reads, I would say to give this one a go. It was a fun, light read with a great setting that is both historical yet futuristic, and Pike's take on it was fairly comparable. If you haven't read this book yet, you might as well stop here because the rest of my review contains quite a few important spoilers and my opinions on them. 
 What I Loved: 
 1. The description of the negative effects that Danica's corset-tightening had on her body I felt like this element was good because it showcased how Danica essentially used this as a form of self-harm because she felt that she deserved to feel pain for her actions. I also liked that Danica's mother was also concerned about what she was doing to herself, because it showed that even through all of her deplorable actions, she loved her daughter. 
 2. The inclusion of people from different racial/ethnic backgrounds This was just generally cool to me, because race was treated solely as character description and nothing more. In other novels, especially YA, authors tend to use the race of a character (usually the protagonist) as the main part of their personality and all of their actions are tied to their race. Luckily, this was not the case here. 
 3. Aaron being gay Again, similar to the point above, the fact that Aaron was gay was not the only part of his personality that the book ever mentioned. Much too often, bi and gay characters are mentioned only for the sake of their sexuality, and that is all we ever see of their character. In Aaron's case, it was never even mentioned that he was gay - we just know that he and Spencer are hopelessly in love, he is a pretty good hacker, and he's an all-around pleasant person to be around. 
 4. The descriptions of Danica's dresses and other historical French traditions The explanations of how Danica was able to modify her dresses to conceal so many Glitter products and euros was fascinating, and really helped me visualize her methods. Also, the lever description was also interesting, because I had never really read about a tradition like this. 
 5.The realistic portrayal of the King's abusive behavior The way that Justin treated Danica was reminiscent of most abusive relationships, more physical than emotional in this case. It also gave us more insight into his personality and his motivations, which contributed to his character. 
  
 Some things that I did not care for: 
 1. Danica supposedly being an advanced programmer, but not so advanced that she can do without Aaron's help It was mentioned at several random moments throughout the book that Danica had left a path towards becoming a great coder to become Queen, yet I can't recall a single moment where she actually showed her "programming prowess". She often commented that she would be able to do this and that if she had "just been able to continue her education", and also lamented her lackluster hacking skills every time Aaron helped her out. Now, I like to think that I am somewhat proficient at computer programming (Java, HTML, and a tiny bit of C++, if you're curious), I know that hacking skills (especially through government software) are not developed in one day. However, given that she was supposed to be at a fairly advanced level, she should be able to do more than whine about how she'll never get to be a "real" coder. 
 2. The constant, and I mean constant, mentioning of M.A.R.I.E. and her existence I cannot tell you how many times Danica talked about how M.A.R.I.E. was always watching and was such a nuisance and had so much to do with security and so on. For goodness' sake, we know M.A.R.I.E. is always there - you don't need to mention it on every page.

April 2014: Still so good. I think this time around I noticed how fully developed Oskar's character is. He is probably one of my favorite literary characters. 
 (review below from first reading) 
 Why does anyone ever make love? 
 It seems like anybody who's anybody is reading Jonathan Safran Foer these days. At least in the English world. His two novels have caused rants and raves among the literary elite, so of course I would give at least one of them a try. 
 Foer is the new name in contemporary lit--he married Nicole Krauss (Author of The History of Love), wrote two amazing novels, and is seen as a talented "kid" in the author realm. (Everybody who reviews Foer always comments on his age. Saying things like, "He's so young!" I felt jealousy because I automatically assumed he was around my age and had accomplished everything I had not. He's 34. Do people my age not write novels anymore? If I wrote a novel, would people even take it seriously? "Look, look at that girl, trying to write. She's waaayyy too young.") 
 When I asked people what this book was about, most answered with "September 11th." Which isn't necessarily true. This story is about a young boy, Oskar, whose father died in the September 11th attacks. Oskar is a peculiar boy--his idiosyncrasies fascinated me the most. Quotes like, "The fascinating thing was that I read in National Geographic that there are more people alive now than have died in all of human history. In other words, if everyone wanted to play Hamlet at once, they couldn't, because there aren't enough skulls!" (3). Or, "Humans are the only animal that blushes, laughs, has religion, wages war, and kisses with lips. So in away, the more you kiss with lips, the more human you are," (99). For a nine-year-old, he is extremely insightful and incredibly intelligent. 
 Oskar and his father used to play little games like circling all of the grammatical errors in the New York Times, or going to Central Park with a metal detector, digging up things, and trying to figure out the connection between them. After Oskar's father dies, Oskar is grieving in his own way...which distances him from his mother. One day he finds himself in his father's closet, and discovers a blue vase with a key labeled "Black." Thinking this is another one of his father's games, Oskar goes through the streets of New York trying to find out the lock that the key fits. 
 While all this is going on, Oskar's grandmother, who lives across the street, has her own story to tell. Oskar's grandfather left her fifty years ago after they realized that they were two lonely people trying to be in love. They got married trying to learn how to live, but instead divided their marriage and their apartment into spaces for existance and non-existance, Something and Nothing places. They needed to be apart while they were together, and made up rules on how to live. 
 What sets this book apart are the images, variances in punctuation, and shifts in narrator. While some might find the images and page-breaks gimmicky, I believe them to have extremely important purpose, especially the narration/punctuation shifts. Oskar's narration is mostly in perfect paragraphs. His grandmother's is in choppy line breaks, his grandfather's (who also has a tale to tell) sometimes fills a whole page with one sentence... one sentence per page for twenty or so pages. Annoying? Maybe. Reflecting each character's internal processing of grief and life? Definitely. The differences in punctuation complimented the character's personalities incredibly well. I found the characters extremely relatable...without better words to describe them...they are so very human. The stream-of-consciousness is represented perfectly, so you are sucked into the mind of the narrator. 
 While looking online reading reviews about this novel by people more intelligent than I, many found the ending to be incredibly emotional, cried their eyeballs out, and claimed this to be the revolutionary novel of the 21st century. ...I am still trying to figure this novel out. It has left me in a mentally reclusive state, thinking constantly about what just came to be. As I said before, it's a novel you experience. I didn't cry, but I am changed, having read this book. 
 The story is essentially about how to grieve, but not quite. I hesitate to even try to write a review on this book, because I am still processing it. It is a book you experience, not simply read. Besides being on the cutting-edge literarily (playing with spacing, pictures, stream-of-consciousness, etc), Foer spun a good tale. The book was extremely captivating. It has layers...meaning when I read it again I'm sure I'll catch stuff I missed the first time around.

 The book does slow down considerably in the last 25% as Winnie deals with a game changer and tries to figure out what it is she really wants from life. It felt as if Brown just stops everything and lets Winnie strings Mark along for a while longer to keep the conflict and anticipation alive. < 
 The Mistakes is perfect for fans of opposite attraction and forbidden office romances who enjoy fun, smart, and sexy couples who have to work at their happily ever after. Some may find the stubbornness of the heroine draws out for far too long but it's an enjoyable romance overall. Though part of a series with previous character cameos and interaction, you can read this comfortably as a standalone. 
 RATING: B-

What I liked about Silent was that it's real. It's not always pretty, there's a lot of heartbreak, but it's real. Sara Alva makes you come to care for Alex and Seb and everything they go through, feels like you experience it as well. 
 I loved the character developments. When I read about Seb coming "alive", that made me break out in a huge grin and root for him. I was so happy that he had someone like Alex to help him and love him. Alex is definitely a strong character. At the end, he figures out that he's better off without his mom and that was great to read. He was right where he needed to be- with Seb. Silent shows you that sometimes you can choose who your family is.

 While i enjoyed the story I didn't love it. it felt as if the author was trying to incorporate all of the cliches in a supernatural novel. the main protagonist who is different; an alpha werewolf and an alpha vampire; romance; insecurities. while all of these things are okay its the way that it was written that seemed forced. the main protagonist and her sisters all got romances in an instant. despite celia saying she hated mishka there wasn't much tension there. I just think this novel would have been better if the author had taken her time to plan everything through instead of just being bam bam bam.

The drama llama has been unleashed! Seriously, there are so many dramatic moments in the first hundred pages that I hardly knew which direction was up. I loved the first one, but it's been three years or so since I read it and I can't remember most of it. I find I just don't care what happens next. Luckily I'm almost through my giant pile of YA sequels.
My first MM book and I absofuckinglutely loved it!

Okay. It's about monsters, so that's awesome. The world itself is fascinating, though the world building at times is a bit forced. I like it better when I learn a bit as I go, rather than having the backstory forced on me, which is how I felt at the start of the novel. 
 However, I have to say things smoothed out for me after a few chapters, and I really got into this. The characters were interesting. Even though I don't feel like a whole lot actually happens in the start of the book, the ending kicked things up a notch. I'm hopefully that this is a great starting point for an interesting series, and the next book just blows my socks off. 
 There were a few things that seemed a bit inconvenient, and it initially seemed to be leaning hard towards romance over fantasy. However, by the end, I would say the fantasy factor was very high, and the romance factor was extremely low. I can't decide how I feel about that, because I love fantasy. That makes me wish more time had been thrown into the issues of the world, rather than the two main characters and the will-they-or-won't-they-be-a-thing conundrum. 
 Despite how wordy this review is, I really did enjoy this story and world, and when book 2 comes out, I will definitely read it. I am hoping book 2 embraces the monsters even more, because when you have a world that dark and vicious, I just want the writing to be a bit darker and . . . bloodier? More painful? Messier? I wanted some additional ugly oomph, I guess, if that makes any sense, which it probably doesn't.

I normally Do Not Like romance novels. I was pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoyed this one, once I got past the 80-or-so pages of teenage relationship angst in the middle. If I have to read one more page of "I am jealous because she looked at another boy or spent time with another boy who was not me", I am going to throw something. Probably this book. 
 I liked the dystopian setting, even if it does feel like a ripoff of the Giver and even though the world building starts to fall apart if you think about it too much. The spouse matching system is a good concept but it does bring up some implications that I wish the author had addressed. Most notably, what happens to the LGBT members of society? Are they allowed to match to same sex partners (doubtful, iirc the book said that the point of matches was to insure the healthiest children)? Do they match with opposite sex partners and live the rest of their lives wondering "what if?", because that's kind of depressing. Do they choose to stay single? As a spinster-in-training myself, I did really appreciate that people could choose to stay single... though I question whether asking 17 year olds to make such a permanent, life-changing decision is the smartest idea. 
 The world building has a bunch of small holes in it if you analyze it too much, but my biggest pet peeve is: if the people in your society can read, and can type on keyboards, there is no reason why they cannot also write! Perhaps they can't write well--it might look like a child's scribbles--but once you know how to read it is not hard to memorize and reproduce the characters. Not to mention the ban on writing is completely pointless from a practical perspective. Even if I'm generous and say that the characters do not know how to write--which is dumb, but whatever, let's roll with it--they can still type things on their tablets. If the society wants to ban the spread of "dangerous" ideas and unsanctioned writings, this is a terrible way to do it. If they were truly concerned about it, they would also take away the tablets and make sure the general public could not read either. 
 End rant. Anyway... 
 The characters were likeable enough, if not particularly memorable. Cassia's internal monologues get a bit heavy handed at times, especially when she starts to realize that her "perfect" society is not so perfect after all. (Who'd have thought, right?) I will say that it's nice to see a coming of age story with a female heroine. Xander, Cassia's childhood friend and original match, also matures considerably throughout the book. Towards the end he helps Cassia and Ky escape  despite the fact that he is still bitter and hurt over their relationship. Apparently I don't hate love triangles as much as I thought when the involved characters can show some maturity. Ky is the least interesting of the three and almost ventures into Gary Stu territory at times. I think a lot of the reason Ky's character falls flat is due to Cassia's biased narration. We do see hints towards the end that Ky is not as perfect as he seems, which will hopefully be addressed in the sequel. 
 I know this will never happen, especially in a teen romance novel, but a part of me is hoping that Cassia will say "screw the system!" and choose both of them at the end of the series. Because polyamory is clearly the best solution to love triangle plots.
Even better than the first one. I loved it.

I thought this was a very well written, family centered contemporary romance set in a small town. The best thing the family/town were believable and normal. I've read a rash of books with OTT zany characters and it was refreshing to read about a down to earth family who pulls together and supports each other. I loved Matt and I can't wait to find out more about Luke and how he bonds with the daughter he just found out about. I liked Allison and I also loved Matt's son. Matt's parents also added to the book in fact there wasn't a secondary character I didn't like. The story was sweet and the pacing excellent. I'll definitely be reading the next book in this series.

Yet another disappointing trilogy ending. 
 The good: 
 - Jeb got marginally interesting. Him getting magic and being the powerful one? Awesome. Do I wish he'd done something with it instead of hiding in a cave of his own creation and wallowing in his neverending guilt and angst? Yes.  
 - Morpheus. Remaining the only well developed character, he's pretty much as awesome as in the first two books. Charming, manipulative, machinating, self-serving yet with this core of decency that he pretends isn't there but that he can't shake. 
 The bad: 
 - Alyssa never really came into her own. She spent the whole book angsting over her relationship issues (instead of focussing on the evil crazy who was trying to take over her body and steal her crown, just maybe). 
 - The flipping LOVE TRIANGLE. The whole damn book was angsting about the two boys. 
 - Any Elsewhere. After how glorious Wonderland was and all the amazing creatures I was SO EAGER to see what Any Elsewhere was like. The thing that kept me coming back to this even though I wasn't keen on Alyssa, disliked Jeb intensely, and needed a microscope to find the plot was the WORLDBUILDING. Nothing, nada, zip, zilch. She's locked inside a mountain basically the whole time she's there. I was so ready for terrifying, convoluted landscapes and twisted creatures. Intrigue and machinations and danger from everything that had been exiled there. Nope. Caves and boys. 
 - Where the $&*PS$ was the battle with Red? Why did Alyssa lose all agency whatsoever? Why did the MAJOR PLOT OF THE ENTIRE TRILOGY WRAP UP WHILE she was apparently SLEEPING?  
 - The $*&PS!*& ending. I saw this total lack of choosing to be a total cop out. And PLEASE. I didn't want to know about her human life, I wanted to know about rebuilding Wonderland. I wanted to know about how they fared with Jeb's stolen magic fueling them instead of human children. I wanted to know about the miracle child bring dreams to the netherlings for real.  
 I dislike it when women get shunted away from being the heroines of their own story. So this was not a win for me.

The escalation in brutality was unexpected, but these days i've been thinking back at the behading of Mother Russia. I have seen too many beheading videos to not find a bit upsetting how celebratory and triumphant that panel was (not that she didn't deserve to die) .

I really enjoyed this book! It made me remember how much I enjoy stories that have Fae in them and that I should really get back to reading more stories that include them. I did read this in conjunction with it's audiobook and though I enjoyed the narration, I ended up reading the physical copy more because I enjoyed the story that much that I just had to find out what happened next.

This is the first book since The Deathly Hallows to steal my heart, beat it to a pulp, gently place it back where it belongs, and attempt to heal it, briefly. 
 This was a harrowing, yet beautiful, ending to the series. I felt nearly every emotion while reading this book. I don't think I realized how much I loved or cared about everybody until this book. 
 Something that I loved, perversely, was how broken everyone in this book is. It feels right. I loved Bitterblue's fragility. So many books recently have forced-strong female characters, as if they need to prove they can be the main lead. Bitterblue was perfect. Broken, self-conscious, fragile... but brave. Daring. Caring. Independent. Doesn't take crap. The complexity of her was masterful. 
 The people WOULD have been that broken, that insane, after 35 years under a sadist's rule. It wouldn't have been easy to sort or or make right, and I'm glad that it wasn't written that way. 
 As far as Bitterblue's love life goes:  I hope she ends up with Giddon. They have shown their compatibility, and she trusts him. He is a good match for her, and could help her lead. Their chemistry is solid and strong, stable. Bitterblue's lust/passion fling with Sapphire was just that: her required life experience of having loved and lost, a fling that could never be. There were several hints throughout the book that Bitterblue and Giddon would be together, and that's what I'm going to believe.  
 I loved seeing the two worlds come together in the third book: Katsa's and Fire's. It felt like the world was righting itself when that took place. 
 Death's Who's Who at the end of the book is a complete and utter treasure. I found myself giggling madly while wiping tears from my eyes. Death himself is a treasure. 
 I recommend this book to lovers of fantasy. Whereas the first two books, Graceling and Fire, I would recommend for teens and older, Bitterblue deals with tougher concepts, and I'd recommend parents read it first before deciding for their kids. 
 This is a story I'll keep in my heart forever. I'll definitely reread them all in the future, and anything else written by Kristin Cashore. What a masterful storyteller.

I was expecting to really dislike this, given that the first line begins with "The first thing that hit me was the smell..." Cliche much? It actually wasn't too bad for the genre, though :) 
 I think my biggest problem with this was that everything just seemed to move too fast, without enough explanation of why, or enough time to be believable. There's the instalove that's a staple of teen paranormal romance, but I felt like Anna's acceptance of what she is, her friendship with Emmaline etc, the conflict with the Ealdwitan and several other things were similarly sudden. 
 Actually, no. My biggest problem was that, when the truck sinks to the bottom of the ocean, it doesn't fill with water until Anna breaks the window. Nope nope nope. Cars aren't watertight. Factual errors in books really bug me :( Especially when they're about things that are regularly in the news, and have even been covered on Mythbusters and Top Gear.  
 All that said, there was a lot of stuff here that I found positive. The love interest isn't creepy. It's the female character, not the love interest, who has the power. Although it's the first in a series, the book feels complete. So, while it's not really for me, I'd be a lot happier recommending it to YA Paranormal Romance fans than a lot of other books I've read! 
 As an aside, is unruly hair the go-to flaw for YA protags? :D

I don't know if I've ever cried harder at a book. Through the first 3/4 of the book, I was thinking maybe I was heartless because while it was touching and sad in parts, I wasn't a mess like I thought I was supposed to be, but  when he breaks the news to her about his recurrence, I got the appropriate amount of teary. And then. Then she just starts the dropping the "that was the last time..." lines and I lost my shit. Lost it. And then just from there on out I was a snot machine and had to get up like three times for more tissues and thank god my husband is a hard sleeper because he would have had some serious concerns about my mental health.  I loved that they had healthy, normal parents and healthy, normal friends. I thought that gave it a relatability that made it even more beautiful and painful. Some of the dialogue did get a little over the top for me, which I know was kind of the point, and I did love it most of the time, but it could get distracting. That's something I'm a little worried about translating to the movie, too, because I think it would be even more over-the-top to hear than to read. I also wanted a little more development for parts of the story like the Caroline back story, it's a short-ish YA book and told from Hazel's perspective only, so I get that it wasn't there and I did like really just concentrating on Hazel's experience, I think I just wanted to know more about everything and have the experience last longer. Overall, I'll love it and I know I'll be reading more John Green in the future.

Wow. This book. I hate books like this because, as I'm reading, I cannot discuss anything with people who haven't read the book or watched the movie. So the rest of this review is spoiler ridden, because there is really no way to talk about Gone Girl without ruining the twists and making it not worth reading, or making reading less of a shock. I'll be buying the movie, as I'm curious to see what they have done. 
  
 In the beginning I really didn't like Nick. Flynn does a good job at making him a distant, weird man who seems to not be able to have a "normal" response to his wife missing. Why he didn't include the cops in everything, why he didn't lawyer up sooner, why he kept telling white lies to the police instead of doing the smart thing and just cooperating fully. By the time we discover that Amy really is lying and whisked herself away, I still don't care much for him. He was handled poorly in the beginning; his story wasn't explained to it's fullest extent and Flynn tries to make us experience the case as he is experiencing it, but without enough inner monologue. I think that, only when Real Amy pops back into the picture do we get the real Nick, and then he actually explains what was going on with stuff like the baby and the pregnancy and trying to pull them together before giving up on it and going for the easy woman. Flynn failed to master the first person narrative until she had the second narrator tying things together nicely. 
 Amy is Amazing, but in the wonderfully psychotic kind of way. She is a sociopath through and through, though I'm not sure if something else was tossed in there for added effect. The diary entries were definitely depicting a good, naive woman caught up with an abusive husband, but even I started to wonder why things seemed to fit together just a little too nicely, especially after the entry where she said she could just disappear and then the scene was staged. The eerie thing is that Flynn writes her in such a brutally honest way that you can't help but relate to her on some level. As much as she tries to be smarter and better than anyone else, the end of the day shows her still being more naive than those grown up in strife. 
 I can't believe she killed Desi. I want to say "poor Desi" but he wasn't exactly innocent either, just a different brand of crazy. I was happy when she got the money stolen from her; she deserved some kind of hardship for being too stupid to keep moving and not keeping quiet about leaving. She holds herself in such esteem that it's her fatal flaw; other people must not be on the same level as her, and need to be dumb as a result. 
 The ending itself is haunting. That he was just about to get out of the prison she trapped him in, but somehow feels enough love for the unborn child that he will stay with her. Part of me hopes he gets the courage to kill her after she has the baby. I don't think it's some weird toxic attraction like Flynn is pushing on us, but more of a fear of the unknown. Now that Nick knows she is a sociopath and psycho bitch, and knows he can't leave her unless she is outed, in prison, or dead, he doesn't want to face the reality. He is stuck because he is worried of taking action. It chills the reader to the bone and left me in shock, almost to tears and wondering why tears were present. Crazy.

Do you ever read a book that seems to take forever to get through? Like it takes a long time to finish? And there's nothing wrong with that, it just takes a while. This was not that book. It could have been, but the moment I picked it up that night, I hardly put it down until I was finished the next morning. 
 Tamara Ireland Stone knows how to catch your attention, knows how to make you fall in love with the characters, their lives, and their stories. 
 As for the story itself, it's brilliant. Time Between Us is told from the point of view of sixteen year old Anna, a high school student and cross country runner. Early on, she sees a young man watching her run, but when she tries to confront him, he has disappeared--literally. As strange as the incident is, it's even stranger that he is the new student at her school, and that he seems to have no recollection of their bizarre first encounter just that morning. 
 Anna feels connected to this unique and quiet boy, Bennett, despite his odd behavior and disappearances and mysteriousness. As they grow closer, Bennett begins to explain things to her, things like that he can travel through time and space, with very particular limits. When he opens up to Anna, he also opens up the world to her. Testing the limits of fate and ethics and everything they believe in, Anna and Bennett glimpse the world together, trying to ignore the very real possibility that they shouldn't be together, should never have met, and that Bennett never stays. They try to live in the present as much as possible, even though Anna's present is 1995 in Chicago and Bennett's present is in 2012 in San Francisco. 
 This story is told beautifully; Stone balances the voice of a naive sixteen year old girl and a wise young woman that has seen and felt and experienced a lot. It's believable, it's relatable, and it's real. I loved the characters. Even if some of them were a bit predictable, that was offset by the uniqueness of Anna and Bennett. 
 What I liked about this story was that there weren't really plot holes when it came to the time-and-space traveling aspect. It was explained in detail, and even with all of the new rules that were introduced, it was still so believable. I love what Stone did with the concept, and I think she made a relatively regular plot line so much more interesting and real with the changes she made. 
 What I loved more than anything was that this book was funny. I don't think I've ever laughed as much while reading a book. I'm used to dry wit and sarcastic humor and dark jokes in my reading, but this book was sincerely hilarious. Like early on when Anna is trying to think of how to explain the stranger's sudden appearance and disappearance without leaving tracks in the snow, she thinks, "How am I supposed to tell my best friend that a guy appeared out of nowhere, smiled at me, and disappeared before my eyes, leaving me with nothing more than an impression of his butt and a nagging mystery to solve?" or, arguably one of my favorite lines, when Bennett is preparing them for a road trip and Anna says, "Okay, so why drive so far when you can just, you know..." I make a weird gesture, as if I know the universal hand sign for time travel. "Ah, look who's getting spoiled!" There are many other moments, but these two just really got me laughing. 
 I also really liked how Anna called Bennett on his shit. If she didn't like what he was saying or she knew he wasn't telling the truth, she never hesitated to ask him about it. She constantly asserts herself as someone who doesn't need protecting, some who is independent, and someone who can make her own choices. 
 I like how the story started with a little preface of Anna as an adult giving a younger Bennett a letter that he won't understand for a few years, but honestly...I kind of based how I thought the story would go on that brief meeting and Anna's warning. I didn't think the story would end like it did, and don't get me wrong, I really liked the ending, but I can't help but feel just the slightest bit...disappointed. (Though, ironically, the ending that I was expecting would have been the end, but Stone's ending...well, it was open-ended enough that a continuation of the story is possible [and even expected! I can't wait!])

This would be a whole lot better if there's a chapter of Tyson's interview. (I can almost imagine him saying peanut butter all the time) :3

A new series of Ms. Novak is always a pleasure to read, but I didn't expect that the story had all the mystery. All her books which I read always prioritized family conflict and romance, but this really surprised me. 
 Yes, Maisey faces various conflicts. An especially painful divorce; have to go back to her hometown to help her brother who has gone through problems with drugs; having to face a cold mother, and in the end, still find out that her family hides a huge skeleton in the closet: there is an older sister of which Maisey had never heard. Why all the mystery? 
 But as we cannot forget the romantic side of the story, Maisey back to meet up with a former boyfriend. Rafe is now a single parent. It's him who unintentionally ends up finding the box of old photos where Maisey discovers her secret sister. 
 Half of the book is focused on second chance at Rafe and Maisey's romance, and the other half, finding out about the missing sibling. 
 A plot that intrigue and makes us want to discover more, to the end. 
 No cliffhanger. 
 4 stars

Just like with the first one, I love getting this extra look into the world of Harry Potter!! The "J.K Rowling's Thoughts" sections are great, I love the "behind the scene" info about her writing's thought process.

Resident train wreck, Samantha West lands a gig at a gentlemen's club (but not a strip club) and quickly becomes infatuated with a client, Harrison Yates. There is an immediate connection between them (it doesn't hurt that he's he's easy on the eyes). But our dear Harry has got a lot more going on than just a healthy appreciation for dance. 
 I'm all about finding love, in the club, or wherever, but these two take it to a whole another level. Maybe it's the body oil, maybe it's the drinks, (I would say smoke, but it's set in California so no lighting up inside) but Scary Spice Sam starts spilling her guts from the get go and get this so does he. Why would these two lonely strangers be pouring out their hearts at the first popping G-string (this train of thought only made more sense later). 
 Kudos to Desrochers for the believable dialogue, well rounded characters and the surprise twist (I love surprises)! Despite the obvious attraction between Sam and Harrison (aka D) Desrochers elects to let their feelings simmer and smolder finally erupting into a combustible inferno. I loved that Desrochers didn't over sell the romance, subsequently, every heated glance and and scorching touch was sweet torture. The secret reveal was genius and one that I didn't see coming.  Okay, I wrote a long ass review and then deleted by accident I'm SO angry with myself. Almost as much as I was angry with this book. When I first finished it I had such mixed feelings I couldn't quite make out what I thought of it. But then, when I calmed myself I tried to analyze everything more carefully. 
 In fact as soon as I started reading the book I couldn't put it down, and for nights I stayed up until 2am reading, which almost never happens to me! But this time it did because a) the style is superb b)the story is very engaging. 
 Here's an overview of what I thought: 
 Plot: what I liked the most about the plotline was that it essentially wasn't a love story, to say, it didn't begin as one. It wasn't "love at first sight". At the beginning Will and Lou couldn't even stand each other, but then a relationship based on internal jokes and mutual trust built up. It was only much later that they realized they were in love with each other. 
 Characters: At first I thought I wouldn't have liked Lou. She promised to be one of those "beam of sunshine" people who I could never stand in real life. But only after a bunch of pages I realized she wasn't that at all. Bright? Yes. But also awkward - like REALLY awkward, not like those self-proclaimed awkward female characters who always know how to behave and what to say-, with a rather peculiar fashion sense, someone who cannot be said conventionally beautiful, and with an unsolved trauma in her past. I ended up loving her and caring about her more than I should have. 
 And Will, what to say about Will. He is precious. He WAS an asshole at first, but I couldn't really blame him for that. He didn't deserve this ending. He's possibly the strongest character I ever witnessed, and deserved so much better. But I'll get to this later. 
 As of the other characters, the family was realistically annoying and narrow-minded but united, and Patrick was a total jerk, I spent the whole lenght of the book hating him. 
 So what is it that didn't quite convince me when I finished Me before You? A few things. On top of it all, of course, the ending. As I said, I was angry. I did not shed a tear (even though in the final part when Lou went through the letter I had a lump in my throat), I just wanted to scream "WHAT THE HELL DID I BUY THIS BOOK FOR??" 
 See, the thing is, I half expected it, but the other half of me hoped so hard for Will to change his mind that I convinced myself he actually would have. I fucked up. But it wasn't the ending by itself, it was how it happened that bothered me. 
 "It's not enough for me. This -my world- even with you in it. And believe me, Clark, my whole life has changed for the better since you came. But it's not enough for me. It's not the life I want" 
 I hated this SO much. I thought it either meant he was lying, that Lou didn't really change his life despite her efforts, or that the author just gave a bad explanation here. But then I realized Lou did change him. He was a stuck up rich man whom no one could ever contradict before meeting Lou. She wasn't only the one who convinced him to get out of the house, or the one who made him laugh and made him gentler. She was the one who made him see he could be loved not for his money or for his looks, but for who he really was. She made him see he wasn't just the one who constantly needed to be cared after, that he could still care after the others (the maze part *sobs*). She made Will see the world from another perspective just as much as he did with her. 
 I still think he deserved better, but after reflecting intensely on this I came to think this ending has got to be the most realistic one. 
 Also, at some point I wondered if some parts could come off as offensive like...when Lou got drunk and kissed Will and then left him there. A carer is not supposed to do that, not ever... Plus I'm always skeptical at best when it comes to couples in which one is in a position of power over the other, so I'd like to hear the opinion of all the non able bodied fellows who read the book. 
 So, after analyzing this with a tiny bit more of detachment my feelings are not that mixed up anymore, and I definitely can say my review is a quite positive one. 
 That said, I won't be going to watch the movie adaptation, oh no. I don't want to see this turned into a sappy love story, thank you very much.

In addition, the author kept writing small paragraph of reminiscences from the heroine which makes no sense until the end of the book but which kept throwing me off the story. 
 As for the world building, it was interesting but not that original and many things are not sufficiently explained or explored. The plot itself which consists of palace intrigues is far too shallow and the ending is too deus ex machina. 
 The characters of the gods were well written. They were humanized as part of their punishment for opposing the most powerful god, but the author managed to let them retain some of their alien aspect. As for the heroine cousins, they are both too stereotyped. 
 Another thing that I didn't appreciate is the custom that the female warrior from the heroine clan must go through for their coming of age : 
  the girls must spend a month alone in a wood and then fight against a warrior selected by their sponsor and lose their virginity by having sex with him in the presence of the council members, the fight determining if the girl is raped or if she controls the encounter, but she still has to have sex. The heroine loss the fight and is raped, but she then killed the warrior with a hidden weapon. I don't understand why she had to do that, she should have killed him before the rape or not at all, it makes no sense otherwise. I dislike mention of rape in novels and in my opinion it didn't serve any purpose here other than trying (and failing) to demonstrate how tough and determine the heroine is.  
 Like I said, it's still a good read despite all those flaws, but given all the awards the book received I was expecting better.

When more than one person mentions a specific author in the context of "if you like X, you may like Y", and if one's own books appear as either X or Y, it seems like a reasonable idea to check out what the other person is writing. And when one of that person's books turns up as a Kindle special, well, what the heck. 
 And so I found myself reading Courtney Milan's The Duchess War. I've never been a voracious reader of historic romances--not like some people I know--though I have my favorites. (Despite certain deep flaws of social consciousness, I return regularly to Georgette Heyer for comfort reading.) But I'm not entirely au courant in the field of straight historic romance these days. (Alas, there really aren't enough lesbian historic romances to consider it a "field", and so I make do.) That said, I can easily see why Milan gets recommended regularly to those looking to go beyond tired old tropes in their historicals. Despite beginning with a bare outline that feels all too familiar -- a handsome and personable Duke being pressured to end his bachelor state, an intelligent and sharply impertinent woman of less-than-exalted birth, with a Dark Past, who collides with him under disruptive circumstances -- we get a result that's far from routine. 
 Milan's strength, in addition to a deft touch with description and setting, is taking the ordinary human foibles of two very different people falling disastrously in love, and making them seem romantic and attractive even in the midst of their chaotic messiness. (Is that too abstract? OK, it takes a good writer to write a realistic wedding night between two virgins and make it both sexy and endearing.) And if Milan's protagonists feel perhaps a bit too progressive and open-minded in their social politics for the setting, they aren't unhistorically so. It's just a matter of devising a story around the particular historic types needed to make it work. There were people like this, and they are no more unhistorical than the more common romance stereotypes. The result works very well, including the inclusion of enough secondary characters and trailing plot-threads to encourage the reader to seek out more of the author's works. 
 If The Duchess War doesn't leave me eager to pounce on every other Courtney Milan novel available, it's only because it is, in the end, relentlessly heterosexual, and as usual I'm caught between the desire for well-written, engaging stories and the desire for stories that acknowledge my own existence. To be fair, one of the features The Duchess War has going for it is that one is permitted to fantasize that the heroine's two older female guardians are engaged in a well-closeted Romantic Friendship. Though you have to be aware of and looking for the possibility to spot it. In a perhaps not-so-odd way, historic romances that have less explicit sexual content make it easier for me to do a cross-gender identification when reading. 
 But setting my own personal quirks as a reader aside, for those who enjoy progressive-thinking, well-written historic romance, with explicit but not excessive sexual content, I can definitely recommend this book.

 My heart ached for Catherine the entire time, even in the end when she became less than pleasant towards her best friend (my heart also ached for Mary Ann). 
 What I liked most about this novel was that it's completely different to The Lunar Chronicles Series, and though you can tell it's the same author, you wouldn't even think about the fact that she also wrote The Lunar Chronicles Series while reading Heartless. I liked that Meyer has such a writing style that she can differentiate her stories and make them all unique and original in her own way. 
 I do recommend this book to fans of Marissa Meyer, but I don't recommend it as a first book because I do believe The Lunar Chronicles Series remains as her best work yet, and I would hate for a reader to be negatively influenced of her writing capabilities if they should not enjoy this book.

 In this fantasy retelling of Beauty & The Beast, Nyx was born with a single purpose, marry the lord who oppresses her people and destroy him. Since birth, she has been in training to fulfill this destiny and on her seventeenth birthday, she goes through with the plan and becomes the lord's wife. Still resentful of her family for allowing her to be sacrificed, while babying her twin, she is eager to complete this task to prove that she isn't as useless as her father seems to imagine and he'll regret never loving her properly. However, Ignifex, the dark lord, is not what she has always envisioned, being charming and even kind to her. Will she finish her destiny or will she fall for this one man who seems to accept her for all the truly is, cruelty and darkness included? 
 Nyx is so very different from any other YA heroine I've read about recently. She is utterly devoted to her cause but harbors such contempt and hatred for her family that it is difficult to keep it all in. She knows that none of what she is being put through is her sisters fault but at the same time cannot help but feel rage at her for never trying to take her place or save her. Does no one love her enough to want to keep her from sacrificing herself for the greater good? Apparently not because no one even hints that there is something wrong with the situation. She holds all the anger and venom inside, but it still occasionally slips out. So once she's with Ignifex, she feels fine expressing her rage at him because he is, after all, the evil lord, right? He makes deals that bring horrendous consequences and he Sundered the land so there is no longer a sky, just a domed ceiling. But the meaner she is, the more she realizes that maybe there is more than meets the eye. I applauded her for her darker side most of the time, but there were occasions when she was overly cruel to Ignifex and I just wanted to smack her. I get that it's your destiny to destroy him, but you don't have to be a bitch after he saves your life! 
 Ignifex was something else altogether. His logic about the deals he makes was so undeniable. After all, people came to him requesting either horrible or impossible things and he gave them what they wanted, at a price. He was really just a facilitator, a middle man, and it certainly wasn't his fault that people didn't always grasp the full cost of what they wanted until it was too late. He's outwardly handsome and charming, always ready with a witty comeback to whatever Nyx throws at him. He's really just trying to make the best of his situation. 
 The other important character here is Shade, a captive of Ignifex...or is he. I can't really talk about him without getting spoiler-y I knew from the beginning that he was a part of Ignifex, that they were the same person split in two.  I wasn't really a Shade fan, he always seemed to have his own agenda and it wasn't always in Nyx's best interest. That part where he almost kills her and we learn that he killed so many of the other wives had me flipping out. How Nyx forgave him is beyond me. I wanted to stay as far from him as possible  
 This has a love triangle, but it's really a love triangle because...well I can't really explain, but just trust me, k? It's a completely fresh take on Beauty & The Beast. It's a bit confusing on the fantasy elements, but that may just be because I'm not very big on fantasy because their worlds always seem to confusing. I think what really drew me to this was the relationship between Ignifex and Nyx. These two are so similar even though their backgrounds are so different and they truly see each other for who they are. Ignifex seeing past Nyx facade of nice, dutiful daughter, and Nyx seeing beyond The Gentle Lord who oppresses the people to the man behind the mask, so to speak. It one of those epic loves that, in the end, breaks all the rules. 
 This retelling of my favorite fairy tale had me digging Luna (my kindle) out at every spare moment, even going so far as to read while I waited in line at the bank, just to get a bit more. Hodge has creating a beautiful world that is breathtaking and heartbreaking. It's a fantasy novel that those who aren't really fantasy fans can wholly enjoy. I recommend it to anyone with a love of Beauty & The Beast or anyone looking for a story a bit off the beaten path!

 I don't have agoraphobia, just an aversion to people as an introvert and a lack of ability to go out due to depression that up until a year ago was untreated. My lowest point was a stretch of 4 years where I could hardly get out of bed, let alone work and function. 
 This however is nothing like what Nora is going through. Equating experiences 
 Agoraphobia is wildly different and is vividly described. The abundance of metaphors and detailed style might be a turnoff for some. 
 The Mental Health Rep: Brilliant. Accurate. 
 As a former cutter, those scenes were on point and shows a side not many see or show. Love the positive therapy portrayal and the therapist being so understanding, helpful, and accommodating, It's an ongoing process. No miracle or savior. Just her working her ass off, taking care of herself, and slowly progressing. 
 Love how the internet and social media were incorporated. 
 The Romance: 
 She isn't saved by a guy or "fixed". She makes strides and progress on her own. She has a supportive mother and a therapist. She is medication resistant for common, understandable reasons. 
 To be honest, the romance could be removed and she'd still improve. The ending would be the same. It wouldn't be as sweet and swoony and adorable, but including that doesn't lessen her accomplishments. It doesn't make her less impressive for having a support system. It'd horrendous having to do it on your own and the odds of success drastically reduced. 
 I am glad it was included because it shows how important talking, and consent is. It shows how it should be done: depending on someone's boundaries. Nora is touch averse, but a romantic and has dreams. However, if you're looking for touch-averse representation beware because Norah constantly puts herself down as a "freak" and wanting to be "normal".

OHMYFREAKINGGOSH. I'M MIND BLOWN. 
 I'm crying. I'm actually crying! 
 Now don't get me wrong. This book has a wonderful, realistic, hopeful ending. I can even categorize it as a happy one. But I'm still crying. Because this book was pure perfection. 
 The action takes place three years after Mia wakes the hospital. And many many things happened in this period of time. I'm not going to give mush away, but I'll just say that each went on his own way. Until one day changes everything. 
 Adam is in New York for a short period of time with his famous band, Shooting Star, one day away from going into a 67-days-world-wide-tour, but for more than twenty-four hours he's all alone in the big city. And one decision leading to another, he finds himselfs at the Carnegie Hall where Mia is holding a concert. And after three years spent in wondering and regret, he wants something. Closure maybe? Or just to see her? So he enters and this is the point where 24 hours full of grief, reawakened memories and forgiveness begins. 
 Adam and Mia were both broken and their intense feelings were overwhelming. Adam, from my point of view, was shattered. Why? Because Mia made some though decisions in the past and plans for herself, which didn't include him. I was mad at her in the beginning, like Rambo-style mad. Not only she dumped Adam without a single word, but she didn't contact him for three and a half years??? I was in battle mode, that's for sure. 
 But in the end I felt conflicted. And I understood her need for distance. Because she really did hate Adam at some point. Because of that vow. Hate is only one step away from love, right? Thank Lord, it works backwards too.(Side Note: I know it looks like I'm speaking in some kind of code, but I'm rambling because I don't have words to really express how intense this story was.) I loved Adam and I ended up respecting Mia a lot. Their journey was heartbreaking, but perfect. 
 Overall, this book is better than the first one, but for this series, Where She Went represents the best possible ending to this fabulosly-written story about forgiveness. I adored the fact that is told from Adam's point of view and I really enjoyed discovering his attachement to Mia's family and understand that he lost them back in that day too. The author's style is amazing, beautiful, unique. Loved the way she alternated memories with the present. It was a nice way to bring some happy feelings and mix it with all the pain. Her way with words will just keep you captivated for one hell of a ride. You'll sob, you'll smile, you'll mourn, but mostly you'll support Adam and Mia with their own loss and grief. But I just gotta say something: 
 THANK YOU, GAYLE FORMAN, FOR WRITING THIS STORY! DEFINITELY ONE OF MY ALL-TIME FAVORITE READS.

I think this review here sums up how I'm truly feeling. 
 But here's my "review": 
 Please do not call this a trans book. 
 This story is told from the view point of Luna's sister, a cisgender girl. Her thoughts, her feelings, all of her is what we really see, not Luna's and is therefore not about the trans person and is not a "trans story". 
 The constant misgendering from the summary alone makes me boil. 
 Reading through other people's reviews of this story, constantly misgendering Luna, makes me even more upset, and they obviously do not know how to respect a person's pronouns. 
 I don't care if the book is doing it, I don't care if the other characters or the author is doing it, you do not misgender a trans person, fiction or not, you don't do it. 
 This story doesn't even help on the side of how to be a good ally to trans people. Regan is the worst portrayal of an ally, you'd learn nothing from her. 
 Obviously books like these are important but this is not how it should be done. 
 And I'm not saying that cis people shouldn't be writing trans stories, I, as a trans person (ONLY SPEAKING FOR MYSELF, NOT ALL TRANS PEOPLE), actually don't mind who writes the story - on one condition - you have to do it right, you have to be respectful, you have to be mindful and you have to be willing to educate yourself on the topic and talk to a trans person in order to write your character instead of just assuming this is how it goes. 
 The amount of times I have read reviews that say that Peters has created an amazing story, full of respect and love for "transgendered" people, makes me so angry, because it's honestly, in no way, respectful. 
 As a side note, stop using the word 'trasngendered', it's not gramatically correct, you'll come across a lot of people, trans or cis, who will tell you not to use it. 
 And lastly, in my anger, if I see this goddamn book on one more "Greatest trans books everyone should read" list, I'm going to honestly throw my laptop at the wall. 
 That is all.

This was a great book on Ancient Greek culture: philosophy, religion, and social structure. To be honest, I probably didn't understand most of it. 
 For example, Alkibiades is mentioned throughout the book, but his presence seems more like a plot driver or a subtle theme and less like a character. Like he's bigger than life. 
 Like in life, some of the characters and the deaths seemed pointless. I cried like a baby when Alexias killed his brother. Lysis's died in battle, and that wasn't a surprise considering their odds. Part of me just wanted them to step aside, let politics sort itself out, but of course they wouldn't do that. It was telling to me that whatever Lysis did, so did Alexias.  
 It was unusual that Alexias was so plucky, but then again, this is Greek culture, so why wouldn't he be? Sure, he had that monologue at the end, when he was yelling at some stranger, but I was still looking for something surprising but inevitable...besides losing his sense of wonder and youth. "I dreamed a dream of time gone by..." seemed to be his theme at the end.

 Rock With Me is by far my favorite With Me in Seattle book! Kristen Proby has a knack of writing about drop dead gorgeous, successful, seductive and absolutely swooon-ish men. First there was Luke, than Nate, then Will and now finally Leo <3 
 Leo, Leo, Leo....where do I begin? Well he is toe-curling delicious. 
 Don't ever lie to me, sunshine. I don't ever want you to run until your legs give out on you like this again. The only time your legs will shake like this is if I'm inside you." 
 Hot damn... 
 Anyways, Leo Nash is a rockstar. Tattoos, piercings, the whole delectable image. When he sets his sights on Luke William's sister, Samantha, he is determined to get under her skin, and into his bed. 
 But Samantha is determined to not fall victim to his charms. 
 That is one sexually potent man. No wonder he's so damn famous. And I am never going down that path again." 
 She constantly pushes Leo away despite the magnetic pull between them. And in true Samantha form she is a complete and utter bitch to Leo. Her disinterest and cunning words are used as her self-preservation, but Leo does not give up easily. 
 I would love to try to knock that chip off her shoulder." 
 Bit by bit, Leo starts to crumble the protective walls that Samantha has put in place. And in return, we see this beautiful couple start to fall in love. But Samantha's defenses are not easily let down despite the growing connection formed between her and Leo. 
 Rock With Me won me over on Team Samantha, something that I didn't think was possible after book 1, Come Away With Me. Samantha has always come off as hard and cold, but she really isn't. Samantha is almost self-efficient to a fault. She views any form of commitment as giving away her own independence and identity, but she met her match when she met Leo. 
 Leo, who is not without is own skeletons, is persistent but patient. He is understanding of Samantha's hesitations and carefully works around their issues. I fell in love with him almost immediately. There is something lurking beneath his rockstar image that has you rooting for him the whole time. 
 I love the glimpses into each of the previous couples current lives. I am usually not a fan of series spin-offs. I normally go for series that focus on one couple only, but Kristen Proby does an amazing job of creating character depth and maintaining individuality between each character/book. After reading Come Away With Me, I wasn't sure if I could love the other couples as I do with Natalie and Luke, but each book keeps getting better and better. Plus, the resounding theme of family that surrounds these group of beautiful, successful people is a bonus as well. 
 If your looking for a book to rock your world, then you have to read Rock With Me. 
 4 stars*

Stinger is the first book I've read by this author...and after reading it I've put every one of the books she's written so far onto my TBR list. I'm always a sucker for the good girl meets bad boy story. But though Carson may seem like a bad boy due to his profession, he's really a good guy at heart...and don't be surprised if he steals yours. 
 The writing was fantastic-very smooth and made for an easy read. The interactions between Carson and Grace were funny, and I really liked seeing them go from the "no way in hell we're getting together" to the "I don't want to leave", even if it happened quite quickly. The author keeps you hanging on to each word-be prepared for one of those all-night, keep reading until it's finished marathons. 
 The transformation that Carson undergoes is amazing, and will make you love him even more. Grace's character seems to stay mostly the same throughout the story, except where Carson is concerned. The secondary characters provide an excellent supporting cast, especially Carson's military buddies-which it would be wonderful to have their stories written as well, I hope the author decides to write them. 
 Sometimes just letting go of your preconceived notions and taking a chance can ultimately be rewarding, the lesson Grace learns here-though it takes her a while to finally achieve that reward...keeping the reader on the edge until the end to see how it turns out. 
 A very solid 5 out of 5 stars...and for the 18+ crowd due to language and sexual content.

3 1/2 stars. This is a cute little book - pleasant, light, and nice. They meet. They like each other. They get along well. 
 STORY BRIEF: 
 Hallie is working in a shoe store to earn money to finish her Sotheby's diploma in East Asian Art. Wealthy handsome bachelor Nick meets her when he comes to the store to buy shoes. He is willing to pay Hallie ten thousand pounds if she will pretend to be his wife for a week. He is flying to Hong Kong to negotiate a business deal with John. On a recent trip John's 18-year-old daughter Jasmine tried to seduce Nick. To avoid offending Jasmine or John, Nick told them he was married. John insisted Nick bring his wife on the next trip. Hallie agrees to the deal. Nick and Hallie spend a day shopping for corporate wife clothing, rings, etc. and then fly to Hong Kong. About 2/3 of the book is their time together in Hong Kong. They enjoy being with each other and with John and his daughter. A side story is someone trying to harm someone. 
 REVIEWER'S OPINION: 
 I like the way Hallie talks to Nick. There was one conversation causing me to chuckle. They had to sleep in the same bed, so she built a wall of pillows down the middle, calling it the Great Wall of China. A few of their comments: he wanted to be the Emperor's finest troops, so she was the Mongol horde. He wondered whether the troops needed to patrol the wall. She said nothing was happening on the northern border tonight. There were more comments about raiding parties, peace negotiations, and traps. It was cute. 
 There was not much relationship development. He offered the trip immediately upon meeting her. From the first day they got along well and enjoyed being together. They were sexually attracted to each other early on, and that happened soon. Both were likeable characters. There was nothing unusual or odd about their personalities. There were no conflicts between them. There were no typical-romance-novel problems such as vague communication conflicts and stupidity, which I appreciated. The few sex scenes were mild and pleasant. To get 4 stars I would have liked it to be longer and a little more depth or interest to the plot. 
 DATA: 
 Story length: 180 pages. Swearing language: mild. Sexual language: mild. Number of sex scenes: 3. Estimated number of sex scene pages: 9. Setting: current day London and Hong Kong. Copyright: 2006. Genre: contemporary romance.

Even though this took me an insanely long time to finish (shut up) I enjoyed it immensely. 
 I actually liked The Ask and the Answer more than The Knife of Never Letting Go. The first book was a little too "bam bam bam action!" for me, I think. This book was a lot more methodical, and the events were placed strategically, and the decisions of the characters were carefully thought out rather than made in a single instant of haste. I'm not the action movie type, so it makes sense that I wouldn't particularly enjoy a novel where once one fight is over, another begins. Or where a certain preacher just does not want to die. 
 But I'm trying to let that go. For the sake of Todd and Viola. 
 In this book, they have arrived in Haven, which has now become New Prentisstown. Mayor Prentiss has taken over, and has really just corrupted the whole town. The men and women are separated again, there is a curfew, and there are soldiers on every street. The Mayor has recruited men from across New World for him army, and they have joined to form a huge army. 
 Todd and Viola have been separated since their first day in New Prentisstown. Viola is in one of the various healing houses, and Todd has been locked up with the former Mayor of Haven. Soon, both of them receive jobs, meet new people, and discover new disturbing facts about the town they reside in. 
 Meanwhile, The Answer, a dangerous group of women has been blowing up the town piece by piece. Todd and Viola will have to choose a side. 
 BUM. BUM. BUMMMMMM. 
 I like Todd much more than Viola, but I found both of their stories and points of view very intriguing. 
 Todd really grew in this book. He didn't have much of a personality in the beginning of The Knife of Never Letting Go, but in this book, he just grew up. He is definitely a man rather than just the boy who ran away from home. He has seen things no boy (or man) should ever have to, and he has lived through just about everything you can imagine. Attacks, war, explosions, more attacks, rogue Spackle (namely number 1017, that piece of crap), working with Davy, the Mayor, the other Mayor, heartbreak, literally everything. He took on responsibilities and he shouldered them and he suffered for it, but you know what my Todd did? 
 He suffered right on through it. 
 Because Todd is strong like that. 
 Him and Viola, the unbeatable team. 
 Now, Miss Viola, we gon' have a talk. 
 I really like you and all, but you got to stop making spur-of-the-moment decisions. You're gonna get yourself killed! Despite this, I do like you. Well, actually, I don't think I like you as much as I just love your relationship with Todd. 
 Because so far, this series has not had the whole boy-meets-girl instant romance thing. I usually am the type of person who swoons over the relationship, but this series has been so . . . refreshing. It's nice to not have all the relationship drama and love doctor stuff going on. Viola and Todd are just friends. Friends. Such good friends that you would think they have known each other for years rather than months. Their interactions are so sweet and innocent. They're young teenagers. Around 14. And they act in ways that, well, normal 14-year-olds act around each other. They hug and they comfort each other and they do what they have to do to survive. It's what makes sense. There are no heroic war moves or sacrifices (although we come close a few times). There is betrayal and heartbreak and such raw emotion, and it hits you harder because some of it is stuff that everyone goes through (not the battles of course). 
 The friendships themselves in this series are what touch you the most. There is Todd and Viola, Wilf and Todd and Viola, Davy and Todd, Lee and Viola, Maddy and Viola, Corinne and Viola. There is peer pressure and pressure from the elders and jealousy and just about everything you can imagine. 
 Todd was, of course, jealous of Lee. I would be if I was him, too. Viola leaves, gets close with Lee, and then when Lee shows up, he's this handsome blonde kid who cares about Viola almost as much as Todd does. I liked Lee, but I feel like he is not a very important character. He was just a substitute for Todd when Viola was without him, and that kind of made me angry, because no one can replace Todd. 
 Davy Prentiss Jr., oh my gosh. The character development in this one was strooooong. I hated him. Hated him. He hurt Viola and he made fun of her and Todd, and he was just an overall terrible person. He still is, don't get me wrong. But he also deserves some sympathy. Everything he does is to please his masochistic father, so can you blame him if he makes a few masochistic choices? 
 I mean, yeah, you could, but I'm not going to. 
 When he first started to become a character who I knew I would end up liking, I tried to deny it, because no one likes a sob story. 
 But I ended up loving him. 
 And I cried like a baby when he died. When his own father shot him in the chest. When the father he worked so hard to please killed him because he had always been a disappointment. When he apologized to Todd for killing Ben, for insulting Viola, for always being so mean. He apologized. Over and over again. In his Noise, out loud, to Todd, to Viola, to everyone.  And he asked his father, "Pa?", just in complete disbelief that his father would choose Todd over him. But he was never bitter to Todd about it. He was mean to Todd before, but not for this reason. When the Mayor told Todd that he was his second son, Davy wasn't upset, he was overjoyed. He was so happy that he could call Todd his brother. 
 But this didn't all happen overnight. It was gradual. It started off with Davy giving Todd the lunch he was supposed to have but that Davy ate every day. Then Davy called Todd by his name instead of calling him Pigpiss. Then he told Todd that even though it was just the saddest thing in the world, Todd was Davy's only friend in the world. And it just all got better from there. It got worse for me, because as soon as I liked him, he was gone. All thanks to the Mayor, that is.  
 The Maaayyyoooorrrr. 
 Humph. 
 He doesn't even deserve a description. 
 Wilf and Jane were wonderful as always. Wilf, sweet, innocent, kind Wilf who risked his own life more than once to save Viola and Todd, who was being controlled by Mistress Coyle, who fought back, and who people finally listened to. And Jane, his amazing wife who doesn't pop up much, but who, when she does, steals the show. 
 Speaking of Mistress Coyle . . . I did like her. I thought she was going to be the character who is really hard on the outside, but who when you get close enough to her, you realize that she is actually extremely kind. 
 She wasn't. 
 She was just awful. Outside, inside, just all around. 
 Allllll around. 
 Maddy and Corinne were Viola's new friends in New Prentisstown. Maddy was quick to talk to Viola and become her friend, but Corinne, not so much. Maddy's death hurt, but it wasn't crazy, because it was so quick and it happened so early on in the book that I hadn't really gotten to know her that well. She was sweet and kind, and I think if she had lived, she could have been a great friend and ally to Todd and Viola, but she didn't. Soooooo.  I'm still not really sure where Corinne stood with Viola. She died, too, but you know. Death.  
 And let me just talk about Todd and his animals. I kept forgetting that Manchee had even existed until Todd would say or do something with his horse, Angharad that was just so sweet, and I would remember how he used to be that way with Manchee and it just hurt me in the worst way. 
 Actually, this entire book hurt me in the worst way. Just every bit of it. So much death. 
 Honestly though, a lot of people died. 
 Huh.

I've been avoiding this serial mainly because I loath most books that I've tried in the format. Meljean Brooks had the only satisfying serial romance/ adventure that I've tried to date, and it's the exception that proves the rule. 
 Still, I was able to score ATTRACTION for free on Kindle (gateway drug, as I ultimately paid $6 for the complete story when I bought sections two and three). The pricing shell game was another minor annoyance, but I finally got started reading.

Suspenseful, surprising twists, heavy on the legalese but still accessible for the layman. What we've come to expect from John Grisham. Set in Kansas and Texas, rather than our favorite Ford County. Texas is fitting, because in this novel his featured issue is the death penalty. The book asks some good, hard questions about the death penalty and wrongful convictions, and also has a subtext about how the right thing and the legal thing are not always the same thing. Racism plays a huge role, and he also addresses tactics of the police when interrogating someone. 
 Though this book definitely has an anti-capital punishment bent, what I took away from it is that the problem is wrongful convictions, not capital punishment. Sure, if we incarcerate someone wrongly we can let that person out when his/her innocence is proven. But is that really better than a wrongful execution? What needs reform is a system that allows racism and small-town politics to influence the verdict of a court trial. 
 Also, every American should learn and understand their Miranda rights, including when and how and how long the police can detain a person for questioning.
Solid and full of emotion, but I had to take it down a star for an ambiguous ending.

Enjoying my re-reads of Courtney Milan, and this book was no exception. Really interesting plot in terms of the heroine's history, which beautifully illustrates the sexism and ridiculous (for us now) conventions that ruled English society at that time. I am sure many would say we have not come so very far when we consider the sweat-shops and working conditions that are still the norm in many countries. Wouldn't be a Milan book without something like this, and I love her for it:) 
 What I particularly loved was the hero's sweet incompetence in the love-making arena and the heroine's willingness to show him what she liked and make him better at it. This is when it becomes clear why the hero, Robert (kind, sensitive, handsome, loyal yet principled and moral- yup, the full package) was so anxious about whether he would be "good in bed". As this had been mentioned- in jest- as a pre-condition for loving him, one can only imagine the pressure he was putting on himself when coupled with the normal male fear of inadequacy in this department! Such a nice change from the suave super-studs we are so often presented with in HR novels. 
 The heroine, Minnie, is fabulous. I felt so much compassion for her, and her situation impacted on everything in her life: her financial future, her reputation, and her relationships (with Robert, with her great-aunts, with her best friend and with Robert's mother). 
 She rose to her challenges so bravely and it was wonderful how Robert loved her for her intelligence (she was an extraordinary chess-player), agreeing wholeheartedly with her teasing statement that in her, he was"overmatched". 
 There is also a beautiful depiction of Robert's mother, who I loathed, initially, but came to understand, even while I did not agree with the choices she made with regard to her son. The message of forgiveness underpinned the story, and it made a lot of sense to me that you would never be able to forgive others if you did not feel you could expect forgiveness yourself. Just loved it.

 Kaitlyn Fairchild and her four friends are gifted with psychic powers and are attempting to escape from those that wish to exploit them - off and away to fend for themselves. Their only hint of possible yet questionable salvation is to head towards a white house that has only been visible in their dreams. Unfortunately, this leads to most of the book consisting of them traveling. You know, where most of the obstacles entail stealing cars, dodging police, getting food, being lost, and so forth. Honestly, I just didn't find those parts that interesting. 
 Sure, some strange things happened along the way. They soon find themselves haunted by opaque grey figures as they become victims of long distance psychic attacks. In addition, they randomly acquire help in the form of a girl named Lydia, whose appearance is found to not be so coincidental after all, yet whose true motives are still unknown.  But I'd have to say it was Gabriel's turning into a true psychic vampire and feeding off of Kait that kept me interested in the book, which didn't really become apparent until Chapter 6. Actually, as a HUGE fan of her Night World series, I was pleasantly surprised that L.J. Smith twisted this series into another vampire story. I have to say that I love the way she describes the mind-link that occurs during a feed (in both series), allowing the two characters to see each other for who they truly are. It's strangely romantic.  As for Kait's romance with Rob, I kind of felt it to be a joke from the start. 
 So really, I found this book to be okay overall, but it was the brief moments of stolen intimacy between Kaitlyn and Gabriel that made me like it. What can I say? I'm a sucker for romance, especially when we're talking about mysterious, dark, tortured souls that need saving. I will say that I did have a hard time relating to the characters because of their age which undoubtedly contributed to the rating. It was difficult to not think about how young they were, which made everything feel somewhat trivial.

Lamb has a lot of... what word am I looking for? Heart? Humanity? It is truly a touching tale of the Christ. 
 It's not a sacrilegious farce, as you might believe by reading the title. 
 One reviewer called "poignant", and I suppose that's not too far off the mark. 
 What went through the mind of Jesus when he was young? How hard was it to grow up? Did He think He was the Messiah? Did he 
 know 
 ? 
 How did Jesus learn everything he knew? Did he learn it or was it innate knowledge? 
 John didn't spring full-grown from the desert. Jesus didn't disappear for 20 years then suddenly reappear to start his ministry (ok, in this book He sorta did, but that's another story). They had lives. They had 30 years of stories - of good and bad times, laughter, sorrow, joy, and pain. They knew people. They has relationships. They didn't exist in a vacuum. I think that's the most important thing this book helped me remember. 
 Plus, Moore did his homework, and I feel like he does his best to paint a picture of the world Jesus would have grown up in, and what it might have been like to grow up being the Messiah everyone was hoping for; that everyone was expecting. 
 (Of course, if your sensibilities are easily offended, there's going to be enough here to send you down the road screaming.) 
 And to be honest, the theology isn't bad. 
 "Love is not something you think about, it is a state in which you dwell." 
 Good stuff. And I like this: 
 "When I told the priests that I would tear the temple down in three days, I meant that all the corruption, all the pretense, all the ritual of the Temple that keeps men from knowing God would be destroyed." 
  
 One of the quotes between the chapters: 
 "Nobody's perfect...Well, there was this one guy, but we killed him." 
 -Anonymous 
 As irreverent as that sounds, could there be any more truth to it? I honestly believe that if Jesus came again today, we wouldn't know Him, and we'd try to kill Him all over again. And, once again, it'd be the religious people who did it. 
 The writing of the week of the passion was pretty intense, even though I knew what was going to happen. 
 Finally, in the afterword, Moore states: 
 "This story is not and never was meant to challenge anyone's faith; however, if one's faith can be shaken by stories in a humorous novel, one may have a bit more praying to do." 
 I couldn't agree more.
