I enjoyed reading this book a lot. The story was engaging and involved a lot of topics I have a special interest in--working in a bookstore, coding, typography--along with cool secret-society type intrigue. The blend of light fantasy and real-world elements worked really well, and the author managed to make scenes that should have been boring (scanning a book all night, finding something in a warehouse) reasonably suspenseful and interesting. 
 I don't, however, think it's a particularly good book, objectively. It has what I call "first book syndrome," which I can tell at 30 paces because I did/do it myself: it's overwritten, with too many vocabulary words and overwrought metaphors. The main character is a total Marty Stu, and the main love interest is a total Manic Pixie Dream Girl. 
 The way technology is portrayed is kind of funny. I know more about almost all of these topics than he does. Not every writer can or needs to be an expert about everything he writes about, but when possible, I prefer delving into a world the author knows and cares a lot about, and really GETS. Sloan doesn't really GET technology. It's clear he's been paying attention when his techie friends talk. He gets a lot of specific details mostly right, but the overall feeling is off. I think it's the way every single character is constantly amazed by the capabilities at their fingertips, even seasoned programmers and people who are supposed to use these tools every day. Really they should be reacting more like those people in the Louie CK bit who are frustrated that their wi-fi isn't fast enough on an airplane: "why won't--this stupid thing--!" It's a mistake people often make with characters in science fiction novels, but it's more noticeable when it's about technology that really exists today. 
 I only had a couple of nitpicks that I had to mentally change in order to continue with the story: 
  
 * The GrumbleGear scanner makes no sense. What good would it do to have a cardboard frame around your digital camera? Especially since it's apparently prefab and not scaled specifically for the size of the book? And the quality of the camera itself was the least thought out part? The fact that is has a bed is especially nonsense, obviously you would just use the table the book is already on. The trip to Dumbo to get a secret tool was cute, but in my mind, the scanning scene is just Clay taking photos of each page with a specifically-chosen, high-quality camera. 
 * I really liked almost everything about the ending. I thought that the content of the secret book was plausible, satisfying, and heartwarming; I liked the reflections on immortality; I liked Clay's cute little presentation where he sort of buried the lede; and I liked the IDEA of the way the key to the code was hidden, but the description of it seemed to imply that it was essentially letter replacement? Like, each character represents a different character? Like a cryptogram? In which case, the computer algorithm definitely would have solved it without needing the key.

Well this was a real shame... 3 stars, but only because I'm in a good mood, I guess. Or maybe it's because it's Colleen Hoover? I love your writing, CH, but what happened here? I didn't cry for Miles, I didn't cry at all. Your writing is awesome, you're one of my favorite authors, but have you read this? 
 Did you even read this...? 
 This is a story about Tate, who crushes hard, and insta-loves her brother's neighbor, Miles. Miles is a jerk. I don't care what he's been through. She meets him when he's piss drunk, and from then on he's either rude or completely indifferent. But still, Tate sees something in him, and she's head over heals. Because of this, when he goes up to her preaching the "guys-have-needs" story, she agrees to enter into a sex-only relationship with him. 
 Their first sexual encounter pissed me off first. From there I was hesitant to move forward.  He has sex with her, is extremely rude and selfish, and when he's finished can't wait to get her out the door fast enough.  Let's just say his respect for her is nonexistent. I know you're not looking for a relationship, Miles, but don't treat her like she's a prostitute you picked up on some dingy corner. Come on... 
 Despite his continued "Nothing will ever happen between us" and "This is just sex for me" lines, Tate still loves him. What? Why? How? He's not even a person I would feel comfortable being around. Tate, from then on, acts like a love-sick teenager, making it difficult for me to envision her as an independent adult woman. She made me want to slap her and tell her to grow up. The sex is just terrible. I started skipping those paragraphs because I just didn't care. I don't care about the characters, I don't care about them "making love." Seeing their relationship so far just made it an eye-sore. This one line, though... After Dillon The Cheating Husband hit on Tate, and Corbin and Miles both defended her? ...two overprotective brothers... No, honey, you don't consider someone a brother if you're sleeping with them. Awkward...  
 A relationship that was on the edge of feeling abusive. He was an ass, she made excuses for him. 
 And the flashbacks to his past? The problem is, when I don't like a character to begin with, I don't sympathize with them at all.  And that tragedy, while sad, was lost to me. It was no reason to treat her like he did. Be moody, be emotional, be a little off sometimes. But not a jerk. I couldn't feel for him.  
 Now to the redeeming qualities. Okay, so there weren't many, but I still gave this three stars instead of less, so there must have been something. I guess I was hopeful because it was CH and, as I've said, I really like her writing. I want to read everything of her, and I think that's the reason I pushed myself with this book. Also the end... it wasn't the crash and burn I was expecting. Love at last, and Miles finally admitting he loved her. But really, does it matter? You treated her like crap, man, even your happily-ever-after feels wrong to me. 
 However, I was really concerned that they'd break it off and nothing would have changed. I thought she'd finally realize it was the worst relationship/arrangement possible, and walk away. Which is what she should have done a long time ago. Everyone could see that... Miles did have some character development, I think Tate was finally walking away, so... I guess that counts for something.  
 Cap! Cap! CAP! Okay, I loved the old man. He was hilarious. Every time he came onto the page I was excited. I really looked forward to him, by far my favorite character in the book. I salute you, Cap. 
 I'm mostly disappointed because I expected something completely different, not something that would anger and offend me. I could never trust for sympathize with these irrational characters to emotionally connect with the story. 
 Three 
 stars is all it's getting from me...

 I honestly still have no clue how I feel about this book. So prepare to read a confusing review. Oh, and I hate using caps in my reviews but it was (sort of) necessary for this one. 
 Siege and Storm begins with Alina and Mal on the run after the events of Shadow and Bone. At the end of the first installment, Alina makes a vow to leave the Grisha life. However, the Darkling's advice about Mal never being able to understand her innate Grisha gifts and the loneliness that comes with immortality starts to settle in, and Alina is beginning to have doubts. Alina's even more confused about her own feelings when she learns that another amplifier exists. She's not sure whether her motivation to seek out the Sea Whip is fueled by her desire to stop the Darkling from controlling her and ruining Ravka further or whether it's for her own avarice. And it troubles her that this possible greed ties her to the Darkling and his selfish endeavors. Siege and Storm is another story focusing on the battle to free Ravka, but this time Alina has to fight the war between right and wrong raging in her mind as well. 
 So I remember being plain upset by the time I finished. Mainly, for three reasons: there was so little of the Darkling, my gosh the bizarre pacing (LEIGH, WHY DO YOU ALWAYS PACK A BUTTLOAD OF PLOT TOWARDS THE END? MY HEART CANNOT TAKE IT.), and Alina's angsty emotions (miserable characters can make miserable readers). 
 From my review of Shadow and Bone you guys may have been able to identify my absolute love for the Darkling. Yes, he's manipulative and evil, but I have always had faith that deep down the Darkling is just a lonely, lost boy. Therefore I feel like if he could get past with his greed for power, Alina could be his healing companion. (YES, I AM A DARKLING/ALINA SHIPPER.) So you guys can imagine how disappointed I was when the Darkling made one (ONE!) actual (you know what I mean if you've read S&S) appearance. So that is the main source as to why I'm deducting a huge star as petty as that sounds. 
 The weird pacing was there but it wasn't a huge issue for me. Like Shadow and Bone, the beginning was entertaining but it was on the slower side and not much happened. It didn't pick up until Sturmhond was introduced (but I may be a tad biased and just think that way because I happen to enjoy his scenes a lot), but when it did the story moved very fast. And as I mentioned in my S&B review, Alina wasn't a special character or one that stood out for me. In this installment, she was much more mopey (for good reason though) but I wasn't of fan of it. 
 What saved this book for me was the many awesome characters introduced. I loved Tolya and Tamar. And prior to starting this, so many readers (thanks, Miguel!) warned me of Sturmhond. So I went into it mentally prepared, and thank goodness that I did. Sturmhond is one of those characters that every reader loves and easily steals the stage presence of all the other characters if this was a drama. He's clever, witty, and normal. It was really refreshing to have a mundane, non-Grisha character that was still strong in strategy and combat. He's also really mysterious (in a different way from the Darkling) and it was interesting to learn all of his identities. And his suggestive and flirtatious nature was fun (I still remain a Darkling/Alina shipper though.) 
 So I would be lying if I said I enjoyed this book less than Shadow and Bone; it still was a fantastic adventure. I definitely recommend this to people that loved Shadow and Bone. As for those that thought Shadow and Bone was on the more meh side, I don't think this installment, aside from the new, amazing characters, provided a uniqueness that will change your perspective on the trilogy. But it's still worth a try if you're curious or invested in the story.

For some very, very strange reason, The Demon Lover by Juliet Dark was incorrectly listed in the Young Adult category. I can tell you without a doubt that this book is not YA, not by a long shot. Did this take away from the book? Absolutely not. As a matter of fact, I can't imagine The Demon Lover being done as YA and still being as good as it is. 
 When we first meet our main character, Callie McFay, she's going through a bit of a transitional period in her life. Having just finished both her PhD and a book based on her adaptation of her thesis, Callie is mulling over various job offers. She ends up turning down more prestigious job offers; accepting a job at Fairwick College where she begins teaching in her field of expertise; folklore. Callie soon finds herself more a part of the College and the town of Fairwick than she ever thought possible with a new house, new friends and a new lover. It's there in the town of Fairwick that Callie begins to learn things about herself and her family that she never knew. 
 The Demon Lover is hot. Hot without being smutty. It's interesting and informative and introduces a paranormal world that is actually quite believable. love. love. love. It took me a little bit to remember what all happened, and to get back into the story but Aguirre does a nice job of reminding the reader without a complete recap. I'll do better with my recap so I'm not so lost next time. Deuce, Fade, Stalker, and Tegan are all settled into their new home Salvation. It is so different from what any of them are used to. Deuce has a hard time with all of the new rules, such as women having their plates, wearing dresses, and attending school. In the enclave she was already considered an adult, but at fifteen Salvation still considers her a child. For some reason both Fade and Tegan are starting over, and don't seem to have much time for their old friends. Stalker and Deuce sneak out at night to continue training, since it is frowned upon for women to fight there. 
 ***Spoilers*** 
 Fade assumed that Deuce is now interested in Stalker because of the amount of time they are spending together. Poor Deuce has no idea of the rules around "exclusive kissing rights" lol she hangs around Stalker because he is available, not because he will ever take Fade's place. Once they figure that out, they are able to pick up where they left off. Salvation's citizens are a little spoiled, with their bounty of food, and safety from the Freaks inside their walls. They must plant outside their walls each spring, to gather enough food for the winter. The freaks are evolving in that they seem to be strategizing their attacks, instead of being driven by their mindless hunger. Deuce volunteers to join the team of guards escorting the planters outside their walls. At first she receives a lot of laughs, and disbelief but quickly proves herself worthy of the position. When their team and the planters return to water, and weed the garden they discover that the Freaks have completely destroyed it. Without it their settlement won't do well over the winter. The town calls for a meeting, but no one has any ideas. Deuce again volunteers for an outpost near the garden to watch over it. Fade, Stalker, and Longshot (he is the one who rescued them, and brought them to Salvation. He's also kind of the head of the soldiers, and makes the runs for supplies) all volunteer as well, but none of the other townspeople step up. The other 16 men are picked at random to accompany them. Most of the men are complete pansies because of their safe lives lived inside the walls. It disgusts Deuce who has better fighting skills, and more honor than the men who are actually from the town and have family living there. Several weeks go by without any large incidents, but Deuce swears she sees a freak sneak into their camp and steal fire. No one believes that the freak would walk past them, intent on stealing and pass up the numerous bodies sleeping. The trio won't rest easy until they find out what's going on. Their trip into the forest reveals a primitive type of settlement, revealing that the freaks are becoming more civilized. Longshot decides to leave them alone, as long as they return the favor. Their job is to guard the crops, and make sure they are harvested safely. When Fade and another guard are taken in their sleep, Deuce won't rest until she finds him. She and Stalker follow their trail, and are appalled at what they find. Beyond the small settlement of freaks is an even larger one, roughly 1000 freaks, with their own society. What's worse is that they are holding Fade, and other humans in a type of livestock pen. She manages to free Fade, but not before others escape and the freaks wake up. Once they return to Salvation, gather all the crops that can be gathered they barely make it back inside the walls. Longshot has a bad knee and isn't able to run, instead he fires at the freaks providing cover for those that are able to get through the gates. Fade is injured beyond just the physical, and refuses to even speak to Deuce. She finally agrees to give him space but it kills her that he won't allow her comfort. For days they freaks run at the gates, and retreat out of shooting distance. Salvation will eventually run out of ammo, and the freaks show no signs of backing off. Some of the women in town are convinced that Deuce has brought all of their problems to them with her lack of knowing her proper place. When the women demand she be sacrificed to save their town, the mayor comes up with a different idea. They both know the town won't last much longer without help, and they decide that Deuce is the only one able to make such a journey. Killing two birds with one stone, she sets off to say her goodbyes. Deuce is surprised that all three of her friends decide to accompany her on the journey. The book ends here with them going for help to save the town that has become their home.

 The name Rachel Cohn used to be synonymous with contemporary urban YA fiction with a bit of a edge. Her Gingerbread series starred the rawer than raw punky teen rebel Cyd Charisse, and when she wrote together with David Levithan, it was Cohn who added the edge, resulting in almost perfect contemporary YA romance novels (Nick & Norah, and Dash and Lily especially are prime examples). In more ways than one Rachel Cohn seems to break with that reputation with her upcoming series of books, of which Beta is the first. 
 Genre-wise, Beta is nothing like anything Cohn has ever written (or published at least). For the first time, Cohn is well on her way to write dystopian romance (yes, that old thing again). With Beta we enter the perfect world of Demesne, where clones are created from a First (a dead person) in a laboratory with the sole purpose of serving the super-rich inhabitants of the perfectly engineered island. Elysia is a Beta, a new type of teen clone. Like all the other clones, though, she was engineered to be soul-less and to serve. In her case she is bought by a rich family who wants her to be a (more) perfect replacement for their daughter Astrid who's gone off to the mainland to study (Astrid, BTW, is the absent character of this book - I'll bet you she's going to be majorly important in the sequels). Clones are designed not to feel real emotions, but to mimic feelings and emotions based on certain bio-engineered implants they have. However, Elysia not only starts to really feel certain things, she also has memories of her First, something which should be impossible... and yet. 
 From the very beginning of the book it is clear that these soul-less clones do have a certain form of self-consciousness. When Elysia feels sad for leaving another Beta she says: "I know the reaction occurs because my chip knows how to mimic human responses, and not because I am capable of actually missing Becky. We feel nothing for one another. We don't need to. I don't know why my stomach also experiences a hollow emptiness at the thought of leaving this other Beta. There is so much for me to learn - about this island, about my own body chemistry. I am so new." (p.6). The observant reader of course knows that Elysia is really feeling anxious for what is going to happen to her. The fact that the story is told in the first person, by Elysia, is an early indication that creating soulless, emotionless beings - even clones - is an illusion, and Elysia will indeed encounter numerous 'Defects', just like her. Elysia, the new-born clone is the perfect metaphor for the life of the teenager she was created from: looking at things with fresh eyes, having incomprehensible conflicting emotions, thinking of rebelling against established orders, making the wrong choices (like e.g. deciding to break free because of a boy, not because it is her own choice - which I for one, was very disappointed by to read!). Elysia is the perfect empty art canvas, and being a teen clone, she is 'still under development', just like a regular teenager. 
 Elysia's voice is in the beginning of the novel the perfect vessel to set the scene: we get to know the idyllic Demesne the way she gets to know Demesne. Her voice is detached, cool even, which is in tune with the soul-less aspect of being a clone. Through her voice, we learn that Demesne was designed to be perfect: there is, for example, oxygen-enriched air to give "the human body and mind a constant feeling of bliss" (p.22), The air on Demesne is its very own soma. Despite the blissful state of affairs, teens on Demesne still feel the need to transgress by doing "'raxia", though, a type of drugs designed to reach true 'ataraxia' (happiness)...well, it sort of mimics the effect chocolate has on the brain... The fact that there are such detailed descriptions and elaborate explanations of life on Demesne, causes the book to have a fairly slow start. It takes a good 150 pages before the story can really take off. 
 The story we get in the second half of the book is unfortunately not the most original one (kind of AI meets I Robot) and Elysia's story is prone to rely on coincidences to really advance. Actually to be honest, the whole book feels too formulaic, and that is because one crucial element is missing: Rachel Cohn's voice. I know, we see what Elysia - the newborn clone - is supposed to see, and as such this book works the way it is supposed to work. It's Elysia's voice: from cool and detached to something more than that at the end when it's clear she's not just a teen Beta, and has real emotions, can fall in love and yearn like any other teenager. However, that doesn't exactly make for the most exciting reading material. Oh, the story flows and ebbs nicely enough, but there is very little that sets it apart from other books in the same genre - not even Elysia's 'new voice'. What I need in especially this beaten down genre of dystopian romance is something that sets it apart from the rest. I don't want middle-of-the-road stuff, I want a unique reading experience. 
 I've known Rachel Cohn to be a writer with a unique voice, one whose voice can lift teen romance to a real 'raxia type of reading experience. *That* is what I want. I don't want great writers being content with yet another dystopian series just because it's hot at the moment. It might sell (just like e.g. Lauren Oliver's Delirium sells like hotcakes), but in my opinion, it doesn't show the author on top of her game. I have the exact same objections I had with Beta as I had with Lauren Oliver's Delirium. I don't want yet another one of those books. I want a Rachel Cohn book, with Rachel Cohn at the top of her game, not something derivative or formulaic. 
 Beta is scheduled to come out on 16 October 2012.

 "...you win some days; you lose others. That's just how it works." 
 Mayra is a girl in Matthew's class that changes his life forever. A simple "Hi" and a sweet gesture leads to an amazing relationship that proves that people can love unconditionally and everyone deserves happiness. 
 I went into this book blind so I didn't know what to expect. I was consumed by the emotion I felt. This gorgeously written story touched me completely. It is unique and the characters are wonderfully complex. Both Matthew and Mayra put a smile on my face. 
 My heart hurt for Matthew as I saw the struggles he goes through. His story, told entirely in his POV, was written honestly and realistically. It was heartbreaking, heartwarming, and believable. I saw how Asperger's not only affected him but the people around him as well. His strength was unwavering and amazing, and I loved his unending bravery. He was wonderfully portrayed and I couldn't help but love him fully for all he was. 
 I absolutely loved Mayra. She is so sweet and understanding, patient and supportive. She is a genuinely kind individual who is so strong and has a huge heart. I felt the love she had to give and I loved how proud of him. Her main focus was always him, encouraging him and believing in him. I loved seeing the inherent goodness she possessed and I wish everyone had the biggest heart like she did. 
 "I want to be with you," Mayra said quietly, and I glanced up at her, wondering if she could read my mind. "Anyone who gives you a chance would know why I'm with you. 
 The secondary characters were amazing; I love the people in his life who loved him unconditionally and supported him were all fantastic. I loved the wisdom his father gave him especially in times he needed it most. 
 Even though some of the subject matter was far from light-hearted, this was still a feel good story that had me grinning from ear to ear. The writing flowed effortlessly and I was captivated from the start. It's definitely a new favorite!!

Unapologetically feminist? I think not... 
 As many reviewers have noted, it has a few superficial things in common with Lord of the Flies. The basic premise requires a certain suspension of disbelief and the characters go from being civilised to savage. That's where the similarities end. The genius of Lord of the Flies is that although it can be read as a parable, with characters representing abstractions such as civilisation, intellect and evil, the characters are also vividly realistic and their transformation is compelling believable. And it's beautifully written. 
 The Natural Way of Things suffers from a pretentious, trying-too-hard-to-be-literary style but it's bearable because of the generally pacy plot. Where is really falls down is the characterisation. The two main characters are the only ones given any kind of depth (mainly through inner monologues) - all the others are crude caricatures. The other women (sorry - they are referred to as 'girls' throughout) are irredeemably materialistic, superficial and vacuous. They are obsessed with removing their body hair, retaining their head hair and beauty treatments. Everything they know comes from reality TV. Even when forced into a survival situation, they remain focused on their grooming or just go completely crazy. Real women simply don't act like this. People I know who have survived the kind of abuse and trauma experienced by these characters REALLY don't act like this. Some are resilient survivors, others deal with living with depression and anxiety, and yes, a few teenagers get into fights or other destructive behaviour; but none of them sit around like the characters in this book, going completely demented, plucking each others' leg hairs, freaking out at the prospect of having to wash their menstrual blood out of cloths, and serving up their companions to be raped by cartoonishly evil men. None of the characters ever seem to speak to each other, none of them discuss their predicament, even at the end when things are looking grim. Hasn't it occurred to them that they can never be allowed to leave alive? Oh wait, only the main characters are allowed to think. They are so stupid and body-obsessed that they allow themselves to be lured to their deaths by goodie bags of beauty products. And the semi-sane protagonist (the other has gone feral by this point) just lets it happen, getting off the Bus of Doom herself but not bothering to tell any of the others that she suspects they are being driven to their deaths.  
 So what is the point of this characterisation (or lack of it)? Is the writer trying to say that all women who are raped or abused are stupid bimbos? Is she trying to say that all young women in our culture are so oppressed by patriarchy that they embrace their sexualisation? Are we being positioned to view these women as men do, as repulsive objects to be used and discarded? If so, what's the point? I get that this is an exaggerated, non-realistic book making a polemical point about how we are all complicit in our degradation but it didn't work for me.

Critically 
 Plot - 4.5 out of 5 stars

 Writing Style - 4 out of 5 stars

 Overall, I am so happy with the character development in this book. All the main character seemed to grow exponentially and that's one of my favorite things to read about. Meghan, while annoyed me quite a few times in past books, in this one she was so good! Strong, brave, powerful, accepting and hopeful. The whole time I was on the edge of my seat. I feel like I've been waiting for this plot segment the entire series. There were so many twists and turns, and although they were exciting and I enjoyed them, I saw most of them coming a mile away. She has this new role to play as the Iron Queen and she accepts it as inevitable with open arms and then kicks some series ass in her new life. 
 It took two entire books and a small novella but I finally connected with Ash and Meghan's romance! Honestly I always felt like they had feelings for each other just because they had no choice but to be in each other's presence but seeing Ash become Meghan's knight was amazing. His devotion to her and to protecting her is intense and to know that it was the first time he had made that type of oath made it so much more meaningful and it made me really connect to their relationship.  I didn't particularly enjoy this book. It was boring. I didn't enjoy Greg's personality or narration or humor. The only thing that remotely interested me was Rachel and his relationship with her. Which wasn't something that was shown in this book. I realize this was the point. Greg's ah-ha moment was when realized that someone he happened to be spending a decent amount of time with and was loosely calling a friend was someone he knew almost nothing about. He befriended this girl per his mother's insistence to lift her up and offer support, set out to make her laugh and only make her laugh, and realized way too late that he didn't know what made her her. He realized what a pity this was and for spending so much time with someone who was never going to have the same eyes or thoughts or memories as her, he knew he should have gotten to know her more. There's a sense of slight regret, a small lesson learned, and Greg moves on, changes his mind about college, which eventually leads him to thinking that maybe he should come out of film retirement.  
 I really don't know how to feel about this book (and particularly the ending) because it holds very little significance. It's like Rachel kind of erected a defining moment in his life, and yet, hardly impacted him at all. It feels too unHollywood/real life. I think if I were Greg, the entire experience would have influenced my life more than it did his so this no-bullshit reality feels more fictional than empathetic.

 It's been a while since I finished this now, and not a day has gone by that I haven't thought of it. I keep trying to make sense of what I read, to choose a rating that would reflect everything this book made me feel, but I've come to the conclusion that this is basically an impossible task. I'm settling on noncommittal 3 stars but I'm not completely satisfied with this rating at all. 
 The thing is, as much as I want to give this book a higher rating because the writing and the characterization were so on point for me, the plot made me extremely uncomfortable and I just cannot force myself to ignore the way it made me feel. And I understand that perhaps the idea of this might have been exactly to make people feel uncomfortable, and to challenge the way we view relationships. But to me, there is no way a relationship between an adult and a teenager because, despite the book beggining with Wavy at eight years old, the relationship between her and Kellen doesn't evolve into something physical until she's thirteen I would definitely have DNFed the fuck out of this if it'd happened sooner  can be excused. I don't care how mature the teen in question is (and it's undeniable that Wavy is considerably more mature than girls her age, given everything she'd had to go through and the kind of upbringing she had). 
 I don't think Kellen ever intentionally abused Wavy, but that doesn't excuse his actions. She was a child with a crush. When a ten years old refers to a close adult as their boyfriend/girlfriend, it doesn't mean that they should actually engage in a relationship with such adult. It means that they are having their first experience with love, and since most of their references are of the romantic love they usually see between their parents (which, in the case of this novel, means the obsessive, hypersexual and violent relationship Wavy saw between her parents), that is what they begin to emulate. That's why a lot of little kids say they want to marry one of their parents, or a sibling. Does it mean that they will eventually do it? Nope. (This is me simplifying a lot of psychological concepts about sexuality, but I think you can understand my point.) So it was Kellen's obligation, as the only adult who cared for Wavy, to put a stop to what was happening instead of letting Wavy build upon these feelings and then, at one point, actually encourage them on the basis of "well she loves me too so this can't be wrong". 
 "(...) I loved her the first time I saw her and I still do." 
 "Love at first sight, huh?" Beth snorted. "How old was she?" 
 "Eight." 
 "That's creepy." 
 He did rob her of a chance of living a "normal" life, and of developing emotional connections to other people her age, by encouraging her feelings for him when she was a kid. She was a child. Children do not have the ability of understanding emotions the way adults do. What Kellen did was emotionally manipulate Wavy during her formative years, which eventually led to their continuous relationship when she was older. Had their romantic relationship started when Wavy was 18 and Kellen 34, things would've been entirely different; she would've had a true choice in the matter. 
 I really liked both Kellen and Wavy separately; I think they were both incredibily interesting characters with well-developed, tridimensional personalities. Which is why it's so hard for me to settle on a rating for this book, because whenever they were having their separate narratives, I was completely engrossed in the story and wanted to keep on reading, but when they interacted, I basically wanted to puke. 
 I also disagree completely with the way the narrative villified Wavy's aunt, who was basically the only person who didn't allow herself to be emotionally manipulated by all the ~true love~ shenaningans because she saw things for what they were: an 11/12 year old having their first crush on someone who should disencourage them but decided to keep the ball rolling. And I don't care how cute the story behind the "relationship" is, this just shouldn't happen, period. 
 Please keep in mind that I'm not trying to say that if you've given a high rating to this book you're agreeing to pedophilia or whatever. Reading is an entirely subjective experience, and the way the same book affects two people is usually completely, and that's FINE, and it's what makes a book community such a great place: comparing reactions and reviews and trying to understand things from other people's point of views. My rating and my review are based on what I felt reading the book and on the way such feelings relate to experiences in my life and my thoughts. It's entirely okay to agree or disagree with me!

Besides the fact that I bent the cover right down the middle, from top to bottom on my last day of reading it, this book was oh so good, oh so creepy, oh so mystical! 
 Every year a book comes out that holds the attention of everyone, even if merely glimpsed at. It's a monster of a book! It's a beast of a book! And it even contains The Beast inside! But when you blind yourself from the length of the book you find a dark and mysterious story full of magical and non-magical, special and not-so-special individuals finding their way across the landscape of New York City in the 1920's - from Central Park where the Museum of American Folklore, Superstition, and the Occult is, to Harlem, to the bright lights of Broadway and its stages. New York City is a character in itself as is the time in history The Diviners and this series was set - a period where the world was growing, changing, rising up from the grounds after a time of heartache in the Great War. Libba Bray has written a truly remarkable tale that still has so much to be explored in consequent books. 
 Although The Diviners allows you to journey across New York through many characters, one character that this book centres upon is Evie O'Neill, the new girl in town. Although she finds herself as the victim so many times throughout this story, she does not dwell on that so much and becomes the heroine that this story needs so very dearly. She was reckless and impulsive, always with the hope that what she was doing would present information that would have remained in the shadows unseen if not for her actions (Evie reminded me of a young, olden-day Carrie from Homeland - reckless and impulsive). But despite her impulsivity Evie is always thinking about her friends and her uncle, even at the worst of times - always thinking about her deceased brother. The rest of the cast was simply divine to read about too and learning about each of their backstories and magical abilities (if they had any) was splendid. 
 "Naughty John, Naughty John, does his work with his apron on. Cuts your throat and takes your bones, sells 'em off for a coupla stones." 
 The Diviners is a four book series, and as it has already begun epically well and Libba Bray has introduced to us an alternate-like New York City habited by a colourful cast of characters the next books in the series can only get more epic, darker, and tantalising. After the mystery of Naughty John the occult killer and the Brethren and the unfolding of the events in The Diviners, I am unsure of what's in store for our characters that we have grown to adore and understood such as Evie, Memphis, Jericho, Sam, Mabel, Henry, Theta and dear old Uncle Will. 
 "Why is this happening now?" Evie asked. 
 Will templed his fingers again. "I don't know. Something is drawing the likes of John Hobbes. Some energy here. Spirits are attracted to seismic shifts, chaos and political upheaval, religious movements, war and invention, industry and innovation. There were said to be a great many ghost sightings and unexplained phenomena reported during the American Revolution, and again during the Civil War. This country is founded on a certain tension." He pressed his fists against each other. "There is a dualism inherent in democracy - opposing forces pushing against each other, always. Culture clashes. Different belief systems. All coming together to create this country. But this balance takes a great deal of energy - and, as I've said, spirits are attached to energy." He let his hands rest on the desk. 
 I wonder what else looms over New York... only time will tell. The Diviners has never a dull moment and Libba Bray has created a paranormal mystery like no other and a favourite of 2012. Future paranormal novels have some distance to cover, because The Diviners is surely a front-runner.

The moments of pure hilarity are sublime in "The Virgin Romance Novelist". The instances of sweet and patient friends-to-lovers interaction are lovely. Meghan Quinn creates the ultimate love scene which is the definition of "Cherish". The situations that the heroine finds herself in, and the naivety she possesses is beyond amusing. The characters, the absurdly funny situations and the set ups also compensate for a multitude of "sins". Meghan Quinn creates loveable characters that are incredibly endearing. The situations that the heroine finds herself and the naivety she possesses is ridiculously comical. However, the mixed messages, and the lack of communication, and some "ass-hattery" brought me down. Some of the heroine's "affectations", such as her pet name for her vagina, can be irritating, but does illustrate how sheltered the heroine was and behind the "sexual maturity" curve she is. The hero although incredibly charming, cannot communicate effectively. Rather than confessing his feelings he vacillates between hinting or jesting about having a closer relationship and yelling or shouting assigning blame on the heroine. Granted the heroine constantly labels their relationship as "just friends" emphatically and with great fervor. I know they both do these things to protect themselves from being hurt so that they aren't embarrassed and/or risk losing their best friend. It is almost one of those situations that I want to slap them up the back of the heads and say, "Pull it together people!" That being said, I did laugh until I couldn't breathe. Which is always a good thing. 
 I did love "The Virgin Romance Novelist" because when all was said and done it was fabulously whimsical and incredibly sweet. But the ultimate Hero pulls some big time asshole moves near the very end. Also her other friends, although they talks to Rosie, they don't seem to talk any common sense into the hero. I understand the doubt and insecurity that Rosie, and the hero feel, throughout the novel - but near the end - the hero's behavior is just douche-y. But when the chips have fallen, both the hero and heroine have undergone incredible growth and maturity. The humor is beyond entertaining and the romance far surpasses tender and loving. The combination of comedy and loving is always a winning combination for me.

 Okay, so I wrote an entire fucking review for this book, and then the tab got closed. STUPID, STUPID, STUPID ME. So let's see if I can recreate it. 
 It's my experience that people are a lot more sympathetic if they can see you hurting, and for the millionth time in my life I wish for measles or smallpox or some other easily understood disease just to make it easier on me and also on them. 
 I have quite a bit to say about this book. First of all, I want to commend Jennifer Niven for her Author's Note at the end of the book. This proves to me that she has had first hand experience with the subject of death and suicide and everything that accompanies those two things. It makes me appreciate the novel a bit more, because when an author bases a story off of something they've experienced in real life, you can't necessarily point your finger at them and say, "You portrayed this wrong!" because everything is subjective. And in my own personal view, I think that Niven did a wonderful job at writing a story about such a complex and complicated issue. 
 Second of all, I want to address the criticism in many of the reviews I've read on this novel. There are a lot of people saying that "the characters become their illnesses" and that the story "romanticizes suicide." Let me just stop you right there, okay? In regards to the characters, I'd say that that's pretty much the entire point of the book. Unless you've been living under a rock your entire life, you'd know that as a society, we are driven by labels. 
 ...because, it turns out, growing fourteen inches in a summer is easy. It's growing out of a label that's hard. 
 Especially in a world where mental illness exists and we continue to stigmatize these problems as though they are the fault of the victim. Theodore is stigmatized because he is different and because his classmates don't understand him and, if we know anything about human nature, we destroy that which we cannot understand. We make people feel wrong for being different. Labels exist because humanity enjoys placing each other into neat little categories; file cabinets that we can be filed away into and boxes that keep us restricted. I think the reason why Niven was so focused on Theo's mental illness was partially because many people like to treat mental illnesses as though they aren't there. As if they don't really exist. And as someone who has dealt with a mental illness her entire life, I can say that it's not so far fetched when characters become their illnesses. I've questioned so many times whether the things I do, the things I say, etc are even a part of my personality or if that's just my mental illness bleeding through and I can't control it because it's apart of me and sometimes it's hard to separate yourself from your illness. So I don't see anything wrong with what she did here, because if anything, I felt more connected to Theo, because I understood him. Because I know how hard it is to separate yourself from your illness. It's pretty fucking hard. 
 And as for the "romanticizing suicide" bit, I don't find that true at all. A lot of people claim that the "they don't love you til you're gone" idea was played out here, but what I think people fail to realize is that, when death happens, these reactions are realistic. Story time: during my senior year of high school, 2 of my classmates died. One was a really popular jock who everyone loved and the other was a nice, quiet boy who wasn't as popular. The reaction to the first guy's death was, of course, more dramatic. Everyone cried. Everyone left school. Everyone went to the funeral. We all drove 2.5 hours to the Away hocker game (he was a hockey player) and we mourned him. The next guy, the response was more muted (probably because he was the third death that year), but everyone still mourned. Even people who didn't know him, people who didn't talk to him--they mourned. Again, it's so typical of humanity to claim people once they're gone. And in that process, they forge them into martyrs and completely forget whether or not they were horrible to them while they were alive. That's how it so often happens. I've seen it. So this whole idea that she "romanticized suicide" by making him a martyr after death is a stretch. If anything, I think this is a book that brings awareness to suicide and forces readers to look for the warning signs. When Violet went to her parents and got him help, that was the author telling the audience: this is what you should do. And for that, I am eternally grateful to her. I feel like this is the only YA novel that has truly done justice to the topic of mental illness (that I've read so far). It's so carefully thought out and very respectfully executed that I give Jennifer Niven mad props. And I thank her. 
 Labels like "bipolar" say This is why you are the way you are. This is who you are. They explain people away as illnesses. 
 I like to think that this book is a social commentary on how fucked up people can be when it comes to mental illness. It's a testament to how selfish we can all be. When we see someone we love hurting, we don't want it to be true. We push away those thoughts because we don't want to deal with that sort of emotional and mental stress that comes with helping that person. Because mental illnesses don't just affect a single person, they affect everyone around you, and I think that the novel does a good job of showing this reality as well. 
 I've also seen people being upset over Theo's eventual suicide . People seem to interpret this as a subliminal message from the author that says: THERE'S NO HOPE, KIDS! IF YOU'RE MENTALLY ILL, YOU WILL COMMIT SUICIDE! And I don't think that's the case at all. Let's do a step by step of Theo's situation: he is undiagnosed (but clearly has Bipolar I Disorder); his mother is inattentive and disengaged; his sisters and his friends don't pay much attention to when he disappears--in fact, they cover for him and say things like, "Oh, that's just Finch. He does that sometimes." So, where in this book does Theo at all have a support system? (I swear to god if you reply with Violet I will rip your throat out.) Here's the thing: love is not the answer to all of life's problems. I don't care if Violet and Theo were in looooove and happy and everything was rainbows for a while. Guess what? It was rainbows because Theo was in experiencing mania. His illness didn't disappear during the time they were together. It was still there. It was still visible. People just decided to ignore it. Write it off. And I for one am glad that, for once, an author decided to be realistic with their audience. Love. Does. Not. Cure. All. Wounds. Say it with me: Love does not cure all wounds. Just because Theo loved Violet, does not mean he was magically cured of his illness. He needed professional help. He needed medication. And sadly, Violet was the only one who recognized this, and she recognized it too late. 
 Though not perfect, I'm a little confused as to why so many people (and a lot of reviewers I respect) have given this low ratings. Maybe it's because I'm a psychology major and I have a mental illness myself that I fully understand and appreciate what was done here, I don't know. Maybe I read too much into this book and all of my deductions are what I wanted it to be. I don't know. Like I said, it's not a perfect book. Violet and Theo are far too mature (we're all a little immature, no matter what our age), and it felt a tiny bit like a reenactment of Romeo and Juliet to me (without the double suicide). Theo was a rapid cycler, which is actually not that common in bipolar patients, and for some reason that bothered me, but not enough to make me enjoy the book any less. I can see why the author made him a rapid cycler (for plot/time purposes), but still. Other than that, this is the most respectful book I've read on bipolar I disorder, and if any of ya'll disagree and have a different book for me to read, I'd gladly oblige. 
 I'd also like to thank my friend Taylor for getting me this for Christmas, as I knew she would, because she has nonstop raved about this to me whenever we talk. It was an overall interesting read. Not in a good way, but not in a bad way either. It's an interesting book.

Oh my, that . . . was so bittersweet. 
 As far as final books to trilogies go, this was pretty good. There were surprises abound in this book and it was actually so freaking cool. 
 Laini Taylor is absolutely amazing. At writing, world-building, characterising, plot line. Plot line is a big one because there were some bombshells in this one. The scope of this story is so much bigger than just uniting two warring races, and you don't really understand that until this book. I mean, yeah, at it's heart, it's a love story. But if you look bigger than that, there is so much depth. Worlds of knowledge in this one book. 
 The way the book was written PoV-wise was amazing, too. Changing PoVs can often feel tedious. There's always one PoV you want to read above all else and sometimes, the other characters views can just be annoying. Laini Taylor changed PoVs in such a way that, most of the time, you're left on a cliffhanger. For all characters. So it no longer becomes a chore to read about all these other characters. And that's awesome and such a rare talent. 
 Probably my only little problem with the book - and the whole series really - is the way it's written. Now, don't get me wrong; Laini Taylor is a brilliant writer. But she can also be very flowery. Very poetic. And that's great! But really, sometimes it's a chore to get through and sometimes, the metaphors and personifications go right over your head. Important moments/revelations can be dulled because of the long-winded paragraphs that come before hand. It's brilliant, but can also be very confusing. 
 As for the ending? So bittersweet. At the end of the day there's still a big loose end that needs to be dealt with - and also leaves the door wide open for a spin-off. Also, I didn't get nearly enough Akiva/Karou personal time. The bits I got were so sweet, but I would love just a wee bit more!

Frost Burned is currently tied with Kim Harrison's Ever After for Best Book I've Read This Year. Review over. I'm outta here... peace! 
 There are authors for me that are the Holy Grail of authors ("What are you going to do, bleed on me?" - I get so distracted...). Authors that, no matter what, I read their books. I won't lag behind on their series' for more than a month. But I also (maybe unfairly) expect great big HUGE things from their books. I've invested hours and hours into their characters and worlds. I'm sucked in and I never want to let go. One such author is Patricia Briggs. 
 Up until this point, Ms. Briggs' Alpha & Omega series was my favorite between her two most popular series. Now I have to say Mercedes is tops over Charles & Anna. I think this time around, it's the supporting characters and that nothing is held back that puts Frost Burned at the top of Favorite Reads of 2013. 
 Characters 
 All of the Mercedes Thompson books start you off by plopping you smack down into her life as it's happening. This time around, we get to witness Mercy bonding with Jesse, Adam's daughter, as they brave the horror (to Mercy, anyways) of what is known as Black Friday. Just the start of the book was enjoyable for me because I think this was the most interaction we've seen between Jesse and Mercy to date. Jesse is growing up and Mercy is treading in new waters with Jesse so we get to witness that new dynamic. I love Jesse and I really hope to see her character more and more in the future. 
 Although the last book, River Marked, was all about Adam and Mercy, I really feel like this book actually delved deeper into their relationship. Adam is still one of my favorite Alphas out there - who doesn't love a wolf in a business suit?!?! 
 While I didn't hate River Marked, that book took us away from all my favorite supporting characters for the better part of the book. Frost Burned brought me back to ALL my favorites! Seriously, I giggled like a school girl whenever one popped into a scene. You'll be extremely surprised by the characters who take big leads in the story and also by some characters who "come out to play" in the story. I about choked on my coffee when one such character showed up!!! 
 Story / Tempo 
 Hands down, this is one of the best stories in the Mercedes Thompson series. Ms. Briggs manages to mix in Mercy's magic, her and Adam's relationship, the pack, the vamps, the fae, humans, her Alpha & Omega series, and all without watering down a thing!!! Seriously, within the first quarter of the book, I was crying over something that happened. NOTHING IS HELD BACK. Listen to the words coming out of my mouth, err on the screen. 
 Really, I was done with this "review" like, about 500 words ago. Mercedes Thompson fans, just go read this already or get caught up...

As a fan of the apocalyptic genre, I'm drawn to titles like this book in much the same way a zombie is drawn to the living. Paul Jones spins a decent end of civilisation as we know it tale, but with a nice twist. There are no zombies in this story, no rampant screaming crowds, or constant masses of blood and gore. Instead the focus centres on a journalist, Emily Baxter, a New York journalist, who seems unaffected by the mysterious red rain that infects the rest of the population. 
 The story has good and not so good points, and I'm reluctant to say bad points as I couldn't really see anything that stuck out as bad, or enough to leave me with a bad feeling after reading. 
 First, the good stuff: 
 Paul Jones captures the loneliness of a city suddenly devoid of human life incredibly well. The humdrum noise of daily activity we take for granted, from crowds of commuters to the drone of vehicles plodding the streets. The eerie silence is unsettling. The story isn't rushed either, Paul Jones takes his time to give the reader insights into Emily's life; her thoughts, feelings and emotions come across well. 
 The unique twist isn't exactly original, in that despite there being aliens, they're presented in a different more subtle way, rather than an obvious "conquer the planet and destroy all life" plan, these new life forms inhabit Earth without a plan or a hive mind driving their actions. They behave as any other organism entering a new ecosystem might, like fungus or moss growing in new places, exploiting a new previously unvisited habitat. 
 The pace was pretty good, enough to keep me turning the page, although I would have preferred to see the tense/action scenes broken up a little more instead of overly long paragraphs. An interesting thing is that there's very little dialogue, and you might expect more given the nature of the plot. However, this doesn't hinder the story or slow it down as the visuals are enough to keep the story ticking along at a decent rate. 
 The scenes in total darkness were gripping, as were the noises, that tap-tap-tap following Emily up the stair well was unnerving to say the least, as was the elevator doors pinging open and shut. The description of the aliens was spot on, just enough for my imagination to fill in the blanks. And the alien trees gave me enough information to ask more questions than there going to be answers for, I quite enjoyed that. 
 Now for the not so good stuff: 
 First thing that struck me as odd (few spoilers here folks!) is the death of Emily's boyfriend. Whilst obviously traumatic, she seemed to cope with it remarkably well. And when the aliens begin to emerge she gives more thought to the baby in the apartment above changing into something alien than her boyfriends own metamorphosis. 
 On the subject of the bike and supplies. I don't read reviews before choosing a book but I do have a quick read before writing my own review, and I have to agree with a couple of other comments about the sheer amount of supplies Emily gathers. At times it felt like severe overkill and I'm sure the story wouldn't suffer if the vast shopping list was considerably reduced. The reader didn't need to know every single item Emily put in her panniers. 
 The bike issue niggled me because it felt wrong. Emily comes across as pretty resourceful, but not that much. It didn't feel right for a New York journalist to suddenly turn into a doomsday prepper and survivalist, though I guess in that situation some people can surprise by giving such forward planning a lot of thought. 
 I suspect the author has read his share of apocalypse stories and is keen to give his own slant on what survival means and how his character reacts. The problem is that the reader is told all humans have vanished. There's been very little widespread looting of grocery stores that you might see in a zombie plot for example. Therefore Emily, also knowing there's plenty of food left, should know that stocking up is a good idea but not to the extent of overloading her bike with food and water to last months. 
 I felt the plot gears grinding with the bike issue and since Emily couldn't drive she figured the safest way out of the city would be on a bike. And the rest of plot hinged somewhat on that fact. I question her reaction to not want to try and learn how to drive. Surely it wouldn't take more than a day to figure out the basics and travel safely out of the city in a car? It's not like she had anything better to do in those first few days is it? It really isn't that difficult to learn, certainly not for a character who comes across as intelligent as Emily. 
 At least she could have attempted it and come up against a barrier like being scared after crashing a car or clogged streets leaving no room to navigate a route out of the city. It felt too easy for her to simply decide not to bother in order for the rest of the story to be played out on the basis of a bike journey leading the reader through the alien forest etc. 
 From her background story the reader knows that Emily had once learnt how to use fire arms. Nothing wrong with that. And it made sense for her to equip herself with a gun. However, it felt a little unrealistic that she was able to master the use of the shotgun so proficiently given her limited training. Again the plot gears were put in place in order for the showdown with the creatures in the forest to carry any sense of tenseness and action. 
 Whilst I found Emily's plan to trek north to find the scientists kind of plausible, I felt her decision was made a little too easily. Not much thought, if any as far as I can remember, was given to travelling to find her parents. I can't recall if they had already died or not. 
 In the first few days of the event taking place, Emily makes a list of things to do, but it seemed to take her forever to start searching the internet for survivors. These days I'd have thought this would be one of the first things to do. After all wouldn't a journalist make best use of the tools of trade? 
 Conclusion: 
 A thoroughly enjoyable read, and whilst I may point out some niggling issues they're in no way bad points at all. The arrival of Thor is a huge relief. Despite Emily's contact with the scientists, I was hoping she'd find another human along the way at some point. Thor's description and mannerisms are well portrayed, and as with any furry companion in such stories I hope he doesn't come to a bad end. 
 My over riding issue with this story is that it wasn't long enough, which is both a good and bad thing. I wanted more. Good thing. I didn't get it. Bad thing. But I am pleased to see there is a follow up. So, yay! A good thing. I'm looking forward to that. I read this book in 3 sittings, and was reluctant to put it down and go to sleep. 
 Paul Jones has given me some much needed respect for writers who publish eBooks. I've read plenty of junk from writers who shouldn't write at all, and honestly I was started to wonder if I'd ever find a writer who had the ability to tell a good story, put together a decent plot, create good characters and not have page after page of spelling, punctuation and grammatical errors. 
 Extinction Point isn't perfect, but what it lacks in niggling little things it more than makes up for it in the best way - being a page turner.

 My first reaction when I finished this book was "OMG there is going to be a sequel!" -immediately followed by me checking Amazon Kindle to see if it was out yet (no such luck), checking goodreads.com to see when exactly the sequel would release (again no luck), and finally checking Tammara Webber's blog spot which shows the next book in the series will be released in FALL 2011. 
 Tammara Webber's debut novel, Between the Lines, was astounding. Told from Emma and Reid's alternating perspectives, Webber introduces several fascinating characters. 
 I especially enjoyed reading from Emma's perspective as she experiences her first big break as an actress and the conflicts that accompany this opportunity. Emma is completely confident on-camera, but once the camera stops rolling, she struggles with real issues: friendship power struggles, family embarrassments, relationship issues and deciding what her future holds (one I can really relate to). Watching her battle through life's obstacles was inspiring, and I'm dying to see how she handles the big curve-ball revealed at the end of novel. (I won't give anything away... but it's HUGE and totally unexpected!) 
 Frankly, I loved to hate Reid (maybe that's Webber's goal). He is a spoiled, selfish slut (look at that use of alliteration) who doesn't care about ANYONE but himself. Reid, (yes, I am talking to you, Reid) I hope a life-altering bomb is headed your way, and until you learn how to feel remorse and respect others I will continue to love to hate you!! 
 Although we don't have the pleasure of reading Grahams inner dialogue, we learn a lot about him throughout the novel. He is the complete opposite of Reid in almost every way: loyal, thoughtful and sweet. And, I cannot wait to see what Webber has in store for him next. (Maybe we will even get the bonus of reading Grahams perspective in the upcoming books in the series!!! Fingers Crossed!) 
 I am desperately looking forward to discovering what's in store for everyone next, but I DON'T LIKE WAITING. Especially because I really didn't expect there to be a sequel. Even at 95% on my Kindle, I would have sworn things were about to get wrapped up, but boy was I wrong. Sequel, just come out already! 
 I gave this book 4 STARS because it was original, entertaining and just plain FUN!! I strongly recommend that you check this book out!!

 Anna Oliphant also known as Banana Elephant (HAHA) is our protagonist who finds love in the place she dreaded to go. Or rather, was forced to go. France! (A thousand exclamations). 
 The beginning of the book shows how she struggles to make friends in a place where she is the ONLY one who is new, who does not know French and is all alone. 
 'I had my own friends and my own inside jokes and my own stolen kisses.' 
 Enter Etienne St. Clair. Ahhhhhh! He is not our regular angst lover, who pushes you to the corner of the wall and makes out fiercely. He is a guy with imperfections. He is short, with buck teeth and wears a purple hat because his mom gifted it to him. He is someone who will not flourish you with diamonds but gives you gifts that symbolizes something.  'French name, English accent, American school. Anna confused.' 
 'No one remembers that I am left-handed.' 
 What's the worst part? He is taken. Spoken for. And he doesn't come out of the relationship either because he doesn't want change. Well, that's acceptable given the circumstances. BUT didn't you all root for Anna and Etienne throughout?! 
 The vivid description about the historical places in France made me want to book a one-way ticket. No, I am not kidding. Also, our character is unique in the way that she likes to write reviews about classic movies. Awesome, much? 
 'Happy Thanksgiving, let's see some dead people.' 
 The book is also funny, making you grin all the way. It spoke of family, of friendship, betrayal and love. 
 The ending.. oh god. It was PERFECT! 
 'For the two of us, home isn't a place. It's a person. And we are finally home.'

Sue has always been the drab older sister, who is forced to stand in her younger sisters shadow, though after receiving a brief makeover by her companions Sue decides to adopt a new persona for the night and call herself Suzanna. 'Suzanna' meets Holden while prancing down the stairs and their night continues on from there... that is until she is caught my her mother and must leave the ball without saying goodbye to Holden..  Her mother actually ruins her costume so when Holden returns he is not able recognize her, she still tries to talk to him but I'm pretty sure he just brushes her off not realizing who she really is  
 Overall I really enjoyed reading this book and liked seeing it all come together, though I did have a few problems with some of the characters and their decisions to do certain things. The relationship between Sue and Holden builds nicely though I felt like the end was rushed and some of the stuff (or issues with their relationship) could have been introduced earlier and had more time to play out. Holden's inability to recognize Sue for Suzanna did not bother me at first because I understand how a little makeup and some fancy clothes can change a persons appearance, but after a while I found his stupidity a bit tiresome as it just seems to drag on and on. 
 Desperately Seeking Suzanna was a fun, enjoyable read. I really liked how everything worked out in the end (even if I did think some parts of it were a bit rushed), and while I did have a few problems with some of the characters and their actions overall they didn't have a large impact on my view of the novel. I hadn't realized that this book was part of a series before reading it, but now that I have read this one I think I am defiantly going to check the others out..

 "A month ago, he would have rather eaten nails than worked for Damien Stark. But then Sylvia had approached him with the kind of project that is any architect's wet dream. To design a resort from the ground up. And not just any resort, but one located on its own private island. And she was handing him a blank slate." 
 Jackson Steele is the best for the job and there is no one who can do what he has envisioned. But a secret exposed from brother to brother may change the game...and test Sylvia in a way she's not prepared for. 
 "Even so, I'm sure there's pain behind both men's masks, and I wish that it was in my power to make this whole situation better for Jackson, whose love I cherish, and for Damien, whose respect I crave." 
 Sylvia finds that her relationship with Jackson has progressed to a point of need. Neither one can go too long without the touch of the other; even though there are still unspoken demons of their pasts hanging over their heads, they fall deeper into a pattern of control and submission. Each bump in the road of their fragile relationship weighs on Sylvia...and Jackson. 
 "I need this, and I know that he does too. This connection. This union. It's power and strength and solidarity. It's proof that we can get through everything that has and will happen. That we can weather the gathering storm. It's torment and treasure." 
 Of course, no love story comes without its strife. Past transgressions, even family secrets are at stake when Sylvia's young adulthood and Jackson's first project (that they want to make a movie out of) is threatened. Now, they have to find a way to make both problems disappear without causing waves in the media...which they are both very much in the spotlight of. 
 Now it's a matter of gaining control of a seemingly uncontrollable situation... 
 This is the second installment of the Stark International Trilogy and picks up right where the first left off. I can't say I was hoping for a happily ever after because, let's face it, I LOVE the angst of new turmoil within a relationship. I love to see the strength develop in the characters and the fight they have in them to stay together and work it out. That is what a real relationship is to me and I love reading about it, especially in the way Kenner writes it. 
 The little twists and turns this story takes had me smiling one minute and cringing the next all the while squirming in my seat. I love the chemistry between the characters, both familial and coupling, I couldn't ask for more. I found the relationship between brother and sister heartwarming and honestly, that resonated with me the most...as well as how the family sacrificed one for the other. That hits close to home for me which just made these characters all the more real. Kenner has a knack for pulling the reader in and making you believe what you are reading is real...one of my favorite aspects of her style of writing. 
 That cliffhanger though... 
 **5 Begging for Book Three, Stars**

This is a horror/crime story about a teenaged boy, Mark Underhill, who becomes obsessed with a creepy abandoned house in his neighborhood. Around the same time, his mother kills herself and a serial killer begins preying on neighborhood boys. None of this is a spoiler -- it's the premise established in the first few chapters -- and all of it is inter-related. 
 The story progresses in a disjointed, "literary" fashion with multiple points of view, scenes repeated with a slightly different emphasis, and much of it told by a character tangential to the story, the boy's uncle, who is (of course) a horror writer. In some books, this approach, like slowly peeling of layers of the onion until the awful truth is finally revealed, is very effective. In this book, it didn't ever seem to gel. 
 On a positive note, I never lost interest in the story and had no problems sticking with it to the end, and Straub is a good writer. I would say that his strength is creating very vivid scenes and images, and the dialogue was good as well. 
 But in this case, I felt that the whole was less than the sum of its parts. The multiple points of view and the repetition really started to get on my nerves. For the uncle's portions, there would be parts told from the third person, and then switch the his journal entries, in the first person, with little hints about "hmm, maybe this isn't true." There were several instances where the author would tell a scene, then flashback and work up to the scene, presenting the same events more than once. As I said, sometimes this approach works, but for me, in this case, it didn't. 
 It's hard to have a truly satisfying ending for this type of story. If the author explains too much, it can destroy the sense of mystery, and if they don't explain enough, it's deeply unsatisfying. In this case, he "explained" just enough, leaving a few tantalizing loose threads, but I thought the ending was stupid.  The ghost of a tortured five year old girl showed herself to Mark as a supernaturally beautiful adult, and had such awesome sex with him on the the very torture bed where she had suffered that he is convinced to somehow join her in the ghostly realm without actually dying first. He's not dead, just gone forever, but don't worry...they're so happy together.

 Like all of the books in this series, and really any book by Gail Carriger, this is just fun. I feel like the ending implies that Sophronia was Alexia's nanny? Throwing in that detail about Italians can't be an accident. I actually went back and reread the short story about Alessandro (Alexia's father), but that falls in the timeline before Finishing School. I really want to go back and reread the original series now, to see if I can spot any of these characters. We know that Petunia, Sophronia's sister, is Ivy's mother, so I kind of love the idea of her having been Alexia's nanny. Also I wonder if we ever saw Soap in any of the pack stuff.  
 Anyway. The dastardly Picklemen are back and they mean business! I kind of love the absurdity of this crew of villains -- they're deadly assassins...but they're answering to someone who calls himself the Gherkin, and they all wear tophats (the Gherkin gets the biggest, highest hat of course) with bright green bands. It's just the kind of delightful detail I've come to expect from Carriger's stories. So we've been hearing about some prototype for the last 3 books now -- I assumed it had something to do with the communication devices we see Alexia and co using in the Parasol series, but they're actually for mechanicals. I've always wondered why no one has mechanicals in the Parasol series -- and we finally get an explanation. Most mechancial servants are set on tracks, but the Picklemen have been working to create "mechanimals"...like Bumbersnoot, only big and deadly, who don't need tracks to move about. The "prototype" is basically a special valve that, if installed in every mechanical, can control all the mechanized servants (and weapons) in the country. Thus allowing the Picklemen to swoop in, "save" the day, and seize control of the government. Also they want control of the school, since it's the largest airship...ever.  As usual, it's up to Sophronia and co to stop them, and avoid being kicked out of school in the process. 
 There's also the tiny matter of Sophronia having indentured herself to the dewan (the loner werewolf employed by Queen Victoria...I want to say it's called the Shadow Cabinet, but I could also be thinking of the Shades of London series). In order to save Soap's life after Felix Mersey's father shot him, Soprhonia promised herself as a servant to the dewan upon graduation -- in spite of a much more attractive offer from everyone's favorite vampire. Speaking of, I was really hoping for Lord Akeldama to get more page time. He's my favorite character of all 3 series, and Carriger keeps hinting that he's somebody...as in an historical figure one might recognize? It's driving me nuts that I can't figure it out, because I feel like it's fairly obvious. We also have an (unnamed) cameo from Professor Lyall, but no Lord Maccon, and sadly nothing from Sidheag or Niall either. I'd actually be interested to read more about the Kingair pack in general. We know at the beginning of Soulless that Maccon isn't part of that pack anymore because there was a coup and they tried to oust him...I know we learn a little more of the backstory eventually, but I feel like there's still more that we aren't aware of -- plus Lyall was involved somehow. And also Niall is dead (recently, I believe) when PP starts.  
 This is a terrible review! Suffice to say, I loved this book as much as all of the rest, and I would be perfectly happy for Carriger to continue playing around in this world, thus allowing me to visit it too.

Consider this review a confession. Kafka's narrative feels like my own. I'm not bragging -- if a straight story more closely matches your experience, you're probably better off than I. Many reviewers have described the world of The Trial as nightmarish or surreal. Sometimes that's true. But, for the most part, I found it familiar and comfortable. 
 I'm not sure about you, but I've spent most of my life bewildered by the world I keep waking up into each day. I do function, brush my teeth, smile politely, and all of that. Yet despite appearances, I'm barely able to piece together the narrative. For me it's all been a series of loosely connected images. 
 I once expected that adulthood would bring some clarity, but it's only afforded me a better view of a labyrinth. My memories are disjointed. They play back like a flip book with missing pages. Your average child has a better grasp of society's mores and motivations. I can study them, but they never internalize. The spiritual longings that pin others or set them free are totally lost on me -- I've tried. I'm too conscious of my own existence to be anything but a passenger in my own body. What kind of screwed up alien world did I end up in? 
 I don't really expect that my experiences are very different than yours or anyone's. Lots of people read Kafka and feel kinship. But, damn. It feels spot on, doesn't it? Next I suppose two strangers will interlock their arms with mine and I too will chase some awful, empty end beside a quarry. Sounds about right.
