This book really resonated with me in ways I wasn't really expecting. 
 The Bully Book is written based on the author's own experience with bullying in school, and I think that's what makes this book so relevant and personal. It's one of the most realistic portrayals of bullying that I've seen, and it shows the real side of bullying: not physical punches or obvious taunts, but also ostracism and exclusion used as a tool to hurt others. 
 The format of the book was very cool, too. There are two different manuscripts that alternate. One is The Book that the bullies use each year to pick and hurt others, and the other is Eric Haskins's journal entries about his experience being "the Grunt". The book takes on a mysterious turn as Eric finds out about The Book and goes in search of information in an attempt to free himself of being the target. 
 It was fast paced and exciting, and I think that the message is perfect for kids. Since The Book actually gives very good advice about how to be manipulative and hurtful, I was uncertain of the appropriateness for kids. However, the book does a good job of showing the full story and making you connect with Eric. By the end, the book gives just as much advice and inspiration for kids to learn to define themselves and reach out for help. I think it would be great for classroom use. 
 Overall, it was a great book. I've known of Eric Kahn Gale through his connections to Team Starkid, and so it was great to read something he has created independently.

The personality and playfulness of the title makes you want to pick it up. Before you crack the spine you know our heroine is strong and resourceful and suggests a magical adventure. The Girl Who Circumnavigated Fairyland... is everything the title promises and has a few surprises. It is silly and full of puns. Rife with nonsensical characters and logic, but it is mischievous and carries a bit of darkness which I feel is essential to a good fairytale. 
 As is traditional we start our story in the mundane world (Omaha, Nebraska), but interestingly during World War II. September, our protagonist, is a twelve year old girl who feels estranged from the other school children, abandoned by her father (who is off at war), and ignored by her mother who works in a factory assembling engines. She is very well read for her age and her non-traditional home life make her unique among fairytale heroines. She knows from her reading what to expect from fairytale adventures and is equipped through the tutelage of her mother to solve complex puzzles and machines. 
 The magical world and characters would feel right at home in a Hayao Miyazaki film and tonally resonated with 
 Howl's Moving Castle 
 . September is joined by the preposterous half Wyvern/half library, A-through-L, and the melancholy marid, Saturday. Together they are forced to go on a quest for the despotic Marquess. Despite her child-like appearance, the Marquess invokes real fear through her cruelty and makes for a rich and complex villain. 
 There are currently three other volumes in this series with a fourth coming out this year. I have not read anything about the sequels, but I hope at least one follows September's shadow. We only get a brief introduction, but it is so unnerving I couldn't stop wishing to follow it into the depths of watery world.

Though the ideas and story behind this book are fun and engaging, I was frustrated while reading it. 
 There were ticks within sentences. 
 Repeated uses of "simultaneously" and "at the same time" and "the same thing" and especially "twin" made me feel like I was being bashed over the head. "Sophie and Josh are twins. Twins, I say! Did I mention? They're twins!" 
 Various emotions and expressions were described as "masks," and then one time when Josh asked Sophie, "Were they wearing masks?" She answered, "No, not masks." 
 But there were also problems with the whole. 
 Though I can forgive sentence ticks if the story and the characters are good, they were frustrating as well. Characters didn't have much depth. It felt forced, like I was seeing bits of the author or another person in his life coming out of each character when it was convenient. 
 I was also frustrated by the damsel in distress plot of the book, despite the nods to Perenelle being more skilled than Nicholas in some ways. It also seemed odd to me that all of the Elders (good, neutral, or evil) we encountered were women, yet Nicholas and Dee (men) are the mortals who know more than they do. 
 A note: I had done research to select this book, in the hopes that I might be the first of a fun series to read. So, perhaps my review is a touch scathing because it let down the hopes I had for it.

I am unsure about how I feel about this book. I think there were scenes where I anticipated things becoming more interesting, but overall the pace was slow and the revelations were not interesting. 
 Beta is the story of Elysia, a teen Beta, or testable human clone. The novel takes place in a sort-of dystopia, after an event called the Water Wars. Humans can either live on the Mainland in enclaves that are scientifically modified to support life (the rest of the world is desert) or, if they are fabulously wealthy and/or powerful, they live on the island of Demesne, where there's pretty much hedonism-lite. The air on Demesne is hyperoxygenated so that everyone is on a high, which makes the subsequent drug abuse we learn about sort of confusing. The world building here is weak; unlike the Hunger Games or Harry Potter's world, it's hard to connect these facts to the actions of Elysia's plot. Mostly, it's concerned with Elysia's social life. 
 Elysia gets sold, like other clones, to be of service. But since she's a teen Beta with a beautiful body, she gets chosen for a slightly different reason other than manual service. She is chosen to be a companion clone, taking the place of the Bratton family's daughter who's now in college (Astrid, who is described by everyone as a killjoy interested in social justice. We never meet Astrid in this book). Elysia calls her buyer Mother, and is introduced to her new "family": a secretive drug-addicted/future military member brother Ivan, a creepy/clone-sexin' father (called the Governor), and bratty but somewhat innocent Liesel. Other clones of the household are Xanthe, who performs housework; and Tawny, the Governor's luxisstant (supposed to provide luxury/exercise to the Governor, but instead acts more like a Massage Parlor Girl). 
 Clones in this world originate from dead people ("Firsts") who've had their souls removed from them. There's a lot to be said about the treatment of clones in this world. There are some implications that I wish Cohn got into; for example, Elysia is a thin, blonde, athletic beauty chosen to be a companion, while Miguel (clearly based on a Person of Color) is a laborer. Even the laws against clone-human relationships resemble anti-miscegenation laws from the past. Oddly, Elysia has information on some aspects of our modern history, but neglects these obvious connections. I'm left wondering if the lack of thematic emphasis has to do with showing Elysia's lack of understanding, or if those themes are left unexplored due to the author's white privilege. 
 The romance writing is shaky--she instantly falls in love with Tahir, has this weird connection with her "swimming God", and an abusive, scary relationship with her brother Ivan. Ivan wavers between protectiveness (he tries to keep his dad from molesting Elysia) and possessiveness (doesn't like it when others have her attention, claims she is there to serve him, and forces himself on her, resulting in Elysia's pregnancy in the end ). 
 I got confused as early on as Elysia's understanding of language wavers. At times, she is confused by idiomatic language, but in many other paragraphs she uses idiomatic English to a great degree. It's not really how I expect a clone to use language from how it's described. 
 The reason I marked this as two stars rather than one is that I'm hoping the second novel irons out the kinks in Cohn's writing. I understand she cowrote Nick and Nora's Infinite Playlist, so I guess sci-fi/dystopia is new to her and I won't hold it against her too much (yet).

My Reaction in a Nutshell: 
 OMFG this book is so good. 
 The Long Version: 
 The opening paragraph: 
 "Imagine four years. 
 Four years, two suicides, one death, one rape, two pregnancies (one abortion), three overdoses, countless drunken antics, pantsing, spilled food, theft, fights, broken bones, turf wars--everyday a turf war--six months until graduation and no one gets a medal when they get out. But everything you do here counts. 
 High school. 
 Cracked Up to Be is probably my favorite Courtney Summers's book (I've also read Some Girls Are and All the Rage). This book, in typical Summers' fashion, depicts a girl who falls from grace. 
 Parker had it all: looks, grades, popularity. And then something happened. Parker starts getting drunk in school, failing her classes, isolating herself from her friends. 
 "I elbow my way through a mass of people to get to my locker because there's something immensely satisfying about the toughest part of my arm connecting with the softest part of everyone else." 
 Parker is the type of girl you usually hate in a book: she is mean, self-absorbed, and doesn't give two-shits about anyone else. But somehow that made me love her even more. 
 I loved this book. It was insanely fast-paced and I devoured it in one sitting. I really like Summers' writing style and her narrative flow. This book (similarly to All the Rage) is told interweaving the events of what happened at Chris' party junior year and present day. Throughout the course of the book, readers get to see more and more of what happened that night until the story comes full circle. This book constantly kept me guessing. 
 This book is an important one about anxiety, depression, OCD, friendship, support, and guilt. Even though Parker spends most of the book trying to push people away, her parents, guidance counselor, and former friends (and sort of enemy) won't give up on her. They put up with her lashing out and try and get her out of her depression. 
 Parker was someone I actually could relate to. Her anxiety and perfectionism are two things that I also have to deal with. And as horrible as it might sound, I don't know if I would act any different from her if I was placed in her position. I would like to think that I would, but I just don't know. 
 One of the reasons why I love this book so much is because of its ending. It really makes a person wonder what they would do, how they would react if placed in a similar situation. 
 I love how this book has romance, but it doesn't overwhelm the plot. Yes, it's there and important, but this isn't a romance book. There isn't pretty courting and fluffy hand holding. It's awkward and cruel and not pretty. Plus Jake wasn't the main person to help Parker heal emotionally. Chris and Becky (and even Evan) all played a large part in her healing. She isn't fully "healed" by the end, but she is able to admit her mistake. And it wasn't Jake who convinced her or guided her. It was her friends in general.  
 I love how this book portrays mental illness. There really is no good way for me to say how well Summers portrayed this without giving MAJOR spoilers, so I'll refrain. But there is no romanticizing of mental illness (but also no shaming of it either). I liked how Parker slowly comes to notice her own OCD. From the perfectionism she had in kindergarten to color inside the lines to her very, very detailed lists to her snapping when nervous. It is a slow progression. In addition, Parker slowly comes to terms with her depression and goes from complete opposition to therapy in the beginning to consenting to it by the end  
 I love how guilt is portrayed. MAJOR SPOILERS are hidden under the "spoilers" tab. Read at your own risk (tw: r). Chris feels guilty because the party was held at his house. Becky feels guilty because she didn't try to talk Jessie out of running away. Evan feels guilty because he cheated on Jessie which made her want to leave. Parker feels guilty because she saw Jessie get raped and dragged away and she didn't tell anyone. All of them were drunk. All of them bare some guilt in Jessie's disappearance (and eventual murder). Whether or not that guilt is justified is up to you. Each of them feels like Jessie's death is their fault. And each tries to cope with it. But it's only through each other that they can begin to heal and move on.  
 I love how this book broke gender stereotypes: Yeah, this is a big spoiler so be warned  when Jake and Parker sneak away at the dance and go to the science lab, the two start making out and removing each other's clothes until Jake stops. He says "no." Granted Parker says something along the lines of "shouldn't guys want to have sex" (I can't find/remember the exact quote) but Jake decides that he isn't comfortable with what is about to happen. They stop, leave, and go back to the dance. I've never read a book where the guy asks to stop.  
 I love how this book portrays friendship. Chris and Parker used to date. yeah Chris did that super shady thing where he wanted to kiss Parker and would let her copy his homework in return which totally wasn't cool or right and pissed me off  But he is still there for Parker as a support system. He invites her to hangout with Jake and Becky on multiple occasions and truly cares for her as a friend. Even Becky who Parker never liked is there for her. Chris and Jake help Parker when she watches her dog die. Chris and Jake help her when she gets drunk at school again. Chris and Jake help her have an incentive to go to the dance. Becky helps her by noticing Parker being uncomfortable with Evan and making up an excuse to get her away.  
 There are so many reasons why I loved this book (and very few reasons why I didn't that being Chris saying that he'll let Parker copy his homework if she has sex with him, and the girl-on-girl hate ). I honestly don't know why Courtney Summers books aren't more widely read. Everyone should pick up at least one of her books. I just have two more to read before I've read them all! 
 ***TRIGGER WARNINGS: R, suicide attempt(s), OCD, anxiety, depression, missing person, mentions of blackmail, mentions of sex for favors,

Review Originally written for Mind-Ventures 
 Tempest seems to be a polarizing book. Either you love it or you hate it. In order to love it, readers need to accept Cross' time travel rules. Forget what you know of time travel and go into this book with an open mind. 
 The book opens with Jackson doing a time travel experiment to prove to his friend and science geek, Adam, that what he does in the past doesn't influence the present time. The theory is shown true until several days later when Jackson is ambushed by several mysterious people, his girlfriend Holly is fatally shot, and Jackson actually "jumps" two years into the past. Now he must figure out how to get back to his present time and save Holly from getting killed. Along the way, he uncovers killer secrets and lies that his father kept while raising Jackson. 
 So, Jackson can go into the past, do whatever he wants, and come back to the future with little or no repercussions. How is that possible? Well, you find out in the middle of the book that  ***SPOILER: Jackson is a half-breed. His mom was a time-traveler and his dad was human, so when he jumps he can half jump (with his body still in the present and mind in the past) or full jump (his body and mind change times) END SPOILER***  This revelation can allow readers to understand the reason why Jackson can't change things in the past when he jumps on most occasions. It is a somewhat believable explanation. 
 Cross creates an interesting plot line that has several twist turns and bumps along the way. It is complex but not overly complicated to follow. It keeps readers guessing who the "good guys" are. Even at the end, it is still a little unclear as to if Jackson can truly trust his dad and his organization. The ending is a tear jerker though. Readers might want to bring some Kleenex for the last few chapters. 
 My biggest complaint is that Jackson jumped back to the present time too easily. He learns about the various branches of time and how he could possibly jump to the present time but on another branch where his actions did affect the future. When he did get back to the current time, he jumped on the correct timeline without any detours. It seems that if he was struggling with his ability and he only fully jumped once, then it would be more difficult to find the correct timeline he was trying to get to. 
 Vortex is the next book in the series and is due out on January 8, 2013. There are still enough questions left unanswered in the book to make me interested in the sequel--especially the young girl who shows Jackson a possible desolate future and says that there are people trying to make that future a reality. So many questions surround her background. 
 The book reminds me of the movie Jumper mixed with a touch of The Butterfly Effect. For readers that enjoy suspense, intrigue, romance, and of course sci-fi, then Tempest might be a good read for you. Just remember to keep an open mind!

Oh, how I love adventure stories. Exotic settings, perilous journeys, treasures to be hunted, and of course fantastic romance. As adventure stories go, I found this one highly entertaining, delivering everything I want in this sort of book. 
 Gabriel, having just retired from life as a soldier, is returning to England for a life of peace. But his plans for an ordinary life are quickly interrupted when a dieing man asks him to take a message to a friend in Mongolia named Frank Burgess. Burgess is a member of a secret society known as The Blades of the Rose. Once in Mongolia he meets Frank's daughter, Thalia Burgess. Together they embark on a journey to recover a magic artifact and protect it from the Heirs, a group of elitist men intent on stealing magic for their own selfish ends. 
 I was very impressed by this book. The plot is entertaining, the pacing is fairly smooth, and the settings and tone build suspense and intrigue. The characters are very likeable and three-dimensional. Thalia is motivated by a lifelong desire to be part of the Blades of the Rose. She's reasonably tough and competent. Gabriel is courageous and steadfast, the perfect soldier. I enjoyed the development of their relationship through all the trials of their quest. 
 My only real criticisms are minor. The development of the characters is slightly clumsy. I felt like the mythology could have been explored in more depth or explained more. 
 All told I felt this was an excellent book. Highly recommended. 5 stars.

Straddling the Line by Jaci Burton was pretty much just fluff. I'm not saying that to be overly critical. I'm just being factual. It was fun, light-hearted, and incredibly smutty so it had all the ingredients necessary to compel me to want to finish the story. But, at the same time I can't call this a masterpiece of contemporary romance either. 
 Straddling the Line is Trevor and Haven's story. Haven is a sports journalist dealing with the grief of losing her father. Trevor is a hot shot athlete who plays both professional baseball and football who is keeping a secret about himself. I pretty much figured out his "secret" immediately. He can't read. Well... he can a bit but he's dyslexic.  And that's kind of it... there really wasn't much of any conflict here. I'm not entirely sure if I liked that or not. On the one hand it was nice to not have to deal with the characters constantly second guessing themselves or some other ridiculous drama thrown in just for the sake of it. On the other hand without any conflict the story just turns into fluff with no real emotional depth. As the story stands we are firmly swimming in the shallow end of the emotion pool. I think I would have enjoyed getting to venture into the deep end a bit more than I got to. But I also kind of liked the absence of useless drama. It's kind of a catch 22 situation here for me. 
 Speaking of the shallow end of the emotion pool, the vast majority of the dialogue in Straddling the Line was just small talk. SOOOOO MUCH SMALL TALK. 
 It was basically like: 
 "Thank you for inviting me to the party." 
 And in response: 
 "I'm glad you came to the party." 
 And that would be pretty much where the conversation would end. And I don't get the sense that this was done on purpose because the author wanted to show a normal interaction. Almost all of the dialogue was about the same. It started to feel like these were conversations taken out of an ESL text book. I just wanted a bit more personality out of the characters because it was starting to feel pretty bland. But even with the bland dialogue, I still found Trevor and Haven to be likeable characters. I was charmed by them enough to care about them having a HEA so I kept reading. 
 Here's the deal with Straddling the Line: I wasn't really reading it for the story. I didn't expect this was going to be a masterpiece. In all honesty, I was reading this one just for the smut. I mean... have you seen the cover? I was totally counting on this being filled with smutty delights and Straddling the Line definitely came through on that one! The smut was super steamy and there was lots of it. So in that regard, the story was very successful. It just couldn't bring that same steam into the other aspects of the story like the plot and the dialogue. I'm not saying this was terrible because it wasn't. It also wasn't amazing either. It just felt kind of average for me which is ok.
After 154 books in a span of 3 years, even though I didnt cry, finally a book has made me shed tear. Amazing.

3.5 stars (not sure whether to rate this up or down...) 
 Here's the deal: I enjoyed this, but I wasn't necessarily wowed by it. 
 Frankly, I think I would've enjoyed this story more had it focused on Alia rather than Diana. Diana wasn't a bad character per se, but she felt so...perfect. Sure, she had her struggles and insecurities, but they didn't emotionally impact me as much as Alia's. I found that some of the most standout moments in this book were from Alia's POV, moments when she was pushed to her limit, when she had to summon every dredge of willpower left in her. As for the side characters, I thought they were fun--but that's exactly it. They were fun, and so was their banter, but I ultimately didn't end up forming a particularly deep connection to them. (I did really love Theo though.) As always, though, Leigh Bardugo incorporates some wonderful diversity in this book: excepting Diana, the cast is made up entirely of POCs, one of whom is fat and also bisexual. The representation was overall fantastic, and that's definitely not something I took for granted. 
 Plot-wise I don't have anything noteworthy to say. There were some scenes that stood out to me--I think my favourite scene was the one where the gang takes turns answering questions with the lasso on them --and I generally appreciated that there was a good balance between plot- and character-development. My biggest qualm with the plot though was with this book's ending, or at least the series of events that led up to the book's ending. The fact that Jason turned out to be the "bad guy" the whole time just seemed a bit far-fetched to me. It was a plot twist--I didn't see it coming that's for sure--but I don't think it was a particularly good plot twist. Maybe I'm just salty cause I had really warmed up to Jason as a character. But Jason really did go from 0 to a 10000000 real quick. I can buy the fact that he was ambitious, that he had plans different from the rest of the gang's, but for him to want to wage war?? for him to order his childhood friend killed?? I just can't buy that. It was too much.  
 That being said, here are some of my favourite scenes/quotes: 
 "'You'll remember me,' he panted, his face sheened with sweat. 'I was your first kiss. I could have been your first everything. You'll always know that.' 
 She looked deep into his eyes. 'You were my first nothing, Jason. I am immortal, and you are a footnote. I will erase you from my history, and you will vanish, unremembered by this world.'" 
 DAMN, DIANA ACTUALLY Did That 
 "He jabbed his finger down on the screen. 'Shapow!' 
 Nothing happened. 
 'Oh, wait a second.' His thumbs flew over the screen again. He cleared his throat. 'What I meant to say was, shablammy!'" 
 this is why I love Theo 
 "I am done being careful. I am done being quiet. Let them see me angry. Let them hear me wail at the top of my lungs." 
 YES ALIA YES 
 "She marched up the hill, tears choking her throat. It wasn't the embarrassment. It wasn't the memory. It was everything that had come with it, every hateful thought she'd ever had about herself like a chorus in her head. The lasso was like looking into a mirror that stripped away each illusion you used to get yourself through the day, every bit of scaffolding you'd built to prop yourself up. And then there was just you. Boobs too small. Butt too big. Skin too ashy. She was to nerdy, too weird, too quiet around people." 
 what a heart-rending passage 
  
 An overall fun read, but unfortunately, I don't think it'll be very impressionable for me in the long run.

"Is that what you were doing in my room?" he asks after a moment. 
 I sigh. Why am I telling him any of this? "Yes. I was on assignment." 
 "I was your assignment?" 
 "Yes." 
 He hesitates a moment, then grins. "That's kind of hot." 
 I read this book at a rapid pace, I loved the concept of the fae world yet I did not expect to enjoy it as much as I did. It was a humourous, fast-paced action novels complete with twists and turns. 
 The book itself centers around guardian in training, Violet Fairdale as she aims to graduate top of her class when she meets troublesome assignment Nate whom she just can't seem to shake off all whilst dealing with her class rivalries and dangerous underground travels. 
 The characters created by Morgan left me in adoration. Violet is spunky and smart and harbours an unexplainable talent desired by all corners of the world  from the the Guild in Creepy Hollow to the evil princes of the Seelie Court. . Nate is sweet and unpredicatable at the same time and so I immediately feel in love with, unfortunately that didn't turn out so well for me  or Violet for that matter . However, my ultimate favourite had to be Ryn, the sarcastic, brooding, bad-boy faerie gave me the emotional edge I needed to push this review up to a 5 star. 
 "You guys dated, didn't you?" 
 "Are you insane? Not even if the continuation of our kind depended on it would I be tempted to do something so awful" 
 The relationship between Ryn and Violet literally gave me life in this novel. The fast flying insults kept a smile on my face but did nothing to take away from the emotional back story the pair share. The temperamental relationship between the two is completely believeable due to the aforementioned past as they already have a fully fleshed dynamic before the novel begins and so they are not thrust into in ridiuclously quick manner as many novels do. 
 "Seelie Court," murmurs Nate. "Sounds familiar. Was it in a computer game?" 
 "Do I look like someone who plays computer games?" 
 A grin stretches across Nate's face. "You look like someone who could be in a computer game." 
 Then comes the fast developing relationship between Nate and Vi which I personally found myself indifferent to as it offered a cute, fluffly romance (for a while) but it all happened so quickly I didn't have the time to attach myself to them. 
 Therefore, the characters of this book really made the story for me as the dialogue and fast paced action scenes is captured my attention for long periods of time. I was intensely addicted to this book to the point I was attempting to read it off my phone in class.

Faefever was desperately in need of more action. Dreamfever might have benefited from a little less. Still, the heightened tensions and the feeling Mac was finally in the thick of things made this a far less frustrating read. 
 The increased activity raises a question though: As Mac's search for information uncovers more secrets and further plot twists, how is Moning going to tie up all the loose threads? Is everything going to get answered in the final installment, or will there be mysteries left unsolved? Because that would force me to get my pitchfork and flaming torch. I don't want all my aggravation to be for naught! 
 As of Dreamfever's end, Mac seems no closer to her ultimate goal of finding the Book and pushing back the Unseelie horde. Fingers crossed that I'm underestimating Moning. The sheer heft of Shadowfever (yes, I already have a copy sitting here) suggests the author didn't do a hasty job of resolving the plot. But looks can be deceptive. What if the whole darn thing is Mac pontificating on stasis and change and the way of the world? 
 That's a scary thought. 
 I shan't recount all the ways Mac gets on my nerves; my other reviews have amply discussed my issues with the protagonist. However, there is one point I would like to make: For part of the story, Dani becomes the narrator. I infinitely preferred her to Mac. She's snappy and relatable, with a keen eye and a sharp mind. She doesn't accept any nonsense and she's always scheming to find out more. She is activity personified. This change in POV clearly shows Moning's ability to create a good story and a compelling voice. Had Dani (or someone like her) been the centerpiece of the tale all along...oh, what an easier read this series might have been!  
 Another cliffhanger-ish ending - Moning does adore them - and Mac is left in limbo once again. I didn't think the final moment was that infuriating. Perhaps that's because I was prepared for it? Or because I have the next book at the ready? Or maybe it's because I've already guessed some things and my predictions are coming true? 
 On to the final book in the series. As my friends have pointed out, getting sucked into the Fever books is not about the characters. It's about the search for answers - a quest that's as infuriating as the hunt for the freakin' Sinsar Dubh!

Actual rating: 2.5 stars 
 Overall: a fun, enjoyable, and easy read. It started out relatable as I am a freshman college and also struggle with social anxiety. I liked reading about a socially awkward main character who had a deep love for something that isn't really seen as "cool" (I have an unabashed love for YA and fantasy books, which no one I know does). However, there were some things I had difficulty reconciling/accepting and feel that so much more could have been done with Fangirl. Minor spoilers ahead so take care! 
 The Good: 
 I was a little hesitant about reading Fangirl because I didn't particularly like Rainbow Rowell's Eleanor and Park, which was extremely overhyped to me and felt quite mediocre to me. I was scared Fangirl might be the same but I really quite liked the characters and their complex relationships. 
 Cath is relatable! At least for me, she is. She's quirky, awkward, and loves something that isn't "cool". I LOVE those things about her. Levi was such a cute and funny guy and even though I was pretty sure he and Cath would get together, it was still a pleasant surprise and warmed me when they actually did! Reagan's sarcasm and biting wit was hilarious. 
 The Meh: 
 The similarity between the Simon Snow series and Harry Potter series really threw me off since it's such an obvious copy and we realize quite early on that Harry Potter does, in fact, exist in this world. 
 Nick's sudden change from potential romancer to "bad guy" seemed a little uncalled for and a little unbelievable. This might just be me and it wasn't so terrible as to infect me with strong thoughts of dislike. 
 The Bad: 
 For me, Cath didn't really grow or develop throughout the book. Everything came way too easy for her. 
 Exhibit 1) She doesn't go out of her comfort zone in order to forge friendships at college. It is always someone else who wants to be her friend, with no real reasoning. Reagan decides to take pity on her and become her friend, without Cath actually actively trying to be Reagan's friend; in fact, she tries to have as little contact with her roommate as possible because social awkwardness! Why does Levi want to be her friend? No clue. It must be because he thinks she's quirky and thus adorable so without even really knowing her or talking to her at all, decides to fall in love and proceeds to win her over without her ever really knowing of it. Nick just decides that he's going to help out an innocent little freshman in his advanced fiction writing class because lo and behold she's the next J.K. Rowling and will help edit his writing to great heights. I'm glad Cath was able to find friends in college but as someone who is in her first year of college struggling to make close connections, I feel that this process of "friendship" has been too smoothed over. I read books like these and fall under the illusion that friends will always come to me because even though I'm super shy in social situations, they will see something special in me that most other people don't see. Cath has such a relatable struggle with making friends that it's sad Rowell didn't decide to explore the two-way process of finding and becoming friends. 
 Exhibit 2) The conflict between Cath and Wren was resolved way too easily. I definitely do not endorse heavy drinking and/or use of drugs so going to the hospital for alcohol poisoning is a really scary thing to me (as it should be for many). Wren gets alcohol poisoning one night and this somehow undos everything she has done to Cath since the beginning of college that resulted in minor estrangement. I understand the gravity of the situation but it didn't seem like the book ever did or tried to present that to the readers. To me, it felt like Wren got alcohol poisoning -> Wren realizes the errors of her past ways in an epiphany -> everything is fine and dandy with no emotional conflict between Wren and her sister and dad whatsoever. PSA: LIFE IS NOT THIS EASY. 
 Exhibit 3) Overcoming her writer's block and finally finishing her original short story. After much stress is put on Cath over this assignment, we as readers don't even get to see her write the story. It felt like the book was building this up and just kind of let us drop with an excerpt from Cath's short story and the tag that it was the winner of the prestigious writing prize. Ugh. 
 Exhibit 4) Cath's complicated feelings towards her mother. After years of no contact, Cath's mother suddenly makes an appearance in this books, just to add even more tension and conflict! Despite Cath's initial anger and resentment, she is shown to actually want her mother to stay with Wren when she is in the hospital because that's what mothers do, goddamnit! Never mind the fact that Cath has been going on and on about how her mother isn't her mother. Now she wants her mother because she doesn't want to be alone! But her mother leaves because that's what she's good at. She leaves and doesn't come back, since she's already exhausted her use as a plot device to drive the wedge between Cath and Wren even deeper and since Rowell needs the two sisters to make up, this complicated little side story needs to be swept under the rug. 
 Exhibit 5) I don't know where Cath went to high school and how she managed to get a scholarship but I highly doubt she can remain on that scholarship without doing shit in college. She is always writing fanfic and never doing school work. She misses her finals and doesn't seem to have made them up. Her professor is allowed to withhold her first semester grade all the way until the end of second semester (I don't feel like this is within the power of one professor. Is there no deadline for grades at this school?). At the very least, she should be on academic probation. Since nothing in this book has indicated to me that Cath is one of those intelligent people who can get straight A's without trying or doing work (she didn't know fanfiction with plagiarism for god's sake!), she should not be able to spend all day every day writing fanfiction and ignoring her school work! This is not how college works! 
 Even though my "bad" section of the review is much longer than the "good" part, I did find it an overall enjoyable read. Clearly, the strength of Fangirl lies in its unique characters and their relationships with each other. It was just never enough for me to fangirl over them myself. I am only so harsh, though, because when I first started this book, I saw something of me in Cath. However, her realness gave way to overused tropes and cliches and I was left with a happy-feel-good book, which while interesting to read, did nothing to go beyond that. I am disappointed because this book could have been so much more and had so much more impact.

Rating: Two-and-a-half stars 
 Jocasta falls just short of three stars for two reasons, which I'll detail below. 
 First, a precis: The novel recasts the myth of Oedipus as told from the titular character's point of view (hopefully, I shouldn't have to recount the traditional version of the myth?). Though the authors have elected to largely abandon any supernatural elements,  for example, the Sphinx is Melanthe, the half-Egyptian Maenad priestess of Dionysus, who poses the potentially fatal riddles to the suitors who come to Thebes after Laius' death,  there's the Tiresias (the prophetic mouthpiece of Apollo), who does seem to channel a divine will when she (he) utters her (his) dooms.[1] 
 The Tiresias prophesizes that fourteen-year-old Jocasta will be queen of Thebes and marry its most famous king. She is chosen for Alphenor, the heir-apparent to Thebes' rulers Amphion and Niobe. But on the night of the betrothal, Niobe blasphemes, the Tiresias curses the family, and all but one of the royal children die. The next day, Amphion is torn apart by a mob, and Niobe goes mad. Jocasta and her family are at a loss, especially in light of the prophecy, but things soon appear to be looking up when Laius, a son of a former Theban king, returns from exile in Pelops' city of Pisa (Olympia), claiming the throne and Jocasta. The night of the wedding things do go well. Jocasta falls in lust at the sight of Laius, and Laius reciprocates the feeling. But soon after the couple consummates the marriage the prophetess tells Laius that any son of his will kill him. The king attempts to repudiate Jocasta but he has no cause, and - of course - she's already pregnant with Oedipus. Nine months later, the newborn is torn from Jocasta's arms and Laius has it exposed, or believes that the man he sends to do it, has done it. The novel passes over the next twenty years quickly. Laius continues to send tribute to Pelops and, living in fear of conceiving a son, never touches Jocasta again. Though Laius proves a most inept king, Jocasta and her brother Creon rule the city, and make it prosperous despite the tribute. 
 The story picks up when Laius decides to consult the Delphic oracle. As in the traditional version, he meets an unrecognized Oedipus on the way to Delphi, there's an altercation, and Oedipus kills him. Subsequently, Creon organizes a competition in Thebes to find a new husband for his sister: Whoever can answer the riddles of Melanthe, the Maenad high priestess, will become the next king of the city. Oedipus shows up to participate, and as with Laius, Jocasta is smitten at first sight. Because Oedipus is the supposed son of Corinth's king and an alliance with that city would counter the power of Pelops, Creon conspires to ensure that the youth wins the contest. 
 Again, the next two decades are glossed: Jocasta and Oedipus rule an ever more fortunate Thebes, and they have four beautiful children: Antigone, Ismene, and the twins Eteocles and Polynikes. And then everything goes sour when Jocasta's relationship with her husband comes out. 
 Why not three stars (or more)? 
 One reason is the writing. It's just "meh" - competent but not particularly beautiful or elegant. And there are anachronisms that jar the reader out of the early Iron Age setting, making her wonder if a Mycenaean Greek would have actually said that. 
 I could have forgiven such clumsiness, however - as I have with other authors - if Jocasta had been a more compelling character, but she has no arc. The child of the first chapter is not all that different from the fifty-plus-year-old woman of the final chapter. Jocasta comes across as rather clueless and passive, particularly in the hands of her brother, whose personal ambitions, machinations and political acumen are what keep Thebes strong. I can accept that a fourteen-year-old girl, growing up insulated from the hurly-burly of politics, would be at sea when suddenly thrust onto center stage. But if I'm to continue to be interested in her at all, she has to show some maturation over the course of the twenty and forty years that the last two-thirds of the novel encompass. It's difficult to see that in this version of Jocasta. 
 I was impressed by how the authors euhemerized the myth. It worked for me, though I'm still puzzled about the role of the Tiresias, the one ambiguously supernatural element. In the end, though, the book reads like a first or (at best) second draft. There's a potentially interesting character in Jocasta, and you can see the glimmerings of potential in Cleon's and Oedipus' but they're not drawn sufficiently well to make me recommend the book. On the other hand, if you like this genre (as I do), it may be just good enough to warrant a perusal. 
 [1] Tiresias is a title for the blinded person who speaks for Apollo. In the beginning, the post is held by an old woman. When she dies, her successor is Jocasta's father, Menoeceus.

This book makes me want to leave a review as profound and poetical as the text itself, but I feat that it would just come across as pretentious. Suffice it to say that A Canticle for Leibowitz is one of those rare books that makes you feel really, REALLY awful . . . but in the right way. It is a clarion call, a cry of warning and protest against atomic weapons, the almighty Lucifer conceived of by Mr. Miiler's generation. It makes you rail against the utter idiocy of human pride, human folly, human suffering. It makes you think. 
 I am *not* a Christian; you don't have to be one to appreciate this work. I admired the religious characters' conviction and faith, and was sincerely moved by parts of the text (though I am no closer to being a Christian after reading it than I was before). Mr. Miller did an amazing job of making his cast relatable, and never stuck with any one person long enough for them to grow tiresome. Their lives (and their deaths) had meaning. 
 This book is awesome, in the original sense of the word. Go read it.

When picking out a book, I am usually drawn to its cover. So when I saw this book by Shirley Jackson, I was curious, drawn to it but curious. So curious, in fact, that I wanted to read it right away. Now, the conflict came when I was halfway through the book. As a reader who is used to reading romance novels and chick literature, I was disturbed by the events unfolding in this story. Let me continue by giving a brief summary of "We Have Always Lived in the Castle". 
 So Merricat, short for Mary Katherine, is a member of the Blackwood family, along with her sister Constance and Uncle Julian. It wasn't always the three of them until a few years ago that the Blackwood family died mysteriously while enjoying their dinner. The suspect, none other than Constance Blackwood , who was the designated cook/chef of the family that night. But she was acquitted for lack of evidence in court. Years later, Merricat, Uncle Julian, and Constance live by themselves in the mansion used to belong to Merricat and Constance's father. Their peace was disturbed by the arrival of their cousin, Charles. 
 I'll stop there because this is where it gets weird for me. A lot happened following the arrival of their cousin. And it seems like everything was caused by Merricat. It's just really weird. There are times that I actually felt bad for them, especially when the whole village was against them and was harassing them. But I go back and think, "Well, you wouldn't be in this situation if it wasn't for Merricat." I keep on thinking, it is all Merricat's fault. Plus, it was kind of implied who killed the rest of the family. But a bigger question is WHY? Why do it? Why kill? 
 It got me thinking maybe, psychologically, Merricat is a psychopath. A psychokiller in the making? And Constance, if she knew that Merricat was the killer, why keep it from the authorities? Was there something going on with the two sisters that nobody knew about?  And poor Uncle Julian, I really felt bad for him. He seemed like a sweet old man who doesn't know what's been going on around him. 
 I got nothing really. I also don't know what to feel about this book. I'm numb on this. I have a lot of questions though. You just have to read it for yourself to see what I mean. Unless, you're the type to enjoy this genre then by all means. The reason I gave it a 4 is because it got me really thinking about the events that happened. And also it entertained me somehow in a weird way. Would I read something like this again, maybe. But honestly speaking I miss reading a good romance novel and I'll probably stick to reading it for a long time after this.

I didn't care who Rachel was or what impact she had to the story so when she was made the next Oracle I didn't really give a shit. ...Sorry?  THEN WHY THE FUCK DIDN'T YOU READ THIS WHEN YOU WERE A KID, GRACE?

Yes, Mel is a Slayer, yes of the Buffy the Vampire Slayer fame, but honestly it's such a different world and different meaning, that there's no need to know about BtVS whatsoever. This has an identity of it's own, seperate of the Buffyverse.

The colourization of this is definitely my favourite part, displaying the city Mel lives in beautifully.

Kat Bastion weaves a story of love, mystery, and yes magic that will have you ignoring family and friends to find out how things are going to play out for Isobel, Iain, and Velloc. It's one thing to have to choose between two men that both feel you belong to them, but to also cross time as well? Isobel get thrown back in time not once, but twice. Yes, that's right, the book is over three different time lines. There's a lot to this book and you won't be skimming this book or you'll miss important bits of information. There are definitely "what the heck just happened" moments. Bastion was able to connect all of the complicated craziness of this story together in such an enjoyable way. There is an element of the paranormal in the story with magic and celestial, mysterious beings. Isobel is not a passive heroine she definitely has her own mind which makes me like her character even more. Now that I have convinced you that this is a good read here's the one negative that you may or may not be willing to accept. Two very strong alpha males are able to accept that the woman they each love, loves, sleeps with, and builds a life with another man. When Isobel goes back and forth I expected at least a little bit of histrionics to happen. Some furniture throwing, Iain or Velloc withholding sex for a bit, or at least some howling and rolling around on the ground. Give me something! These two alphas were way too calm about the sharing for me. Although Iain initially said that Isobel was his and he did not want to help her learn to manipulate her ability to time travel he still gave in to her. I really expected him to refuse to let her go back. Maybe I'm just being a drama queen, but this mamma wanted some drama! This book is well written, the plot is unique and will pull you in, the love scenes are steamy, and at the end of the story you will be left wanting the next book to come out as soon as possible.

"We thought we could do better. 
 Better? I say, in a small voice. How can he think this is better? 
 Better never means better for everyone, he says. It always means worse, for some." 
 There are two types of people : those who can read the Handmaid's Tale and think " ah, good thing that'll never happen!", and those who are chilled to the bone, and think "this could happen. This is too real". 
 To be a woman - a western woman, with rights, and legal protections, and the benefits of modern medicine and hygiene and so forth - is to be grateful. I can vote, own my own property and indeed even open a bank account. I can wear trousers and use birth control and remain unmarried. I'm not subject to virginity tests or forced to marry a stranger by my parents at age 14 or many of the other injustices perpetrated against women around the world. 
 To be a woman, though, is to be angry. At lower salaries for women, at the aforementioned injustices still being perpetrated, endlessly, at catwalks and harassment and threats of violence, of sexist "jokes" that I must laugh at, or "don't you feminists have a sense of humour?", at unwarranted opinions about my face, my body, my mind, my outfits, my choices. At the unending condescension. Yes, please explain this simple thing to me. 
 So, this book hits close to home. Because it's a future holds have to *hope* never happens, but can't really have any faith that it won't.

What price is too high to pay, even for love? 
 City of Lost Souls picks up nicely from City of Fallen Angels, with the story continuing its new arc following the first three books. I'm glad I took that little break from the series though, because immersing myself back into the world Ms Clare has created makes me love it just that little bit more. The story, the characters, the writing, all of it is rich and pulse-pounding. Plus, come on, the last two books' cliffhanger endings? Who wouldn't want to dive into the next book right away. On the darker side of things, and I don't think I really noticed it before, I feel this entry to the series is just a tad bit too long-winded. 
 Jace is gone. 
 After the battle with Lilith and the arrival of the Shadowhunters, Clary finds herself stuck in her own personal purgatory. 
 Terrified of what's happened to the love of her life; terrified of what she knows she'll have to do to bring him back. 
 But with Sebastian waiting in the shadows to strike. 
 What will the consequences be for the choices Clary and her friends make in the name of love? 
 Like I said, City of Lost Souls' story is a great continuation in the series. It's intricate and fantastic, filled with magic and promise and scenes that force your heart into your throat. The build-up is also pretty darn awesome, with events within the plot steadily ratcheting up the suspense for the finale, not only the finale of this entry, but also the finale that is the final book in the series. 
 What weighs it down in this instalment though is its length. I'm sure it's around the same as the others in the series but, something about City of Lost Souls just makes it feel like it has far too many pages. It isn't helped by the fact that about every other paragraph is dedicated to describing our characters' features in explicit detail. It's another thing I'm not sure I noticed in the previous novels, but here it feels slightly overwhelming. We're five books in, I have a decent visualisation of our main characters without being reminded every five minutes. 
 Our cast of characters though are all great. They have distinct personalities that show just as well as before, with some solid development occurring with them that doesn't detract from the bigger picture. The two standout people in City of Lost Souls, for me at least, are Clary and Sebastian. Starting with the latter, I think Ms Clare has done a fantastic job of creating a sinister villain with multiple layers of nightmarish-ness. Sebastian is a much, much better bad guy than Valentine, and I can't wait to see which direction this boy goes. 
 Clary on the other hand has divided me once again. It was just a simple and short scene with her and her mother. The way our main character treats, speaks and antagonises Jocelyn really rubs me up the wrong way, and strikes me as slightly off key. I was fully behind Clary when she vented her anger the first time, but as events have unfolded and Clary herself has grown, she should now have a better understanding. But - SLIGHT SPOILER - to blame her mother for her life being hell, after the decisions Clary has made, angers me. 
 No, honey, your mistakes are your own. Your mother protected you from that hell all your childhood, giving you something others within the book didn't have. Be a little, no, a lot, more goddamned grateful. 
 But on a positive note, Clary's a bad-ass! During the second half of the book I really started to see how she's changed, how strong, both physically and mentally, she's become. There are some truly great scenes that redeem her for the reader. I also cannot help but love her recklessness and stubbornness. I think some people are a little put off by those traits, but for me, it's those bull-in-china-shop decisions that keep the world from crumbling. Before everyone else can come up with any definitive plan, Clary dives in to hold back evil's spread until they have one. 
 I didn't realise I had that much to say about City of Lost Souls. 
 Although it's definitely got me pumped for the final book.

The fact that I knew this from the first sentence is a testament to Levithan's memorable prose. I'm trying to think of another author from whom I would not only tolerate but enjoy a first-person-plural present-tense narrative. John Green, maybe. There's a reason they wrote a fantastic collaboration. Anyway, I digress. 
 This book is great at what it does, which is represent gay teenage boys. Extra points for one of them being trans, and integrating that into the story without making it a Big Issue. It is not great at, say, including women who are characters in their own right, but that's fine, it wasn't really the point of the novel. I just wish there would be a high-profile YA novel about two girls kissing. Whatever. 
 Really extra awesome bonus points for the narrative voice of the gay men who died in the AIDS epidemic, lending some gravitas to what was otherwise basically a book about some high school kids trying to pull a crazy stunt. The phrase "shadow uncles" really jumped out at me and made me think. There's a whole segment of a generation of gay (and probably trans) people who should still be here, right now, witnessing their legacy. I like the idea that they're watching and rejoicing the way the narrators of the book do. The haunting collective voice, the trademark poetic prose...Levithan does it again.
Though this book series didn't blow me away as much as I thought it would, I throughly enjoyed reading all three books

Ulysses is not for the faint of heart or anyone who dislikes modernism and/or stream-of-consciousness. 
 This book is so unusual and I'm not sure where to start in a review. The book amazingly takes place in the span of one whole day. We start with Stephen Daedalus (I am not sure if this is supposed to be the same of Stephen Daedalus from A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man; however, given the name I imagine they are the same). Then we quickly shift to the story of Leopold Bloom. Most of the story stays focused on his day but we occasionally change back to Stephen's perspective and at the very end we get Bloom's wife, Molly's perspective. 
 As I think everyone knows going into this, Ulysses was written as a counterpoint to Odysseus, with Bloom being Odysseus and his journey to try and make it back to his Penelope that day (Molly). With that in mind it makes sense in an irreverent sort of way. The book is interesting and has some beautiful prose; however, it was just convoluted and I didn't appreciate the stream-of-consciousness. I could write more but it was so bizarre that I don't think I want to.

But well, thank goodness around three-fourths of the book everything went pretty well - the part where she started totally understanding everything and admitting to herself and others her mistakes. 
 I almost gave this a lower rating than 3 but the ending changed my mind. And how can I not move it up without considering how brilliant a character Zac was! Zac was a unique character. It has been a very long time since i last read a LK book. And i was really looking forward to this one. 
 The book didn't disappoint but it also didn't really have that distinctive LK wow-touch - I remembered her books used to have bit more pull when it comes to feelings and plot twists. This story is interesting enough as a start of a series but comes across as a bit mainstream to me somehow. However, her characters are as adorable as ever...but what does it say when the story makes you love the side characters more than the main ones? 
 Devon Ravenel, as the main guy here, did come across as a mean a-hole at first. He's selfish, lazy and lacks the urge to be more than he is. He grudges the fact that he's saddled with new responsibilities as the Earl of Trenear and he's eager to get rid of it as soon as he could. The estate and land that seems to be more a liability than a profit made him more adamant in his decision to sell off everything and inadvertently kicking out all the inhabitants, namely the widow of the late earl and his three young sisters. However, one love-hate exchange with the feisty widow Kathleen made him reassess his decisions. Kathleen is so proper and controlled, wanting to do the right thing by society yet at the same time she uses sarcasm as her tool and wields it well with the two Ravenel brothers. Love the dialogue and the witty banter although there should be more. Devon as a hero is not a wholly noble and gentlemanly character. He has his moments where he could be calculating and a bit callous. Kathleen comes across as a woman who is struggling to stay within the appropriate boundaries she was brought up to heed. 
 The side characters are endearing. You have Weston/ West, Devon's younger brother who was saved from life as a wastrel by Kathleen's scathing set-down (ouch...but it did him good). He turned out to be a very good brother-figure for the younger girls - the gentle and intelligent Helen and the two spirited twins Pandora and Cassandra. And you have the grumpy rich bachelor friend Winterborne (who's story is up next in the second book of the series) who also almost stole the show. 
 So, to sum up: hero is a jerk who came into title that he doesn't want, sees heroine and because she is clever, hot and sassy despite dowdy widow costume he lusts for her, brother of hero becomes a better man thanks to heroine and becomes a valuable ally to all, hero sets about seducing heroine but she is confused with hero's advances, hero schemes ways to save the land in whatever way he could, but in the end hero becomes a better man. 
 Although there is a nice sweet ending for the MCs, there is a cliffhanger epilogue involving the next couple (aaarghhhh!) and we have to wait for half a year for the rest of the story.

Tess and her sister Kristina are complete opposites. Tess is smart and quiet, and Kristina is sporty and popular, but both of them are okay with having their own place. But when Kristina is diagnosed with bone cancer, everything changes. Suddenly Tess is the center of attention with everyone looking for updates, and senior boys are flirting with her. Home life changes too; her picture-perfect family is cracking, and it's up to Tess to hold the pieces together. 
 I'M NOT HER was a powerful, emotional story dealing with a frequently-used topic - illness of a sibling - and, while not exactly putting an entirely fresh angle on it, refrained from resorting to cliches. It's easy to empathize for Tess as she struggles with not just the relatively trivial issues of high school made complicated but with her possibly dying sister. She had always felt weaker than Kristina, but now she needs to be the strong one. 
 There was really only one thing that bothered me about this book, and that was an event that occurred towards the end. (Highlight to read the blanks if you want the spoiler.) I felt that Jeremy's death was just completely unnecessary. Kristina was suffering enough without that, and I thought that he died too late in the book for the author to fully explore the impacts of it, not to mention that he was my favorite character. 
 All in all, this is a novel that could have been just a bit more original but remained fresh enough to provide an honest, gritty account of a family member with cancer. I'M NOT HER is a book everyone can relate to, regardless of whether they've had similar experiences. Though a certain event felt a bit soap-opera-ish to me, I greatly enjoyed this book and would recommend it to anyone who wants a touching, emotional read.

 I have been fascinated by 'And Then There Were None', since watching one of the movie versions when I was a child. I'm not really sure what took me so long to read it. I think I mistaking thought that it would be difficult to read and hard to keep track of the characters. Neither was the case,however. It is written with such precision that it was easy to understand what is happening and equally easy to remember the background of the characters. 
 The premise of the story is that ten strangers are sent to a secluded island. They are each lured to the there for different reasons. When they arrive they realize there is only the ten of them on the island and that someone has a vendetta to settle with the guests (how fascinatingly creepy). 
 It really is a testament to how good this book is in that at eighty years old this novel is still so entertaining and relevant. The story line was able to both creep me out and keep me guessing. This is without it being overly graphic or gross. 
 Up until the end I had no idea why or by whom the crimes were committed. This rarely happens for me with more contemporary mystery/thrillers. I think this goes to show what a true genius Christie was. 
 This novel is also relatively short and with the suspense I zoomed right 
 I can't wait to read more of her novels. I also can't wait to watch one of the movie adaptations. It will probably be the newest T.V. adaptation though. It turns out the movie I watched as a child,' Ten Little Indians' strayed from the novel quite a bit.

 ORIGINALLY READ 2013 AUGUST 19-31 
 So I read somewhere in a review that the reader didn't feel the love between Avry and Kerrick, and sad as it is, I also felt that way. Sure there were sweet and mushy moments, as well as moments that were heavy and tense, but I didn't quite feel Kerrick's change. 
 The Plot 
 Laying hands upon the injured and dying, Avry of Kazan assumes their wounds and diseases into herself. But rather than being honored for her skills, she is hunted. Healers like Avry are accused of spreading the plague that has decimated the Territories, leaving the survivors in a state of chaos. 
 Stressed and tired from hiding, Avry is abducted by a band of rogues who, shockingly, value her gift above the golden bounty offered for her capture. Their leader, an enigmatic captor-protector with powers of his own, is unequivocal in his demands: Avry must heal a plague-stricken prince--leader of a campaign against her people. As they traverse the daunting Nine Mountains, beset by mercenaries and magical dangers, Avry must decide who is worth healing and what is worth dying for. Because the price of peace may well be her life.... 
 Plot: full of twists and plots that intrigue. That's what I love the most about Maria V Snyder's works. 
 Magic: Was cool, but like I've mentioned before somewhere, it sounds like the same healing system in The Shifter. Then again, it's also different, because Healers in this series are constantly healing themselves, but in The Shifter, if I'm not wrong, the healers could only heal each other and not themselves. 
 The Characters 
 Avry reminded me alot of Yelena from Poison Study, they're very similar yet they are also quite different. While liked her overall, I didn't feel like her reason for disliking Prince Ryne was strong enough. I was constantly looking for that reason for her strong hatred, and yet...when the reveal came, I felt hardly a thing. Sure it was a reasonable reason, and I get her pain, but it didn't seem bad enough for her to really hate him. 
 Kerrick was a bastard at the start. For a smart guy too, he also fails to perceive one of the many reasons why Avry refused to heal Ryne. Yet, while I did say I didn't really feel the change between Kerrick and Avry, I didn't think he was a badly created character, just not the best. 
 Supporting characters are a bunch of males, fellow soldiers who follow Kerrick and are around to keep an eye on Avry. Belen is Avry's strongest ally despite being Kerrick's man. He watches over Avry, advising her whichever he could. Flea reminded me of a little brother-like figure.  His death was pretty heavy  
 The Setting 
 The Fifteen Realms. 
 The Writing 
 Is exactly like what you see in Poison Study, simple, yet imaginative. There's no flowery poetry, there's nothing fancy. The language is straight forward, with a strong, female voice. 
 Overall 
 I'm intrigued. I do love the adventure I get when I read Maria V. Snyder's works, and I am curious enough to read athe sequels of Touch of Power.

 The Storyline 
 Fighting to Survive picks up a few weeks after The First Days left off: Katie and Jenni are helping establish a new life on the fort and working to minimize the ongoing danger of the zombies. Nothing much happens (in my opinion) in regards to the zombie as this book focused mainly on expanding on new characters, the growing of existing relationships, and establishing more problems outside of the zombie issue. The writing was still a bit stilted for me and I still love the zombie action scenes far more than the character interaction scenes. 
 The Relationships 
 So I totally get that everyone is living day to day not knowing how much longer one another will survive, but does that give everyone the right to become a bunch of hussies? 
 "We just decided today," he explained. "Life is so short. We just don't' want to waste time. We've been sleeping together in my tent. Might as well make it official and be a family." 
 Uhh... okay? 
 Jenni and Juan were already together in the last book and their relationship steadily progresses until they are eventually living together. Jenni and Juan's relationship is strange though and I'm not positive whether they actually like each other or not. And I swear... I was going to snap if I hear Loca one more time. 
 Then there's Katie and Travis. In the last book Katie kept trying to keep Travis at bay by continuing to remind him that she is in fact lesbian and no she will not be with him. Her reasoning behind this was explained in the last book as she didn't want to tarnish her memory of her wife Lydia even though she did have feelings for Travis. But Katie has a dream where Lydia tells her it's okay and that she should be happy. Uh-huh.  I felt that whole storyline and the ending was anticlimactic and definitely inevitable. But... how they decide to have a baby in the end?! I'm sorry but that almost took it down to 2 stars for me because that really pissed me off. I understand that life's too short and everyone should live! But does that really include bringing a baby into that screwed up world? That's completely irresponsible and what did they go on like two dates before they decided to procreate? They deserve to be eaten by zombies.  
 Final Thoughts 
 Reading these books back to back has caused me to become quite cynical. I do plan on finishing up the trilogy but will come back to it at a later date when I've managed to forget some of my irritations. I'm hoping the third one has lots of zombie action scenes and EVERYONE gets eaten! hahahaha

***4 'You make me lose control' Stars*** 
 Already being a fan of Melynda Price's Against the Cage series it barely took me a split second to grab it and once I started it I had a difficult time putting it down. It was a fun read with characters I ended up really liking, even when they had me rolling my eyes at some of the things they did and though there were some things that I saw coming and guessed at, I still enjoyed the journey and couldn't wait to see how they would react with everything was said and done. 
 I really liked Asher and Quinn, I did, but man did they have a lot of baggage weighing them down. Guilt, feelings of inadequacy, trust issues. I swear they would be a scientists/psychologist/psychiatrists dream to be able to observe. And with all of these issues the walls they've constructed around them are as high as Mt. Everest and equally as dangerous to try and conquer. But underneath their kevlar shells are two people who have the need to protect and do the right thing, even when it seems impossible. 
 Their relationship reminded me of that little boy and girl on the playground who like each other but can only show it by picking at each other constantly. It was amusing even as it was irritating to watch the push and pull between them. They were so blinded by how they saw themselves that they couldn't see past it. Insta lust runs rampant and I know some would say turned quickly to insta love, but considering the situation they found themselves in ~ life or death situation and being forced into close quarters ~ it didn't bother me because despite everything they did get to know each other along the way. I liked the story (jousting!) but there were several times I thought it stretched believability. The second half was interesting since it was covering new ground - except it got repetitive so the new ground was...not so new very quickly. 
 Specifically: I thought it was a real stretch to believe the bad guy (or his men) were able to sneak in, get in touch with evil girls, and kidnap Gisela all while soldiers were on guard searching. After 4 books, my feelings about the series have cemented - very cute but simple. It's been several decades since I first read this particular installment of Stevenson's work, and with that in mind, I'd like to mention that the same guy who wrote this novel (which would almost surely be classified as YA these days) also wrote Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde which is a dichotomy that has a certain charm in and of itself. Stevenson did, of course, write a lot of "adventure" or "sea" stories, but it's interesting to see the range of such an artist. A lot of writers stick to a particular genre and engage in a long, career-lasting repetition of theme, presenting their audiences with a seemingly endless rhythmic variation of a single core idea, and then there are those who swerve. There are merits and demerits to reading either kind of author, but it's worth bearing in mind which kind of author one is reading. Stevenson may not be the exemplar of writers who swerve, but he's definitely in that crowd. 
 This re-re-read of Treasure Island was inspired by the TV series Black Sails, which I'm sure many folks will know is set two decades before the events of the novel. Given the classic nature of this book, there have been any number of reviews/discussions of it, and there's very little that I could add to that existing commentary, so I'm going to talk about the relationship of the book to the TV series rather than just review the book alone. Though the TV show may diverge from the novel at any point, it hasn't so far that I've detected, so I suppose that means fans of the TV series could look at the novel as a massive spoiler for the show. I'm a "read the book first" kind of guy where practical, and this is a site dedicated to books, so I don't think that should be a problem, but should anyone see things that way, here's a list of Black Sails/Treasure Island spoilers that I gleaned from this reading: 
 From Treasure Island we know that: 
 1. Captain Flint is dead. He dies bitter and drunk on the island of Savannah. 
 2. Billy Bones has a personality change. He's rather a nice guy in the series, but he's a very aggressive, intimidating jerk in the book. 
 3. Also, he dies in the book, meaning he'll survive the events of the TV series if the producers of that show keep to the events of the book. 
 4. Long John Silver loses more of his leg. It's gone nearly at the hip in Treasure Island. 
  
 There are a lot of non-spoilers for the TV series that we can also gather from the book. Not the least of which are: 
 1. New characters: the blind pirate, Pew; Black Dog. 
 2. Long John Silver owns a tavern in England with "a negress" in Treasure Island, which is interesting for those who are fans of the character Max in the TV series. There's nothing other than the note of his partner's race in the book to indicate that it could be the same character, but it is an interesting possibility. 
 3. The treasure that the characters are seeking in Treasure Island may not be the Urca da Lima treasure that features so prominently in the TV series. At least, it's described very often as "silver" and in details that differ from the "gold" most often described in the TV series. 
 4. Characters in the TV series that are based on historical figures (Charles Vane, John Rackham, Ann Bonny) aren't in Treasure Island but that's all history, shall we say.... 
 It is interesting to read this book and pick out which elements are and aren't aspects of the latter day interpretation of a prequel. Maybe it was the influence of the TV show on my reading this time around, but it had a much "grittier" feel to it decades after the first read. The body count is an awful lot higher than I remember it being. The pirates are just as dissolute, but the lack of female characters in the book (other than Momma Hawkins) mean that they are generally limited to drink and violence as expressions of their moral character. 
 Speech patterns are very different, of course. Many contemporary period pieces (Black Sails, Deadwood, etc.) have found that trying to use "old time" terms and vocabulary more than a little laughable to modern audiences. From time to time, movies and TV shows are able to pull that kind of thing off to some extent (Boardwalk Empire, Miller's Crossing--Hmm, both gangster-oriented I wonder if that's why?) but Black Sails has made no attempt to update "Yo-ho-ho!" or the phonetic spellings of Treasure Island into their product--a wise choice in my opinion. 
 Last, it's also interesting to note that the relationships of power that feature in the TV series are very much present in Stevenson's work. For instance, early in the novel there is an encounter between the rough and crass Billy Bones and Doctor Livesey in which the doctor quickly threatens to have Billy hung, and Billy takes that threat quite seriously. The doctor having a governmental position later makes that threat very real, and we are confronted with the life or death aspect of power politics that is a theme of the TV series. There are other aspects of this conflict that appear throughout the book, such as Long John Silver's attempts to talk his way out of situations, and the affectations of "civilization" or "patriotism" as it relates to lawlessness. It's fascinating to see how that manifests in a 21st century "inspired by" project like Black Sails. The latter day interpretation of core values and ideas that are, by and large, the same now as they were when Stevenson was writing is very likely the reason such ideas work in both the novel and the revisioning of that world for a modern audience.

 Finally! I finally finished the book! You have no idea how eager I was to finish it. I bought Wayfarer the day it was released and didn't properly read it until the 9th. Yes, I'm that lazy not to mention I get distracted. 
 But we're not here to talk about me being a lazy mofo, we're here to talk about Wayfarer! 
 Let's get started! 
 After the events of Passenger I was wondering what would happen in Wayfarer. Etta and Nicholas are separated and they must find the astrolabe before the timeline is completely altered. Not only that, but apparently, a new enemy emerges and is a powerful threat to all of them. 
 Alexandra Bracken has done it again! She not only wrote a good book, but also a satisfying ending to the series. She did a great job with the characters, creating alternate timelines, not to mention tackling subjects such as racism, gender, and even going into sexuality. When an author does that, it makes the book all the more better. 
 Plot wise, I enjoyed the journey of both Etta and Nicholas. They travel to many different locations and time periods while also fighting off the Ironwoods and their new enemy. Nothing is ever simple for them, is it? Not only that, but we also get to see the characters grow more. I like them even more after reading Wayfarer. 
 One thing I should mention is that there isn't much of a romance. It's still there, with Etta and Nicholas thinking about each other. And I liked it. It's clear that they still care about each other even though they are not together for the majority of it. Still a good romance. 
 My only complaints would have to be the pacing, being too descriptive (there's a time to describe a setting but not to go overboard and describing how an item feels in their hands). 
 Also, here's something I want to talk about. So we get a new enemy who is apparently an immortal being who is after the astrolabe. He's like that because of the use of alchemy and how he absorbed power from the astrolabe to become immortal. Along with that are his recruits known as Shadows, people who basically follow this guy (I forgot what he was called) and are also in search of the astrolabe. To me, they felt out of place. I mean, it was good we got more background information on the creation of the astrolabe and the passages, but I couldn't fully comprehend as to why this immortal guy was involved. He came out of the left field. It does advance the plot and answers some questions, but it felt too forced.  
 Verdict 
 Another great series! I'm really looking forward to what Alex will be writing next. 
 Thanks for reading my review!
