Frankly speaking, I'd encourage readers to skip #scandal entirely. Seriously. If you haven't read Ockler before, I'd dissuade you from beginning with this novel and if, like me, you're a fan, you're simply better off re-reading one of her previous titles. 
 #scandal dealt with one too many issues for it to handle with aplomb. When Lucy's best friend, Ellie, is down with the flu and unable to attend prom with her dashingly handsome boyfriend, she forces Lucy to be Cole's date instead. Only, Lucy has had a crush on Cole since before he began dating her best friend and now, at such close proximity with him for an entire night, her feelings rush back, all at once. As luck would have it, however, Cole returns her feelings--a truth he can admit to, as he and Ellie broke up before prom--but before their break-up becomes public, an image of Lucy and Cole kissing goes viral instead. 
 Now, I don't know if it's because I spend more time on Goodreads than on Facebook, but I felt oddly distanced from this story. Lucy begins the novel already in love with Cole, which left their romance a pile of disappointment as I was unable to become emotionally involved in it. Ellie, from the first page itself, stood out as an odd type of best friend, forcing her friend to accompany her boyfriend as his prom date, and I cannot claim to truly feel the bond of friendship between these two girls. Even more than that, though, #scandal deals with cyber-bullying in a manner I find to be woefully disappointing. Lucy is attempting to clear her name from the scandal she is associated with, all while trying to find out who stole her phone and posted the picture--along with other incriminating ones--online. Thus, the entire problem of cyber-bullying is dealt alongside a heavy dose of gossip and drama, which didn't work for me. Quite simply put, I barely have anything to say about #scandal except for the fact that its characters failed to resonate with me, its plot felt flimsy and underdeveloped, and with the exception of that gorgeous blue background color, I'd prefer to entirely forget about the existence of this novel. Excuse me while I hunt for my copy of Bittersweet to remind myself of what a classic Sarah Ockler story reads like; this innovative approach just didn't do it for me.

I'd been saving this book as something to look forward to after finals. It seemed like exactly the type of fluffy read that I crave after hours of pouring over stiff and serious academic textbooks. I was very pleased to find that not only did it give me exactly what I was hoping for, it gave me more. 
 The book is written by Carol Goodman, author of several mysteries and thillers, but for some reason this was released under a pseudonym. The original title of this was [[ASIN:B005VQFQMU Incubus]], so if you're one of the people who got the UK release, this is the same book. (Just want to make sure that nobody picks up the same book by mistake!) 
 While this is shelved as a paranormal romance, I was pretty enthused to see that like others have said, it does tend to take on more of an urban fantasy feel at times. The sizzling hot sex scenes are what really reminds us of its PNR classification and I'm glad to say that the sex scenes are chock full of chemistry and sexy goodness. They're well written, which is good since a poorly written or even worse, boring sex scene can absolutely ruin a book and its tone. It's the smaller elements of this book that really make it come to life, such as the iron mice (Ralph!) and the magical creatures that abound in Fairwick, both known and unknown. I'm really hoping that some of my more favorite characters (such as a certain vampiric professor) will show up and be fleshed out more in the future volumes. He's just a good example of one of those characters that aren't really dwelled upon in the books but you can't help but get drawn to them nonetheless. 
 The only drawbacks is that at times I kind of felt like reaching into the book and giving our heroine a good hard shove for being a little overly oblivious to everything. Some of it I could rationalize or overlook, but some of the bigger plot elements were so obvious that they all but had a neon sign blinking "sinister" or "obvious plot point" over their heads. Normally I wouldn't really be so picky about this, but I really enjoyed this book and the details here are so rich that I can't help but hold it to a higher standard.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I went into it with excitement - Hurray, new Harry Potter content - and fear - the reviews haven't been that great. 
 Having read it, I find myself somewhere in the middle. I don't hate it, but I also don't love it. In essence it's a delightful story about growing up under the pressure of high expectations, self-doubt and unlikely friendships. To some extent I enjoyed reading about Albus' insecurities, and the time-travelling bits were exciting as well, but I have to admit that my rating has merely been given out of nostalgia. 
 I simply can't get around the fact that this story is a mixture of weak plot and out of character situations. 
 Voldemort having a daughter is frankly absurd. Are we really supposed to believe he had sex with Bellatrix Lestrange? If so, why did he do it? Surely not out of love, because we know he wasn't capable of that. Did he want an ancestor? Seems unlikely, since all he cared about was himself and his fight for power. So, why did that happen? 
 Harry threatening Minerva McGonagall is insane. That's not something Harry would do. And talking about McGonagall: why is she Headmistress of Hogwarts? Didn't J.K. Rowling tell us that a new character would fill that post after the Battle of Hogwarts? 
 And then there's that whole Time-Turner quest. First of all, Cedric Diggory's death wasn't Harry's fault, as Albus Potter put it. Nor do I see why saving Cedric Diggory seems to be much more important than any of the other dead characters. Why do they go to all this trouble to save the spare Cedric Diggory, without even bothering about Fred Weasley, Remus Lupin and Nymphadora Tonks, to name a few? Also, if there's a Time-Turner powerful enough to go years back in time, why not simply save Lily and James Potter? Or even better: Kill Voldemort when he's still a child. 
 There's so much going on that doesn't make sense with the Harry Potter books as we know them, that I've got trouble accepting that J.K. Rowling actually agreed with this play. I'm not sure how much input she had in the story, but at the least, she must have given her permission to take it to the stage. Why? This story is a million miles away from J.K. Rowling's view on the wizarding world and her characters. It really is nothing more than a crazy fanfiction story. 
 Despite its many flaws, nostalgia made me still enjoy parts of the story. So, when the time comes, I will go see the play, which I'm sure will be spectacular. No thanks to the plot, unfortunately, but there's no doubt in my mind that the actors will do a great job and the special effects will probably be splendid.

 ***Minor spoilers*** 
 Incarceron is a prison world full of forests, cities, caves, and more. Nobody ever comes, and nobody ever leaves. Everything there is recycled, even flesh. When there is no more flesh, Incarceron creates its children partially metal. Finn, an inhabitant of Incarceron, comes across a crystal key which he swears he recognizes, and somehow the key connects him to a girl named Claudia, who has an identical key from the Outside. Her father is the Warden of Incarceron, and only he knows where Incarceron truly is. Finn believes he is from Outside and wishes to escape, and his best bet is getting assistance from Claudia. 
 I am so grateful to be finished with this book. I didn't like it at all. I had this book sitting on my shelf for around 3-4 years because I bought it based on a recommendation from a friend, but never felt the urge to pick it up. Based on that and some reviews I read on Goodreads, it seems that this is one of those books where you either love it or hate it, and I'm part of the latter. I had too many issues with this book. 
 This book had such potential. There's an entire prison world, someone is trying to escape, there's a girl on the outside who is yearning to learn about Incarceron, and so many other details that could've made this a great book (to me, at least). But I found the storytelling so dull, and descriptions lacking, and the writing style just wasn't for me. It was lacking suspense and excitement. Some things are given away much too early and leaves no mystery for the reader. To me, the entire thing was just boring. 
 My other major problem was that it was so confusing! So many things aren't explained well enough, or when it was explained, I still had so many questions. It seemed that a lot of the "what," "why," and "how" were all glossed over and it left me feeling really uneducated about the world. There are some terms thrown in that are never explained, such as something called Protocol which is some sort of law Outside that I still don't know the meaning of. I still had a ton of questions in the end. Also, what time period was this? Is it set on our Earth? An alternate Earth? There are no cars and barely any technology (something enforced by Protocol, I think) but they have electron microscopes? I'm a person who has a lot of questions, and I felt like this book overlooked too many of them for me to enjoy. 
 Overall, I'm glad that I've finally wiped this from my to-read list, but I didn't enjoy it whatsoever. I struggled to continue reading and a lot of the time I wanted to just give it up. It seems like a love it or hate it book so you may have better luck, but in my opinion there are much better sci-fi novels out there that would be much more enjoyable than this one.

The Development of a Criminal...The Development of a Good Man? 
 What a fascinating psychological study! This epic story begins when Theo Decker is 13 years old and ends when he's twice that age. Wow, does the author torture him in this story. What does not kill us, makes us stronger? I'm not so sure that's true in this case. Tragic events weaken Theo and it's unclear if he will ever regain his strength. 
 Theo lives with his mother in New York City after his alcoholic father abandoned them. His beautiful, fun mother has to take him to a late morning disciplinary meeting at school, so they stop in an art museum on the way. Then a terrorist's bomb explodes. The blast rips Theo's life apart when it kills his mother. In the ensuing surreal melee, a dying man insists Theo take "The Goldfinch": a famous painting. 
 The painting haunts Theo for the rest of the story just like the story has haunted me. 
 The characterization is raw, real, and detailed, and the author made me care deeply for Theo. Every time he suffers a post-traumatic symptom, I wanted to hug him. Every time he veers into drug use, I wanted to smack his neglectful father. Here's a vivid description of Las Vegas Dad, who has shifted from abusing booze to pills: 
 From his genial cursing, his infrequent shaving, the relaxed way he talked around the cigarette in the corner of his mouth, it was almost as if he were playing a character: some cool guy from a fifties noir or maybe Ocean's Eleven, a lazy, sated gangster with not much to lose. 
 Thank goodness for quality mentors like furniture-restorer Hobie, who is connected to the dying man from the museum. 
 Theo's Ukranian friend Boris is simultaneously endearing and infuriating. Boris is the saving grace to a lonely boy, and the loving shove to a boy perched on the precipice of a deviant, criminal life. I freaking love how Boris nicknames Popper the dog "Popchik". 
 The writing is exquisite. I dog-eared so many pages with impressive passages, like these: 
 Tormented by what was happening, yet unable to stop it, I hovered around and watched the apartment vanishing piece by piece, like a bee watching its hive being destroyed. 
 When I got off the phone, I felt sick -- like someone had just reached a hand in my chest and wrenched loose a lot of ugly wet stuff around my heart. 
 Spring in New York was always a poisoned time for me, a seasonal echo of my mother's death blowing in with the daffodils, budding trees and blood splashes, a thin spray of hallucination and horror. (What a vivid description of PTSD) 
 My moods were a slingshot; after being locked-down and anesthetized for years my heart was zinging and slamming itself around like a bee under a glass, everything bright, sharp, confusing, wrong -- but it was clear pain as opposed to the dull misery that had plagued me for years under the drugs like a rotten tooth, the sick dirty ache of something spoiled. 
 Speaking of pain, Theo pines for a girl who also survived the museum bomb: Pippa. But she doesn't seem to requite his love. 
 "Well, girls always love assholes," said Platt, not bothering to dispute this. 
 No, I thought bleakly, untrue. Else why didn't Pippa love me? 
 Aww, Theo. You are quite lovable! 
 One of the reasons I became so involved in the characters is the impressive length of the book: 770 pages. Unlike some readers, I didn't find the story unfocused, though the end did drag just a little. I'm glad I invested the time to read this moving drama.

 Let me start off by saying that Dava Sobel undoubtedly knows what she's talking about. The amount of research that must have gone into this book is astounding! I find it so incredible the way history can be sewn together from so many pieces to create such a detailed tapestry. 
 Throughout the book are letters written in the hand of Galileo's daughter, Suor Maria Celeste. From these letter you discern not just how devoted a daughter she was, but also that Galileo himself was an honest and generous man, with dignity, strength and faith. It is truly a travesty that his letters to his daughter have been lost. 
 I found the names confusing (as so many were named Vincenzio, I often got disoriented), but Dava Sobel has foreseen this problem and provides friendly reminders throughout which I found tremendously helpful. 
 There were several points in the story where I found goosebumps dancing down my arm as though I were truly witnessing Galileo paving the road of modern science. Galileo was able to balance science and religion in a way that is relevant even today. 
 The end of this story is where Sobel's brilliance truly shone. Of course there is no doubt what the outcome will be, as history has already been written, but the way in which the details were unraveled for me brought me to tears. 
 I can highly recommend this book to those who love history, science and truth. Enjoy!

On one side of the Rift is the Colloquium with its technological advances and complacent society. Everything is as it should be. The world makes sense. 
 Sixteen-year-old Glenn Morgan has lived next to the Rift her entire life--staring through the forest at the bright, red lights marking the border between the Colloquium and somewhere else. Kevin Kapoor tells her that the other side of the Rift is filled with magic and mutants--wolf-like creatures and maybe even witches. 
 Glenn doesn't have time for magic. Or Kevin Kapoor. 
 Ever since her mother disappeared ten years ago, Glenn's life has taken on a singular focus: get good grades, join the Deep Space Service, travel across the universe to planet 813 and get the hell away from everything and everyone else in her life. Her father hates the idea. But her father has been a shadow of himself since Mom disappeared--wasting away as he works on the mysterious Project that he might never finish. 
 Except he does finish; building something that looks more like a piece of jewelry than a piece of technology with the potential to change everything on both sides of the Rift. 
 Entrusted with the Project, chased by Authority, all of Glenn's plans for the future become irrelevant as she and Kevin are forced to run with only one place left to hide in Magisterium (2012) by Jeff Hirsch. 
 Magisterium is Jeff Hirsch's second novel (following his debut The Eleventh Plague). 
 Magisterium is a satisfying blend of fantasy and science fiction as Hirsch blends together the best elements of both to create a unique, exciting story. I hesitate to give too much away but Hirsch has conjured two dramatically different worlds on either side of the Rift to create a strong, evocative setting. As the story progresses the land itself seems to become a character in the novel as Glenn and Kevin learn more about what lies on the other side of the Rift. 
 Glenn is a conflicted heroine, forced to negotiate between her own agenda and the tasks that circumstance have forced upon her. She is also strong, grounded and determined--all nice qualities to find in a character. She is accompanied by several great characters throughout the story--notably Kevin Kapoor who is funny, cheerful and stalwart even in the face of Glenn's feigned indifference making them a great pair to read about. 
 Hirsch's writing is also excellent as he creates a gripping, exciting story. Sometimes there is almost too much action between the dramatic chases and dangers across the Rift. In the midst of all that, Magisterium also raises interesting questions about family and the ideas of unconditional love, home, and even the nature of friendship as almost everything Glenn trusts is stripped away. 
 I also have to say, I love Jeff Hirsch for writing stand alone novels. It's so refreshing when everything seems to be part of a series or have some kind of cliffhanger. Magisterium is a nicely contained story with action, magic and some very difficult decisions as Glenn realizes that after some choices there is no road home. Highly recommended for readers looking to transition into the fantasy or science fiction genres. 
 Possible Pairings: The Drowned Cities by Paolo Bacigalupi, False Memory by Dan Krokos, Sabriel by Garth Nix, Daughter of Smoke and Bone by Laini Taylor, Uglies by Scott Westerfeld

Pros 
 *A very entertaining historical fiction novel. 
 *Unusual subjects-A modern recurrence of Bubonic Plague, San Francisco pre-1906 quake, women's rights, and Chinese-American life in the early 20th century. 
 *Wide Appeal-The story includes hints of romance, action and derring-do, is based on true historical events, and provides readers with a Downton Abbey-esque window into the daily lives of history's ultra-wealthy. 
 Cons 
 *Meandering plot-There was a lot going on here--Lizzie+Gus, Lizzie+Noah, Lizzie+friendships, illegal street fighting, Bubonic Plague, early 20th century newspaper wars, racism and genocide, early 20th century medical technique, proper etiquette for women, women's rights, etc... I didn't feel satisfied with the amount of coverage any of these topics got, and I wish the book had been about 100 pages longer so that we could have delved a little deeper into them. 
 *Lizzie-Not my favorite character. She was a self-important know-it-all who whined about not having any friends, but then didn't reciprocate much when they invited her out. Sometimes, being a brilliant pest can come off as oddly charming, but there just weren't enough things I liked about Lizzie to balance her out. 
 *Did we really have to kill off the brother as punishment for his Devil May Care attitude and lukewarm feelings about doctors? Geez. As soon he started trash-talking medicine because it couldn't save their mom and was therefore worthless, I knew he was a goner.

It's rare to read an autistic character's POV. It's also quite rare to read a depressed character's POV.

 This book is beautiful beyond description. I cried at every chapter : sad cry, happy cry, angry cry, frustrated cry... This book has it all. 
 I love the way it's written too. It focuses more on the inside of Emmet's and Jeremey's heads, and through that we see how they face the world every day. We see our simple daily tasks through a different set of eyes. I love that the problem is real and not overrated. The romance is real and common, and not crazy bang-bang with unnecessary details. At most times, I feel like I'm reading a non-fiction book that explains both autism and mental depression instead of a fiction, but you know what? It works for me. I enjoy reading it. 
 I cheer Jeremey's little winning against his worst enemy: his negative mind, and I super looooove how Emmet overcomes his autistic barriers creatively. 
 This book is different than any other fiction books about autism or mental disability. The story made me think, feel, smart, inspired, grateful, and sensitive altogether.

World After literally picks up where we left off with the resistance having just attacked the aerie, Penryn being reunited with her family, and Raffe trying to get his wings back. 
 This series is seriously one of the most gripping, intense YA series I've ever read. Susan doesn't hold back on the horror and gruesome imagery and I love it. 
 I think one of the main reasons I love this series is the variety of interesting characters. 
 Penryn in this book is still badass but this time we get to see a bit more cracks in her persona due to the intense responsibility she has to protect her sister, Paige, whilst trying to comprehend and accept the changes her sister has gone through. What I love the most is the development in Penryn's character as she tries to balance her responsibilities to her family and her need to help others. We also get to see her take more risks and chances, some that work, some that don't. 
 Paige is another character that has more of a focus in this book. We see her trying to deal with the changes they made to her and also deal with Penryn's reaction to these changes. Paige has endured so much at the hands of the angels that we can visually see. We also get several revelations about how that really impacts the book and quite frankly surprised me in the best way possible. 
 Now onto Raffe. He's not as heavily featured in this book as he was for Angelfall but in the mentions we do get of him I love. One thing I loved was the glimpses we got of Raffe before the invasion, and we also get a better understanding of the motives behind some of his actions. Also the moment he does physically show up is pure epicness. The chemistry between him and Penryn is undeniable and we see the two of them become emotionally closer to one another as their trust in each other deepens. 
 Dee and Dum are also very interesting characters. On the surface they add some comic relief and their banter with Penryn is on point. A part of me thinks/hopes they're not all they seem (in a good way) and I hope we see more of them in the next books. 
 We also get a glimpse into the motives behind some of the angels actions. We also get more answers regarding their plan with the scorpions and the action is definitely kicked up a notch. It's bloodier, more violent, horrific and gruesome. 
 My only issue is that while we get some answers we get more questions and it can be quite frustrating. Also whilst I understand why there wasn't as much Raffe in this book I did miss him and wish we saw more of him. 
 Overall it's an epic instalment to the series and I cannot wait for the next book.

I hadn't realized before I started reading this that the title, If I Stay is actually a perfect synopsis of the book. High schooler Mia gets into a car crash with her entire family, who die. Her consciousness is separated from her body, and she watches herself get taken to the hospital and operated on, and all of her family and friends come to visit her. She gets to choose her fate: if she dies, or if she stays. 
 That might sound really interesting, but it was actually so dull. I don't even know how it was as distant and uninteresting as it turned up to be, since the subject matter almost necessarily makes it exciting. But through the book, Mia herself feels next to nothing. She tells us she feels things (ie/ how can she go on without her family) but doesn't feel them, which makes them feel hollow. 
 The book is interspersed with flashbacks to her living past. We get short snippets of her with her parents, boyfriend, best friend, brother, etc. I suppose this is supposed to make us sad at the thought of her leaving them, but since getting to know the characters comes after the shock of knowing she might lose them, none of the emotional factor is there. Plus, all of these characters are Big Stereotypes. Her brother's a Christ Child figure, with no depth at all beside being blond, cute, and perfect. Her parents are Cool Parents, who give her money for condoms when she gets a boyfriend and encourage her to go to mosh pits. Her best friend is the Jewish Sidesick, with no extreme personality of her own, beside dropping the occasional Yiddish slang. And her boyfriend is Love Conquers All, which is a trope I cannot stand. In fact, that's the point of the entire book, which also strikes me as unrealistic. 
 In addition to that, there are just little details that annoyed the beezus out of me and made it a less enjoyable read. For one, I don't think the author knows what a hipster or a punk is, because she uses them completely interchangeably. About halfway through the book, the author must have realized that teenagers swear, because the S- and F-bombs start coming, where there had been none previous. Also, during Mia and Adam's first romantic encounter, he tells her to "play him like a cello", which is somehow supposed to be sexy, and she taps him on the chest where the frets would be (whatever is the cello equivalent of frets), and then runs the cello bow along the line of his pants, which actually sounds kind of painful and not at all romantic. 
 Some younger readers might find this book more to their liking, which is why I'm rating it 2 rather than 1 star. But I was looking for something profound and emotionally resonant, and this just wasn't it.

This is not the type of book I would normally pick up on my own and read. I would never even have considered this one if it hadn't been listed in a mini-challenge I'm participating in this month. So, thank you, Phrynne, for recommending the Mistborn series! 
 The book was a little slow going for me at first, but about one-third of the way in it started to become more interesting and by the time I had finished two-thirds of the book, I didn't want to stop listening. Brandon Sanderson created a very fascinating world with many interesting characters. I'm very interested to see where this series goes.
I am embarrassed by how much I am enjoying these books (I'm currently on #4), but they're like crack and I can't stop.

3.5 
 How to write a fun YA contemporary? 
 Well, just follow Kody Keplinger's recipe cause she's got it down to a science! 
 "I'm serious. They'll call me a pussy." 
 "And if you help them, I'll call you a dick. So no matter what you do, you're going to be some form of genitalia." 
 She was constantly cracking me up with her dry humor. And what I loved most about her? She felt like a real teenager who at times-let's be honest, more often than not- made mistakes. 
 She was also strong. She wasn't perfect or had some constant God-sent advice for all her problems. She sounded real, and yes, I was annoyed with her at times, but when I sit back and think about how I was at that age, I have to admit, I was a pain in the ass too. 
 "I didn't do this to end the fighting. I did it because I know it's important to you. And you're important to me." 
 This was what made me fall in love with the book. Not the boyfriend, the high school drama or even the plot. It was the effin amazing friends that surround her! The friendships were breathtakingly beautiful and I don't mean in their perfection but in their realness. I mean I know that Chloe was one of the supporting characters but to be honest she could have been the lead for all I care. That's how much I loved her. Effin goldmine here. 
 "I'll always come if you want me to, Liss." 
 And that's the thing, she didn't only have one amazing friend. If you've read other reviews you'll know I usually rant about the fact that nowadays authors tend to only make the female lead and her best friend the only characters you like. But Kody Keplinger managed to wow me with countless friends and thank the Lord with the absence of the cliche mean girl. She was able to give depth to not only Lissa(which btw her name's Melissa, just felt like I had to point it out :P) but to every character. They're all distinct in their own ways. Can I hear a hallelujah?! 
 "Because I want to see you with someone better than him. Someone who will see how lucky they are to have you." 
 I bit my lip, nervous but determined to ask my next question. "Do you happen to have someone particular in mind, Cash?" 
 "Maybe." 
 I'm not even gonna gush but 
 I don't know what the heck is wrong with me lately but I am falling hard for good guys and Cash is freaking amazeballs amazing! 
 AMAZEBALLS AMAZING! 
 "Chloe didn't have all the answers, either. I knew that now. But she had known something all along that I hadn't: that being ashamed of what you want or how you feel is pointless, and letting anyone else make you feel ashamed is a waste. We all wanted different things, and that was okay. Chloe wanted sex without commitment. Mary wanted to wait until she was ready. And I wasn't sure what I wanted, but I didn't want to make any decisions until I knew. And I was proud of that." 
 I don't know if you've ever noticed that most YA kind of fall flat. I mean, it's not like I expect great wonders from these books or anything but I do tend to expect some difference in the characters as the book progresses, especially if the point of the plot has some kind of maturity(not that this plot was mature or anything, sex strike is not a sensible way to go). What I mean is some plots tend to lead the characters to growing up and finding themselves. This was one of them. And we see her growth in the way she learns to deal with her family, in the way she starts to accept herself and in the way she starts to carry herself as a person. And I loved that. 
 And finally... 
 Do you know how sometimes books are preachy or you feel like the author is just shoving their own beliefs down your throat as you read the book? You know how sometimes it's annoying as heck? Well, while it may feel like the author is driving her advice home through these characters, I couldn't help but wholeheartedly agree. 
 "It's so screwed up, the standards...You should like it, but you shouldn't like it too much or talk about how much you like it. You should do it, but you shouldn't do it with too many people or talk about how much you're doing it. It's like there are so many rules, but none of them make sense." 
 We're taught at a young age that sex is a taboo subject. That it shouldn't be broadcast like some news at 6. We're taught to judge a girl's worth by the amount of guys she's slept with but at the same time taught to admire guys because of how many women he's been able to take to bed. Girls are taught that if you like sex too much, you're a whore but if you don't like it you're a prude. Guys are taught that the more women you sleep with, the cooler you'll be and if you don't like to sleep around then obviously you must be gay. 
 Sometimes life and choices aren't as black and white. And I loved how Shut Out portrayed it. 
 In the end it wasn't perfect but it did manage to make me think. And if that's something I could take away from a YA contemporary romance then great.

2.6hrs, 2 stars, 1 for world building, 1 for the 20% that actually interested me somewhere around 70% and -3 for mild sexism and drudge. 
 This is the story of Gren and his girlfriend, Yolanda. Or something beginning with Y anyway. They live in a world that has stopped spinning, where life has devolved into vegetables and humans are, apparently, 1/5 their current size. 
 Starting from the beginning, we have a tribe where women rule, but only the boy children hold any value. Then one kid dies so the older people fuck off and turn into moon-butterflies never to be mentioned again. All of the other kids die except Gren who is a boy and more intelligent than the others, who feeds himself to a Cordyceps. The others then exile him and his girlfriend, she dies rather quickly. He wanders around for a while and then meets Yolanda during a daring escape from a rotten log. 
 Gren and Yolanda then travel through the jungle for about a year, during which time they show no interest at all in anything around them. At one point they meet some tree-bound idiots; the comic relief; who they rescue from their tree, much to the idiots dismay, and Gren is taken over further by the Cordyceps and is driven around like a donkey while the fungus shouts about how smart it is. 
 That's it basically. They all blunder around for a while before being rescued by the moon-butterflies and going off into space. Except for Gren and possibly Yolanda, who decide to die of old age instead.  
 Highlights include, "Look, a castle!" A long talk on evolution from the fungus, during which none of the people go "wtf is evolution I was born in a banyan tree", a moment where the Cordyceps goes through Grens mind and pulls out images of cars and boats and roads, and the strange plastic Miners-Strike kite thing which flies around them shouting slogans for no apparent reason, before being eaten by a bird. 
 For such an imaginative world, it was really quite a boring book.

WOLF WITH BENEFITS follows the same enjoyable path that can be expected with a Pride Series book. With Toni we get a strong lead female character who has to be serious and organized to the nth degree all because of her very large and rambunctious family. Toni is depended upon to keep her wild siblings in order and doesn't often have time for herself. It's hard for Toni to step outside of her comfort zone but when she does things get crazy. Assigned to protect Toni's family Ricky Lee seems laid back and nonchalant but there's more to him than meets the eye. 
 There's a lot going on in this one which does distract from Toni and Ricky Lee a bit. I do wish that they had been the sole focus of the story instead of having the other story weaved in as well. The story is still a fun read with enough twists to keep me engaged in the story despite the extra characters making appearances. Shelly Laurenston can be counted on to provide lots of humor, sexy love scenes, along with well written and enjoyable paranormal stories. I have yet to read a Laurenston book and not enjoyed a good laugh and WOLF WITH BENEFITS is no exception.

Full Rating: 4.5/5 
 This book did a really good job of taking a somewhat ridiculous sounding premise (Nazi skin-shifting motorcycle racing?!) and making it serious, believable, and compelling. The writing was the perfect blend of poetic and descriptive, and the history was well supported and respectfully treated. Yael was a strong and complex heroine--Graudin did a great job of describing how she dealt with the horrors of her past without making her sound whiney or unrelatable. I felt the romance was very well done, subtle yet with enough umph to make the reader care. I also appreciated the fact that the book didn't dissolve into a somewhat incestuous love triangle between Adele's brother and ex. It definitely helped that both Felix and Luka were well rounded and complex in their own right. In fact, all of the characters, even those barely mentioned, felt real and whole. And, although not much actually happens, much of it set up and uneventful racing, the plot was laid in a such a way that I was never really bored. Basically, this was a really well-written, interesting, and believable book, and I cant wait to see where Graudin takes it next.

Wow! After reading Cinder I was pretty impressed, but even more impressed after reading Scarlet. Marissa Meyer does an amazing job weaving sci-fi/fantasy in with a traditional fairy tale. Scarlet is meant to be Red Riding Hood, although unlike Cinder, it wasn't super obvious. There's her hair, and the red hoodie (cape), her grandmother  captured by the lunar wolf pack,  and Wolf himself. The little details make it known what she is modelling the story after, but the plot itself is very original and complex. 
 At first I was more concerned with finding out where Cinder was now, and how Kai was handling the situation, but the more I read about Scarlet, I almost started to like her more. She's a pretty feisty person and her quest to find her grandmother was pretty compelling, and I really enjoyed Wolf being thrown in there. There was just enough action and mystery from both points of view in the story (Cinder and Scarlet), with a little bit of romance thrown in (enough to root for them, but not enough that it overshadows the main plotline). I thought the ending was perfect between Scarlet and Wolf, and I am excited to see what Cinder does next. 
 There's probably a lot more I could say about this, but I'll just leave it at 5 stars for Scarlet, Marissa Meyer is a very talented writer, no complaints, and I am very eager to have the next book (2014, noooooooo) in my hands!

I appreciate this series. I know a lot were upset by the ending, but I totally get it. It's realistic. Everything isn't perfect in life, and it means so much more when tough decisions are made and deep feelings are felt. 
 Four and Tris have so much love. It's the real kind, the true kind, the kind you don't think of for people so young. 
 But now I know I am like the blade and he is like the whetstone-- 
 I am too strong to break so easily, and I become better, sharper, every time I touch him. 
 That is how it feels. Like everything between us is twisted together, friendship and love and family, so I can't tell the difference between any of them. 
 "I can't wait until tomorrow, when I'm back and you've done what you set out to do and we can decide what comes next." 
 I like how Four finally comes to know himself, his inner struggles. 
 "No," I say. "I was afraid of my considerable capacity to kill." 
 How many men fear that there is a monster inside them? People are supposed to fear others, not themselves. 
 I like how Tris is always true to herself and isn't swayed by others. I also feel it's important how her inner monologues show her struggles, how her decisions didn't come easily. 
 This story shows an accurate depiction of life and war. 
 It seems like the rebellions never stop, in the city, in the compound, anywhere. There are just breaths between them, and foolishly we call those breaths "peace." 
 There are no second chances after you've died for something, at least as far as I know. 
 There are so many ways to be brave in this world. Sometimes bravery involves laying down your life for something bigger than yourself, or for someone else. Sometimes it involves giving up everything you have ever known, or everyone you have ever loved, for the sake of something greater. 
 But sometimes it doesn't. 
 Sometimes it is nothing more than gritting your teeth through pain, and the work of every day, the slow walk toward a better life. 
 Yes, I'm upset. Yes, I'm emotional. But isn't that what reading is about, feeling. Thank you Veronica Roth for the devastation and the encouragement to go on. 
 toni

 It has some issues that would normally bother me, but they didn't even make me pause. I love Keir and Lara. The secondary cast was stellar. And there were several moments in the book that just made me happy to read about. During the dance, and also when  Lara learns she is free  were times when I know I was reading with a ridiculous smile on my face. 
 I also thought the author did a good job of creating two different cultures and showing how hard they were to mix. 
 So the issue where Lara just didn't sit down and ask about the Warlord's culture? It didn't even bother me. I can't wait to read the next one!

 This clearly deserves a 5-star, but few things bothered me. The 27 Club is the type of book that's impossible to review without giving away spoilers and since I believe that you should go into this book blind to experience the feels it will undoubtedly leave you with all I'm going to say is this... If there's one book you need to read this year... This is it!

Okay almost like how everybody else keeps saying.....THEY ONLY NEEDED ONE BOOK!!!! 
 What the hell is with these people?!?! Everyone in this series has some strong case of insane bipolar disorder......except for Lexi and Lucinda OH! and Damien. 
 Rita....bipolar 
 Remy.....bipolar

 Sara's mom (name I just can't remember).....hypocritical bipolar 
 Jaxon......hot bipolar

Bad pacing; great world-building. Better than I expected, but worse than it could have been.

I liked the narrative, especially the sarcastic tone of the protagonist. But the plot was empty and there wasn't any real character development. Anita Blake, the female protagonist, was an expert in raising the dead and making them testify for legal matters. As a side hobby, she killed and hunted vampires, mostly because she hated them because of what they were. She was forced to help vampires find a murderer, but this challenge did not change anything about her and she remained resentful. 
 The mystery was not really engaging and it was fairly easy to guess who the murderer was.

Exceeded expectations! Had a wonderful, magic atmosphere. Typical southern gothic. 
 "Mortals. I envy you. You think you can change things. Stop the universe. Undo what was done long before you came along. You are such beautiful creatures." 
 This quote is the best one in the whole book. It is said by my favourite character- Macon Ravenwood- Lena's uncle. He's witty, elegant, smooth...I love him! 
 Another thing which I loved about the book was that Ethan was this, typical, normal boy. Wore the same t-shirt for days, never cleaned up his room and all that. It made him real.
A successful novelization of a classic Russian fairytale. The beginning and end were compelling, although it sags in the middle. The prose is either beautiful or purple, depending on your mood.
I love John Inman's books and while this wasn't my favorite of his, it was still a really fun read.

The Good: 
 There are some interesting philosophical ideas in Jekyll's lengthy exposition, however the best thing about this book is its overwhelming sense of authenticity. This was set in the same time and place in which it was written, so you'd hope so. 
 The Bad: 
 Overall I found this dull. It is slow, and very little happens immediately around the protagonist. Instead he experiences the events of the novel through various second person accounts, some of them written. 
 'Friends' character the protagonist is most like: 
 Mr Utterson is described in the opening paragraph as "dreary and yet somehow lovable", so a bit like Ross Geller.
I loved this story! And no, I wasn't tearing up. Someone was cutting an onion around me.
It was ok! Not fantastic, not as good as Dresden Files, I'll keep at it. It seems like the next book is gonna be the typical "kid goes to school and get bullied" book, purely from guessing.

There is a lot of pain in this. Prince Jorg is a complex and intricate character that deserves close attention. Listening to his story is like being dragged into a tornado. You're spun round and round and round until you land (dead or alive it doesn't matter) completely wrung out. As I said in my status update, there is a heavy theme of 'loss of innocence'. Despite the gore, I really enjoyed this. I enjoyed it in the sense that Lawrence created the kind of character that I could lose myself in.

I feel like I have to preface any review of this by mentioning that my knowledge of Pride & Prejudice is limited to multiple viewings of the BBC miniseries (the dreamiest Darcy) and the 2005 film version. (And also the movie Pride & Prejudice & Zombies... and all the Bridget Jones movies [because again, Darcy]) 
 I adored this book, mostly. Despite a bit of trouble initially with the mingling of modern-day paleo/crossfit/millenials lingo into Austen-like florid, overlong sentences, it got into its flow and really, I thought, put some new life into the story. I loved the author's interpretation of the Bennets in modern day society, home shopping addictions and bowling leagues and all. 
 I had one issue, which kept this from being five-star for me, and it was how the author dealt with Lydia's storyline. 
 I kept waiting for the shoe to drop in Lydia's storyline, wondering how she was going to wind up with Wick. When it did, though, I was kind of horrified. It was a total "wait, really?" moment for me. 
 In the original story, Lydia's actions were impetuous and brought literal shame to the family. She ran off with an already detestable character, and remained ignorant and insufferable throughout the ordeal. Darcy saved her dignity in a way she wouldn't understand. 
 I give the author the credit that, as a modern retelling, you can rethink character arcs however you want, and I was glad that she chose to make Lydia a little less insufferable and give her a lot more depth instead. But while Lydia's actions still brought a hypothetical "shame" to the family in a different way -- playing off the intolerance and ignorance of the parents -- it just felt like a really weird choice. 
 I wasn't as vehemently turned off by it as other reviewers were, and I can understand their reasoning behind their feelings, but... despite that, it just felt strange and it took me out of the story for a bit, making me instead consider the author's treatment of the issue.
Scratch that. Alaska is officially the third book that has the ability to make me feel emotional.

I love these books by Grossman. What I love the most is the language that he uses and how he tells the story. 
 The world building and characters run a close second. The plot is excellent, but with this one and the first one, I started to get restless as the end came. Perhaps the book was just a smidge too long and some of the plot elements slightly drawn out. The writing is superb though. I would highly recommend this book and the first one for anyone who enjoys fantasy. Lev Grossman is a writer to watch closely. 
  
 I am also very curious to see how he is going to handle the next book. I can't wait to see what happenes to Quentin, or is he going to follow Julia? In the Fillory books written by Plover, each book starred a different child plus the one in the story before. I am wondering if these books will mimic that? I haven't read anything about this series anywhere. Quentin was left in an interesting place at the end with having lost anything. I almost had this feeling of....now the story is really going to get started. So very curious to read more. :o)
Extremely strange - Joss went some weird places in season 8.

Lib Wright, an English nurse who trained and served in the Crimea under Florence Nightingale herself, doesn't realise what exactly she's letting herself in for when she accepts a posting to a remote Irish village to investigate the claim of an 11-year-old Irish girl being able to survive without food. Apparently little Anna O'Donnell has been able to live without eating anything for the last 4 months, surviving by the grace of God alone, or as Anna calls it, her "manna from heaven". Religious folk from all over the world are flocking to the remote village of Athlone to catch a glimpse of this "miracle" child, believing she has the power to heal them of their ailments. There is even talk she may be hailed one of Ireland's new saints. Fully prepared to expose the girl and her family as frauds, and their claims as a way to make money, Lib and an Irish nun commence alternating eight hourly shifts in their charge's modest home to make sure that she is indeed receiving no food. But what was supposed to be an easy assignment soon turns into an emotional roller-coaster ride as Lib realises the full extent of little Anna's resolve to refuse food - and her reasons for it. Torn between her duty and her heart she must fall back on her intellect and training to do what is right, even if it means sacrificing everything she has worked so hard for ... 
 I loved this book! Donoghue does such an excellent job at bringing her characters and the setting to life that reading The Wonder felt like time travel, and I was so totally and utterly absorbed in its pages that I could not put the book down. What starts off as a gently and rather straight-forward tale soon throws the reader into a world where superstitions reign, where religion has such a strong hold on people that they even accept the demise of their most loved ones as "God's will". A world, where intelligent strong women like Lib are frowned upon, whilst men who value their own ego more than common sense get to make all the decisions. I loved the way Lib slowly grows as a character, changing from an emotionally cold and remote personality to a strong, determined woman fighting for her patient's rights in the face of adversity. As a nurse myself I very much enjoyed the character of Lib, reflecting on how the profession of nursing has changed over the years but that in our hearts we are all in it for the same reasons - to fight for the nest possible outcome for our patients. 
 With its remote and somewhat claustrophobic setting Donoghue creates an aura of mystery and suspense as the story unfolds and casts its spell upon the reader. Donoghue's eye for historical detail is reflected in the astute way she explores the hold religion has on the poor in the aftermath of Ireland's catastrophic potato famine - presented in a way which shows both sides, through the eyes of fervently religious Anna and Lib's fierce intelligence and scepticism. As a reader you can feel the conflict in every pore as the story takes us to its inevitable finale. I loved the ending, which brought tears to my eyes - but no spoilers from me! 
 I applaud Donoghue for her latest novel, which is definitely one of my favourite reads for the year - I loved it much more than her previous bestseller Room. Very highly recommended, a full 5 stars from me.

 I totally guessed the "twist" before it happened, and then hated the actual ending.
