4.5/5 stars 
 Yay! Absolutely loved this!!!! I actually devoured this story! 
 The writing: I thought it was pretty good. Sure it could've used a little more editing (especially the first few chapters), but nothing that bugged me too much. I'm a huge fan of dual-POV, so I was grateful for that. But I have to say the voices weren't that distinctive, and from time to time I caught myself asking if that was a Hannah or Garret chapter. 
 The characters: Man, I liked Garret. I really enjoyed his backstory. I loved Hannah, too. Her rape story and how she dealt with it? *claps hands* well done. 
 But I loved more about this was the romance, the relationship. It kind of had two of my favorite tropes in one: hate-love + friends to more. How could I not love that??? Plus, they Garett and Hannah were pretty funny together. There were more than a couple moments I laughed out loud, and that's a big yes on my list. 
 So, yeah, I truly enjoyed this!

** spoiler alert ** 
 Click to Subscribe had such a cute concept judging by the blurb. The first half the book introduced West's vlog pseudonym Sam Green and Harper Knight, a girl who comments on his vlogs at precisely 2.02pm. It's obvious the two get along very well through their amusing chats and they finally decide to meet up (conveniently Harper lives only 20 minutes away - but we already know who she is!) 
 The blurb pretty much summed up the whole story with respect to Cat and West's relationship. Many parts were cliche and predictable as they continued to have a push and pull relationship. West pushes Cat away because he doesn't want to risk losing the friendship they have but he pulls her back because she is one of the few bright spots in his life. Repeat three more times until they're finally together. 
 What the blurb doesn't tell us is West blames his father for his mother's death in a drink driving related car accident and since then his father has been an alcoholic wreck. This runs continually throughout the story but was never resolved with West's forgiveness. The vlog was an interesting idea as West's outlet of expression but it didn't turn out to be a majorly central to the storyline. Overall, it was an okay read.

This is a wonderful read. The focus is more strongly on the historical fiction aspect, which is really done. The world is rich and intricate and pulls the reader into the political intrigue of court life. The fantastical aspect comes in the form of Ismae's relationship with Death, which is gradually developed and revealed over the course of the book. It adds a nice dimension to the story. Very intriguing and perfect for those who enjoy both historical fiction and fantasy reads.

When Mark Nolan's sister dies, he finds he is the guardian for his six year old niece. Maggie Conroy is afraid to love again after losing her husband to cancer. When Mark brings his niece into Maggie's toystore, it's the beginning of magical changes in all their lives. This is a cute Christmas romance with such likable characters that I was sorry to see the book end.

The Truth About Alice is a story that will stay with you for a while. It's well written and the characters are well developed. 
 Alice is 'the slut who slept with 2 guys at a party.' One was Brandon Fitzsimmons (the star quarterback who also dies in a car accident) and now everyone blames Alice because she sent him racy texts. Supposedly. 
 Told from 4 POV's of students from Healy High; Elaine(the popular pretty girl), Kelsie (Alice's best friend who turned against her once the rumors started), Josh (Brandon's best friend) and Kurt (the nerdy guy who never hangs out with anyone and knows a secret that no one else does), they tell you stories about Alice Franklin and their version of events. The very last chapter is told in Alice's POV. 
 I liked this story a lot. It's not common where you find a book where the author knows what she is talking about and makes it sound realistic. The characters in this story are like everyday teenagers. You have the popular girl, the jock, the nerd and etc. The way the story was written like a diary made me read through it in a couple of hours. Out of everyone, Kurt was by far my favorite character. He's just so smart and nerdy and he doesn't care if people don't hang out with him. He's unique and rare.  And he is also in love with Alice.  
 I personally think Alice could have spoken up at times and not hidden in her over sized sweaters but that is what happens in real life. Some people are too scared or too afraid to really do anything. They just let it happen. 
  As for the other characters, I could understand why they acted the way they acted. They're only human. Elaine is the most popular girl in school and thinks everything she knows, is the truth. If she thinks Alice is a slut, Alice is a slut. Josh was in the car accident with Brandon but the seat belt saved his life so he's left to tell the details. When Mrs. Fitzsimmons asks him what happened, he immediately thinks of Alice and says she was sending Brandon racy texts during the time of the accident. Josh knows this isn't true because he took the phone out of Brandon's hand himself. That's when the accident happened. Brandon took his eyes off the road to stare at Josh and bam. Kelsie started to ditch Alice and start even worse rumors because she was mad over the fact that Alice said she didn't understand some things because she was a virgin. Well, Kelsie took care of that problem and ended up getting pregnant by Tommy Cray (the other guy Alice supposedly had sex with at the party). No one knows of course. Her mom took her to the clinic and she had an abortion. It's still not right to start rumors of something like that but she was hurt and she wanted to do something. As for Kurt, I loved how he was nerdy, shy and stalkerish. He'd take notes on Alice on what she likes and what she looks like but he never acted on anything. And he knows the truth about really happened at the party. Brandon told him while they were drinking beers on Brandon's roof. Alice didn't want to have sex with Brandon so he made up the rumors to get back at her. He thought it would pass and then she'd finally say yes. Well, he died so the rumors spun out of control. At the end, Alice tells us that she knows Kurt likes her and she feels the same way.  
 It was a fast, enjoyable read and I recommend it to anyone who enjoys contemporary YA. 
 ***Complimentary copy provided by the publisher via NetGalley in exchange for an honest review***

Re-read in September 2015: 
 I loved this book! I took a long time to read this book again, but I am glad I did. It made me feel the same emotions the second time around. I enjoyed the concept of time travel. The storyline was interesting with the bloodlines of each family and what gem stone the represent. The characters were amazing. 
 Gwen is a girl who was always the "black sleep" of her family. She thought her cousin, Charlotte, was the time traveler. However, it turns out that Gwen is the one who can time travel. She is thrown into a world that she never imagined. Her journey was really cool throughout the book. Gideon is Gwen's time traveling partner. He is sometimes really sweet, and sometimes he is a complete jerk. 
 I also loved Gwen and Gideon together. I love that they kind of have like a love-hate relationship. It makes the story more relatable to me. It made the book funny at times for me because they would fight a lot in the beginning. The ending was great. Overall, an amazing read.

I wasn't expecting to read this one because I didn't care for the character of Costigan in the first Cyberlove book. I was wrong. Fast Connection was even better than Strong Signal. The dialogue between Luke and Dominic is great, both chat and in person. Dominic was an a-hole to Garrett in Strong Signal but that's addressed in a reasonable and believable way. I enjoyed the focus on a different aspect of cyber-relationships -- whereas Strong Signal was about connections made through gaming, Fast Connection is about Grindr hookup culture. The sex was pretty hot except there's no way Dominic would be able to take a hard pounding with a thick eight-inch dick with no prep his very first time at bat without damage!  The personalities of Luke and Dominic's families were nicely developed for the most part and the dynamics felt real. I did think that Duffy's financial problems were waved away too easily at the end, especially when he is still using his credit card for apparently thousands of dollars of purchases after taking money from his son to fix his deli  but that was a minor complaint. Overall, I loved this book and highly recommend it.

When you just spent 4 hours reading a book and then it's over and you're like what day is it? who am i? what is life? 
 This was so good. 
 I expected it to be good but damn it was absolutely amazing
Gets a little shmoopy toward the end, but still a strong entry into the series fantasy genre.

Gail Carriger is the newest name on my list of favourite authors, for the pure and simple reason that her books are damn good fun. Over the last year or so, whenever I've needed a literary pick-me-up, I've turned to the Parasol Protectorate series because nothing else puts a smile on my face more. These books are so funny, incredibly witty, highly entertaining, and filled with the most wonderful cast of characters. Every time I read one, I go through a mini-obsession phase with all things Alexia Tarabotti (my love, my queen, my everything). Are these the greatest books in the world? Not by any stretch of the imagination. Plotting is iffy at best, and oftentimes tea and hats are described in more detail than the action scenes. Then there's the small (or, more aptly, HUGE) matter of problematic fave Conall Maccon. BUT, in spite of all of that, I've loved all of Miss Carriger's books that I've read so far, and I'm already craving the next one like Alexia craves tea. 
 Blameless is not my favourite of the three Parasol Protectorate books so far (that honour goes to Changeless, which was near-perfect until that ending), nor is it my least favourite (the bizarrely plotted first book, Soulless). It sits nicely in-between the two, mostly because I found the plot more cohesive and well-written in this one, but I missed the glorious romance that this series began with. Blameless picks up pretty much exactly where Changeless left off, and That Significant Event (I won't specify what it is because spoilers) drives most of this book. As a result, Blameless feels like it has direction and purpose, which isn't a feeling that I necessarily got from Soulless or Changeless, no matter how fun they were. Rest assured, Blameless still has its wacky moments; I still don't fully understand the ladybird thing, and the Lord Akeldama plot went a bit amiss in amongst everything else. However, I'd still say that, in purely plotting terms, this is the best book of the series so far. 
 The shining star of this series for me is Lady Alexia Maccon. Oh, how I adore Alexia. I'm quite obsessed with her wit and her bossiness and her clever bluestocking side which she only lets out every now and again. What I especially loved about Alexia in Blameless was the amount of vulnerability that was shown. Up until this point, Alexia has been a very stoic woman - hiding any negative emotions with a clever quip and recovering from traumatic experiences by drinking tea - but, in Blameless, her feelings become harder to suppress. We see her break down in tears multiple times, and we're exposed to her serious doubts about her future with Conall and which path she should take next. As she is primarily written as a comedic character, it was so wonderful to see another side to Alexia. I feel as though she went on a real character-development journey in this book, which was unexpected but greatly appreciated. 
 Also: I am still 100% interpreting Alexia as bisexual. Her flirty banter with Madame Lefoux absolutely kills me. Given the events of the last two books, I'm half tempted to jump ships and devote myself to Alexia/Madame Lefoux instead of Alexia/Conall. Lord knows that the Frenchwoman has been a way, way better support system for Alexia than her husband has through these difficult times. 
 Speaking of Conall Maccon... most of my problems with this book lie with him. And that really sucks because I still love him as a character. The way he jumps from blushing sweetheart to angry, raving Scotsman is the most incredible and lovely thing. And, in terms of comedy, Carriger's use of him is inspired. I think he had a total of about three clothed scenes in this book and spent the rest of the time inappropriately naked. It's hilarious. Yet, no matter how much I love Conall's personal attributes and his dynamic with Alexia, I have to take issue with how his behaviour was dealt with in this book, particularly at the ending: 
 In a lot of ways, I'm happy that Alexia forgave Conall. It was clear that they'd both had time to think over what happened and still loved each other and wanted each other back, so I do believe that reuniting them was the right move. I even liked their initial reunion scene because I thought it captured the argumentative-yet-affectionate Alexia/Conall vibe sooooo perfectly. My issues lies with Conall's seeming lack of repentance, and the way that forgiveness is attained. Even though Carriger makes Conall's regret at his reaction to Alexia's pregnancy super obvious, I don't think that he ever once says that he's sorry. He just makes excuses for why he did what he did, which is no good because his behaviour was straight-up out of order. The only one of the characters who seems to share that opinion with me in Professor Lyall, who continously insists in his narration that Alexia will be equally as hard to convince. Unfortunately, he's wrong. In actual fact, all it takes for Conall to win Alexia back is an encounter with her at an opportune moment, lots of neck kissing, and some sex. In the context of everything Alexia went through in this book, I suppose that's understandable because, if I was pregnant and held captive by monks who wanted to use me as a weapon, I'd be damn glad to see my husband too. However, I think that an apology should have accompanied that relief. Leaping straight from an argument about Conall's behaviour to sex is a little icky to me. I'm a firm believer that the way to solve problems is through talking, and for Carriger to imply that a short conversation in the middle of a sexual encounter solved Alexia and Conall's shitload of problems is ridiculous. That is not the right way to address the situation at all; Conall should have been made to grovel and apologise more before Alexia welcomed him back into her affections again. Also, it felt to me like the sex scene was only there because this series classes as romance, and, as Blameless on the whole is very light on romance, it needed sex to justify that label. Am I still on-board the Conall/Alexia ship? Yes, because I like their dynamic and I do feel as though Carriger was trying to keep things both in-character and lighthearted, but I'm far more wary now than I was to begin with. End rant.  
 All things considered, I thoroughly enjoyed Blameless. It was just as entertaining and funny as its predecessors, yet I also feel that it showed development. As well as the aforementioned improvement of the plot and complicating of Alexia's character, I also really appreciated the focus given to some of the historically quieter characters in this series. In particular Professor Lyall, who I have come to love and adore, but also Biffy and Floote. I NEED a Floote prequel, Gail Carriger, because there's so many things I want to know and I highly doubt that all of them will be answered in this series. Then, of course, more Madame Lefoux is always appreciated. I adore Madame Lefoux almost as much as I adore Alexia. And this is precisely what I mean about this series - there's so many things I want to critique and which deserve critiquing, yet I'm completely in love with it anyway. This is one of those obsession-inducing series that you want to devour all in one go, like a really good cake. I'm not entirely sure when I'll be reading the next instalment, but I'm sure I'll be saying much the same things when I do, because Gail Carriger can do no wrong in my eyes. This is guilty-pleasure reading at its very finest.

A Man with Asperger's Delightful Journey to Love 
 Books like these make me appreciate my book club even more because I probably wouldn't have tried it without my friend Colby picking it this month. 
 Don Tillman is a 39-year-old genetics professor in Australia who knows he is socially inept but doesn't know he has a raging case of Autism Spectrum Disorder. He would like to date but his difficulties with emotions and subtleties of interactions have made that difficult. Being the scientist he is, he decides to write a questionnaire for potential partners he dubs "The Wife Project". He believes his data driven approach will weed out unsuitable candidates. 
 He has a married psychologist couple, Gene and Claudia, to help him sort out these puzzling social interactions. Sadly, Gene and Claudia are his only friends. 
 When Don attends a dating event, his unique perceptions of the world are hilarious. 
 Olivia resumed talking to me while the others engaged in small talk -- an extraordinary waste of time when a major life decision was at stake. On Claudia's advice, I had memorized the questionnaire. She thought that asking questions directly from the forms could create the wrong "dynamic" and that I should attempt to incorporate them subtly into conversation, Subtlety, I had reminded her, is not my strength. She suggested that I not ask about sexually transmitted diseases and that I make my own estimates of weight, height, and body mass index. I estimated Olivia's BMI at nineteen; slim, but no signs of anorexia. 
 Every time Don meets someone new, he mentally calculates their BMI. BA HA HA! I've met quite a few characters through dating but I've never had one come out and ask me my BMI--Don would totally do that if not for Claudia's advice. 
 Don's friend Gene sets him up with Rosie, a "barmaid". Rosie comes over for dinner prepared by the excellent cook Don. 
 I commenced retrieval of vegetables and herbs from the refrigerator. "Let me help," Rosie said. "I can chop or something." The implication was that chopping could be done by an inexperienced person unfamiliar with the recipe. After her comment that she was unable to cook even in a life-threatening situation, I had visions of huge chunks of leek and fragments of herbs too fine to sieve out. 
 Once Don discovers Rosie smokes and runs late, he automatically discards her as a candidate for The Wife Project. But when Rosie tells him she's trying to discover the identity of her biological father, geneticist Don is suddenly all in to helping her with The Father Project. 
 They narrow down potential fathers based on her mother's medical school class, and proceed to obtain DNA samples from over fifty men in a madcap manner. 
 Don eventually learns that Rosie is a doctoral psychology student who's smarter than she seems. Don and Rosie test a sample from one probable father. 
 "But I've never consciously thought of him as my father." 
 "He's not," I said. 
 The results had come up on the computer screen. Job complete. I began packing up. 
 "Wow," said Rosie. "Ever thought of being a grief counselor?" 
 "No. I considered a number of careers, but all in the sciences. My interpersonal skills are not strong." 
 Rosie burst out laughing. 
 Don is just so damn endearing! The funniest scene is when Don and Rosie pose as bartenders at a medical school reunion in order to swab cocktail glasses. Memorizing orders and drink recipes is where computer-mind Don excels, and he performs so well that the bar owner wants to go into business with him. 
 Equally funny is when Don wants to woo a ballroom dancing champion, so he practices his dance moves with a skeleton from a nearby lab. When he tests out his dance moves in front of a crowd, he learns Unfortunately, this requires cooperation on the part of the partner, particularly if she is heavier than a skeleton. 
 When Don decides he would like to have sex with Rosie, he talks it over with Gene: 
 "So why the stress?" said Gene. "You have had sex before?" 
 "Of course," I said. "It's just that adding a second person makes it more complicated." 
 "Naturally, said Gene. "I should have thought of that. Why not get a book?" 
 So Don buys a book and memorizes all the sexual positions. Naturally, he brings out the skeleton again for practice, and naturally, the dean walks into his office while Don is getting into compromising positions on the floor with the skeleton. *laughs* 
 In addition to the charming humor, there's some depth to this story about love and growth. I definitely want to read the sequel. Highly recommended.

Hayley's voice is clear and strong, even though I didn't always agree with it. Her situation is heartbreakingly impossible to contend with, and yet she frustrates us with her stubborn pride and inexplicable memory loss. 
 Initially her new friends are presented as level headed and 'normal', but just as Hayley does, we come to see them with troubles of their own. Hayley knows it's not all about her, but sometimes I wish she had shared more with Gracie as a way to show her support. She does that eventually with Finn, but the way Gracie seems to just disappear by the end had me questioning her role in the narrative. 
 This journey of despair to acceptance is a tough one to go along. Hayley has some missteps along the way, but gosh, these adults that fail her need to look at themselves too... And Anderson is very critical of the education system that cares only about restructure and lock-downs. She takes a few stabs there. 
 How to sum up? It's brutal but also beautiful.

One of Scalzi's best--a terrific story cycle in the Colonial Union universe, reminiscent of some of the most pleasant SF from the 50s and 60s. The stories all feature interesting dilemmas, good lines, and a clever resolution. The problem is that every voice is Scalzi's: pragmatic, no-nonsense, and insightful, but also heavily mixed with wit and sarcasm. It's a good voice, but every viewpoint character has the same one, even the alien.

As the youngest sister of three boys, Charlie is well versed in all things boy. Which explains her absolute lack of knowledge on anything girly. If it's soccer, basketball, or pick-up game of football, she's all in. Make-up and fashion? Not so much. Unfortunately her third speeding ticket does not go over well with her dad, and he tells her she has to get a job and pay it herself. Somehow, without even trying she ends up working in a small boutique, which is totally out of her element. While stepping outside of the box is stressful, it also allows her to learn more about herself. Braden the actual boy next door, and best friend of her closest brother Gage, has always been an honorary brother as well. While dealing with what seems as her new double life, she ends up meeting Braden in the back yard to talk. Their conversation is innocent to start with, but she quickly understands that maybe she hasn't been so honest with herself about her feelings for him. Braden isn't just some guy though, he's like her best friend, and acting on those feelings could cost her an invaluable friendship. Charlie also suffers from a thing pretty common in women, in that her perception of herself is somewhat skewed. She sees herself as one of the boys, not feminine enough to attract the attention of most guys. Luckily she has plenty of people around her to point out her misconception.

I am genuinely in awe; I liked the first book of the series but I was somehow puzzled by the fact that the main character was 8 years old. 
 This book though follows Owen's adventures when he is 17. As a side note, I genuinely find Kiskaddon as musical and I smile every time I hear it. 
 I listened to the book while I spent most of the day in the car and I was absolutely entertained. Owen, Evie, Etayne are just characters I like, clever, hard working, hiding secrets. The villains - that are not really villains - are well described too. I would actually go as far as to say that the villains is a very fluid category and the people in this category are not necessarily bad people. 
 I find the book is construed in a way that there is an explanation for all loose ends. 
 I enjoy the magic system - so unique, linked to the fountain, such a powerful fountain, connected to the water even visually. Impressive clever idea! 
 I feel like there is a reference (if not an entire retelling) of King Arthur and I cannot stop being in love with this aspect. 
 The only aspect that is somehow missing is action; better said, there is action but it is very limited. The book is just perfectly tailored though despite my personal interest in more action driven books! 
 I cannot wait to start with the next book of the series!
Saving my review for the finale.

Prior to reading Gardens of the Moon, I read another user's review that went something like this: "After 200 pages, you won't have any idea what's going on. That's okay, keep reading. After 400 pages, you still won't have any idea what's going on. That's okay, keep reading." It's so very true. The first half of GotM is difficult to get through. Erikson throws so many characters, places, gods, history and magic at the reader that it's almost impossible not to feel overwhelmed, and it makes you wonder if there's any point to it all. There is. 
 Keep reading. :)

A beautiful tale of self discovery and love, interwoven with heartbreaking revelations of past horrors. 
 The audio of this was fabulous. Kim Fielding's words and K. C.Kelly's narration worked very well together.

...So what's this book about? 
 This is a novella (approx 100 pages) about Tenzin, one of the main characters from the Elemental World quartet (A Hidden Fire #1, This Same Earth #2, The Force of Wind #3 and A Fall of Water #4). Elizabeth Hunter published this story two years after she had completed and published the Elemental World series and so I actually think this should be read after you've read them all too, in fact, I think this story could also work as a stand alone tale. 
 This book is broken down into seven chapters: Prologue: Tell Me a Story, Chapter 1: The Girl, Chapter 2: The Monster, Chapter 3: The Madness, Chapter 4: The Fire, Chapter 5: The Warrior, Epilogue: The Heir 
 ...So, what did I like about it? 
 I am already a fan of Ms Hunter; her writing style, the characters she creates, and the way she unfolds her stories to us. This book didn't let me down. Reading this story, I felt transported to the pre-historic steppes, the way people lived; their priorities, hopes, fears. 
 I feel that The Bronze Blade is a story more about Tenzin's emotional and mental change from human to vampire rather than just her physical metamorphosis. I loved that! I liked getting into her head in such an all encompassing way. This story gripped me from start to finish and yes, a few tears did fall on a number of occasions. 
 ...So, ummm, was there anything I disliked about it? 
 No. This particular story was about her beginnings, however, Tenzin has such a long life, I would love Ms Hunter to write more novellas about her other experiences throughout her extended history. *hint*hint* 
 ...So, basically what I'm saying is... 
 I loved this book! I was already completely enthralled by Tenzin so this brief insight into her beginnings only added to my love for this amazing female character. But be warned, this story does contain many scenes of graphic violence and horrific abuse, so it's definitely an "adults only" story!

A powerful message, but the story itself didn't make me feel all the things it should've. I cared about the shooting and the kids and everything, yes. But did I care about the characters? Not particularly. The writing just seemed off to me. Or maybe I'm just a terrible person, I don't know xD

Neil Gaiman opens this collection with a discussion about storytelling, in which he is asked to provide a quote for the wall of a library. His contribution, which he believes lies at the heart of good storytelling, is: "And then what happened?" 
 That feeling, that desire to know what happens next, is an important part of a good story, but this collection shows that it's not enough by itself. There are some good stories here, but there are plenty that draw you in and then leave you feeling hollow, promising a resolution that they don't provide.

5 stars. Or 4-1/2 but I'm rounding up because Reese King. 
 This book was amazing. 
 I don't know if it's when I read it or if I was just in the mood or what. But I am literally shocked by how much I loved this book! 
 After a terrible mishap while working as a production assistant, Paisley's name means trouble in the entertainment industry. Her best friend/roommate, Jonathan, pulls every string he can and gets her a job as personal assistant to the most notorious diva, Bellini, who is starring on her own reality show. To say that working for Bellini is the worst job ever would be an understatement. The only perk is looking at Bellini's boyfriend, Olympic swimming superstar, Reese King. He's total mancandy--Paisley had posters of him on her dorm walls. He's also strictly forbidden--as the significant other of Bellini and as her boss. 
 Reese is taking his last shot at Olympic Gold--he's been labeled the Silver Stroke by the media since he chokes up at the last moment, always coming in second place. Since he's retiring after this, his publicist thinks it's important to get as many endorsements and sponsorships as possible, even if the cost of which is entering a fake relationship with reality star Bellini. Though Bellini grates on every nerve of his, he is determined to put up with doing the promos and making appearances with her for the short length of the contract, until he sets sight on Paisley. She's the most beautiful girl he's ever seen and she's sassy. He can't stay away. Paisley has to fight the growing attraction between them or risk losing her life's passion, but how long can she hold out when Reese King won't let her? 
 "Finding your soulmate is never easy, Paisley. The luckiest people have to work at it, because once you find that true match, hyou will be that much more grateful for the journey you took to find them." 
 Like I said, I was shocked by how great this book was. I loved it so much, I decided to make a Top Ten reasons you should read Stroked right now. I mean, right now. 
 Reese King. I mean, did you think I was going to start with anything else? I loved him. He was sweet and swoony and sexy. I love that he respected Paisley and loved how good she was at her job. He was a dirty talker and just totally take charge. But he had a vulnerability that Quinn captured perfectly. He didn't want to be the Silver Stroke. He wanted Gold. He also wanted other things in life, and I just loved him. #favorite 
 Pope Francis. He needs no explanation. 
 Paisley. It's not very often that I love the heroine in the book, but this time, she blew me away. She was sassy but had a genuine desire to prove herself. I liked that she was willing to do whatever it took to get her life back on track, and when she was faced with an ultimatum, she accepted responsibility for what she had done. She was a lot of fun, and I loved the progress her character made throughout this book. 
 Chemistry and the Hotness Factor. The chemistry in this book was so off the hook, it needed to be mentioned separately. I believe in love at first sight, and I could literally feel it with this couple. 
 "We would be so fucking right." 
 And this book was hottttt. For real. 
 "What are you doing?" I hiss, hoping no one saw him take me in here. 
 He presses his hands agains the door, bracketing my head and bringing his lips inches from mine. "I'm showing you who I belong to." 
 Olympics It's hard for me to describe what I mean here, but Reese has been working for this moment his whole life. Quinn really captured his feelings during the events, and that was one of my favorite parts. I was actually anxious while I was reading the races! 
 "I want to impress you so fucking bad." 
 Also, the ambiance of the Olympics was just amazing. Walking the flag with Reese and feeling like I was right there with him was amazing. I loved the camaraderie and the historic feeling. Paisley was in the crowd, soaking all of that up, and it was just so...magical. 
 Authenticity. I appreciated how authentic this book was, and I'm sure Quinn had to do a lot of research. From Reese's diet to the way Olympic trials work to the film industry. It was amazing. 
 Jonathan. He might have done some things that made me want to punch him in the throat, but he was a good friend. And he was so funny! 
 Nicknames. Bellini was ridiculous, no doubt about it, but the names she made up for people were hilarious. 
 Reality TV. I Reality TV (Well, I The Bachelor), and I thought this aspect of the book was done really well. 
 Last but certainly not least, Truth or Dare. I don't usually like don't like Truth or Dare in adult books, but damnnnnn this one was hot. It's the most original version I've ever read, and it was a great idea! 
 "I dare you to howl like a wolf." 
 And an Honorable Mention goes to the set up for the other books in the series. I can't wait to read them!! 
 There were two things that I didn't like. First, Bellini. I mean, really? I wonder if there are people who are actually like that. Then I see this and know that there are. Just watch the first part, about the earring. 
 Though Bellini provided comedic relief, I could have done without her point of view. I also didn't care for a twist that happens with Jonathan. I felt like it was out of left field and it really wasn't addressed with Paisley. Other than that, I loved this book. Can you tell? :) If you're looking for a hot athletic romance book with a fresh storyline and characters who will make you laugh out loud and fall in love with them at the same time, you have to read Stroked by Meghan Quinn. It's awesome.

3.5/5 stars 
 What a fantastic debut from Lauren Morrill! Such a lovely, cute book. It's set in London, and Morrill describes the city so well and vividly that you feel as if you're really there (and anyone who knows me in real life knows how much I drone on about wanting to go to London, so I definitely loved that). The writing is fantastic, descriptive and flows really well. The plot is a little predictable, but there are twists and turns, and somethings I didn't see coming -- especially near the end. 
 I loved the characters! I predict that some people won't like Julia or Jason, because they're not made to be exactly likable, in my opinion. They're very real characters with surprising depth. I know that some people have found they could not connect to Julia, but for me at least,Julia is extremely easy to relate to. She follows the rules, gets straight A's, over-thinks things constantly and at times (even though she probably wouldn't admit it) she thought she was better than everyone else, smarter than everyone else. She also has the urge to correct people when they get something wrong. Sometimes, I swear she was me. Jason, on the other hand, is that rude, obnoxious guy that you loathe who is always vying for attention, but all of a sudden he says something sweet and you can't help but like him. I adored how their relationship developed throughout this book and how much they developed as characters as well. They brought out the best (and sometimes the worst) in each other. The supporting characters don't really appear much in the book, so you don't really care for them at all. 
 Meant To Be has a lot of witty banter, which is always a good thing. It also has a lot of references to The Beatles and Shakespeare, which I'm sure people will like. But with all that said, it didn't wow me as much as Anna and the French Kiss did, but I did enjoy reading it, and I'm excited to see what Lauren Morrill writes next. 
 Overall, Meant To Be is a light and fun romantic read, with lots of witty banter and hilarious moments. Definitely one to put on your "To-Read" list.
Wow! Just WOW! So sad it is over...

 The Witch Hunter was another one of those books that I wanted to love and was super excited to read. When I was approved to read it via Netgalley I was super stoked and dove into it right away. I love, love, love strong heroines, and adventure, and magic. 
 Sadly the amazing premise of this book was ruined by the poor execution and illogical characters. Our main character, Elizabeth, is supposed to be one of the best witch hunters in the country of Anglia. I expected bravery and stubbornness, and instead got a wimpy, useless heroine.

Personally I thought it worked very well - appropriate tension had been introduced at appropriate times, but resulted in a satisfying enough conclusion in regards to gratuitous character and emotional payoff that I'm left bursting to read the sequel to see what happens next, and not caught up in heartbreak. 
 I think one of the reasons why I adored this book so much from the get-go was not only the fact that its epistolary format kept things dynamic and fast-paced, but also how much it spoke my language. 
 See, I've put a LOT of hours, and a LOT of money into understanding tech-speak. Literally, I'm doing a degree in it. So when I opened this novel and, for the first time in my entire life, saw actually complicated and (Lord help me) accurate tech-speak, my ego gained about fifty kilos. Beyond my own narcissistic tendencies, however, it showed just how much research and time had been dedicated to getting these details right. The inclusion of binary code, of programming lines, of the concept of executing and debugging programs before they actually make sense and do what they're supposed to - THESE are the tiny details which so many sci-fi and technology-based books so often leave out. And the best way to make something so inherently inhuman seem organic? Add in these details. Don't make it seem like technology is all wizz-bang wonders and miracles, and once you've got the skills, you can do it all perfectly first-go. 
 I'm gonna try to make this review a little more coherent now; because holy cow we gotta talk about those characters, man. 
 Look, I'm not going to lie, when I first read what Illuminae was about, and how it was structured, I was very concerned as to how Kaufman and Kristoff were going to craft characters that we as readers would not only relate to, but somehow become attached to - and I honestly don't think it could have been done better. 
 These characters felt real. They were interesting, and they felt different. Kady was flawed - she was abrasive, and insubordinate, and cold, and arrogant, and damaged. But she adapted to her situation in a way which felt so very, very human to me. Her lack of connection to the fleet gave her a perspective which enabled her to ask those questions which rippled into the Illuminae files. Her part in, and emotional and psychological reaction to every breath-stealing event in Illuminae felt genuine, and felt real. 
 Ezra was delightful - I wish we'd gotten a bit more of his 'perspective' (as much as is possible in an epistolary novel), because I feel like there was a lot of untapped potential there. But at the same time, I'm glad that some parts of him remain a mystery - not just so that there's room for further exploration in the later books, but also because that makes him seem even more like Kady's person. His character didn't belong to us, the readers - he was a person who was Kady's to love, and to loathe, and to grieve, and to rediscover . It added a very human element to the text, and had the bonus effect of helping to add to the somewhat mysterious element of the documents.

 AIDAN was on a whole other level - a point at which I'm no longer talking about how phenomenal the characters were, and talking about how mind-blowing-ly amazing the themes were. I don't think I've ever read a novel which has forced me to confront the concept of humanity and morality and understanding and perception and creation and every other philosophy-questioning topic as intensely, and as gloriously as this before. By the end, I was crying. As in, there were actual tears. Because of course AIDAN would come to consider these higher-level things. If you create artificial intelligence, and you put it among living, breathing creatures and give it a job - no matter what kind of restrictions you place on it, eventually it's going to ask the questions that human kind has been asking since day one: who am I, what am I, why am I? 
 The evolution of AIDAN was one of my favourite things about Illuminae. Besides it being one of the best representations of an AI in general that I've ever read, its progression from mindless, order-following AI, to pre-teen temper tantrum AI, to thinks-it's-a-deity AI, to self-questioning AI, to the final product was so deliciously organic that I honestly don't have the words to describe how much I loved it. And the final product - a creation which was somewhere between human and artificial, somewhere between being and not being, somewhere between a rock and a hard place, made it the number one thing that I loved the most about Illuminae. 
 Overall, my feelings for this book could be summarised by the fact that by the end, I was feeling so many wonderful and horrible things that I was completely crying, but so absorbed by the break-neck pace and wonderfully, gorgeously juxtaposing moments of silence that, despite literally not being able to read the page sometimes thanks to those wonderful tears, I kept fucking reading. This book was one of those phenomenal, gorgeously intricate novels in which the language on the page made my head spin and my heart pound and my ears rush and my fingers twitch and my hands cramp and my breath quicken and my eyes spill and so many other fantastically, fantastically human things. Illuminae's words were its own soundtrack, its own music. I was so, so happy to sing along. 
 Read this book. 
 Read it.

I didn't write a review for the first Stormlight Archive, so I will for this one. The tone, prose, plot, action, etc. are all similar for both books so the general parts of this review can serve for the whole series. 
 Sanderson's prose is simple and straightforward... much like his other novels (Mistborn and Elantris being the books that I have currently read). It is actually pretty refreshing to me, most fantasy books that I have read recently have been heavy handed and tend to sound like the author had a thesaurus sitting next to him or they contain philosophical inner monologues that drag on and on... so Sanderson's prose is a nice change of pace! He keeps it simple and it works for him. 
 Where Sanderson really excels is in his world building. The Stormlight Archive has a world that is nothing like I have ever read before... it is hard to compare to any other books. Roshan is full of highstorms that the people have to gear their time and cities towards, the plant and animal life is completely diverse, and the culture and history of the people is intriguing to say the least. 
 The one major complaint that readers have for WoR is that the plot drags on a bit. For me, that is not the case. The action is nonstop in the main parts and the flashbacks/interludes are a great device that add history and storylines where the main plot isn't happening. Spoilers for WoR below: 
  
 Likes: 
 1) Kaladin finally accepting that he is a Knight Radiant. His hatred of lighteyes and his depression was beginning to wear on me. Now that he has accepted his role and said the words I think he is really going to come into his own. Not to mention his badass battle with Szeth and saving Elhokar had me on the edge of my seat! 
 2) All things bridge four. I continue to love Rock, Lopen, Sigzil, and Teft... these minor characters keep the story rolling when you have had enough of Kaladin/Dalinar/Shallan. Lopen finally sucking in stormlight had me rolling on the floor. I also have high hopes for Shen/Rlain to play a huge part in later stories. 
 3) Finding out the different factions and some of what their goals are. The Ghostbloods, The Sons of Honor, and The Knights Radiant all have their own agenda and I'm glad we are starting to see the main members of these groups and their inner workings. I hope Sanderson can keep the different groups to these 3 and not dilute the story. 
 4) The Spren. Syl and Pattern are one of the most fascinating aspects of the series. The more and more Syl opened up to Kaladin towards the end, the more the story unfolds and keeps me coming back for more. 
 Dislikes: 
 1) Lots of people coming back to life. I really don't want this to turn into another Game of Thrones. I can understand why all the characters did come back to life... but at some point some characters do need to stay dead for there to be a believability factor in the future books. You lose some of the anguish or worry when you think they are just going to sprout back to life a day later. 
 2) Nothing else! Maybe wish the next book was already published? Can't complain though with the pace that Sanderson pumps out books. 
  
 Easily a five star book and highly recommended to any fan of fantasy.

 This book is a whirlwind of emotion. It's got plenty of heart, a great voice, dry humor, real emotion, and a memorable main character. Leila Sales knows how to write a thoroughly compelling and totally flawed protagonist that still makes you sympathize and empathize with as she struggles to find a place in her world. A vast improvement on her fun but shallow Past Perfect, This Song Will Save Your Life takes a familiar YA plot and adds in originality and flair to create an engrossing, raw, heartfelt and impossible-to-put-down novel. 
 The depiction of Elise is the best thing about This Song Will Save Your Life. Hands down. She is so genuine and real, it's pretty much impossible to not recognize some aspect of yourself in her. I loved this character so very much, and Sales hit her difficult characterization with precision. Elise grows and learns and changes over the rather short course of the book, but it takes time, experience and thought to get Elise to where she needs to be. Her foibles and flaws make her all the more interesting (and compelling), and her humor keeps things light enough to keep this from being a total downer for the first half. Socially awkward, smart ("precocious"), Leila Sales nails what it is to be an outsider with no real place to fit in. 
 Besides Elise, the author packed This Song Will Save Your Life full of real, dimensional secondary characters. With the exception of the pack of mean girls at Elise's school (and also the only reason this is a 4.5 instead of a full 5-star rating), Sales imbues these characters with personality and problems. They are all so real - the mom's obsession with fairness? I get that. The friends Elise feels are not good enough? I loved that they were shown to be so much more than Elise had assumed. This book takes a lot of tropes and stands them on their heads and is so much better than its contemporaries for doing so. First loves aren't perfect. Mysterious aloof guys aren't always the ones you should be with. 
 This is a short book, and though I have so much love for it, I don't want to say too much and spoil the experience for other readers. Bullying plays a key part in the plot, but there is more to This Song Will Save Your Life and Elise herself than a simple story about being bullied and ostracized. It's about growing up, moving on, finding yourself and being okay. It's a wonderful novel and I hope it finds the wide audience it more than deserves.

 First of all, I came into this book with low expectations. Maybe because I had never heard of it but it surprises me how books like All the Bright Places are lurking around in the NYT bestseller list and this one isn't. 
 I know there are a lot of books with similar plot lines but this beauty by Stokes exceeded my expectations. I had nearly given up on young adult books based on illnesses and mental health (Thanks, John Green!) but it's books like these which have kept me from completely losing faith in them. 
 So, what is Girl Against the Universe, you may ask? Well, it's an engaging read with spoonfuls of quirky, relatable and charming characters, a dynamic plot, eloquent writing and a dash of feels. It is not about a dull girl meeting a cocky boy and suddenly becoming all sunshine and rainbows. It's a sad, realistic and not-so-manipulative tale about survivor's guilt, PTSD, anxiety, survivor's guilt, paranoia, sports, overcoming your fears, depression and giving yourself a damn break because you're a human being and have every right to be happy once in a while. 
 Yes, it is a love story but that's only the subplot. It's about two teenagers helping each other heal. Not just the boy "fixing" the girl or vice versa because let's face it: no one can save you but yourself. The main characters of this book didn't only have therapy lessons where they complimented each other's tennis rackets and talked about their feelings. They did what normal teenagers do; go to parties, have angsty moments, eat burritos, tease each other, go rock climbing, etc. 
 So, after witnessing tragic incidents following a car crash which killed her brother and dad but barely left a scratch on her, Maguire Kelly comes to the conclusion that she is "cursed" and develops a habit of blaming herself whenever someone gets hurt, from minor scratches to unexpected deaths. She starts a life where she stops socialising in fear of hurting someone with her mere presense, lives on lucky charms and good luck rituals, refuses to travel in a vehicle with people and avoids human interaction. 
 Maguire was relatable. Especially when she jumped from her bedroom window to make sure she wasn't invincible. That was completely absurd but it's totally something I would do. I had my sympathy for her but I liked how her character wasn't screaming, "I have a sad life. Cry for me, bitches!". What truly made me like her was the fact that she was trying hard to get better and trying hard to get rid of her demons. Following her psychologist's suggestion, she comes up with seven different goals; driving with people, enrolling in a sports team, etc and the final one - travelling in a plane to Ireland to attend her deceased family members' memorial service. 
 I loved how Tennis was portrayed in this novel. I don't normally like team sports but if I had to pick one, it would be Tennis for sure! I've also read a lot of books where the girl signs up for something new and is suddenly the best at it but thankfully, Maguire doesn't fall into that category. She does have a knack for the sport but is not the ultimate best. She occasionally needs help with her serve, loses quite a lot of times, has a problem with nerves, ends up (CRINGE ALERT) hitting her tennis ball on a boy's crotch (You may run around screaming "Ewww" now.) and is often, on the verge of quitting. 
 Enter Perfectly Assembled Boy - a professional tennis player who has a million names - Jordan, Jordy, Jord, Stanford, Stan, Dolphin lover, etc. I feel like his life was a very accurate representation of struggling with society and family's expectations and your inner desires. I don't like boys who act a little psycho when they see a cute girl ("Can I touch your hair?" No. You don't ask to touch random girls' hair.) or get very sensitive when they're rejected but I liked how he apologized for being slightly bitchy about it. Eventually, he grew on to me because I have a weakness for sassy boys. Sigh. 
 The major and only problems I had with this book were certain problematic aspects of Jordy and Maguire's relationship. I liked her honesty, how she refused to hang out with him at first, because for all we know, he could've been a serial killer (take notes, Hazel Grace) but how many times have I read about an athletic and almost perfect guy falling for the new, plain and uninterested girl? Dozens. At times, Jordy was so desperate that I had to roll my eyes and snort. I don't really interact with men much but are all boys as desperate as him? It's pathetic. 
 "It means this is harder than I thought." 
 "What is?" 
 He lowers his voice. "Sharing you." Before I can reply he continues, "I'm glad you felt comfortable enough to come to this party. I want you to get over your fear of being around other people, but man, I hate watching other guys hit on you." 
 Um...is this supposed to be cute? Are you her third parent that you don't like her being hit on by "other guys"? I appreciate your honesty but you're practically an other guy too, sonny. And you're not even involved with her ffs! Is she a box of pizzas that you don't like "sharing her"? Ugh. 
 I don't know. This may appeal to some but I guess it just shows how unromantic, cold and emotionless I am :( 
 You're not a toaster, Maguire. You're not here to be fixed. 
 The only character I would give an A* would be Daniel Leeds. I loved him. Not because he's perfect but because he was just so admirable. I mean, Jordy and Maguire were relatable and all that tosh but this guy was brilliant. I'm so glad he wasn't one of those cliched, usless therapists who don't do much apart from making their patient regret their existence even more. I liked how constantly he reminded Maguire how she was the one incharge and the only one able to make herself get better. I liked how he wasn't a big fan of the word "fixed". I liked how he told her that medication and antibiotics don't always guarantee a recovery. And he was a musician! If I ever end up becoming a psychologist, I aspire to be half as good as him. 
 Maguire's stepdad was awesome too. He had those cliche, over-protective qualities but that's what made him so interesting because he was a stepdad. A not evil or abusive stepdad like in most YA novels. It was nice to read something different for a change. 
 "Your mom told me you had a visitor tonight. Does someone need to kick that kid's ass?" 
 "No, you don't. Because as soon as he said that, I basically pushed him away." 
 "Yessss." Tom pumps his fist. 
 I frown. "Not helping." 
 "Sorry. That's just every dad's dream answer." 
 Aww. I think I have a Dad crush on him. 
 There were some one dimensional characters like Kimber the mean girl (who is also a dumbass) and I found it very unbelievable how normally Maguire communicated with her peers. If she had cast a wall between her and the Homo sapiens agenda then how is she not having problems socialising with them now? 
  
 Apart from the romance, the other thing which stopped me from rating this book at least 4.5 stars was the extremely cheesy, vomit-worthy ending. This book ended with Jordy and Maguire confessing their love for each other. Groan. I have a dirty feeling Stokes didn't know how to end her book because I'm a writer, and whenever I'm facing the same issue, I write a cliche ending too. Guilty as proven. 
  
 Stokes's writing style was very gripping and I think I cried once. I liked how she portrayed mental health. What a disappointment this book was. I gave up on it without finishing it. So many people had told me to read Pat Conroy, and how good an author he was. So I borrowed this one from the library. How did I choose? This one was in paperback, and I needed to take it on the road; also it was flagged on other Conroy novels. But it felt like a make-weight book to me. It was almost like the Beatles did in Abbey Road, throwing all the half-completed pieces of work into a pot and seeing how it turned out. On Abbey Road it turned out OK. Here it felt like there was a limp storyline (Father takes daughter to Italy to escape fall-out from wife's suicide) that then was a canvas on which to paint the storyline of all the other people from their small South Carolina town. I didn't like the people, I didn't like the way the story jumped about without really adding anything to the real story; in short, I gave up. Maybe his other books are better? One star out of five.

Old review I wrote on my blog (http://douglascootey.com) on 21 November 2005: 
 Last summer I waited in line with my daughters for the most eagerly anticipated book of the year: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince. The book was well worth the wait. It was the best written since Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban. I pegged some events correctly and was surprised by others. I found the book entertaining, and would even recommend it to non-Harry Potter fans as a place to start the series. I'm going to be discussing some plot spoilers in this review so if that sort of thing bothers you you've just read my review in a nutshell and don't need to read further. 
 I had problems with Book Four, Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. Although I enjoyed much of what happened in the book the ending nearly killed me. Once we learned that Barty Crouch Jr. was posing as Moody we were treated to a full chapter of exposition as he recounted the entire story all over again, but from his point of view. I found it dreadfully dull and often skipped through it. Only this year did I learn that JK Rowling enjoys Dorothy Sayers and that Goblet of Fire's ending fit the classic Sayers' style ending. 
 I had problems with Book Five, Harry Potter and the Order of the Phoenix, as well. I found it overly long at times and in need of a good edit. Interestingly, JK Rowling felt the same. 
 "There are bits of all six books that I would go back and tighten up. My feeling is that Phoenix is overlong, but I challenge anyone to find the obvious place to cut." 
 This isn't to say that I didn't enjoy those books. I've read them so many times I've lost count. I'm just saying that these books had flaws in execution and length. The same couldn't be said for Book Six, Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince. This is the tightest book she's written to date. The narrative was woven well. The characters were well fleshed out, there weren't any personality changes pulled out of a hat like Ginny's character in Book Five, and the back story balanced well with current events. Not only did we see an end to CAPS LOCK Harry, but exposition was much improved from earlier books. Instead of having the story explained from the mouths of Hermione, Dumbledore, or Crouch, we had pensieve episodes which worked much better in my opinion, proving the old writer's adage: "Show it, don't tell it." This was a well written adventure story. 
 Interestingly, I had three predictions proven to be true, which is good even for me. First, Dumbledore died, paving the way for Harry to finally stand on his own. Until now, and as Harry himself had pointed out in Book Five, he's been very lucky and always saved by somebody else. Now there will be no teachers to rescue him. No guardian angels waiting in the wings. Our hero cannot be a hero until he fights insurmountable odds on his own. Second, we discovered the horcruxes. I had predicted a few years ago, based on events in Book Two, that Voldemort had obtained immortality by imbuing inanimate objects with his soul, as he had done with the dairy. I was delighted to be right about this one, and the third prediction: that it would be too much to expect the horcruxes to be laying about Hogwarts so Harry would have to go on a quest to find them. There are still mysteries to be revealed in Book Seven, such as the importance of Harry's green eyes and how that relates to Lilly, his mother, or what significance his scar has yet to play beyond it's iconic purposes. Book Six tied up enough loose ends to satisfy, but left enough untied to keep the reader looking forward to the next installment. 
 Much has been made of how dark this book is compared to the others. I'm not sure where people's heads have been. Harry Potter and the Sorceror's Stone started with murder, abandonment, and child abuse. It was garnished with bullying, hinted with dark disembodied cloaks that fed on fresh unicorn blood, then topped with life threatening trials and ordeals. And that was all before facing the grand baddie himself. All that has changed is Harry has grown up, gone through his angry teenage years and now is ready to be a man. The framework for this was laid in the first book for this progression, but the books have always been dark. 
 As for romances, much has been made about them as well, but JKR will not be known as a great romance novelist. The "romance" in the books is, as we Americans would put it, High School stuff. Meeting at lockers, making out in the equipment room, etc. No surprise there. They're still students. We have yet to see if Harry and Ginny have the greatest written love scenes of teen fiction yet to come. In fact, I suspect that it is quite plausible for Ginny to die, sacrificing herself and protecting Harry with the same charm his mother once used on him, but I'm not holding my breath. The romance will be there, but secondary to the action and adventure experienced by our hero, Harry Potter. It is his story, told through his eyes, and unless Harry suddenly becomes a hopeless romantic the story's narrative will focus on the same elements it always has. Could a Harry Potter fan ask for anything more?

This was a refreshing read for me in that I haven't picked up a contemporary adult fiction novel in a while. The book itself was kind of a mixed bag. 
 I didn't have any expectations going in. The story was interesting but not completely engaging. Quite a few moments seemed pretty far-fetched and really tested my ability to believe what was happening. I'm thinking specifically of Lotto's big incident at his prep school. (I had to put it down and then power through when that particular bit happened). Lotto as a character I didn't find that likable. I'm not quite sure how to describe it, but he's pretty frustrating. 
 Mathilde's history is intriguing, although the deeper it delved, the harder it was to suspend my belief (similar to Lotto's prep school incident). I liked her, but am conflicted with her portrayal and her actions to support her husband. She went without meals while he pursued a fruitless acting career and while he obviously loved her, he never recognized that. I know that's part of Mathilde's character, but it made Lotto a lot less likable. The 'contract' in her past was pretty troubling and I can't tell if the author was trying to make some kind of statement or if it was merely for shock (I feel it was more the latter). That sex scene with the sushi in his apartment was so...it just seemed incredibly unnecessary and very pandering to straight guy humiliation kink. I don't mind sex scenes at all, and there's obviously a lot of loaded and problematic things about that particular relationship, but JEEZ. It felt like the oddly descriptive stripper scene in Water for Elephants. It doesn't add the story, the character, and feels like it was inserted for the purpose of getting male readers off, honestly.  
 The writing was dense and thoughtful. A lot of reviewers said it was pretentious and I can definitely agree with that, but again, I enjoyed it if only for the fact that it was breaking up some of my reading habits as of late. Whether you hate it or you love it, it certainly sparks quite a lot of discussion. I also have to wonder if this was written by a male author, would it still be getting the same kind of criticism? Maybe. 
 I have heard compared with Gone Girl a lot, and from what I know of that novel, I don't think this is true. While I haven't read it, I feel like that's become a sort of tagline to get readers interested in the next big thing. This is a slower paced novel about a marriage between two people you don't think will make it work, but they do. One thing I liked about their marriage is that they never cheat on each other although Lotto came very close with his operatic friend, which I'm still surprised didn't actually happen . This may seem like kind of a stupid thing to praise, but marriage and adultery are represented pretty strangely in novels and films. I also appreciated Mathilde's ending. It's not something you see terribly often and I felt like that part of the book was realistic. It wasn't quite the happy ending most envision after tragedy, but it was real. 
 I don't know if I could really recommend this book. I'm glad I read it, if only to see what all the hype was about. Is it the greatest novel written? I don't so, but the writing was still very good, if a little pretentious. It's sure to make you think a little bit, if you love it or despise it.

Okay, this book was so much fun to read. It's interesting because it originated in "Fangirl," where the protagonist was obsessed with a Harry Potter-esque series and wrote fanfiction about it. "Carry On" is the result. 
 We are clearly living in a post-HP world, and Rowell takes advantage of that. It tidies up messes that exist in HP while still honoring the source material. It's predictable and pandering at moments but never overwhelmingly so. The characters are fresh, realistic, and fun. My favorite chapters were from Baz's point of view. 
 The one thing that drove me insane was that the punctuation is placed within the parenthesis. Why?! So irritating. I had to pretend that it was because the book was "written" by a college freshman to move past it. 
 I stayed up until 2am to finish this book.

This book was fantastic. 
 The first hundred pages of this book is buildup, because it's Stephen King and buildup is basically his middle name, but even throughout the buildup there's sprinkles of excitement and wonder and then everything gets intense so quickly and it stays intense, apart from a few little bits of reprieve. 
 This is 'the last Castle Rock story', and it was great to see little references to The Dark Half and Cujo - mostly The Dark Half, because the main character in this novel is Alan Pangborn, the sheriff in The Dark Half and he makes a few references to Thad Beaumont and his issues. Either way, it was nice to see a familiar face. 
 The plot of this novel is something that starts out simple and blossoms into something that's still... essentially simple, but with a lot of little moving parts. A new store opens up in Castle Rock, Maine, owned by Leland Gaunt, called Needful Things. Inside, one can get the thing that they need 'the most'... and Gaunt is definitely willing to bargain. 
 The characters and description, as always, are the strongest points, although this novel was so well plotted that I loved every second of it. It did take me a while to finish, but that was more of a fact of me taking my time on it than not wanting to read it. 
 Overall, fantastic and a great 'last Castle Rock story.'

 In Frau Totenkinder's story, we see her send the Pied Piper to steal the children of Hamelin. You all know I love JLA's books. I was a little apprehensive before reading Bitter Sweet Love a few months ago, knowing it's a fantasy series about Gargoyles. I mean... Gargoyles? The only ones I know are the stone ones in NYC. And they don't look so inviting. But I gave it a shot, since It's JLA. 
 And ever since I finished, I've been waiting for White Hot Kiss. 
 You remember the half breed charge in the DC Warden house, right? Layla. 
 Layla is torn. She considers herself Warden, even though she's only half that. Her other half is Demon. The Wardens' enemy. How'd that happen? Read the book. I'm not revealing that itty bitty detail in this review. 
 You probably remember Zayne, too. Her pseudo-brother? He's fiercely protective of her, her best friend. He's also in love with Layla, every bit as she's in love with him. But they can't ever be together for fear of her sucking out his pure soul. Promising, right? 
 Layla is allowed to attend school, and one of her extracurricular activities is tagging demons for Wardens to easily spot and rid of when they're out to hunt late at night. 
 Layla so deeply wants to belong, she does her best to suppress her demon side all the time. But Layla comes of, at first, as a little whiny. And then one day she meets Roth and her whiny self turns less whiny and a little rule breaking. 
 Roth is a drop dead gorgeous 17 year old. He's also a demon (a special one) and he seems to know all there is to know about Layla. Even things she doesn't know about herself, or ever tried finding out. Layla is attracted to Roth, who seems to always be there, when she wants him to, and mostly when she doesn't. 
 Layla and Roth go on an adventure behind the Wardens' back. And they get into a lot of trouble. But then, most of this trouble affects Layla, not so much Roth. For the time being. 
 I loved the love triangle type in this story. There's a distinct battle between good and bad, and right and wrong. But not the way you'd think. The battle between good and bad is within each of the characters - and that makes things fascinating, and also makes the reactions they have all the more unpredictable. 
 As with all of JLA's books this one is fantastically written. I consider Bitter Sweet Love to be an introduction to this world. But I definitely consider White Hot Kiss a fantastic preparation for some great romance, fabulous action and a lot of plot twists and turns in this series. I just hope we get more from... well, I can't tell you. That would be a spoiler and I don't do spoilers. 
 The story ends with a bit of a cliffy, one that I wouldn't consider as such but more of a get-me-the-next-book-pronto type need-to-read-further end. 
 It also left me with a bit of a hangover and a confused heart over Zayne versus Roth. I kept thinking a threesome would be fine by me. And then I remember it's a YA. Sigh.

 Poison Study is one of my absolute favourite fantasy novels. Magic Study and Fire Study didn't have as much impact on me as the first book in the series; they seemed to lack some of the magic in Poison Study and the characters didn't seem consistent. But when I learned that Snyder was writing more books about Yelena, I got excited because I hoped it would redeem the rest of the series for me. It did, mostly. 
 Shadow Study has a unique narrative technique. There are multiple POVs, but not in the way you'd think. Yelena's chapters are told in first person while Valek and Janco's chapters are told in third person. Don't get me wrong, I love having the extra insight into Valek and Janco because it made them very complex, but the decision to not tell the whole book in third person POV startled me with the first POV switch. I'm not sure it was the right decision, but it didn't hinder my enjoyment of the book too much. 
 Yelena has had a hard life, but she fought and survived and now she has a family and happiness. She's also accepted herself for all that she is even though all that she is sometimes makes things difficult for her. In this book, we finally get to see the Yelena we know and love. She's smart, insightful, resourceful, caring, and determined to survive. When Yelena loses her magic, it's easy to see that she's devastated at losing a part of herself that she's come to love. It's a nice pay-off to see the character growth she's undergone over the course of the series so far. What I don't understand, however, is the fact that people still don't trust Yelena even though she has endangered herself to protect people again and again. I just don't understand why Snyder keeps returning to that attitude towards Yelena when it seemed to mostly be solved in Fire Study. 
 Valek was always a main character in the book, but in Shadow Study we get to know him a lot better. We get to see his motivations and struggles that led him to be an assassin and we come to understand a bit more of why he's so loyal to the Commander. A good portion of the novel is spent on these flashbacks. An interesting dynamic is the relationship between him and the Commander since he's loyal to the man above all else, even sometimes Yelena. In this book, we see how he's changed since meeting Yelena. He has someone else to think of now, and his life isn't only consumed with making the Commander happy anymore. He wants to be happy and have a life that he thought he could never have. 
 I will say that sometimes the characters aren't written consistently, however. For example, Janco comes across more ridiculous than fun and wise, and Leif returns to his old self, just a little. I'm also surprised that one character seems to have gone back to his old beliefs completely  i.e. the Commander decides he still hates magicians even though he is one . 
 The many mysteries in this novel kept me absolutely riveted. I had so many questions about who was behind what, why this was happening, etc. Sometimes I guessed things fairly easily, or almost guessed things. Other times, I thought "whoa". Not everything is solved in Shadow Study because there will be two more novels in the series. But what this novel uncovers about characters makes me super interested in seeing how everything will end. 
 Shadow Study is a riveting, smart, and action-packed novel that reminds me why I enjoy Poison Study so much. While it has its issues, it's an improvement on the previous two novels about Yelena and co. I can't wait to read about these beloved characters in the next two Soulfinders books!

A couple drive an endless dark country road to visit his family's remote farmhouse. It's all atmosphere, atmosphere, atmosphere. And talk. This couple does nothing but talk, and it's all philosophical. I can't shake the feeling I am reading a book version of the French film Haute Tension (aka Switchblade Romance), and things aren't what they seem. People just don't talk this way. Most people talk about other people, and things, their work day, shared memories. Not this couple. Their conversations are abstractions filled with underlying secrets. 
 When they get to the farmhouse, things get weirder. Mom and Dad are even worse at conversation, and one half of the couple - the half that should be smoothing the conversation along - stops talking altogether. We wander around the world's creepiest, darkest farm, talking through a glass darkly. Then we drive to the world's creepiest Dairy Queen, and finally to a school where this book ends in the only possible way it could end. 
 I am guessing the really extreme 1-star and 5-star reviews of this were from people who were surprised by the ending. I was not surprised.

 John Dies at the End is what they might come up with.

I will echo everyone else and say that The Hate U Give stands as one of the best YA books ever written. The story follows Starr Carter, a sixteen-year-old who struggles to navigate her identity between the rich, mostly-white prep school she attends and the poor, mostly-black neighborhood she lives in. Her entire world gets shattered when she sees a white police officer kill her childhood friend Khalil, even though Khalil held no weapon. The controversy surrounding his death and the ensuing court case takes over Starr's life and the lives of her family and friends. With little time to grieve, Starr realizes that she must speak up to have even the slimmest chance of securing justice for Khalil. 
 I am amazed by how Angie Thomas incorporated so much in this book without any individual part feeling under-developed or confusing. In addition to the central plot involving Khalil's death, she addresses so many issues pertinent to Starr's identity as a black girl and social justice for black people overall: how to handle a racist friend who has tons of white fragility, the challenge of developing intimacy with a white person as a POC, learning how systemic discrimination leads to black people selling drugs and then going to jail, and much more. Thomas writes all of these nuanced topics into Starr's story and interactions with great skill, always moving the plot forward while giving us a ton of important material to think about. 
 I loved The Hate U Give most because of its characters and their relationships with one another. Thomas creates such real, flawed, and personality-filled characters that you cannot help but feel heartbroken and angry when they experience racism and discrimination. Amidst all the hate Starr and her community receive, their genuine love for one another imbues this novel with hope - and it inspires me to see how Starr uses that love as a launching pad to engage in meaningful activism. 
 Overall, a fantastic book I would recommend to literally everyone. With the awful white supremacist stuff that has happened as of late, white people and non-black people of color must educate ourselves and one another, as well as take other actions to fight racism and prejudice. It gives me some hope to see The Hate U Give do so well in the literary market; may the youth rise with love and power to resist America's hate-filled past.
