Flora Segunda lives pretty much by herself in Crackpot Hall, the house of eleven thousand rooms. Her mother is too busy being General to stay around much, and her father drowns his life in the bottle. So maybe it's not so surprising Flora gets into a little trouble trying to help Valefor, the House's resident Denizen, regain himself. A lot of trouble. And suddenly she's going to need every skill she possesses (and quite a few she doesn't) to get out. 
 Flora's sheer vocabulary makes her an amusing narrator. The slang is explained well and used often, but the variety of descriptions is one area where this book shines. But the book's chatty tone keeps it from bogging down in big words. 
 The characters themselves are all larger-than-life in some way, from Udo's fashion sense and bravado to the General's impenetrable Will. Flora never has a dull moment as she races from adventure to adventure. 
 Unfortunately, Flora herself is extremely irritating. She says it best: "I thought I was so clever and rangery, and I wasn't anything at all but a stupid heartless mindless snapperhead!" And given it takes her nearly 300 pages to come to this realization, I almost put the book down several times before finishing it. Valefor was just as bad; he came off as a whiny teenage brat (which I suppose he is, in Denizen years) that just won't shut up. The pair of them had me hoping they would kill each other, preferably sooner rather than later. 
 On a smaller scale, I never got much of a sense of setting for the overall world Flora lives in. She describes her immediate surroundings well enough, but just enough of a wider picture to assure readers that history and possibly even geography is wildly different. Particularly with magic, things happen and explanations follow; this would not normally be a bad thing, but it happens so often it feels like Flora keeps pulling rabbits out of a hat. 
 Thankfully, the end of the book is much better than the beginning. Characters stop feeling like caricatures and reveal multiple dimensions. Flora ends up being wrong in some of her key assumptions about people and situations. But it's such a long slog to get there I wonder that it's worth reading this book, much less the sequel. I rate this book Neutral.

I came across "The 100" after watching the first season on Netflix. I really enjoyed the show so I decided to give the book series a shot. And that probably affected my reading of the original source material. I liked the book, I just felt like the television series a bit more. 
 The structure of the book is one of three narrators; Bellamy, Wells, Clark, and Glass. This is a common style and it often fails. It tends to get a bit convoluted, jumping from story to story. But Kass Morgan handled this style quite well. The plot did not become disjointed at all and it was easy to follow because three of the four story lines were very well connected. 
 The fourth, unconnected story line was the one I enjoyed the least. While Clark, Wells, and Bellamy were all back on Earth, Glass remained on the space ship. A ship story could have gone a long way to tell the reader what was going on in space. But instead of answering questions like why the 100 were sent to Earth or how long the Ark has left, we were treated to a high school love story. It was all kind of unnecessary. 
 "The 100" is more or less a setup book. We learn about the Ark, the back stories of the four narrators,and it isn't until the very end that we get some real conflict that will hopefully fill the following two books. And if setup was the purpose of this book, it was highly successful. While the book was not and amazingly griping story, the last few chapters definitely get the reader excited for the sequel.

1.5 stars. 
 What compelled me to try this book was--guess--the very professionally done cover. That's right. It just goes to show that if you hire a good cover artist*, readers will flock to your book. You spend good money on a cover, so the editing must be good too, right? Right? 
 Wrong. 
 All this shows is that anyone can hire a good cover artist. Feiwel and Friends publishing company, you've shown me exactly the quality of books you release. I've been burned and warned for the future. Not reading your books again. 
 I had to read this book in small steps, taking looooong breaks in between, in order to finish it. 
 At first glance, the writing looks like purple prose (because of the long sentence lengths and all the semicolons and descriptions/adjectives/adverbs, but once you taker a closer look at the words, you see some odd choice of words that make it a little awkward. The user Mary -->https://www.goodreads.com/user/show/8... did a fair job of collecting a bunch of quotes to illustrate this with her commentary in her review of Lailah-->https://www.goodreads.com/review/show.... 
 The book had a plot--a very thin plot. Basically Lailah is on this mission to find out who she is. At the end of the book, she finds out. We find out at the very beginning--at the prologue. 
 Not very effective planning there, Miss Nikki Kelly. You kind of ruined the entire mystery for us. Unfortunately for the plot, nothing much happens during the entire middle. We also had a bunch of scenes (eg. that Christmas scene and movie night scene) that did nothing to further the plot. We learned absolutely nothing new in those scenes. Though the author did take the opportunity to shove some HEAVY light/dark symbolism on the reader during the Christmas scene. 
 This story is riddled with cliches: love triangles, super duper all powerful female main character, female main character jealous of other women near her two love interests (which by the way was sickening to read). 
 It's a shallow story. Not only that, the main character doesn't have much in the way of characterization. She is bland and boring. That's right, take away her strange version of immortality and there's nothing left. No substance to her. I don't want to know her. I don't care about her. She isn't a powerful character. In fact she doesn't even rate as a weak character. 
 It's not just the female main character I have a problem with. The side characters as well. What a good story has is a strong cast of characters. That's right. The main character can't be the only developed one. You can only showcase the MC when the supporting cast is interesting as well. The villain in this book was not only PURE EVIL and boring, but so lacking substance that it's not even funny. 
 At the end, we find out Lailah's specialty and why the villains want her so much. It was so weird that it made no sense. The author forced an explanation on the reader in the hope of the reader just accepting it. 
 As for the weird choice of words, I think that this will fix itself overtime as long as the author keeps writing. It seems like the author just needs to experiment; see what it feels like to use those words. Once she gets that out of her system she'll see why it's better to keep things simple. For example: 
 I was confused as I watched him raise [my strands of hair] to his orifices. 
 Let's be clear about this... I would expect an alien to use 'orifices' but not someone who lives among humans. If I were to narrate, I'd say 'nose'. The author needs to better get in character. That is just unnatural sounding. 
 This author needs to go back to the drawing board and ask herself why we should care about Lailah. What is it about Lailah that would make us want to spend time with her if she had no powers? This author needs to work on her greatest weakness first: building strong characters. This is achieved by asking what their goals, motivations, and drives are in each scene. Also, the same question should be asked about the character what the answers used to be before the story began. After the author has achieved that, then she should move on to improving her plotting. This is done by questioning the goal, problem, resolution, and new problem (that appeared) of each scene. 
 *And it's not like the cover artists have any clue about the quality of the book they've been hired to produce a cover for. They don't actually read the books, you know. Cover artists take the jobs because they have bills to pay... and considering how long it takes to create this type of cover on photoshop and low payment ($500-$700 is the high-end which still doesn't pay enough to live on) they take the jobs. The cover artists ask very basic questions like themes in terms of visual aspects, which in the case of this cover shows a sweet girl bathed in light being dragged down into darkness. Kind of falls with the theme of this book: light versus dark, good vs. evil.

And I'm extremely happy to say that this one definitely did not disappoint and it was certainly the perfect book to get me out of my reading slump. 
 To say that I'm officially hooked to this series would be an understatement. I actually am starting to dream of suddenly being whisked away into a parallel fantasy world/realm/time and meeting an extremely hot alpha male, who also happens to be a royalty and leader of some sort. 
 Yeah... something like these... 
 Cora Goode found herself suddenly thrust into this fantastical world where she can talk to animals and she's surrounded by lush gardens and scenery... no joke, it's like the perfect setting of a Disney fairy tale. And what is a Disney fairy tale without a hot strapping young (okay not so young here) lad-slash-prince mounted on a horse? And how can we forget the cruel evil witch as well? Yup, that's the world Cora found herself in but thank goodness she has Prince Noctorno "Tor" Hawthorne, who also happens to be her husband, to rely on every step of the way. But just one slightly major problem... Tor hates her guts. Or at least he hates the Cora-of-their-world's guts. 
 Thus begins Cora and Tor's journey together in realizing that fate (actually it was an evil witch) had twisted their destinies and they actually held half of each other's souls. Do take note that this is first and foremost a romance story so that aspect really comes first, more than the action, the fantastical aspects, and what have you. The story really focused on the developments in Tor and Cora's relationship and KA did a fabulous job of creating another swoon-worthy alpha-male of a hunk and a very sweet and steamy romance story. Of course, this story is without challenges posed by outside forces and I loved how Tor and Cora powered through it together. 
 I highly, HIGHLY recommend this book to those who are looking for some epic fantasy romance. I do have to admit that this was not as riveting and mesmerizing as The Golden Dynasty, but it was a very worthy read nevertheless. In fact, I'm now convinced that I have to read the first book in this series and I'm definitely looking forward to more from this fantabulous series!

 The Mime Order picks up where The Bone Season ended, on the train to London. Paige is back with the Seven Seals, and while Jaxon is perfectly happy pretending the whole thing never happened, Paige is a changed person from her time being enslaved by the Rephaim, and she can't pretend it never happened. Needing Jaxon for protection against Scion and Nashira Sargas, Paige is faced with a whole host of problems as she tries to get back into her mime-lord's good graces at the same time as trying to figure out what to do about the Repahim situation. 
 I really enjoyed this book. It is slow-paced, but the world building is exquisite. I really enjoyed being in the Underworld of Scion London, learning how it worked and being introduced to the mime-lords and mime-queens. The world building dominates a little over half of this novel, but with good reason. Everything has been set up perfectly, and it will allow Samantha Shannon to just go for it in the next books. 
 The characters in this are just beautiful. Paige is such a perfect MC, she's such a perfect heroine, and she's by far my favourite strong female character. Warden is so unreadable, I just can't quite fathom him out, but I think that's predominantly a good thing, because he's battling between Paige and his fellow Rephaim and he can't just put his heart on his sleeve for the whole world to see. The Seven Seals are great, Nick is the sweetest and I can tell that he's the ultimate worrier, Eliza is so lovely, Zeke is nice, Nadine is desperate for approval and she hasn't quite accepted anyone in the Seals but Jaxon, closing herself off from the world. Speaking of Jaxon, he's horrible, but his personality is intriguing. 
 Also can we take a second for the ending because I KNEW IT. When Paige uncovered the Abbess and the Rag and Bone Man it kind of clicked that maybe Jaxon had a part to play after Nashira wanting to find him while she was in Scheol I. I CALLED IT, MAN.  
 I think the reason that this wasn't quite a five star for me was that I was dipping in and out of it at first, still in a bit of a hangover from book one, and I spent a lot of time hating on Jaxon. After the first book it didn't have quite the same umf. Not to say that it didn't have any umf, because it did, but I don't know. Maybe I'll change my mind after it's all sunk in. 
 Overall, this is a terrible review but a fantastic book, and my thoughts are still whirring around my head. Maybe I'll write another review that makes more sense but I just love this book.

You know, I used to be a big reader of literary fiction. Really. But there's this terrible epidemic, and The Age of Miracles is a great example of it - in which literary fiction is basically like other fiction with all of the blood removed. (In particular, this is Life As We Knew It with all of the life taken out of it. Read that instead!) 
 To be fair, I only read the first 150 pages of this. I couldn't read any more: this book is totally bloodless. There is no spark. Everything is told to us in this incredibly heavy-handed way - all telling, all the time. This world doesn't feel real. The characters seem like people, but without any of the things that make people interesting. 
 This isn't Walker's fault, really. There seems to be this feeling among writers of literary fiction (and presumably among readers as well, or this would go the fuck away) that you can't comment seriously on the world if you engage with it. And so you don't. These novels are written in this weirdly detached voice. You can't get too close or else you might not be able to be so knowing/sardonic/"literary" - or something. It's bleak, is what it is. And not even the human kind of bleak - not even real melancholy - this shadow of what would, in any other kind of novel, be a real emotion. 
 When I was in high school a therapist diagnosed me with dysthymia. In this particular disorder - a kind of chronic depression - you aren't horribly deeply sad all the time. It's just that everything is a little bit worse, all the time, than it used to be. You don't really experience extremes. Everything is gray. It's more boredom or fatigue than anything else. Nothing holds your interest. Your emotions just kind of flatline. 
 That is how all of this literary crap makes me feel these past few years. I don't want to read any more dysthymic novels. I want passion and color and spark. I want my novels to come alive, and to make me feel more alive. Otherwise, why bother? If you just want people to read your clever/heartfelt/articulate observations about the human condition, start a blog. No reason to pretend it's a novel.

I looked at the reviews and the blurbs again and realized that I read this sometime last year and was annoyed to no end by the heroine. Quite simply put, she was stupid. That immediately means the story goes nowhere. And it didn't.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Ok, I will admit that I picked up this book completely because of its cover. After all, it was pretty and pink and fluffy and romantic, if not entirely historically accurate. I mean, cover art so rarely matches up with the story. 
 I wish I had known that this cover was my warning label. 
 The characters in this book were probably the worst part. They were very flat and stereotypical. Elizabeth was the typical "good" daughter who was doing everything that her mother wanted but was so deeply in love with someone below her station (something completely unacceptable in 1899.) However, she entered into a loveless engagement with Henry, typical womanizer who just HAPPENED to fall in love with Elizabeth's younger sister Diana. And Diana just HAPPENED to tame Henry's womanizing ways by being full of life (if not a little rebellious herself.) 
 Of course, the person getting screwed in all of this was Penelope, the bitchy, mean, manipulative best "friend" of Elizabeth, who found out about Elizabeth's affair with the help and told her if she didn't give Henry up to Penelope, she would ruin Elizabeth's reputation. We're supposed to hate Penelope, but honestly, what I hate is that because she's the only woman who thinks for herself and goes after what she wants (oh, and by the way is NOT a virgin), she is automatically bitchy and a slut and she's the one we're meant to hate. I think she's the only one who has any sort of a personality. 
 The plot in this book was so predictable. We find out in the first chapter that Elizabeth has died. However, I am no more than a third of a way into the book when I know what happens through the remainder of the book, and certainly the big secret. Elizabeth is not really dead and has decided to run off with Will.  The writing of the book is not that complicated and really, should be more engaging than it was. I shouldn't be able to figure out a plot within the first third of the book because, honestly, it makes the rest of the book not really worth reading. 
 Also, the were a lot of things that really bothered me. First of all, woman who weren't married didn't wear make-up. Yet Godbersen was constantly referencing how Elizabeth and Diana did their make-up and Diana was barely out in society. She also continually referenced Lord & Taylor which, I always find it off-putting when authors drop names in their books. It's like their promoting the business. And yes, Lord & Taylor was around in 1899, but it wasn't the shop like it was today. I feel like Godberson wrote this book like 1899 New York City was like NYC was today and that just wasn't the case. I felt like she kind of researched 1899 and then just winged the rest of it and it showed. 
 Overall, I wasn't that impressed with the book. I felt like an 1899 fashion show was being paraded in front of me. I don't know; maybe Lord & Taylor paid her to write the book. X amount of money for mentioning their name X amount of times (because let me tell you, it was in there a lot.) I hated that the characters were so stereotypical and that she was sending out such stupid messages like sexual independence = mean spirited and bitchy. I don't think I'm going to read the next book (mainly because I'm pretty sure I already know what happens.)

I am extremely late to this review party. I picked this book up given its prominence on "best new fantasy series" lists, but finished with confusion over why it was picked for such distinction. Since I'm behind on the posting, I'll skip the plot summary so many others have described and jump right into my problems with the book. 
 I am confused by the ridiculous amount of praise for the "world-building" Shannon creates. She used a metric shit-ton of words to create a place where so much goes unexplained. Shannon provides a heap of indecipherable exposition-dump text to establish her world that includes clairvoyance, Scion, the syndicate, London, Oxford, the Rephs, and the Emites without actually explaining or helping me understand any of it and how it interacts within the world she created. Maybe I just missed it in the dump, but I can't buy into the world you built if I can't even understand it. The entire set-up just left me with so many unanswered questions. And these questions were not minor issues of structure or miniscule detail that would have added depth to a scene or character, they were major issues of how the world was established and functioned and how the people within it lived and acted. 
 For example, Paige is in the Seven Seals, a crime syndicate in section I-4 of London, and engages in "mime-crime" which is using clairvoyance to make money. How do they make that money and what tasks do they perform, you ask? Well, I can't tell you because it was never explained. 
 Also, this alternative-future London is ruled by Scion, an oppressive, totalitarian government that captures, punishes, and kills any clairvoyant that does not work for Scion in catching "free" clairvoyants. What threat do voyants pose to society and why is the government so adamant in removing them from society you ask? Well, clairvoyance in unnatural and something, something. 
 How to clairvoyants obtain their power? No one knows (okay, I can buy that). How do they use their power? Well, they tap into the aether (spirit realm). It can just happen just by doing it. Not one individual even attempts to explain or describe the process. And don't even ask about what types of clairvoyants exists and what powers they have. According to the ridiculous flow charts at the opening, 52 separate types of clairvoyants exist, and not even that explains the specific powers each uses. Remembering what each one can and cannot do, other than Paige maybe, is tiresome and a chore. 
 Okay so clairvoyants are presumably powerful and threaten the government so they are killed or captured. Why? Well, part of the reason for capturing voyants is because a whole race of beings from the aether, the Rephaim, have a deal with Scion to funnel voyants and some regular humans into slavery for the express purpose of training them to fight the Emim. The Rephaim also "feed" on voyants.  
 The Rephaim? Well they are mystical beings from the aether that purportedly fight the Emim (although they are forbidden from fighting the Emim; that is the job of the captured voyants). They are maintaining a balance between Scion and the Emim. How? Somehow. Why are they based in Oxford? Why not? What purpose are they here for other than torturing and using humans? Your guess is as good as mine. 
 Oh, you saw the mention of the Emim? What are the Emim you ask? Some mystical being that likes human flesh and come from the aether. And they apparently really like the area around Sheol I (Oxford). Why just Sheol I? They seem to be drawn to the Rephaim. The glossary states that the Emim's existence, "is shrouded in mystery". No shit. Probably why none of the humans are unaware of them prior to the arrival in Sheol I. But if the Emim eat human flesh, why are they not running rampant in London or other cities around the world? If they are attracted to the Rephaim in Sheol I and not other locations, why does Scion have an agreement to funnel voyants to Sheol I? What purpose does that serve?  Sweet fancy moses, my head hurts. 
 All this world-building by Shannon lacked substantive details that actually established a functioning narrative. With a new set-up, I just have seventeen more questions that are explained away in the glossary with "it is shrouded in mystery" and  a toss-off comment from Seb's ghost that he knows "a secret, but I cannot tell"  which will seemingly explain all over the course of the next six (SIX!) books. I kept going down the rabbit hole of my mind trying to answer obvious questions about this world that Shannon had no interest in sharing. 
 And that isn't even getting into the flimsy characterizations of the people populating the book. Paige, the feisty heroine, is feisty. She is a little unsure of herself and her powers, but she isn't going to be pushed around. Luckily, she doesn't get pushed around and remains feisty. She also learns to harness her amazing powers, but keeps her feistiness. She also falls in love, because what is a fantasy novel involving an angsty teen without a love story? Not one at all. Especially one so ridiculous and unconvincing as this one. Warden is a handsome, stoic Rephaim that is stoic, but he is also respectful. Throughout the book he remains handsome and stoic while he trains Paige, and she also aids him, but he also remains respectful. And he also falls in love. And then they work together to defeat their enemies (but not really defeat them since this is only book 1 of 7 (SEVEN!)). And then at the end Paige remains feisty, but also in love, while Warden is still handsome and stoic, but also very respectful. It's character depth that you would expect from a 21 year-old author with no other books to her name. 
 Basically, they hype surrounding this book is unwarranted, IMO. It is a slog of a book, that has a ridiculous amount of convoluted and trying prose to explain a very, very basic plot. And not a good or unique plot either.

Emotionally poignant, your heart will hurt for the heroine who seems to be cursed with having her dreams ripped from her time and time again. Readers are sure to love this twist on the feisty ingenue and bossy alpha trope.

Boneshaker takes place in a largely abandoned section of Seattle. The area was sealed off by a wall after a man-made disaster released a steady stream of poison gas. The few people that remained live underground, and must rely on gas masks to survive whenever they leave their carefully sealed and maintained pockets of air. Getting a dose of the Blight gas is literally a fate worse than death - it turns humans into zombies. 
 The setting is fantastic. It's imaginative and richly described, with plenty of fun steampunk detail. The story is action heavy and fast paced, though sometimes I found myself wishing for fewer chase scenes and a little thicker plot. I liked the writing style for the most part. But at times the we follow two different characters, and their stories occasionally mirror each other in an awkward way that kept reminding me I was reading a novel. 
 My main problem with the book (and the reason that I didn't like it as much as I'd wanted to) was the characters. The most developed character is Briar, and she has a promising background for a protagonist. She was the wife of the inventor who supposedly caused the disaster, and the daughter of a lawman who, in some circles, is seen as a hero for his actions during the evacuation from the Blight-ridden area. In the sixteen years since the wall was built, this hasn't made Briar's life easy. 
 Briar's past, together with a predictable secret she still holds from those days, turns her into a guarded person concerned only with getting through each day. She distances herself from her son, so all the boy knows of his family history is the rumors that he's heard. It's as if Briar is as walled off as the section of the city that she used to live in. Sounds pretty great, huh? But the way Briar's nature is handled closes her off to me, as a reader, as well as to the other characters around her. The only time I was really able to emotionally connect with her was when she first discovers that she'll need to search for her son. 
 The other characters are all fairly average. Briar's son, Zeke, is typical for a teen in a fantasy story. He's brave, determined, overconfident, and a bit too smart for his own good. The people they meet behind the wall are mostly scrappy survivor types, interchangeable air pirates, and mysterious Chinese men. The villain is a bit cartoonish for my taste, but that fits with the style of the story. 
 I enjoyed the book overall, and would definitely read more from the author. If the characters in her future books start to feel as real to me as her setting and style, those will be five-star reads for sure.

This is the second Kleypas I (partially) read (the first being Then Came You) and exactly like this one it also features a completely modern (in her behaviour and thoughts), feisty and "strong" heroine grafted onto a Regency setting and into Regency clothes. 
 Yes, I have heard the clamour for strong heroines, but damn it, that doesn't mean--at least for me--that you should have anachronistic heroines. I already hate the "strong, kick-ass heroine" in contemporary romance (which is why I avoid contemporary romance and prefer historical fiction), but that this epitome of alleged Regency Romance excellence of all people, Lisa Kleypas, writes such utter nonsense, that is a revelation! 
 So, the heroine stalks the side streets of London gambling quarters with a pistol in her reticule (Mrs Kleypas, the wording alone does not a historical fiction make!) and is forgettable modern drivel, but it doesn't stop there. The hero is the same unlikeable idiot Cockney criminal alpha-hole we already met as a side character in "Then Came You". Yuck! I'd really like me a male lead for once who isn't an alpha arse and who doesn't cheat. I'm over every variation of the rake as well. 
 That all still would not have been reason to rate as low, if at least the prose had been something to write home about. But once again Kleypas' prose sounds artificial, put on for reasons of sounding "Regency-like, righto?" and stilted. The plot and its devices were very constructed, and the Cockney dialect exaggerated (listening a bit to Sir Michael Caine would have helped there). 
 I'm actually taken aback at the amount of hype these books get. Well, that was my last, this could else easily become an expensive hobby.

3 stars because it just didn't keep my attention like I'd hoped so. My bad. 
 Not my favorite Tahereh Mafi book ever, but I liked it enough to keep it in my library. Furthermore just didn't grasp me like the Shatter Me series. Perhaps a second reading would help me. 
 But I like this book, nonetheless. I just do not see it as a book or even a novel. I see it as a poetry. I am totally mesmerized by its lyrical tale of love, strength, and friendship. There were times where it made me cry, too. 
 The plot started off strong. Mafi created an intricate and well-developed setting al. Although I felt like I could not connect well with some of her characters. Still, I adore Alice, the protagonist. (I like how that rhymes.) 
 Alice, nourished by experience and pain, comes of age by realizing that magic exists in her and that she herself can use it to help others. Oliver, Alice's friend, dares to defy his own conviction and belief where human friendship is prized and demonstrated. Familial relationships are also examined in touching tenderness. 
 Furthermore is composed of a sad, magical, happy and imaginative story. I like how Mafi wrote it with light intensity even though it's full of adventure and mystery. It is very well written, yes. Accessible to young and old alike, yes. 
 Furthermore pulls you in and wraps around you for a rollercoaster ride that doesn't disappoint. 
 Even though it's built on fantasy it radiates lessons on truthfulness, empathy, family, and hope. Read it for the wondrous storytelling or read it for its deeper meaning. But, for goodness sakes, just read it and then give it to the adult or child sitting next to you.

9/10 Stars 
 As a black hole forms it creates an immense gamma-ray burst, blinding whole galaxies with light and destroying millions of worlds. You could disappear at any second. This one. Or this one. Or this one. make sure, as often as possible, you are doing something you'd be happy to die doing. 
 Pros:

 - A good balance of comedy and serious introspection 
 - Beautiful prose that was also easy to read 
 - Deep exploration of what it is to be human, with all its faults and illogical joys 
 Cons: 
 - A rather predictable/cheesy storyline 
 - Who are the Vonnodorians? We never really learn much about them beyond that they don't die/hurt, their religion is mathematics, and their world is violet 
 - Somewhat flat secondary characters that could have used more fleshing out

Between 4 & 4.5 stars. 
 Most of the Romances I read have some kind of paranormal element. This one is Contemporary, but it is a Romantic-Suspense with a REALLY evil big bad in it. It's also different in that it's not fully contained in one book. The main relationship is, but the overall mystery will span 3 books, each with a different couple as the main focus, but still with the other characters involved. This is very different from other romances I've read and I think it really works for me. If everything had been solved by the end, it would have been too neat. Too easy. I've read a few too many Romantic-Suspense books where in between the all night marathons of fantastic sex to the exclusion of all else, the hero and heroine are also able to capture the villain who has been giving the authorities the run around for years. I'm not saying that this concept hasn't been done well (for instance, I loved Linda Howard's Dream Man), but in more than a few I haven't been satisfied with the end, mostly because there wasn't enough balance between mystery-solving and romance-building. 
 I liked the characters. There are a lot of different POVs here (it's all 3rd person, just following several different characters), but that didn't bother me. It worked for the story. Being in the killer's head was creepy as hell. He's a sadistic torturer-rapist-killer. You don't get really graphic, explicit details, but sometimes what's NOT told is even scarier as your mind makes up the difference. 
 Lena, our lead female character is blind with a fierce independent streak. She's worked hard for the life she's built, is fiercely loyal to her friends, and has a wicked sense of humor. Ezra is a cop on leave following a shooting - I won't spill what happened, as it's pretty crucial to his whole attitude, but I thought it worked. There were plenty of times I called him an idiot, but his actions were understandable. I bought their relationship. It's not one that starts because of the villain, although circumstances involving the mystery do bring Lena & Ezra closer together. The romance was hot - there was no skimping on that end at all. 
 I am definitely reading the next one.
Emiri - November 2011

 As a woman Kestrel must either get married or join the military, her father has always expected her to be his good little soldier. Kestrel has little talent for fighting and little desire to marry, but she must choose. When Kestrel purchases a slave that she connects with she'll learn that owning him will cost her far more than fifty keystones. 
 Kestrel is a fantastic character, and so deliciously different from most fantasy young adult protagonists. Kestrel doesn't want to fight, but she's expected to. In young adult literature it's often the other way around, princesses and highborn ladies who want to shun their femininity in favour of a sword. Kestrel is strong without being violent, she proves that there are ways to write good female protagonists without devaluing traditionally feminine traits. 
 The protagonists cleverness is also incredibly valuable to the conflict. It's interesting to see a story where the battles are fought not only with strength but with secrets, strategy and intrigue. Rukoski has developed a politically complex world and the fact that we see if from both the well-off lady Kestral's point of view and that of her slave makes it have much more depth. 
 The book dealt with both slavery and love with skill. To often love in fantasy novels feels destined or immediate so the slow boil of this particular romance, along with the realistic difficulties, was beautiful. Slavery isn't something many books touch on, and rarely this well. The slaves are not treated terribly, because they don't have to be mistreated to make their status as lesser beings wrong. 
 Kestrel is complex, flawed and strong without being a strong fighter. The world is unique and interesting. There are parts of the book that are slow, but it'd necessary. There are weak bits and weak characters but The Winner's Curse can more than hold it's own against other similarly toned fantasy novels.

I enjoyed this book, even if it does show its Harry Potter roots a bit too much. Percy is a misunderstood almost teen with a bad habit of attracting mysterious monsters and strange happenings which ordinary people don't seem to see or notice. He's dyslexic, ADD and the butt of most of the bullies in school. When he finds out he is the son of the sea god Poseidon and is sent to Half-Blood camp where other children of gods and mortals train to become heroes, he thinks life might get a bit better. But that would make for a very dull story. So Percy, along with a brainy female sidekick and a brave satyr friend, get to fight monsters and outwit gods on a quest to save the Big Three - Zeus, Poseidon and Hades - from tearing apart Olympus in a civil war. Rick Riordan has learned his lessons well and throws in all the right elements for a fun romp.

Because everyone on the planet excluding me and maybe some of the Kardashians have read this series, I'll skip the plot summary and go for a less formal review. I can see why so many people adore Harry Potter. While Rowling does not introduce anything particularly groundbreaking in terms of fantasy or plot or characterization, she does abide by the hero's quest with great precision. Harry is the underdog from the start and you can't help but cheer him on as he overcomes obstacles with the help of his friends and his mentor. Each of the characters has a distinct personality, and Rowling's simple writing style leaves room for brevity and enough imagery to pull you into the setting. Story-wise, she includes all of the necessary elements: foreshadowing, conflicts that escalate to the climax, a pretty satisfying plot twist, etc. 
 I'll probably read one other book in between each installment of this series. I'm looking forward to seeing the characters mature and the plot become darker as many others have said it will!

Passenger opened up this series with a bang introducing us to Etta Spencer and Nicholas Carter who find themselves traveling through time on a rescue mission and to retrieve an ancient artifact that will change the world as we know it. Chock full of adventure, romance, exotic locations and time periods, and pirates. Suffice to say, I loved it. If you enjoy books like Outlander and reading YA then definitely check out Passenger. 
 I eagerly anticipated getting my hands on Wayfarer since, oh boy, the way Passenger ended I definitely needed closure. Taking place right where we left off, Nicholas and Sophia (who really deserves her own book; she is such a great character) race through time to try to find Etta, who has woken up in an unknown place and time and is soon in the hands of unexpected individuals. Wayfarer dives deeper into the mythology of the world that Bracken has created, leading the reader across the globe and time as we find out more about the astrolabe as well as the motivation of key players. Fast paced, well written, and just plain fun, this was a fitting conclusion to the story. I also like that the ending was somewhat open...perhaps we will visit this world again one day? :)

"The Sherlockian" begins with Arthur Conan Doyle contemplating murder--the murder of Sherlock Holmes. Doyle's literary creation has made his life a misery. Perhaps the crowning blow is his own mother requesting him to sign a book for her next door neighbor as "Sherlock Holmes." This misery must end. Doyle writes "The Final Problem." Moriarity and Holmes fall to their death from the top of Reichenbach Falls. Upon the story's publication, Doyle is mystified by finding citizens on the street wearing black arm bands in mourning for the demise of the great detective. He is shocked to be swatted by a lady of advancing years swinging a large hand bag. It is 1900. Although Britain is changing and gaslights are being removed to be replaced with new electric street lighting, the citizenry want their hero back. They will always see Holme's lean profile appearing out of the fog, barely visible in the swirls of fog, a dimly lit figure in the spare glow of gaslight. 
 In 2010, the most elite group of Sherlockians is meeting in their annual convention. Alex Cates, one of the most esteemed authorities on the Holmes' canon of stories, has announced his discovery of the "Grail" of all Sherlockians--Doyle's missing diary covering October through December, 1900. 
 However, Cates doesn't reveal the missing diary. He's been murdered. Written in blood on the wall of his hotel room is the word "Elementary." The newest member of "The Baker Street Irregulars" is Harold White, a young copyright attorney. He is a voracious reader and has gloried in the Holmes stories since childhood. Harold leaves his dull profession behind to take up the quest to discover Doyle's missing diary. The game is afoot. 
 Graham Moore, the author of "The Sherlockian," succeeds in adding a new chapter to Holmes fiction. The writing is sharp. It is smart. Most of all, Moore presents a package of dry wit, delving into the life of Arthur Conan Doyle who actually began to consult Scotland Yard on a number of cases for several years. Moore puts Doyle in the middle of the investigation of the murders of two young women. As Doyle takes on the persona of his most famous creation, Bram Stoker will be his Dr. Watson. It is a delightful pairing of personalities that entertains the reader throughout the novel. 
 Two thumbs up!

First of all, I want to thank my Goodreads friend, Shannon, for recommending this wonderful book. My life was so enriched by the reading of it. I also want to thank Ms. Simone Elkeles for putting fingers to keyboard and bringing this incredible story of the love between Alex and Brittany to life. 
 Life is cruel and harsh, and we all wear armor to protect ourselves against the pain of loss and the hardships we face. In Perfect Chemistry, we see two very different people who have a kindred soul. They are both walking through life wearing protection and disguises for their survival. One of the most illuminating and fascinating parts of this story is when these two reluctant chemistry partners are asked to tell the class a little bit about each other. What they say represents what the two of them want the world to see about themselves, even if that's not who they want to be. 
 Alex is a tough gangbanger, macho (and very appealing) Latino young man. He has pretty much had to join the Latino Bloods gang because his family and his own life would be in jeopardy otherwise. So far, he has managed to stay out trouble with the law, and to avoid crossing the line and killing and selling drugs. But the time is coming where he may not be able to prevent that transition. He sees Brittany and she is all he ever wanted but couldn't have. He tells himself that she's just a blond princess type, no substance, but he soon finds out that is far from the case. 
 I fell head over heels for Alex. He was not perfect, but even his imperfections endeared him to me. Under the scary, macho gang facade, he is a very perceptive, intelligent, and loving person. His caring nature is evident in how he treats his brothers and his mother, and even his friend Paco, and also how he treats Brittany, despite the teasing and sexual innuendoes. He comes off as being hardcore, but his heart is very good. I have to say that he was a very sexy guy. I was surprised at how much charisma this eighteen year-old kid was. I could imagine this drop dead gorgeous guy with black hair and dark eyes, a seductive smile, and a hard-body, riding his motorcycle. I am not big on gangs or the urban lifestyle, but this was so much a part of him, that it didn't lessen his appeal at all. 
 I loved seeing the world through his eyes, and enjoyed the authentic Latino/Mexicano flavor of his thoughts and language. I have a deep appreciation for Mexican culture, and I feel that Ms. Elkeles showed this in a manner that did it justice, adding to the depth and the characterization of Alex and flavoring the life he lives. Gosh, I cannot tell you how much I adored Alex. He made some bad choices, but also suffered for things beyond his control, and my heart ached to see what he had to go through. But deep down, I never doubted that he had a good head on his shoulders and he would end up doing the right thing in the end. I wanted for him to get out of that destructive lifestyle, and I was holding my breath hoping that he did. 
 I loved Brittany as well. She was a very three-dimensional character, even from the beginning. She might seem like the girl that I would avoid like the plague in high school, one of the shallow 'beautiful people,' but she had a really good heart, and was a very loving person. She was under tremendous stress trying to keep things together and maintain a perfect facade that was getting harder and harder to keep up. Her homelife was very difficult, with her hypercritical mother who was on the edge of emotional collapse, and her father who spent more time at work and thinking about work than interacting with his family. She is weighted down by her family's enormous expectations to always be perfect and to represent them well. Her steadfast love for her disabled, mentally-challenged sister really opened my heart to her, from the first page of the book. Shelley was very important to Brittany, although even her boyfriend was uncomfortable being around her. So she didn't let people come to her life or talk about Shelley. Not out of embarrassment, but because of the fact that Shelley was a private, personal part of her life that others didn't understand or know how to deal with. It meant a lot when she introduced Alex to Shelley and he hit it off with her right away. 
 Like Alex, Brittany impressed me as a very level-headed, mature for her age person. I really appreciated how she was able to look past Alex's scary gang facade and see the warm, loving boy inside. She inspired Alex to want to strive and to be the person he was meant to be. This book really teaches a lesson about judging a book by its cover. Brittany would be the kind of girl that would be envied by many. But the truth is, her life was very difficult, despite living in a big, beautiful house, driving an expensive car, and wearing designer clothes. Being the captain of the pom-pom team and dating the head quarterback isn't all it's cracked up to be, and Brittany knows this first hand. And it's clear that she would willingly give that up without any regrets to have a true love, even with someone so different from her as Alex. However, the fear of what will happen to Shelley if she lets go, keeps her on the narrow path that has been given to her to walk. It is wonderful when Brittany decides to go where her heart leads her, although she does have to deal with some anguish and heartbreak along the way. 
 This couple is one of my favorite couples of all times. That's saying something for this serious romance fan. I never thought I could feel that way about a couple in a young adult book, but I believe Twilight did open the door for me to young adult romance, and I am very glad about this. Alex and Brittany meet each other's needs in every way. They had blistering sexual chemistry between them, yet Ms. Elkeles wrote this book in such a way that I didn't feel conflicted about reading these teens expressing themselves sexually. You could see that every encounter came from a deep connection on a mental, emotional, and spiritual level. I loved how they saw each other clearly in a way that no one else did. That is what soulmates should do for each other. 
 The cast of secondary characters added to the flavor and the depth of this beautiful story. Some of the people in both Alex and Brittany's life are not good for them, and do much to hinder their growth, but people like Paco, Alex's best friend, Isabel, a childhood friend of Alex who becomes Brittany's friend, Ms. Peterson, and Sierra, Brittany's friend, do their part to help Alex and Brittany on the journey to self-discovery and finding a future together. Ms. Peterson, their chemistry teacher, was the kind of educator that we need more of. She works hard to inspire her students, and didn't give up on Alex and write him off as just another Mexican gangbanger who was going to end up dead or in prison. 
 This book has some parts that were hard to read, but they needed to be there, because it is a story about a young man who is surrounded by violence and crime on a daily basis. There had to be some of this in the book, or it would have lacked authenticity. Fortunately, this does not detract from the story, but helps you to see what Alex is dealing with, and to respect him for the choices he makes to have a better future. 
 The climax of this book will have your heart in your throat, and tears welling up in your eyes. But the way this book ends gives the reader so much hope and joy. It's truly a perfect ending to this book. 
 I could go on and on about how wonderful Perfect Chemistry is, but I will end by saying, if you read one young adult book, please put this on the list to consider. You won't come out of this book without having your heart touched.

The Android was always one of my favorite Animorphs books when I was a kid because, even before I knew what it was, I loved worldbuilding in fiction. This is one of the reasons I love serialized storytelling so much, because serialized stories (no matter the medium) are the ones that have the most room to deepen and define their fictionalized worlds without sacrificing character or theme. And The Android does quite a bit of worldbuilding in a short period of time. 
 We're introduced to several important new concepts, like zero-space (or z-space), which is where ships travel at faster than light speeds, and also happens to be one of the secrets behind the morphing technology. Ax lets it slip to Marco that due to the laws of physics, when morphing an animal smaller in mass than yourself, the mass has to go SOMEWHERE, and that somewhere is z-space, and there is an infinitesimal but still possible chance that a ship in z-space might hit your extruded mass and vaporize it, thus causing you to become stuck in your morph forever. This is not a pleasant thought for the Animorphs, but it is a cool bit of sci-fi. (They don't inquire further, and I can't remember if we get answers in the future, but what happens when you morph an animal with a larger mass? Does it pull in excess matter from z-space? If so, whose mass are they borrowing?) 
 But I'm burying the lede, here. It's Marco's old friend Erek and his "family" who are the real focus. Because Erek turns out not to be human, and he might even be involved with The Sharing somehow. The Animorphs end up doing recon at a Sharing retreat, but end up exposing themselves when Marco gets eaten by a crow, and he has to demorph in front of Erek. But Erek doesn't immediately betray them to the Yeerks. Instead, he tells them to meet at his house in a few days, that they are allies in the fight against the Yeerks, and promises to explain everything. 
 And man, is it ever a weird explanation. 
 Erek is an android, a robotic artificially intelligent being. He and his "family" are called The Chee, which was a name given to them by their creators, the Pemalites, an extinct race of pacifist aliens who died out 50,000 years before. They pass as humans using advanced holographic technology, and they have been doing so since humans developed civilization. They, too, are pacifist by design. The Pemalites programmed so they could never hurt another living creature. Only some of them, like Erek, are frustrated by their limitations, and want to be able to join the fight against the Yeerks. They enlist the help of the Animorphs to steal a Pemalite crystal in Yeerk control, not only to keep it out of Yeerk hands, but to use it to re-write their programming.  
 It sounds pretty straightforward, but the way Applegate handles it is an example of why I love this series so much. Erek and his friends see the war with the Yeerks happening, but feel like their programming prevents them from getting involved in the fighting. But there are some Chee who do not wish to overturn their programming, who believe that nonviolence is the best option. The Animorphs unsurprisingly take Erek's side. Nonviolence is nice and all, but from their perspective, they can't afford philosophical stances when real lives are at stake. Marco's dad is in danger of being made a Controller for his work. Jake's brother already is one. Marco's mom is Visser One, and his whole life was torn apart because of it. Things will only get worse if the Yeerks aren't stopped, and stopping them is not something that can be accomplished with nonviolence. 
 Basically, the book acknowledges that the ethics of nonviolence, especially in a time of war, are not black and white. They're grey as hell. This is made especially clear when Erek does rewrite his programming in the midst of battle in order to save the Animorphs from certain death, but in doing so, he kills twenty Hork-Bajir and human Controllers (both the Yeerks and their innocent hosts), and he does so in an unbelievably brutal fashion. And because he's an android, the memory of doing so will never leave him. Saving the Animorphs, who are pivotal figures in the conflict to come, whose survival may mean the difference between a Yeerk victory and defeat, was the right call, but it also meant killing innocent beings, which is something that can't be celebrated and shouldn't be forgotten.  
 There's also some little stuff in here, both funny and serious that deserves a mention. The Pemalites, and the alien race that destroyed them, the Howlers, are not just one-off aliens. They will both come back, and we will learn much more about them. We don't get much regarding the Howlers here, but any race that destroys what are essentially intelligent dogs is big trouble. Speaking of dogs, the only thing left of the Pemalites, , it's sad and so weird that the Chee want to save Earth not for humans, but for dogs. I haven't mentioned much about Marco in this review, but he was a nice way in to this story. His investment in the fight has steadily deepened, and his protectiveness and anger over his family is starting to affect the way he goes into missions. Aside from Ax, he's also lost the most to the Yeerks, even if Jake is the only one (and now Erek) who knows about it. He also got a new haircut in this one, which he agonizes over at length throughout the book, but it turns out that the reason he got the haircut is that Scholastic had a new, cute model they wanted to use for Marco, but he had short hair. So Applegate gave him a haircut. Behind the scenes! 
 Next up, time stuff!

I loved everything about this book. The actual idea of it, of Forgetting, was something that I'm pretty sure has been done before, or at least the whole amnesia things has been overdone, and I was very surprised by The Forgetting and the world and set of characters that Sharon Cameron wrote. 
 Nadia was a strong character, she had to be strong with everything that was happening to her and with her being the only one in the city of Canaan that remembered everything from 12 years ago when she was just a kid. A lot of things were going in the background, and after befriending the glassblower's son, Gray, they really start to dive into the whole conspiracy and problem that was Canaan because something wrong was definitely going on. It was a great book that kept me guessing and wondering about the truth behind the Forgetting and who really was that bad guy in all this. There were a lot of surprises here and there, but overall it was a great story with just about everything: a little romance, bit of humor, action  heads up, one brutal and savage death near the end of the book , mystery, sci-fi (somewhat), and a whole new world to discover it all. 
 I enjoyed the love interest, Gray, and how much they loved each other, especially during the heartbreaking moments. Seeing together throughout the story was totally one of my favorite parts. As for the love rival, boy was I in for a surprise when I thought that Eshan had a crush on Nadia! Finally a love rival who likes the guy instead of the girl, yay!  I mean, I also liked the Liliya and Jonathan moments the last few chapters, it was nice. 
 I admit that I was confused with the cover of the book and how it tied with the actual story. It wasn't until well into the story when things are revealed by the antagonist and the forgetting that things started to make sense. Of course, I won't spoil anything but man, the cover sure is pretty to look at. 
 I feel like if I say anything more I'll just end spoiling the whole book and I really want for anyone that reads this book to be surprised by all the twists and turns just like I was. The Forgetting is definitely worth reading!

The ways in which Lev AC Rosen plays with gender and sexuality in All Men of Genius is astoundingly brilliant. Seriously. The fact that Twelfth Night and The Importance of Being Earnest interpretations are wrapped up in it makes things even better. Basically, what I'm saying is that I want some of the kool aid to which Lev AC Rosen obviously has access. 
 One of the first things I plan on doing now that I've read All Men of Genius is to reread The Importance of Being Earnest. I don't think I've read it since high school, and remember very little. Twelfth Night is my favorite Shakespearean play, so I had no trouble eating up all those references. But the Oscar Wilde pieces? Much less so. But, I loved All Men of Genius so much that I want to be able to love it even more! The Importance of Being Earnest here I come. 
 Steampunk. Classical retellings. Victorian London. Cool scientific stuff. Gender role reversals. Plays on sexuality, feminism and homosexuality. That is quite a list, y'all. Lev AC Rosen nails all of it. Violet, a scientific whiz, wants to go to the prestigious Illyria College of science. Too bad it's all all boys institution, right? Good thing she has a rather devious twin brother willing to let her take on his identity! (Are y'all feeling the Twelfth Nighty goodness?) 
 What follows is a delightful ImportanceofBeingEarnestian comedy of errors worthy of a Shakespearean play. (I'm ridiculously proud of that sentence.) People fall in love with people who fall in love with people (even if it is a man instead of a woman...or so they think) who are in love with the same people who...well. Really, just pick up All Men of Genius and see for yourself. 
 Seriously. I had so much fun while reading All Men of Genius! I couldn't put it down...Violet is such a fantastic character. I'd follow her anywhere. I'll also follow Lev AC Rosen anywhere. I'm so excited to see what he comes up with next. 
 I highly recommend this for fans of fantasy and classic retellings. You don't want to miss it - promise.

In the end, however, THIS> Vee turned out to be a Nephilim  < HAPPENED and lets just say, she was included in the plot a bit more ;) I think the THING THAT HAPPENED was a bit of a rush decision by Becca and was only really done so everything tied off nicely. In the end, this plot twist could have been made way more epic, had the exposition been better. 
 The other thing I had a problem with, and part of it ties in with what I just said, but the Epilogue. I can understand that the reason Becca chose to include it was because she wanted readers to know how the characters were doing, and that they were ok.And, WHO'S GAVIN?!  
 There was a death that I think could have been played out better. (instead of just mentioned) I think this certain person's death should have been witnessed, not just recapped. 
 There was a death that I didn't like, simply because I LIKED THAT CHARACTER. Ugh, why couldn't they have just been happy?! 
 A few of Nora's decisions and mood swings were a bit weird. An example that I can remember is when her opinion of the Nephilim war drasically changes from "I have to lead this army only because my jackass birth-father made me swear and oath" to "It is my obligation to lead this army with pride, as they are my people." And, like, I mean this happened in just a couple chapters. 
 Now the good things! 
 Nora and Patch's relationship played out well. The ending may have been predictable, but there were a few things that I was just like "WoW, didn't see that coming ." All in all, I was very happy with their relationship. (They're adorable!) 
 The plot was interesting and there were plot twists. Let me tell you something, review reader: I LOVE PLOT TWISTS. And there was basically the best plot twist in the series in this book, that I did not see coming involving a certain Detective Basso . 
 The setting was classic Becca Fitzpatrick setting, Coldwater, Maine, nothing changed there. 
 The writing was classic Becca Fitzpatrick writing, a bit descriptive at times, but I easy to read and interpret. Chapters don't end on a cliffhanger. I love when they end on a cliffhanger, but this didn't bother me much.

 Full Review: 
 *I received an ecopy of this book from the author. This has not influenced my review.* 
 This was a very character-focused book with a slow pace and not a whole lot to the plot, but it was a good start to a series that I have most definitely been enjoying so far. 
 Both Scarlet and Liall were unique and interesting enough to keep my attention. Scarlet was feisty and stubborn (I loved how he stood up to Liall) but also kind of lost and still struggling to accept his sexuality. Liall was a bit more of a mystery, but he was clearly lonely and regretful. He was also imperfect but showed a great capacity to learn from his mistakes and grow as a person. 
 I also liked the slow burn of the romance (if you can call it that, since this book was just barely the start of the relationship) as Scarlet kept trying to sneak his way past the toll and Liall kept catching him, amused by all his antics. Of course, Scarlet wasn't quite as amused, and I couldn't blame him. My favorite scene in the book was the one when their back-and-forth reached its boiling point. The scene started out so fun with a little play on the Red Riding Hood story, but then it suddenly took a drastic turn and became so intense and charged with anger and tension. And Liall's thoughts, the way he immediately became kind of defensive because he knew he was wrong but didn't want to admit it to himself, were nicely realistic. 
 Another thing I liked was how the author took something that could've been problematic and turned it on its head so that not only was the character's behavior pointed out as being wrong, it really added something to the story and the character growth. *SPOILER ALERT* Liall was charging a toll for people to use the road, but from Scarlet he demanded his body rather than money (first he charged a kiss, then he upped it to an hour with him on Scarlet's next attempt, then he upped it to a whole night with him on Scarlet's next attempt, and Scarlet kept refusing). Scarlet eventually got so angry that he called Liall a rapist for how he kept trying to force himself on him (not physically, but by charging that toll for the road he needed to take). Scarlet's father also said to Liall when he met him, "So, you're the Kasiri who tried to make a whore of my child." And upon realizing how wrong his actions were, Liall was ashamed and tried to make up for his mistakes.  *END SPOILER ALERT* 
 The only thing I didn't like about the romance was that I'd have preferred the word love not been used since the two men had hardly spent any time around each other. To be fair, I think it was only used once by one character, and it was just a thought in his head, but still. The characters' actions were still believable though; just being interested and drawn to each other was a plenty good explanation for why they made the decisions that they did. 
 As for the writing, it wasn't flowery or anything, but it pulled me into the story and seemed to match the high fantasy world. 
 Speaking of which, this was a super detailed and thought-out high fantasy world, There were all these different regions and cultures and types of people and words. I had a bit of trouble keeping track of things since I've only recently started getting into high fantasy and am not used to that kind of stuff, but not so much trouble that it affected my enjoyment. 
 So overall this book was mostly just setting up the romance and the situation and the world, but I enjoyed it, read it quickly, and was interested enough in the characters to keep reading the series! 
 Recommended For: 
 M/M high fantasy readers who like slow-paced, character-focused books with sweet relationships.

Bayou Moon, the second installment in the husband and wife writing team's Edge series, is even better than the first. Although I have to admit that some parts of it made me feel like I was experiencing deja vu (Rose and Cerise are a little too similar if you ask me). 
 On the Edge introduced us to the magical world of the Weird, the unmagical, but technologically advanced Broken (ie. the world as we know it) and the world in between, called the Edge. We also first met William, the hero of this second book, there. In On the Edge, poor William didn't get the girl, but after reading Bayou Moon, I can say that's okay, because Cerise was definitely the girl meant for him. 
 The story picks up two years after Rose and Declan return to the Weird for their HEA. William has been living in the Edge, licking his wounded pride. When he is approached with a job to go after his enenmy, the Spider, William jumps at the opportunity to get justice and end the Spider's threat to Changelings. The job however, takes him into the Mire, the worst corner of the Edge but allows allows him to cross paths with Cerise, a worthy female lead for this story. Bayou Moon borders on epic in its scope; in depth world building, plenty of action and yet it doesn't slack on character development or the story between Cerise and William. William may be a born fighting machine, but his upbringing has stunted him emotionally and socially, and it's entertaining to read as he works out what social nuance means and whether he reacts correctly or incorrectly in certain situations. His growth into a well-rounded person takes time and is believable. Cerise's struggle to take up the family reins and her effort to retain the control and respect of her unruly clan is also well portrayed. Cerise is sure of herself but knows that she must prove that she can hold the family together. It was refreshing to have a heroine that could hold her own throughout the book and didn't have quite as much growing to do as the hero. The action which the Andrews team is known for fills the pages of Bayou Moon as well as danger, suspense and mystery. The book is flooded with magic: good and bad. Twisted magic, tormented souls, romance. What's not to love? Bayou Moon is a keeper in my opinion.

 Interesting concept. Dark, grungy, and a touch whimsical (particularly when it comes to the alternate-reality pecking order of certain rodents.) 
 In a Nutshell: Richard Mayhew, a weak-willed and unremarkable man, loses it all when he decides to help an injured girl. His version of reality rejects him, and he finds himself in a parallel London fraught with urban fantasy danger. 
 "There are two Londons. There's London Above--that's where you lived--and then there's London Below--the Underside--inhabited by the people who fell through the cracks in the world. Now you're one of them." 
 But Richard has an agonizing amount of difficultly accepting what's happened to him. Even when he does, his dull inability to adapt to new cultural and conceptual nuances makes his survival seem more than improbable. 
 While this reader never formed any particular empathy connection or attachment to any of the characters, the biggest problem for me was Richard Mayhew. He was so dense and lacking in sensical self-respect, I just couldn't cheer for him. I would call him TSTL (Too Stupid To Live), but the author is British and so is the book's setting. So I guess that makes him TDTL (Too Daft To Live.) Fortunately, the point of view isn't limited to Richard, and actually does a lot of moving around. (I'm not sure I could have made it through if I'd been stuck with him alone.) 
 At one point, well past the middle of the book, Richard takes on this attitude:  Oh, so the people who've been keeping me alive in this horribly dangerous place think I shouldn't be consorting with this mysteriously interested woman. But surely I know better than they do about the potential hazards of their world... >.>  
 Oddly enough, the threads of this book left unanswered held better in my memory than the plot itself did.  
 -What was Hunter's curse? What would have happened if she'd gone to London Above? 
 -Is Door really the last of her family left alive? 
 -Why was Richard able to see Door in the first place? 
 -Why would Richard even consider choosing the unmitigated horrors of London Below over the reality he is accustomed to? 
  
 The intention may have been to leave room for a sequel, but to me, it just ended up feeling like the worldbuilding was less distinct than I would like--fuzzy around the edges. 
 I generally like Gaiman's works better when he writes shorter. Although in this case, I liked it only slightly more than American Gods but not nearly as much as Stardust or The Graveyard Book. (Where that sits on my sliding mental scale, I'm not even sure.) I also think there's a bit of a pacing and info buildup toward the end, which made the last 15% of this book significantly more interesting and satisfying than much of the rest of it had been--at least to my mind. 
 Favorite Quote: 
 "I have always felt that violence was the last refuge of the incompetent, and empty threats the last sanctuary of the terminally inept."

 This book is described as a cross between Across the Universe by Beth Revis and A Handmaid's Tale by Margaret Atwood so my expectations were super high since Across the Universe was fantastic and The Handmaid's Tale is one of my favourites. 
 This book follows a girl named Ava who lives on a ship that is constantly in space. The crew of the ship has set roles for the men and women on board that reflect traditional gender roles (women take care of the cooking, cleaning, sewing and their main purpose is childbearing/ men take care of over thing else and take many wives). 
 Ava flees after something (spoiler) happens to earth where she is faced with taking care of herself in a world that is vastly different from that of the ship. 
 This book was described as a feminist science fiction book and there were many feminist themes (women in the work force, gender roles, etc.) I feel as if the themes were non existent. I was expecting the protagonist to go through a feminist transformation, but the transformation she went through was little and she fought her own transformation every. step. of. the. way. 
 The plot was nonexistent and about 200-250 pages could have been cut from the book and make the book flow better as well as connecting the major plot points in a more tangible way. Although, the plot points that were in the book were fantastic and had a lot of potential for development into an interesting feminist science fiction. 
 We spend only about 100 pages in the most interesting part of the book, the life on the ship. And the time we spend there is very confusing and leaves you asking questions. The people on the ship have a different vocabulary which further tells the reader how different they are from earth, however their vocabulary is never explained. For example, the protagonist is described as a "so girl", which I still have no idea what that means. 
 The love interest is insta-love and when I say insta-love I mean INSTA-LOVE. I've never read two characters who fall in love so unbelievably fast. I couldn't stand when she went on and on about how much in love she was. 
 Overall, this book has sooooo much potential but it fell so flat. The author skimmed over the interesting plot points and drags out the useless ones. The ending contributed something interesting to the story, but once again that was no developed. I really wanted to like this book, but I found myself skimming over useless description and inner monologue. 
 As a last note about this book... Across the Universe and The Handmaid's Tale should feel insulted for being compared to this book.

Warning. Major furious ranting ahead. And spoilers that you should not get into if you can. 
  
 I don't consider cheating a black and white business. In only a few cases though, because most of the times, cheating happens in a book because characters couldn't control their inner ass-holes. I despise it even more when they try to cloak this under long drawn emotional speeches. - Wake up jerks! That speech is not getting an Oscar from me! 
 The main hero of the first half of the book, is in a dying marriage. No questions about that. His wife, Sabrina, loves her job more than staying at home. She hires people to send gifts to her family and husband. She has basically become so distant that it is understandable that the marriage is in name only. 
 I also don't find it wrong to find people attractive other than your spouse. A crush is not that big of a deal. 
 But I draw a very thick line at a point. When you know you're feeling way more than attraction to a person, and you might be entering a morally grey zone, you need to check yourself. Talk to your partner about it. It is difficult but it saves so much hurt. 
 The hero of the first half, Gus and the heroine, Parker, cross the line. They don't have sex. But really, at that point, sex was just a formality. I feel a little bad for Parker, because she constantly tries to push back Gus, but he just has to push against her resistance. 
 "Someone cheated on you. And you're so fucking mad about it because you can't understand it. But love is an emotion that resides in your head and your proverbial heart." 
 Bullshit. Complete bullshit. Parker knew how it felt it to be cheated on. Her own boyfriend and twin sister hooked, got married and now had a kid on the way! Astronomically high levels of crap were happening. I can't condone her behaviour but she did try so hard to resist. It broke my heart for her. 
 Just what stopped Gus from talking to his wife , Sabrina, and clearing everything out. If they're both on different planes in life that can never again meet, then he should've gotten out of the relationship. Trying to stick to two relationships is ....wow, I have no words. 
 And then Gus and Sabrina have to die. And then the second love story starts. With Levi. And guess what? Levi is related to Sabrina and Gus. Perfect soup of crap and drama.

When I first tried to read this book almost a year ago, I couldn't get past the first fifty pages. After the incident here on GR surrounding it, I was mad. So mad, I think, that there was no possible way I could have read The Selection unbiased. Every little thing about it got under my skin. But now that some time has passed and things have settled down some, I decided to give it a try again since I purchased the first book for cheap. Originally, what drew me to it was the cover. I'm not usually a huge fan of ones featuring pretty dresses, but these are simply gorgeous. The pose of the model is a little weird, though. 
 The Good: 
 - I ended up enjoying this more than I thought I would. If you go into it knowing what to expect (it's a book almost entirely focused on the love triangle), it's entertaining. 
 - The story itself is quite addicting. Despite whatever issues i was having at any given point, I still wanted to finish it. 
 - Though I still find the Selection itself to be little disturbing (Shows like The Bachelor have never been my thing), I liked reading about ask the different stages/interviews and such. 
 The Bad: 
 - Weird thing to complain about, but I hate how much this is compared to The Hunger Games. The only similarity is a big competition and though I don't like the selection, I'd still be in that contest over the games ANY day. Other than that, they're completely different. 
 - America is not the greatest protagonist. In fact, she can be incredibly annoying sometimes. She is repeatedly told that she's pretty, but she can't take a compliment. She is also very indecisive, floundering between one decision and the next. Personally I think that's why she wouldn't be the best princess for the country. 
 - In particular, I really didn't like the part where America knees Price Maxon in the leg when they're simply walking together in the garden and she fears for her virtue. She's incredibly lucky that she didn't get kicked out right then and there because she basically accused him of trying to rape her. 
 - What's with the weird names? I'm kind of eating my own words here, but The Hunger Games did have the same sort of oddness to it. However they didn't bother me there, maybe because I felt like a lot of the names were after the districts or something. In the Selection, it seems like they're just there to be there. America, Aspen, Clarkson, Sosie, etc. 
 - The world building is questionable to say the least. I'm not going to pretend to understand about how the counties operate, but China suddenly invading the USA seems kind of weird. The rebel attacks were scattered throughout the novel, but there just felt kind of random. Like a subplot I wasn't getting into. 
 - I wish there was more substance to the characters. I feel like I got to know America and her story and all that. I also got to know Maxon a little. But Aspen wasn't around much, so at this point I'm undecided about who I like better in this love triangle. I didn't really care when a contestant left because I as a reader did not know anything of them besides their names. 
 I can't say I have much hope that any of my issues will be fixed in The Elite (based off a lot of reviews), but I own it. And I'm interested enough to want to know what happens next. If I recommended The Selection to someone, it would be lighthearted entertainment only. Not a lot of substance/world-building/character development to be found.
