There were lots more coming to the surface in Savage Delight. I didn't see some of them coming at all. 
 I so badly just wanted Isis and Jack to start off where they finally left off near the end of the first book, but they had a long way to go to get back to that. Plus there was the added complication of Sophia. I got the impression through the first book that she only liked Jack as a friend, but I started to see a whole new Sophia in this story. One that I wasn't sure how much I liked. I understand why she was how she was, but my perception of her changed. 
 The Lovely Vicious series is dark and wounded. These characters are so deeply flawed but they are able to find comfort in each other after all of these awful things happened. I loved that they each faced some of their fears in this book. And I loved how they stuck together. The ending was tragic and intense once again and it left us hanging, just like last time. I am so sad that there is only one book left in the trilogy, but I am so anxious to see how everything will wrap up. This is a really unique series. There is not anything quite like it out there that I have encountered. I love it.

I love Roshani Chokshi's writing and I really enjoyed this story and it's characters so much!! Gauri, Aasha, and Vikram were A+. 
 About 4.5 stars tbh.

I did not see that ending coming it just blew me away..... omgeeee!! I loved this book it was a little slow at first then BAM your hooked!! It had a mix of thriller,family drama,mystery and a love story. 
 No spoilers here just read it! If you love elephants, psychics, scientists, more elephants this book is for you.

They were both descending further into silence. 
 A very dark and disturbing book. We see Yeong-hye's descend into madness as described by her husband, brother-in-law, and lastly her sister. Her husband and brother-in-law focuses mostly on how it affects them, whereas her sister is much more emphatic, and really tries to understand why this is happening. The three voices are very distinct, and it almost feels like you are reading three different books. In a sense this novel reminded me of a movie, The Piano, the scenes and imagery, especially in the section two and three, were beautiful, brutal but always distant. Definitely not for everyone - part three pulled it up to three stars.

This definitely felt like a second book in a trilogy. I'm getting a bit annoyed by Bard's lack of self preservation. I know she's supposed to be a tough cookie, but she seems to make some really irresponsible decisions but always manages to narrowly escape death. For once, I'm happy that it's going to take a while for the third book in this series to be released because maybe by that time, I will forget all my issues with the main character and want to read the finale.

A decade ago a blood fever swept though, killing adults and leaving the surviving children with strange markings and a few with powers. These children are referred to as malfettos, and blamed for everything wrong in the society. Though there are a shadowy few who's powers have brought them a level of reverence and infamy, they are the Young Elites. 
 Rating 4.5 
 Holy Crap I really enjoyed this book. This book dark fantasy, and our main character Adelina is complex. She isn't your typical 'good girl', she is dark and mean but it's easy understand why and how she is the way she is. Personally I couldn't really relate to most of her feelings about Violetta, but Marie Lu wrote the family dynamics in a way that I could see how and why Adelina is the way she is. I enjoyed how the group of young elites interacted and the way that Lu chose a few characters to really develop complex characters, hinted at the complexity of others (who I'm sure we'll seem more from in later books) and then left others as simple characters. I feel like a common problem in some fantasy is that characters seem to all be overly complex or all fit a simple archetype. Because of the way Lu wrote characters like Adelina, Enzo, Raffaele, and Teren, it is easy to imagine the other characters have complex story and personality. 
 While all of the powers of the Young Elite are interesting, I liked seeing how Adelina's powers grew and how she learned to use them. I also like that her powers seemed to really pair with her stone alignment. 
 I would recommend this book and can't wait for The Rose Society to come out I need to know more especially given the epilogue curve balls.

Better than the second one. Standard romance arc; the differences come from the mystery of the disappearing vampire (with unsatisfyingly psychopathic villain) and the supernatural society in Victorian England.

This book was surprising. Although it was written in verse, and I probably would have guessed it was by Ellen Hopkins had I not already known, it was not her usual story line. These characters didn't have EVERYTHING that was bad that could happen be thrown at them, and most of the time they made the choices completely clear minded knowing exactly what they were getting themselves into. This book made me laugh, cry, it was sexy, and spicy. I really thorough enjoyed this book and would recommend it to anyone.

Monica is trying to leave her relationship with Jonathan behind. She made the decision to leave him but the more time she is away from him, the more she realizes how much she really cares for him. It's a struggle for both. 
 Jonathan will not come for her. He wants her to make the decision and commitment on her own. Although, he kind of makes things flow his way. 
 In the mix of all this we still have Kevin and Jessica causing trouble. 
 This series keeps on being entertaining. Maybe this one was my least favorite. There is a cliffy but we only have to wait a couple of months, so it's tolerable. 
 4/5 Fangs

Found this a bit bland. It was diverting, and I wasn't compelled to throw it across the room, or anything, but after such a lovely cover and such a fascinating blurb, it was disappointing. 
 I went in expecting dazzling female heroism, but it was actually more like watching clumsy caricatures of Buffy and Hermione skulking around the dark, multi-leveled streets of steampunk London. They both spend far too much time having their breath stolen by assorted men, being shown up by assorted men, being knocked out or drugged or outsmarted by assorted men. 
 And of course, there's also the fact that their prominent, name-drop identities are irrelevant. Miss Holmes has a bit of vaguely Holmesian internal monologue to her credit, and she does figure out where they need to go a few times, but the local constabulary apparently as at least one member who can do everything she can, but with a floating motorcycle. Miss Stoker is a Chosen One of the vampire-slayer variety, but that fact has literally no impact on the plot. She beats up a flock of ruffians once and bests a man at arm-wrestling, but otherwise there is very little reason for her character to be superhuman. 
 The inexplicable kid from the future also had no real reason to be there, especially as a (love interest?). If relationships absolutely must be set up, I far prefer Grayling and Pix. 
 The Egyptian aspect, however, had a little bit of that kitschy, intentionally-ludicrous flavor I particularly love in Hammer films. Kudos to Gleason for capturing that vibe. 
 On the whole, not very Holmes, not very Stoker, and not very steampunk.

EH - This book was O.K. but a bit discombobulating. 
 It was written well when the author focused in on the story, and you can tell extensive research was done about the subject. But I am really not sure if I would consider this a horror novel, and for the most part this is geared towards young adults, with an occasional taboo curse word used. It feels very PG-13. 
 As a reader, I was very disorientated, and distracted at times. I found myself skimming through parts that were confusing and not relevant to the story. 
 Although this was definetely an original idea, and the use of a third party narrative through video camera was pretty cool. 
 I did like the MAIN characters, especially the Gothic butler, and the settings were definetely intriguing. 
 I dont find that my answers were solved, and the ending felt a bit rushed, and I am still scratching my head a bit, wondering what in the world was going on at the end.
A silly book, left me with no desire to pick up another by her.

Imagine you had the power to come back to life, to be re-incarnated into a different body, year after year, century after century. This is what Seraphina's life has turned into. That one night where the boy she loved used alchemy to keep them together for eternity has left Sera hanging on by a thread. She doesn't want the life she's been given anymore, so she sets out to die for the last time. 
 Except everything changes when she saves a teenage girl from a car accident one night. Sera finds herself not just taking over the girl's body, but her entire life. Then when Cyrus - the one who gave her immortality - catches up with her, not intent on letting Sera go - things start to go awry... 
 I still don't know what to make of this novel - I enjoyed it, but at the same time I didn't. The novel opens with Cyrus giving Seraphina immortality, explaining that she can have it all - and Sera chooses that life. We then get a glimpse of what it's like to be an Incarnate, and how Sera finds life as one. Considering that she's planning her own death, it's safe to say that being an Incarnate isn't all that it's cracked up to be. Yet when it comes to choosing whether or not she wants to watch someone die or take over that body, Sera makes it very clear that she can't give up life as an Incarnate just yet. 
 Sera learns to adapt to life as a normal teenage girl, and one thing that I liked was the fact that she didn't automatically 'get' life as a teenager. Sera finds it awkward and strange to fit into Kailey's life, especially as she doesn't know a single thing about what this girl was like to anyone. She's awkward, hesitant and wary - like a timid version of Cady from Mean Girls. And then there's Noah, the boy next door, who Sera finds intriguing, but apparently Kailey didn't like him. At least, not anymore. The only issue is, everyone seems to accept Kailey's change in behaviour. Sure, they give her the odd raised eyebrow and maybe a sarcastic 'Didn't you wake up on the right side of the bed for a change' comment, but no-one really questions her. No "Who are you and what have you done to my daughter/friend/sister?" 
 Yet Sera's growing relationship with Noah doesn't really seem like anything to me. It's very vague and quite instant, and although we can see that she's interested in Noah, that intensity you get in most novels (most recently, Jack from Everneath who has stolen my heart, big time!) just isn't there. I don't feel compelled at all to worry about what might happen if Cyrus, who eventually finds Sera, gets his hands on Noah (dad a duummmmmmmm). There was no drama, no real action, and characters that you don't learn anything about - for example, Taryn, the girl who supposedly steals Sera's backpack and car. It's almost as if it was a filler, but I'm hoping that it has something to do with the next novel. 
 In saying all this, I was fairly intrigued still. Williams puts together two types of legends together - alchemy and incarnation, and spins a great tale. Reading The Alchemy of Forever was kind of like reading Wither for me. I enjoyed it, but it just didn't do anything for me. 
 I love the idea of incarnation however, and this new take on it - body swapping - was a great premise to the story, and really helped push the dramatic ending a bit. I definitely want to read the next book now, as I know it'll be way more interesting than this one, but you have to start somewhere, don't you? 
 As I said, the mixed feelings are still determining whether or not I liked this novel. I definitely enjoyed it, but there was no wow factor for me. If it hadn't ended the way it did, I probably wouldn't even consider reading the next one, but as always curiosity killed this cat. I have to know how things turn out!

Just when Raine Cooper gives into her love and attraction for Torin, Torin's memories of her are erased by a group of norns. But Raine is intent on reminding Torin of what they had. But that is not all she has to deal with. Between ignoring snide comments and insults in school, training about Runes, trying to keep up with her father's illness and trying to be a good friend, Raine is stretched thin. Will she be able to hold on to all her projects or will she lose someone in the process? 
 I was happy to see Andris play a larger role in this book. The dynamics between Raine, Cora and Eirik are ever changing and interesting. We find out a little more about who Raine really is and the extent of her power. The character of Ingrid is kind of confusing - one never knows what she is all about. The plot continues to unfold, revealing more secrets and information. I have started to like the author's narration style except for the continuous repetition of Raine Cooper telling us that Torin makes her go weak in the knee. No seriously, the number of times she thinks about it to herself is way too much and half way through the book I was shouting at Raine -'Okay woman I get it!' 
 This second novel in the series gives us a look at the bigger picture and the possibilities are immense. I will be sure to pick up the next in the series.

The 'Matched' series is a FANTASTIC example of a series that COMPLETELY LOSES THE PLOT. Both literally and figuratively. 
 Matched itself is decent enough; a pleasant and mildly exciting read. But the trilogy spirals into a complete mess. 
 I imagine that reading the books again would solve a lot of the problems I have with it. But it's so hard to pick up a book that you know you so strongly dislike.

This one was a hard read for me, because it feels both apocalyptic and like present-day life (in some areas). Set in California, it's a future story, but much nearer to us now--2024--than when she published it in 1993. There is a spine of hope, and the teenage narrator does not shake her belief that things, though they have been awful her whole life, can change for the better. But those first hundred or so pages are wrenching. 
 "Do you think our world is coming to an end?" Dad asked, and with no warning at all I almost started crying. What I thought was, "No I think *your* world is coming to an end, and maybe you with it." That was terrible. I hadn't thought about it in such a personal way before. I turned and looked out a window until I felt calmer. When I faced him again, I said, "Yes. Don't you?" 
 --p 62 
 Lauren Olamina eventually leaves her walled neighborhood to travel north, trying to find a place and work that paid cash. But first she must survive a road trip filled with the horrors common to the genre, but this time also with some pleasures. 
 I stared down the hill from our camp where just a glint of water was visible in the distance through trees and bushes. The world is full of painful stories. Sometimes it seems as though there aren't any other kind and yet I found myself thinking how beautiful that glint of water was through the trees. 
 -- p 263 
 I like Butler's strong, straightforward writing style, and especially the people she creates. Lauren's good-sized family and neighbors are distinct, as are the many people she meets along the way. Their responses and their voices feel true, even as some play a "role" in the "parable." 
 Lauren seeks meaning; she's studied religions and beliefs and is developing a philosophy/religion of her own. I'm not sure she's there yet when she starts sharing it with others, but I enjoyed her questioning and stretching early in the story (when she's only 15!). 
 "A lot of people seem to believe in a big-daddy-God or a big-cop-God or a big-king-God. They believe in a kind of superperson. A few believe God is another word for nature. And nature turns out to mean just about anything they happen not to understand. 
 "Some say God is a spirit, a force, an ultimate reality. Ask seven people what all of that means and you'll get seven different answers. So what is God? Just another name for whatever makes you feel special and protected?" 
 --p 15 
 To me, the new-religion stuff wasn't as interesting as how she builds a community of people who despite all evidence still choose to trust one another. Unlike Cormac McCarthy's The Road, there's a better balance here between crazed terror and conscious decency. 
 Late in the story, a new potential member has many reasons to distrust the group, but one was a surprise to me--he distrusted the sole white guy. Then I thought, why wouldn't he? Why wouldn't they all? It's the white guys that have held and hold the power all these centuries and look what's happened. 
 All struggles 
 Are essentially 
 power struggles. 
 Who will rule, 
 Who will lead, 
 Who will define, 
 refine 
 confine, 
 design, 
 Who will dominate. 
 All struggles 
 Are essentially 
 power struggles, 
 And most 
 are no more intellectual 
 than two rams 
 knocking their heads together 
 -- from "Earthseed" (Lauren Olamina) 
 --p 94

"When given the choice between being right or being kind, choose kind." 
 I love thought provoking, feel-good books. Palacio's story was beautiful; it portrayed children (and adults) as they actually are. It took me back to those days, even made me feel kind of nostalgic (not for the "bad" parts ;). Most importantly, it reminded me how important it is to be kind. Always. And for that, this book was truly a wonder.

A Little Too Much is the second book in the A Little Too Far series. The book tells the story of Alessandro Moretti, the almost to be priest we met and fell hard for in A Little Too Far. 
 I enjoyed reading this book, but am rating it only 3 stars because of the POV. The reason I chose to read it was because I really enjoyed the character Alessandro in A Little Too Far and wanted to learn more about him. I can't say this book didn't deliver - it did give his life a closure and had I not known Alessandro before I picked up the book, I probably would have rated it higher and just concentrated my review on the story and the writing - which both were deserving of at least 4 stars. 
 But I can't ignore the fact that I was disappointed. I wanted the book to be from his point of view or at the least a dual point of view. I didn't know Hilary and felt I was cheated moments from Alessandro's life and given a sorry substitute. Hilary was okay, but Alessandro was what I 'came for'...and the reason I hoped getting deep into his soul by reading this book, kept me from connecting with Hilary and left the reading experience to be only 'okay' for me. 
 "I feel like a half a man when you deserve someone whole. Letting you see what I really am scares me, but I will, if that's what you want. And after you know the real me, I won't hold you to any promises if you want to leave me." 
 I need to add a praise to the author thought for setting both of the books in beautiful locations and making the city a part of the storyline. The first book was set in Rome and concentrated a lot on the museums and art pieces the city has to offer. This one was set in New York and included many interesting tourist attractions when Alessandro and Hilary explored the undiscovered New York regularly every Thursday. I think the city exploring in both books was an excellent idea and added the extra something for the books.

I thought that this book really just expanded our knowledge of the world and people we were introduced to in Unholy Ghosts. This book picks up about four months after the events in the first book. 
 Whereas Unholy Ghosts really introduces the readers to the characters and gives us a look into their past, and introduces us to the world of Downside, Unholy Magic digs even deeper on the character side of things. There's not too much additional knowledge of the world that we learn, instead we learn a lot about our characters. Namely, Chess and Terrible. 
 There are reviewers who have called this book heartbreaking and I would have to agree. There are moments that I feel so sad for these two characters and what they have been through and what they will inevitably go through. I know Chess has a lot of problems in her past and she uses drugs in her present to keep those thoughts from coming back and haunting her. I think if Chess could find that one thing that is worth more (cough* Terrible cough*) she would see herself better. I was saddened by the comments she would make about herself not being worth it. While I'm not much for a pity party, I think Stacia Kane did the right amount to remind readers how Chess feels about herself, but not throwing it directly in our faces at every turn. 
 Terrible really grows in this book. We get to see beyond the enforcer that he is, and we really get to see his heart. We saw the beginnings of it in Unholy Ghosts, but in this book he really opens up which makes it that much harder to see what he believes in come crashing down. Stacia Kane really did a wonderful job with making you want to see the characters find happiness, only to watch it get ripped away. 
 But I haven't given up hope. We do see at the end Chess fully realizing what it would mean to lose Terrible and it really is a beautiful moment. I am interested to see how things will be for them in City of Ghosts. 
 I really am enjoying this series and I can't wait to read the third book. I little sad that I will have to wait until March for the 4th book, but from there I don't thik there will be as big of a gap between the books in this series. Until Then!

The Unlikely Pilgrimage of Harold Fry is a well-written, absorbing story of a shy man, who is often mistaken for being dull, and his epic journey in yachting shoes. Of course, I had to look up what yachting shoes are... Joyce tells the story of a marriage gone silent, a few new friendships, a broken family, a pilgrimage always threatened by failure (and facebook!), and most importantly, of "ordinary" people. 
 Harold walks through memories of his childhood, of his marriage, his son, and his friendship with a woman, perhaps his only close friend in life, who he feels he has failed many years ago. Walking toward his friend from the past, we meet Harold's painful childhood, his inability to connect with his only son, and his painful regrets. We also meet the many people who help Harold along the way, who accidentally inspire him, and who use him. Harold is a coward, a gentleman, an introvert, a loser, and sometimes an angry, old man. But Harold is also brave, honest, compassionate, and more in touch with reality than anyone realizes. Though he is and therefore the book is focused on if he will make it, the real question is what will happen once he does. 
 I did not think the book lost its focus after a while. Instead, I thought the disruption of Harold's solitary journey by the media blitz and facebook heroes was perfectly paralleled with the life of a painfully shy and lonely man, who had managed to disrupt his lonely existence once with a brave deed across a dance floor, had briefly managed to have a family, to return to a painful loneliness in the end. Perhaps Maureen, Harold's wife, presents us with the true emotional range, when one is faced with such a history. 
 This may be the saddest uplifting book I have ever read. Though more heavy-handed, some aspects of the storytelling and character development reminded me of The Heart Is A Lonely Hunter. As a whole, Joyce produces a touching story that centers on what must be one of the most unlikely heroes of our time.

When "Perfect" Parker Fadley begins drinking at school and failing her classes, the entire school goes on high alert. Her parents have put her on suicide watch and all of her teachers watch her like a hawk. How, though, has Parker fallen so hard? What has happened to cause the captain of the cheerleading squad and the most popular girl in school to become such a mess. Parker doesn't want to talk about it though and would rather everyone just left her alone. Things are made worse when a new kid, Jake, joins the school and takes a shine to Parker. So much so that he's constantly there, constantly present and is always asking questions. But Parker can't tell him what happened that night. She can't tell anyone. Because the truth is, it could well be Parker's fault. 
 I actually have no idea how to review this book. I literally cannot think how to put into words just what this book has done to me. I'm kind of speechless. One thing I do know is that I have totally underestimated the Young Adult genre. When I decided to buy Cracked Up To Be I wasn't expecting the read I just got. One thing's for sure, though, I'm very happy I did buy Cracked Up To Be. When I got into the Young Adult genre I expected light and fluffy reads with a typical happy-ever-after ending much like the chick lit books I enjoy so much. Yet so far the YA books I've read haven't really had much lightness or fluffiness or happy-ever-after endings. 
 When Cracked Up To Be arrived on Monday and I had finished my latest book I decided to give it a read as I knew I'd be able to finish it relatively quickly as it's only 214 pages long. The book starts pretty much as it means to go on: Parker Fadley is no longer known as "Perfect" Parker Fadley and I suppose the easiest question at the beginning of the book is, "Why?". If you're looking for an easy answer in Cracked Up To Be then you aren't going to get it because Parker's fall from grace isn't told in one swift moment. No, Parker's fall from grace is fed to us slowly. Kind of like when people are on a drip. We get snippets here and there of the night Parker's life suddenly unravelled but for the most part the main focus of the book is Parker's bid to push everybody away. 
 But still, Parker's bid to push everyone away begs the same question of why. It's easy to ascertain that she's guilty for some reason but nothing really becomes clear until we're told exactly what happened at that party that night. And that doesn't happen until the end of the book (as you would expect). I was surprised by Parker's attitude throughout the entire book as she's very snipy and sarcastic and constantly puts people down. I found myself questioning Parker constantly and I couldn't get it right in my head whether or not I actually liked Parker. I think more than anything I admired her determination. Everyone was watching her constantly yet she still persisted in trying to get everybody to leave her alone. It was futile but Parker still didn't give up. 
 What really brings everything into focus for Parker is the arrival of new kid Jake. She's just as snipy and stubborn with Jake as she is with everyone else yet he still takes a shine to her and begins, in a roudabout way, stalking her and constantly asking her questions. This is how we got to know the real Parker. The Parker underneath the facade. Sure she was projecting a hard-nosed front but it was the exchanges with Jake that show she isn't as hard as she likes to make people think she is. I actually loved the rapport between Parker and Jake. I loved that he refused to give up on her and that, slowly, Parker began to reveal more of herself to him. I liked Jake, really, full stop. He was nice and persistent and, to be honest, seemed to be just what Parker needed. There are other characters in the book. Chris and Becky, friends (kind of) of Parker. I quite liked Chris but wasn't really a huge fan of Becky. The only other main characters affected by Parker's actions were her parents. I found it so hard to read the scenes between Parker and her parents. I could feel the helplessness radiating off Parker's parents and I could see Parker doing her best to make them feel even more helpless. Parker even manages to get a dog, Bailey, from her parents due to her actions; she was a master manipulator, that's for sure. I actually quite liked the dog and I thought even the dog got more out of Parker than her parents did. 
 Cracked Up To Be then hurtles towards the inevitable revelation of just what happened that night and I have to say I was mildly stunned. I had the feeling that I should have figured it out and it was like a lightbulb went on in my head and said, "Of course!" but I just didn't see it coming. It was definitely full of suspense and I have to say it impressed me. What makes the book though is Summers' writing. She writes Parker so well that you have to like her. Or you have to at least try and like her no matter how mean she may get. There are a few twists in the book and I admit the book did make me cry at one point. The ending of the book kinda leaves the door open for a potential sequel - right now, I would devour a sequel - but I'm sure after a few days of thinking it over (I need to think it over) I will accept the end of the book. It wasn't a bad ending but anybody that knows me knows that I like my endings tied up in a neat bow. 
 Cracked Up To Be quite simply blew me away. I wasn't expecting so much emotion to pour from the pages and I certainly wasn't expecting so much suspense. I actually don't even think I've done the book justice in my review. The book was truly outstanding and I think I'm going to have to read it again soon just to absorb everything about the book. It may well be only 214 pages but it's 214 emotionally-packed pages.

I didn't like this nearly as well as Divergent. It felt sloppy, and Tris made a lot of decisions that seemed out of character and, well, stupid. I don't really enjoy reading conflict that's just a result of refusal to communicate when there's not a plausible reason for it. I know she's sixteen and not sixty, but Tris's decisions just make me want to scream. 
 I finished the book, because I still wanted to know what happened, but by the time I got to the end I wasn't particularly interested in reading Allegiant. I feel like it's already clear that the characters shift and change in unrealistic ways according to the needs of the plot, and the plot isn't particularly well thought-out anymore. I'd rather keep it so I'm willing to reread Divergent, at least.

** spoiler alert ** 
 I just finished reading this book to my four-year-old daughter for the first time. What a treat it was to share it with her and to see it through her eyes. I have so much fun watching the stories we read make an appearance in her play. I was surprised that she wasn't upset about Charlotte dying. She asked why she died, but took it fairly well in stride when I explained that she was old and that every living thing must die one day. She seemed more upset when Charlotte's children flew away and that Wilbur was sad about that.

This was a great romp from Wilkie Collins, a mix of mystery, gothic terror and swapped identities. 
 The real hero of it for me was Marian Halcombe, who must be a prototype female took-a-course-in-badass. She spends half the night listening from a rooftop, in the rain, just in case someone is up to no good. What a girl! Unfortunately, since she isn't the protaganist or the love interest, she has to be ugly (at least to a Victorian audience) so our hero Mr Hartright won't be tempted to fall in love with her. I'd take her over Laura Fairlie (who is supposed to be our heroine, and is useless!) anyday. I actually wanted Hartright to come to his senses and marry Marian instead, but alas! It was not to be. 
 There are some great characters in this book, Marian being one of them and the other the wonderfully devious Count Fosco. They really carry the book more than anyone else, and the story flags when they aren't around. 
 There's even a quote I'm considering adopting as a motto: 
 My hour for tea is half-past five, and my buttered toast waits for nobody. 
 Great stuff.

There are some books you know you will love just by the cover and the blub. This is one of those books. I have to give five stars for creative presentation. 
 I have never worked in retail per se, but I have worked for a large healthcare corporation for several years in a service capacity for the public. Mr. Hendrix has the corporate speak mindset down pat. One of the things I liked best about the story were the descriptions of the employees, er excuse me, floor partners. They are totally relatable. I have been Amy and am currently Ruth Anne. I've had bosses like Basil. I've worked with Trinitys and Matthews. 
 I love that part of the horror of this workplace based book is work.  Both the penitent spirits and the floor partners have to endure a form of work therapy to be "cured"  
 My only minor quibble is that everyone was afraid to go on the bright and shiny path without a flashlight or cell phone. Note to characters: I know the dark is scary, but you don't want to draw attention to yourselves by using the light. I had a few unanswered questions about Carl, but it wasn't enough to bring down the rating. 
 The ending leaves an opening. I would love to read a sequel with Planet Baby.

After loving Life After Life, I decided to go back to Atkinson's backlist and read her debut novel. 
 With the story of Ruby Lennox, I immediately saw similarities to Ursula Todd and as a storyteller Atkinson has only improved. Of course, she had a pretty strong start with this one. 
 While there were a few things with this one that didn't seem to work, overall it's a wonderfully weaving story of several generations of Ruby's family -- Alice, her great grandmother, Nell, her grandmother, and Bunty, her mom -- and we see over and over how history manages to repeat itself despite all the different paths taken. 
 Spoiler: The one thing that threw me was that Ruby apparently had a twin, Pearl, but we don't know about it until MUCH LATER. Which doesn't make a lot of sense because Ruby starts narrating at the point of conception.... So that kind of distracted me from the story.  
 I think the story could have survived without that piece, but it also didn't take away from my overall enjoyment of the novel.

This series is much along the lines of George R.R. Martin's A Song of Ice and Fire series in that everyone you love is going to be killed or damaged. Good luck, readers. What I learned as I kept reading, don't underestimate this author. 
 Gavin's story... omg. There are a number of literary traps that I thought this series was making, but as I continue to read, Weeks is actually subverting them rather cleverly. The Gary Stu that Gavin starts off being, the perfect hero with the perfect body and perfect morals along with being the most powerful person on the planet, has such a journey that completely undermines what made him great while simultaneously giving him depth and a dark nobility. (The last line in this book froze me. I had to read it about five times as the weight of it settled). 
 The story of his brother in the trap seemed so odd at first. There's a great deal of time developing this story line, then it ends so abruptly. Huh? What I thought was a plotting flaw, though an interesting one, in the second novel is coming around like a sledgehammer. 
 Kip, who has to be my favorite character so far this year, keeps growing on me. I love reading his journey. His humor and struggles have so much heart. Even when he stumbles (his initial thoughts when Tia becomes his slave before he frees her, for example), there's such a sweetness to him, I can't stay mad. The plucky turtlebear continues to amaze me. His sections in the story were easily my favorites. 
 Truly, the characters in these stories are fully realized and finely crafted in detailed strokes, with all their little idiosyncrasies lovingly rendered. 
 Like many others, I am saddened by the long wait for the next novel, but as I was reading, I understand it. I do enough writing as a hobby to see when something is a happy accident and when an author really slaves over a phrase to get it just right, when s/he spends the time to write something profound that will change how you think. Weeks is an author who polishes his stories until the awkward phrasing or odd comment is fixed. I admire him more for it. 
 Novels like this make me feel cared for as a reader.

 If there's something I love about Amy Plum's books, that is her neat writing and her awesome characters. 
 That was After the End. 
 I don't want to say much about the plot because I think the synopsis is very descriptive and I don't want to give spoilers. But I can say I was very surprised by the magical elements in this book. 
 I've seen some people say After the End is a dystopian book but I'm not really sure about it. Even though Juneau had lived all her life with lies, the other side of the story, the real world, is modern and it didn't feel dystopian. Not that it matters, but this book felt quite magical. 
 After the End is told in alternative POV between Juneau and Miles. Amy Plum did an excellent job creating different voices. 
 Juneau is smart, loyal, and brave. I loved the way she acted after she discovered the truth, I loved that she was serious and determined. 
 The only thing I didn't like about Juneau is that she lived with her people far away from the modern world, and yet she understood everything so fast. It was like Juneau was super-smart. 
 Miles, in the other hand was awesome. He was hilarious! He was smart, a little arrogant but sweet and courageous. 
 It made me really happy when the hints of the romance started to show. 
 It wasn't a huge romance, but it was enough. Juneau and Miles were a badass team. Their relationship is one of the most natural I've seen. It started slowly but then it became something solid. 
 I'm so thankful because this book doesn't have insta-love, they even didn't trust each other at the beginning. 
 After the End is full of suspense and mystery. Shocking betrayals and some jaw-dropping moments. 
 It has everything to be an amazing read, but I was still left with a lot of questions and the ending somehow felt a little rushed. Like there was something missing. 
 Anyway, I really enjoyed After the End. I think this will be a great series. Plus, the cover is amazing. 
 After the End has action, drama, and great characters. With an amazing plot and secrecy that will have you on the edge of your seat, After the End is the best beginning of a new series.

This book has been getting rave reviews. Both here on goodreads, in magazines, and in other media. 
 And I just don't get it. 
 I felt that the writing and story were inconsistent. Atkinson essentially recycles a handful of scenes throughout the book, sometimes hundreds of pages apart, which irritated me. I always felt "Hey, I've read this before...earlier! Why am I reading the exact same words again? Am I supposed to have gained a deeper understanding of this scene? Because I haven't." 
 There were sections that were heartbreakingly beautiful and/or wonderfully tense. But there weren't enough of those to hold the flimsy story together. 
 Ursula's voice was inconsistent, although I suppose Atkinson would attribute that to her protagonist having multiple lives and therefore multiple upbringings and therefore a personality that shifts depending on how happy/easy/violent her life has been. But again, I found this more aggravating than intriguing. 
 I honestly skimmed the last 150 pages. This story wasn't holding me to anything. I had to work too hard to connect characters from past lives into new lives and recalling scenes to suss out whether they were slightly different now than before. This book would be easier to read if I charted it out on a large chart as I read it, tracking Ursula's lives. But it still wouldn't be enjoyable.

I didn't find it her heroic and I wished she DID get thrown out the ship. They did what they thought could get them through the journey and while it wasn't a perfect solution, it was justifiable (unlike a certain main characters idiot thoughts + actions -__-) they just had the best in mind. His/her reason for doing what he/she did were true! that the ships passenger were either going to be slaves or soldiers  I loved the 'villain's' in this book more then the main characters but in the end, I will be looking forward to book 2, A Million Suns.

While I have no objection to romances where there is a significant age gap ('These Old Shades' by Georgette Heyer, pairs 19-year-old Leonie with a 41-year-old Duke and it's superb), the harsh truth is, teenage heroines in adult romance novels are tricky beasts. 
 Mature readers need to be able to identify and connect with the heroine, and teen girls share exactly none of their life experience. Regency form dictates that an 18-year-old upper class lady be a naive ingenue: virginal yet impulsive. Reality dictates that teenagers are excessively given to drama, and annoying hormone-induced outbursts. 
 In the case of Morgan Bedwyn, the heroine of this book, not only is she a sheltered teen, but also beautiful and loved. Her life is charmed. She comes from a close family, where she's the baby; cossetted and indulged, courted and adored. She has no acne, no money worries, no deep dark secrets... it's all smooth sailing. 
 This makes her about as engaging as a plastic Barbie doll. 
 Where the author's voice proclaimed Morgan's actions "strong-willed", I saw "spoiled" and "unaccustomed to opposition". Her purported love of painting manifested itself in one weak little afternoon of drawing a river and tree; not exactly a sustaining passion. Her disregard for society's rules was another example of supreme privilege - the rich don't need to follow rules or mind gossip. All in all, not lovable. 
 It's hard enough putting yourself into the satin slippers of a woman from the early 1800s, without making her a hotheaded, deliriously gorgeous, pouty teen who can have her pick of men and chooses a French dude who waggles his eyebrows a lot and screws her when she's alone and vulnerable. Not even the Duke of Avon would be so bold. Hi, Gervase? You're a freaking adult, maybe you could keep it in your pants when an emotionally compromised girl comes on to you at a rough time. 
 Aside from not being able to get inside the head of a girl with no employment whose major feature is not sass or intellect, just "beauty", I was also not a fan of the hero. Consensual but ill-advised, ill-timed sex aside, he keeps WAGGLING his freaking EYEBROWS. I had to pause in case the next line of dialogue turned out to be "wacka wacka!" Who waggles their eyebrows to indicate sexual suggestion outside of a Woody Allen comedy? Just no. 
 What kept me going was familiarity with the rest of the Bedwyn Clan, who have made me a somewhat unwilling captive through three full novels already, and who are going to hook me in for two more. Why? Because much as I don't really care about Alleyne, I need to know what's going to happen to icy old Wulfric. Here's hoping that the author antes up for the last two installments of the "Simply" series. 
 N.B.: Props to Balogh for trying to work a little same-sex action into the story. Since it is a plot piece, I won't go into detail, but yay?

This book had me in tears. I read the ARC that a friend left me when she stayed for the night and I really enjoyed it! I would say this falls in the same vein as John Green, David Levithan, Rainbow Rowell YA books--quirky teens, trying to find their way. This focuses on mental disorders and parental abuse rather than physical illness, which was intriguing. I liked the characters and was rooting for them, mostly. I thought it was so interesting to see and feel how bipolar disorder felt to someone close to it and to the person with it. Finch was such a bright, crazy character. I wasn't sure what to think of him at points, but I ended up being really interested in his character. I wish we heard from him a little more during his descent into his disease and depression. His sister Kate seemed to have it together, but really, she didn't and she needed help. I wanted a little more from her, why was she covering up his crazy? His mom was a basket case, his dad was a jerk, but someone should have seen what was going on and helped him. It was hard to have any sympathy for his mother and it was hard to believe she was so clueless since she was so one dimensional she didn't feel real. Asking Violet to go looking for Finch was kind of crazy, what adult would ever do that?! But, it goes along with her detachment from reality. Violet was a great character--her parents, overcoming adversity, I was really interested. I liked her parents because even though they were a grieving, they felt the most relatable to me, as did Embryo.  At the end of this book I had tears running down my face, some of them felt unearned because it was such an emotional plot moment, not emotional character moment, but still, I'd recommend this to anyone looking for a cathartic cry and who likes John Green type characters.

Wow.. This one is quite a challenge - not because it isn't a quick, compulsive read (it is), but because it is mostly so cringe-worthy. How can a book told from the point of view of a sociopathic, female, sexual predator be worth reading? I knew there would be a lot of controversy about this one, and I was intrigued. 
 I read an interview with Alissa Nutting who talked about her attempt to create a monster in Celeste Price. It was important that she be beautiful and desired by all her students, so that the typical older woman/younger student dynamic be surrounded by the usual wink wink-nudge nudge attitudes that so often follow these scandals. 
 While the comparisons to Lolita seem obvious, Celeste is no Humbert Humbert - she is calculated and determined and predatory in the most horrifying way. Celeste becomes a teacher to have her pick of boys. She has her own private rituals she performs when selecting a boy to go after, and makes sure there is no way he can possibly say no to her. Nutting makes it very clear that consent couldn't be made. 
 This was a very interesting interesting read. It is graphic in a stomach-churning way, so it's definitely not for the faint of heart. Alissa Nutting was successful in creating her gorgeous, wealthy, terrifying pedophile.

I have read pretty extensively in the vampire genre - have read Dracula numerous times, starting when I was about 10, then Interview with a Vampire/The Vampire Lestat/Queen of the Damned (I didnt' go any further in Anne Rice's series); Suzette McKee Charnas' The Vampire Tapestry, about the first 10 Anita Blake books, thus far the first four of the Sookie Stackhouse books, Guillermo del Toro's The Strain, Stephen King's Salem's Lot, Elizabeth Kostova's The Historian. Probably others as well, but that's what I can recall right off the top of my head. I've also watched all of the 1960s' Hammer movies with Christopher Lee and Peter Cushing, as well as most of the film adaptations of Dracula, plus of course Buffy the Vampire Slayer, Angel, Moonlight and other TV series. (I have not read the Twilight books, nor do I plan to [the author apparently knew absolutely nothing about the vampire genre prior to writing her books - that is, she was familiar with none of the tropes of vampire literature. What kind of writer writes a genre novel without knowing at least basically what has gone before? Or else why bother to make it a vampire novel?] Nor do I plan to get into any of the other 374 vampire series that have been spawned in the past 10 years.) 
 My point with all of this preamble is this: I like it when an author takes one of those tropes and spins it a little - explains why it's true, or gives a more modern, scientific explanation for its existence, etc. Like why a vampire doesn't cast a reflection in a mirror, or why you can't take a photograph of one: both have to do with silver - the silvering on the back of the mirror, and the silver emulsion on film. Ah, except now (according to Mick from TV's Moonlight) you can take a pic of a vampire, as long as you're using a digital camera. 
 In Robin McKinley's Sunlight, the existence of such things as vampires, demons, and magic is known, but they exist only on the periphery of society (even more so than in Laurel K. Hamilton's Anita Blake series. No citizenship for these vamps.) Rae lives a comfortable life surrounded by family and working at a job she loves, as a baker for the family diner. She also has some odd relatives, including her father, who is a major magic-worker. Rae herself knows a few tricks, taught to her by her grandmother, but for the most part she goes about her business and doesn't concern herself with those issues. 
 Unfortunately, one day she finds herself the captive of a band of vamps who plan to use her as bait for an old and powerful vampire. Here's where the fun spin comes in: in Rae's universe, the older a vampire gets, the more susceptible he becomes to sunlight, including being unable to go out at night when the moon is full or nearly full, because the amount of reflected sunlight can kill him. So on a full moon night, Rae ends up chained in a room with a starving vampire. He's an ethical vampire, and he doesn't want to drink her, but he's losing control. Being a smart woman and not one to panic, she employs some of the magic her grandmother taught her - and some skills she wasn't quite aware she possessed - to save herself and the vampire, who has impressed her with his non-evil nature. 
 Let's just say from there on out, Rae's quiet life is pretty well shot. Now she has ticked-off vamps who want to know how she got away, her family's history is obviously much more complex than she was ever led to believe, and there's a super-secret police unit that would like to pick her brain. 
 Robin McKinley's one of my favorite authors. She repeatedly takes something you think you're so familiar with, no one could possibly say anything new about it - Robin Hood, The Beauty & the Beast, Cinderella - and turns it inside out. If you don't know her books, you should.

Dog Stars tells the story of Hig, his dog Jasper, and his plane, The Beast. Hig lives in post-apocalyptic America, which has been ravaged and essentially wiped out by a strain of the flu nine years ago. His days consist of tending the garden, killing off intruders, flying the perimeter, and maintaining an awkward relationship with his survivalist-extreme roommate, Bangley. Bangley leaves a bit to be desired on the comforting front, so when Hig hears a radio transmission from an airport just outside his "point of no return", he feels a temptation he cannot ignore. And so he sets out- to discover. 
 This is a story of loss, and it's a story of survival. It is told through a more complex version of narrative verse. Some entire sentences are, 
 "But." 
 or, 
 "And." 
 But I cannot stress enough that this does not detract from the story. Let me be clear: My husband and I listened to this on audiobook, and the narrator was out-of-this-world. He made the story flow. If you do not like to read stream-of-consciousness on a page, I would suggest listening to the audiobook. Either way, I suggest listening to the audiobook- it was amazing. 
 The style of writing is what I would consider art. Look, I've been reading a lot of dystopian novels. There isn't a lot of new material out there. This novel is new and fresh because it's told in a different way. It's a hero who is not all that skilled, and not all that charming, but loves things fiercely. Hig does not understand the world around him, but he understands his airplane. He does not beat us to death with repetitions of his thoughts- but explains his thoughts through his actions. We see his grief in not just the actions of Hig, but in the sentence structure. I cannot stress enough that the stream of consciousness of this story lends itself to this story of loss and sadness. 
 Not to mention which, Hig was an aspiring poet- he feels and sees things through a poet's eyes. Thus, we see everything through a poet's eyes.But it's not kitschy or forced- at least, it wasn't for me. Hig feels things that I think a genuine human would feel in the world that he lives in. He acts in the way that I feel a tired, but headstrong, but very sad man would act. 
 There seemed to be only a few personality types in the book... Cima/Hig- the poetic moral-compasses of the story.... Bangley/Pops- the survivalist, bad-ass men who do not waste time over-thinking things... and the side-characters: the Families or the Bad Guys, neither of whom get much time in the book. Perhaps these are the only people who will survive- the bad-asses, and the people they choose to take care of. 
 I love how it all comes back to Jasper. In the end, everything is about Jasper- and that's saying something considering  Jasper dies halfway through the book.  
 Peter Heller is brilliant, and staggeringly so. He has written a book about hunting and guns and the cruel people at the end of the world, but made it a story about love and loss in a way that can be accessible to almost everyone. If, that is, you can get past the writing style. Which I suggest you try to do. 
 I actually think I will read this book several times. There are so many books right now that I put down and say, "Hey, that was fun" like a movie. Like a summer blockbuster. But this is a book that made me want to pick it right back up as soon as I was finished. I already miss Hig. And Jasper. And Bangley, even. 
 If I could add the whole book as a quote and "like" the quote here on Goodreads, I would. The style, the characters, the story... it was just plain amazing. 
 Note: This book is not for everyone- this is not a fluffy book. There are many parts of this book that are very disturbing. But then, this is a book about the depravity of the human race at the end of the world.

16-year-old ecumenical Indian boy Piscine (Pi) Molitor Patel's life is turned upside down when his father decides to move the family, and several of the family-owned Pondicherry zoo's residents, to Canada. When the cargo ship sinks during a storm in the middle of the Pacific Ocean, Pi suddenly finds himself stranded on a fairly small lifeboat with a very large tiger. Survival becomes paramount, though seemingly impossible, and Pi has to rely on his knowledge of animals and his faith in various deities to stay alive. 
 First of all, how has this book been around for a decade before I discovered it? Must a book be adapted to a major motion picture before it comes to my attention enough to pick it up and read it. If so, I'm really glad they made a movie, because I REALLY liked this book and I'm glad I finally read it. How do I describe what I liked about this book?... Let's just split it up into separate elements: 
 The characters: They were engaging and real. Putting aside the sea and sky, which are practically characters in their own way, Pi is a wonderful person who I wanted to know personally. Richard Parker (brilliant name) is an animal in every sense of the word, and the writer never tries to anthropomorphize or humanize him. He was never cute or cuddly (beautiful and powerful, of course), and they never became snuggle buddies or anything like that. Their relationship was realistic and tense. The story: Could anything be more compelling?? I had NO idea how it was going to end (though the author thankfully informs us early on that it will have a happy ending), and though it sometimes took me a little effort to pick it up, it took even greater effort to put it down. I never thought it was slow or boring. At times it was miserable and bleak, but there was just as much joy and hope (or at least enough to balance it out) so that I never felt it was laborious. The writing: Beautiful! It was vivid and true and I could actually see and feel the things that Pi saw and felt. I was grossed out when he witnessed violent, gruesome (natural) behavior from the animals. I was afraid, I was excited, my eyes shot open with each exciting turn of events, and I groaned with agony when disaster struck. I was even pretty willing to go along with the more bizarre elements, and made ready excuses when ideas entered my mind that the story might have gone a bit too far (meerkats?...). The themes: While it seemed to have a definite purpose, this book didn't seem to have an Agenda (in fact, it seemed to debunk various agendas). The beauty of this story, especially regarding religion, is that it doesn't shy away from it at all (a story that will make you believe in God? Yes, please), and in fact it's quite open in its message. The story is built in such a way that in can be taken in various directions, but it seems pretty clear to me the message the author was trying to get across, and it's decidedly positive. My personal religious beliefs obviously steer me in a certain direction regarding Pi's all-encompassing religious beliefs, but the fact that this was a boy who truly loved God and wanted to do good was awesome. Also, it could just be my perception, or based on what I've read recently, but it seems like few modern books are willing to address so overtly themes of religion and transcendentalism, and that was a true breath of fresh (sea?) air. 
 And for the record, I'm not confused AT ALL as to which of the two stories is the true one. Silly shipping company personnel. 
 Also, as a side note, um, I hope I'm not the only one who was totally fooled into thinking this was a true story, and that the Author's Note was actually truly what the author experienced and what prompted him to write this book. If it's not true, at least it's written in such a way that I was thoroughly convinced that it COULD be. 
 This book is marvelous. I'm sometimes wary of trendy books, but when they turn out to be really good, they change from a trendy book to a popular book, and I'm so glad I finally read this. It's actually kind of a challenge for me to find anything I dislike about this one. I think for those who have ears to hear, it IS a story that makes you believe in God. The movie is pretty great, but the book is excellent. Tigers are still cool, but also still scary.

 What new stuff Soule/Garney bring is pretty bad: a new sidekick character called Blindspot who has a cloaking suit - geddit?! Yeah, it's another shite Soule original - toss it onto the pile of awful hackneyed Inhuman/Wolverine characters he's cranked out since he joined Marvel!

Instead of moving Carrie immediately or accepting Carrie's resignation, Carrie's boss counter offers an interesting plan. Find Finn Dalton, the best selling author of ALONE, get an interview with him for the Sun Times and Carrie can write what she wants to write. Carrie hungrily accepts the offer-dying for a chance to prove herself. Her editor informs her that it won't be easy- Finn is a person everyone wants to find and interview, but no one has had luck. 
 Carrie begins the search for Finn and within a few days has managed to track his whereabouts down. With a little help from a friend of Finn's, she makes it to the cabin in Alaska- where she is met with a chillier response than the weather. Finn is not happy to find that a reporter has found him and he makes his feelings very clear. Due to the weather, Carrie has to stay with him, though. As they get to know one another, both are surprised at the attraction they feel- yet neither act on it. Right before Carrie leaves, Finn kisses her and tells her to not write the story. 
 Back home in Chicago, Carrie weighs the pros and cons- and decides she will not write the story. Finn and Carrie begin emailing and talking to each other daily- falling in love even though there is miles between them. Both recognize they are very different, and yet; the feelings the city girl and the rustic outdoorsman have for each other are real. Their relationship is like a fairy tale, until a misunderstanding causes them to question everything that has happened between them. 
 Can Finn and Carrie find common ground? Will Carrie decide to write the article on Finn? Will Finn step out of his comfort zone and into an unknown world with Carrie?

Max is in trouble. Her parents are coming, expecting her to be the well-behaved and presentable young lady they think she should be, and then there's the matter of the non-existent perfect boyfriend. Okay, so she does have someone, but he's nothing like the kind of guy they think she should be with, and that means she's got to come up with a plan. Enter "Golden Boy," perfectly dressed, well-spoke, and absolutely presentable. Now they just have to convince her parents that they're a couple, wait till her parents leave, and then they'll just go their separate ways... Right? 
 The Verdict: I absolutely loved Losing It, and watching Cade walk away broken hearted when Bliss fell for Garrick was hard. So I was thrilled that the super-sweet guy would get his own story -- and happily ever after, with any luck -- in Faking It. 
 I suppose the plot is a bit standard; there are an awful lot of stories that start with the whole "will you pretend to be my significant other?" bit, but that didn't make me look forward to it any less. On the outside, Max is edgy, refusing to conform, but she's really quite normal in that she simply wants the independence to pursue her passion - music. Cade, on the other hand, is not what he seems at first glance. He looks straight laced and somewhat conservative, but we know he's fun loving, teasing, and even a bit mischievous at time. He and Max may at first seem like an odd couple, but they really are quite perfect for each other. 
 Unfortunately, I read Faking It directly on the heels of Losing It, and it's impossible not to compare the two. In fact, I loved the first book so much that I was dying for more, so I guess in that sense I went in with really high expectations. But where Garrick and Bliss were both sweet and hilarious, where I spent just as much time laughing at Bliss's antics as I did swooning over Garrick, Faking It, while sweet, lacks a lot of that crazy fun. I imagine if I picked this book up entirely on its own, without having a clue about the story that came before it, I probably would given it a higher rating, but since I picked it up primarily because I wanted more of what book one so perfectly offered, I ended up being a little disappointed. Faking It is a sweet, solid love story, and it's great to see Cade get his well-deserved happily ever after, but I wanted the insanity of the first book, and it didn't really carry over into this one.
Well, I honestly didn't see that coming.

 It's about Lina, who's mother dies, and she is sent to live in Florence with her dad whom she never met. While she is there, she is given one of her moms old journals that tells the story of the year that her mom spent in Florence. As Lina reads the journal, she explores all the sites that her mom mentions, and also uncovers a deep secret that changes Lina's life. Of course, her cute Italian neighbor, Ren, is there to help her. 4 "Tick and White Feathers" Stars! The Air He Breathes is my first read by Brittainy Cherry. I had been hearing such great things about this author (who also penned the popular 2014 title, Loving Mr. Daniels) that I decided it was finally time for me to dig in and experience her writing for myself. Well, I have to say that I was thoroughly enchanted with Ms. Cherry's talented intermixing of complex characters, mild suspense, heartfelt romance and even a touch of humor! 
 However, please note that a large component of this book is learning how to survive the death of a person you were in love with. In fact, The Air He Breathes compounds this sad theme times two, as both the heroine and hero are faced with this devastating reality. Thus, be prepared to break out the tissues, because this story is surely going to bring out the tears. 
 While I have to admit that death and loss are not among my favorite subjects when reading a romance, I was truly mesmerized by Ms. Cherry's talented prose and I loved how Ms. Cherry was able to weave together several sub-plots, along with the romance, to keep the reader truly on their toes. Therefore, I'm looking forward to experiencing more of Ms. Cherry's talented writing in the near future!

Liesel Meminger is a young German girl who lives during the World War II era. Her story starts years after she becomes a foster child and moves in with her new family. While living through the Holocaust, Liesel steals books. Her father helps her learn to read them and pretty soon she has her own shelf. The novel isn't only about that, it does have dialogue and other subplots. She has a friend, Rudy (he was my favorite) who's very charismatic. But that isn't what was most interesting or what I liked most about this novel. The structure of it was captivating. For every book, an important event happens. For every issue there's a solution. The author is very clear and consistent with his plot, setting, characters... everything. 
 Death narrates this novel. It's as depressing as it sounds but somehow I kept reading. I didn't expect to love this book as much as I do. Mainly it isn't a happy book, but there are happy moments. I also liked death's personality. I know, death has a personality? Yupp. It was interesting to see how he spoke, especially about the Holocaust. It's empathetic. Something I did not expect. 
 "On many counts, taking a boy like Rudy Steiner was robbery--so much life, so much to live for--yet somehow, I'm certain he would have loved to see the frightening rubble and the swelling of the sky on the night he passed away. He'd have cried and turned and smiled if only he could have seen the book thief on her hands and knees, next to his decimated body. He'd have been glad to witness her kissing his dusty, bomb-hit lips. 
 Yes, I know it. 
 In the darkness of my dark-beating heart, I know. He'd have loved it all right. 
 You see? 
 Even death has a heart." 
 I can't write a review on this novel and not talk about Rudy. I loved him. I loved how the author made him, what he stood for, and everything and anything he said. It's amazing how he Zusak used a kid to show the true problems of this era. 
 I do recommend the book to someone who is looking to expand their reading. I will say it wasn't a quick read. It did take a while to get through the whole book and when I finished I felt like I had to take a really deep breath in order to shake some of the feeling off. I wouldn't read the book again but for the right reasons. It was SO impactful that I don't think I can bring myself to read it without getting emotional again. It opened my eyes, sometimes even a sad book is a really really good one. It's a classic.

*4.5* What a book! It put me through a rollercoaster of emotions. Scarlet and Theo are complex characters. I think what made this book so interesting is the moral ambiguity of it all and yet each decision or reactions these characters made, I understood. 
 This book started with humor. Theo was an asshole from the beginning and I liked how Scarlet handled him. There's a sensitive trigger  terminal cancer , but I liked how it was handled. I really dislike it when a heroine chases the hero, but in Scarlet's case and what she had gone through and all her philosophical musings I saw her as someone wanting to save Theo because this man is consumed with revenge. She did have her breaking point. 
 Losing the will to live cannot be understood until--it happens. It's not that the pain is too much; it's the ability to feel anything has been suffocated by the pain. It's literally mind-numbing. 
 ... letting go takes far more strength than holding on. 
 Scarlet's father, Oscar was also a great character and I was sad with how things happened. 
 I'm so glad we got Theo's POV. Some of the things he did to Scarlet would have been unforgivable, but we could see how loving her is killing him. I don't want to reveal more, the nature of his revenge ... etc... but if he goes through with it, he won't be coming back from that. 
 I'm just glad it ended in a  HEA . 
 Why not 5 stars. The "I am Scarlet Stone...." became a bit too much. 
 This book has also encouraged me to juice carrots. I really believe in the natural healing of food. I'm hoping in a month I won't need reading glasses. ;)

I'm going to start by emphasising that I really enjoyed O'Shea's Rock Bay series. Those are solid contemporary romances, which work well within the usual formula. I like things which do exactly what they set out to do and do it well. This one sounded as good - teacher protagonists, childhood sweethearts negotiating adult relationships, just enough conflict to make it sound interesting. It sounded like a perfect rainy Sunday book. 
 Instead, it kept disappointing. This felt like it would have been a short story if the characters had been allowed to finish a conversation. Every time they started to talk about their issues (the usual stuff: teenage jock boy pretended not to know geek boy boyfriend, relationship crashed and burned, geek boy still holds grudge as adult, jock boy pines) the conversation just stopped. There wasn't even the usual sort of convenient interruption. They just kept wandering off in different directions mid-conversation for no reason except to prolong the conflict and make the book a bit longer. All this, whilst they were sharing a bed, but not managing to mention all the feels they were supposedly having. 
 Besides that, the characterisation was paper-thin. All I learnt about young Rory was that he had shiny hair, lived next door, and Ben fancied him. Given the whole emotional arc of the book rested on their history, some sort of vague character sketch beyond that would have been helpful. 
 So, points for writing about teachers in a way that didn't make me want to stab someone. Minus points for author plot manipulation completely unsuspending any disbelied I might have.

Disclaimer: This review is for all three books in the trilogy, and speaks of all three of them as a work as a whole, not each book as its own separate entity. Therefore, the three star rating is for all three books as a trilogy, not each book separately. 
 The Hollow Trilogy by Jessica Verday is a series of three books: The Hollow, The Haunted, and The Hidden. The series deals with high school junior Abbey Browning as she grieves for her recently deceased best friend Kristen Maxwell. Abbey seeks solace at the Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, where Kristen is buried and a place where she and her best friend used to spend time visiting the covered bridge and the grave of Washington Irving, author of the story the trilogy draws its main inspiration from. At the funeral, Abbey catches the eye of a handsome stranger, soon to be known as a teenage boy named Caspian, and from there they find insta-love and insta-hardship and all shit hits the fucking fan for the rest of the series. 
 Okay, let me pause for a second to say I was raised just outside of Sleepy Hollow, NY. I literally had a five minute drive to get to this town, and it is near and dear to my heart. I love the legend and all of the history the town holds, and I like seeing and reading adaptations of the legend and anything else to do with the town. That probably is one of the reasons why I was extra judgmental on this series. When I saw that there was going to be a YA paranormal romance retelling of The Legend of Sleepy Hollow, I became excited - although a bit apprehensive (I was a teenager myself during the whole Twilight fiasco and was well-too aware of the boom of poorly written schlock that authors tried to pass off as paranormal YA romances). I didn't want to assume that this first book or this whole series was going to suffer from that same syndrome, but it was hard to ignore. I was hoping for a good story that showed not only the legend but my own basically-hometown of Sleepy Hollow in a good light. 
 I got what I didn't want, but Sleepy Hollow got so much worse. 
 First off, there is no covered bridge near the cemetery. There are several small bridges in the cemetery, and a bridge claiming to be the Sleepy Hollow Horseman Bridge just outside of it - although if Kristen were hanging out there, she would have been hit by a car, not murdered , as it is a heavily traveled, four lane road. Sleepy Hollow is not some cutesy little town where they obsess over the story every single day of the year - the only time you really get anything to do with The Legend of Sleepy Hollow is during October, when everything in the area tries to jump on the tourist train and create any event possible that can involve the Headless Horseman. People come from everywhere and eat that shit up, but it's hardly the locals that care. The high school's prom is during June, just like any average prom, and it is not some Halloween-themed shindig called "The Hollow Ball". The students at the high school just about care about the legend their town is named after - trust me, I taught there for a few months. The town is mostly made up of immigrants and really preppy rich families who live in the fancy rich areas just across from the cemetery - this was a detail that Verday got right by placing Abbey's house there, though again, she wouldn't have been able just to walk to the cemetery all peacefully whenever she wanted to. That four lane road I mentioned? Yeah, try crossing that any time of the day sweetheart. 
 I could complain more about the bad hand the town of Sleepy Hollow was dealt, but I understand there is some creative license allotted to an author and I'll leave my complaining at the former paragraph (but again, just to say, nothing irked me more than that damn Hollow Ball. NO ONE WOULD HAVE THEIR PROM IN OCTOBER WHEN STUDENTS ARE TAKING LAST MINUTE SATS AND FINISHING COLLEGE APPLICATIONS. IT JUST DOESN'T HAPPEN, WHETHER YOU LIVE IN SLEEPY HOLLOW OR SALEM OR WHEREVER ELSE HALLOWEEN TOURISM RUNS RAMPANT). 
 Here are some things I did like: Abbey and Kristen's friendship was really well done. Verday did a good job getting across Abbey's grief and it was nice that Abbey grieved throughout all three books. Ben was a great character, all sweet and goofy, and actually didn't end up becoming that dreaded third piece in a love triangle, so kudos to her for that as well. Cyn was also a nice addition; it was nice to see Abbey start to make more friends and attempt to have a normal life. Her passion for perfumes gave her a hobby and something to flesh out her character a bit more. 
 But here's what was bad. 
 First off, Vincent Drake. As a villain, he was just horrid. Stupid motives, stupid attempts at making him scary or creepy - that whole way she had him say DE-LICIOUS was more annoying than effective.  He was lame, and I can't believe any of the characters struggled against him. The other Revenants were okay, outside of Cacey and her pointless obsession with Coke, which was probably supposed to be funny but also came of as just stupid. Abbey's willingness to just up and die  to spend forever with Caspian was not well done, and the whole ending of The Hidden was so rushed just to get her to complete him that you feel like Verday really cheated her of a chance to ever chose the other option - life, her perfume shop, some other guy.  
 Perhaps the worst parts of the book, however, where what Verday attempted to do with the actual legend. 
 I really don't know if Verday thought out how she wanted to use The Legend of Sleepy Hollow properly, or if she just wanted to write a scary ghost love story and toss in the legend as an attempt to market the trilogy to a larger audience. It didn't need the addition of the legend at all, and the legend certainly gains nothing to its adaptation cannon by having this trilogy attached to it. We get glimpses of the story's importance in The Hollow, but it is literally all mentioned right at the end of the book in a way that makes me think Verday just tossed it in to make it relevant. There's next to no more mention of it or how it relates to the plot in The Haunted. In The Hidden, it basically is thrown in as last-minute exposition to make the villain's already stupid motive even more stupid. Caspian is descended from Ichabod Crane - and that's literally it. No other mention of it before one brief mention in the third book at the end of the story, and it basically doesn't relate to the plot at all. Katrina Van Tassel and the Headless Horseman are happily protecting the cemetery as Katy and Nicholas, in love forever and ever.  And that's it. That's all the purpose the legend serves. 
 What a waste of a great short story. 
 And finally, Caspian Crane 
  Vander himself. He's boring. That's really all I can say. For a YA love interest, he was just dull and boring. Certainly not someone worth tossing your life away for , although Abbey sure missed the note on that one. I can't think of anything worth saying about him. He was written all moody and deep and as a suffering artist/poet boy, but he was just boring. 
 The sad thing is, Jessica Verday's second series that deals with Edgar Allan Poe and many other works of classic science fiction is so much better than this series. That that wasn't what she wrote first is a shame, because maybe she'd be a bit more popular. That this series was allowed to define her is sad. 
 That this series is allowed to define anything involving The Legend of Sleepy Hollow at all is the true crime. There is fanfiction out there written better than these books, and that is all you really need to know when sitting down to read this.

The premise of this novel is preposterous, but if you can get past the implausibility, as I did, you might enjoy it. 
 Kendra Donovan is a present day, kick-ass FBI agent. After a mission goes horribly bad, she goes rogue and takes off for England to exact revenge on one of the men to blame. While taking part in a reenactment dressed as a 19th century maid, she escapes into a secret passageway in an old English manor. Something happens, and she emerges in the same manor in the 19th century. 
 She plays the part of a Lady's maid at a manor house party while trying to figure out what has happened to her. She is absolutely hopeless, of course, and very American to boot. (That is used as an excuse for almost everything she does wrong.) Then a woman is found murdered, and her FBI training kicks in. 
 As I said at the beginning, it's preposterous to think that upper class English men of the 19th century would allow a woman, a servant no less, to investigate a murder, interview her betters and watch post mortem exams. But the writer did a good enough job convincing me to play along that I quite enjoyed it. 
 There were some plot twists I did not see coming, and the interactions between the modern day American and the 19th century English men were a hoot. Kendra is a strong female lead who foolishly allows herself to get trapped in a dangerous situation but gets out of it without any help from a man. . 
 If you like mysteries, Regency romance, historical fiction, time travel, strong female leads, or some combination, you might want to read A Murder in Time.
