When I picked up Vitro and read the premise I was absolutely sure that it had the potential to be just my kind of book. I tend to pick up anything related to biological engineering because I find the possibilities to be endless and it's just so fascinating. This stood out from the other books -- I guess I'm drawn to the lighter, interesting covers, especially amongst the dark and angsty covers that are so common... 
 In some ways, this book was just like its title. It was fresh and I enjoyed that. I think what stood out most to me, surprisingly, was the humour in Jim's narration. I actually really enjoyed reading things from his perspective, his thoughts were very funny and it was so much nicer than some of the heavy "SHE IS MY WORLD AND I AM DRAWN TO HER" possessive narrations of many other MMCs. Lux would have been my second favourite, even though it at times came close to annoying. I think what worked for me here was the imprinting idea  -- that was amazing -- and I loved how her narration showed it. The only complaint was that I feared it was going to lead to conflict between Lux and Sophie over Jim.  I'm glad the novel stayed away from that. 
 That being said, the love was working really well until the end ready to take a bullet for him because love?? Why couldn't her motivation be the fact that she dragged him into it, or that they were childhood friends and she wanted to protect him? Like I get that they're saying it grew out of that, but they'd only been back together for two days. I've met friends I moved away from and the first two days can be awkward as hell as you try to work out how you fit together again.  
 I think the problem was it kinda fell flat for me. I loved the ideas, but Sophie didn't really catch on too quickly, and when she did she accepted things way too easily. If someone told me I was a Vitro I would question it a hell lot more. The proof given was a photo of her 'mum' holding her in a lab, but that didn't seem all that weird given the explanation she was given. Believing something for 17/18 years means it's supposed to be hard to let that go, especially when they one telling you is who 'Nicky' was.  
 Another problem was the villains. They seemed kinda...I think they had potential, and in one I think it kinda deflated, and in the other I think it became cartoony. I loved certain elements like Nicholas using his ability to guilt Sophie to get her to do what he wanted, the lengths he was willing to go do and the way he was so far detached from it all.  But... his motivations seemed all over the place and he spent a lot of time talking?? Like, it's kinda the cliche badguy blabbing in critical moments -- he should have shut them up, got what he wanted or demonstrated his power. He had an entire group of Vitros at his command-- why not keep some behind and use them as back up when the others are caught? Also Strauss and the gas chamber?? Jim was right when he called it fascist. The connection meant that it seemed rather extreme? I'm not sure if that was intentional but it just really didn't work for me. I think it would have made more sense for them to have a euthanasia to put the Vitros to sleep, clinically killing them rather than torturing them and leaving a very very dangerous gas on an island with people like Mary and Nicholas around??? But I digress  
 In all, it was a really quick read and aside from a few minor things here and there it was kinda a nice read. I love the ethics and the questions it brought up, especially because it made it clear without rubbing it in to the reader's face. That was nice. The technology behind the chips and code  also worked well for me. I think part of why this book didn't completely work for me is because I had higher expectations because this kind of premise is what I adore...

Penelope Wallace meets Charlotte Ferris at a bus stop, when the latter insists Penelope accompany her to her Aunt Clare's for tea. It is 1950s London, and the two young women, seemingly very different, become fast friends, moving through elegant parties, sharing a crush on singer/heartthrob Johnnie Ray, and exploring various love interests. Together they weather the changes in British post-war society, and in their own family situations. 
 I really enjoyed this novel. Through her characters, Rice lets the reader experience a taste of high society and Bohemian counterculture, landed gentry living in genteel poverty, the excesses of youth, and the fascination with flashy Americans. Despite our many differences (age, nationality, social standing, etc), I connected to these characters. I loved how they developed as they matured. Penelope, Charlotte, Harry and Inigo are witty, thoughtful, confused, eager, charming and vulnerable. 
 I applaud Rice for what she did "not" have the characters say and do, as much as for what she did have them comment upon and experience. They felt real to me, and while I have no desire at all to relive my teens, I was happy to go along with them on their journey towards adulthood.

Voltaire was one of the prominent philosophers from the Enlightenment movement, an era in which religious dogmatism, the aristocracy and intellectual dependence were frowned upon by thinkers who employ reason and the scientific method in attempting to understand their environment and form a just model of society. Such "enlightening" ideas feature prominently enough in his infamous novella Candide ; but to perceive it solely as a product based on the principles of the Enlightenment Age is to miss out on half the novel's satire, and almost all the fun. 
 Voltaire was clearly a man who disliked his society. While Candide is foremost an attack on Leibniz's admittedly absurd theory of Optimism (that every misfortune or evil is justified by the benefits in which it will eventually result, based on the idea that a perfect God would only create a perfect world - in which a minimum of evil is a necessity), but also fiercely criticizes the nobility, religious orders, colonialism, war, art, futile traditional practices and even individual writers, contemporary or otherwise. The story follows the young Candide, thrown out of his German household, traveling the western world in search of love, all the while encountering events which either plainly contradict his private tutor's teachings of Optimism, or which reflect the lunacy, cruelty and hypocrisy of western civilization. Although Candide was written in the eighteenth century, the modern reader will with certainty recognize such flaws in his own society. 
 The book's mere 100-odd pages comprise more ideas and opinions than most philosophical novels; it is rich with insight and witty in its satire. Candide's most comical moments are however directly related to the narrative itself; Voltaire seems to revel in satirizing the quintessential novel of the 1700's, by developing characters in complete contrast to their ideal roles (Candide's long-lost love, Cunegonde, is continuously raped by men)  , and by ceaselessly depicting ridiculously over-the-top situations. A very insightful and funny novel.

AT LAST I have read the sequel to the wonderful Sunbolt! Intisar Khanani is a fantasy author who really deserves a good, let's say, 75% more fame than she is currently receiving, so let's all get on spreading the word far and wide, okay, team? Read the novella Sunbolt if you haven't yet, and then get straight on to the superb sequel, Memories of Ash. 
 Our protagonist, Hitomi, is learning magic from the secretive, kindly mage Stormwind, with whom her vampire friend Val left her at the end of Sunbolt. Many of her memories of her former life are gone, and she is focused primarily on cultivating her powers and staying under the radar. All of her peace is shattered when the High Council (led by Hitomi's old enemy Blackflame) summons Stormwind to stand trial for treason. Though Stormwind accepts her fate, Hitomi is determined to go after her and save her from unjust imprisonment and possible death. 
 If you are needing (as I am) some straight-ahead fantasy adventure stories, I can't recommend Intisar Khanani's work enough. Her worldbuilding here, as in the last book, is superb, everything from the limitations to Hitomi's look-away charm to the differing societal norms for the desert nomads as opposed to the people of the Mekteb (the school where magicians get trained). Possibly my favorite thing about watching Hitomi travel to so many different locations is that Khanani seems to believe in the fundamental goodness of people. Wherever Hitomi goes and however slim her chances seem of rescuing Stormwind, she always meets people who are kind and good. At a time when the world feels less and less hospitable to strangers, Memories of Ash was a balm. 
 As with Sunbolt, this book ends in a satisfying way that nevertheless leaves the door open for many more adventures to come. Hitomi finds herself, at one point, in a land that's been shattered by vicious magics, and she makes a promise to come back someday to try her hand at fixing it. Part of this is my current state of mind, but most of it is Khanani's gorgeous world- and character-building: I absolutely cannot goddamn wait to see Hitomi throw her considerable energy and talent into healing the whole world.

Powerful stuff. 
 'Grey' a young English student comes to Tokyo to speak to a Chinese professor whom she believes has evidence of a war crime in Nanking. As a child she read about the crime, acted in a tragic way upon what she read, but has been unable ever since to make anyone believe that the account existed--which would thus exonerate her from her crime. In exchange for the information she seeks, the old man wants her to investigate the strange longevity of a local crime lord. He is reputed to be taking some kind of Chinese rare medicine, and the old professor wants to know what it is. 
 Desperately wanting answers to her questions, Grey becomes entangled in a horrific web of violence and deceit that has its very roots in the secret she is trying to uncover. 
 This story is pretty harrowing. Be warned. I couldn't put it down. Highly recommended.

This is it. This is it . This is the imaginary friend story that culminates into a fantastic novel by Matthew Dicks, an author I've never heard of, writing the novel I've never heard anything about. Thank goodness my Adolescent Literature class offered this book, because this was a wonderful world to get lost in. 
 Budo, the imaginary friend of Max, has been around for quite some time. It's not until a teacher believes she can "cure" his friend that they become separated. Budo hurries to save his friend Max when everything is against them. 
 It shows that this book is written by a teacher who understands kids, perhaps even worked with someone who is characteristically on the spectrum. Matthew Dicks led me to believe that Max was a real child who I knew from being in the classroom with. Budo also made his way into my heart. 
 I'd highly recommend this novel for those who are looking for a great novel about imaginary friends and what happens when their time is up. 
  
 I personally think that when Max finally does let go of Budo, he still lingers as part of Max and his growing up. He absorbs him, if that makes sense. All of the lessons that Budo taught him and how he kept him safe, this becomes a part of him.

This is the second in the trio of Wattpad stories Marissa Meyer wrote to compliment the Lunar Chronicles books and it tell the story of Wolf's past, before he came to Earth and met Scarlet. 
 The story opens with Wolf as a twelve year old boy called Ze'ev, or Z for short, being taken from his home by the queen's thaumaturge to join her bonkers army of wolf-man hybrids and then goes through his training in the army. 
 I really liked this installment of the short stories. It was very violent because it details the way Wolf became the Alpha of his pack, but because he's my secret boyfriend (so secret he doesn't even know it) it was interesting to see where he came from and a snippet of his life from before the army. It bodes well for our future as a couple, I think. 
 To get all the references in this story it would probably be best to read it after Scarlet.

I was so excited to read Poison Study because I knew it would be one of those books I fall in love with. Everything I read about it excited me, and for me, it lived up to the hype. I finished it in two days, and though near the end I wasn't digging it quite as much, this book still held my interest and gave me exactly what I wanted. 
 So the premise is that Yelena is slotted for execution when she's taken to the Commander's adviser. What she believes to be a sentence end up being a job offer, one she readily takes. Becoming the Commander's food taster is a far more appealing future, but Yelena soon discovers the dangers inherent in her position and that there are those who wish her dead. 
 The Good 
 * Yelena!!! I love her so much, I just want to hug her and keep her safe. I seem to just have a soft spot for traumatized characters, and I've especially empathized with Yelena. I also really loved how she was desperate for friendship, but also less open to trusting, and struggled to reconcile the two. She was so caring and kind, but wrestling with so much, and by the end of the book I felt like a proud mother. 
 Oh, and when she told Margg off? One of my favorite little moments in the book.  
 * The side characters. I'm not as goo-goo eyes over Valek as everyone else seems to be, but Janco and Ari are the loves of my lives. Apparently they don't end up together but let's be real, they're gay. I won't accept anything less.  Also I love Irys and wanted more of her, so I hope the next books feature more of her. The Commander also grew on me, and I love the relationship between him and Valek. 
 * The premise is really interesting, as is the world-building. I just love the idea of military districts and this castle stripped of its history to be used as offices for its new occupants. It's not something usually seen in fantasy, and I'm a big fan of it, the Code of Conduct especially. 
 The Bad 
 * The prose is exceptionally clunky at times. I was disappointed because I thought it would stop me from getting into the book when I first started reading, but I eventually was able to look past it. But still, there were some phrases that just read strangely. And the characters kept saying things, or Yelena's narratives would have more modern-sounding words and turns of phrases that it kind of mucked up the setting for me. Speaking of... 
 * The world-building, as interesting as it is, also confused the hell out of me. Mainly because I have no basis for what era this is supposed to be set in. I was thinking this would be late medieval, but changed my mind to early industrial before I realized there's no gunpowder. Then it starts talking about conveyor belts, so now we're at least in the 20th century. 
 It's a secondary world so not everything has to line up with the real world, but there should be at least some coherency. It feels like the author wanted medieval weapons, but the plot required post-industrial technology, so she mixed the two of them together without explaining why they have conveyors and are still using wagons, and why there's factories but guns don't seem to exist. 
 * The romance. I loved how it was being handled for most of the book. The relationship developing between Valek and Yelena intrigued me, but then it went from 10 to 100 near the end. I guess I'm not convinced of the strength of their emotions, and that all of a sudden they'd be confessing their love so eloquently, especially considering the circumstances at the time. 
 And it was so corny. I'm sorry, but it was so weird having one character who is this assassin/poisoner be waxing poetic about his love for Yelena. This is honestly just subjective, and I'm more into subtler romances, so I was kind of disappointed that by the end of the book the romance seemed to take over everything else. I also wanted to see Yelena overcome trauma in order to be with Valek, but that didn't happen. 
 * One of the reasons I was really interested in Poison Study is because there is a trans character. And well... I was annoyed at the handling of the Commander being trans. But according to spoilers I've read, the character isn't actually trans? So idk how to feel about this, it was just one of those "huh ok" moments for me.  
 It looks like I disliked more about this book than I actually did, but that's just because when I don't like something, I want to explain my feelings thoroughly. 
 Overall, I really enjoyed this book and I'm looking forward to reading the rest of the series!

When I first got this book from Amazon, I thought there were some sort of weird marks on the cover resulting from it being at the warehouse for too long. When I couldn't scrub it off, I checked the book cover online and saw that the book was meant to look like it was scratched up. After finishing the book, it was quite clear why this was: the lines crossing the brick heart were meant to show Yunior's fragmented self, plus the way the story was told (in 9 fragments that were only loosely connected). 
 The jaggedness of the lines symbolized the vivid and raw view it portrayed of Dominican immigrant life. Junot Diaz does not attempt to tone down his language, which leads to total immersion (dare I say drown-like) into the lives of these people, showing the hardships that they experienced accurately, and not being afraid to address controversial issues. Junot Diaz once again proves himself to be a master weaver of the immigrant experience in America.

 Sean Griswold's Head is a quirky, cute, humorous, book about a girl, Payton Gritas, who used to have a different color highlighter for all the different types of literary devices. That is, until her dad is diagnosed with MS and suddenly she can't even find a pair of matching socks! Payton's parents make her go to the school guidance counselor after she finds out, her counselor tells her that she needs to choose a focus object that will help her to concentrate her emotions. Needless to say Payton chooses the back of Sean's head as her focus object. All of Lindsey's main characters are very unique and well rounded characters who are all easily liked, and connected with. 
 Most YA books center around romance and everything else comes in second. I really liked that this book was more centered on family and friendship but also had that romance aspect without drowning everything else out. So quit judging books by their cover and go pick this one up. You'll be glad you did!

Sigh... I'm kind of disappointed in this one. Not completely distraught but not absolutely thrilled either. There were a lot of interesting gears turning but it just never got to ignition. I just wish it had been put together better. I found the writing to be pretty good in general but I just didn't really care for the story. 
 I found several things to be entirely unrealistic. Mind you, most of the story takes place in a land called Algid where magic is a real thing. Even with that being the case, there were unrealistic things. For example, in the beginning Snow is in an insane asylum. However, she's been in there for 10 years because of one thing she did when she was 6 and sometimes she has a bad temper. THAT'S IT. What? I'm pretty sure they don't lock up children for their whole lives and drug them constantly for one incident where no one even got killed. Also, she never goes to school there. Snow even says there's no school and everything she knows comes from reading the encyclopedias in the library. HOW DOES SHE EVEN KNOW HOW TO READ IF SHE'S NEVER BEEN TO SCHOOL AND NO ONE TEACHES HER ANYTHING!? I could go on and on but I'll just stop there. On the bright side, one thing I actually did like was how Snow described all the different drugs she had to take by naming them after the seven dwarfs. 
 I think the main issue here was that Snow is a genuinely insufferable character. She's just one of the most self-absorbed characters I've even seen. The whole time, the people of Algid are begging her to help them (because she's the special snowflake prophesied chosen one of course) and she's just like "O so the King is evil and kills people... Too bad! Sucks to be you! Now why don't you help me find my boyfriend and get out of here? O and I'm going to be super ungrateful the whole time too. Sound cool?" What an asshole! Why would anyone attempt to help you when you won't do anything in return for them? It's utter narcissism. The whole reason her mind starts to change and she kind of cares about Algid is because she meets her twin sister. It literally took someone who has her exact same face to get her to care about Algid. The narcissism level here is off the charts!  Then she like has a romance with literally every guy she meets. Girl... aren't you there to find and save your boyfriend? I understand that she's been in an asylum and all so there weren't really a lot of options in romantic interests before now. But still... EVERY boy? Why do they even like her? It's entirely unfathomable to me. 
 I'm willing to put up with quite a bit if I really like the characters. The problem is that I downright loathe Snow. She's just so terrible of a person/character that I don't think I would really bother to continue on with the second book whenever it comes out. Which is really unfortunate because I think this was well written enough to get me to stick with it if I had actually liked the heroine.

This story took my breath away but made my heart heavy. It was a difficult read, and if possible, was far more emotional than the first book. Despite this, I love the swoony, old-fashioned romantic language of this novel. Simons intermixes the heartache with just the right amount of sex, and like the Bronze Horseman, I couldn't put it down. 
 Tatiana and Alexander are separated by continents, and each wonders if the other is alive. There is no way they can be sure! Both are morose in their loss of the other and dream of their beautiful days together in Lazarevo. 
 With death all around him, Alexander faces the darkest depths of hell: a bloody war, inquisitions and torture at the hands of the NKGB, injury, starvation, and war camps. Through the hardships, he remains admirable and strong, but his situation keeps growing increasingly more desperate, and I felt defeated for him. Soviet government was cruel, unjust, and absolutely insane! A small misstep, or unfortunate circumstance could get anyone declared an enemy of the state and imprisoned in hard-labor camps. 
 Tatiana, now in America, is living a much easier life, but she is in her own hell, too. Years go by, and still she is unable to stop aching for Alexander. She blames herself for leaving him behind, and struggles with the temptation to move on. How can you let your greatest love go ... when he might still be alive? And suffering? You can't do that without having regrets. Her desperate hopelessness tortured her, and me as well. 
  Through her doggedness, and much bravery, the two are reunited, but with an uncertain future. The last third of this book is devoted to very descriptive combat scenes. Lots of detailed gun talk , which I thought odd for a love story. I skim read these parts. 
 My greatest disappointment was the end of the story. I was imprisoned with Alexander, wept with Tatiana on her balcony in New York City; I ran with them through the hills of Berlin under enemy fire and cheered with them when they reached the American Embassy in Germany. There, we were forced to face a brutal reality. Despite having gotten this far, Alexander is considered a war criminal, and the Soviets are desperate to keep him from leaving the country. He may not be able to go back to America with his wife. 
 I died a little with them as they contemplated a life without each other.  
 For all my worry, I expected relief in a major way - fireworks or a marching band were in order, but damn it, I didn't get that. I was offered one line of comfort. ONE lousy sentence, which I had to re-read to be sure it meant what I thought it meant. It was a small, insignificant light at the end of a very dark tunnel. I felt bereft, cheated. I moped around for hours in my despair. 
 I will read the Summer Garden, praying the final book in the series will give me the ending I crave. The author cannot possibly offer us a meager HEA after all the anguish we've suffered. Or can she?

I thoroughly enjoy Butcher's plots where greater overarching story-arcs, sub-plots and uncertainty are present. Side Jobs, however, is a collection of short stories presented as tight packages (often) with little to no ambiguity at the end. Don't get me wrong: many of Butcher's stories in this book are entertaining and well-written; but many of the mysteries ended with each short story. In other words, minimal guess work for me after concluding many of them, reducing my personal reading satisfaction. What can I say? I like fantastic urban mysteries because they increase the likelihood of options and plot-twists I might never consider. 
 Overall, I enjoyed reading Butcher's short stories in Side Jobs with a personal preference towards"Aftermath."  As I alluded earlier, this tale has the greatest amount of details unanswered at the conclusion of its plot.  
 I prefer Butcher's most recent writing style, and it was apparent which stories were older as I read this collection. His style is evolving as he hones his writing-craft (it was most apparent to me after reading his Dresden Files: Small Favor. 
 I am looking forward to resuming my reading of Ghost Story, the next book in his Dresden Files series. His opening presentation (to avoid spoilers) is coming out strong.

I read Going Clear and saw the documentary. Both are chilling in terms of their frankness and you learn so much about Scientology from people who gave most of their lives to it. You get peripheral information on the big names involved, though, which is why I wanted to read Leah's book. She came into the "church" via her mother, who went in via her second husband. What you get in Troublemaker is not an involved Hollywood memoir that delves deep into Leah's career - she talks about it, but her acting is the backdrop. This is an account of Scientology told from a celebrity POV, somebody this organization would normally revere for their status (and money), and it left me with my mouth open in a WTF right to the end. 
 I watched Leah on "The King of Queens" and I remember hearing she was a Scientologist and asking myself, "Wha? How'd she get roped into that?" Reading her book helped me to understand how Scientology appealed to her in her youth, and how it drained her of money for decades and did her few favors. It took four simple words out her mouth ("Where is Shelly Miscavige?") to destroy her standing and consequently crush her faith. Leah prides herself on being a troublemaker, a big mouth, and a badass, and it's interesting that one moment where she showed concern for a friend got her into big trouble. 
 I enjoyed this book - it's blunt and engaging and emotional. You're going to read things here that will piss you off. I leave it with the hope that Leah will find closure by finding out the truth about Shelly.

In some ways I think this may be one of my favorite of Sanderson's works - in a lot of ways I identified with Kenton (constantly seeking approval despite the array of odds against him, the frustrating knowledge that no matter what you do you'll be judged for what you can't do) and for the first part (when he's undergoing the Master's test) I was rooting for him the whole way. 
 So of course when the meat of the story - the attack on the Sand Masters and Kenton meeting Khriss - I was a little let down.  Also GDI another instance where our clever, but socially considered useless hero breaks with tradition and in return he's left orphaned and alone by the narrative. This is why people don't try to break the rules you know  
 The story suffered for two reasons - 1) if you're a fan of Sanderson's works you're used to a more detailed introduction to the world and its particular blend of magic and political atmosphere. Words on a page with more words and sometimes illustrations, but that's it. For a reader like me, who focuses on words not visuals, this is wonderful. WHITE SAND however relied on comprehension of the words while busy visuals were crowding around also trying to make their point. 
 While the "big" illustrations herein were eye-catching, the average panel distracted more then it helped to convey the story. Much of understanding what's happening involved reading the panels, then going back and looking at the illustrations for each. There was a disconnect for me between the two that made it hard for me to comprehend both at once. My problem wasn't with the illustrations themselves - like I said some were eye-catching and the overall style is pleasing - but with the layout of the action and paneling. I'm so far outside the world of comics I'm not sure if the illustrator has done superhero comics before, but it didn't have the easy transitioning between panels you'd expect from a more veteran illustrator. 
 The second problem is more of a "what if" sort. Sanderson has an introduction that details where this idea came from, how he's tweaked it and what made him finally bring it out again but in a different (read: non-prose) format. This is part of his larger "Cosmere" universe (I believe this is set at the earliest point in the timeline), so fans will see hints that tie it in (as this is the first volume of three its largely speculated the next two volumes will contain more clues, hints and information), but not so much that non-fans will be like "what is even?". Moreso the issue is that this was adapted from a novel - one that has not been published and I don't believe there are plans to publish it as such in the near future. 
 It both reads like a Sanderson novel and doesn't. The meat of his novels isn't the dialogue between characters (which is almost always fun), but the world building. A lot of this is shown in context, though some is, by necessity, explained (for instance in WARBREAKER, biochromatic breath is explained to us several different times because its a very visual magic system, whereas in the Mistborn books its shown to us through the characters' actions and reactions). The Sand Masters' (and other spoilery characters) magic may have had more of an effect on me if it had been explained without the visuals to me. 
 If this has been published as a novel first, I would have gotten more out of it. The pacing feels off - not enough time is given to Kenton and his fellow before/during/after the Master's test (it was over and done before I could blink!) so it lost some emotional resonance with me. I liked Khriss quite a bit, but she just...appeared in the story after the too short introduction to Kenton's people. 
 tdlr; - I enjoyed this, I'm happy Sanderson is branching into (yet another) type of media to conquer, but I wish more thought had been put into the pacing and overly busy illustrations.

First, I love the nod that the 12th book in the series is themed with the twelve days of Christmas (the English festival of twelfth night, not the insufferable yuletide carol). Barron's penchant for meticulous historical detail brought to life has always been one of the primary recommendations of this series, and providing glimpses into Austen-era holiday traditions is wonderfully transportive. 
 On one hand, this work nearly rediscovers the best qualities of the earliest books in the series; on the other, it seems to try to recapture that magic by thinly remaking specific scenes, characters, and developments from those very narratives. For instance, one simply cannot escape deja vu when reading of Jane's nighttime hallway encounter with a mysterious and dashing gentleman while clad in a nightdress with her hair loose down her back . 
 No matter. Austen devotees are well-served not only in the details of Jane's lifestyle, travels, and insights, but also -- perhaps most especially -- in the revealing relationship with her beloved sister Cassandra and the character inspirations she may well have drawn from life. Though there are hints of familiar personalities who will eventually appear in different novels, it is the most ridiculous characters of Persuasion who bear the brunt of exposure here. 
 One additional quibble: the structure of dividing sections with "The First Day," "The Second Day," and so on would have made more sense if those chapters didn't repeatedly contain events that crossed evenings and mornings. The technique of retreating a few steps to explain context is fine, but it's distracting and unclear when paired with calendar day separations.

Anticolonial 
 In 1626, the Spanish explorer Panfilo de Narvaez landed in Tampa Bay with six hundred men to claim La Florida for His Catholic Majesty. Through a combination of misfortune and bad leadership, the party was split up, hounded by hostile Indians, decimated by disease, and forced to take to improvised rafts in search of a friendly port. After coming ashore at Galveston Island and remaining there for some years, the survivors then set out on an epic march through Texas and Arizona, crossing the cordillera and going down the west coast to finally reach their compatriots in Mexico City eight years later. Of the six hundred, only four survived: Alvar Nunez Cabeza de Vaca, who wrote a celebrated history of the ordeal, Alonso del Castillo Maldonado, Andres Dorantes de Carranza, and "his enslaved Moor Estebanico." Laila Lalami, who was born in Morocco herself, is interested in the last of these, wondering how the actions of the Spanish colonists must have seemed through the eyes of her fictionalized African protagonist. 
 It is a good story, well told, but it has two quite different audiences. Estebanico (proudly named Mustafa ibn Muhammad ibn Abdussalam al-Zamori before his forced baptism), is writing a "minority opinion" to set against the account by Cabeza de Vaca. It therefore has a special meaning for those who know the official history, who would be enraged or delighted to see the boasts of heroic deeds counteracted by tales of a much less admirable nature. But for those who, like me, do not know the story, Lalami must simultaneously recount the facts and show them through the Moor's eyes. She does this by placing emphasis on all the most arrogant acts of the conquerors: the reading to the empty forest upon landing of the formal Requerimiento declaring the land the property of the King of Spain; the brutal torture of four captured Indians whom they hope to use as guides, on the assumption that Indians are not to be trusted otherwise; the obsession with finding gold to equal that of Moctezuma--Narvaez's envy of the more successful Cortez is a large part of his motivation. 
 I was enjoying the book quite a bit, but had no difficulty putting it down when a more interesting novel arrived; unfortunately, it no longer had the same grip on me when I resumed. The first half was powerful but intermittent. Lalami alternates the Florida chapters with others showing Mustafa's birth, education, early success, and the circumstances that led to his slavery. I did not enjoy these so much, but they made the scenes in Florida that much more vivid. I returned for the second half, which is much simpler, the story of a long trek and feat of endurance. Although Mustafa gradually begins to carve out a new destiny for himself in the New World, the rest of the account becomes something of a slog. But parts of it are very good, the history is fascinating, and the sympathetic protagonist has the beautiful last words.

This was incredibly frustrating. 
 It hits the same problems I had with Before I Fall and the ten pages of The Time Traveler's Wife I managed to get through: if you're going to have a literary book that hinges on a theory of quantum mechanics (alternate universes and divergent timelines), you need to explain your mechanics. It doesn't need to be rigorous. You just need to acknowledge that yes, you're screwing around with timelines, and that, in the universe of the novel, that is permissible. 
 And there's the racism, sexism, homophobia, misogyny, antisemitism, ableism that one is just supposed to expect of a period novel. I'm tired of that. I hate how psychiatry and mental illness is treated in this book. Of course it's going to be awful, it's written to take place between 1910 and 1970! Everything just sucked then! 
 Sure, but if we're going to go through it ten times in five hundred pages, you better start looking at it more carefully. 
 The two sets of arc words are at odds. "Practice makes perfect" versus "needs must"? As Ursula is written as being aware of her own narrative weirdness, neither. makes. sense. 
 It's a cleverly-done trick to explore the different paths available to a woman in interwar Britain, without having to develop more than one character. That's like having four save points for the same Sim that you like, so that one can be a rock star and another can be a scientist and a third can be a politician and another is a housebound novelist who gardens. It's literary cheating. I feel cheated. I never got a narrative out of this; I got a portrait of how much it sucked to be alive for half a century. 
 Of course, the book is beautifully written, and Atkinson did some very, very smart things when shuffling timelines. She took every opportunity she had to build up the background characters more, so the end result was like this character ensemble portrait where one person just happens to be ten or twelve people in the picture. Her word use is gorgeous and I'm looking forward to reading other books of hers. 
 I think I'm just cranky because Connie Willis does this right, and seeing it done wrong, or almost right, or fudged so that it'll be swallowed by lit critics, feels like an insult.

Not only did this defy all those rules^, but damn that Rogerson Biscoe! From a sexy, fun, boyfriend, how did he turn into a psychotic asshole? He starts to dominate Caitlin and suddenly out of the blue, starts hitting her. She doesn't run away, or end things with him, though. She accepts it and fears it. The worst part is nobody notices anything wrong with her when her body is covered with bruises and she starts to become invisible. Even when her mother does say something, it's about something incredibly stupid- she has stopped wearing primary colors, and isn't showcasing her goddamn eyes. I mean, seriously? She hides in herself and seeks solace only in photography. In the end, Caitlin's mother catches Rogerson hitting him and he is arrested. Caitlin ends up at the Evergreen Centre and slowly pieces herself back. Not as the girl she became with Rogerson, but not quite who she was before either. She remade herself, better, and just the way she wanted herself to be. 
 This is a heart wrenching story. Sure, it's a little dark, but it deals with what could happen to any of us. And out of the darkness comes light. Written beautifully, Dreamland By Sarah Dessen is a must read

I decided I would withhold official judgment until I finished the second half -- I'm still wavering between 3.5 and 4 stars...maybe 3.75 is a better estimate? I ultimately enjoyed the story, and the pace picked up quite a bit this time around, but there were still elements that bothered me (some of which appeared in both books and some of which were simply carry-over annoyances from Blackout). 
 When we smash-cut to black (heh) at the end of the last book, our heroes had all finally crossed paths with one another, and come to the awful realization that the drops to Oxford weren't working. They spend much of the first part of the novel comparing notes, and realizing that, thanks to the slippage, all three of them may have altered events -- each historian worries that he/she alone could be responsible for the Allies losing the war. Mike untangled the propeller and rescued Lieutenant Hardy at Dunkirk; Eileen prevented two of her evacuees from leaving the East End; and Polly may have committed any number of small actions, simply by being in 1941 longer than necessary and interacting with so many different people. What follows is a lot of reconnaissance -- trying to locate other historians who may have been in London during 1941 (regardless of the year they may have left from Oxford), trying to determine if there are any noticeable discrepancies in events (which is made more difficult by the fact that misinformation and false reports were a contributing factor to the Allied victory). And also theater rehearsals. Many, many pages of tedious theater rehearsals. Polly is still with the crew she met on her first night in the Blitz, and they're still calling themselves a theatre troupe and putting on plays -- it's interesting from a character development standpoint, I suppose, and it plays a role in the endgame (albeit a tertiary one, and it's a doozy of a stretch, in my opinion), but I wanted there to be more of a payoff. Polly seems to think Sir (can I just say that Game of Thrones has ruined me on nobility titles? It bothered me for 1200 pages that it's not "Ser") Godfrey knew all along she was a time traveler -- I wanted him to turn out to be an historian in the end as well. I suppose there could have been a cheesy "You've had the power to get home all along" quality to that sort of reveal, which is why Willis avoided it. But then again, the ending itself is sort of cheesy as it is.  
 We also catch up with Colin, who is still not the protagonist, no matter what either cover blurb will lead you to believe, but he's still searching for Polly and Eileen across the years. I actually wish we'd seen a little more of his search and less of Polly's rehearsals and Mike's various extracurriculars. Can I just say I felt so dumb not realizing Mike was Ernest in Blackout? Like...duh. It was obvious by the end of Blackout that Mary was Polly, but we saw so little of Ernest in the first book. His chapters were still dull, however. I'm not sure how you can turn espionage into a snoozer, but there you go. Mike/Ernest is just sort of a charisma void, as a character, and given that he only realizes in the last few minutes of his life that he hasn't irreparably fucked up the timeline...I wanted him to figure it out sooner and stop sucking the life out of everything with his despair. He's a little like Angel in the first few episodes of Buffy: "Waah, waah, poor me, the weight of the world is on my shoulders and mine alone. No one has suffered like I have suffered, blee blah bloo." There's just an absence of anything else in that character, he exists solely to bemoan the fact that he couldn't save Eileen and Polly (and plus it's painfully dull to watch him write fake newspaper articles).  I also had issues with the characterization of Eileen. I get that she's supposed to be younger than the others (the evacuated children were her first assignment), but the entire time, the other two treat her not just with kid gloves, but as though she needs to wear a helmet to avoid hurting herself. She's sort of flighty, yes, but not actually stupid, and it bugs me that Mike and Polly expect her to have perfect recall of every conversation she may ever have observed between historians, because she was apparently supposed to intuit that it would be important months later. She's just treated as very simple, and it bothered me, because to me, she didn't read as a simpleton. The constant withholding of information got old really fast too, might I add. Mike and Polly spend the first two hundred or so pages NOT telling Eileen everything they know, on the grounds that they don't want to upset her (because in addition to being simple, apparently she's fragile, because we aren't hitting enough stereotypes at once!). It bothered me on Lost when no one talked to each other or asked questions, and it bothers me when this happens in books, because 99.9% of the time, it's a stall tactic. Kate and Jack refuse to share information with Sawyer because the writers haven't figured out their convoluted mythology yet. And Polly and Mike aren't telling Eileen everything they know because we still have 500 pages of book left! Bah. Quit stalling and get to the point. 
 Ultimately, the ending is satisfying, and the time travel logic mostly doesn't make my head hurt. We get a different understanding of the whole "slippage" concept here as well  at first Mr. Dunworthy (who managed to find a functioning drop and make it to 1941, so he's poked holes in his own theory already) tells Polly that it's a safeguard against alterations -- the drops have shut down so the continuum can repair itself, thanks to the damage historians have caused. The two believe, erroneously it turns out, that the timeline will repair itself by undoing any damage they have caused, i.e., killing everyone they've ever come into contact with, because thanks to Polly/Mr. D./Mike/everyone else -- lots of people are alive who shouldn't be. So Polly spends about 200 pages running around trying to be a coldhearted bitch (which she sucks at) in an attempt to drive people away so they won't get close enough to her to be killed by the timeline's self-defense, or whatever. THEN, about 200 pages later, Polly nearly dies in a V1 explosion, manages to save Sir Godfrey, and has some sort of memory trip/hallucination, wherein she realizes the real real function of slippage. For real this time: 
 "I think we may have been wrong about why they're not opening, and about the slippage. What if it's not to prevent us from altering the course of history? What if it's to put us where we can? To keep us here until we do?" 
 It's a little cheesy, but it's a good deal more optimistic than typical time travel logic! In 11/22/63 we have the opposite -- the past actively resists being changed. So many forces conspire to keep Jake away from situations where he could have the potential to alter the past (what these folks refer to as "divergence points," I believe). When he actually saves Kennedy, he rips a literal hole in the space time continuum, and he has to go back and reset, knowing exactly what he will lose in the process (and what others will lose too). Here, there's a bit of a safer way out -- the past is NOT obdurate (I had to), and the historians in fact have to be there in order to make their small, war-winning alterations. As Polly assures Mr. Dunworthy, they didn't lose the war, "It was always won because we had always come. We were always here. We were always a part of it." And this? This right here is why time travel still ultimately makes my head hurt. Colin goes to collect Polly at the theater, and he only knows where to find her because Binnie (not Eileen) told him in 1995, which occured before he went to 1941. And when Binnie sees him in 1995, she knows that this is when he learns where Polly is, and she knows it because she remembers him being there in 1941, so he had to have figured it out, since it already happened, and ouch.  I mean, at least we aren't mucking about with multiple timelines and alternate universes. It could be so much worse (ahem, Vortex...and also Shadow of Night, because that is just the laziest excuse for time travel I have ever read). 
 Overall I would say this is just shy of 4 stars. I had too many issues with character and structure to give it a full 4, especially since it's so hard to evaluate these books separately. Plus, I read them back to back, and I'm already sort of forgetting what happened in which book! I do with the structure had been more...balanced? I realize that as it's set up, it would be nearly impossible to go the "all of the story for some of the characters route," a la A Feast for Crows...even if book 2 was entirely Colin's story, so much of it is wrapped up in what happens to the others. Though I stand by my assessment that I'd rather have heard more from Colin than we did -- he turns out to be rather important and we barely get to know him. But I'm not at all sorry that I got myself into this 1200 page commitment, and it's actually made me want to check out more of Willis's work.

Smitten's Blog Review 
 My Thoughts 
 I, Kat McCarthy, paranormal fantasy addict, am choosing a contemporary romance about a drag queen as my most loved novel of 2012. Yep. I'm as surprised as you are! 
 I'm finding it hard to find words to explain why this novel affected me so much. It opened my eyes and mind to a completely different world that I knew existed but didn't understand. It's akin to how Fifty Shades of Grey made me feel. But please don't get me wrong; it's nothing like FSoG. It's only the same in how it feels to find a novel that is so different and compelling that it rocks your world and will forever change how you look at things. And you just can't bear to pick up another one for a little while because you don't want to lose that 'high' that comes from reading a novel powerful enough to have that kind of impact. 
 I mentioned in one of my GoodReads status updates I posted that I fell in love with Painted Faces after reading only the Dedication. So obviously before I even read one word of the story itself. If I may, let me share it with you: 
 "For all the men who are women and the women who are men, the men who are men and the women who are women. And those of you who are a little bit of both. You colour my world." 
 I knew immediately that this novel was going to have a significant impact on my thinking. And I was correct. It is a romance that takes time to develop (which I loved) and even though there are lots of issues and happenings that keep the story interesting and made me fret, it's not full of serious angst that we've seen a lot of this year. It's more realistic and true to life. 
 If any of you remember the song Christina Aguilera sang back in the 2003, "Beautiful", you'll remember that it's about how everyone is beautiful, no matter what anyone else says or thinks. It popped in my mind several times reading this novel. If you've never heard of the song, google it. I wasn't a fan of the singer at all, (and this author seems to really be into music so she may kill me for mentioning that artists name in this review, lol!) but that song is incredibly moving. It's guaranteed to arouse all kinds of emotion for those who are considered outside society's perception of 'norm'. That's why it came to mind reading this novel. Many of the characters are perceived as freaks by society but they are truly beautiful. 
 ________________________________________ 
 Freda (Fred) is absolutely fabulous character. As the author summary says, she's offensive at times and doesn't think before she speaks. Which is awesome and hilarious because her wit is an art in and of itself. 
 As an example, this to her gay friend Harry about his fear of vaginas... 
 "As a gay man I have to admit I'm quite squeamish when it comes to women and their downstairs business." 
 That's awful Harry, says Nora. It's just a vagina, why would it make you squeamish? 
 "It's the unknown," Harry replies. The unknown can be frightening to a delicate flower such as myself. 
 I snicker. "Delicate my arse. You can suck a dick, but you can't take the idea of a hairless vagina." 
 It's a good thing her friends love her for who she is. There's also a lot of soul-searching and reflection in this novel and since it's written in 1st person POV (Freda's), it's hers. At times, I would have loved to hear what Nicholas was thinking but the author does such a masterful job at dialogue and describing his reactions, facial expressions and body language that I knew what he was thinking anyway. Plus some of his background of why/when he started dressing as a woman is in the prologue, epilogue and throughout the story's dialogue. Nicolas has many issues, as does Freda, and I just love them both. 
 There are some great supporting characters as well. Enough so that even though this novel is a stand alone, there's potential for a follow up on some of the other characters. I really hope this happens as I found myself not wanting to let go of this story. I'll even wait a while before I pick up another novel because I don't want to replace the story with something else just yet. 
 I guess you can see how much I loved this novel so I'll finish up the review by sharing a few favourite quotes to whet your appetite while not giving the story away. 
 Freda on herself: 
 "The art of laziness is something I perfected many years ago. Often it's nice to just sit back and be a spectator for other people's love lives. I might not have a boyfriend, but I have cupcakes, and those tasty bastards haven't let me down yet." 
 Freda on Nicolas: 
 "I'm thinking he might be a sex pest." 
 Freda trying to figure things out: 
 "Am I attracted to the man behind the costume? Or do I want the man in the costume? It's hard to tell. I think I like the entire package." 
 "Well, I was just wondering about how you classify yourself. Are you a drag queen, or a transvestite or a cross dresser? Or are they all one and the same thing?" 
 Freda on her mother's doctor: 
 "Dr. Knobhead (her nickname for him) clearly got into the profession for the money..." 
 And just one of my favorites from Nicolas... 
 "Every woman is different," he explains. "Some of them make you feel satisfied, others make you feel high, most just make you feel used and dirty, but you Fred, you make me feel cleansed." 
 ________________________________________ 
 So bottom line is if you are looking for an unconventional romance that will impact the way you think and give you an amazing reading experience, Painted Faces will do it for you. I cannot recommend it enough and I believe EVERYONE should read it. I will even go as far to say that if this novel makes it into the right hands, it will make this author famous. 
 Happy Reading!!

 Officer Off Limits by Tessa Bailey 
 Book Three of the Line of Duty series 
 Publisher: Brazen 
 Publication Date: June 10, 2013 
 Rating: 4 stars 
 Source: Bought from Amazon 
 ***Warning: this is an adult book, and for the eyes of mature readers*** 
 Summary (from Goodreads): 
 His need to possess her is non-negotiable. 
 Story Brooks' fiance just called off their wedding two weeks before the happy day. As if that isn't bad enough, her semi-estranged father, an infamous NYPD hostage negotiator, has suffered a heart attack. Not wanting to examine her lack of emotion over the broken engagement, she hops on a plane to reconnect with her father before it's too late. 
 Playboy hostage negotiator Daniel Chase has never, not once, been refused by a woman, so when a debate over hospital snack foods with a delectable kindergarten teacher ends in flat-out rejection, he makes it his mission to seduce her. His only obstacle? She's the daughter of his mentor who implicitly forbade Daniel from pursuing her. 
 Despite her father's warnings and Daniel's troubled past, Daniel and Story can't resist their intense attraction to one another. But when the reason for her fiance's abrupt wedding cancellation comes to light, can Story and Daniel's already forbidden relationship survive? 
 What I Liked: 
 I bought four Brazen books during their Brazen Bash back in July (I know, it's been that long since I read this book!), and of the four of the books, I think this one was my favorite. Maybe. I really liked this book! It was recommended to me by Jessirae from Words, Pages, and Books, so this one was the first of the four that I bought, and read. Back in July. 
 I absolutely LOVE how this book stars. Story and her soon-to-be ex-fiance are in a restaurant. A seafood restaurant. Story HATES seafood. Fisher is such a jerk. He takes her to a place she won't enjoy, forces her to sit through his little I'm-breaking-off-the-engagement speech, and doesn't even let her get dessert! I love how Story handles the situation... she is hilarious! 
 When Story and Daniel meet at the hospital, sparks immediately fly. It's almost expected that after they formally meet each other - as the boss's daughter, and the father's co-worker - and they are alone, things happen. Steamy things happen. Both of them seem to have zero control when they're around each other. 
 It's funny how they go through the entire story tip-toeing around one another - especially when they're around Story's father. I love how Bailey constructs the scenes where Story and Daniel get together. It's clear to me that they are completely physically attracted to each other; at the same time, I can see how they begin to care for each other. 
 The end: I KNEW there was something up with Fisher, and Story's father, and EVERYTHING. I knew it, I knew it, I knew it! It wasn't obvious, I'll give Bailey that, but oh my gosh! Story's father is... sneaky. And Fisher is one big JERK. Poor Daniel! Poor Story! I'm glad they got their happy ending though. I'm glad Story made it work for them. 
 That was something I really liked - the guy didn't drop everything for the girl. It was the other way around! Sort of. I don't want to spoil anything. There's a happy ending, just trust me. 
 What I Did Not Like: 
 This is something I'm going to complain about with all the Brazen titles, but I wish they were longer! I generally buy the longest one - the ones that are close to 200 pages or longer. But seriously! Full lengths novels would be fantastic. 
 Also, I was kind of annoyed with Story and her indecisiveness with Daniel. I'm glad that she made the decision that she did, in the end. But I seriously could not understand her expecting Daniel to make the decision. Poor Daniel... oh, well. Everything ended nicely! 
 Would I Recommend It: 
 Out of all the Brazen titles, I'd probably recommend this one the most! I loved it! Granted, I haven't read any of the newest titles yet. But this one was fabulous! But seriously... this is a very adult title. You are warned! 
 Rating: 
 4 stars. I need to go back and read the other two books in this series! Good thing I don't have to read each one to follow the series. That's the beautiful thing about companion novels!

 The Books of Ember, Book 1; YA SF; 8/10 
 I first heard about this book when the trailers started appearing for the film that is due to begin screening any day now. The trailers looked interesting and comment on the books was also good so I decided to try it for myself. This is a very solid, well done YA novel that tells a fascinating story. While the main characters, teenagers Lina and Doon are well realised, it is the city of Ember itself, built underground and rapidly running out of everything that is the star. It is atmospherically written and easy to imagine. The shortage of everything was well described, so that a precious piece of drawing paper is actually the back of a tin can label and everything must be reused and reused until it can't be used any more. Lina and Doon's quest to find the way out of Ember to a new beginning parallels the collapse of the city itself and they slowly find the answer not only to the "Instructions for Egress" but to the hows and whys of Ember's construction as well. The journal they find of the woman who was one of the first settlers is a touching document that also helps the final pieces of the overall story fall into place. I hear the movie is essentially true to the book and I'm looking forward to seeing it. I also have the sequel, The People of Sparks sitting on the PDA waiting for me to find the moment to read it.

The Silent Waters (Elements #3) by Brittainy C Cherry 
 5 stars!!! 
 "Not all broken things need to be fixed. Sometimes they just need to be loved." 
 Two five star books on the bounce and two authors also receiving their first five-star review from me, it has been an amazing reading week. 
 Brittainy Cherry never fails to deliver with what I crave the most...emotion and with The Silent Waters she delivered one hell of an emotional read. A story that was gripping and captivating from the start, a story that was powerful and emotional, a story that makes you dig deep, a story that resonates, a story that you will never, ever forget. This was a story that definitely left its mark, an indelible print on my heart and my soul, because this book touched me, this book made me think about myself, this book made me think about the author and this book has had me tossing and turning all night thinking about the characters. This is me typing a review with tears streaming down my face as I relive the unbelievable story I read last night, so please excuse my ramblings. This is a story that you should read blind, expect the unexpected and for that reason I am keeping my review about my emotions and a little about the characters. 
 "It amazed me how a heart could shatter in a crowded room and the sound couldn't be heard by a single person." 
 When I read a Brittainy C Cherry book I know that I will probably cry, I know that she will deliver something unique, I know that she will deliver something powerful, I know that she will deliver a story with meaning and I know that she will deliver a message and this message was received loud and clear. Every single character in this book had his or her place, nobody was superfluous to the story developing around them and every character was magical in their own way. I may have wobbled with a couple of characters but alas, I should never have worried, they totally redeemed themselves. 
 Maggie Mae Riley was a beautiful character and when we are first introduced to her as a little girl she will have your heart melting from the very start. Maggie was the apple of her daddy's eye, a single dad that always put his Maggie at the forefront of his thoughts and actions, so when he finally finds "the one" he can finally give Maggie something that she has always wanted...a loving family. Moving into his future wife's home, Maggie is now the proud owner of a step-mother, step-brother and step-sister who welcome her into the family with open arms. They become a tight family unit and the "step" is soon dropped, Maggie was one of their own. 
 "The world keeps spinning because your heartbeat exists." 
 Brooks Griffin was Maggie's brothers best friend. At first, Maggie was a fly in his ointment, that annoying little bugger that kept following him around, dreaming of their wedding and making all the arrangements in her fairy tale bubble. Maggie sent him love notes on the regular and no matter how hard and mean he was back, she never got the hint, she carried on regardless, as far as Maggie Mae Riley was concerned she would marry Brooks Griffin, she loved him, even from such a young age and we all know that little boys "hate" those girls they secretly love. 
 "Love didn't come with guidelines. It flowed into a person with only hope as its current. There wasn't a list of rules to follow, making sure you cared for it correctly. It didn't give you instructions to keep it pure. It simply showed up quietly, praying you wouldn't let it slip away." 
 The Silent Waters follows these two through life as little kids, as teenagers and as adults and because of this there are time jumps. All jumps are relevant and really piece together the lives that these two lead, both together and apart. Told in alternate POV's this book delivers that character connection in spades as you are treated to the thoughts and feelings of both characters. Their growth from little kids, to friends to lovers and everything else in between was tangible. Their connection was solid, they were each other's anchor, they were true soul mates. Their communication through their love of music and books was ingenious and really cemented the bond that these two had. Sometimes life was with them, sometimes life was against them, but even apart these two were tethered. You never forget your first love but you also never forget your soul mate. Brooks' nickname for Maggie was Magnet because 
 "there's this magnetic pull of friendship between us...You're my Magnet" 
 and no matter what life threw at them, they always pulled back together. 
 "You can't just read these books and think that means you're living. It's their story, not yours, and it's heartbreaking to watch someone so young toss away their chance at writing their own story." 
 The synopsis of this book sums it up perfectly, this is a collection of moments, some hurtful, some hopeful and some full of promise, heart breaking moments and breath taking moments. This is a story about a boy and a girl who loved each other, but didn't love themselves. Despite the highs and lows this was their journey, their promise to each other and their fight to deliver on their promises. Brittainy C Cherry is one super talented lady. I felt this authors blood, sweat and tears in these words, I felt the truth behind the characters, but most of all I knew because I had been there. I lost my voice once albeit not through the same circumstances, speech Is a powerful weapon, it's something we take for granted but should be cherished, but as the saying goes, sometimes actions speak louder than words. 
 "Everyone has scars. Some people are just better at hiding them." 
 This is an incredible story; one I would urge everyone to read. Not only is this my favourite of this author but is also one of my favourites of the year, of all time even. Brittainy C Cherry, you nailed it, your authors note broke me but united we stand, don't ever lose your voice again, the book world would be a sadder place for it.

 Adam. Parker. Django. WHY WERE THERE SO MANY GUYS THAT ANNA THOUGHT WAS NICE OR CUTE OR FELT LIKE THEY LIKED HER BECAUSE THEY WERE CONSTANTLY COMPLIMENTING HER?

 Am I the only that thought that Ben was making up that story? Maybe it was real but honestly, it sounded fake...

 There seems to be a lot of debate about if this book is a good read or not. For me, I enjoyed the book, however, I'll admit, I can completely see why so many people were disappointed in it. One of the most obvious reasons (to me) is the fact it is expressly labeled as a young adult fantasy novel. Let me tell you something, there is nothing fantasy-related in this entire book. Not one element that would earn it that genre and yet, even on the back it claims to be just that: fantasy. I'm not one to get overly upset over this as fantasy can be a very hit and miss genre for me, regardless of how much I love it. But there are people out there that love their fantasy and expressly go out of their way to read those books and I can see how they would be highly disappointed about being deceived into reading a book that is 100% NOT FANTASY. 
 Another thing that seems to have bothered a lot of people is how glaringly obvious that Osfrid and Adoria represent England and colonial/post-revolution United States. I actually didn't have a problem with the author using something as commonly known as their past to create her world. Is it obvious? Yes. Did it bother me? No. 
 Now, for the positives. I actually liked this book. Even though "Adelaide" was a bit too perfect for my taste, I enjoyed her tale and I found it to be an interesting journey to a (familiar) new world. I'll admit, I wish at least a little more effort would have been put towards the training the girls have to undergo. They literally skip from day one to eight months in. We aren't even given a glimpse into Adelaide's assessment of the schooling before we jump right to the final exams. I think it would have been interesting if maybe the author could have had her write journal entries about some of her mistakes... like bleaching the vegetables as well as the troubles she had trying to reign in her knowledge and ability of the finer aspects of the curriculum. By doing so, it would have really strengthened this aspect of the book as well as allowed the author a stronger introduction to the attraction between Adelaide and a certain someone. 
 I got the sense this might be the next series for the author and I can't help but hope it isn't. Even though I'm curious to discover more about what happened to Tamsin and Mira, I really didn't feel this was a strong enough book to keep going with the story lines. As a one shot story, this is a decent read, but if you are expecting it to stand up to the standard of Vampire Academy or Bloodlines, this isn't the right book for you. However, if you enjoy a Victorian-inspired culture and the prospect of early U.S., I think you'll enjoy this story and will be able to appreciate both the similarities and differences of the true cultures to that of these fictional ones.

 Scourge of the Betrayer is one of those rare books. A novel that takes the familiar tropes of a particular genre, tweaks them ever so slightly until you (a long time reader) find that your expectations of that genre have been suddenly raised to a new level. 
 And how did Jeff Salyards do that, you ask? 
 Well, mainly, he did it by refusing to be confined by the familiar, formulaic pattern of grimdark fantasy. Where most "grims" cover their pages with equal parts gore-coated combat, cynical characters, sexual situations, harsh language, and gritty worlds, Scourge embraces those elements but does not stop with them, adding a layer of realism and attention to detail that elevates this standard "grim" story into a realistic, tour-de-force of fantasy. Indeed, Mr. Salyards creates a world where armor actually does protect you in combat. Where there are no "Chosen Ones" or godlike heroes or all-powerful villains. Where magic is present but not scattered around like motes of dust. Where your favorite character might appear as a "good guy" one moment only to seem a "bad guy" the next. And where anyone, ANYONE can die if plans do not work out or a blow is mistimed or too many foes appear. All things that might sound like normal grim but are so much more in this story. 
 Mr. Salyards throws readers into his realistic grimdark world from the first page; the first person narrator of the tale being a young man named Arkamandos (or Arki for short.) This youth has just been hired by Captain Braylar Killcoin, leader of a band of Syldoon soldiers, to be their company's scribe. And while Arki is very wary of his new employers (They are the fiercest, most vicious soldiers in the world), he explains his reason for joining up with them as: 
 I had no family, or none that had claimed me as such for years, and no friendships of any lasting duration. The promise of being part of something larger than my life--which admittedly, up to this point hadn't exactly been consequential or noteworthy--was exciting, even if my involvement was restricted to observing and recording. At least it would presumably be something worth setting to parchment for once. And there was no denying the draw to that. 
 This desire to be part of a grand, epic adventure is exactly why Arki is the perfect narrator for the story that follows, for he is in the exact same shoes as his audience: a spectator completely in the dark as to what is actually going on. For there doesn't seem to be any dark lord to defeat here or epic war to wage or apocalyptic event to stop - well, not that Arki knows about anyway. Instead, Captain Braylar and his men have their own secret agenda; a plan that they have no intention of willingly sharing with anyone. And so, Arki is left to listen to the conversation of his employers, gather clues as to their intentions, and piece together theories about their motives, goals, and true aims. All the while never knowing if his guesses are anywhere close to accurate. 
 And as Arki leads readers along on this grand adventure to discover the why of it all, Mr. Salyards carefully uses the interactions between the young scribe and the other characters to slowly sculp vibrant people, not grimdark caricatures of humanity, but real, living, breathing people who gradually come into focus. Don't be surprised when there are not any long soliloquies where the characters intentionally reveal their inner demons or hidden desires or troubled past to you, because Mr. Salyard does not spoon feed anyone. Instead, he forces you to live day to day along with Arki, reading his interpretations of his traveling companions, his beliefs about their personalities, and his assessment of their actions, making you use the youth's observations to form your own opinions about these three-dimensional people who surround him. 
 While this gradual development of plot and characters could have ruined the pacing of the story, it did not do so. For even though the beginning is slow and a tad confusing, Mr. Salyards deftly places clues throughout the narrative, stringing a reader along. Each suspected insight into Braylar's plans building a little more excitement, each small revelation about his history adding a touch more drama to the tale until you can't wait to turn the page, hoping to find the next part of the puzzle that Mr. Salyards has so expertly hidden from view. 
 But this is a grimdark, so where is the bloody combat, you ask? 
 Oh, it is here. Braylar is a man of action, willing to trade a few humorous slurs with his opponent before wielding his exotic flail to crush their skulls, and his Syldoon are constantly in the thick of the action. Blood and gore coat the pages, especially after the halfway point of the book, with the fighting coming fast and furious (though Arki presents it more from the point of view of a witness than a participant), and always Mr. Salyards deftly crafts these fights with utmost realism. No overpowered godlike warriors here. Even the most experienced fighter only one step away from getting struck down in battle. A fact that makes the fights even more gripping, as you wonder if anyone is safe from the grim reaper in this world. 
 As you can tell, I thoroughly enjoyed this novel, and there are lots of further things I'd like to say about the story, but I can't - to do so would reveal too many spoilers and ruin the fun for you. Perhaps it will suffice for me to write that Scourge of the Betrayer took everything that I love about grimdark, added in a touch of realism, and coupled those things with a slow-developing, character-driven story that made me constantly strive to figure out what was going on. It is quite simply a great fantasy read. 
 So, with all that being said, I highly recommend this one to grimdark fans, lovers of character-driven stories, fantasy fans, and all those that just adore tales that make you think. Have fun reading!

The Dagger and the Coin is a series that keeps spreading. It is a tapestry, intricate and finely woven, which is being unrolled in front of you. Except, it is so large, that you just cannot see where it would end. 
 Marcus Wester has woken the last remaining dragon. Cithrin has rejected Geder Palliako and left Suddapal. Geder cannot see beyond having her - even if it means sending out an army to retrieve her. Clara Kalliam, the loyal traitor, has finally realized just what it is that she's facing - and that she has to stop it. 
 Until now, Antea has won victory after victory. Conquered cities they should not even have reached - not just because of the spider priests, but also because no one knew of the danger they posed. But now the Antean empire is coming apart at the seams. Reality is catching up and more importantly, information is spreading. 
 And finally, finally, people are starting to fight back. From the soldiers who were in Kiaria to the Medean Bank and its bounties to save the Timzinae and hurt Antea - unlikely friends are coming together to get their own back. It is not just about freedom and neither is it about revenge. It is a bone deep thirst to fight back because enough is enough. 
 This series brings together so many elements of human nature to the fore - loyalty, love, friendship, tolerance, kindness, hatred, distrust, intolerance. All of them are there - sometimes even in the same people. And that makes them characters that truly stay with you - that make you think about them and their fate even after you have kept the book down.

 Bailey Glicks welcomed the New Year in the least expected position...in a club's restroom pressed up against the wall being given her own private fireworks show. Rewind a few days and you'll see she's not your usual club hussy who hooks up with random strangers...no matter how sexy. In fact, her humble upbringing Amish-like roots (I'm betting on Mennonite)  would portray a strikingly different image of what behavior is expected of her. Having caught her cheating fiance in a lie, she's recently entered the single life and is in no rush to jump into another relationship. That all changes after the lustful encounter with a certain green eyed sexy Scotsman refuses to leave her thoughts. 
 Just when Bailey decides to steer clear of men, become emotionally unavailable (like George Clooney) and focus on her career, the universe has a very different idea. She gets hit with not one, but two hot men looking to win her over (one more aggressively than the other). Enter Kalen Brinner, the green eyed, smooth brogue talking, walking sex god. He came into her life like a shooting star, granting every wish and desire. With his Alpha Male persona that oozes seduction, Kalen quickly gets under Bailey's skin. Is it possible to fall in love after knowing someone only a few weeks? If only life were that simple. 
 Recently graduated with a degree in accounting, Bailey gets her first job as an auditor. During her first assignment, she discovers certain discrepancies in a company's books which put her in some seriously hot water. Someone doesn't want her getting to the bottom of this financial crumb trail. Let's not forget what killed the cat. Determined to uncover the questionable Office Space-like practices (insignificant figures being withdrawn from accounts), Bailey continues her relentless search disregarding various warnings not to. When she seeks out the company CEO to inform him of her findings, she's met with the some pretty shocking news. Not only is the CEO not who she expected...he happened to be Jeremy Kalen Brinner Glenn. She knew he was well off but never did she imagine him to be the son of a billionaire...BILLIONAIRE! Worst of all, just when her personal life seemed hopeless, he goes and drops the L-Bomb. Kalen never intended to fall for Bailey; nevertheless he confessed he loved her at a critical moment. And they lived happily ever after, right? Not so fast!  
 With a storm brewing on the horizon, Bailey decides there's no place like home. What she doesn't realize is that old flames die hard... 
 Assets is a refreshingly new twist on the devastatingly handsome billionaire meets the ordinary not-so-privileged girl. Although I found the writing style to be slightly awkward at times, the overall plot was engaging. I definitely look forward to reading the next installment in this series.
