Shadowfell is the story of Neryn, a girl with the unusual canny ability to see faeries. Neryn has spent years running for the King's Enforcers, a group of soliders sent out to destroy any hints of magic. Her grandmother, who also had a canny gift, was greviously injured and later died because of the annual Cull. Her brother died fighting for freedom. All that's left of Neryn's family is her father. Once a good man, he's no longer much of a father, turning to drinking and gambling to deal with his loss. 
 When her father loses Neryn in a gambling match, a mysterious stranger saves Neryn from the other gamblers and the King's forces. He wants to offer her a choice, but she flees before he has the chance to explain. Neryn heads north, towards Shadowfell, a place she's never been. At Shadowfell, people with canny magical abilities can be safe. At least that's what Neryn's heard. She has no idea if Shadowfell even exists. 
 The journey takes Neryn across the countryside, where she encounters the Good Folk nearly everywhere. They tell her that she might have a destiny if she can prove herself in a series of tests. As a reader, the tests are a bit tedious because it's obvious fromt he beginning that she's going to pass them all. Books with journey quests are always the same. The main character encounters all the tests and pass them, usually struggling with at least one. 
 As for the romance in this book, I'm torn about how I feel. I saw it coming from a million miles away. There was no surprise or twists. It had a lot of tropes that bother me, such as "You'll hate me if you know what I am," that I feel like I've seen a lot, particularly in paranormal YA, as well as the main character claiming that nothing is going on when something is clearly going on. But at the same time, the romance did develop slowly and by then end I was happy they were finally acknowledging it. Partially because at least the characters would finally stop denying it, but also because the romantic lead gradually grew on me. 
 Now that I'm writing this I'm realizing predictability was the biggest flaw in this novel. Yes there were obstacles, but I always knew the main character would overcome them. I was never surprised by what happened or by a characters behavior. The book and the characters behaved exactly as expected throughout the whole book. 
 However, I will still say I enjoyed this novel and will probably read the next in the series. I'm a sucker for Marillier's use of mythology, her fantasy worlds rely heavily on Irish folklore, and I love that. I just know that Marillier can write better books because I've read them. There is nothing horrible or bad about this book, just the sense that I always knew what was coming and could've read the beginning and skipped straight to the ending and it wouldn't have really mattered.

This was classic Russo...in-depth look at a normal family living in very specific times and places that come alive with the everyday details. Despite the focus on the normal and everyday, Russo as usual makes these settings and people come alive in a way that provides depth to their experiences. 
 This story spans the lifetimes of four interlinked characters. The first one readers meet has a very interesting perspective. This perspective is what drew me into the book and in a very strong way kept me going even when I tired of the dialog (I've found Russo's dialog less than captivating at times in other books, as well) and even when I thought the length could have been trimmed just a hair to tighten the narrative. 
 Overall, a book I would recommend. And be aware that you'll want to read it slowly. It's a thought-provoking book even though it can't be described as "thoughtful" in the usual manner. You won't be confounded by deeply meaningful discussions of issues; instead you'll find deep meaning in very simple events and the characters' responses. 
 3 stars. 
 Want more fiction that touches on intergenerational movements and families? Try The Family Made of Dust: A Novel of Loss and Rebirth in the Australian Outback, a story of Australia's Stolen Generation.

 Last year I immensely enjoyed Behind Closed Doors, B.A. Paris's debut, and so I was looking forward to reading The Breakdown. I pre-ordered the ebook some months ago and, when it appeared on my kindle, I couldn't help starting it immediately. And I really wasn't disappointed! 
 The thing is, Paris's novels are not the most original, mind blowing thrillers you will ever read, but they are terribly exciting, gripping, and hard to put down. She has a knack for creating very involving stories, claustrophobic atmospheres and characters it's very easy to identify with (even if you don't always agree with their decisions). I couldn't wait to see what would happen to Cass, and how the mystery would turn out. 
 Paris also did a good job creating an unreliable narrator: this is a device I love, and which has become popular in the last years, but it is not very easy to pull out. In this case, I found Cass's portrayal believable, and I often questioned her mental status. I was almost completely sure that she wasn't really losing her memory, but it wasn't as obvious as it is in many novels of this type.  
 The mystery aspect is much more developed than in Behind Closed Doors, even if it is still secondary to Cass's mental state and personal struggles. However, I think it was really well done. True, it is a little unbelievable that Cass stumbled upon the truth as she did, but the solution, and how it came about, was still very satisfying.

 I'm rewriting this because I don't think I laid out my thoughts clearly enough. 
 Here's the thing: I ADORED the first Hunger Games book. I liked the second one. The characters and action were entertaining enough to move past the fact that a lot of the death was for the sake of shock value. The world was interesting and unique, and the main character had a unique voice that I could appreciate. 
 Now, The Hunger Games has never been a heavily character-driven story. It's always about the action. While, yeah, a few of the characters were 'developed', there was always the risk that they would die. You would choose a few to root for, then get heart broken when/if they died/got injured. 
 And this is where Mockingjay falls. 
 There is no Hunger Games in this book, and perhaps that was the one thing that made the series work. I was all on-board for a more serious, more depressed, more paranoid Katniss. After all, she had been in the Games twice now, and look what happened to a few that had only been in one! 
 What we got, however, was really, really over the top. There's a logical jump in character, then there's Katniss. She literally hid in the broom closet, snapped at everyone who passed her way, whined about how much her life sucked, etc. Even the two love interests finally pointed out how angsty she was. And she mistreats them, too. 
 [image error] 
 It got to the point that by the end of the book, Gale basically said "lolPeetashe'sallyoursbye". 
 Then there was the horrible 'propo' shots or whatever. I didn't get it. Wouldn't actual footage of, you know, and actual battle be more efficient? Especially since Katniss is camera challenged and can't even say her lines right when Haymitch is telling them right to her. They even brought the fashion team back (minus Cinna, whose death obviously meant nothing to our selfless hero, as she never really mentions him unless it's about her outfit) to 'make her over' or whatever. I didn't really see the point in it other than to waste a good hundred or so pages. 
 And then we get to the most troubling part of this book. The deaths. 
 Oh man, there's a lot of blood, a lot of death, etc. There's always been a lot in the series, but there was more of a reason for it. Only one winner and all that, survival... yadda yadda. 
 The deaths in this book felt so completely worthless. Finnick and Cinna's felt like the most needless, because none of the characters were really... affected by it. Finnick had finally gotten his happy ending and its completely blown out of the water. We don't find out what's happened to his wife, and he's just sort of forgotten. While yeah, it's a war, and yeah, people die... There was no point. Literally. 
 My mind was completely void of all emotion by the end of the book. Like, every death just became a 'cool story bro'. In the past books I'd be rooting for a character - in the first it was Rue, second it was Finnick and the drug-addicts - but in Mockingjay I just wanted them all to die for the cause. But you know, whatever. It's a war, I guess. People are gonna die. 
 Then Prim dies. And the entire point of the books is completely lost. We literally wasted our time. 
 [image error] 
 Now, if it had been a good death, I wouldn't be as upset. But it was pulled out of nowhere. You say she was 'manipulated' to the front lines. Um, HOW DID THAT HAPPEN?! Seriously, she was a medic. She had no reason to even be that close to the front line unless she was helped carting soldiers, which wouldn't be ideal for a fourteen-year-old girl (or however old she is) to be doing! Collins wanted a shocking death, but this just literally killed the book for me. I could (almost) forgive everything else. Even Finnick's death. Even the way the love triangle was resolved. 
 I felt no emotional bond to Prim as she died, and apparently neither did Katniss (though she had one redeeming moment when she shot President Coin instead of Snow). She cried a bit, angst-ed a bit, etc. But it wasn't the same person who had been willing to sacrifice herself for her sister two books ago. I get that the Hunger Games changes people. I'm just sure that Collins didn't want Katniss's reaction to everything to be 'whatever'. 
 The spirit of the books was lost as soon as Katniss stopped caring about those who she loved. The series was about war, but it was also about sacrifice and passion. All we got in this final book was the war. 
 I still do recommend the Hunger Games. It's a good read. The ending however, lowered the series in my eyes. 
 Two stars because Peeta actually grew a backbone and snapped back at Katniss, which serves her right for taking advantage of him.

The last thing Calliope wants is glasses, but she needs them. However, the eye doctor has to order in a pair for her, and the loaner pair is super ugly--thick, black, square frames. Then she discovers something about them: they allow her to read other people's thoughts. At first, she's not sure what's going on, actually, but once she figures it out she learns all sorts of things. Granted, some thoughts are better off not being shared, even if no-one knows that Calliope is looking in. 
 It's a year of best friend changes and discoveries, of finding her own place, and figuring out life a bit. 
 I liked this one. Fairly predictable, but it's got a sweet message. Even with the glasses, Calliope has some growing up to do, and she manages it gracefully. At the base of it all is learning compassion for others. We could all use a good dose of that magic.

Loved. Atkinson is being promoted to my A list of modern female authors, along with Elena Ferrante (also discovered this year), Margaret Atwood, Hilary Mantel, and tentatively Sarah Waters, although I really need to get around to more of her stuff. It would be fun to pick one of them and really work through all of their work, the way I did with David Foster Wallace a few years back. Although this gets pricey now that my NYPL unlimited ebooks membership has run out :( 
 Not that Kate Atkinson is really a new author to me- I read Life After Life in 2013 (sidenote: how has it been that long?!), but it didn't really capture me in the same way that Behind the Scenes at the Museum did. The essential elements that I loved about this book were there- complicated family relationships, British stoicism, funny caustic one liners, but I think for some reason the rebirth aspect distracted me. 
 Not to say that BtSatM was any more of a straightforward novel. After just these 2 books of hers, I think it's safe to say that the passage of time is one of Atkinson's authorial obsessions, and the idea of telling a story linearly doesn't fit with her concept of the world. There is, in fact, an anchoring time and storyline here- the life of Ruby Lennox, born in the 1950s to the cantankerous Bunty and the philandering George, but her story is interspersed with "footnotes," which aren't really footnotes but instead entire chapters taking place in a different generation of Ruby's family, ranging from her great-grandmother on down. I didn't treat these like footnotes at all, and instead just read them when I got to them like a chapterbook, and was kind of annoyed at the conceit of calling them "footnotes." 
 But anyway, I really liked these intervals. They were always triggered by the appearance in Ruby's life of some physical object that turned out to have some significance in the life story of a previous generation, creating an echo feeling in the storyline, like what is happening in Ruby's life is somehow rippling back in time or vice versa. At one really low point in Ruby's life trajectory she explains her theory of a life "lost and found locker" (there was some much more quaint British term for this), where the detritus from our lives, from memories to childhood toys to our lost buttons, is waiting for us in the afterlife. Ruby, in some ways, takes on the characteristics of a human lost and found locker, as she becomes the repository of the memories of her tragically lost sisters, and even eventually taking on the whole twisted family tree . 
 But beyond the story, Atkinson creates an atmosphere that I love, one that is dark/mysterious at times and moving at others and all in all feels true to the experience of love and family relationships as I've experienced it. The line somewhere towards the end where Ruby realizes how important her sisters are to her, despite their non-traditional and even combative relationship, brought real tears to my eyes. Characters do not undergo some deathbed redemption, and are made to live with bad choices and bad hands in life. The wars, especially, play a starring role in the unwinding of family lives. 
 There is a bit of what I would call magical realism, but never completely beyond the pale of everyday life. There is an interesting trend of the "golden child" in each generation, completely beloved but  doomed seemingly inevitably to an early death. This is never really explained, but makes the contrast between the largely sour and unhappy surviving members and these angelic likeable children particularly strong. Are the good doomed to early death? Is cynicism a necessary acquired trait for survival? None of these darker characters seem dark from the beginning- instead they are often described as of malleable personality, changing depending on who is around. But when we are reintroduced to the same characters at the end of life, they are invariably thoroughly unpleasant individuals.  
 I already looked through all of Kate Atkinson's other novels, but none of the blurbs beguiled me as much as this one. Write a new book soon, please!

 The Beautiful Ashes is the first book in a new series by Jeanine Frost about a young man and woman who are battling against fate--their own, and the fate of the world. 
 I liked Ivy. She had just been through some traumatic events, but the girl was scrappy and feisty, and she just kept on going. Adrian was an interesting character--it's hard to know whether I like him or not at this point, because there is still so little about him that's been revealed. What we do know is that he is resigned to and dismayed by his destiny, and he doesn't believe it can be changed. 
 The pacing of this book was good. Most of it centered around the world building, which it has to in a book like this in order for the reader to 'see' things. There were a lot of demonic realms and creatures that needed to be established, and I think the author did a great job with this. It was very descriptive, and I was able to picture each jump the characters made into the demon world. 
 While I thought there was chemistry between the characters, I didn't think it was strong enough to warrant such dramatic feelings. This story relies heavily on what their fates are as opposed to developing feelings, and I'm hoping this will be fleshed out more in the books to come. 
 So...here it comes. It's hard not to compare this book to the Night Huntress series, and I have to say...while I find the Night Huntress series to be an incredibly character driven series, I find The Beautiful Ashes to be more plot driven, and I think that showcases Jeaniene Frost's versatility as a writer. It's easier to write about supernatural beings in a human world than humans (sort-of) in an entirely different world. 
 Overall, I thought this book was a decent start to a new series. Like a lot of series introductions, the focus is mostly on the world building, but having read Jeaniene Frost before, I have no doubt she has a master plan. And I'll be there to see it play out!

Emma, Emma, Emma. Conceited, vain, spoiled, self-absorbed Emma Woodhouse. I was afraid of you, afraid you'd be intolerable and unlikeable, afraid you'd prove uncaring and undeserving of the happiness that is inevitably bestowed upon you. 
 I'm terribly sorry. 
 This was my most dreaded Austen book, because I genuinely believed Emma to be unlovable. Where did that come from? There's no doubt she's not the most easily likeable Austen heroine, she meddles, she overestimates her own capabilities and she's full of extremely ill-placed, but well-meaning intentions. 
 The only unforgivable thing about her is, perhaps, that she tends to overestimate her own worth at the expense of others (namely Harriet), but I see this rather as a product of the time this was written. A woman of Emma's status would have grown up being told she was "above" certain others, and she'd have been treated as such, because that's how it worked. 
 Emma is also the character who transforms the most. This is not only because she's the protagonist, her ability to change is there from the start. What impressed me the most about Emma was her self-awareness and ability to admit her mistakes. At times she doesn't see how badly she's ruined something, and it'll take a nudge or two from friends to get her to consider how badly she's acted, but she does consider it - and learns from it. 
 While reading 'Emma' I constantly thought of mirrors. Characters seemed to mirror each other, to be worse and better versions of each other, and depending how well you chose your partner and companions you could end up better or worse off. Emma is at times close to being worse off. Her acquaintance with Mr. Churchill is positively disastrous, because they highlight the very worst in each other and call it forward. Together they're arrogant, dismissive of the feelings of others and proud. They're really fucking unpleasant. So for a happy ending to be possible, they can't end up together. 
 'Emma' is chock-full of both couples who are perfectly matched and those who aren't. You might say that's the case for other Austen novels as well, but it's crystal clear in 'Emma'. There's a constant mirroring of characters who resemble each other, but depending on the partner/companionship they end up with they become better or worse. 
 It's, of course, also a story of hubris. Emma almost flies to close to the sun and is saved by the grace of her friends and her own, actually fairly reasonable, disposition. She's got pride, but she's humble enough to admit her mistakes and make amends. Mr. Knightley falling in love with her is not for nothing; I found Emma annoying, yes, but also wonderfully lovable. She wants to do the right thing, but has no idea what the right thing looks like and is too stubborn to listen to others. She learns her lesson and earns the love of Mr. Knightley - another important point. She's had it from the beginning, but only in the end, having paid her penance, can she return it with all that Mr. Knightley deserves. 
 It's really a brilliant book. 
 I'll also say if I hadn't known this was a Jane Austen book I would have expected Emma to be aromantic, perhaps asexual too. I loved her complete and utter disinterest in all things romantic on her own behalf, her total confusion whenever men were courting her and her sort of dull acceptance of her fate and trying to convince herself she's in love when she realizes she'll probably have to become engaged to Churchill after all that flirting. I'll say she's a perfect candidate for a modern adaptation where she ends up on her own, happy and independent, and I hope that happens someday.

Between the Star Trek: The Next Generation marathon on yesterday, blustery winds and a lack of desire to do anything, I read a bunch of romances. 
 Here is a three star rating which is more of a 3.5 star. 
 At the wedding of the h's best friend and the H's brother, the two hookup. This could be/is a huge mistake as the h is a good girl, daughter of the parson, and the H is a bad boy aka bad son. She has had a crush on him for years which was tough as she was over-weight and bullied when she was younger. They have a one night stand with consequences. 
 The book starts at a party the newlyweds are having. The h sees the H arrive with her arch-nemesis from HS and loses it. She takes her EPT stick and shoves it on the H's burger which is a little over the top for me but works for her. 
 The hero is horrified, not about the burger or the baby on the way, but horrified that he up and skedaddled after the best night of sex/romance he ever had. He's not exactly Heathcliff, but he does have some serious guilt issues and baggage to work through. 
 He runs after her and has an uphill battle to convince that he wants to be there for her and the baby. In addition to being a hunka hunka burning love, he is a nice guy that wants to do the right thing. Both characters are pretty sweet and seem good together. No outrageous idiotic behavior other than the norm. She's a little reluctant to get involved with him, and he's a little shut down but all believable. Good news is they actually grow as characters. 
 The h has issues with perfectionist, harping mother while the H has a very serious and dark backstory that his own brothers don't even know about. Two of the brothers work in the construction company owned by the father. The brotherly banter gets a little old. The H was the renegade and resident bad boy of the town and the family, and his brothers never let him forget it. There is a big reveal of what motivated his bad behavior, and I found it to be a shocker. 
 So definitely not a 4.0, but it's a nice read. I only wish the evil arch-nemesis had gotten a little bit of a comeuppance as given her nastiness in HS, she deserved it so Ms. James, we need an episode here please.

 Leigh once again pull the team together in a scheme like no other. The fast paced of the plot made it's hard to stop reading (because if you do, you might afraid of missing some amazing actions). This series would probably be the first where I enjoy the main couple. 
 Inej and Kaz 
 I would mostly focus on the drama especially of Kaz and Inez (they are my fav so far), because the action is no doubt, one of the best I've ever read. Unlike any other romance stories I've read, I love how, instead of 'trying to change' Kaz, Inej told him to embrace it at the end. Moreover, they could relate to each other even without many words spoken, although yes at some part it's a bit annoying how they misunderstood each other. 
 Matthias and Nina 
 At Six of Crows, I enjoy Matthias and Nina storyline the most especially at the beginning. I believe their stories were the one which developed the most. How with Matthias faced his devil and how Nina finally manage to overruled her addiction. Maybe it's my preference, but when Leigh focused too much about their romance, I became 
 bored 
 . It became a bit cliche with how they were like star-crossed lovers and I've to be very frank that I dislike how Leigh ended Matthias like that. Boom. Voila, suddenly he's gone - 
 very anticlimactic 
 Wylan and Jesper 
 *inner fangirl squealing* I thought it was only my imagination that Jesper flirted with Wylan, but apparently it's not and how I'm so happy with that. Their interactions were so cute, like any other teenagers falling in love. If this were a university/college-universe, I might think of them as two students - one very popular, another a shy one. Voila, they met, bantering, and fell in love. 
 Overall, I love the characters' development (despite Matthias' ending) through the entire stories. If Leigh would decide to make them in another story/universe, I would never say no.

I did not expect to like this book as much as I did. This book really makes you believe. Believe in fate, believe in destiny but also believe in the flip side of things. It challenges your disbelief and makes you believe in frivolous things such as "meant-to-be" through experiments and observation. 
 We read from the POVs of our two main characters, Natasha and Daniel. They both have completely different thought processes and reasonings. Natasha believes that if something cannot be explained by science, it does not exist. She is a realist who prides herself on her precision and practicality. On the other hand, Daniel is the kind of person whose heart blooms with hope and who has absolute faith in love and it's power. They have clashing personalities that compliment each other. Reading about them just made me feel so good. 
 The whole book takes place in the span of a day and it follows our protagonists as they fall in love, while fighting their personal battles the whole time. Considering that the protagonists fall for each other in a single day, insta love would be assumed. But their journey is captured so well and the characters and their feelings for each other developed to such an extent that it didn't feel like insta love at all. That's probably what I like most about this book. I also loved the small tidbits of science we get and the POVs of minor characters that are interjected into the story. It really made me think about how all the small events in our lives are responsible for the consequences we face; how so many things lead up to a single impactful event in our lives. 
 We also see the troubles that Natasha and Daniel are facing. We see them try to overcome them and emerge as wiser individuals.  Natasha's family is being deported from America on account of them being uncharted immigrants and her life is falling apart. We see how she blames her father for toppling her life and simply thinking about himself and his dreams. We also see from her father's perspective as he tries to justify his actions. You begin to resent her father,Samuel Kingsley, as much as Natasha does. You feel whats she feels. You feel her grief, her anger. Meanwhile Daniel struggles with trying to meet his family's ridiculous expectations and wishes. Daniel's family wants him to attend Yale and become a doctor, against his own desires. His father is genuinely curious to know why he thinks that what he wants matters. He has to deal with the pressure of doing what his parents expect of him instead of following his heart's desire, that is, to become a poet. Their encounter helps them both make important decisions and change them as individuals. They both learn new things from each other. Natasha learns to be passionate and Daniel learns to make definite and clear choices. 
 At the beginning of the book, we are introduced to a security guard, Irene who starts off the chain of events that leads to Natasha meeting Daniel and I love how it ends with her being the cause for their reunion. It reinforces how the little things that you ignore play a major part in shaping your life.

Ten is the perfect book for a hot stormy summer night and if you're home by yourself let's just hope the power doesn't go out and that windows and doors are locked. Meg and her best friend Minnie are invited to a party hosted by the most popular girl in their town. The problem is that the party is hosted on a remote island and their parents don't know they are there. Well that isn't the only problem. The guests, their are ten of them, start dropping like flies. After they play a creepy homemade movie that freaks them all out, the guests of the party start dying off and when they die a red slash appears in the foyer for each person who is murdered. 
 This book was great. I thought it was going to be really cheesy, a big cliche, and that'd I'd figure out who the murder was right way. I thought I knew who it was but there was a major plot twist at the end. (I will say that I was half right though.) I honestly got scared while reading this. I had to sleep with the bathroom door cracked open because their is a night light in there and I was terrified that someone was hiding in my room. Just thinking about it creeps me out. Ten is like a combination of the game Clue and the movie Fear Island, it is a must read!

Thoughts on the Overall Book: I've been wanting to read this one ever since it came out, and I was not disappointed in it either. It made a quick, creepy gothic read with an enjoyable cast and interesting storyline. 
 Cover--Yea or Nay: I love the cover, it's dark, and the font it awesome. 
 Characters: I really liked Sterling (apart from her name) she was a strong heroine, without an attitude, and she was a good sister, which always makes me happy. She also handled the situation really well, and once she figured out that no one remembered her brother, she gave up trying to talk about it, which so many characters don't understand and people think they're crazy which causes all sorts of problems they easily could have avoided. It's a hard situation, but she deals with it well. She does have an eating disorder, and sometimes things like that bother me, but her reasons behind it are very understandable, and even she knows it's silly, but since it's psychological (she's stressing over her brother leaving for collage) she can't help it. Though we really don't get to see Phin a lot in the book, the reader gets to know him really well though Sterling. People who follow my reviews probably know how much I love sibling stories, and this was a really good one. I loved Sterling and Phin's relationship. He was a really awesome, and protective big brother and Sterling's devotion in getting him back was nice to see. Sterling's friend Candy was funny and kind of a typical bestie that you see in these sorts of books, but she was just the kind of person Sterling needed. Heath was also a likable character. He was quiet, and kind, and was a really nice guy, despite his own issues. I liked him a lot. Lenora May, the girl the swamp traded Phin for, was also an interesting character.  I wasn't sure what to think of her at first, but I did end up feeling really sorry for her after we find out exactly what went down  
 The Romance: Sterling and Heath do have a bit of romance, but it never goes beyond a little kissing, and it really doesn't take precedence in the plot as they are both just as eager to figure out what is going on and why people continue disappearing in the swamp. They're not even qualified as 'insta-love' either because they had had a crush on each other a few years previously too, but after Heath lost his best friend in the swamp, he kind of went off the reservation for a while since no one believed him. Anyway, I liked their pairing. 
 Writing Style: The story is told in first person present tense from Sterling's POV. Not my favorite style, and not as pretty as Victoria Schwab's, but it wasn't so bad either, and it did work out for this story. The feel of the book was the important part, and that I really liked. One thing, that wasn't necessarily disappointing, but okay, I was a little disappointed in, was that this book really wasn't as scary as I thought it would be. I was hoping for it to be way creepier, but it's really more of a classic supernatural adventure story than an actual horror story. On the other hand, it felt very much like an old backcountry folktale, which is I think what the author was going for, so that's never a bad thing in my book. And there were creepy parts, but nothing that kept me up at night. It was still a good story, even if the plot twist was pretty easy to see coming, the end was still fast paced and had me on the edge of my seat, and I enjoyed it. 
 Accuracy/ Believability: Not applicable. 
 Problems/What bothered me: The only thing that bothered me was that the author just seemed to randomly throw in that Sterling's other friend Abigail prefers girls. There's no reason for it in the story, and it's only mentioned, so what was the point? 
 Conclusion: 4 stars. A fun supernatural adventure. While I don't care for the American south overmuch, I love reading about it when it has a folklore base. I'm guessing this is a standalone, but it was a very good debut novel, and I look forward to see what Natalie C. Parker comes up with next. 
 Recommended Audience: Girl read 16 and up, if you liked Victoria Schwab's The Near Witch and Maggie Stiefvater's books you would probably enjoy this one.

 All Lined Up is a great novel about finding love in unlikely places. It's about a girl who grew up around football and has come to resent it. Throughout the novel, though, she finds the love she used to have for the game and that helps her to understand her father better. 
 Dallas has lost her love for football. Her father gives more energy to coaching his players than he does to parenting her. She's bitter that he's making her stay in Texas with crappy dance programs, when really, she wants to go to New York. And to top it all off, he's accepted a coaching position at Rusk University, where she's going to college. Dallas is a stickler for rules. She and her BFF Stella balance each other out. Stella is carefree, sometimes too much so, and Dallas reigns her in. And Stella makes Dallas loosen up every once in awhile. I loved the dynamic between this unlikely duo. I've mentioned this before in past reviews that I hate it when a girl hears a rumor and immediately doubts her boyfriend or she decides she knows what's best for him and breaks up with him to protect him. Dallas is not one of those girls. She hears a rumor, considers it for a moment, doubting Carson, but then she realizes that he would never do that to her. I loved that about her. She's smart ;) 
 The only thing Carson has ever been good at is football. He does averagely in school, but he has to work hard to achieve that. He's never had to work hard to be good at football. He doesn't have time for a girlfriend because he has to focus on football so that he can possibly obtain a scholarship or a starting position. He's funny and cute and understands Dallas in a way nobody else does. He was unbelievably sweet. 
 All Lined Up is not only about falling in love, it's about learning to love football again and it's about family. Dallas and her father don't have a good relationship at the beginning of the story, but they try to work out their differences and understand each other.

For Kayla Green, Christmas means pretense, she has to act as if she cares about the whole cheer of the holiday when in reality it only brings up painful memories. Kayla is great at her job, she is in PR and lives and breathes her job and she gets a perfect opportunity to get out of the cheer for a job, helping their new client Jackson O'Neil , publicize his family's resort. The only caveat is that she has to stay at the resort for a week and she asks for an isolated cabin. 
 Of course at her first meeting Kayla feels the spark with Jackson but she is an expert at avoiding things. When she arrives at her temporary home, she finds herself under-dressed for the weather and then her meeting with the hero's family is a disaster, his grandfather's comment makes her wander down sad memory lane to when she was thirteen and an outsider in her dad's new family. 
 She of course decides to make up for it and spends her time familiarizing herself with the hero's family and resort. Now, I loved the whole cast of characters, hero's brothers and their possible life partners, mother, grandparents, even the town people. Their whole snow-mobile ride was great and their first time too. I liked Jackson's dedication to his family, he left his own business to help take care of his family's business after his family's death, even if that meant dealing with his grandfather's interference. 
 The hero Jackson was great with Kayla, he didn't let Kayla put him off and despite the short time span the romance was believable and sweet and sexy, all in all if you are looking for a good holiday themed romance with a great family Sleigh Bells in the Snow is for you. 
 ARC provided the publisher through Netgalley.

UGH. SO MUCH UGH. 
 I feel like it's prudent for me to mention that I am extremely finicky when it comes to certain details in books. If something bothers me it will usually nag at me for the entire story, regardless of its merits. I also tend to be quite literal, so arguments of metaphor won't quite do it for me. That being said, if my reasons for disliking this book seem flimsy to you, you were warned. 
 The biggest issue I had with this book was the sheer mis-classification of age. I have spent the last few years working with 9 & 10 year olds, and I can assure you they are about 1000x more intelligent than this supposed 9-year old protagonist, Bruno. The sister, Gretel, also suffered from this, but as she is not the focus of the book she didn't bother me quite as much. Had the characters been written as 6 and 9, respectively, I may have had an easier time understanding why Bruno was SO STUPID. 
 Then we have the language. I did listen to an interview with the author in which he speaks about the book as a book for all ages. So I understand that some of the language quirks were intentional in order to reach the widest audience. However, I can't accept the English idioms used as misunderstandings of German words. Auschwitz is referred to as "out with" by Bruno throughout the book. I'm sorry, a German child is not going to confuse a German word with an English phrase. Just no. He also misunderstands the meaning of "heil" as in "heil Hitler" to mean goodbye, even though, again, HE SPEAKS GERMAN. His father is an officer and his son apparently doesn't know who the Fuhrer is; he refers to him as "the fury" throughout the book. UGH. 
 Additionally, Bruno is just. so. naive. He lives directly aside Auschwitz for a year and still spends ample time being jealous of Shmuel for having so many friends to play with while he has none. He witnesses the brutal treatment of his Jewish friend and his utter starvation, his father (who is a Commandant, I might add) tells him the people in the camp are "not people at all", there are soldiers and fences surrounding the area, and yet Bruno makes no connections as to the horrific nature of the camp he is living next to. 
 Then we have the incredibly selfish nature of Bruno himself. He has absolutely no compassion whatsoever, and I came to despise him and his treatment of his "friend" Shmuel. He is constantly making thoughtless comments and eating the food he carries to the starving boy during his visits because he just gets so hungry on the walk to the camp. 
 Speaking of the camp. There is no way a young boy in a concentration camp could have disappeared to sit by the fence every day without a guard noticing.  A fence, I might add, that can be easily lifted for a child to crawl under. 
 And then we have the manner of Bruno's death. Even if I bought into his complete lack of understanding, Shmuel would have understood. He would have known that Bruno would be in extreme danger inside the camp, and that he would not be able to leave it once he had entered. So now I'm left thinking Bruno is an idiot and Shmuel is malicious.  
 This is a book about an incredibly serious event in history, and its utterly ridiculous simplification of matters is gross. JUST UGH.

I love all of the intricate word play and literary references. If you consider yourself a bookworm or bibliophile in even the smallest sense, you would enjoy the series. I can't wait to get the "Well of Lost Plots" and see what happens next. They are wholly original, genre-bending books with very likeable and interesting characters. I hope he adds more to the series!

I never thought it would be possible to love a book so much when I hated absolutely all the characters. A moment didn't go by where I wasn't cursing the actions of someone in the story. Strangely, this didn't bother me or keep me from enjoying the story. I guess you would say it was a good hate. The one exception to this might be Waverly, who seemed the most sane and reasonable. She did go off the deep end a bit towards the end, but I still liked her. I'm honestly in awe by this author. This is one of the rare times that I find myself sucked completely into a story and invested in the characters. It's not as wonderfully creepy as 'Glow' and the egg harvesting, but it makes up for that with other things. This book mostly focuses on the characters reactions to everything that occurred in the first book. It's sufficed to say that most of them are traumatized and it results in various mental breakdowns and moments of psychotic rage. It was interesting to see how each of the kids were affected by what the New Horizon and what Anne Mather's had done. The longer I read, it got a little Lord of the Flies on me. There was still a focus on the ongoing conflict from the first book about getting the parents back, getting revenge on the New Horizon, etc. As far as sequels go, I wasn't disappointed at all. 
 The person I hated most of all had to be Kieran. I was only like seven pages in and he already had me contemplating murdering him. I take back any vaguely nice thing I might have said about him in my review for the first book. He had a few moments where I thought he was being reasonable for once and then two seconds later he'd do something stupid and petty that negated whatever respect I'd had for him. The only time I might have liked him was towards the end of the book, but that was probably just because he was up against Anne Mather's who instantly trumps when it comes to me hating someone. I really thought it was disgusting how he used his preaching and religion to manipulate the other crew members. It seemed like he was mostly out for himself and didn't care about any of their opinions. I even recall someone referring to him as a dictator. Even though I can understand why, the way he treated Seth was horrible. I liked how Seth told Kieran that Kieran was just as bad as him. It reminded me of this movie I watched called 'Land of the Blind'. A horrible, ruthless dictator is overthrown by the 'good' guys, only for the new leaders to end up being just as horrible and ruthless. Kieran was just a selfish douchebag, concerned about power rather than what's best for the ship. The whole Empyrean blowing up  could have been avoided if Kieran had just listened to Seth instead of blowing him off. 
 The biggest surprise of all was Seth. Other than Waverly, he is my ultimate favorite. After the first book, I was prepared to hate his guts again, but somehow he changed my mind. The book starts with Seth in the brig for trying to kill Kieran and start a mutiny. He's had a lot of time to think after his tirade and realize what he's done was wrong. I wanted to be annoyed by the personality switch, but it was done in a way that was realistic to me. The way he was portrayed in 'Spark' made me more sympathetic to his character and I was willing to forgive any crappy thing he'd done before. I honestly never thought I'd say this, but I'm seriously hoping that Seth and Waverly get together. They're actually kind of cute together and I got so happy when Seth finally kissed her at the end . I got so sick of Kieran telling Seth he would never be good enough for someone like Waverly. 
 The ending had me pissed, but in a good way. The cliffhanger was terrible. You can't leave things like that and make me wait a year. I feel like the next book is going to be f-ing AMAZING! There's bound to be ten times the conflict and I need to know what happens to the characters after this latest travesty. I'm sure Anne Mather's will give me more reasons to hate her and Kieran will annoy the crap out of me. I'm more interested to learn more what's been happening on the New Horizon. I'm feeling like there's some brainwashing going on. However, the thing that had me most pissed concerned Seth. WTF is going on here?! I was so giddy about a certain thing and then Seth decided to stay behind on the Empyrean. If I was Waverly, I would be so damn furious that I risked my life to save him and then he's like peace, I'll stay here . There better be some logical explanation for that. I'm probably going to look around other people's reviews to see if they understood that part.

A reread. 
 This is a straightforward detective fare, the sort of material you wish you'd see more in local bookstores, less of the shit romantic taglish stuff. It's CSI: Philippines with priests. Batacan's priority was to tell the story, not to make a guessing game for the readers. Virtually no one believes the Philippines has a bunch of serial killers on the loose; Batacan makes it plausible using 'missing' statistics that the overworked/inept police don't keep track of. 
 The characters are fairly lovable, but if this we forget this is also a literary piece, the way Batacan fleshed them out smacks of pretention. Fr. Saenz and Fr. Jerome are the archetypes you see on long running pop crime shows like CSI and Bones: they are not bogged down by angst or the mystery of why an ever omnipotent, ever benevolent god allows evil. Joanna, the upgraded version of Lois Lane, leaves the NBI and the police in the dust with her social savvy and nose for information. Joanna learns the identity of the killer as quickly as Saenz and Jerome, although her sleuthing is unwritten half the time. The novel suffers from the Smurfette Syndrome: the important ones are all male, save for one lone female. For the peripheral characters, there are mothers, fathers and boys; there's a lack of girls. 
 Saenz, Jerome, Joanna (I'll refer to them as Saenz trio for ease) are polyglots, educated abroad, and culture ooze from their pores. One thing I know this country is that these are indicators of high social status and it can overshadow the fact that education, languages spoken can be intellectual indicators ("Good taste" for Bach and Mozart and the rejection of the Biebers tells someone has enough resources to know the gems from the fads). Saenz's wealthy background is emphasized and juxtaposed with the killings embroiled in poverty, in a dump site, Payatas. 
 Saenz himself is not rich, but his family is rich enough to support his education, priesthood, CD-collection, emergency travel expenses while he works in a lab in which the equipment is (sometimes) supplied by grants. While this can be read as pop-fare detective novel, the "haves" and "have nots" don't go away. The scene where one of the mother of the victims thanks Saenz for 'doing everything he could for her son' is not a thanks related to finances, but for solving the crimes and helping identify the victims -- Saenz's most important job, although there's that elephant: had anyone given these boys or a particular boy a chance, the killings may not have occurred. The politician who forgoes sleep to help Saenz and Jerome is the anti-stereotype of "lazy money-grubber". Nothing on the politician's finances, but usually those who run for office in this country are moneyed. Maybe politicians are men of action when it comes to good friends, like everybody else. Meanwhile, Arcinas, the bureaucratic character who rose from poverty to a civil servant somebody, is vainglorious and a deterrent to everyone until he was checked by his superior. 
 Perhaps Batacan was writing against poverty and that Saenz trio, flawed they may be, are the ideals born from secure finances? Who knows? There's enough sartorial morality here for the music lovers - it seems Batacan has genuine appreciation for it, having worked as a musician. In contrast, the peripheral characters don't have this wee problem, and the short paragraphs Batacan gives them makes them more believable, endearing and their poverty, heart-breaking. 
 Batacan contrasts the not-local education of the Saenz trio with that of the killer. Jerome and Joanna flourished under the kindness of good mentors like Saenz; a child turns into a neurotic, then a killer, after a teacher repeatedly rapes him.  
 One very disturbing scene was the confrontation between Saenz and the killer. The killer, mentally unhinged by prolonged sexual abuse, is lured by Saenz by impersonating his abuser. Anyone who cares enough to know how some Catholic churches spend Sunday donations finds out the Vatican has protected one too many priests who evaded the law and abused more children. While there's no hint of the predator in Saenz, only the conscious lack of frigidness, it does bring this ugly issue to the forefront. Those damaged by abuse are lucky if they have some sort of redemptive closure that does not involve death. Either these details are unintentional, or Batacan is more skilled than we give her credit for. 
 "Not everybody can be saved." It's an acknowledgment that sometimes grates against our wishful notions of good and evil. Saenz and Jerome will remain priests. This is a detective novel, not a philosophical contemplation. Tomorrow, many people will thank deities for the good. Evil and suffering remain.

Blog review @Scaredy Engines End of Line Library 
 From the start I wondered whether this was fantasy or sci-fi especially when it mentioned flying beasts and three moons in the sky.. 
 But even though the world building is pretty scarce I would say this is high fantasy... 
 So.. this is quite a dark one and right from the start it never bored me or had me losing interest. There is a lot of action and suspense in this book which keeps the narrative flowing fast. My main problem is the lack of descriptions/history on the world. There was a map in my copy showing what appeared to be waterfalls in the ocean.. I mean cascading waterfalls like Niagara! These were hardly described. But on saying all of this perhaps I will find out more in the other two books.. but I really do like my world building! :( 
 Okay the characters, right from the start I will admit I liked Adelina in strength and personality. I was able to see things through her eyes very well and her panic was all too real. The other characters were also very complex with many layers to their personalities. But most of all I felt Adelina's loss at the end not to mention the fact that I didn't see it coming. At the end there also appears to be the introduction of more characters from faraway lands. There is just so much potential here and there was a massive build up of suspense with that ending so therefor I would recommend this book for those who are looking for a different darker YA novel but also don't mind a scarcely described world.

Book about prediction by the author of the 538 political blog, which became particularly famous in the 2012 presidential election (after the book was written) due to the author's high confidence in an Obama victory due to polling evidence in marginals. The author was prior to 538 spread over two jobs - online poker (until it was made illegal in US - see below) and baseball stat evaluation (where he developed his own site which he sold to a professional site for which he then worked). 
 The book's central themes are the importance of Bayesian stats (as opposed to Fisher type confidence intervals based only on data) as the optimal blend of expertise and data and the difficulty of distinguishing the true signal from underlying noise which can either obscure the signal or create false ones. He continues various areas in turn - all of which have their own forecasting issues, which are often very different leading to his third point the difficulty of drawing hard and fast rules around prediction. Generally an interesting book - more a compendium of ideas and so lacking the really big idea/takeaway - which seems deliberate due to the last point. 
 In respect of the financial crisis, he identifies various failures of prediction (housing bubble, rating agencies, failure to see how it would cause a global financial crisis, failure to realise how big and deep recession would be) which he largely ascribes to over-confidence and inability to forecast out of sample events. In political forecasting he claims his ability think probabilistically, revisit and alter past forecasts and look for data consensus means he outperforms what is a poor level of competition (biased and unscientific political pundits). For baseball again he initially competed against simple rules of thumb but sees the real skill in continuing to combine the best of stats with properly incorporated qualitative information to continue to look for edges. Weather forecasting he sees as largely a success story especially when you account for bias (for example to over-predict bad weather as that is less catastrophic an error) and allowing for chaos theory which makes precise long range forecasts difficult. Earthquake forecasting by contrast has had almost no success (here he talks about over fitting). For economic forecasting there are lots of challenges (Uncertainty principle type ideas such as Goodhart's law, self-fulfilling prophecies so that talk of a recession causes one, natural biases of commentators including either not wanting to go away from herd or being deliberately provocative) not least the sheer noisiness of economic data. For infectious diseases he discusses self-cancelling prophecies (epidemic warnings change behaviour in a good way) and although it's a challenging area he believes practitioners in this field (perhaps due to their Hippocratic oaths) are more thoughtful about their predictions. In chess he discusses in detail the psychology of Kasparov's defeat by a computer - an error it made in a losing position convinced him it could think more deeply than it could as well as where humans are better or worse than computers and how blended programmes are very strong. For Poker he takes the view that the Poker players are very natural Bayesians, adjusting their knowledge both as cards appear and also assessing chance of different hands by an intuitive posterior analysis based on how they think their opponents would act with different hands. He also takes the view that he standard of opponents is key to if you can make money. For stock picking he discussed the efficient market hypothesis (especially with transaction costs) and the psychology of bubbles. For climate change he discusses healthy scepticism and also his conclusion that scientists are a lot more seekers after the truth than politicians. For terrorist attacks he discussed power laws to extrapolate to major attacks (which actually dominate costs and deaths) and the importance of lateral and imaginative thinking around threats.

I don't know how I feel about this... 
 Let's clarify: I knew this was going to be written as a stage script; I knew that, while it was inspired by a story written by JK Rowling, the final product wasn't completely written by her; I knew that it wasn't going to be the fully fleshed-out, living, breathing book I was hoping for. 
 And I was still excited. I wanted to know what the characters would be up to in the future, how they were dealing with the ghosts of their pasts and so on. But, while I enjoyed this story, it didn't ring true for me. Spoilers ahead. 
  
 Things I liked: 
 1. Harry wasn't a perfect parent and wasn't trying to be one, either. His relationships with James and Albus (unfortunately there wasn't much of Lily and only slightly more James) were complicated. His struggle to parent was very relatable. 
 2. Despite not always liking Albus, his character felt real. There was bound to be one of Harry's kids who would struggle living under their dad's shadow, no matter what. 
 3. Albus and Scorpius's friendship and rapport was excellent. 
 4. Ginny and Hermione still kick ass. 
 5. Having Rose start out very stuck-up and being smarmy was interesting with a mother like Hermione. 
 6. The perspective of Hogwarts from two kids who didn't fit in or have their own crowd was very refreshing. 
 Things I didn't like: 
 1. Ron isn't Fred. He is his own person and in this story, I feel like the writers were trying to make him more like Fred than Ron. 
 2. The idea of Voldemort having a child. The only slightly possible way I can think of this happening is if someone convinced Voldemort that he could have a child using Muggle technology without having sex or there was some kind of really ancient magic that would allow for creating a child. Voldemort was unloving, unfeeling and didn't like to be touched. Even if it was hatef*&@ing (sorry for the language, but I really couldn't think of another way to describe possible Voldemort hatesex), I seriously couldn't think of Voldemort having sex with anyone, or even masturbating. I get that this was a device to link all the stories together through parent/child relationships - but this was a very square peg being hammered into a triangular space. DOESN'T WORK. 
 3. The characters didn't sound like themselves. Yes, I realize it's been 19 years - but even when people grow and become adults and different versions of themselves, there are some mannerisms and quirks and tics that remain. There wasn't any of that in here. 
 4. The Time-Turner plot wasn't incredibly outlandish, but I didn't like using Cedric Diggory or his father as part of it. 
 Also, I think Harry was the Cursed Child. 
  
 My feelings on this story still aren't resolved, so maybe I need more time. Final thought: this doesn't change how I feel about the series overall, but I don't quite link them together. It's a good story, I did want to find out what happened and it wrapped up well. But I'll say it again: it didn't ring true to the previous books. Ultimately, you won't know how you like it until you read it yourself.

 It breaks my heart to give a KA book a bad rating! I am a huge Kristen Ashley fan, I read something like 26 of her books last year alone. That was the only reason that I actually finished this book. I had this nagging voice in my head telling me that it was going to get better...it didn't. There were some sweet moments but the majority of the book was painful to read. 
 I was actually super excited to read this book. As soon as I read the blurb I was excited and I hadn't even finished the early books in the series yet. The blurb talks about how Justice had a 'Poet's soul' and I thought this was fantastic because I would consider myself the same thing. I'm a little too reflective and melancholy with a passion for poetry and philosophy to consider myself anything else. I was anticipating relating to Justice over a shared passion, but this book had the opposite effect. 
 I hated Justice and her 'Poet's soul' which apparently gave her the right to whine constantly about her life while being completely ungrateful. I rolled my eyes at so much she said and I all I could think was: OH MY GOD I hope I don't act like this! In all, I found Justice to be over dramatic and plain annoying. On top of that, she was just so selfish and caught up in her own fame (that apparently she didn't want people to know about even though she told everybody she met). Man, I wish I had a dollar for every time I wanted to slap Justice because I'd be a millionaire by now. 
 I didn't hate Deke like I did Justice and actually, I think he could have been a pretty likeable character...that is if I could actually understand anything he said. I don't know if it's just me, but most things Deke said sounded like gibberish. Sometimes I wasn't sure we even spoke the same language. I re-read so many paragraphs but still couldn't wrap my head around the dialogue. Either I was completely disconnected from the story or the dialogue actually made no sense. By the end of the book, I think I had given up on trying to understand what he was actually saying. Sometimes he spoke so cave-man like (I'm guessing it was to show that he was an 'alpha male') that I just wanted to scream in frustration. I know KA specialises in badass me, but I'm pretty sure an alpha male should be able to actually speak in full, sensical sentences. 
 I didn't dislike every part of this book even though this review will make it seem like I did. There were times towards the end of the book or when Justice and Deke first got together that I was really enjoying. For that reason, as well as the fact that this book wasn't offensive, is why I've decided to rate it two stars instead of one. 
 This was a pretty long book and it felt like a lifetime when I wasn't enjoying it. I fell into this trap of skim reading because I just didn't care enough about the story. The more I read, the less connected I felt with the story. To be honest, I don't think I could accurately recount many events that happened because everything just seems to blur together. This also had to do with the fact that I didn't understand much of the dialogue and because I found the story itself pretty uneventful and boring. I also didn't connect to the characters and didn't care what happened to them, which just furthered my disinterested in the story. 
 I'd say that the final straw for me was when I wasn't enjoying any of the side characters and especially their interactions with the MC. The Kristen Ashley speciality is to have a huge cast of characters who are always so vibrant and fun to read. I just don't think Justice fit anywhere with the characters and instead of having fun hearing about them, I just got annoyed. The new friendships that were formed were so unbelievable and superficial. Justice met a couple of characters once and then we were meant to believe that they had this life long friendship...no, that's not how life works. By this time in the book I had basically given up and it's an awful thing to say, but I felt relieved when the book finally ended.

Look, last time I knew Ethan he was a five years old. Please tell me I'm not the only one conflicted about the boy on the cover! I almost didn't want to read this book because I kept expecting Chris Hansen to come in and tell me to take a seat. 
 Then I'd be like, "I swear! He's sixteen! I just READ about him when he was five! He's totally of age now!" 
 Then I'd cry dramatically JUST like this. 
 But, facts are facts, folks. Ethan's aged like a fine brandy if brandy had washboard abs and a butt built for spanking. AAAAAAaaaaaannndd, I just reach my creepy quota for the review. Wow. That didn't take long. 
 So Ethan meets up with Love-Interest while trying to avoid the Fae working their darndest to ruin his life. To save his and the Love-Interest's life they escape into Fairyland to track down his sister and solve the mystery and try to save the world. 
 More Facts: you don't need to have read the Iron Fey series to read this book. There's enough back history and explanatory exposition to make it through. I certainly haven't read The Iron Fey series and I managed to enjoy this one as a standalone. 
 Like angst? Ethan's your main dude. Seriously. Kid could bottle that stuff. I'm sure there's a roaring trade in teenage self-pity tears. But he's balanced out so nicely with Kenzie who would, by herself, be kind of a meh character. I might have found them both insufferably frustrating except they seemed to bring out the best in each other. So if teenage hot boy angst is your thing - hit this one up! It has it in spades. 
 Other than that you have all your old friends back. Meghan, Ash, Grimalkin, Puck et all and then you have some newer ones and then you have a pretty decent and solid mystery/action story going on. 
 Julie Kagawa's come along way since the first novel of hers that I read, The Iron King. I didn't get bored, kept eye rolling to a minimum and largely enjoyed the narrative. 
 There's one young man in the book though, I won't mention who he is. But I will say this: Son. SON! Don't go breaking our hearts, m'kay? You've reduced me to quoting Elton John here. It doesn't get more serious than this. 
 So, over all summation is that I want to hunt down the Iron Fey series and read that. Then I want to hunt down the novellas and read them. Then I want to start badgering the Harlequin Teen's publicist to put me on the list for the next one. I'd say that's a ringing endorsement. Wouldn't you?

Will the YA community stop tricking me?! I keep hearing people raving about how wonderful this book is! Lies! All lies! I'm having a really hard time trusting the YA community now, because so far, I've been really disappointed by all of the popular books! 
 And I really wanted to like this. I went into this book expecting to like it. I can't finish it. I just can't. 
 First off; why the hell would the King want a criminal as his Champion? Why does that sound like a good idea? Is he an idiot? All of the potential Champions are assassins, thieves, murders, or soldiers who were too violent for the army and got kicked out. None of them are good people. These are not the people you want defending the King! They will kill him and steal from him! Stupid premise! 
 Also, I personally hate love triangles. I'm so sick of them. The YA genre seriously needs to stop with the love triangles. I know, I know, everyone is following in "Twilight"'s footsteps, because "Twilight" had a love triangle. But "Twilight" was one of the first YA books to do that (obviously, "Harry Potter" did too, but you know what I mean) and that was why people liked it. It was different at the time. It's not different anymore. It's tiresome. Please, please, for the love of J.K. Rowling, stop! 
 The worst part thought, was our heroine. 
 If she is the most deadly and dangerous assassin in this land, everyone else is really incompetent. 
 There is absolutely no way at all that Celaena (or however you spell her name) is the best assassin in the land. So many little things made her stomach churn, and made her vomit. There is absolutely no way at all she had the stomach to be an assassin, let alone the best there is. We kept being told she was this bad-ass who could brutally kill people, but it was never proven. We were just supposed to accept it. I don't believe it. 
 She spent most of the two-hundred pages I read admiring herself and other peoples' dresses. I'm very tired of descriptions about dresses. And I'm not saying a bad-ass can't also like looking nice, but she was so shallow and preoccupied with her beautiful looks. And everyone had to remind us that she was beautiful. I wanted some brutal ass-kicking! Not some dainty characters admiring dresses and occasionally smacking each other with a wooden sword. 
 I truly don't believe Maas understands the ramifications of being an assassin. Killing people, taking someone's life, is not something for a character who's just like the reader. If you want a real assassin, they should be strong willed. They should not flinch just at the sight of the King, even if he is despicable. Someone who has the stomach to kill lots of people, and for money too, are made of steel. They can enjoy reading, and dresses, and whatever, but they are still hardened people. This heroine is not. I firmly do not believe she is emotionally and mentally capable of killing anyone. 
 Also, when the Champions were being introduced, there were two who were murderers, and who were brought out in chains. Why the hell wasn't she, as well? She's also supposed to be a murderer. I don't care if they're pretending she's a jewel thief (which I thought was a stupid plot device). She is a murderer just the same. If anything, an assassin is worse because they don't care who they kill; they do it for money. But no, because Maas really does not comprehend what being an assassin actually means. 
 On top of that, it was incredibly boring. The only interesting parts were when some of the Champions started dying, but that was only just barely interesting. 
 Still, I made it nearly two hundred pages and was going to keep reading, until I heard this was going to be six books. I could have maybe attempted three. But six? I just can't.

The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes by Arthur Conan Doyle is a set of short stories, about Doyle's famous detective. 
 I've written a review of each short story. They all are acceptable, and quality stories, however some of them have issues. A few haven't aged well, a few are easier to solve due to changes (for instance the rise of the second Ku Klux Klan in the 1915 and their lineage up to the present) and some are fantastic. 
 But overall, I'm hesitant to call this book great. There's The Red Headed League, and The Speckled Band and both are top notch to the point it's easy to recommend someone read just those two. A majority of the stories were four or five stars for me, which is good, but it's odd that there's a few questionable choices as a whole anthology. 
 For me the first story was a little flat, it felt a bit too easy and obvious, and I felt Holmes acted more like Encyclopedia Brown than Sherlock Holmes. There's also a number of stories that seem to be just too similar. Red Headed League is great, my first guess about the solution was wrong. However The Adventure of Copper Beeches at the end of the book is set up similarly and my guess for Red Headed League came true in that story. 
 In addition a number of stories aren't exactly "mysteries" but rather long stories. The Engineer's Thumb has a small mystery as a part of it, but 90 percent of the story is just a tale. It's a good tale, and quite enjoyable, but I don't believe the client needed the master detective to solve it. In fact having a short chat with Scotland Yard would have been good enough. 
 The book is worth reading, there's no horrible, unreadable stories in the anthology, but the reader will find a rollercoaster of quality. Some will be excellent, some will merely be adequate, but if one is prepared for that, there's a lot of enjoyment that can be gained from this collection.

I did it! I met Joe Goldberg. Though, I don't ever want to really meet Joe Goldberg. You was both wildly entertaining and horrific, funny and terrifying. I had a crazy good time reading and listening to this book. The writing was really great and the Joe's character made it all that more riveting. 
 When you start this book, it doesn't take you very long (first paragraph) to realize that the story's narrator is more than a little off. At one glance, he's already deduced that the female patron of his book store is a "dirty girl" and that he is in love with her. So the completely normal thing for him to do is take note of her name on her credit card, find out where she lives, stalk her social media accounts, find out where she lives, buy costumes so that those in her neighborhood don't notice the same person standing on the corner staring at the same window night-after-night, break into said apartment, and desperately try to know her by insinuating himself into her life. Totally normal. Well, to Joe it's normal. And he's played this game before. 
 It was Kepnes's characterization of Joe that stood out to me. We are in Joe's head the entire time, so everything we learn about his backstory is filtered through him. He briefly glosses over his childhood and how his father didn't care when he went missing. His relationship with the book store owner is more than a little creepy. He repeatedly mentions that he didn't go to college--which led me to believe that he felt inferior to those that did--but it's clear that he is a very intelligent person. 
 What made this book so compelling to me was Joe's voice and dark humor. His sharp wit was magnetic and attractive, but not in a romantic sense. I found myself laughing out loud at what he would say and the lengths he would go to to try to win Beck's affection. 
 But, I'm not gonna pull away from you. Sure, you are uniquely sexual. Case in point: You devour the "Casual Encounters" section on Craigslist, copying and pasting your favorite posts into a giant file on your computer. Why, Beck, why? Fortunately, you don't participate in "Casual Encounters." And I suppose that girls like to collect things, be it kale soup recipes or poorly worded, grammatically offensive daddy fantasies composed by desperate loners. Hey, I'm still here; I accept you. 
 LOL!! I'm still laughing at this more than a week after finishing. Okay moving on.... 
 It was downright disturbing the way he would nonchalantly mention how he's stalked other people before or talk about the items in Beck's online shopping cart, like he was asking a waiter for more ice. If you read this one too quickly you might miss some of Joe's gems. 
 And sometimes you have to play around with the facts to get the girl. I have seen enough romantic comedies to know that romantic guys like me are always getting into jams like this. Kate Hudson's entire career exists because people who fall in love sometimes tell lies about where they work. And Candace believed that I was a scout. I waited until we'd been together for a month before I told her the truth. She was mad at first (girls get mad sometimes, even when the guy is Matthew McConaughey) but I reminded her of the comedic, romantic truth at heart: The world is an unfair place. I know music. I'm smart. 
 Joe is kind of like a more disturbing version of television's ultimate serial killer, Dexter. But unlike Dexter, Joe isn't out there trying to rid the world of the bad people; he just kills the people who get in the way of his love. Joe describes himself as a romantic and maybe in the very true sense he is a true romantic. Like many of us, Joe is just looking for his one and only, his one true love. Beck has the chance to be the recipient of ALL of Joe's love. The question is whether she can handle his love. ;) 
 You sigh and I love you for trying to spin this into some sort of strike against complacency and what fun it is to play with you. 
 This book was well-written and Joe is a character I won't soon forget. I wanted more plot and story, rather than Joe being creepy. The plot was rather predictable, but that didn't take away from my enjoyment. I'm looking forward to more of Joe's adventures in Hidden Bodies. 
 Audiobook Comments: 
 I started reading this book and then the audio copy came in at my library and I switched. Santino Fontana narrates the crap out of this novel. Joe's voice is magnetic all on its own but combined with the narration, Joe that much more creepy. Fontana's comedic timing made me laugh so many times. I think this may be one of my favorite audiobooks ever just because I really appreciate dry humor and a sharp wit and Fontana captured the essence of Kepnes's beloved Joe perfectly.

This is the weirdest anthology I've ever read. I wasn't aware that Zombies Vs. Unicorns was a thing (still not entirely sure it is), but this collection of short stories had some of my favorite authors included so I knew I had to pick it up! This is not one of the better anthologies I have read, though I still enjoyed a few stories.

 Love Will Tear Us Apart by Alaya Dawn Johnson--3 stars: This one was SO weird. It was basically about this zombie who murders people until he falls in love and it was written in a very odd way and had a lot of sexual metaphors. Not really my cup of tea. 
 Purity Test by Naomi Novik--4 stars: This story was honestly so ridiculous, but in a good way. It had a very cynical tone and knew when to poke fun at the fact that this was a story about unicorns. The dialogue was hilarious! 
 Bougainvillea by Carrie Ryan -- 1 1/2 stars: A story that constantly switches between "before" and "now", this felt disjointed and confusing. I guess it was a prequel to her zombie series? Didn't really enjoy this one at all.

 The Care and Feeding of Your Baby Killer Unicorn by Diana Peterfreund--3 1/2 stars: The beginning didn't grab me but once the baby unicorn actually came into play I was much more interested. I always love a good human/animal bond so I enjoyed this one in the end. 
 Inoculata by Scott Westerfeld--2 stars: Didn't care about the characters, didn't care about the romance. Skimmed for the most part.

Eragon, the first novel in the Inheritance Trilogy by Christopher Paolini, is a story about a farm boy who finds a dazzling sapphire-blue stone which, as it is revealed later, is in fact an egg that hatches a blue-scaled dragon. 
 The dragon, Saphira, establishes an unbreakable bond with the young man who learns that he is the only dragon-rider to have come into existence in many years and that he will have to choose whether to resist the evil king/dragon-rider Galbatorix or surrender and join him. 
 With his home destroyed and his uncle murdered by the Razac (evil dragon hunters employed by Galbatorix) Eragon sets out on a journey with his mentor, Brom, to learn the dragon riding craft and enact his revenge on the Razac. 
 Eragon has all the traditional ingredients that make a fantasy novel enjoyable. 
 While Eragon is a very entertaining story, Paolini's writing is still somewhat immature. 
 The novel's pace is quick and exciting throughout most of the book.The only lag was the 40 page, desperate last-leg of Eragon's journey. 
 Packed with action and magic, Eragon is a fun read.
