I'm a bit embarrassed to say that there was quite a bit I had missed! But at this point, I was getting a bit tired of flipping pages and re-skimming the same bits anyway, so I just read the ones I had missed and called it a day. 
 My favorite passages: 
 Haha WOW this is your first conversation with her and she's already bringing up religion and being devoted to her eternally. You wanna bail, Romeo? 
 Shout, "Hah hah hah right um I'm gonna go over there, bye" into her ear and bail: turn to 85.

Well, I did like Allegiant better than Insurgent. That's something. 
 I just have to say this: I love Tris and Tobias' relationship. It's sweet and healthy, and I like how they actually talk to each other, about the hard stuff too. And the little touches and looks they exchange are adorable. Their relationship is probably my favourite thing about this whole series. 
 But so much of this book is NOT sweet, and it is not well written. The most obvious example is how Tris and Tobias sound like the same person. There were so many times when I thought I was reading about Tris, but then a memory from Tobias' childhood would come, and I remembered that this was Tobias's chapter. I felt almost lucky when I got these reminders, because other times I would wonder why someone was explaining something to Tobias that he had just experienced, and then realize that the previous chapter had been about Tris. Ugh. Very confusing. 
 Speaking of confusing: it was difficult to follow some of the action sequences, especially within the compound. There might be something wrong with me, but I had a hard time imagining what the compound looked like, and I felt like the distances and placements of elements there shifted. I had to re-read some of the action sequences just to understand what was going on. 
 The action sequences weren't the only things that were murky, though. The plot often felt brittle and contrived, and I kept thinking "... but that doesn't make any sense". Ever since the series moved on to the more big political stuff, I've gotten the feeling that Roth is not mature enough to make the Divergent world entirely believable. I like the messages behind the plot, like who do we discriminate against and why, but the story she tells is not tight enough for it to make an impact on me. I like the sentiments, but Roth does not make me think. She does not make me question my own society, and I think she means to. 
 And, finally. I did like the ending.  I think Tris' sacrifice is believable, both with regards to her character and the situation. She entirely believes that you should only sacrifice yourself out of love, and she loves Caleb, so she cannot let him sacrifice himself for the wrong reason. It makes perfect sense to her in that moment, and it makes perfect sense for her as a character.

Della's story begins with blood. 
 Della only wants one thing in life - freedom. 
 And even though she feels guilty, even though she doesn't know if she can ever overcome them, she wants to try to outrun the demons from her past. When she's given a set of car keys and hope for the future by her best friend, Braden, Della takes it. 
 She's going to go out, explore the world, find herself. 
 There's just one problem. She's in the middle of nowhere, her car has just run out of gas, and she has no idea how to pump it. 
 When Woods decides to help her out, he assumes it's just going to be a one-time thing. Della's on her way out of town and he has his future perfectly lined up, a future that definitely doesn't include someone like Della. 
 The two know exactly what they want from each other - one night, one night to let their inhibitions go and to just feel. 
 I'd wanted to know what good sex was. Now, I knew what earth shattering sex was. Mission accomplished. One thing was for sure, I'd never forget Woods. 
 Della and Woods both move on. Months later, Della relocates to Dallas and quickly befriends a guy named Tripp. After an incident with her boss that leaves Della shaken, Tripp offers to get her a job and let her stay in his condo in his hometown. He doesn't tell her where, just gives her directions, and those directions lead her back to Woods. 
 But things are different now. Woods is nearly engaged to a woman named Angelina - the arrangement isn't out of love, it was set up by his father. Woods likes to refer to it as a "business transaction" and it is exactly that. If Woods marries Angelina, the Greymark and Kerrington lines will be connected and he will have access to more money, more power, and more stability than he could ever have dreamed of. 
 When Della walks back into his life, though, Woods is torn. Is it worth throwing away his father's approval and what he has worked for his whole life for a girl who might run out of his life? 
 My heart picked up its pace and I realized it always would around Woods. He had connected with it and I couldn't stop that. I had tried. 
 Twisted Perfection is a story about overcoming your fears and living life. It is HEART-WARMING, HOT, INSPIRING, AND a OH-MY-GOD-LET-ME-THROW-MY-BOOK-OUT-THE-WINDOW-BECAUSE-OF-THE-ENDING read. Woods and Della are definitely my two favorite Abbi Glines characters. Woods is just as hot as I knew he would be. And Della? She has the dimensions of a perfect female lead - she's vulnerable, yet tough as nails. She isn't afraid to go after what she wants and I love her for it. 
 Overall, I'm going to give this a solid 4 STARS. The only problem I had with the book was that I wish there had been a little less sex and a little more substance to Woods and Della's relationship (I'm not saying it didn't have substance, IT DID, but I wouldn't have minded a slower build). After that ending, who ISN'T on the edge of their seats waiting for Simple Perfection?

Reading Bright Lines is a bit of an immersive experience. It brings to life the multicultural sights, smells, sounds and people of the Atlantic Ave. area of Clinton Hill in Brooklyn in the early 2000s. It has a variety of characters of all different ethnicities converging in this one place. It primarily follows the Bangladeshi Saleem family - Anwar and Hashi, their beautiful daughter Charu, and their orphaned, just finding herself to be queer niece, Ella. 
 It has to do with family secrets, and memories, elaborate gardens, political unrest, first loves, hallucinations, identity and fabric. I really loved each of the characters in this book and enjoyed following their lives. It also made me miss spending so much time in Brooklyn.

Really liked this short, extra look into the story from Genya's point of view! 
 I feel sooo sorry for her though!! Why did she deserve all of this :(( *cries*

This is one of those rare instances where I feel like this book is objectively great in both narrative and writing but I just didn't really connect with it. I understand how this book was amazingly creative and the characters were richly detailed, making it a really good book... but maybe just not the book for me. It's sort of a literary "It's not you, it's me" situation. It was objectively great but not great personally. 
 I really can't complain about anything nor can I think of any instances where I felt the author faltered. What it really comes down to is a matter of taste. (Again, it's not you, it's me!) I could talk about things that I would have wanted to see, I.E. romance, but I think that would be a bit disingenuous to the characters themselves. This had a sort of Romeo and Juliet vibe but minus the romance. I respect the hell out of Victoria Schwab for making this decision. Personally, I like books better when there are smooches. Hey... at least I'm honest about it. Ha! 
 Overall, This Savage Song is such a wildly original concept: acts of violence have become so pervasive that they now spawn real live monsters from the aftermath. LOVE IT! Kate and August are such complex and interesting characters and their inner monologues were some of the best writing I've seen in a while. AGAIN, PROPS TO VICTORIA SCHWAB! If it came down to it: Would I recommend This Savage Song? Yes, absolutely! Did I personally like it? ...Sort of.
It's alright, I guess. It's somewhat motivational despite offering vague advice and making problems that are kind of problematic in real life kind of too simple.

I really love the romance in these books. The way the POV is in first person for the main character and in third person for everyone else took a little getting use too, but I mostly just because I thought it was a strange concept, not because it was necessarily irritating. Beside, I am very forgiving if the author can deliver in the romance department. Oh, and they are actually clean books with the exception of the lack of respect for Deity's name. It's too bad more people don't count that as swearing.

5 Words: Magic, cruelty, bravery, adventure, hero. 
 Not my favourite book, but I do love the Lockhart scenes.

I spent a good deal of this book feeling superior about how much of the ending was obvious to me. 
 Turns out, it wasn't exactly as I thought. It reminds me of that scene in Jurassic park where the ranger is attacked by Velociraptors. He looks straight ahead and is surprised from the side. So, Lisa Unger, clever girl...
Heartwarming. I loved the main character's determination. Wonderful read. <3

(+) Fun read! Love the heroine's snarks, the heroine/hero's banters, and how the story progresses.

I think there might have been a few too many plot twists and time shifts. Also, I'm really getting sick of Nesbo killing off his most sympathetic female characters,  and this is only the second book of his I've read! In spite of that, I will be coming back for more.
More post-apocalypse, and this could have felt very cliche, but something about it really worked.

I've read just about every book Harper has written and this is the lowest rating I've given one to date. The story was interesting and the plot engaging. I even liked the characters. But the friendships were too fast and complete, with immediate in-jokes and banter, that strained credulity a little too much. I liked them. I just didn't buy them. That break in engagement was near constant after about the halfway point. The relationships (and I don't mean simply the romantic ones) felt like they were played on fast forward... 
 I did like the originality of the haunting, though. Good set up and excellent delivery. 
 A note about Steamy: Light, for Harper, actually. One or two explicit scenes, some uncomfortable spiritus interruptus...
Review posted at So Many Books, So Little Time

1.5 Stars, the half star being only because I actually like steam punk and Victorian England and paranormal characters but the way it was presented to me was not done well at all and I'm frankly insulted, if not pleased knowing that at least I can write a novel better than this one. I got 150 pages further into it than I expected I would and all I've got for it was a raging headache and a sneaking suspicion that Cassandra Clare doesn't have any concept of what an editor is there for.

Clare, I'm so disappointed in you. How dare you interrupt TMI to promo ur new series..... The first thing we read is about TDA. I mean COME ON! I thought I was reading the wrong book. I was like, where the hell is Jace and Clary? Anyone? A bunch of new characters are just thrown in and I'm left wondering how this is relevant to TMI. In fact, a quarter of this book is Clare pushing the next series in our faces. I'm sorry, this is freaking TMI, don't give me premature TDA crap. I'm sure it is very relevant to the next series, but I'm looking to finish up the one I am reading before starting a new one, which I won't see for another year or two. 
 Okay, maybe, I would have gotten over it if the bloody TDA characters, who are like 12 and younger, act their ages! I mean seriously! Tiberius sounded like a Dictionary come to life and he's ten. Clare would try to make him sound younger when she mentioned a stuffed bee, but I felt like she was trying to save the freaking Titanic. And Emma and Jules don't sound like they're 12. Maybe shadowhunter kids act older as they are warriors, but it's still weird... 
 And holy crap! This book was LOOONG!!!! If we didn't have all the TDA build up, then the book would be a lot shorter. I mean, 700 pages? SERIOUSLY? 
 I was really pissed that there was a huge deal about who would die in this book. But honestly, the people who died were secondary characters, not even, more like tertiary characters. I mean who cares if Maureen dies? Or Raphael? Or Meliorn? And then Jordan dies just so Maia doesn't have to deal with her feelings? There were a few close calls, but come freaking on! And then we lose Simon, only for him to come back! WTH?! I guess she didn't want to pull a Allegiant ending. But that has made Roth famous, while we just a fail-whale of a conclusion. Even Clockwork Princess left me more devastated.  And we get a happy ending! I don't know if I was ready for it. I was ready to be emotionally ruined. But I was left just feeling stunned, like seriously? 6 people died? When did that happen? 
 I was fairly happy what happened that was TMI though. There was some humour to lighten the mood at points and there was some character development. Alec became a better character, a little more than just an annoyed dude. I was a little disappointed that Jace and Clary seemed to be done developing their relationship. And where was Simon and Izzy relationship? I was hoping for more with them. 
 I was really happy with Tessa and Jem's involvement in this book. I wonder how everyone knows each other though. (because all the adults are like, OMG! TESSA! and I'm like, what?!) 
 I'm excited to read The Bane Chronicles, that are written for Alec. I will be really disappointed if there is no letter to Alec in the front of this book. And I guess I might read TDA because I want to see everyone from the previous series. I'm interested to see what's going to happen as the aftermath of this book.

Good-bye, and may you find a better life, find comfort again and your breathless smile, and when your beloved face lights up once more at the Western sunrise, be sure what I felt for you was not in vain. What a great story. 
 I was horrified to learn what poor Em has gone through with that sick fuck Frank. I swear to God I want to kill him so dead.

It wasn't like he banned her from doing something or other. He wanted her to have it all, he freed her from her nightmare. He just didn't like other guys making advances at her. I have very fond memories of The Chronicles of Narnia. When I was young, we would gather as a family and my dad would read these books as we all listened along. It's one of my fondest memories as a child and it helped solidify these books as a permanent part of my childhood. 
 As a young child, I was unable to really grasp the religious allegories within when I was first being read these books. Because of that, it's much more interesting to read through the story (with this particular one being essentially the 'creation story') and see what I get now. 
 Some of the allusions are extremely obvious, like  the garden of Eden and the tree of knowledge , but others actually bring on more interesting questions. Most notably: was the impetus for Aslan's creating Narnia the appearance of the two children, their Uncle, the Caddy, and the witch queen? Would Narnia have been created at all if it weren't before their eyes? If the latter, and we take the Chronicles of Narnia as a direct retelling of Christian mythology, then who do Diggory and Polly represent? Indeed, would Narnia have been created at all if it weren't for their sudden arrival into that world, or was it just perfect timing; a deus ex machina of sorts? These types of questions are fun to think about, and I'm excited to be keeping them in mind as I compete the rest of the series. 
 The writing was light, the story was short, and there were plenty of nice illustrations within the text. All in all I really enjoyed it. The reason I didn't give this five stars is because, in some places, it moved too slowly and in others I thought it rushed along a bit too much.

Greg Gaines has an overbearing Jewish mother and an affinity for avoiding real friendships. He finds the lack of deep social connections essential for surviving high school and his own lack of self-esteem. However, when his "former girlfriend" (read: he didn't realize everyone thought they were dating until it was too late) is diagnosed with leukemia, Greg's mother guilts him into spending more time with her. Earl, the only person Greg considers a friend also starts pushing Greg, and suddenly, Greg has to learn what having a real connection with someone is like... all while going through the most emotionally traumatizing period of his life. 
 Rachel's cancer is clearly a background element to the story of Greg's developing life. This is surprising to those who expect a "cancer book". I really enjoyed reading The Fault in Our Stars, but I felt like the messages were too overt about how beautiful life/death is and explaining how a person can gain a new outlook or fall in love or whatnot just from being close to someone you know will die. In real life, people are too self-centered. Most people don't know how to interact with someone who has a terminal illness. Jesse Andrews recognizes this, and his characters are honest about how they experience Rachel's illness. We get to witness how Greg, Earl, and other recurring characters are dealing with this situation- and everyone experiences it differently. 
 It's powerful watching Greg grow. He talks about how he should be moved my Rachel's illness, and how he feels like he should want to hang out with her-- but he doesn't. He doesn't really want to help or get involved. His reaction is something many can relate to: I wish I could ignore the whole situation. However, you can't just willfully ignore a situation like that and expect it not to affect you.  For example, Greg's teachers all notice this is taking a toll on him. They let him know they are here to support Greg as he suffers through this ordeal with his girlfriend. Greg immediately dismisses this. So what if his homework has been late? It's definitely not about Rachel.  Greg's experience with Rachel pushes him so subtly throughout that he goes from a character who didn't seem like he cared to one who was obsessed with helping a friend. 
 This story also strongly affected me because I listened to the audiobook. What makes his audiobook unique is that it's narrated by the actors who play these characters in the film. Thomas Mann (Greg) and RJ Cyler (Earl) already thoroughly understand these characters from their experience on set. Also, when Thomas Mann is impersonating the other characters, you can hear the actors he worked with in his voice. For example, Molly Shannon plays Denise in the film. Mann's depiction of Denise's "Grrrrreeeeg." is a spot on impersonation of Molly Shannon. I felt like Greg and Earl and Rachel were all real. Acting is magic. 
 Never have a read a book, or listening to an audiobook, before and thought to myself, "Huh. I should probably see the film version of this." Well. There is the first for everything. 
 This book, as you can tell, really spoke to me. I even found another great piece of life advice in it: 
 Go. Find this book. Read it.

A quickie read with my breakfast coffee. Like many Alexa Riley's stories, this is like a scrumptious piece of cookie you sneak in in between doing other stuff. 
 The premise is as expected, insta-love and a hot and quick cherry-popping action. H sees h, they both feel a connection but were not able to pursue more at that time. Fast forward a few years till she's just about legal (yep, we can't have underage action going on here) and our H is hot on her. This book is a "dripping with lust" fantasy love story it's got all the ingredients for one but unfortunately it's just not memorable enough for me. Maybe i'm bored with sweet virginal young heroines. Maybe it's because the Hero is very much like any other macho AR Hero in the last few books. In other words - it's not something i'd revisit in the future unlike some of the older books. 
 However, the "objective" of this book, if you can describe it that way, is to offer a fast, hot and sexy read and it does its job decently. But i'd rather save my stars for something more outstanding.

I am completely smitten over anything involving dogs so I was excited to read this. It has a childlike feel to the narrative but it works perfectly. It will make you laugh and it will make you cry - if it doesn't then I'm afraid to tell you, you might not have a heart, I'd get that checked! There's parts that aren't perfect but it's a feel-good book about unconditional love, that made me want to go hug my dog and never let go after finishing it.

This book was an easy one to get sucked into, with a really interesting and original storyline and a romance angle that hooks readers even more. It wasn't the first adult book I've read by this author since I had previously read book one in her "Darkest Powers" series and I didn't really find it gripping but I really enjoyed this book and would look forward to the rest of the books in this series and other series' by the author. 
 The main character is Elena, a one of a kind female werewolf; turned after her ex-boyfriend bit her she acted as an investigator of sorts for the pack she had inadvertently joined. But she got tired of the life and moved away getting herself a proper job and a serious boyfriend who doesn't know about her alternate life. She gets dragged back when killings are getting blamed on her pack and she has to return home and back to the ex. From there on out the Elena finds it difficult to turn back to her normal life. Elena was a cool yet confused character for most of this book, but cheating on her boyfriend for her ex doesn't really surprise me. 
 There are a lot of secondary characters in this book and I suspect some of them will be making appearances so I'm only going to talk about my favourite characters; these are Clay and Philip. Clay is the ex, a werewolf who is strong and Elena seems to be the centre of his life and the only good thing he has going on. Philip is the boyfriend who honestly seems to have a lot of stuff going on in his life and although he feels a lot for Elena he doesn't always put her first. 
 The storyline is brilliantly original, gripping and easy to read although I would have preferred if the chapters were shorter it didn't detract from the reading experience. The pacing was good but I did think the ending was slightly rushed. 
 3.5 stars a good read

I can't quite pinpoint what it was about this book, but there was something that bothered me more than usual about this latest Scarpetta Series book (which I think have been pretty bad over the last few years). This one started out by confusing me with what was happening. I felt like I had suddenly tuned into a conversation between a party of people that I knew nothing about. The events being discussed in the first several chapters had me confused and wondering how it related to what would be happening throughout the rest of the book. *Start rant. To skip over, go to paragraph four.* 
 Thankfully after the first few chapters, it started to get a little more interesting because there had a been a murder and Scarpetta with her trusty husband Benton Wesley, her conniving niece Lucy, and volatile cop friend Marino jump in to try to save the day and figure out "who done it". This is where things started to yet again go south. I think Patricia Cornwell needs to get everyone out of the routine of lying, withholding information, and giving too much information. The earlier books were so good because you knew who to trust and they were truly about finding the bad guy. The latest books (this one included) are too much about trying to figure out Scarpetta's closest relations through her point of view. For instance: "Why is Benton not telling me things?" (Seriously, it's because it's part of his FBI job and if you can't get over his withholding of information, then maybe you shouldn't be with him.) "Why is Lucy being so distant and why does she keep lying/not telling me things?" (Because Lucy first makes sure that she is correct and that the timing is right for everything that she does and says. Scarpetta (and Benton for that matter) has analyzed Lucy for years and it's pretty obvious that Lucy's affinity for doing/telling things only when they benefit her will never change.) "Why is Marino such a loud mouthed ass?" (Clearly Marino has been an ass since book one and since Scarpetta has married Benton, Marino has felt the need to one up and attempt to humiliate Benton as much as he can, which unfortunately pisses off multiple people and agencies in the process.) 
 So, since we have gotten all the negative emotions that Scarpetta has throughout this book (their answers contrived from the earlier books in the series) we should be able to actually have a normal plot right? Right! Except, by this point, the book would be down to about 150 pages. Then Cornwell has the gall to not even wrap up the book sufficiently, which then forces you to buy whatever the next Scarpetta book will be in this never ending, downward-spiraling series that has become more about the dysfunctional relationships between the characters than about catching the "bad guys" and hearing about the tactics and tools used to catch them. *End Rant* 
 Overall though, it was very interesting the way multiple murders wove together by the end of the story and I definitely did not see "it coming" so to speak. I am getting a little sick of dysfunction between the main characters (Kay, Benton, Lucy, and Marino) and think the series would get better gain if we could focus on what the series started with - who is the bad guy and how are we going to catch them? Please get it together Cornwell, I'm not sure I can stand more books like these last few.

 Actual quotes:

 - "I wouldn't care if you were alive or dead." 
 The protagonist wasn't much better -- after page 50 I gave up trying to like Tate. I hated her back-and-forth with Jared & her inexcusable treatment of other girls. 
 And, the constant slut-shaming -- don't even get me started.

I figured out the who-done-it as soon as the word sweatshirt  was used. I've watched enough after-school specials to know the deal. But I was left oddly disappointed in the ending of the marriage . I really was hoping for a happy-ish ending. Overall, a solid addition to the genre.

This is the story of a boy and his horse (and a girl and her horse, too, but I guess titles can only get so long before they become unwieldy), and their escape to Narnia and the north. 
 I had a lot of trouble getting into this one. Every time the adventure starts picking up, there's a sudden Grownups Are Talking scene that just seemed to go on and on and on. My poor son has taken to drawing pictures during bedtime reads because, advanced in so many ways as he is, he just can't find it in himself to get excited about Calormen politics. And I honestly can't say that I blame him. 
 I might have felt differently if there had been something interesting or creative about the Calormenes. But, instead, they're pretty much just a hodge-podge of "oriental" middle eastern stereotypes. Which really only serve to date the book. 
 I'm also unsure of what this does to the Narnia universe. In both The Magician's Nephew and The Lion, The Witch, and the Wardrobe, there was a sense of an empty world. Sure, there was the cabby who served as the first king of Narnia, but his court was comprised of talking animals. And in TLTWaTW, everyone makes a huge fuss over there being actual human children in their world. 
 Now, just a few years later, we find out that there are whole nations of humans less than a day's ride from Caer Paravel. 
 It reminded me of the book of Genesis: God creates Adam and Eve, who have three sons, who then go off and get married. And, suddenly, we have near descendants going off to other lands and living in the cities there. Knowing a little of C.S. Lewis's religious perspective, I can't help but wonder if he wasn't having a bit of a larf when writing this. 
 In conclusion, I found this to be a very pale follow up to TLTWaTW. There are too many grownups and grownup doings, and the use of stereotypes just comes off as lazy.

Whenever I need a break from traditional romances, I turn to either paranormal or historical. I'm so very glad I did. This is my first by Meredith Duran and definitely not my last. It often takes me some time to acclimate to the genre. Not this time. I was completely swept away by strong characters, political intrigue, attempted murder, and an unlikely couple. This was a story to be savored. 
 I was immediately caught up in Duran's eloquent prose. I felt myself enamoured by Victorian England, the etiquette, the scandal, even the decor all brilliantly laid out as a powerful suspenseful romance. I usually get frustrated by the lack of conversation in historical romances. I just want them to talk it out. Clear the air, but the time period, doesn't lend kindly to those. Women have their place. Men have their place. Usually it's a tug of war to get a fully developed thought out to one another. Not in this one. Yes there are some jilted conversations but they're deserved of the plot. 
 I love strong female characters and Jane is definitely strong. I would even be so bold as to call her pioneering for her time. She's in a terrible position of needing a husband. She longs to change her life and those less fortunate for the better. She believed in education for women and longs to see women schooled the same as men. It was fascinating seeing her character come into herself. I really felt like she grew as the story progressed. When faced with challenges she found herself stronger than I think even she realized. 
 Crispin is not whom she wanted for a husband. In fact she didn't think he would be her husband for long. But this new Crispin is one she finds herself liking. The old Crispin was a scoundrel, a maverick, someone she could easily use as a means to an end. I don't think she ever counted on helping the new Crispin or falling in love with him. He's got one heck of a mess on his hands, he doesn't know who tried to kill him or why. The plot is thick, the secrets closely guarded. 
 I cannot wait to run back and read all the previous books in this series. A Lady's Code of Misconduct can be read as a standalone quite easily. However now that I've had a taste, I want all the rest! 
 * I voluntarily reviewed an Advance Reader's Copy of this book *

Better than the last one. High praise, indeed. And, sure this couple was also boring, but the story was sweet and actually a little bit believable. There was actual chemistry. 
 So, we have Phoebe, a blind girl who gets all annoyed when people want to help her walk without falling into a hole. And, James, her bodyguard who is a bit crippled from injuries to one of his legs who gets annoyed if anyone wants to help him in any way. Perfect match. 
 They fight, she resents him, he secretly loves her, he leaves her, she misses him, he kidnaps her for her "safety", and then... 
 The only thing that annoyed me about this book, other than the idiotic scene where she convinces him to let her walk unassisted along a hole-ridden, uneven road and she falls over and over again, but hey, "independence", was how utterly stupid James has suddenly become. When he was the captain of the police, he was uncannily perceptive and smart at figuring things out. But, suddenly he can't figure out the most obvious kidnapper ever. The guy practically screamed "it's me" from the start, but Captain Unobvious couldn't see it. Perhaps he also knocked his brain loose when he hurt his leg. I was unimpressed.

I've been keeping this book in my tbr list for quite sometime now. I heard of the plot but I wasn't interested until now. 
 The book is a lot like "The Bachelor" but in a dystopian setting. They have a caste system from 1-8, 1 being the richest and most influential in the community. 
 The heroin of the book is America. She's a five, lives with her parents and two siblings. She's a performer, sings and plays music. 
 Then here comes an opportunity to make America's family to have a better future. The government makes The Selection wherein the Prince will find her wife from women in different castes. Every girl will have an opportunity to join and be drawn to be a part of 'The Selection'. 
 But America is in love with someone. Someone who she's not supposed to love, a lower caste citizen. She'd been stubborn to join but in the end was urged by her mother. 
 I like America. I like that she has her own personality and she's not afraid to say her opinion. She's been strong throughout the book. 
 On the other hand, there's Prince Mason. There's something mysterious about him at first but as the story went on I learned to like his personality. 
 There are different issues that are put into consideration about the book. There's romance, betrayal, family and politics. 
 I like how the story flowed effortlessly, I read it in one sitting.

*Sigh* 
 Actual Rating 1.5 Stars 
 I enjoyed reading about Illarion and Edilyn and I wish there was more of it. I wish the author just sticked with their story because it was amazing, she could have focused the story on those two but she did not. She had the whole Kikimora storyline to explore but no. 
 I was really disappointed with this one and I can't help but feel that the author is getting lazy and taking for granted her readers. I love Ms Kenyon and her works but I can't help but feel slighted. 
 The large chunk of this book was copy and pasted from Cadegan and Maxis books with a sprinkling of Illarion and Edilyn. As in whole trunk full of chapters were lifted from Son of No One and Dragonbane. 
 Verbatim. 
 Word for word. 
 I feel cheated 
 I feel robbed. 
 I just finished Dragonbane right before I read this one that's why the book, story and writing feels redundant because it actually is. And this book didn't come cheap, it sells for $14.99 on amazon! 
 I think Ms Kenyon needs new materials. I love her but her betrayed, abused and neglected from childhood/tormented hero storyline is getting old especially after so many books with little to no variations. And this lazy piece work? Tsk. Tsk.

I'm so torn about this. I love Lockhart's prose. I love her snappy dialogue and the way she folds social commentary into her narratives. But this book isn't just inspired by The Talented Mr. Ripley (or, as Lockhart says in her author's note, "I cannot possibly name all my influences but particular debt goes to Patricia Highsmith for The Talented Mr. Ripley"): it's pretty much a modern day, genderfucked TTMR AU fanfic. Like, a lot -- a lot -- of characters and plot points match up: not just Tom and Dickie, but Dickie's parents, Dickie's unwilling to be spurned ex-lover, Dickie's overly suspicious other friend, Tom's potential love interest who he has to lose to win the game. There's even a canoe paddle. 
 So this was fun, but it hewed incredibly close to Highsmith without, I felt, giving me quite enough of a twist or a "take" to justify the similarities. And I'm all for lady versions of previously male narratives, but I think they should be a little more upfront that that's what they are.
Rating: 90% (4.5 stars)

5 Stars 
 Awesome book!! It was exactly what I was looking for. I wanted a break from bad boys, and I love when the hero is a virgin! 
 Bennet was amazing, I loved his personality and the way he treated Avery. Also, he was a tattoo artist, a very sexy tattoo artist. He was perfect, sweet and caring and really hot. 
 This book has one of the most intense, powerful and incredible sexual tension I've ever read. I spent most fo the time swooning and drooling. Seriously hot, I loved it. The sexy moments between Avery and Bennet were amazing. 
 Avery was a nice heroine, likeable and strong. She wasn't annoying, and the way she acted was understable given her past. 
 I enjoyed this book a lot, and I highly recommend it.

Wonderful story to go along with Graceling! In Dell there are monsters. These monsters can be birds, bugs, and fish. They are beautiful creatures who lure their victims with their fashly colors then take over their minds to bring about their death. Fire is the last monster human. Why I'm not sure, but would love to hear more about that story. Her country is on the verge of war and she finds herself in the King's court for the sole purpose of digging around in minds to find information. This is something she swore after the death of her monster father she would never do. But for the sake of the kingdom and the people she loves will she become the monster she is? 
 And now we know how Leck, from Graceling, lost his eye. I'm glad Leck was not a huge character in this book, but I am curious to find out what will happen next will all the characters from Cashore's stories.

*3.5* 
 The beginning started off good, but the diary entries came in after the flow of the story had developed and so I was a bit thrown off. The diary entries seemed long and boring at first, but just before the halfway point, I began enjoying the diary entries and the story just took off. It's crazy how much my opinion of the book changed over the course of the book. I never really got attached to any of the characters, maybe Andi a bit...overall not an emotional read despite some strong themes. 
 I feel like I'm a sucker for books set in Paris, there is just something so magical about them. I also found the history of the French Revolution was really well done and came out in an interesting way, not a boring textbook kind of way.

 I really enjoyed reading the adventure that was The Great Hunt. Even not having a clue about any of the story it was based on or anything it related to, I got lost in this fantasy land with Kings, Queens, arranged marriages, and duty to your country over living out your personal dreams. And there was lots of blood and gore, lots and lots of blood. I loved it! 
 You see, there's this "beast" roaming the countryside randomly killing people (check out the amazing map above - nice world building, eh?). It may be one person one night, or a couple of people the next night. At first, it was only people in the countryside outside the Royal Lands getting "mauled" to death. Then someone close to the royal family was killed and the King finally took notice. When nothing short of a 'Great Hunt' will see this beast's demise (see what I did there? I'm so clever...) all sorts of manly riff raff from all the kingdoms come to camp on the castle's footsteps. 
 And you just know someone is going to get googly eyes for the Princess. 
 The romance was done so well that the mom in me totally approves. Subtle and sweet, the kind of love that is meant to be (swoon). Even the side characters had a swoon worthy romance that had me thinking that their book would be the next book in the series. 
 See where my need for closure clouds my every day? For some reason, I was just reading along, utterly enjoying this book and WHAM! I hit face first at the surprise ending and I didn't like it. No sirree Bob, I did not.

 I do want to go on record and say that I WILL be continuing with this series because my driving need for closure will compel me to pick up the next book.

 As a big fan of Fiona Paul's Secrets of the Eternal Rose series, a beautifully written historical fiction series with romance and mystery, I was more than ecstatic to find the author had a contemporary fiction novel publishing under the name Paula Stokes! 
 Back in March I had a guest post with Paula Stokes about character flaws. At the time, I had yet to start this novel but I was intrigued by the post because character flaws can make or break a book for readers and everyone seems to respond to those flaws differently. So when I opened up The Art of Lainey on my Kindle, I was honestly not sure what to expect of our main character. Lainey begins the novel by getting dumped, publicly, by her boyfriend. And she takes it hard. With the help of her best friend Bianca, or Bee as she calls her, she comes up with a plan to try and get him back using The Art of War, by the Chinese military strategist Sun Tzu, as inspiration. The thing about Lainey is, she didn't really know her own worth or who she was without her ex-boyfriend. During the course of their relationship she let herself get wrapped up in his world, with his friends. She embraced the popularity and the lifestyle she earned from it. The breakup wasn't just a loss of someone she 'loved', to her it was a fear to also lose that lifestyle she had become accustomed to, of the unknown on what her Senior year would bring. And I think that is Lainey's flaw. She could be a little fake and superficial. But I think that is part of why I loved her character. Inside she was just someone who was unsure of herself. She needed this break to step back and look at her life and what she had become. To open herself up to new possibilities. To find what was real. 
 Throughout Lainey's journey we find some great relationships. The friendship between Lainey and Bee is one I adored. Bee was a truly amazing friend, the type of friend who was willing to help Lainey with whatever she wanted and needed but also one who could challenge Lainey to think about what she was doing without pushing her away. It was a very positive and healthy friendship and one Lainey needed at this time in her life. And of course there was Micah! Never have I been so attracted to a person, er character, with a mohawk! lol Lainey and Micah agreed to help each other win back their exes by faking a burgeoning relationship and going on public dates. And these two couldn't have been more different, on the outside at least. Micah hung with a different crowd, but you couldn't let his appearance fool you. He was crazy sweet and all around amazing. He was someone who was very dedicated to his family, his job and love for baking. A guy after my own heart right there! I loved his playfulness when he'd take innocent jabs at Lainey to get a reaction out of her. He was a huge reason I had a hard time setting this book down when real life was demanding my attention. Even though I was rooting for him and Lainey, I couldn't help but admired his longing for his ex. It showed us a sensitive side to him to go along with that playfulness and edge. Basically, Micah has now become one of my favorite book boyfriends! Swoony, sweet, funny yet with a bad boy flavor, what is there not to like? 
 Whenever Lainey and Micah were together on the pages a huge smile would light up my face. By far my favorite parts of the novel were the dates between Micah and Lainey. These dates they took each other on truly pushed them both out of their comfort zones, from pancakes at a torture house to dancing at a club. But you know what? They both embraced it with often hilarious consequences as well as eye-opening ones. So much fun! 
 Everything about this book was exactly what I enjoy in a contemporary read - relatable characters, great friendships, and swoony moments all combined with good fun and a little side of angst. I am deeply impressed with Paula Stokes ability to once again write a book that got me hook, line and sinker!

While I generally have enjoyed each of the books in Castillo's Kate Burkholder series, I'm finding that this series is straining credibility a bit too far. From the intensity of focus on the Amish residents in Burkholder's jurisdiction - who are known as gentle people who value family and community, and who are strictly adherent to their religious beliefs - to the frequency of major crimes in a small town to the staffing of the small Police Department, the reader is asked to avoid thinking very hard (if at all) in order to accept the premises on which these stories are based. 
 For example, Painter's Mill PD employs 4 full-time officers and 1 part-timer, and 3 dispatchers. Questions come to my inquiring mind: Who fills in for the 6 shifts per week when the dispatchers are off-duty? This is never addressed, or even mentioned. Neither is the fact that the PT officer, being in his mid-70s, is generally given very routine and low-key assignments, and does not fill in for the full-timers. Again, not enough coverage for any week, let alone ones in which manpower needs are heightened. Yet there is never a problem convening the entire force within 30-60 minutes any time the Chief decides a briefing is necessary. Nor is there ever a lack of response by a particular officer when she finds herself in need of immediate back-up. Do these officers never have a day off AND never sleep? 
 Serious crimes in this small town happen far too frequently - every few months at times, a minimum of twice a year - which seems to be a function of how often Castillo needs to address the progression of the Chief's relationship. Unfortunately, the crime/mystery credibility factor suffers. 
 I am also beginning to wonder about the reason for Castillo's focus on the Amish community. Seven books into the series, the Amish have sometimes been crime victims but far too often, have been the villains. This is wholly inconsistent with reality. I am beginning to wonder why the author has chosen the setting and community she has, as it seems ill-suited to the stories she wishes to tell. Is there any autobiographical component involved? Chief Burkholder was raised in an Amish family but didn't fit in with the strict Ordnung and left the Plain life. Those who leave are looked down upon and are banned from fraternizing with those who remain, including one's own family. Might Castillo have a personal ax to grind? I have no idea, but I do know that - just as Amish women are not allowed to think for themselves and are subject to first their father's, and then their husband's, decisions, without questioning - Castillo is asking her readers to accept her series without questioning. 
 There are so many ways this series could broaden, which would easily remedy all of these discrepancies. I hope this author will do something differently soon or I don't see this series being worth such complete suspension of disbelief when there are so many other great authors in the crime/mystery/suspense genre to spend my reading time, and money, on.

Margaret Hope returned to England where she was born, unwillingly, to oversee the sale of her newly deceased grandmother's house. That her paternal grandmother was not long dead was a surprise to her; the aunt who raised her was deeply estranged from her mother and had allowed Maggie to believe she was dead. 
 It's 1940 and Maggie has something rare and wonderful for a woman in that time: acceptance into the graduate program in mathematics at MIT, after obtaining her B.S. from Wellesley. Delaying her entry for a year to go to England is totally not what she wants. 
 And then the house doesn't sell, and she's stuck for a while, and starts to make friends. Some of them move into her grandmother's house with her. 
 As the book opens, a young woman in the secretarial pool in the Prime Minister's office is murdered on her way home. A replacement is needed quickly, and Maggie's connections are just good enough. It's true she wanted a position as a private secretary, doing research that her education eminently qualifies her to do, but it's no real surprise to discover they won't consider a mere woman for such a position. She takes the lesser job, because she's increasingly committed to England and wants to contribute what she can to the war effort. 
 What Maggie doesn't know is that something far more significant than her gender is keeping her from the coveted post, and nearly barred her from the job she did get. She thinks both her parents died in a car crash when she was a baby. She thinks that one of her housemates, Paige Kelly, is simply another American girl, a Wellesley graduate, who worked for Ambassador Kennedy before he was removed from his post. 
 And no one tells her that the young woman she's replacing, Diana Snyder, wasn't killed in a simple mugging. 
 As Aunt Edith tries to persuade her to come home, as determinedly as she once persuaded Maggie to go to England, Maggie decides she's finally ready to face her parents' graves--and makes a startling and unsettling discovery. 
 This is overall a really well-done book. It captures the delicate balance of the time well with regard to gender relations: older ideas still prevailed to a great extent, but women had the vote, were working in a growing range of occupations, and with the coming of the war, were about to have an even wider range of occupations opened to them, reinforcing trends begun during and after World War One. Gay men need to be cautious, but Oscar Wilde is in the past, and the post-war horror of the persecution of Alan Turing yet to come. The complicated nature of the conflict between England and Ireland is not explored in depth, but enough is included to make sense of some important plot elements. 
 And if you grant Aunt Edith the right not to properly understand the character of the young woman she raised (trying to order her home without a real explanation of why is a bad mistake), the character development is wonderful. Everyone's motivations make sense for who they are. There are no elements of idiot plot. Even the bad guys have, from their point of view, real reasons for what they do. 
 Recommended.

I have heard so much about Robert Heinlein, and was excited to start reading this book. In fact, I picked it up at the used bookstore, in its original cover from 1957. I loved the idea of reading something from the 1950's, in what is now considered classic pulp fiction, from an acclaimed giant of science fiction. 
 I still had that feeling after reading this book. The execution of a brilliant idea, except for the part about the cat and the labour-saving robots, (and the wickedly scheming Belle) is not that great. A lot of ink is spilled over the machinations of the stock ownership of the small firm that Dan, the central character, shared with two other partners. A lot of this book could be characterized as "corporate speculation" much like "Barbarians at the Gate." 
 The book picks up speed again when Dan meets with the time travel scientist. Their exchange is classic and mesmerizing. It is one of the greatest dialogue I have ever read in a science fiction book. 
 But for the 75% of the book that seems to focus on plotting by Dan, and the corporate takeover machinations, it was a bit of a drag to read despite its slim volume. The object of Dan's interest, Frederica, isn't much of a compelling character. Only Belle and Dan (and his cat Pete) stand out as memorable characters. 
 If this book was done by an indie author, I would give is four stars. For a master of science fiction, I would give it three stars. But I do defer to the wide acclaim this book has received. Perhaps in its time it was truly brilliant writing from cover to cover. And the author does wordcraft very well with his put-downs, astute observations, and use of metaphors.

I started reading this book as a buddy read with a Goodreads friend, but she decided it wasn't the right book at the right time for her, so I continued on alone, grateful that it had been her suggestion and I got it off my to read shelf, and I'm so glad that I did. 
 There is a helpful map and I love maps in books, though I wish it had been even more heavily labeled as many places were mentioned didn't appear on it. I also appreciated the photos. Each chapter started with one photo, though I wish that that many more photos were included. Why there are so relatively few is certainly understandable though. 
 I found it helpful to read the notes for chapters that are at the end of the book as soon as I read their corresponding chapters. They're not long and I think that there is great benefit to reading them when the chapters' contents are still fresh in the reader's mind. 
 While I wanted more, more people and more updates on each person and more information, it's just because what's there is so good. 
 When I read books such as this I go back and look at what I was doing, eating, etc. during the periods and on the days mentioned. (I have schedule books going back to 1977.) I'm always stunned to read what some people have gone through during my lifetime, and unfortunately that includes now. 
 Somehow this feels like a perfectly crafted book. It's non-fiction that reads like fiction, so much so that a few times I caught myself thinking something such as oh that's too bad but it is realistic, and then realizing of course it's realistic because these are real people's real stories. The reader really gets to really know the six main people and gets a clear sense of how it was for others mentioned and also for the general populace. 
 While a tremendously upsetting account, it helped me to know that the six people focused on had all gotten out of North Korea (though it's impossible to not think about the people still there or who were stuck there and are likely dead and those who did die) but these are brave and strong people, and there was some humor, and the storytelling was so riveting, that despite the horrors, it wasn't exactly a depressing book, though there were plenty of heartbreaking events I will likely always remember. I felt a lot of suspense wondering how people were going to manage to escape. The way their stories were told did not disappoint. 
 This is an excellent book. I had none of my usual contemplating whether it should be 4 or 5 stars or whether I needed to include a half star. 5 stars it was, and I knew that most of the way through. It would have had to go way downhill for me to give it anything other than 5 stars and that never happened. Top notch! Very hard to put down! It's a true page-turner and always engaging. Very well researched. It didn't improve my mood about people or governments though, including the North Korean and also my own United States government. I already knew a few things about how things were in North Korea, but I learned so much more about the country, and while much of what was described was highly disturbing it was also fascinating. It helped that for the most part the people were likeable and at least relatable, even with the cultural differences and often experiences vastly different from anything I've experienced. 
 I really can't recommend this book highly enough. The author's other book also looks intriguing. She certainly chooses interesting and challenging topics. I'm eager to see what she will write next.

I was going to give this 3 stars simply out of loyalty to the series at a whole, but then as I was writing this review I realized how poorly the book was written on the whole. If I were being impartial I would have given it 1 star... so, 1 star it is! 
 There are some books where you get to the Big Reveal and realize, "Damn. [Author's name] knew all along what they were doing, right from the beginning. That was so clever; I can't even deal with it right now." J.K. Rowling comes to mind, and N.K. Jemisin or George R. R. Martin are two others. 
 ... And then there are books where you realize that maybe the author had no freaking clue what an amazing story he or she had on their hands, and was merely making it up as they went along. If the poor characterization, nonsensical explanations, and hastily patched-up ending are any indication, then Allegiant definitely falls into the latter category, much to my chagrin--and that of what appears to be a large chunk of the readership. Be prepared for a lengthy rant. If you liked this book/series, please avoid the spoilers (related by yours truly in a somewhat aggressive manner) below. 
 An aside note: I think I may have done Allegiant somewhat of a disservice (albeit not as large a one as it does to itself) by reading it concurrently with Deity by Jennifer L. Armentrout. I started that book later than Allegiant and ended up finishing it earlier because it drew me into the story much more effectively than, alas, Allegiant. But I'm getting ahead of myself. Lack of in-drawing is something I will discuss at a latter point in this review. For now, a list: things that simply did not work for me in re: Allegiant. 
 Poor character development. Tris Prior has never been my favorite of heroines, I'm going to be upfront about that. I found her to be a Mary Sue in the first book, a whiny mope in the second book... and in this book I found her to be a cardboard cutout of what she was supposed to be at this point in the story. Honestly, I felt like Tris was merely a vehicle with which to drive the plot forward, the eyes and ears of the narration without truly being a three-dimensional character. I actually felt myself missing Tris circa books one and two, which says a lot about the situation... I think I just missed Tris, I dunno, not defining herself by other people. In this book, that's all she does--all her emotions are delineated by her interactions with others: Tobias, her brother, etcetera. It seemed to me Tris was demoted to a mere point of view and no longer a character. 
 Out-of-character tendencies. To continue in this vein, I felt like Tris was not acting at all like herself in this last book. She was extremely out of character to the point where I had to check the chapter heading to confirm that it was, indeed, Tris who was narrating that particular section. For example, Tris whined so freaking much about Caleb. Yeah, yeah, we get it! He betrayed you! Now shut up and move on! Or aren't you the strong, special snowflake you were made out to be in books 1 and 2? Whiny!Tris from book 2 made another appearance in Allegiant. *shudder* Tobias was no different, really, but I'm too exhausted to go into detail about him. Suffice it to say, Tobias went from coolheaded, badass, mysterious leader in Book 1 to a petulant, jealous, poor decision-maker who doesn't seem to know his right from his left if you gave him a map. Honestly, the two deserved each other; they must be the only two who can tolerate one another. I sure as hell couldn't tolerate either of them by the end of the book. At least the secondary characters (Cristina+ and Uriah, in particular) were by far more tolerable. 
 Slipshod, slapdash, and altogether hastily/poorly done explanations for... everything. I get that Ms. Roth only had one book to tie up the rest of the series, but honestly? Like... seriously? People in factions, divergents, are just basically genetic experiments? What is the point of being Divergent, then?--they're not special, there is no importance behind the moniker, they're simply... genetically whole?  What a waste of potential plot. Furthermore, the information dump that was housed in this book was not only extremely boring, but also seemed like Roth had no idea what she was doing and was merely making it up as she went along up until the end of this series. There is no Endgame, no Big Plan that overarches the plot of this trilogy. Honestly, I'm still a little confused as to what really happens at the end of the book. Which leads me to: 
 No answers, just more questions. As I came to the Big Climax, I realized something, or rather a series of somethings that all had the same theme: I didn't realize a point to Tris and co's plan. And once they carried it out, it was really underwhelming. So, great, Chicago is factionless again, people are existing in harmony, but... people's memories were erased?  And Tris and friends let this happen? Seriously? Who the heck gets to decide that kind of thing, ever? It's no one's place to take away people's memories, regardless of whether it is in their best interests or not. That raised so many questions as I was reading this. Why would you even attempt something like that? What is the point of the last few books, then? 
 A crappy, cop-out ending. The only reason that seems legit as to why Roth decided to kill of her main protagonist was to lend some modicum of gravitas to her story and to set it apart from other series in which main characters, against all odds, manage to live while everyone else around them dies.  While I applaud Roth on taking such a huge risk, I have to honestly say that it does not work for the story whatsoever. Tris' death came so out of the blue that I didn't even have time to be shocked or angry or whatever... I just laughed. Seriously, I laughed out loud when I read Tris' death scene, because it was so ridiculous and at the same time infuriating. Countless authors have proven that you can kill off a main character and yet maintain credence and improve the story at the same time.  John Green does this all the time. So does George R.R. Martin. But Roth took a swing and a miss and all that's left at the end of the story is a jumbled mess with unresolved character relationships, a giant question mark in regards to the future of what Tris and co fought for, and, somehow, a sinking feeling like the huge war that was waged over the course of the trilogy didn't, in fact, change much of anything for the now-factionless dystopia that Roth has constructed. 
 TL;DR: 
 With not enough substance, a weak explanation for the events of the past two books, and poor character development, I felt like Allegiant was a completely different book than what I expected for part of the Divergent series. Instead, I was left with no closure on any front--not something a reader should feel at the end of a trilogy. Color me disappointed; it appears that in the end, the Divergent trilogy subscribed to its own hype and failed to deliver when it mattered. 
 + Interestingly the only version of Tobias I liked in this book was the "aftermath/two years later" version sans-Tris, when Tobias is interacting with Christina. For some reason, when he interacted with Christina he was much more... stable and mature, I guess? I found him to be 100x more tolerable than when he was with Tris for this book... I think a small part of me ships Christina with Tobias now, at least where the book ended up.  Strange, indeed.

 Review: I can't even...I don't know where to start.  Obviously, this book revolves around voodoo, the culture, the traditions, the legends. An urban gang named Loa Ogoun, after the god, formed after Hurricane Katrina to help protect and preserve the families of voodoo. There are four original families, three of whom still reside in New Orleans: Dubois, Touissant, and Igbos. The return of the fourth family is prophesied and with that return can come great evil. 
 Adrienne St Croix has won a scholarship to a prestigious school in New Orleans. She moves from Atlanta, Georgia to New Orleans to live with her father so she may attend this school. Jayden Washington is the hot quarterback, son of the rich "black Steve Jobs." As Jayden starts school, his father reveals a secret family history to him. A burden, really. 
 Of COURSE you know that Adrienne and Jayden are bound to cross paths. She's petite, pretty, and gifted with a marvelous voice and Jayden is the jock of the school, revered and desired. 
 I am fascinated by magical tales, voodoo, paranormal, etc. This was no different. Voodoo is especially fascinating for as much as is revealed and reported, there is so much more that is swept under the rug, hidden behind locked doors, and only passed down from family to family. 
 Even when you have multiple families working to preserve their ways, they withhold information from one another as you see Marie Touissant do from Candace Igbos. I am probably going to be the only one to say this, but... 
 I DID NOT LIKE JAYDEN WASHINGTON. There are characters in this book that I just couldn't stand. I don't know if it's because I come from a more privileged (although not like Jayden's) background than Adrienne does, but her father was REVOLTING. (And by privileged, I mean I have 2 parents who love me and when I was a kid, I was not given adult responsibilities like help me pay the rent!) I don't see how any parent treats their kid that way! She's not even an adult and she's paying her own way?! I understand chipping in because times are hard and you want to ease the burden on your parents. I do. But then he turns around and chastises her with thoughtless, jerk statements like "that fancy puffed cereal you like ain't free." 
 Okay, so that's her dad. But I didn't like Jayden for the SAME reasons. Firstly, while his Uncle Tommy's comments are messed up, Jayden has no love or respect for his grandmother. He dismisses her as crazy with her "voodoo" crap. You know, my grandmother was very superstitious as well and I never dismissed it. You, kid, are a rude, insufferable jackass. Then, he is thinking about how attracted he is to Adrienne, but since she's poor and his daddy is rich, "can't be anything serious between us but I wanna have a little fun and won't be told I can't by anyone!" You typical jerk male. UGH! *slaps him* 
 I also didn't like him for  lying to Adrienne, not warning her of the malicious intent from Kimmie (that selfish, vicious COW) that he KNEW about well ahead of time (he could have WARNED Adrienne!!!!), and then he is dismissive towards her as well, after asking for a tarot reading and dismissing it TO HER FACE as "a card trick." ARE YOU KIDDING ME? And she is STILL fawning over him? No. Just no. 
 No amount of money makes this kid worthwhile. Besides, he's 17. It's not his money anyway. It's his father's! Just because the dad is rich doesn't mean this kid will be. The dad could leave it all to charity or his sisters. Not that Adrienne really thinks about his money; she's bowled over by his handsome looks. She does think about it, but not in a money-grubbing, gold-digging way. Still, I'd rather she choose Rene, who is very what-you-see-is-what-you-get. I want Adrienne to be with Rene. Rene is rough on the outside, but gooey on the inside. He has this strict street code he sticks to that I find honorable and admirable. Jayden better be doing a whole lot of self-sacrificing, heroic, white knight on a fiery steed kind of crap in the upcoming books if she is going to choose him. (Are you listening to me, Adrienne? So far the one who is looking out for you and cares if you end up in a ditch isn't Jayden; it's Rene!) 
 Adrienne has to face some hard truths about the sister whose disappearance she is looking into. She already knew that Therese had crossed the line into black magic (blood magic) and its evil ways, but she didn't know just HOW much. And oh look...another betrayal from someone that is supposed to be on her side. How is she ever going to learn to trust the right person? While I pitied her, I was also frustrated with her on this point. 
 The story is twists and twines and reaches faaaaaaaaar back into the past and messes with the present. And you just KNOW that the resolution should lie with the Chosen, the Devil, and the Warrior. And you THINK you know who is who, but then...you're wrong. Or are you?! 
 So as I'm getting all revved up, CLIFFHAAAAAAAAANGER. Major things happen and then no matter how hard I was tapping on my kindle, it stubbornly remained at 100%. I can't...I can't even.

It's an Anne Bishop novel with no sex. If you don't know what you're getting into with one of those, this is not the right place to start. 
 I have started every review of the books in this series this way and everything I've said up until now still holds true. But I want to turn from Bishop's handling of gender politics for a moment. 
 I'm four books into this series and I STILL can't tell whether it's a brilliant examination of imperialism or racist. 
 I think it might be accidentally both. 
 Here's the thing - the terra indigene are very clearly modeled on indigenous peoples, right down to the name. They also draw on the animal and shape shifter legends of indigenous people. They are under attack by the inhabitants of Europe Cel-Romano and the introduction that accompanies every book in the damn series recapitulates the first contact. 
 BUT, and it's a big one, the terra indigene are a fantasy of power. The shifters, the Elders, the ACTUAL OCEAN are the terra indigene. Humans are always here on sufferance. Unlike the Imperialist fantasy of dominance, this is the fantasy where the only humans allowed to stay are those who can learn to live in harmony, who can cooperate with those unlike themselves, who can submit to the strictures of living with the land and its stronger inhabitants. The narrative still turns on the fulcrum of power and dominance, but this time it's Nature's order, rather than human imposed might-makes-right, and while nature can be both altruistic and cruel, it is not duplicitous and that makes it better than humans. 
 The Others is basically the story of what would have happened had humans been forced to reckon with power in their attempts to conquer and subdue the world. The group Humans First and Last consistently gets what is coming to it and the moral is that those who put in-group survival above helping others and cooperation deserve all of what nature red in tooth and claw can do. 
 Here's the second but. The terra indigene don't stand for indigenous people. They replace them. So, first of all, the pristine Americas is itself an imperialist white fantasy and is problematic in pretending indigenous people never lived here. And second, if you read the terra indigene as stand-ins for the indigenous inhabitants rather than the mark of their erasure, then Bishop is playing into their dehumanization by, quite literally, making them animals (some of the time). Also a problematic imperialist trope. 
 At the end of the day, our sordid history is things that Europeans did to other humans. And while this series, told predominantly from the point of view of non-humans, manages to defamiliarize the human experience by making our priorities and attitudes look weird, it also relies on native erasure and dehumanization to do so. 
 Bishop also combines "city-folk are evil" and "anyone intolerant deserves to die" into the same story and I have to love her for it.

"I see a world that is terrified of me. Terrified of someone who would reject manhood. Terrified of a girl who knows who she is and what she's capable of. They are small, and they are weak, and they will not hurt me ever again." 
 A YA trans superhero? HELL YES. Danny Tozer's greatest wish has been granted - thanks to the death of the biggest superhero in the land, Danny gains amazing powers and her body transforms to match the person that she is on the inside. Danny (now Danielle and not Daniel, thank you very much) faces many hardships and tough decisions, along with trying to master her new powers. The shining star of his book is the relationship between Danny and the enigmatic gunner Calamity. Their friendship is what really pulled me into the story, and Calamity is a deep character who accepts Danny for who she is, which really changes Danny and brings her a ton of confidence. I really loved Doc Impossible, for her personality and her crazy awesome inventions. In fact, this book is full of great female characters and relationships that I was fist pumping with girl power through some parts. The action was great, the world was explained fairly well, and the heroes and their powers were all interesting. Plus a pretty bad ass female villain! 
 Now, that's not to say that this book is flawless or anything. It took me a while to become invested in the plot, because the first bit of the book is such a bummer. I was so excited for Danny, but to see her so beat down by people who should have been there for her (parents, best friend, etc.) was terrible. Graywytch and Danny's dad can go jump off a cliff for their blatant and consistent transphobia. Fortunately, with the introduction of Calamity and their mission to uncover Utopia's plans, I was able to become fully invested. Also, I wish Carapace and Valkyrja could have lived longer. I really wanted to see Carapace grow to know Danny, and Valkyrja would have been the perfect role model! =(  The whole book felt like a prelude, like the origin story. Even when everything is revealed at the end, it felt a little rushed, and a lot of info was dropped on the reader very quickly. Now that the world is set up and Danny has one major victory under her belt, I can't wait to see what is next for Dreadnought! Solid 4/5!

 Well, this book didn't make me feel weak in the knees like Falling Kingdoms, but I still enjoyed it. I'm a little disappointed, but I had a bad feeling this might be more on the filler side. It did have some pretty swoon worthy moments, which completely captivated me. It's still very hard for me to ignore the Game of Thrones aspects. Especially with this book introducing Melisandre Melenia. 
 This book picks right back up where Falling Kingdoms left off. King Gaius now rules all three kingdoms. Magnus is still battling with who he really is versus what his horrible father wants him to be. Cleo is still trying to figure out how to reclaim her kingdom. Jonas now has a somewhat strong group of fifty-ish rebels, who are willing to risk their lives trying to bring down The King. We are introduced to a new female character, who I absolutely adored, named Lysandra. She's amazing with a bow, and has a very strong voice in what the rebels should be doing. Her village was destroyed, with her family as well, when they refused to help with the building of a road into the Forbidden Forest. 
 Confession time: I do not like Lucia. I didn't love her in Falling Kingdoms, but in this book I just down-right disliked her. Like, she acts like her brother's infatuation is disgusting, but she is constantly leading him on. Then she chooses to be all catty towards Cleo. It's like, have some freakin' compassion. The poor girl just lost her family, friend, boyfriend, home, and kingdom. Then this little moody girl chooses to have no empathy. I know she tries to redeem herself at the end, but it was mostly Cleo extending the olive branch, not bratty Lucia. I'm completely, 100%, without a doubt, shipping Cleo and Magnus. I seriously reverted back into a sixteen year old gushing teen when they still had to get married. Then that kiss later on in the book? Like, please sign me up for all of that. Sometimes intervening and giving information away that they shouldn't. The sanctuary scenes were kind of underwhelming for me. I found myself struggling not to skim.

I don't know what to rate this (5 stars, or 1?) My Harry Potter lover side tells me 5 stars, but then again I was hurt (yes, actually hurt) by some of the decisions made regarding the plot of the novel. 
 I'll start off with what I found most important about this play, which I think all Harry Potter lovers will agree with: There were a couple of scenes, words said, moments between characters - that had been missing from the series but which were included here. And that warmed my heart up, more so than the actual plot itself. 
 So yeah, that's the number one thing I like about the book (and what makes me want to rate it 5 stars - and it's enough of a factor to push it that high up into my rating.) 
 The next thing is my love for Scorpius, because I actually think his character was excellently developed and very realistic. 
 And thirdly, I like how this book stands quite on its own, how it's a whole world apart from the other books in the series. (It's not even part of the series, it's a standalone - so that says it all right there). The reason why I like that is because if it had tried to be an imitation of the rest of the series... I probably would've despised it. But it feels so far off that I don't really associate it with the ACTUAL Harry Potter, you know what I mean? 
 Anyhow, let's just get to the cold truth of this: Yes, some parts were fabulous, but many others weren't. Instead, they were awfully cringy - like badly written fan fiction. In a sense, Harry Potter and the Cursed Child IS fan-fiction, because JK Rowling didn't even write it. But still, I don't see that as an excuse, because I don't understand why she agreed to the plot of this play, why she agreed to take part in it - is this REALLY what she imagines to be the next part of Harry's story? 
 Here are the two things that I think are a complete dishonour to the series, and which I can't get over why JK Rowling could possibly agree with:  
 Firstly, Ron is portrayed as a weird, almost pointless background character throwing around stupid jokes. How could this possibly honour Ron? I just cannot agree with Ron turning out as a pointless, cast aside character. 
 Secondly, Voldemort has a daughter. And with Bellatrix, on top of that. Excuse my language (and I don't often speak like this), but what the actual F**K????? I cannot possibly IMAGINE for one second that this is what JK Rowling believes to be true in her world of Harry Potter. Maybe I'm wrong, but I just don't believe this. It's so fake, and I think everyone wants to vomit at the thought of it.  
 In the end, Harry Potter "8" had SO many expectations from fans everywhere, myself included - and it's important to remember that this book isn't another 7 book series, written in the same way and with the same feeling. Our three main characters have grown up, so how could reading this still feel like it's the same, like its the Harry Potter series we know? It can't. 
 I was very scared about reading this book, because I knew it wouldn't feel right, it wouldn't be right to have a next Harry Potter - yet I am still glad for the parts of it which warmed my heart and added what was missing from the 7-book series (like I mentioned above). But here they are, in more detail:  how Petunia kept Harry's blanket - I feel it's something she actually would have done - , being able to relive parts of the Triwizard tournament again - I particularly liked the description of Hermione clapping loudly for Harry, and learning that the Yule Ball jealousy was what truly defined Ron and Hermione's relationship. I was also very, very much warmed by the scene where Snape learns Harry had named one of his children after him.  
 So yes, there are moments I loved in this. But it's also true that I hated the larger concepts. I won't rate this book, as it's a 5 star and a 1 star all at the same time - and it's not like I can simply find the average score. For me, Harry Potter will always remain the 7 books JK Rowling wrote. Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is something separate.
