 I had the hardest time trying to work out what to rate this book. I'd heard a lot about this book, some of it good, some of it bad, all of it quite controversial. I wanted to read it with my own eyes, to see where my own opinions fell on the spectrum. 
 I had a vested interest in this book, as someone who a) had been a depressed teen and b) is someone considering specialising in child and adolescent mental health in my medical career. My general feeling is that I'm struggling to vocalise what I felt about this book. It didn't feel like my depression at all, but I know that I can't speak for everyone. Depression is an amorphous entity, as varied as there are people suffering from it, and everyone's 'black dog' is different. I would say that I didn't think the book delved into Hannah's depression particularly deeply, it made the decision to focus on external motivators for her suicide, which, in my opinion, made this book more about how people treat others than suicide. 
 I liked the message that people should always be kind as no one knows what anyone is going through, but I also felt very uncomfortable with the idea that depression, and suicide, had a basis that could be entirely based in environmental interactions. Depression and suicide are very very complicated subjects and part of me did feel that this story oversimplified that. 
 I was also wary of the message that all of these 'crimes' towards Hannah were 'reasons' for her suicide. One of the characters only crime was to let a friendship drift? That's not a crime against Hannah, that's life. I feel uncomfortable with the idea that someone who lets a friendship drift (and herself is assaulted later in the story) is in the same league as a rapist. I'm also wary of the message that it sends teens, watching these 'reasons' stacking up in their own lives and wondering at what number their life starts to become unliveable. As someone who lived through a not particularly happy high school situation, that experience does not have to follow a person. Who cares who your friends and enemies were in High School? Odds are that you're never going to see them again. Yes, the issues and problems born in teenage life can plague a person, but there's therapy and medication and life beyond High School, and I worry that this book did not give that as an option. I wish Clay had challenged some of what Hannah had said, rather than believing it word for word. Depression can make people bitter and angry, it doesn't necessarily make them the perfect sage counsellor for a book about how people should treat others. 
 That, I think is key. I don't think this book was written for suicidal teens. I think it was written for teens who couldn't even begin to consider that feeling. That job I think it does very well. People should be considering how their actions affect others, one person's actions can create a domino effect. 'Treat others as you'd want to be treated yourself' is the lesson we try to instil in all kids, but sometimes it just doesn't seem to get through. So, I hope that all kids reading this book take that message away, but for kids reading this who are suicidal, this is not the only path you have ahead of you. Please talk to people in your life, don't waste your precious breaths on a cassette recorder... 
 Here's a list of some resources for people who are currently struggling, or those who know someone who is struggling: 
 -currently suicidal or having thoughts of suicide? Here's a list of suicide helplines around the world. 
 -for parents or educators who want help in raising the conversation of suicide. 
 -for American Teens, 'teenline' offers phone/ text/email support from fellow teens in discussions of mental health and social problems. 
 -As always, if you feel in danger, whether it be from yourself or others, your local emergency room, accident and emergency department (UK) or crisis centre should be your first port of call. Mental health is health and you deserve to have your illness treated just like any other illness.

 The premise of Foreplay, by Sophie Jordan, is what drew me to this book, the first I've read by this author. This story's strength is its characters. There is nothing especially unique about the plot. In fact, it was incredibly predictable, though not uninteresting. Again, I think this is because Jordan did an exceptional job making me interested in her characters, making me truly care about them. 
 Pepper and Reece have both had less than stellar upbringings, and both tend to hide behind their damage, locked away from embracing life for different reasons but neither fulfilled. Pepper wants Hunter, her best friend's older brother. He represents stability, family, an ideal life. But she can't get him to notice her. When she finds out through the grapevine that he and his girlfriend have broken up, she realizes this is her chance to be with him. The problem is she doesn't feel confident enough to turn his head. After all, she's only kissed one guy and it was an utter failure. She decides, with the influence of her college suite mates, that she needs to find an experienced man to show her the ropes, to literally teach her the art of foreplay. The candidate is Reece, a hot bartender with a promiscuous reputation. He's the opposite of Hunter in every way--pierced, tattooed, blue collar, wild--but Pepper's attraction to him is undeniable, and winning Hunter's heart is enough motivation to make Pepper leave her comfort zone and act, to embark on an education that challenges what she thinks she wants out of life. 
 For me, this story was a tiny bit flat, a little too predictable to really fall in love with it. This book could have benefited from alternating points of view. I wanted inside Reece's head, to understand his motivations instead of just guessing at them. The no-strings arrangement with Pepper fit better with Reece's appearance than his actual character. Yes, I realize this is stereotyping, however, the same can be said for Pepper's conclusions about Reece's sexual prowess which she based solely on rumours and the way he looked. He was so much more than that, as was Pepper more than the "nice girl." 
 Reece and Pepper had great chemistry. And she had no chemistry with Hunter whatsoever.  So her focus on Hunter always felt weird in a way, as though she was trying to convince herself that she had feelings for him. I'm just going to say it despite my shock: I was expecting more of a love triangle. In general, I hate them, but the lack of passion from Hunter's direction left the story feeling unbalanced for me. The connection between Reece and Pepper was alive. And I understood that Pepper fought her feelings for Reece because he didn't represent the 'safe' life she thought she wanted. I guess when it came right down to it, I wasn't convinced that her past would have made her seek out a predictable, secure future in the face of real love. And yes, in the end it didn't. But she simply resigned herself to living without Reece. I would have liked to see her go after what she wanted. It simply fell into her lap. If not for faulty wiring, she would have ended up alone.  
 Jordan's writing didn't wow me, though in large part the hang-ups were mine: word choice and repetition. For me, there are words that once used should be avoided for a while for maximum impact. When these words were used again, it felt repetitive. Also, I found some of her phrases were of the pretty-but-awkward-sounding variety ("I slid him a long look." Pg 61, for example.) I felt she relied too heavily on certain things to tell the story: Pepper's breathing, tucking her hair behind her ear and her blush. It's not that any of this was bad, simply overused for my taste.

I didn't read any of the reviews for this book until after I had finished it. Yeah...I'm sensing a certain dissatisfaction with its ending. 
 Well, let me be the contrarian here and say that I liked it a lot. In fact, based on clues scattered throughout this book and its predecessors, I figured that it would end much like it did. And I'm OK with it because I don't think it's a cheap cop out. The clock has been reset, but Kelsea has paid an enormous price to save The Tearling - she's lost all of the people she had come to know and love even if their counterparts are still alive in the new timeline. 
 I will say that I thought the new Tearling sounded a little too perfect but I think I'm just being a curmudgeon. We don't get to see much of the new world so I shouldn't judge. And history hasn't stopped just because Kelsea's gamble paid off and Katie was able to establish a Tearling that was (far) closer to William's ideal. There are still plenty of Row Finn's in the world to threaten it, I'm sure, and provide fodder for future stories. 
 I also wanted to mention Jonathan Tear's death. Some reviews have questioned why it was necessary, and I think the answer comes when Katie-Lily-Kelsea comments that New London cannot tolerate a Tear. As abstract figures to admire and emulate, William or Jonathan Tear were acceptable. Much like any saintly figure. But as physical presences, they were too obviously reminders of how far most people fell short. That was the poison corrupting New London, not Finn's machinations nor the spread of the old world's religious beliefs. And you'll remember in the last minutes before K-L-K killed Jonathan that they looked at each other and seemed to be silently communicating. If so, I think they were realizing that Jonathan couldn't survive even if Finn was killed, and he accepted that.  
 Strongly recommended, and don't be put off by any of the negative reviews. The series ends exactly as it should.

 The Edge of Never tells the story of Camryn and Andrew, two strangers who meet on a bus headed to Idaho, via Wyoming. Camryn is trying to escape her unfortunate past (the fates have dumped a lot in her lap over the past couple of years) and Andrew is travelling across country to visit his dad, who is dying of cancer. 
 I quite enjoyed this book. It's told from the dual POV of Camryn and Andrew and although it's primarily a romance, the author steered clear of instalove - the two characters do some quality sniping at each other when they first meet, which was very amusing. She also didn't fall back on a love triangle to create tension, and I was so glad. Love triangles are starting to absolutely do my head in. Seriously, if you read much YA or NA fiction, you'd be forgiven for thinking that every girl out there is constantly having to make the tough decision between two hot guys. Because that happens to me, like, every day. 
 Anyway, that's what the author doesn't do. Instead, she builds in tension with Andrew and Camryn's sad back stories. One of Camryn's ex-boyfriends died in a car accident and the other turned out to be a bit of a scumbag, so before she meets Andrew she has sworn off men. Andrew, on the other hand, has never met a girl he likes enough to commit to and is now travelling across the country to visit his dad, who is dying of cancer. 
 I have to say, there was a point in the first few chapters where I thought that this was going to be my first DNF of the year. I didn't connect with Camryn very much in the early part of the story and I think she made some odd choices, but I'm really glad I stayed with it because she grew a lot as a character once she got on the bus and I started to really enjoy her POV. 
 There was a twist at the end that I didn't see coming and I thought the ending was maybe a little bit rushed because of it and everything surrounding the twist was wrapped up a bit quickly. Other than this, though, I thought The Edge of Never was a really enjoyable read and a very sweet romance.

"We create art for man reasons - wealth, fame, love, admiration - but I find the one thing that produces the best results is desire. When you want the thing you're creating, the beauty of it will shine through, even if the details aren't all in order. Desire is the fuel of creators, and when we have that, motivation will come in its wake" 
 This book left me feeling good. Hunger satiated, wisdom fed, and life inspired. 
 Whatever Zappia's specific intentions were, the book definitely extracted numerous emotions and reactions from me. Eliza's anxiety, fears, and sadness - they oozed out of the pages and gripped my soul. 
 Initially, I thought, "Predictable." Of course the new kid is rainmaker. Of course they'll be romantically involved. 
  But ultimately, my disappointment dissipated like it never existed at all. I absolutely loved the main characters. Their vulnerability is so touching. It's authentic and endearing. 
 "Orcus itself is my favorite location. If I could live there instead of on Earth, I would do it in a heartbeat. I would build an airship and fly over the monster-filled oceans, and I'd visit all the places I've only ever seen in my head" 
 This novel is very symbolic and relatable especially to those with depression, anxiety, or panic disorder. 
 Eliza Mirk is fortunate enough to find solace in her art. Her imagined world provides more than an escape from a cruel and insipid world. It is also a place of serenity, passion, and adventure. 
 Not everyone can be as creative as Eliza or Wallace, but there is always something. 
 Loved ones to hold on to. Hearts to treasure. A ground to push yourself off of. And stars to reach. 
 This is what I'm taking with me from this story. I bought them with genuine tears and a piece of my heart. 
 P.S. About "You found me in a constellation". Eliza mentioned a truth behind it grasped differently by everyone who knows about the quote. I think I understand its truth for myself. I wonder what anyone else felt about it. 
 P.P.S. So what's next for Francesca Zappia? Monstrous Sea and Children of Hypnos please! 
 P.P.P.S. Apparently, Children of Hypnos already exists!

I read this book in the span of two afternoons and I am not ashamed. I really really loved it. I feel like a reread of the prior books is definitely in order because it reminded me of how much I love these books. If I could marry a book series, this one would be it. 
 This book kind of does it's own thing, which, if you're used to the vague formula of the other books, can be a little jarring. In this book, they're really getting into the meat of the overarching plot of the series as opposed to hinting and doing a scene but having the story be more about whatever big, bad monster Atlanta got stuck with this month. Glancing at other reviews, I can see that that's thrown some people off or made them feel like it went too fast. This is not a book where the characters get to catch their breath and it does go by very quickly. That being said, I don't think it felt rushed to me as others are saying. Streamlined, perhaps, but never rushed. There is a set of goals from very early on in the story and they work toward them the whole book. 
 I'll put the rest behind a spoiler for those who haven't read the book yet. These are just some of my thoughts about the book in no particular order. 
  
 Hands down, I think getting Roman to officiate their wedding was great, hysterical fun. There was nothing better than picturing the black priest of Chernobog designing wedding invitations with cutesy flowers on them and helping Curran pick out wedding cakes. I fully believe that if they hadn't had him forcibly helping to plan their wedding, it would have been a wedding where everyone showed up in leather armor, carrying crossbows and swords. 
 Curran and Kate had a lot to deal with in this book, though I feel like a lot of the problems might have been avoided if Kate were simply honest with Curran. He points this out himself, of course, but, in more ways than one in this book, it is shown that Kate is her own worst enemy sometimes. 
 I loved having Erra back as a mentor instead of as a true enemy. Sure, she's still a force to be reckoned with and violent as hell, but we got to see more of her world in this book and her perspective. It gives you a brief glimpse into Roland's world as well, though it doesn't manage to explain away his megalomania. I don't think that can truly be explained. I do wonder about this family and their habit of turning themselves into bone weapons for the heir to their families. It gives a whole new meaning to these swords being a family heirloom. 
 I'm so glad Ghastek chose Kate over her father. I assumed he would after the last book, but I feared the worst. 
 I'm also very very glad for Christopher being able to find his sanity after what was done to him. That was a hellishly tense scene when he initially transforms. I look forward to seeing how he and Barabas continue to develop, since there's obviously shared feelings there. Lord knows they both deserve to be happy. 
 I think the only thing that was kind of a red herring for me was when it was mentioned that Curran had eaten the spiritually blessed saber-tooth tiger. I felt sure that was going to do something interesting aside from just being a thing that he just randomly decided to eat. Like he gets stabbed by Roland and is able to bounce back because he had eaten a divine creature. But no. Never mentioned again. Alas. 
 I was glad to see more of Derek in this book. I remember feeling that he was mostly absent in the last book, which was understandable but sad all the same. 
 Thank goodness Julie's not under Roland's thumb. I know that was a concern there. 
 Jim had more of a stick up his ass than usual this time around, but I am so very glad Dali didn't die. I love Dali. I love Dali and Jim together. I love their nearly polar opposite natures coming together so nicely. Losing her would have made me tremendously sad. That being said, so would losing Andrea's baby. I'm glad they have their first child. I do adore Andrea. She's so kick ass. All the ladies are so kick ass. I love them all. 
 I wish there was a way for Kate and Nick to bridge the gap between them. I know he hates Roland for really understandable reasons, but Kate isn't Roland. Even on Roland's best day, Kate is still a better human being than Roland is capable of being. I feel like Nick should be smart enough to understand that. 
 I look forward to seeing how much of a terror Kate is when she's pregnant and has a colony of people doting on her. Curran, Adora, Julie, Derek, Andrea, Barabas, Christopher - I could keep going. If she gets put on bed rest, I'm pretty sure she'll lose her shit. It will also be hysterically funny.

Oh, and she also doesn't remember anything about the "accident" that put her into a coma. She continues to repeat things like: "is it me who's missing something or is it them?" I understand and empathize with Jenna, but at the same time, sometimes she talked like Charlie from The Perks of Being a Wallflower.

I mean, every time Jenna sees/meets a guy, you immediately feel tension. You shouldn't feel that. I never saw her ending up with any of the guys that she meets, but whatdoyouknow, she does. It just felt forced and overall uncomfortable for me and I never felt anything but bored with the relationship. 
 Other than that, everything just felt so..artificial to me The characters. Dane, mainly. Like, what did he add to the book? Why was he so strange? No one will ever know. I don't know, I never felt like I was entirely in the story. I have to be fully immersed in the world and characters and story to actually love the book. This one, I was just reading it and I never had that feeling like I have to keep reading this. 
 On to the good, I actually liked the author's message at the end and how she got the inspiration for this novel. It explained a lot and was interesting to read about. I also liked the overall setting. I felt like it fit the kind of creepy plot well. I did speed through it but that may just be because it's a pretty simple book and you can easily fly through it. 
 Basically I like the idea/concept of this more than I like the actual book as a whole.
I loved the way it was written but it scared me witless. For me this was closer to a horror story than I am comfortable with.

If you liked RUINED, AVENGED will leave you feeling just as excited! 
 Picking up where book one left off, AVENGED continues the Ruined series with action, deception, politics, love and turns that will leave you wondering why you didn't see that coming. The characters continue to grow together and as individuals and the storyline is smooth and easy to fall into. 
 Cas and Em still have me loving them as a couple--not that they are always a couple. They are torn apart by their warring sides, but fate still finds ways to push them together. They don't have much romance time, but I still enjoyed their interactions and I could feel the connection between them, even when they weren't allowed to show it. 
 I enjoyed the addition of Aren's POV. It is easy to like him and root for him in everything he does. Olivia is beyond crazy and it shows in every decision she makes. People see it, but I don't think they fully understood how much crazy was there until the end when it was too late. There are a few other secondary characters--especially Iria and Violet--that I enjoyed getting to know more about as well. 
 I'm dying to know what will happen next and I really want Em to get her happily ever after at the end of it. She has sacrificed so much--and for people that don't fully appreciate it--that she deserves some good to come of everything that's happened. Book three doesn't have a name yet, but it's already on my wishlist.

 Oh, oh oh. There are so many things I want to say about this book. Rarely am I left in such a tizzy when I finish. So this is enthusiastic but not terribly organized. The books is well organized, and we get a well-thought out, well-constructed world with great continuity. The characters are well-developed and could play to type but don't. The writing is also very good, well-balanced with descriptive language nicely meshing with internal monologue and dialogues. 
 This world's development is hampered by the conditions present in it, the division between predator and prey creating a subsistence economy with sharply divided classes and a lack of art. Technology, such as it is, is available but not advanced. 
 WICKED AS THEY COME is so romantic; imagine pages and pages of dark deliciousness. It's very sexy although it takes a while to get to actual sex, when that occurs the actual sex is steamy. I would like to read more with expanded accounts. 
 The world of Sang where Tish is transported reminds me of the film The Imaginarium of Doctor Parnassus. Just the world's feel, not the story. It's that same gritty carnival darkness with less skin and a bit of blood. 
 I didn't really catch the techno vibe of steam-punk, more like mage-punk. In steam-punk there is a pretense of a scientific foundation to all the technology, here it's not really explained. You can assume there's science or not. 
 Tish goes from being a upstanding nurse to doing what she must to prevent genocide. She chooses a path that brings her freedom and love when she was escaping a relationship with a violent, controlling man. She has to go through the same struggle or darkness she predicts for her clients when telling their fortune. And part of that is discovering her own darkness, understanding the violence of it. It's heady, hot stuff. 
 And Criminy Stain is like Mr. Darcy mixed with Barnabas Collins, a tempting vampire magician with the body of a male stripper. 
 Letitia longs for love, but she needs to find herself again. Criminy longs for love and wants to find his other half in it. His love for her is unconditional, his spirit and responsibility are generous, his ingenuity amazing but not infallible. He is a gentleman thief, a rogue with honor. The humans are generally an intolerant lot. A few have honor, but most seem a nasty bunch afraid of people they don't have to fear. Tish, or Letitia is never bigoted in that way, she is bigotted against love, and hampered by loving responsibility. And, oh! The bludbunnies! 
 Steam-punk, Paranormal Romance or Urban Fantasy Fans, I call this a MUST READ and call for MORE!

We will call that a 3.25. It started a bit slow, but after the major plot twist at around page 200, I paid more attention!  I also wasn't sure what the depiction of Evon's love life had to do with the rest of the story--pretty much nothing, as it turns out. Maybe he did it with a future story in mind? When I first started reading the Pretty Little Liars series I couldn't put the books down, but now I'm finding them extremely tedious. The structure of each novel is exactly the same; the introduction hinting towards secrets that the friends are keeping from each other and the ending being a resolution with a hint of things to come in the next novel. The cliffhangers have become smaller and smaller as the series has grown, with this one being a simple crack in the pavement of shock. 
 Ruthless continues the life story of Spencer, Hanna, Aria and Emily. Emily has fallen in love with a stranger at a party, Spencer is convinced the girl she framed for her crime is back for revenge, Hanna's started another bad relationship and Aria's returned to an old love after her break-up with Noel. 
 Shepard always seems to introduce characters for one book and then they never appear again (Chloe, Caleb) which is the only reason the return of Ezra Fitz shocked me. However, the change in his character seems too dramatic and takes away from the magic that he held in the first arc of the books, which I believe comes down to pure laziness. If he really had written a novel for the girl of his dreams, I'm sure he wouldn't run away and kiss someone else in the coat closet at the first sign of a rift, as he is still in love with her after her childish breakdown when he left and her getting him in trouble with the police. If you can put up with a girl for those things, while being in an illicit student/teacher relationship, I'm pretty sure waiting a couple more days would make no difference. 
 The reunion of Aria and Noel at the end of the novel is predictable and, I felt, unwanted. Aria and Ezra's relationship was so beautiful at the start of the series and Shepard made him let go without so much of a fight, which completely ruined their history for me. 
 A shock for me in this book was how much Spencer was growing on me! While the other Pretty Little Liars are obsessing over relationships and are barely thinking about Tabitha, it was great to see Spencer's breakdowns while rehearsing for the role of Macbeth. Yes, she had a kiss with her attractive co-star Beau, but the pairing was over almost as soon as it had begun, which made her a much more bearable character. I'm still annoyed that Andrew was written out so abruptly, but I hope he reappears in the next two novels and they get things sorted out. 
 Spencer also seemed to be maturing much more in her new family situation with Mr Pennythistle and Amelia. In the previous book she complained so much I felt like pulling my hair out, but it was good to see that she seemed almost happy with the new additions by the end of this novel. 
 Emily the on again/off again lesbian (seriously, just admit you're bisexual!) seems to be growing more into a character in this novel, as she always seems to have faded into the background compared to the other three girls. Her obsession with Ali and a possible return is a bit repetitive and I can assume that it's foreshadowing to the next couple books (if it is, this isn't subtle at all). It's good to see her referring to herself as New Emily and the party scene with Beth and her "bad-girl bucket list" did make me chuckle, but the finale with Kelsey just disappointed me; saying "Poor Kelsey" after she nearly got killed by the girl? Emily, get it together! 
 Similarly to Emily, Hanna needs to get it together too. After her previous relationship disasters I'm surprised this girl hasn't claimed celibacy yet, but she starts another one off, with her fathers political rivals son, Liam Wilkinson. Meeting him and immediately saying "that's a beautiful name" (with Liam being one of the top 20 most common names?!) just shows how shallow Hanna really is. I was slightly surprised by the revelation that Liam was actually a serial dater, but the fact that Hanna spilled his secrets after one betrayal, which she didn't even give him a chance to defend himself over, didn't surprise me at all. Hanna has a moment of realization during a conversation with Liam earlier in the novel, deciding that Ali really was just a bully, but that's all that Hanna is too. 
 The only thing that's making me pick up the next book (other than the determination to finish the series) is this secret between Hanna and Aria from Iceland. I hope it's worth it.

I had to read this for my book club otherwise I would not have finished it. The passive voice that begins each chapter, especially in the beginning, was really annoying. It was probably meant to reference the inevitability of the rise of the third reich and the main characters' helplessness but mainly it just irritated the hell out of me. 
 All the characters were cardboard cutouts until page 150. Marie Laure is blind, likes to read and is interested in life sciences. Despite aging from 10 or 12 to 16, she does not change from page 20 to page 420. Werner is a mechanical genius, is really good at math and cares for his sister. He also does not change from page 20 to 420 despite aging from 10 to 16. Marie Laure's father is a typical Dickensian good guy. Presented with difficulties, he makes the moral choice over and over again. Werner is also faced with moral choices, in fact there is much more at stake with Werner's choices. The moral ambiguity is high. Werner chooses the path of least resistance again and again. There is no tension in his choices. He is as passive as the chapter beginnings. 
 So what happens around page 150? We finally get some interesting characters! Characters with depth that change and we can care about because there's more to them than a list of interests. Etienne has PTSD from WWI. He hasn't left his house in decades. We don't even see him for several days after his existence is brought to our attention. Then when he comes out, his love for Marie Laure and for imaginative adventures and his fear of the outside world shines off the page. We also meet Madame Manec and she's awesome. She cans the best peaches, she's talkative and friendly and warm. I won't give away how these characters develop, but they do. Meanwhile Werner and Marie Laure operate in their circumscribed paths and make me feel soo sleeeeppeee 
 Yaaawwwnn 
 And now for spoilers of things that made no sense! So Marie Laure likes going into a grotto filled with slimy creatures and cold sea water that saturate her shoes? Maybe she is a dedicated naturalist but that doesn't explain the shoes! She doesn't have spare shoes. The leather is being ruined. Her only escape is to walk to the bakery in shoes that she is quickly destroying. 
 And then! to get away from creepy cancer guy, she locks her self in the grotto in the seawater and waits him out? Seriously? The town is occupied by Germans. He could simply post a soldier to wait for her or he could wait for her himself. And much more comfortably than she can wait. He can get a chair, get some food, a blanket, all kinds of things to make waiting easier for him than for her. We already know he is a patient man. But apparently locking herself in a grotto completely defeats cancer man. 
 The first person that Werner is directly responsible for killing is cancer man and this is treated as if he killed a cockroach. Werner is being haunted by a 5 year old girl he did not directly kill. How does this make sense? As odious as cancer man is, how worthy Marie Laure is, there's got to be some sort of impact on Werner but yet there's not. 
 Werner's death was so predictable. Of course he's going to die. But I didn't care. Bye Werner. I won't miss you because you're made out of cardboard and missing cardboard is kinda crazy. 
 The entire story is missing tension and drama. The author chooses a beautiful and unusual setting - Saint Malo. He chooses a time of upheaval and heartbreak and sacrifice and honor. And this book is so milquetoast. The jumping around in time was the only thing to bring some tension to the story and that was me rolling my eyes and silently telling the author to just write the fricking story already. The jumping around in time did nothing for the story except make it annoying when it was merely dragging along. 
 The tie between Marie Laure and Werner - the science recordings - became merely a banal coincidence when it should have been a moment of poignancy. 
 Finding the key in the little model house was a so-what moment when it should have been a moment of poignancy. A can of peaches would have been better - a tie back to a character I actually cared about. The key harkened back to Marie Laure's father, a flat character, and the grotto, a cold slimy place, and the museum, a place where very little happened. 
 The Sea of Fire was so uninteresting that I just now remembered to mention it. 
 The references to light weren't bad but they also felt pretentious to me. They had so little to do with the story that it seemed more like a lecture than anything poignant. 
 I'm rarely interested in delving this deep into my book reviews so I guess bravo for that. Nevertheless. This is not an author I need to follow.

I had a hard time relating to Luisa because I can't imagine not having any school spirit. I firmly believe that you should attend at least one major sporting event for your high school each season (even if you don't like sports. Everyone is there and it's fun) and I can't imagine not being in any clubs. In Luisa's defense, she does have a job that keeps her very busy. she's a waitress and sometimes she has to cover her older sister, Grace's, shifts (usually when Grace is taking care of her daughter or going on a date with her baby daddy/on again-off again boyfriend Paz. In addition to (at first) not being able to relate to Luisa, I was irritated by how as soon as Luisa engaged in an extracurricular, boys were falling all over themselves to talk to her. True you meet more people at after-school events, but I find it hard to believe that without changing any aspects of her appearance or personality, she would discover all these new admirers (who were not all admirable). And let me just say that there's no way the city of Chicago would ever sponsor a contest as awesome as this one. Throughout the city of Chicago (although there is a tiny issue with this because I thought the story takes place in a suburb which would not be in Chicago...), schools are competing to see who can get the most money. The winner gets a full month off of school for winter break and in the battle of the sexes, the winning gender gets an extra three days off for spring break (the battle of sexes is only for Dunfield High School). 
 Obviously I loved the high energy of the columns. There are plenty of (mostly clean) innuendos, insults and retorts thrown about. A battle between genders is always intense and fun to read about and this one did not disappoint. One of the best parts of the book is trying to guess who the male columnist is. It's not easy and while it becomes clear towards the end who is NOT the columnist, I didn't expect the big reveal. I thought the whole time that it was the first guy. The relationships Luisa has with family and friends are borderline three dimensional. The characters are developed but not quite fully there. Luisa, Grace and their mother have issues but these issues are never addressed head on so there is no resolution or goal setting. I really liked Paz though. He was the typical rough-exterior-soft-interior guy and I was rooting for him and Grace to work out (and for him to stop picking on Luisa). Luisa does become a character that is easier to identify with as she tries to balance four (!) different guys, she struggles with self-esteem and going too fast. 
 Girl v. Boy was an indulging, not wholly realistic and somewhat cheesy read. It becomes predictable but the sparkling banter between the two columnists keep the story moving. It's especially amusing to see the effect the two columnists have on the entire school. Girls become more vocal about what they want and guys have even more questions about what girls want. Trying to figure out the identity of the male columnist will keep you constantly turning the pages as will seeing the big finale and figuring out who wins the winter break competition and the battle of the sexes.

WOW. Just wow. 
 This book was amazing. 
 At first glance, it seems like a perfect set up for a typical "love conquers all" outcome, complete with the love triangle and authority challenges. But there is so much more to this book than meets the eye. 
 Set in a futuristic world, where people called the guardians dictate everything (and I mean everything; from what you eat, where you live, where you work, what you do in your free time, all the way to who you marry, how many children you will have, and even when you die. The story begins with Cassia meeting her match, Xander, who happens to be her best friend. It isn't until the next day when she looks at the information of her match, that she sees another boy's face on the screen, a face that is not of her match, Ky; the aberration that lives at the end of her street. And so begins the love triangle. It is also important to note that there are only 100 songs, 100 poems and 100 paintings available in this world, a result of the "refinement" of culture. This is explained better in the book. 
 Matched starts off slow at first, with minimal progression in the story line, and most of the time spent to building on the relationships between Cassia and those around her, her family, Ky and Xander as well as a few others. This is necessary for the story to play out as well as it did. 
 Cassia is a strong character with unwavering beliefs and a growing sense of unease with the world she lives in. The thing that made this book so fantastic was the fact that the story wasn't solely reliant on the love triangle, it was more a story about challenging the norm, which was brought about and propelled by the love story. I can't say too much about this without giving too much away. 
 I love the way Condie works poetry throughout the whole of the story; it's not simply something that is placed at the beginning of a chapter (which seems to be becoming the popular thing to do), it is something that works its way into the story, meaning something to the characters, encouraging the rebellion that you can just see coming, and giving hope to those who know about it. 
 This is a fantastic book, and definately goes on my 'favourites' shelf. I really can't wait for the next one in this series "Crossed"

 For Me and Earl and the Dying Girl, I'd heard mixed things. Basically, you either loved it or you hated it. Luckily, I loved it. 
 Greg Gaines is a high school senior who makes films with his "friend" Earl. When a classmate, Rachel, gets diagnosed with leukemia, Greg's mom forces him to befriend her. Then things just go downhill. 
 I really liked Greg. He was witty and self-deprecating and just felt so real. He was the perfect narrator for this type of book. From my experience in public high school, he was exactly like a senior boy. He was profane and kind of an ass at points, but it made him so real and tangible. 
 Earl, on the other hand, felt a bit too...stereotypical. He, too, was funny but his race was so exaggerated, to the point it felt fake and a bit racist. He may have been my favorite character, however, because he put Greg in his place and had very heartfelt moments. 
 The story was funny and snarky, but when Rachel went back in the hospital, it became touching and sad. Basically, I felt all the feels when reading this. 
 The only warning I give with this is that Greg and Earl can be very, VERY vulgar. If you're into that type of humor in books (like myself), then by all means go ahead. But if you don't go for that, be wary as you read. 
 Overall, it's a fast, fun read and I would definitely recommend a sad book that isn't too sad.

GLITCH was one of the books I was really excited for. So when St. Martin's Press approved my request for it on NetGalley, I was naturally ecstatic and couldn't wait to get started on it. 
 There were many things I disliked about this book. I was not a fan of the world-building (if it could even count as that); the characters were poorly crafted out and extremely awkward; the dialogue was jerky and strange; the writing was childish, and did I mention that the way the characters interacted was REALLY awkward? 
 Zoe lives in a world where emotion has disappeared, and everyone sees everything in drab grey. They have no thoughts of their own, and everywhere you look, it's always neat and orderly. 
 To be honest, I found it hard to like any of the characters. When I first started reading this, I was touched by how much Zoe cared about her brother, and how much she wanted to see some sign of emotion on his face. I really liked how Heather Anastasiu introduced the Link and Zoe's glitching to me. It wasn't dumped on my head all at once, like some books. 
 And then Adrien comes into the picture. He's described as this boy who has brilliant aquamarine eyes. (So now all love interests have great green eyes? Great.) Zoe was, of course, immediately attracted to him. And so began one of the worst romances I've ever seen. 
 The insta-love was really obvious. 
 I mean, come on. Do you kiss a guy who introduces you to a group of rebels seeking to overthrow the government? A guy whom you thought was going to kill you? A GUY YOU MET ON THAT SAME DAY ITSELF? I most certainly don't! But that's exactly what Zoe did. She hardly knew anything about him, other than the fact that he's part of a resistance team and occasionally has visions from the future. 
 Probably the only thing I was happy about during this part of the book was that Adrien's mom did NOT approve of this instant relationship between her son and this mysterious girl. 
 Apart from the insta-love in this book, there was also the horrible love-triangle. I hated Max. Hated him from the bottom of my heart. He was creepy--nothing short of a pedophile. And whenever Zoe was around him, she acted like this dumb girl who didn't know what was going on between both Adrien and Max. It was also pretty clear what Max wanted from her: sex. At this point in GLITCH, I was ready to throttle Zoe with my bare hands and then electrocute all witnesses. I also found the way the characters interacted with each other to be extremely jerky and awkward, and it really didn't fit with the book at all. I think that contributed a lot to the lack of depth in the characters. 
 Oh, and then there was the part where Zoe's powers only came in when it was convenient. Seriously. 
 The world building in this book was also a little on the 'meh' side for me. I knew almost nothing about the Community and the Uppers, only that the people were nearly robots, controlled by a chip. 
 Perhaps the only thing I really liked about GLITCH was the concept and the cover. 
 1 1/2 stars.

started running for pretty much the first time in my life about a month and a half ago. Sure, I'd done the one-mile run for the Presidential Fitness Test back in school, but that was literally the extent of my history with the sport. I still don't completely know why I decided to pick it up recently, but I'm sure part of it was that I'd been feeling extremely lazy and my couch was starting to look a bit too worn out. Now that I'm into it more, I started looking for tips to make me a more efficient runner. Katy suggested this book to me last week, and I was hooked from the start! 
 Born to Run starts with a simple question: "How come my foot hurts?" What follows is a mix of personal narrative and explanations of various discoveries related to evolution and the science of running. When Christopher McDougall said he wanted to find the answer, he wasn't kidding. His expansive search took him from respected medical professionals and experienced athletes to perhaps the most authoritative source on the planet: the elusive Tarahumara Indians living in the dangerous Copper Canyon, just across the Texan border in Mexico. He wanted to know how they can run for days with little more on their feet than a sandal, while he could barely get a few miles down the street in some of the most expensive running shoes designed by man. So he went directly to the source, on an adventure that led him meet a cast of characters, including: Caballo Blanco (the White Horse), an American man who shed his old life in favor of living like the Tarahumara; Scott Jurek, the best ultra-marathoner in the world; and Barefoot Ted, a man who jump-started a sort of revolution by finishing the Los Angeles marathon barefoot--and fast enough to qualify for the Boston marathon. Over the course of the book, McDougall goes from running with incredible pain to completing a 50-mile trail race in one of the most dangerous places such a feat can be done, and his account of the journey is both thorough and fascinating. 
 Yes, this is a running book, so people who participate in, or appreciate, the sport are bound to get the most out of it, but it also contains a genuinely engaging story that ends with one of the the most impressive races you've never heard about. I can't say that I've been all that serious about running so far--only going for runs two or three times a week--but this book gave me a lot of ideas and inspiration to help change that. I am also somewhat interested in the idea of strengthening muscles in the feet through the use of Vibrams FiveFingers shoes, and may have to check them out someday.

Detective Hank Palace is a newly promoted police detective in the small city of Concorde. He's investigating a death that everyone accepts as suicide in the washroom of a McDonald's, but which he is sure is murder. His sister's new husband is getting himself into trouble, and cell phone coverage is disintegrating, along with the internet. 
 Oh yeah, and there's an asteroid that is going to hit the earth in a little over six months, which will kill most of the world immediately, and condemn the rest to a slower death in the resulting nuclear winter. 
 The big question of the book is, if the world is going to end in October, why bother investigating crimes? Suicide is endemic (in one scene, a character talking to Palace just casually throws himself in front of a bus), and services are breaking down as people walk away from jobs, either to commit suicide, or to go 'bucket list'. 
 But Palace is one of those people who cope by throwing themselves into their jobs, and yeah, it might be pointless in the end, but for now, he wants to do a good job.

 Tbh this book probably is more of a 3/3.5 stars rating, because although it's good, it's not extraordinaire. The reason why I'm giving it 4 stars is because of the amazing family dynamics we see throughout the story, starting with the main characters Hazel and Ben, who are siblings. I love a good family dynamic, and it's upsetting for me to see so many authors willing to explore all kinds of romantic relationships with their characters, but forgetting to develop the relationships they have with their families, which should be a crucial thing because families are, in a way, responsible for shaping out personalities and they can either make you or break you. If there's one thing The Dark Part of the Forest does well, is showing the all-consuming love/hate relationship pretty much anyone with a siblings knows so well. 
 Another good thing about this was the romances. At one point I was scared of a potential love triangle that, thankfully, never happened. It was all very natural and I was rooting for all the couples in this book. And I was also very sad with the make-out scenes because they made me realize how dull my actual love life is. I never wanted to make out with a hot faerie dude in the forest before reading this, but now that's been added to my goals list. Thank you, Holly Black!

It's hard not to compare it to another book by one of the Bronte sisters (Jane Eyre). As much as I love Jane Eyre, this book made me realize what a fantasy it is. The horrible, horrible childhood might be realistic for a lot of people, the falling in love with your angsty employer might be realistic for some people  (The wife in the attic thing? eehhh I hope that's not realistic)  
 But for the most part, life's circumstances are more mundane than all of that. 
 Like Jane, Agnes is also a governess but the similarities pretty much end there. 
 No one in Agnes' family believes she can hold down a job. So she gets one to prove to herself and her family that she can, just as much as she does to make money. 
 The job is no picnick. She's un-appreciated, but she's also not a star at her job either. Sometimes she's less than competent as an employee, and she has to learn her place and what's expected of her there (which she does a pretty poor job at, reason numero uno she has to leave imho). 
 Ultimately she has to leave her first job because she's not willing to play the part of a parent and an educator. 
 Her second job she has a bit more luck, but I got the sense that she didn't find it as fulfilling as she thought she would. She spends a lot of the time wishing the boys were old enough to be sent to school. And, weirdly enough, Agnes seemed surprised at the thought that one of her female pupils would want her approval and esteem as she entered adulthood. (I would be, like, really proud of that. Agnes seems resentful.) 
 Like Jane, Agnes does eventually marry. But it's to another working class guy (from her neighborhood back home, I think); and really then it just seems like an escape from having to continue governess work. 
 This should be the most boring piece of rubbish, literary wise, except that I feel the reality of it. It took me back to when I was a babysitter, wondering what was appropriate for me to do when a kid misbehaved. It made me think of those children, and beautiful young women they've grown unto. As a caregiver, you're in a unique position and sometimes you're not sure of what your role is. You're an employee, but you get to see people more intimately than most people do. You can never be sure of the impact you have on the lives of other people, and most of your concerns are of the day-to-day kind. That was captured in this book, even if Agnes didn't appreciate the significance of it much. 
 Note: 
 Agnes comes across as extremely blue-collar. She's a very very different type of person from me. I would have taken failure personally, whereas she's just like "Eeehh, it wasn't the right job for me." In some ways I really respect that she's got thick skin, but other times she comes across as kind of a jerk.

Up until the ending, I really did not understand why this book is widely considered to be the best (or at least the top five) of Christie's books. Then it happened, and I was like WHAT!? 
 Actually it was more like a double what, because not only was it a really daring ending, especially for being published in 1926, but I actually guessed the murderer! That has never happened to me before. I am THE WORST at guessing mystery endings. I am gullible and trusting and passive as a reader. Authors: take advantage of me shamelessly, and I will enjoy it. Make no mistake, it was entirely a guess. No deductions involved whatsoever. I merely thought of the thing I thought least likely and picked it. That it turned out to be true, and worked beautifully, is entirely accidental (on my part, not Agatha Christie's-her part was brilliant). 
 I'm going to split the rest of this review up into spoiler and non-spoiler sections, because I just have to talk about the ending. 
 Spoiler Free Zone: Knowing the ending for me is coloring everything I have to say about the rest of the book, but there are some things I am free to say without spoiling you. Firstly, the premise. The titular Roger Ackroyd, fresh off the suicide of his fiance, is murdered mysteriously in a country estate. Hercule Poirot is living next door in retirement, and is brought in on the case by Mr. Ackroyd's niece. The narrator, and Poirot's assistant for the case, is Dr. James Sheppard. He lives with his spinster sister Caroline, whom I adore. She plays daft but is actually very sharp. And of course, there are an assortment of relatives and friends who all behave mysteriously enough to warrant suspicion, and Poirot does his Poirot thing of being small and cute and condescending all at the same time. 
 As a sidenote, I would highly recommend the audiobook for this one. Hugh Fraser does a wonderful job. His voice is like butter. 
 Spoilers Ahoy: Seriously don't keep reading if you don't want to know. At the end of the book, Poirot warns all the major suspects that he is going to tell them everything, and that it would be in their best interest to give up all their secrets before he does it for them. This includes our narrator, Dr. Sheppard, who turns out to have been helping conceal the main suspect in the investigation, and having given no evidence of it in his account even to us the readers. And there's a reason for this, which is that the book we are reading is actually a document Sheppard constructed for the sole purpose of being read after the fact. He was convinced Poirot would be unable to solve the case, and like Poirot's past assistants, he could publish the document to acclaim. Only Poirot does solve the case and Dr. Sheppard is found out. Dr. Sheppard is the murderer. There were subtle clues all throughout the book, more in what he as narrator doesn't say than what he does. It was one of these instances that caused me to wonder, Hey, what if he was the murderer? And then I giggled a bunch, I'm sure. The book then becomes an artifact of the mystery itself. To get even more spoilery, Poirot allows Sheppard to finish up the book as a sort of confession, before Sheppard kills himself to save face. It was all very British.  
 The ending retroactively made the rest of the book rise up several levels in my eyes, and I'd love an eventual re-read to see if I can pick up on all the clues.

 This book came as a recommendation from a close friend of mine, and I wasn't sure what to expect going into this. I've heard from the booklr and booktube communities that people either love it or hate it. I am glad to say that I really liked this book and found it surprising. 
 So, one of the biggest complaints I heard about this book is that many find this similar to other YA series. While I do believe there are characteristics that are seen in many other series like Graceling and even the adult series Mistborn (Mare's background and role in the plan was just so similar to Vin's in The Final Empire) I found this to be incredibly unique. 
 Mare Barrow is unique in the way that all of her flaws, every single bad quality, was apparent from the beginning. I actually kinda didn't like Mare at first. She's bitter, selfish, a criminal, and insanely jealous of her younger, more talented sister. She judges all Silvers and sees them as monsters that need to be destroyed, and although I can't blame her for her feelings, I did think that for awhile she refused to see Silvers as people who also love and care about one another. She judges the Silvers as a whole based off of the faults of only a portion of the group. It's a problem all individuals of society have, judging one group based off of the actions of a select few. It's a problem every person in this novel has basically. 
 However, as the book continued Mare really grew on me. Her blinding hatred for all Silvers cooled down and she came to care for Maven, Cal, and Julian. The more invested she became the more she understood that while what the Silvers have done to the Reds, which might as well be slavery, she knows that violence will not solve the problem. Her eyes are more open now, and she also gains a better understanding of her powers and the world around her. Speaking of powers, her power is so cool. I don't want to spoil it, but it is very freaking cool and she kicks major ass. 
 The twists and turns of court games left my head spinning and after awhile I just stopped trying to guess what would happen. The antagonist of the story was kinda surprising, but it was more of a I-had-a-feeling-this-would-happen-but-I-really-wish-it-didn't sorta thing. The signs were all there and I saw them, but I just didn't want to happen because I had grown so attached to the character. It was a hard fact to accept. 
 Perhaps the most surprising thing about the book was the love square and how much I enjoyed it. That's right, I said love square. There's Mare, and then there's Kilorn (childhood friend), Cal (crown prince), and Maven (younger prince and her betrothed). Three guys, one girl, and it didn't bother me! It wasn't poorly written! The romance didn't take over the book, and each remotely romantic moment was so subtle and well done I never cringed while reading them. Each boy is special to Mare, but all three have their own flaws that Mare can't overlook. There's a scene where one of the boys makes her choose, and she says the best line in the book: 
 I choose no one. 
 She picks no one! Three boys, and she doesn't end up with any of them in the end. Mare is a strong woman who does not need a man! And it's because she's been hurt by them and she just can't help but see them in a new light.  
 My biggest problem was the worldbuilding, or lack thereof. I understand that this takes place in the far future, and the governments have just regressed to monarchies with the Silvers on top. So while there are guns, electricity, cool future technology, there are Houses and their nobles and the superpowered people on top. Each House is known for one power because children usually inherit their father's power, so only those married into a House would have a different power. However, I wanted to know more about the surrounding lands and what the environment was like. I just want more, and I hope I get that in the next book. Also, this is a really weird gripe, but I wish the book had a map in the front! Every time a new place was mentioned I wanted to look it up on the map only to remember there was no map. It was disheartening. 
 Also, I totally called that ending! I knew that was gonna happen so hah! That's one twist that I caught. 
 Overall, this was a really solid first book and I can't wait to read the next one. Aveyard managed to write really well-developed, complex, and flawed characters. There is no one in this book that is strictly good or evil, they are all somewhere in the middle, which I found to be refreshing. I hope in the next book the world will be explored more as Mare travels and I hope for even more plot twists and action. 
 I recommend this for fans of the Graceling trilogy, the Grisha trilogy, and anyone who enjoys YA fantasy with complex characters.

 My first Lovecraft, and while I felt something was missing in the storytelling, I see the appeal, and will try more.

Read this review on my blog! 
 Alright. Let's review this train-wreck. 
 How is this possible? How can the woman who wrote such a good debut novel fail to deliver so spectacularly in this book? I thought that writers were supposed to get better through experience, not worse. 
 Apparently, Veronica Roth is the exception to that rule. If Divergent was awesome and Insurgent was pretty good, this book continued the downwards spiral and ended up being terrible. 
 The book is told from both Tris's and Four's point of views, a choice I don't really understand, since this has always been Tris's story, right from the start. I get why she had to do it, but I think she should have come up with a different way to patch up the holes that using only Tris as a narrator left in her story. 
 Especially since she is clearly not able to give Tobias's voice the same charm that she gave Tris's. Mostly because he sounds exactly like her. 
  
 The book was full of plot holes. The whole genetic experiment thing didn't make a whole lot of sense. Scientists should know better than pick a large number of people from different backgrounds, tamper with their genes and then just send them out into the world. 
 Couldn't they have started with a bunch of volunteers and put them in a facility like Tris's Chicago and see what came out of it, instead? It would have made a tad bit more sense. 
 And then to the ending. Which I hated, and not because I wanted an happy ending. I mean, I wanted an happy ending, but I can enjoy endings that don't go the way I want them to if they feel natural. 
 Tris's death didn't feel natural. It didn't feel like the story was supposed to have that result, like there just wasn't any other way. It felt like it had been constructed in order to give Tris the possibility to sacrifice herself. 
 The ending was rushed, and the epilogue was just a way to tell us through exposition what a bunch of characters I don't really care about did after Tris's death. It didn't have any real purpose in the story, it didn't serve to establish the message. If anything, it made it more confusing - since we went from "we can't be defined by our genes" to "life sucks, but some moments don't". 
  
 This novel was a huge disappointment. I was really excited for it and it was just a mess. You're better off not reading it. It felt convoluted and rushed and it didn't give me a sense of closure at all.

I was hesitant to read Courtney Summer's 
 This is Not a Test 
 because I'm not a fan of zombies. However, This is Not a Test keeps zombies to a minimum, with them mainly appearing in flashbacks and in the denouement. I can see how zombie fans would be disappointed with the lack of action and epic fight scenes, but I was fine with it because the all of characters were rendered with such complexity, from their inner motivations to their flaws. I was skeptical how Summers could make being stuck in a school last 300 pages, but she did--and beautifully too. This is Not a Test is a wonderful, poignant character-driven story and what happens when you are stuck in a school with five less-than-perfect people in a hopeless situation, which may be more evil than the rancid zombies looming outside. 
 Solane, The Girl Who Wants to Die...But Can't Seem To Do It Right: 
 Solane is a unique protagonist, while everyone is fighting for survival, she's contemplating the best way to die without being a burden on everyone else. She's not the fierce survivor who slashes through hoards of zombies with a strong will to survive. She also tries to get herself eaten by zombies, but somehow her plans always foil. Oh the irony! It's through Solane's eyes that we get her story behind her suicidal intentions; even though I find her character gloomy, I could understand her motivations. I found her character realistic, especially when she voices her disgust towards Harrison, the wimpy freshman who always makes the already dire situation worse with his crying. I could relate to her (don't worry, not the suicidal part), even if she isn't the nicest of people. 
 She's a gloomy, passively reserved character, but I also found her surprisingly thoughtful. It would be so easy for her to slit her wrists, but she decides not to do so for she doesn't want her peers to deal with her corpse. I would also like to think that part of her doesn't really want to die. We find out her father's abuse and her being abandoned by her older sister that made her sink into depression. I liked the complexity in her relationship with her older sister, she wants her to be safe, but she also blames her sister. It's as if she wants to use her sister as an excuse to wallow in depression. The suicide note she keeps in her pocket is written to her sister, as if she wants to make her sister feel guilty for her death. 
 Harrison, The Crybaby That Everyone Secretly Wants to Punch in the Face: 
 He is the reason why I think all the others are very nice people: they manage to put up with his whining. If it was me, I would have slapped this kid in the face, and probably gagged him so he would stop crying. He somewhat redeems himself in the end, but I suspect he was kept unlikable because Sloane wanted nothing to do with him, so we never got his back story. I was annoyed with him, but I don't know if I would have been able to muster courage either amidst a zombie apocalypse where everyone I ever knew was either dead or developed an palate for my brains. 
 He pretty much faded in the background for much of the story. I pitied him, because he knew he was being dead weight. 
 And he tries desperately to be in everyone's good graces, or at least stay out of everyone's way so they won't feed him to zombies. For some reason, I was expecting him to extract revenge. Hey, it's always the silent ones you have to watch out for. 
 Grace, The Student-body President and Nice Girl: 
 For a nice girl, I didn't expect her to be that promiscuous. She's the only one that kept Trace, her twin brother, in check and acted as a peer-mediator. She's secretly weak even if her position calls for bravery. She has her flaws, but I found her to be a flat character and the most boring out of the group. Sure, she was nice but that was it. No one had a reason to dislike her, but she wasn't the brave, righteous person either. 
 Trace, The Jerk Everyone Loves To Hate: 
 He's the one that stirs up unnecessary problems to get on everyone's nerves. His anger is not completely misplaced for he does have his reasons. He just doesn't know how to deal with his grief, so he displaces it with anger and blame. He blames other so that he won't have to live with the guilt--but deep down, he knows it isn't working. I'm surprised at the maturity of his peers to let him go on his tirade instead of giving him a cold, hard reality check. Underneath his anger is just a lonely guy. 
 Cary and Rhys, Because I Am Too Lazy to Give Them Each Their Own Section: 
 For an Asian guy (I am guessing from his last name), Cary Chen breaks the stereotype. He doesn't do well academically and he is a drug dealer. And apparently he is also a sexy beast. Cary might not do well in school, but he gets an A+ in survival skills, even if had some evil intentions. He didn't survive by being a nice guy. Rhys' back story is heartbreaking, and I admire him. There's no reason to dislike him, but I have nothing to say about him either. Go figure. 
 Romance: 
 There's a tiny pinch of romance. Although I would rather call it "being desperate" instead. It's more of trying to make light of the dire situation than a romance. 
 Overall, I loved the story. My only gripe was Sloane spent her time being emo and made the pace slower than I would've liked. There were also a few minor events that weren't fully explained. But it's definitely on my list of top YA reads of the year. The characters were so well developed that my heart ached for them throughout the story. A refreshing new direction for the zombie genre (even though it barely had anything to do with zombies). 
 On a separate note, what's the best way to stop yourself from becoming a zombie in the middle of a zombie fight? Would drinking cyanide be fast enough before a zombie bite? Just wondering. 
 Spoilery Thoughts I Need To Get Out of My System: 
 So...what was Roger doing lying out there? Did Mr Baxter really ditch him? 
 And what about the suspicions about "medical processing"? 
 Why did Trace have to die like a jerk? Go slit your wrists or something, not lure every zombie in hearing distance!

This book was all over everyone's timelines last year, so I added it to my TBR but the descriptions just didn't grab me so I kept putting it off, even though it was getting so many 4 and 5 star ratings. Eventually I read it, mainly because I needed a book with an airplane on the cover and not because I was really excited about reading it. But boy am I glad I did! I'm sad I put it off for so long instead of listening to everyone. 
 In the first section of this book, Louis Zamperini is in high school, training to run super fast miles to keep out of trouble. He learns to love running and eventually makes it to the Olympics at the 5000 meter (5k) distance. I was listening to this as an audiobook, describing the training that he went through to get ready for the Olympics, as I was doing distance training to prepare for a marathon. I loved every second of it -- it was really inspirational to listen to while running, and very interested the differences between training for a fast mile and training for long distances. Louie makes it to the Olympics, but doesn't do as well as he'd hoped. But he's young yet, and plans to return in four years to knock everyone else out of the water. 
 But of course, the running wasn't the point of the book (although I bet Louie wishes it were). 
 Instead, World War II comes rushing in, the Olympics are canceled, and Louis goes off to war in the Pacific. 
 The war starts out well for Louie -- he's well respected and his crew is well known for their successes. But they are shot at one day and although their plane survives long enough for them to land safely back at the base, it is no longer usable. For their next mission, they are given a replacement plane -- one that makes strange noises and is difficult to steer. The unwieldy plane has difficulty keeping up with the other, faster planes in their unit and they fall behind, so no one is around when they make a crash landing into the Pacific Ocean. Most of the men do not survive the crash. After 7 weeks of floating on the ocean and barely staying alive, Louie and the one other surviving man are "rescued" by the Japanese and taken off to a string of prison camps where they endure some truly horrifying forms of torture designed to rob them of their dignity and will to live. 
 Louie's story is heartbreaking and astounding, and really made me admire the strength of character it must take to survive in such situations. His life and relationships upon returning to the real world were all strained and colored by the life he had to endure while a prisoner of war. Although in the end he finds religion (which would seem cliched, but it's his life), I think the book dealt with it tastefully and I wasn't put off by it for the most part.  
 I'm very interested in seeing the movie about his life that is coming out this December. I hope it can do him justice. I was sad to hear that he died in July of this year.

The Da Vinci Code by Dan Brown is the second involving symbologist Robert Langdon. 
 Before we go too far. I don't care about the lawsuits, or the historical inaccuracies, or the religious inaccuracies. If Dan Brown had advertised this as the truth, I'd care, but....he wrote this as fiction, so he can say what he wants. If you are a religious fanatic, you probably wouldn't like it, but Brown is telling a story....and I enjoyed it! 
 Police Captain Bezu Fache calls Langdon to the Louvre in Paris where he finds the curator has been murdered. He had left a cryptic message (a Fibonacci sequence out of order), and lay sprawled in the manner of Da Vinci's Vetruvian Man. The last line of the message read "P.S. Find Robert Langdon" (which was erased before Langdon arrived). The police cryptographer, Sophie Neveu, secretly tells Langdon that the curator was her grandfather, and that the P.S. was meant for her. She convinces Langdon that there is much more at stake, and that Fache has his own agenda. From then on, the two become a team trying to stay ahead of the police, and a murderer, while trying to solve the message that the dead man had left them. But the deeper they dig, the more Sophie realizes she really didn't know her grandfather well at all. Apparently he was the grand master of the Priory of Sion, a secret society formed to protect the secret bloodline of Jesus Christ. And then suddenly, they are chasing the Holy Grail. 
 This is another fast-paced mystery. Just remember, people. It is fiction, so enjoy it for what it is...a story!

I loved the writing. I love the storytelling and the time travel. 
 However. I think the author and editor really messed up on this one. 
 The ending, for me, was beyond problematic. Because it felt like in the end Natalie's life didn't matter--at least not as much as Beau's--and this seems like a pretty negative message. When she visits the world in which she's died in the car accident, Beau sees her family. And they're happy and smiling as if they don't miss her at all--and while it's been 12 years since their daughter's death, this seems like a risky scene. Natalie was adopted and feeling unloved and unwanted, like she didn't belong to her current family or her birth mother--then we learn that they actually would've been ok without her? Sheesh. 
 Also, the fact that she's an American Indian--while initially wonderful, since there are not enough Native American main characters in YA--could have been handled much more gracefully. The recognition Henry gives to the history of adopted Native children is a nice detail. But let's remember that this is a demographic that was all-but erased from this country once already. And the climax of this book is that the Native American girl no longer lives so that the white boy can? (Ok, so we aren't sure that she dies, but she's at the very least given up her life.) I think someone in editorial should've talked this plot point through a bit more before it went to press . . .  
 And I hate that Emily Henry didn't get permission from the Nations to use these stories. So many of these Native people's stories shouldn't have been written down and included in the context that they were, incorrectly and for the entertainment factor of a novel.

 This books deals a lot with the issue of "right to die". Will, previous to his accident, lived a "big life" and has not made the adjustment to his life as a quadraplegic. Because of this, he has chosen to go to a facility that will enable him to "die with dignity". I want to point out that he is wealthy. His family is able to offer him all the best - a physical therapist that comes to his home several times a day (maybe this is part of UK's health program, but I don't know), a computer that has special voice recognition software, a personal companion, and an exotic vacation (accompanied by said PT and companion). He also has the love of his family, and a woman who loves and accepts him as he is. Despite this, he can't be happy. It's almost like, if he can't be happy in these circumstances, who can be? 
 I admit my perceptions are colored by watching my sister struggle with multiple sclerosis. She suffered with the disease for 13 years, before passing away a couple of years ago. I watched her lose the ability to walk, become completely bedridden, and even lose her mental faculties. And all of it, amazingly enough, without a bit of complaint and a smile on her face. And she did not have any of the financial blessings of the character in this book. Will's attitude seems very shallow in the face of that. 
 I know this is a difficult issue, and I'm not even saying that it's always the wrong choice to make. However, Will's story did not convince me of anything, or even make me sympathetic. And no, I did not cry. Not even close.

When I was in the fourth grade I transferred from a Catholic school to a public school. It was there my fascination with Greek mythology emerged, and ironically, the first story I was ever taught was that of Hades and Persephone. To this day I remember drawing a poster of Persephone being dragged on a fiery chariot to the Underworld with Hades. When I stumbled across The Goddess Test by Aimee Carter I was immediately intrigued, not only by the beautiful cover but also by the creative twist on my favorite Greek myth. I have to be honest and say that this novel did not live up to my expectations, but maybe that was because they were a bit too high. 
 The novel begins, prologue aside, with Kate moving to Eden, Michigan with her dying mother. This pulled at my heart strings and I related to how Kate felt responsible for her mother. The writing in the first chapter was fantastic. It was descriptive and carefully thought-out. This seemed to dwindle by the second and third chapter. Kate had only been in school for one day, and she already has a best friend (James) who would do anything for her. By I think the third day Kate's witnesses the death of her recently acquired enemy. It is in that moment that we meet Henry (Hades). He raises Ava back from the dead and from that moment on Kate belongs to him. In exchange for Ava's life Kate promises to stay with Henry for six months in the year, as the myth goes... Kate thinks he must be insane and brushes him off. Somehow, Ava (the enemy) and Kate become best friends. They are practically attached to the hip. This is the one of the things that really irked me about this book, everything felt so rushed. I didn't understand the relationships that were built between Kate, Ava and James; it was as if they appeared out of the blue. The other thing that bothered me was that the characters, everyone except Kate, seemed very flat. They developed a bit as the novel progressed but not by very much. Anyway, Kate is supposed to go through with the agreement or Ava will die for real this time. Since Kate thinks Henry is a lunatic, an attractive one at that, she doesn't go through with the plan and Ava dies. James rushes Kate to Eden Manor, where Henry lives, and without thinking twice about it Kate moves into Eden Manor. Ava does not return from the dead but is still present in the story as a "ghost". Henry has a new deal to strike with Kate though. If Kate lives at Eden Manor, her mother will live long enough for Kate to say goodbye to her properly. Of course she accepts, but she doesn't know what she is getting herself into. She learns that the reason why she is here is because Henry needs a new queen, or he will eventually fade away. In order to become queen she must pass all seven tests that are presented to her. She also must stay alive because someone has killed off all the other queens in training. As the story progresses, Kate obviously falls hard for the lonely and tortured Henry and for a while he isn't that receptive. He tries to distance himself because he has given up on himself and can't stand to see Kate be hurt. We also add in the fact that he lost the love of his life, Persephone, who actually never loved him back. Kate tries her best to win over Henry, she is determined to stay alive and become immortal not only for her mother's sake, but for Henry's. Eventually she realizes that she is doing this for herself as well. 
 Though The Goddess Test did not reach my expectations, it was honestly a good book. I was just not thrilled with how the story felt rushed in the beginning or how one dimensional the characters were. I know that this is Aimee Carter's first book though, so it is understandable. I intend to continue reading the rest of the series with hopes that the minor wrinkles have been ironed out. I also hope that the next novel brings more legit mythology to the table. 
 If you liked this, I recommend: Jessica's Guide to Dating on the Dark Side.
