So, here's what this book seemed like to me... 
 It seemed like Deborah Harkness has done a lot of research about 16th century England and France and Prague. It seemed like she knows quite a bit about how people dressed, how shops would have been set up, how people interacted and what traveling by barge would have been like. It seemed like she has a lot of IDEAS about how it might have smelled, how people spoke and what Queen Elizabeth and Emperor Ruldolf II were like. It also seemed like she has a bit of an obsession with William Shakespeare and a very strange love-hate relationship with Christopher Marlow. 
 Mostly, it seemed to me like Harkness REALLY wanted to fit all this knowledge and all these ideas into a book...and when they didn't actually FIT, she just put them in, anyway. 
 I got SO SICK of all of the historical tidbits that were just THROWN into the book. Perhaps it's because I am a bit of a history buff myself, but it just seemed like Harkness showing off to me. 
 And if Matthew deClermont ended up being one more shadowy historical character or was involved in one more historical event I was going to scream. 
 I found the "plot" annoyingly disjointed. 
 Here's what happens in this book. Matthew and Diana travel back in time to the year 1590. They find a coven of witches to help Diana learn her craft. They develop their relationship a (TINY) bit and end up pregnant not once, but twice. They learn why this impossible thing is possible for them. They meet monarchs and authors and all manner of famous historical characters and it turns out that Matthew has been a part of every major and minor event from the beginning of time. They come back to the future/present.  
 That's it. Hardly enough to fill 600 pages, and yet it did. 
 The characters bugged the CRAP out of me, too. 
 I should amend that to say the MAIN characters bugged the crap out of me. I actually really liked Gallowglass, Phillipe, Henry Percy, Mary Sidney, Goody Allsop and Susannah. 
 Matthew and Diana sucked, though. 
 In A Discovery of Witches Diana is an annoying, Pollyanna type character - but by the end she is much stronger, much surer of herself. She's been through scary stuff and come out better for it. As she became a more likeable character, her dopiness was explained in a way that was quite satisfying to me. 
 In Shadow of Night she's right back to being an annoying Pollyanna. Really, Diana? Your REALLY this dumb? You're REALLY surprised to find out that your 1500 year old vampire husband has all these regrets and sadnesses? Your SHOCKED to find out that he's possessive??? That he wants to drink your blood and control your every move? REALLY? I must have rolled my eyes at Diana's idiocy at least a dozen times. I actually spoke out loud to her - asking if she was an idiot - at least half that many times. Her lack of initiative in finding a tutor annoyed me. Her use of the word "witchy" annoyed me (as in - "one of my witchy talents" - uhg.) Her being submissive, but not really annoyed me (passive-aggressive people always do.) And finally, the way that she called her father "daddy" annoyed the bejesus out of me. 
 Matthew was almost as bad. In ADOW I found Matthew to be "everything a vampire should be - strong, broody, dangerous and tragic." 
 I said that. 
 In Shadow of Night I found him to be a whiny, ornery, b*tch. I got so SICK of him denying himself for the greater good. Give me a break. Go drink some damn blood! Hunt, you big freaking baby! How in god's name would such a weak suck live for 1500 years? Suicidal but without the balls to do anything about it, one way or another. I hate guilt-wracked characters. They are uninteresting. 
 There were flashes during the book that he was strong, but not enough. Mostly, he just seemed sad. Sad is annoying. 
 In the end, I didn't find this book a complete waste of time, but I'm certainly glad I listened to it as an audio-book. At least I was able to get other things done as I read it.

 A rough start again for the third book in the Divergent series. It falls into a lot of the tropes that dystopian YA novels have a tendency too and for a while I was stuck trying to get through it. 
 It was saved by the final third of the book which was powerful. Roth makes a few very brave choices that I wasn't expecting her to. It nearly brought me to tears. 
 It's not a book I loved. The dual narrating was particularly upsetting because I often forgot who was narrating at any point because unless Tobias or Tris were thinking specifically about themselves they had very similar thoughts and nothing sets their narration apart. 
 I found Tris a little too much everything, brave, strong, kind, selfless, intelligent, resourceful. She also had a few too many special qualities (belonging to three factions, resisting serums no one else can resist). 
 It also didn't seem to commit to it's themes. It's back and forth about sacrifice and love. It says that everyone is a little evil and there's no black and white but then a particularly disappointing moment occurred when a character who'd been developing and changing was tossed off as "just plain evil because that's how they were". It's views on memories are interesting, but the view that they are all that forms a person is a little simplistic to me. 
 Overall the end of this book made it, and as a trilogy it was enjoyable. I will say that the final few chapters are the best bit of writing in the series.

"Are there gods, Croaker? I never believed in gods." 
 "I don't know, Lady. No religion I ever encountered made any sense. None are consistent. Most gods are megalomaniacs and paranoid psychotics by their worshippers' description. I don't see how they could survive their own insanity. But it's not impossible that human beings are incapable of interpreting a power so much greater than themselves. Maybe religions are twisted and perverted shadows of the truth. Maybe there are forces which shape the world. I myself have never understood why, in a universe so vast, a god would care about something so trivial as worship or human destiny." 
 "When I was a child... my sisters and I had a teacher." 
 Did I pay attention? You bet your sweet ass I did. I was ears from my toenails to the top of my pointy head. "A teacher?" 
 "Yes. He argued that we are the gods, that we create our own destiny, that what we are determines what will become of us. In a peasantlike vernacular, we all paint ourselves into corners from which there is no escape simply by being ourselves and interacting with other selves." 
 "Interesting." 
 "Well. Yes. There is a god of sorts, Croaker. Do you know? Not a mover and shaker, though. Simply a negator. An ender of tales. He has a hunger that cannot be sated. The universe itself will slide down his maw." 
 "Death?" 
 "I do not want to die, Croaker. All that I am shrieks against the unrighteousness of death. All that I am, was, and probably will be, is shaped by my passion to evade the end of me." She laughed quietly, but there was a thread of hysteria there. She gestured, indicating the shadowed killing ground below. "I would have built a world in which I was safe. And the cornerstone of my citadel would have been death." 
 The end of the dream was drawing close. I could not imagine a world without me in it, either. And the inner me was outraged. Is outraged. I have no trouble imagining someone becoming obsessed with escaping death. "I understand." 
 "Maybe. We're all equals at the dark gate, no? The sands run for us all. Life is but a flicker shouting into the jaws of eternity. But it seems so damned unfair!" 
 Do you know what kept me glued to the page without fail throughout Chronicles of the Black Company? Do you know what was the main reason I was able to finish the final book in The Books of the North trilogy in the span of a long day and night of waiting in terminals and sitting in airplanes on a return trip home from a 14 day visit to Mexico that was the first time I had been in the country in 8 years? It wasn't the fights, skirmishes and battles, though they were heart-pounding. Nor the twists and turns in the schemes, plotting, and intrigues though they made me intensely curious as to what happened next. Nor the presence, charisma, and banter of the colorful, lively cast of misfits and scoundrels Glen Cook has created. 
 No, what had me hooked more than anything else in The White Rose and indeed in The Black Company and Shadows Linger was the budding, complicated-as-hell relationship between world-weary mercenary, physician, and Annalist Croaker and the evil, enigmatic sorceress overlord the Lady. By no means should Cook have been able to make something so tripe and wish-fulfilling as the-incredibly-attractive-monster-falls-in-love-with-our-protagonist plot work. 
 It just shouldn't. 
 That is the domain of bad writers, professional and amateur; published and fanfiction. And when I say monsters I mean monstrously evil characters, even when said monsters are massively entertaining and compelling. 
 And perhaps this is why, even with scenes and passages like the quote above peppered throughout the war between the Lady and Her empire and Darling and a beleaguered Black Company, and the looming, pressing knowledge of the Dominator's inevitable escape from his prison, Cook was able to make this work. The war has been long and grueling to all of the participants, and knowing that Her husband will break out and wreak havoc, slaughter, and total enslavement on everyone in his path should he emerge victorious (which he will if he isn't destroyed immediately after reentering the world) She performs, off-page, a divination ritual at a point before the above passage takes place that puts Her into a deep, reflective mood throughout the rest of the book. Her glimpses into the possible future have never proven to be wrong, see. You can imagine how despondent She was when She learned that of the handful of possibilities She had visions of, none of them were of Her standing triumphant.  
 Learning what She learns would make anyone, irredeemably evil or not, seek some sort of comfort, or amusement that can serve as a distraction. For a considerable amount of time the Lady actually goes undercover as a normal woman with Croaker in order to attempt to form an extremely tenuous, highly circumstantial alliance with Darling without a fight breaking out. And, during this time where every one of the other mercenaries assumes Croaker must be hitting that, She's having so much fun. 
 In the oddest voice I ever heard her use, the Lady replied, "Loneliness. If you want to kill Tracker the easy way, lock him up in a room and go away." 
 I felt a chill that had nothing to do with the weather. Whom did I know who had been alone a long time? Who, maybe, just maybe, had begun to wonder if absolute power were worth the absolute price? 
 I knew beyond the glimmer of doubt that she had enjoyed every second of pretend on the Plain. Even the moments of danger. I knew that had I had the hair on my ass, there in the last days, I could have become more than a pretend boyfriend. There was a growing and quiet desperation to her in that time as going back to being the Lady approached. 
 Despite all his professed cynicism, Croaker is of the disappointed Romantic variety of cynics. He doesn't throw the word "evil" around lightly, and even when he does he doesn't let that stop him from working with, or liking, or sympathizing with someone he considers evil. And he has considerable trouble accepting the notion of anyone, no matter how monstrous, could be absolutely evil. That includes the Lady's own husband. When he wonders that surely the Dominator, before he became the Dominator, had to care about someone like his mother or somebody at some point, the Lady instantly retorts that She'd be surprised if he didn't kill her early on in his life. 
 So while the relationship that's buds between the world-weary, smartass mercenary and the immortal, totalitarian sorceress is incredibly dynamic and compelling throughout these first three books, that's partly because it's so goddamn crazy and foolish, as Croaker's Company brothers never forget to remind him. Love can be as blind and stupid and self-centered as it can be powerful. 
 If for some inexplicable reason the seven remaining books in The Annals of the Black Company were to suddenly vanish off the face of the Earth I would only be somewhat saddened and not for long. I wouldn't be despairing like I would be if that van had actually killed Stephen King before he could finish The Dark Tower series or if George R.R. Martin were to die before A Song of Ice and Fire could be completed. Even though I'm eager to start reading the other two remaining books in The Books of the South another part of me has no problem with putting them on the back burner. And although I found The Silver Spike to be a more than worthy account of the aftermath and fallout of the colossal events in The White Rose I was also a little annoyed at myself for finding out what happened afterwards instead of leaving it to my imagination (and more than a little annoyed that I did so before writing this review down). This should give you an idea of the sense of closure Glen Cook provides to the explosive, nerve-wracking, bloody climax to the Lady's war and the crucial roles the soldiers of the Black Company played in it. 
 It should be obvious by now that the last novel in The Books of the North trilogy is the reason why I gave Chronicles of the Black Company 5 stars. The ending needs to be as strong as the beginning and The White Rose overachieves. I haven't even rambled about the Plain of Fear (one of the most fantastically weird locations I've encountered in fantasy) or it's sovereign Old Father Tree, or Darling's growth into the compassionate, battle-hardened White Rose, or finding out the truth behind Bomanz (the sorcerer who unwittingly started this whole catastrophic mess), or the mystery behind some man called Corbie and how he figures into all this, or a creepy canine called Toadkiller Dog for some inexplicable reason.

I have problems with that. We were in her pov often enough that it feels like the author held out on me. First Lord's Fury is the sixth and final book in Jim Butcher's Codex Alera. Set in a Roman inspired world whose citizens control powerful elementals called furies the Codex Alera is a fast-paced action intensive series. In First Lord's Fury both speed and action are ratcheted way past 11 making for an exciting, though somewhat rushed, read. If you haven't read any of the other books in the series yet then even reading past the blurb of the later books, or glancing at the titles, provides some minor spoilers. Still if you haven't read other books, or aren't quite caught up to book six then stop reading now.... 
 First Lord's Fury picks up almost immediately after Princep's Fury with Tavi, now Octavian, rushing to the aid of the beleaguered people of Alera who are crumbling under the onslaught of the vord. Along with Tavi are the last surviving Canim under the leadership of Varg. Back in Alera proper Attis Aquitaine has taken the title of First Lord and is leading the people of Alera in a desperate defense where the only real surety seems to be defeat. 
 Despite being a solid 480 pages First Lord's Fury feels like a book half that length. At the beginning of the novel Tavi isn't even in Alera and Butcher really pushes the limits of credulity with the speed at which he manages to converge the geographically disparate POVs towards the final battle. Of course, slow and steady fantasy has never really been Butcher's strong suit. Indeed, high action is something that Butcher has come close to mastering, and the final battle (say the last 100 plus pages of the novel) is as close a magnum opus as we're likely to get. 
 Despite the seeming rush to get all the pieces into place Butcher does manage to drop a number of tantalizing ideas into the mix that I would love to see explored further. Little tidbits such as the hints as to the vord's origins, the idea of subconscious furycrafting, and the first binding of furies by the first First Lord are cool elements that are thrown out in passing. Indeed the concept of Alera itself, as in the literal personification of Alera glimpsed at the end of Princep's Fury and seen more frequently here, is explained. Over the course of her training with Tavi we learn how she came to be in the broadest sense of the term but the specifics of her nature, and even furies in general, remain something of a secret. In fact the notion of a physical representation of an entire nation dovetails nicely into the themes of national identity and the natural rights of man that Butcher only touches upon in the barest of ways. Of course Butcher's musings on the philosophical and sociological underpinnings on the world he has created take a serious backseat to the action. In fact it is never handled at the same level as his almost seamless examination of faith and religion over the course of the last few Dresden novels. (Side note: I find it a bit odd the religion is almost absent in this series, but maybe it's just me) 
 As I mentioned the epic final battle between the remnants of Aleran society and the vord is impressive and downright thrilling in execution. In terms of memorable battle scenes in a fantasy series it ranks right up there with the best of the best (for reference The Battle of Emmond's Field, Dumai's Wells, the final battle at Hogwarts, and just about everything from Memories of Ice rank among my favorites). Even split into several major scenes across several points of view the action never relents and each different point of view manages to provide a fascinating perspective on how the battle unfolds. It is truly some impressive stuff and a major payoff for readers who have been following Tavi since book one since the majority of the battle plan is his. 
 There are a couple of standout characters, other then the main crew from previous books, that deserve some mentioning. I absolutely loved the Marcus/Fidelias point of view. Butcher does a fantastic job of walking the line between heroic and tragic and the final culmination of his role in the story is, I think, both fascinating and appropriate. In almost deliberate counterpoint to Marcus/Fidelias we have Invidia Aquataine. Kept alive by a vord symbiote she has betrayed her people to side with the vord Queen and her naked ambition and self-serving nature serve to throw Marcus/Fidelias into sharp contrast. However, thanks in part to her interaction with Isana (whose watercrafting allows her to sense emotions) she is a character that on one level you can't help but pity. 
 High action and some entertaining hi-jinx, thanks in part to Tavi/Kitai relationship, make for a gripping page turner and I can honestly say that I wish it wasn't over. Butcher has an undeniable ability to create memorable and ultimately likable characters that are, quite frankly, difficult to part with. The ending of First Lord's Fury is satisfying though somewhat rushed. It ends with several of unanswered questions that leave the door open for future volumes while at the same time still providing a definitive conclusion. I'm sad the series is over but given Butcher's penchant for publishing something every six months I won't have long to wait for the something new, and who knows, maybe next year we'll see a new book set in the realm of Alera. I for one will be looking forward to it.

I have to thank Suzana for bringing me to this book. Because like Max Vincent or "Heathcliff" as he's affectionately known, I think I would've done a whole lot of wandering, before I realized this perfection was in front of my eyes. 
 I love this book. No bones about. 
 The heroine is very philosophical, and since I'm a very philosophical person in general, it was a marriage made in heaven. I'm all about abstract connotations, and seeing how shoes symbolize everything about a person - whether they're staying or going. Repaired over and over again or brand new - wow. Hawthorne (or Clare) has been through more than the average person - and like me, older than her years. Her relationship with Uncle Gregor reduced me to tears at two points in the book. The first time when he passed away into a coma, whilst Clare and Max danced in front of him, and the second, when she went to visit his grave with "Mams" ashes. 
 Clare is a very unique YA protagonist, and I suspect a heroine, not everyone is appreciating as much as they should. 
 Most people would be screaming, "Why is she letting him go? Again?" (in reference to Max) and she lets him go at least twice throughout the plot. Never pins expectations on the male lead or tries to tie him down - which I suspect many women wouldn't understand. Surely love is about fighting for it, till the very last breath? Holding on, and not letting go? So why is this book telling me, that love should involve letting go? 
 The thing about this book, is that it treats subjects like love and death with maturity. 
 The author has a deep understanding of what love is - you should never hold someone back - you should let them go if they want to leave - and if your love is meant to be, then he (or she) will always find their way back to you. Love is different from responsibilities, highlighted nicely by her absentee parents. They left responsibility behind when they abandoned their daughter. Max didn't leave any responsibility behind, only love which he carried - which is the key difference. What does this mean? That love shouldn't be born out of responsibility? Powerful message. 
 I appreciated their separations - particularly because Clare is a woman who understands the philosophy of free-sprit and the worse thing you can do is pin it down - she is self-effacing and utterly in tune with the universe. Seriously. People like Clare are rare! (Heehee, that rhymed.) 
 One minor point: 
 The author backtracked on herself. There is a point where Heathcliff teaches Clare to drive, asking if it's her first time, and she doesn't reply leaving us to assume it is...but a couple of chapters later, it's revealed she has a license already?! Minor editing error? What's going on there. 
 The writing was beautiful. One of my favourite YA's published this year I think.

 Charlie, on the other hand, I did not like. Maybe I didn't have such a big problem with her as a character, but with how she was made. She is supposed to be an avarage teen, but from the decription Scott gave us, I created an image in my head and she looked everything apart from normal. This bullying is even given as a motive for murder later but when it happens I had to read a few times to be like what??? why  
 Some of the inconsistencies 
 What's with the whole secret society? They're a Russian one but 2 of the key figures are a Pole (who they murder) and someone who only speak English and Swedish. Why are they a communist society if they're centuries old? Why did the Pole give the knife to the victim in the first place? Oh and the Pole is referred to as speaking Russian and not Polish - why is he called a Pole?? How did the society even find out the Pole had given away the knife? When the society all get arrested, why did Alleyn come through the chimney when all the other police apparently got in fine at the same time by just walking in? I think he was hidden the whole time? I guess? Which is uh. Sounds very uncomfortable. What were the secret society even doing? They were arrested for sedition and treason but they didn't seem to do anything except murder each other. They're a big red herring subplot but none of their actions really make sense. 
 With the murder, the murderer is specifically allotted *exactly 8 seconds* to get from the bathroom to downstairs, do the murder and turn the lights off. His method relies on the victim being in *exactly* the right place to get stabbed (he could never have turned around, he couldn't have moved away from the stairs). In those 8 seconds, after apparently sliding down a banister, he got the knife in EXACTLY the right spot between bones that was considered so impressive that the murderer needed to know anatomy well. His alibi was 2 people thinking he was in the bath but as well as those 8 seconds he also got out the bath to get a glove from his wife's dressing room. That would take some time. Surely someone would have noticed the splashing had stopped? Bath noises are actually pretty distinctive - you can usually tell when someone's getting out. And there's door noises, footsteps too. In fact, the servant who comes into give Nigel shaving water would surely have seen him on the landing? The timescale is even less than the 8 seconds allotted and it seems extremely unlikely. He'd also have dripped water EVERYWHERE! I can't believe nobody noticed. (Realised iirc he actually wasn't in the bath. He was just pretending to me. Even then splashing about would get you wet and you'd drip. And the noises are noticeably different when you're not in with your whole body. Ah well) The attempts in the scene before the murder to make it work just... don't. He also decided to do this plan even though he only had a single glove - he tried to avoid leaving prints but completely failed. Surely his wife would have thought "oh I'm sure I put those gloves in the drawer" too and realised something was up - but she doesn't; Alleyn actually misleads here by claiming he found one in the hall so the wife doesn't question it.

 the murderer is in no way revealed except for Alleyn accusing him and him saying "damn you".

Great book, I really enjoyed it. 
 This was a book club selection, and people invariably ask "What's your book club reading?" and "What's it about?". Describing what this book is about makes it sound a lot more ridiculous and silly than I felt while actually reading it. 
 The main gist is that a lighthouse keeper in the 1920s, in Australia, and his young wife are unable to have children. A dead man and a live baby wash ashore in a boat, and the wife convinces the husband to keep the baby rather than reporting what has happened. Later, they find out that the mother they were sure was dead is actually alive. 
 This is where the book gets meaty for me. The wife is steadfast in her commitment to keeping this child, but the husband is conflicted and plagued with guilt over what they have done to the natural mother. 
 I know, kind of soap opera like. More than kind of. 
 But I liked it anyway. OK, I like soap opera story lines (except generally actual daytime soaps - way over those), and enjoy following the story to see how things turn out. 
 Beyond that though, a couple things stand out: 
 The book is mainly from a man's perspective, which is fairly unusual for this type of story. The man deeply loves his wife, and is trying to ease her pain. The descriptions of the setting were vivid, and it was easy to "be right there" with the characters on their island. 
 Also, I have a personal affection for lighthouses, so I enjoyed a story taking place mainly in one. 
 Overall, I recommend the book, although it's admittedly on the overwrought side of things.

Reader thoughts: Short, funny, sarcastic, yet hinted at bigger things that might be happening between the Egyptian gods and Greek ones. Carter wasn't too bad in this one, though Percy will always be my favorite.

Now, some of these are actual short stories, and some are true novellas, but it still seems to be a newer trend.

So, I guess I'm in the minority here, but I've rated these last few books as 3 stars, rather than 4. 
 While I don't think the writing style has declined, per se, I think the rating has more to do with the content, and my perceptions of both the content and the series itself having changed over the years I've been reading these titles. 
 I've found the last few books (since at least Volume 11 or so, and maybe a bit longer) to be "joyless", for lack of a better word. 
 Bear with me as I try to explain, and I hope this makes sense... 
 In the beginning of the series, we met Harry Dresden, who was competent wizard with a compelling backstory. He had enemies who hindered him, and friends who helped him, and had his back, and vice-versa. And he was frequently outclassed by his opponents. 
 As the series progressed, it became harder for a new reader to jump onboard, abd becamse(IMO: YMMV, of course) much less of a "Case-File" type series, than an ongoing serial more about the world, and less about Harry himself. (And this connects to my similar theory about both the Wheel of Time saga [and the Vampire Earth saga]; I think most people had some misgivings about that series when the focus of the books shifted from Mat/Perrin/Rand to the larger world. WHile it may be a necessity to get to the grand scale of the story, it's nonetheless initially offputting to the reader to change their scale of reference.) 
 The other offputting thing (for me, at least), was to see Harry grow in power, and yet he routinely gets the crap kicked out of him by his opponents still! YEs, you want a challenge for your character to give the reader that visceral thrill, but at the same time, don't ABUSE him just for the sake of it, only to have him have a last minute surge of strength/burst of inspiration, etc. It just cheapens the experience for the reader. 
 So, I"m still onboard with this series for now, but not sure how much longer...

"We have met the enemy, and he is us." Or similar. 
 I really liked this one. I stayed away for a long time, thinking it was just another "braaaaaaains" horror show. But it ended up not really being about the zombies at all--it's about how humans (individuals, groups, families, governments) behave when they're trying to survive. Think The Road, not Night of the Living Dead. 
 The book is told as a series of Q+A interviews between a narrator and a sampling of survivors from all walks of life around the world. This has pluses and minuses--we get personal and global perspectives (for once!), but we don't get the typical connection with a protagonist and supporting characters. I do think that Brooks did a good job of getting across a story arc despite the lack of a "main character" other than himself as narrator. 
 It's hard to judge the pacing because I read it as an ebook--I have trouble with them anyway. The ebook format also made it difficult to pop in and out of the supporting "footnotes" as I went along. 
 The only substantive negative comment I have is that I would have preferred a bit more buildup before the outbreaks got going...for example, how did the infection get outside of China, or at least the initial villages? Maybe he could have had an airline rep be one of the interviews? But really, this is just nitpicky. 
 It's funny--the movie isn't really about the zombies, either; it's about Brad Pitt, Action Hero. But the book is so much better, well, fleshed out. (moan)

After the hints, I kept telling myself to be prepared and not be over emotional when the inevitable happened. But stupid, hopeful, unrealistic me thought Oh, he's going to make it. They'll find a cure and it will be a happily every after, etc. 
 . But I soon realized to give up my hopes on that thought. Don't get me wrong, I've read plenty of cancer  books, but this was by far the most emotional one I've read. It's either close to beating The Fault in Our Stars or tied.  I felt like adding that factor to the abuse in this book was almost just too much for me to handle. Those two things are at the top of my "Worst Things in the Universe" list, or at least in the top five of the things that make me the most emotional cancer  probably being number 1. 
 My taste in books varies from chick lit to dark, like this book, and it's been awhile since I've read a book that really opened my eyes to life and made me want to not take advantage of every second, and this book was a good reminder that things can change in an instant and the things you love most in life can be jerked away from you forever and you won't know if speaking or seeing this person will be the last. 
 One thing that makes me hate abuse so passionately is that it can be prevented. I'm not at all blaming the victim. I'm saying that most times cancer  cannot be prevented or changed. It just happens and it's no one's fault. But rape and other types of abuse, that's at the hands of a human being, someone who was born innocent, but time and circumstances changes that for the worse. It seems almost impossible to me that someone can think the way they do and that that abuse is in any way okay. I don't know what causes people like that to be the way they are, whether or not it's experience or if it just is. But, if they are the way they are because of being raised to have a dark mind, what made the person's mind before him/her dark, and the person before that, and before that, and so on? It hurts me so much that people all over the world suffer just because they knew the wrong person or was at the wrong place at the wrong time. It's all just circumstances, and that's what makes me hate it so much, because someone who doesn't deserve what they get, get's it only because there are people out there that are not right. 
 Even though things would have been a lot easier if Kate had talked to someone about what happened to her, or realized that it wasn't her fault, I understand why she couldn't. As much as I'd like to believe that if something like that ever happened to me, that I wouldn't blame myself, I probably would. Like Kate, I'd probably torture myself with a million what if's. What if I wasn't so naive? What if I had seen the signs? What if I had just done this differently? What if I hadn't somehow put out the wrong signals? That's another reason why rape/abuse irks me so extremely. It's not fair for someone to ask those questions and to somehow in 
 any 
 way believe it was their fault. I know that there's a reason for everything, and that somehow (I don't quite positively know, though) that these events lead to how people become who they are and how they overcome and end up where they belong, but I just wish it wasn't such a devastating and crushing way. 
 The only reason why I didn't rate this book 5 stars was because it was kinda slow during a lot of the book and it was so overwhelmingly tragic, but I know it had to be that way in order to get it's message across. It still sucked though. 
 I would definitely recommend this book, but only if you're extremely prepared to ball your freaking eyes out for half the freaking book. 
 You'd think I'd be used to it by now with all the tearjerker books I've read, but it still feels like a new feeling every time I read a devastating book like this one.

"Just when he thinks she will have the energy to run forever, to escape his sight, she pauses. Turning back, breathing hard, her hand on her hip, making sure he is there." 
 Jhumpa Lahiri's Lowland read like one of her short stories enlarged to a novel and thus a story so very completely told. Most impressive of her feats is that she could manage to express emotions, the inside of humans through simple outside gestures; the one I quoted is just an example. 
 There are a lot of details - which at times does annoy you, but more often than not, these details are brought to proper use, establishing a proper tone. It is through them that author is able to make you see the point of view of all the major characters. You are able to enter the skin of each of them. 
 The author also uses these tiniest details to show story's movement in time. You could actually see the kids growing in time, people developing notions and everything. 
 Lowland is definitely not a political novel. You must not raise your hopes on mention of communism in first few chapters. Lowland is a story of an average middle class family, and its characters do not influence politics than members of such a family would. Politics do influence the family but only as much as it would influence one of its average victims 
 Similarly, do not, at any point, start building up an image in your mind as to how the story shall go - your imagination is going to be probably be inspired by some movie and you shall be disappointed. There are no surprises, there are no shocks (except for death but that is in keeping with reality). 
 At no point, Lowland's characters become heroes and heroines of a movie. They are almost always mere mortals, struck with their lives. The story goes on smooth like a river with few sharp turns, explicable in hindsight -which may make it boring to those who are used to drama. 
 For some reason, the author refused to use quotes, although that doesn't affect reading experience; but the problem is that there is so much of silence especially in the middle. I understand that it was a dysfunctional family and everything but there is no way people can go on living wit out talking, without having any internal jokes or sharing laughter -even they don't share love. The reason for my argument is simple - people need someone to talk, especially Gauri who had no one to talk outside either. 
 Also I believe with everything happening, Subhash seems to be too-out-of-world a person to not show his frustration more often. Similarly, I find it difficult to absorb that a mother can stay away from her daughter for decades - refusing to even check on her - these are though minor doubts in what is otherwise a great read.
Overall I enjoed it but the beginning was a little slow for me.

Opening Line:"I clasp the flask between my hands even though the warmth from the tea has long since leached into the frozen air." 
 At the conclusion of CATCHING FIRE two words entered my head "Wow" and "Really!?" Then I caught my breath, checked my heart and re-read the final chapter because I'd been so engrossed in finding out how Suzanne Collins was going to end this unpredictable ride that I'd really only scanned the words the first time through. Not many books have the ability to leave me breathless and on that note not many books surprise me anymore either. Catching Fire managed to do both and what a fantastic time I had. 
 Starting soon after Katniss's victory in the Hunger Games we re-join her back in district 12. Now a reluctant celebrity of sorts Katniss no longer has to worry about money or feeding her family however things are far from perfect. At odds with both Gale and Peeta there is unrest and change brewing in Panem, old rules are being reinforced amid rampant rumours of a rebellion against the capital. A revolt Katniss and Peeta may have unwittingly started but are certainly being accredited for. As the pair make plans for the upcoming Victory Tour and the 75th anniversary of the Hunger Games a visit from President Snow contains a grave warning, forcing Katniss to publicly reaffirm her love for Peeta as well as trying to find a way to stop the desired but deadly and growing civil unrest. 
 Of course this is just the first half of the book (and the boring half too) Once the President decides on his form of revenge you simply won't believe what happens and then you won't be able to put the book down. I wondered how Collins was going to be able to trump the excitement of The Hunger Games, well she does ten-fold and I never knew what was going to happen next. Full of surprises, innovative themes and fantastical creatures, we also get violence, heartbreak, page tearing suspense and a healthy dose of politics. The pace never lets up, making up for the weak and wandering part 1 where I felt like Collins was never really sure of where to take her story, giving us one possible direction before heading off in another. Silly me this was undoubtedly her intention all along letting me think I knew where she was going before she finally gives us...Wow. 
 Events have now been set up brilliantly for the third and final instalment; Mockingjaydue Aug 2010 and I can't wait. Cheers

So many feels... I swear every time I read a Tillie Cole novel I go through three phases. 1. I want to hug her 2. I want to throttle her and 3. I want to bow down to all her awesomeness. I have never read books by an author where I can admit each one made me feel, took me away from reality and became one with my blood. A Thousand Boy Kisses is no different. Don't let the YA genre fool you, Tillie still managed to create a beautiful heartwarming story with characters who are wise beyond their years and put through trials most adults never have to suffer. 
 If you've not heard this is a tear jerker. And I don't just mean one paragraph or chapter will do you in. I mean invest in Kleenex, open a few boxes, scatter them around you and delve in. You won't be able to put this down and once you get to around 50% all bets are off. Your eyes will not be able to adjust. Every next page I thought I had a handle on myself, but no, the tears just fell like a waterfall. I don't think I cried this much through my entire over dramatic teen years. 
 I knwo I havent really given any of the story away and I won't. Simply this is a best friends to lovers with some added drama and heartbreak Tillie style. If she's a top read for you or you just want to read a damn good book, pick this up, hell pick up all her book, not one is disappointing, but again don't think you can start this at work like I did. Save this for a wintry night or long weekend where you can read and give your emotions time to deal and move on. The epilogue was something I've never read before and it was just the cream on my cupcake. I couldn't be happier with the way things turned out even as the tears still pour out.....

So how silly is it to write a review for a book that already has a million-trillion ratings and reviews? Just more words to get lost in the siege of already-said sentiments about the book, right? 
 But I liked, really liked, 'The Decisions We Make". And, though I can't add anything to say about the book that has not already been said, I liked it enough to at least chime in with the crowds to say so. 
 Daniel. I sure did love him. He was not your average 'foster kid' character. So refreshing. Oh, he had his past issues that tagged along with him into his new home. But his were unique from so many other in stories I've read. A breath of fresh air from the oft told story of past abuse and something or someone in the new home being the healing balm to it all. Nope. Daniel did just the opposite. Went out from a perfectly wonderful, supportive environment to find his own resolution to his past. A character who realized the answers could not be found and magically resolved through a boyfriend or even through simply living with a loving family. A character who I didn't feel sorry for, who didn't drive at my heart though angst but instead touched me through his beautiful, oh-so gentle personality which belied incredible inner strength and maturity. 
 Then there's Daniel's foster brother Jamie. 
 Their adorable tip-toeing into their attraction for each other is endearing and sweet and perfect. Not contrived, not over-the-top, but believable and very, very natural. 
 Oh, Jamie! This is also his 'coming out' story. And, boy, oh, boy, an incident in the wake of this coming out could easily have been used as a high powered angst marathon. But I applaud Ms. Scott for taking it, instead, to manifest one of the most encouraging, inspiring scenarios ever. She used the near-tragedy to bring out the fighter in Jamie. It inspired me, seeing how some young folks do fight back. Sure, they suffer a set back, they are NEARLY derailed from their own truth. But, thanks to a strong family to back him (oh, my gods, what a TRUE relief THIS was to see in fiction, as there really, really ARE supportive families out there), they face it head on and come out on the other side with their true selves still intact and proud. Being a parent who would be supportive to my child, no matter what, it was a joy to see 'our' type protrayed in this story. 
 Just a beautiful, pure tale of two young men---alike as night and day---gently discovering who they really are and the effect their love for each other has on not only them but everyone in their lives. 
 A must read. So pleasant, in spite of the obstacles. A book I'll not forget.

 Blood Red Road is the first book in the Dust Lands trilogy. This was a strong start to the trilogy. 
 Before I say anything else, let me first warn you that this book does not use quotation marks. Yes, there's no quotation marks to discern speech - I think the purpose of this is to symbolize the main character's lack of education. In addition to the lack of quotation marks, the characters have accents and to further emphasize their rural upbringings. I got used to this about halfway through the story, but it's something to keep in mind before going into the book. 
 Saba is the protagonist - she's tough, capable, and unapologetic. I absolutely loved her tenacity and unwavering mindset. Her physical and mental strength may have been unrealistic at points, but that arguably made parts of the book even more fun to read. 
 There's an emphasis on family in this book. It made me yearn for strong sibling relationships myself after feeling the family love and struggles vicariously through the characters. Whether or not you have any siblings that you're close to, you'll feel the despair, frustration, and limitless love that comes with the territory of having siblings.

I loved that she saved Alex's life many times and cared about him more than anything.  I hate the fact that Darla didn't have a major part in the book. This book could have got 5 stars from me, that's all I'm saying.  
 Two characters who left an impression on me are Alyssa and Ben. They are siblings and Alex rescues them from a bandit gang. Ben is autistic. He has a passion for anything military and knows everything about their weapons and cars. He was so smart and adorable. Once he told the people who had their weapon pointed at him to stand in a different position so as to cause maximum damage. 
 Alyssa, is brave, in a different way than Darla. I want to praise Mike for creating such smart and strong female characters. I felt for Alyssa and what she had to go through to keep her brother safe. She gets my respect. 
 Do you remember the scene in Dark knight when there were two ferries, one full of civilians and the other has prisoners and the joker gives the passengers a choice to either blow each other or else he will kill them all. I love that scene and I would like to believe that people will react the same way in real life too. This book isn't that hopeful, it's presents a world where some people are willing to do anything to survive. It scared me. Seeing the ugly side of humanity is not comfortable but again I praise the author for not shying away from showing the gory details. 
 Mike Mullin has impressed me. He now features in my list of favorite authors. I recommend this to all the people who like the dystopian genre and even if you don't try this book I am sure you won't be disappointed.
a little hard to get into, but it got really good about 100 or so pages in.

Stewart rocks! Wow awesome suspense! Dysfunctional Family! Gorgeous Rich Guy! Castle in the Sky in Foreign land! What more can you ask for! All of her books are great- must reads but this one and My Brother Michael are my two favorites!!

Booktube-a-thon book 5. Challenge 6: Read a book you really want to read. 
 Weeeeeeeeell, this was a pretty good conclusion to an amazing paranormal trilogy. The story wrapped up nicely, although a little too fast for my liking. The love triangle finally got solved out and I am 10000% satisfied with the choice Clara made. I fell in love with the guy all over again. 
 The epilogue was so sweet, I was grinning like an idiot while reading it. 
 4.5 stars for me, taking out half a star because the problem got solved out in a couple of pages, whereas before it seemed larger than that.

4.5 "New Beginning" Stars 
 Riley Mackenzie has done it again. These two ladies have brought forth a story full of heart and emotion with the mother of all twists. Guy and Jules are two characters who aren't looking or expecting anything else but the life that they are currently leading until they are brought together during a time in their lives when they needed each other. They just didn't know it at first. 
 Hunter is a doctor. At one time he had a gorgeous wife after a new baby made an unexpected arrival. Four years later and his life is nothing like he expected it to be. He has a little girl and a young son that needs constant medical attention. His life took a detour and he is now living his it so that he can support his kids. Jules life took a detour as well which led her to a career change where she meets Guy in the pediatric unit with his sick son. 
 Jules and Guy's relationship slowly built as they were both very cautious to trust each other and their circumstances. But when they finally went all in, it was beautiful. Filled with steam and heat as well as devotion and adoration, Jules and Guy had me rooting for them. Both had been broken by their pasts but together they were stronger. Watching Guy interact with his children had me swooning and when Jules was added to the picture, my heart soared. 
 Since their pasts were only revealed bit by bit, I was constantly on the edge of my seat waiting to see how all the pieces fit together. When all was revealed I was blown away only to be gobsmacked at the ultimate plot twist. Intricately woven, this story was full of heart and passion as well as friendship and everlasting, finding your way true love. 
 ARC provided to A is for Alpha B is for Books for honest review.

Not my favorite Jane Austen, and for the same reason as Sense and Sensibility - the main character, Fanny, isn't my idea of a model woman. She definitely was the type you would strive to be in the Victorian times - modest, pious, morally-strong, patient and devoted - but to me, she was annoyingly weak. She is no Emma or Elizabeth. She got a little better near the end, or perhaps this was because every other woman grew progressively less likable, but overall I wouldn't even go so far as to call her a heroine. Still, the story overall was engrossing. Like all Austen novels you pretty much knew how it would end, but whether it would actually get to that point is where the suspense arises. To be honest, I kind of hoped it wouldn't end the way it did.  I was hoping Henry would maintain his conviction and win Fanny's heart and she'd break out of her shell a bit, and Edmund, marrying Mary, would as well . The way they end up they pretty much are just going to be boring the rest of their lives. I didn't care for most of the supporting characters - Mariah and Julia were spoiled brats, Mary was conniving, Mrs. Norris was the archetypal loud-mouthed, know-it-all older female character, Sir Thomas was a good guy but super-sexist (I try to overlook the sexism as a product of the times, but when Sir Thomas berates Fanny for not marrying Henry in extremely sexist terms I just about lost it), and Edmund was boring. Tom and Henry was interesting and Yates was funny. Overall, I was never bored by the story and there wasn't anything I overly disliked about it, but I wouldn't never re-read (or re-listen to, as this one was an audio-book I listened to while commuting) it. 
 I did like how Lady Bertram had a pug named "pug". :)

Oh Harry, how I missed thee....

Jim Butcher excels at creating situations that stack impossible (but believable) odds and executing shocking plot twists and edge-of-your seat action on the roller coaster ride of Harry (and friends) surmounting the insurmountable. 'The Warded Man' starts off with a fantastic premise - mankind at war against demons with wards, or symbols that keep the demons at bay (barely). Against this backdrop, we meet three promising young characters, their pasts scarred by encounters with demon-kind. 
 The book has good action that keeps up throughout the story. However, I found some of the dialogue, and the romance to be a bit odd and melodramatic. The characters also seem to do an excessive amount of screaming - when they're angry, when they're sad, when upset, or even when they're in love! 
 All of this aside, the book keeps your attention and the series is off to a great start. I am very much looking forward to more.

2 1/2 stars 
 The problem I usually have with literary fiction is that you have to wade through some pretty dense fog before you finally see where you're going. And even after you've arrived, you're not quite sure where you are. At least Lillian had some destinations in mind when she took her walk. That is more than I can say for this book. 
 This author loves to employ imagery. (Was this her way of screaming "MY NOVEL IS LITERARY FICTION!"?) 
 "I decide not to tell Sam that I dislike Times Square. Times Square, much like these TV ads, expects little of us, if not quite the worst. Instead of treating one like an overgrown six-year-old with impulse control issues and a huge piggy bank ready for the smashing, as the ads do, it treats one like an enormous genital. A penis with a wallet, if one prefers." 
 "People didn't always hate pigeons in the city--in fact, one could look up and catch glimpses of homing-pigeon lofts atop a lot of the lower buildings, owners doting on the dear little things, circling on their wings high above the rooftops. But people have come to make a hobby of detesting the birds, I think, because they've come to see that pigeons are much like people: dirty and murmuring, greedy and abundant, flocking in a corpus of such shit and weight that one fears they may permanently deface or crush whatever they congregate on." 
 "But recently, even on the hottest nights, I couldn't fall asleep without being covered up, couldn't quite rest without at least the lightest sheet settled lightly over me. In my mind, I'd come to see it as the physical remedy for a vulnerability I'd begun to feel--a material attempt to ward off my own light sheet of anxiety, ever-present, ever-covering." 
 I am not a fan of imagery... especially when it is so heavy-handed.

Can I just say I love this story. It had so many cute moments and the way she retold a classic fairytale and made into a modern one was so nice. Hate me but I'm a sucker for a perfect love story so deal with it. It was so perfect and this might throw off some people but I loved it. Kyle(Adrian)  is the cutest character and his change was so dramatic but still bearable. The chatroom was really fun, keeps the modern fairytale feeling fresh. I think I understand what the chatroom is about but I still don't. Totally recommend this book who likes a good love story.

I'm kind of sick of cliffhangers... 
 It seems to be a popular trend of young adult novels, well, that and dysfunctional romances. I can hear the publisher rubbing his/her moisturized hands together and saying, "It's sells, doesn't it?" 
 Blood Red Road doesn't really end as a cliffhanger but more of a view-from-the-top-of-the-hill-and-you-can-see-what-lies-ahead. "The End". 
 The story is good, and it kept my attention, but several times I was jarred from the text saying, "Really? You had to go and write that?" For example, "Let's get this party started!" Groan. You can sog through it because there's a cleaver crow, crows are very intelligent, and lots of action. Then comes the anticipated romance, along with several forehead slaps as you read the idiotic things Saba says. And then, oh and then, you're left with the craziest ending of all. You're thinking this is a good crazy, but don't get your hopes up. Not that kind of crazy. Stop reading now if you don't want to hear about the ending. 
 I don't understand what possible reason there is for Jack to go and hunt down this briefly mentioned 'Molly' when Ike could have gotten off his lazy bum and done it himself, then to fuel a quasi-suspenseful ending. Seriously! The sequel-tension was already built up with DeMalo and his mysterious, and slightly threatening, message to Saba, to write Jack off (hehe). You know what's coming, right? Oh, yes. Jack will get captured and then Saba will have to go after him. Come on! There's so much more going for this book than going that route. Okay, I just need to calm down. 
 Let's hope there's something better tucked up Young's sleeve than a cheap, been there done that plot for book two. 
 Would I recommend this book? Yeah, dystopian is very "in" right now. 
 Will I read the sequel? Undecided.

4.5 stars. This was good. This was really good.

Eh, I'm not sure what to rate this one. Such potential, but it somehow felt very... stale? unfulfilled? disengaging? 
 The beginning was full of action and rather intriguing, but then the plot tapered off for a while, only to be hurried up again toward the end. At first I was wondering if Bardugo was interweaving lots of hidden magic within the subtext, for a huge payoff later. But by now I don't think that's the case -- all those coincidences really were coincidences, and the romance really is that easy, and the villain really is that... dry? 
 After a while, I've realized that it's probably because everything in this book is recycled material -- secretly pretty heroine with pretty name learns to overcome her meager place in society, find emotional and physical strength, and fulfill some sort of greater destiny, meanwhile dilly-dallying within a love triangle, struggling against a super-villain... It just wasn't unique enough for me to rave about. 
 Plus some random sexuality is thrown in, plus the magic has unexplored potential, plus the beginning love triangle Mal is left out for the first third, only to show up just in time to save the day, then later declare his love... from then on the main romance was boring to me.  
 Three stars for a creative universe inspired by an under appreciated culture in fantasy (albeit one that became kind of flat and old after a while). The characters were sympathetic, and I was interested enough to finish -- but not interested enough to dig up the sequel.

Fantastic book!! I loved how Miranda's family developed through such hard times and in their struggle to survive with such little. It's strange to think of what seemingly insignificant things can turn out to mean so much, even as much as life or death. 
 If you're looking for an action thrill ride, then this is not the place to be. It was exciting in the way that I couldn't be sure what would happen next or when the family would run out of food and other essentials because wasn't a matter of 'if' but 'when'. Just as things seemed to look up, some new turn of unfortunate events would bring the family into even more difficult survival situations. Hunger, thirst, cold, illness, air..are all working against Miranda and the world. For some the book may be slow, because events don't happen page after page, but in the order of true life..like a diary. :) 
 Okay..now onto the characters.... 
 Miranda: I think I relate most to Miranda. Not only is she around my age but a lot of the things she writes of are the same as how I think sometimes..if that makes any sense. I would hope that if I were in her situation that I would be able to make the same hard decisions and sacrifices as she does. I think Miranda is stronger than most teenage girls would be in the end of the world situation. I really liked Miranda and can't wait to read more about her and her family, although I don't think they come back until the third book. 
 Matt: He was definitely my favorite!! As the eldest brother, and only father-like figure in this little family, Matt has the world on his shoulders. The most responsibility is thrown his way by way of decision making, and muscle work. He would rather give up food and die than let any one of his family members go hungry and die themselves. I love him! =) 
 Jonny: The youngest of the kids, but can be just as strong as Matt. He isn't told directly of the family's problems, but he isn't stupid. He knows, and contributes in any way he can. 
 Mom: She sacrifices everything for her family, always trying her best so atleast one of them makes it out alive. She's a very strong character. Not a lot of mothers would be able to admit to themselves that all of their children might not make it through. 
 Overall, I loved this book and thought it a great story of a family's love and survival. I reccomend it. =D

DNF it... 2.45 stars 
 nope

 NOPEEEEEE!!! 
 *sighs profoundly* 
 **A fair warning, spoilers will follow and a lot of rant!!** 
 I know a lot of people just love this book, but it just wasn't my cup of tea at all!! 
 The world building, the magic system are well done. But I just couldn't bring myself to like it. 
 I found Vin a very annoying sixteen-year-old teenager that acted more like she was thirteen and that to me made a lot of difference. Also, for someone who lived until then her entire life on the streets, her sense of self-preservation and survival instincts seemed way too many times non-existent. 
 Ham, for a character that is supposed to be twentyish, reminded me of my teenage self, with all those basic philosophical questions that were just one more annoying factor. 
 Brisa and Sazed along with Kelsier were the only characters that I really liked, seemed to be the more mature, wise and funny ones. But even that got screwed along the way. And unfortunately, Brisa barely appears as much as Sazed or Kelsier. 
 For a translated book of 618 pages, the relationship and bonds between the characters for me were not as developed as it should have been, having as a comparative basis the six of crows characters. I know the past story of Vin and Kelsier, but what about Brisa and Sazed?? Or even Ham?? The bond between them was there sure, but it was barely visible most of the times. 
 And the pace of the book...OMG, the first one-third of the book is all info dumping, world building and introductions of characters, a when that was done I honestly thought that it was finally getting better, but it only did for a few pages because shortly after the slow, boring and lack of action came back...too many useless balls, and many other scenes and situations that I really didn't care about and only made me feel more bored because they felt that much bland and useless to me. 
 I like to binge read my books but I just couldn't with this one. The repetitive, too much useless use of words style of Brandon Sanderson was just torture for me. I found myself having to take a lot of breaks and couldn't read more than 30/40 pages each time I picked it up. 
 By the time that I had only 160 pages left to read I just snapped and jumped more than half of the pages, actually I passed my eyes quickly and barely paying much attention to some select pages that were less than 40 out of the 160 and I still got to know every relevant thing that happened, and that just goes to show that those 160 pages could have been summarised into a more decent pace, with more action and less waste of words and paper. 
 And the romance...don't even get me started! It felt so forced and out of nowhere. I mean, when the hell did Lestibournes fell in love with Vin?! And for a fantasy that was taking their sweet time getting to the good action parts it certainly did not take time at all for Vin in her first encounter with Elend feel like she was her true self with him and that she knew him better than many. Insta love much?? For someone who has a hard time trusting and being herself around others it sure as hell only just took her a small encounter of a few minutes to let her guard down and start to be obsessed with him. 
 I guess the major thing in the book that made me keep reading it was the Lord Ruler, because of the brief and teasing quotes of his record book/diary. It made me think that "the villain" of the book had a lot of layers and story behind him, and in my mind, he was the most interesting and unique character. I badly wanted to know why did he change so drastically based on the person he seemed to be in the past before the Ascension. Why from a person so worried to be fair and end the conflict between the existing nations of that time, he turned to be a tyrannical, detached ruler towards his subjects and their suffering? Buuuut even that was screwed royally for me. Sure the plot twist I didn't even saw it coming, but still, it was very disappointing and frustrating. 
 If you liked or loved the book, great I'm happy for you. But it just wasn't for me and I don't intend to read the other books, cause I really just can't bring myself to care about the character and what happens next.

I *loved* the first big chunk of this story. The breakneck pace pulled me in at once, the info-dumping was kept to a minimum, and Frankie/Leila seemed like a very interesting heroine, with unique powers and a nice amount of resourcefulness. Sure, some of the plot points were predictable, but I looked forward to--rather than dreading-- their inevitable reveal. 
 And then, when Leila moved into Vlad's castle, things started to go south. I'm sorry guys, but you should not go shacking up with actual dictators that use torture as standard practice, no matter how hot they are. Sure, Vlad's got a sad past and sure, he actually has depth as a character; he's not a generic alpha a-hole. That doesn't change the fact that he routinely tortures people (something he has no intention of changing), murders people, and uses physical force, along with threat of torture and murder, to co-erce people who he has no actual jurisdiction over to comply with his will. 
 We aren't talking about punishing evil-doers harshly, or even the way he rules the roost over the people at the castle. There's a valid argument that if you volunteered to be one of Vlad's vampires, you also agreed to live under his draconian rule. But Leila(at least at the beginning), Marty, Leila's family, and potentially others as well did not in any way, shape, or form, agree to Vlad's system of government. He forces them into submission because he can, because he has the power and no one stops him. That straight up makes him a dictator, and a pretty vicious one at that. 
 The action/adventure parts of the book are exciting, and there are no big logical gaps to bang your head over. But I couldn't get behind the romance at all, and that obviously soured my enjoyment of this book.

 The Winner's Curse is an amazing tale full of intrigue with characters who will melt your heart. 
 How do you review a book that left you without words when you finished? That is The Winner's Curse for me. All I want to say in this review is OMG THAT WAS AMAZING. WHAT DID I JUST READ? THIS BOOK IS FABULOUS. BUY THIS BOOK NOW. 
 SERIOUSLY. 
 My thoughts surrounding this book are still crazy even though I read it a while ago. Therefore this is not really coherent review this book, so bear with me. 
 Can I just say that the cover for this book is ABSOLUTELY STUNNING? I can honestly say that I have stroked the cover-and I am not even ashamed of it. And I would have killed for that dress for my year 12 formal last year. 
 Author Marie Rutkoski has an extraordinary way with words that allows the reader to be fully immersed into the world of Herran without overloading the information. And the world of Kestrel and Arin, our two leading characters, is amazing; there are beautiful dresses, balls, sieges, stolen kisses and DUELS. Who doesn't love reading about a good old-fashioned duel? The story flows beautifully and I was so reluctant to ever put this book down (gosh darn those university interruptions). 
 With such an amazing premise, I was hoping for brilliant characters as well. And I was rewarded! Kestrel Trajan, our leading lady, is a character I would love to meet in the real world. Her passion in everything she does, especially playing the piano, is incredible. I've been going through books where the main character has irritated me at least once and I can say without any doubt this did not happen with Kestrel. She is such a strong character, and I don't mean that in the sense that she is a skilled fighter. Kestrel is strong as she uses her mind to find the best possibly outcome, which is especially needed as a general's daughter, and I really admire her for that. 
 And then there is Arin. DEAR GOD ARIN. Where does one get an Arin? Surely I'm not the only one asking! He is just as passionate as Kestrel, and just wants to do what he believes is best for his people, the Herrani. And I can't fault him at all in this. With the slavery of Herrani people, Arin is trying to find everyone's freedom. 
 This places Kestrel and Arin on opposite sides yet an affection or fondness develops between the two, which gradually grows and blooms into something more. This had to be my favourite aspect of the book. The fact that the attraction between the two is slow going really lets the characters learn more about each other. 
 That ending though, my heart was screaming at me! All those feels were getting to me! 
 I cannot wait for the next installment and am eager to try anything else by Marie Rutkoski! 
 Thanks to Bloomsbury Publishing for this review copy in exchange for my honest review.

This book was so much fun to read. I do not think there is a weak story in this collection. Maybe the poems, but I have never been a poem person, so I do not think that I should judge. Of course, some of them stand out. 
 "Down to the Sunless Sea" is a sad moody story and it is written beautifully. 
 "Adventure Story" and "Orange" tells their story in a unique way. I get so excited when authors explore different formats to write their stories. They were very amusing. 
 "A Calender of Tales" is a collection of twelve very short stories. They are short but very powerful. 
 "And Weep, Like Alexander" was also very amusing. It reminded me Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, which is always a wonderful feeling. 
 "Nothing O'Clock" is a Doctor Who story. It was quite enjoyable. As I was reading it, I was able to picture everything as if I was watching the show. At some point, I thought to myself "Was this an episode, did I watch this?". 
 "Feminine Endings" is the story that disturbed me the most. It was well crafted and nicely written. 
 After I read the Introduction, I was expecting creepypasta level stuff. I do not think this collection was that dark. I think it is worthwhile for everyone who enjoys short stories.

I have mixed opinions regarding this book. The writing is very crisp and sharp and didn't immediately draw me in. The appeal, I have to say, is largely in the dry, biting, and sharp humour. But there are other problems. For one, the plot seems pretty extraneous considering you never have any idea what's happening, which should be fine in a detective fiction, and could even be an essential element of it, but it takes a whole another shape in this book, one that I did not like. The other part that I did not like was, as has been pointed by many, many people, the protagonist, the bigoted Philip Marlowe, who thinks women can get used to being slapped around, and who is contemptuous towards every woman he comes across. What I did like about this book is that in my opinion it would make a great film noir (I still have to watch the 1946 adaptation of it, and I desperately hope that Humphrey Bogart's Marlowe doesn't sound so bigoted, but I'm pretty certain I would like it if not for any other reason than the fact that it has Humphrey Bogart). Is that reason enough to like this book? I don't know. So I'll stick to giving it 3 stars for now.

I enjoyed this quite a bit more than expected. I had thought to just watch the movie but figured I would give the novel a shot. SO glad I did! Nicola Yoon did a great job bringing these characters to life. The reading is light and fast. It is part comedic in how Maddie expresses herself in the book. I enjoyed the journalistic style. The romance was a bit unbelievable, especially Olly's patience. But overall I loved this. Easy to get wrapped up in and read in one sitting.

I really expected to love this one, and am a bit baffled as well as disappointed that I didn't. Part - or, really, a lot - of it was down to Shelby, Alex's sort-of, maybe-he's-blown-it, can-he-have-a-girlfriend? girlfriend. I got to the point where her repeated "I had venomous snakes as teething toys in Australia was just super-irritating, and it didn't say much for the relationship that she kept telling Alex about it. I also found it incredibly convenient that she just happened to be who she was, in such an unlikely and out-of-the-way spot, where Alex also just happened to be. Incredibly convenient. Finally, there was something off about the way Alex kept thinking of her as "my girlfriend". As in, "I have to go rescue my girlfriend", and "there's no other way I can save my girlfriend" and on and on... Maybe it was supposed to indicate how poor Alex felt about the actual possibility of having a real relationship, but still, when the situation is a big old disaster, wouldn't you just think of her as Alex. 
 I did love seeing Sarah in her recuperative stage, as the cuckoos as "family" is such a great concept and so well handled here. Best thing in the whole book, and it was a really good best thing. Pity the rest didn't come near to matching it for me.

When the Hand of the King dies, Eddard Stark is prevailed upon to take his place. Yet there are whispers that the Hand's was murdered. Eddard must discover the sinister truth that plagues the throne and the seven kingdoms - but will getting too close to the secret cost him his head? 
 I enjoyed 'A Game of Thrones' far more than I expected to. It is a large book and very character based. Some might find it slow or lacking in action but it is very character driven and Martin never passes up a wrench in the workings or allows his characters an easy way out. The novel is written in third person from eight different perspectives, primarily the Starks with the exception of Tyrion Lannister and Daenerys Targaryen. The focus on each character is surprisingly captivating and each does their part to pull the reader into the intrigue of the story. 
 My favourite characters were Tyrion, who has a way with words and a refreshingly conflicting outlook on life, Arya, whom I found more sympathetic than most other characters, and of course Eddard Stark. Him I found the most enthralling to read about because he seems to be the best of men but his honour and loyalty are a double edged sword. 
 It was interesting to read from all the different perspectives. It made for a more rounded and less biased view of the novel. The Lannisters are established as the antagonists, and yet Tyrion is one of them. Eddard doesn't know who he can put his trust in. Both the characters Little Finger and Varys seem at times seem to be for and against him but the truth of it is that they put their intelligence and their survival instinct before any loyalty. They are both cunning and think before they act. The separation of the characters means that they often don't know the truths past their own speculation and hearsay. The reader is the raven that flies over Westeros and sees more than any character, even Varys. 
 I had always assumed that 'A Song of Ice and Fire' was an epic fantasy but in the seven kingdoms magic is but a whisper in the dark under the light of the moon. The novel is very much what its title promises it to be: a game of thrones. One reason I liked Daenerys was because she was wrapped in the intrigue of the dragons. Hopefully sub sequential volumes will have more magic than just on the outskirts - whether it be fiery or something to send a shiver down the reader's spine. 
 One of the main reasons I was so drawn into 'A Game of Thrones' is because I listened to it on audio book, narrated by Roy Dotrice. It is a very long audio book to be sure but I am not sure I would have soared through the book so fast had I read it myself. Dotrice in an excellent narrator, who doesn't just read the book but rather acts it out. If a character laughs or whimpers, he doesn't just state it but shows it in his voice. There were a few times he slipped up and said "Jeffrey" instead of "Joffrey." I personally prefer the pronunciation "Just off him already." 
 A Song of Ice and Fire is a series that has been recommended to me for years but I never paid it much mind. When HBO's 'Game of Thrones' reared its head, I didn't even realise that it was adapted from George R.R. Martin's novels. I had only had the faintest of spoilers from glancing scenes from the television show in passing - which I have for the most part successfully avoided - and intend to listen to the audio books before I watch the corresponding seasons. 
 'A Game of Thrones' is a novel I would highly recommend to anyone who appreciates a novel with excellent character development, tumultuous tension, and the intrigue of magic.
