I have to admit that I wondered if I would enjoy a book overflowing with magical realism. But Gabriel Garcia Marquez is a wonderfully imaginative author, weaving together reality and fiction, the everyday and the supernatural, history and magic. The reader has to suspend disbelief and accept it all as reality. By the middle of the book, I was hooked. 
 One Hundred Years of Solitude is set in the mythical Colombian town of Macondo. The isolated town changes as gypsies bring in new inventions, civil wars are fought in the country, the railroad connects to the outside world, foreign investors set up a banana plantation, and years of rain drive away the population. 
 The Buendias are the founding family of Macando, and the book follows the family for a hundred years. Garcia Marquez plays with time with some things proceeding in a linear manner, and other things in a circular manner with repetitions of family names and personal characteristics. The repetition of names was the most challenging part of reading the book with all the males being named a variation of either Arcadio or Aureliano. But each character had a distinct personality, and there is a family tree in the front of the book. There is love, hate, passion, incest, wealth, poverty, death, ghosts, magic, and humor in the story of the Buendias. Social and political changes in Macondo affect the family members. The atmosphere ranges from intense solitude to crazy parties to visits in the red light district. The one hundred year saga closes in an ending that seems very appropriate in an imaginative, magical way. 
 It is the 50th anniversary of the publication of One Hundred Years of Solitude. Although I had read Garcia Marquez's nonfiction book, News of a Kidnapping, this was the first time I had read his fiction. He's a talented writer who paved the way for other authors of magical realism.

I felt the author's enthusiasm on Japanese culture. It was very evident in the book. I also think it was smart of him to take a different route from the usual. I don't often come across books like these. It definitely piqued my interest. And anything Japanese (or Asian) inspired is a major win for me. 
 Stormdancer 
 is innovative and completely, hands down bad-ass. If only was too ambitious. 
 It tried to incorporate as many ideas as possible which either impressed me or overwhelmed me. It's like a glass full of water but it kept pouring even though it couldn't accommodate it any more. So many ideas. Heavy on descriptions. Some were pretty remarkable. Some were unnecessary. And because there so many stuff going on, the utilization of these ideas had suffered. 
 It also didn't help that I didn't like how it presented the facts. I don't like the Q & A style, probably my least favorite way of handling information. There were several times someone had asked the "what is" question. (e.g. "What is a RONIN?" What is DAIMYO?" "What is Kyodai?" and so on and so forth.) I know it is important for readers to know these things but there have to be another way to get your information across. There has to be. 
 I think some reviewers had already voiced out their disappointment over the improper usage of the Japanese language: there's the honorific 'sama' and if I may say it again, the abundant of the word 'hai.'But as for me, I don't know what to feel. I don't know if I'm going to laugh it off or get boiling mad. I'm not going to pretend that I'm an expert of the language. My familiarity comes from being an anime/manga fan. Years of being in the fandom helped me familiarized with certain Japanese words. At least the very basics. So having the basics wrong was really an eyesore. Plus, there's something really, really off with the way they speak, like is this how authentic Japanese conversation should sound? Should I assume that they were originally talking in Japanese? Or they were really talking in English and were just trying to sound Japanese by throwing some words in the conversation? I don't get it. I don't know how to approach it. 
 I think it's a sign of respect to one's culture (subject) to invest time on proper research, especially if it's something you're not familiar with. I remember Amano Akira (of 
 Jia Ting Jiao Shi hitsutomanREBORN! 
 [Katekyo Hitman Reborn!]) she asked someone who's fluent in Italian (she can just use google translate, y'know) to help her to name/translate terms she uses in her manga. Ooooh, another perfect example I think is Takashi Hashiguchi (of 
 Shao kitate!! ziyapan 
 [Yakitate Japan!!]) he even hired a baker to make sure the breads he featured are possible to bake in real life. That folks is dedication. 
 But this book has merits. I understand how it sweeps off a lot of readers' feet. So let's give credit where credit is due. Did I just say it was bad-ass? Yes, it was really action-packed. Bursting with exhilarating action. The author didn't hold bars. When it is kick-ass time, it is really kick-ass time. Yukiko could be annoying but she is strong. She owns herself. She relies on herself. And while the romance? (lust?) almost made my eye roll (wait, I did roll my eye!) I like that it didn't consume her like other heroines I've read before. 
 And well, there's Buruu. This creature had me heart and soul. More than Yukiko actually. I also like the background story of the first Buruu, and it made me cry reading his story. It was very heartbreaking. And quite honestly this was the only time I have genuine emotional connection with the book. Then there's the new Buruu. I liked Yukiko and Buruu's connection, interaction. One, if not the only aspect that made the book worth giving two and a half stars. 
 Even though I sound so negative, I still think the book is worth the curiosity. There are a lot of people who loved the book and I can see why. And maybe you could be one of them, so go ahead and try it and judge it for yourself. The book's idea is impressive, if only it was executed properly.

Man, I enjoyed this -- it was a loopy little detour into a fairly standard horror story set in an Ikea-esque store. The real strength is the unity of design and story -- the book is laid out like a fake Ikea catalogue, with diagrams, store maps, and advertisements one of which at the end is really effective, because it sets up a sequel, or just a horrific pondering to ponder.  
 Maybe I liked it so much because Ikea is the hottest topic in my city at the moment. One's just opened, and everyone lost their collective minds -- right down to the local government putting up traffic warning signs and sending out "whole of government" emails for when it opened, because people were expected to gridlock the streets around it. So I've recently been wandering around an Ikea, which makes the whole Orsk experience a bit more real. 
 In terms of the book itself, it's one part Ikea parody, one part fairly juvenile humour, one part stock horror story. The horror elements are very familiar "haunted house" stuff, and it's clear that the author really knows their paranormal fiction and TV (ngl, as someone who loves to chill out watching terrible faux-paranormal TV, some of the comments around these shows made me laugh). The horror is generally effective, but it's not show-stopping or genre breaking; but then again, I didn't get the impression that was what Hendrix wanted to do. The characters are all quite unlikable, and I only really found myself feeling sorry for Basil; poor Basil. 
 At times it reminded me of John Dies at the End, but less fratboy, more retail. Worth reading just for the stunning design.

Fire was such a breath of fresh air. I started it after trying out and giving up on another book where beauty is an important part of the main character, but I was just turned off by it in the other book. It's funny, because many attributes of Fire might add up to form a picture of a Mary Sue - "I'm so beautiful, it's like a curse," powers no one else in the kingdom has, strange-colored hair, multi-talented (she's a musician and an archer). Instead, what I read was an intricate journey about grief, family, self-acceptance/forgiveness, and learning how to do right when there are no easy choices. 
 And there really are no easy choices. Fire has done awful things in her time (won't spoil the big one that looms in the background of her characterization throughout the book). But which is worse: using your power to do something horrible to a few people, or sitting back and letting these people unleash evil and destruction on the world? Fire doesn't take a black and white view to this, and the answer is genuinely difficult to live with - and she must make the choice over and over as she gets embroiled in the buildup to a civil war, trying to help the royal family keep power. 
 Something I want to note is the bulk of the cast. There were a lot of characters, and they were all so skilfully drawn - I never found myself mixing them up or getting lost. They had their own motivations, viewpoints, ways of dealing with things. And so many side characters had journeys of their own, as well, and I enjoyed that. The ending /is/ a bit Lord of the Rings-esque - you know what I mean: a whole lot of epilogue-esque scenes, each of which could conceivably be the end. But I didn't mind at all, because they were tying up loose ends, both in Fire's journey, and in the journeys of the people - so many people! - she, and I, have come to love over the course of the book. 
 I am also endlessly sad about one of the deaths, still surprised at how many revelations there were regarding parentage etc., and still have the heebie-jeebies over the single crossover character from Graceling. (I wonder if he'll be the only crossover character in Bitterblue, too?)

Definitely recommend this book. I had heard so much about it and thought that it was another book that was being overrated and over exaggerated. And then someone mentioned that if I liked Gone Girl then I would enjoy The Girl on the Train. So I gave in and bought the audiobook. Totally glad I did. 
 I thoroughly enjoyed the suspense and the mystery that surrounds the characters and their lives that are seemingly unconnected, but forever intertwined in the strangest of ways. The anxiety that Rachel feels throughout the entire story never lessens and actually continues to build right up until the very end of the book. It kept me on my toes, that's for sure. Not to say this book outdid Gone Girl, though. That last sentence in Flynn's novel takes the cake for me. But this story seemed to keep me a little more on the edge, maybe because the mystery wasn't solved until the very end? Either way, if you liked Flynn's novel, then The Girl on the Train is a pretty good book to move on to. I enjoyed the writing, but it is a little difficult to judge it based on an audiobook. By the sound of it, the novel flowed really well. However, the performers were spectacular, so it might have just been their talents that made it read well. If you are looking for a great audiobook, I highly, highly suggest this one because you will be entertained all the way through. 
 The downsides to the novel would definitely be the characters. Rachel kind of turns me off at times and then at other times I feel downright sorry for her. *Spoiler maybe*: She is an alcoholic who can't seem to get her shit together. Every time you turn a page, she is back at the bottle. She is one of those characters that you really want to root for, because you sit there and listen to all of the injustice in her life. But, yet, you hate her because she doesn't do a damn thing about any of it. She just takes it all. I hate those kinds of characters; the ones that just sit there and apologize without even trying to fix what's broken. Without even standing up for themselves. Yet, I liked her. It's all very confusing, that's for sure. The other characters: well...you'll just have to read the book to figure out my frustrations with them. All I can say is I found every single one of them disagreeable in some way. And then there are certain characters that Hawkins just stops writing about. That always frustrates me, when I feel as if there are loose ends that still need to be tied up. I also feel like once everything is solved, the end drags a bit. Even though there seems to be a lot of grievances, they are pretty tiny compared to my enjoyment of the book. 
 Overall, I thought it was great! A great mystery, a great thriller and a great story. Anyone looking for a fun audiobook should definitely look into listening to this one, and anyone looking for a good read can find it with The Girl on the Train.

 It's always an excitement to read anything that has to do with J.K. Rowling and the magical universe she's created, she never runs out of ideas. The story of Harry Potter and the Cursed Child is no exception. I loved the plot, but the writing itself lacks emotion and creativity. I know, J.K. didn't write the actual book, but I can't help being angry at all this. This is not the 8th Harry Potter book! There is no such thing as 8th Harry Potter book! 
 Since it's a theatre play, I had to focus a little bit extra on the characters, and I was kind of disappointed to realise that they're not exactly themselves. Ron, whom I loved in the HP series, doesn't look like Ron at all. He's barely there, actually, and he seems so bland and so not himself. Don't blab that he's a grown-up now and he got mature, I know Ron, and this certainly isn't him. Also, the most important question I have, WHERE IS GEORGE? I mean, he was supposed to run Weasley's Wizard Whizzes, not Ron. I so wanted to read about George again, to see how he's doing after losing his other half, but he wasn't there! He's not even mentioned. 
 I was expecting so much more from Albus's friendship with Scorpius! I wanted to see some development, some chemistry, some intrigue, and I got none of that! I believe there's so much more to a friendship between two persons whose fathers used to be arch enemies! Since Scorpius is Draco's son, I wanted some angst (how can you speak of Draco Malfoy without mentioning how angsty he is?). 
 Speaking of Draco, who's a beloved character of mine, I was actually happy with him in this novel. He got the redemption he deserved, but he kept his old habits of teasing The Golden Trio. I missed this, and, fortunately, I got some of it. I have believed in Draco all this time... 
 Delphi was not very predictable, but she's definitely not worthy of being a Harry Potter villain. Once again I found a plot hole and ruined everything: if Voldemort is not capable of love, then how on earth did he leave Bellatrix pregnant? Voldemort was hungry for power, he'd never wanted a heir, he wanted to live forever and rule the world. Then how was this Delphi actually born? Hmm... 
  
 But I can't end this review without mentioning the biggest and most obvious mistake in the book: how did Albus and Scorpius manage to prepare Polyjuice Potion is a few minutes, when preparing it takes at least one month. You can't fool me, muggles, I've read Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets...

A war between Earth and Faerie has left the world changed and ruined forever, where even the plants and trees are no longer to be trusted and will even kill you if they have the chance. Sound awesome? I think so! But unfortunately for me, the execution made on this story about a post-apocalyptic future touched by the effects of magic just didn't live up to my expectations. 
 As I said, I really liked the idea the author was working with here and is the reason I read this book. A war between the people of Earth and Faerie sounded too good to pass up, and the general story itself was interesting enough to hold my attention the whole way through. However, the characters were so flat and uninteresting half the time that I felt zero connection with any of them save for perhaps Allie. I felt like I was thrown head first into the story without getting to know the characters so that I could feel for them or care about their struggles. Matthew is a great example of this. Even the elements of surprise, those I felt that the author was trying to achieve, were lackluster and had no meaning because it was like they were dumped on me too soon without any sort of build up. I did like some of the characters, but I wish they could have been fleshed out more so I didn't have to feel so disconnected. 
 My biggest criticism about the story is the main character. I just plain didn't like her. And the fact that the narrative was spoken by her, it made it all the worse. She was two-dimensional, depressing, and straight out annoying. However, considering her situation, like her father abusing her and other sad things that's revealed about her life, it's somewhat understandable. But again, the writing here couldn't bring it all together in a way that I could relate to her. If you don't mind an "emo" (couldn't think of a better word for it) character and narrative then you will probably like this book a lot more than I did. I'm just not into that sort of thing. 
 A lot of the description in this book was really nice, and the way the author painted this post-apocalyptic world was, as I mentioned earlier, interesting enough to hold my attention, although some of the ideas to describe somethings were just plain bad in my opinion. For example, magic touched people have clear hair. Hair as clear as glass. I can't help, I think that's really stupid. On the other hand, the way the forest operated was awesome. I wouldn't want to live in such a place but reading about it was great. 
 So, you may be thinking "why give this book three stars if you sound like you didn't like it that much?" Perhaps it sounds that way but I honestly did like the story itself well enough. Even though I found the execution not to my liking, the main character annoying, the characters two-dimensional, I thought it was a good little story about a post-apocalyptic future and magic. It's not the best story I've read but it was still good.

For claiming to be the end of a 'saga' (though can you really be a saga with only three books?) this book does not quite have the closure I expected. It was all right, but not much more was truly resolved than the last book. 
 Out in the world with memories returning, Nick begins to have more constant memories of a girl, one that he can't tell if he hurt or not. He feels compelled to track her down and does. The book alternates between his and her POV. 
 Seeing things from Nick's perspective was interesting. While quiet, he is not the jerk that he seemed to be from the other books. But then, it has been obvious that was changing since the second book. He also seems like he wants to prove himself different from his father; yet he continues to drink himself to oblivion just like his father. However, he is driven to find Elizabeth, and once he finds her she becomes his everything. This rankled me, being rather like insta-love, and never really having a reason.  After all, it turns out he literally just met her for a few minutes in the forest, saved her life, and dropped her at a hospital. And that is supposed to be the basis for this deep and protective love? Feels a bit much to me.  However, I did enjoy that his relationship with the others, especially Anna, has improved. He truly sees them as his family and trusts them and loves them in a way that I liked seeing. 
 Elizabeth is not exempt from insta-love either. Hers at least has some basis- hero worship. When she sees Nick she sees the guy who saved her; the rest of the story takes time to come out. Then, beyond that, he is a smoking hot guy with interest in her. Still, a bit insta-love-ish. Regardless she is an interesting character in that she is a person struggling through panic attacks and finding ways to live a normal life around it; also that she is a mystery as to what happened and why the Branch interest. I enjoyed that. 
  The fact that at the end Riley gets away bugs the hell out of me. I know that it makes sense, that not everything has a perfect happy ending, but that isn't what bothered me. This more felt like a way for Rush to leave it open so that if she felt like it she could come back and write more. I don't know, it just felt cheap in that way.  
 As an overall it was a fast, easy, passable read, but the series itself is rather unremarkable and forgettable so not something I would be jumping to recommend.

Will Robin ever find out that Matthew had deleted that voicemail? Will it matter continuing on in the next book? 
 The breakup between Robin and Matthew had me cheering for her and the "breakup" scene between Robin and Strike had me in tears. Thankfully, we see a glimmer of hope at the end of the novel that I hope will translate into Strike getting into some jobs and money that'll bring Robin on as a partner and get her a raise in the next book.  
 There doesn't seem to be a mention of it yet, but I hope there's book four to see where this story goes!

 The Trapped Girl is another entertaining addition to the Tracy Crosswhite series. There is a new mystery for Tracy to solve, with lots of twists and turns along the way. The pace is steady, if a bit slow, and the character development continues to be great. The shifts in POV are a bit abrupt, as they change from third to first person, and disrupt the narrative flow. 
 Robert Dugoni always brings something new to his novels, but remains faithful to the characters he's created. This novel still has something that is uniquely Tracy, which grasps the reader's attention. A few of the twists are quite predictable this time around, but this is still a fun mystery read. 
 I just didn't connect with this novel. As it seems to be the case with all Dugoni books I've read so far, the beginning is a bit of a struggle for me, as it takes me a while to get into the story. The slow pace remains steady throughout all of it, which definitely helps readers keep flipping pages, and things do pick up after the first few chapters. 
 Tracy is still my favorite! She continues to be an amazing narrator, and her character continues to develop with each novel. The core of who she is as a person is still the same, as is her motivation for doing what she does, which ties with the very first novel of this series. It's lovely how Dugoni keeps bringing that up, as it's such a huge part of who Tracy is as a person. 
 Something that did throw me off were the abrupt shifts in POV. The change from third person to first person are really jarring, especially when there is yet another POV in some chapters that is also told in third person. It just feels odd, not in a good way, and it disrupts the otherwise smooth narrative flow. 
 In the end, The Trapped Girl just isn't for me. The different narration format doesn't do the plot any favors, and the twists can be easily figured out. It is still an interesting mystery read, but not as good as the previous installments. The ending is rather sweet and adorable, though, which is definitely a highlight!

His family the hangmen know its only a matter of time until he completely shatters and is gone to them forever but his emotions take an unexpected turn when he meets Maddie.

I really liked this series. I know there is another one, but it is more of a companion, if I'm not mistaken, so I am going to read that next. I actually think this ending was better than the one for The Raven Cycle. I didn't mind the bit of the open-ended-ness because it allows us to decide for ourselves what happens to Grace and Sam at the end. I also think having a concrete answer would have ruined the mythology a bit for me. 
 Stiefvater's writing, as always, is perfect. I love how engaging her writing is and how descriptive and beautiful. I thought she really fleshed out the series in this one and made me really happy. I definitely understand why this series was the breakout for Stiefvater because it is magical. The writing really draws you in and makes you feel as though you are running through the woods with wolves. You're basically Kevin Costner. 
 I still really like Grace and Sam as individuals. I also like their relationship but whenever she talks to her parents I'm just like "no bby no." I still think they were rushing into things and I definitely rolled my eyes when Grace was like "I don't know what to say to Sam" and then ten seconds later said to him, "Want to get married?" I was confused by the 180 there. And then their relationship just went downhill from there for me. I did get pulled back into them when they were wolves together at the end,  but it still almost wasn't enough for me. But individually, I REALLY enjoyed them. I liked that Grace wanted to finish school and go to college. I liked that Sam wanted to take care of the wolves and work in the bookstore. I liked that they both had their own dreams that semi-overlapped with one another. I just couldn't get there with some of the other things they discussed. 
 I also really liked Isabel. I mean, she was the best character in this series. I was really glad that she was a part of this story. I just felt like she was only around when someone else needed something. I felt like she was under-utilized until the very end and even then it wasn't enough for me. I needed more Isabel (and less Cole). Because honestly, Cole didn't do it for me. He took a lot of risks that weren't necessary. I liked that he was science driven and realized he didn't want to die. But I just didn't get it. I don't get the appeal. At all. And every time we were in his POV I wanted to skip ahead. 
 There were also a lot of other things that happened in this one that just kinda felt out of place. I understand that the police probably would suspect Sam but it felt like it was thrown in there last minute and not really developed in a way that made sense. It also ... went away pretty easily. A lot of things that were introduced either in the late part of the last book or the beginning of this book were easily cleaned up at the end and that was meh to me. But I am okay with the overall ending of it, so I wasn't too hung up on this. 
 I highly recommend this series! The mythology is SUPERB and I have discussed it in both of my reviews for Shiver and Linger so I don't feel the need to restate it here. If you are looking for something a little different in terms of werewolf mythology, check out this series!

 BUT.

I have read a number of fast-paced novels -- they tend to be my favorite type of leisure reading -- but The Heist was, by far, the fastest novel I have ever read. The prose was quick and sharp, was not too heavy on details, and was shaped to fit the racing, action-filled plot. 
 That being said, there were definitely things wanting. While the quality of the novel was not too compromised for briskness of prose and plot, I do not think the novel reached its full potential. Given another one hundred pages, or at least more finesse in some of the scenes and dialogue, the novel would have improved dramatically. The plot itself was not the problem; though there was only one major twist that was unpredictable, albeit bordering on ridiculousness, the storyline remained relatively fresh. (Disclaimer: that may be only because I have read few novels centering on grifts and cons.) 
 What lacked in the novel, in my opinion, was proper character development. As a fan of the TNT drama Leverage, a TV series about a handful of specialized criminals (and one honest man) who become a team of con artists working as modern-day Robin Hoods, I was more than excited to read a novel where there was potential for a similar group of con artists to band together to take down a big-time criminal. Such was not the case. All across the board, the characters seemed more of bas reliefs than actual people -- slightly more than just standard stock characters, but nowhere near fleshed out enough to be interesting. The villain was unremarkable, and the amateur people who were recruited to be part of the con team were hardly given enough screen time, if you will, to leave distinct impressions on the reader's mind. 
 The stars of the novel, FBI Special Agent Kate O'Hare and notorious conman Nicholas Fox, are in no way remarkable, either. O'Hare is the typical female government agent: tough, independent, mostly unfeminine unless she must be (in which case she just happens to be drop-dead gorgeous and perfectly seductive), and single because of her job -- or, rather, her intimidating persona and occupation. While I am all for tough and independent female characters, the one touting a military background and a bottomless pit for a stomach, thereby allowing her to woof down all manner of greasy foods, seems a bit worn out from being reused so often. Nicholas Fox is the standard slick, handsome, charming con artist who can have any woman, O'Hare included, soaked within a minute just by talking. Their connection throughout the novel is a bit bland and rather forced, as though the writers are indulging the readers with the "necessary" romantic plot line, regardless of whether or not they truly intend to "go all the way" with that narrative arc. No true chemistry between the two is properly built up in the novel, which does not leave enough room (or opportunities) to give O'Hare and Fox any chance to even realize if they truly are experiencing chemistry. 
 The redeeming aspect of the novel, in regards to characters, lies in O'Hare's father, an ex-military man with enough tricks and favors up his sleeves to help his favorite daughter out of nasty situations. The character proves to be the most developed, as evident in how he shines in whatever scene he appears in. Perhaps subsequent novels should focus on his previous experiences instead. 
 Regardless, I enjoyed reading the novel, and I may pick up its sequel, merely to see where O'Hare and Fox are called to next. After all, there are plenty of "legal" criminals who need to be tossed behind bars, or at least paying for their devious exploits. Perhaps I will go and watch an episode of Leverage to fulfill that desire...

She decides to go back to her normal life and find out more about what she is, and learn to control her powers. At the same time, she is also having visions about the future that intrigue her. 
 Skye is pretty muc the same as she was in the last book, but she is becoming more independant and gaining control of her life. Initially she decides to join the rebellion but as the book progresses, she reconsiders everything and goes with what she thinks is right. Asher has changed a bit. He isnt so much the cocky, flirty bad boy we met before. He has been tamed (sadly) and a bit too sappy for my liking now. Devin kinda annoyed me, with his constant whining about how he is helpless and controlled by the rebellion when he can obviously do soemthing to stop it. 
 The love triangle continues and things do progress a bit. She is offically with Asher but continues to have feelings for Devin. We are getting closer to the war between the light and the dark side, and the ending was really good. It set things up for the next book wich will undoubtedly be epic. This book is easy to get though and pretty enjoyable.

3 Friends to Lovers Stars! 
 This is the second book in the All Saints series and this time it revolves around the other owner All Saints. 
 Marcos is dedicated and loyal to All Saints but leaves nothing left for his personal time. 
 The greatest, most honored job a parent has is that of loving their child. Raising their child. Giving them hope for a happy future. Unfortunately, many parents are continuing to forget that. They turn out their children, and so many of those children have nowhere to go except the street. 
 After being kicked out from his family his biggest loss was his best friend Anthony whom he mourns daily. So when Anthony's sister comes to him for help he grudgingly agrees to help. Marcos is skeptical from his past hurts and personal experiences and doesn't know what to expect with Anthony since he's turned to drugs. 
 Marcos knows what its like to beat down the demons of addictions but doesn't know if he can do again with Anthony but letting down his best friend isn't an option. 
 We quickly find out why Anthony dove down the rabbit hole and it breaks your heart that both boys didn't have to go through that if they had any support from their families. Marcos quickly finds out that Anthony wants more than friendship but is scared to go there with him being an addict plus not wanting to ruin their tentative re-kindled friendship. 
 This was sweet but it didn't pull me in like other books. I had to make effort to keep engaged and then Marco's stubborn ways got a bit annoying at times even though I did understand it. I did like it but it took me too long to get into the story. Otherwise it was sweet and full of hope and second chances plus I'm always a sucker for friends to lovers and straight to gay. So it fit the bill in that category.

"It's so hard to leave-until you leave. And then it is the easiest goddamned thing in the world...Leaving feels too good, once you leave." 
 We all leave eventually. No matter who and what we are, or where we're from, we will someday and somehow leave our comfort zones or the norm of our lives to find ourselves a place in this world. Some people take their time into actually doing it. They spent much time planning and scheming on how they should gloriously plow into life. There are some who tried a few times before succeeding, by accepting that their heavy butts are beginning to be a burden to their family and to the economy. 
 Then, there are those who are used to having things come to them in a rush; and when it's not fast enough they go for it instead... Such is Margo Roth Spiegelman and many other teenagers out there who cannot wait to be themselves without the restriction of the norm. My dear nephew, Jaff, calls it emancipation. This is perfectly normal; it's a matter of how they are properly motivated and inspired. They should be equipped, so as not to become scattered dandelions, gliding aimlessly waiting where the wind will blow them. Unfortunately for Margo, she has uninspired parents to motivate her. They are like the paper cut-outs Margo described, who boxed themselves inside this very peculiar thing called normal life. They regard Margo's actions as rebellion. 
 "It is easy to forget how full the world is of people, full to bursting, and each of them imaginable and consistently misimagined." 
 Margo, on the other hand, sees life as a colorful journey filled with dark abandoned buildings, knee-high grasses, endless road, moonlit roof and plenty of exhilarating risks. But all this is unknown to her family and friends. All her life, she has coated herself with a shell of Margo Stuff- the cool ones. It then became difficult for her to remove her coating and be herself. So the only option is to leave it all behind. But there is still one string attached to this papergirl - Quentin Jacobsen. She wants Q to know her; understand her; love her for who she is inside, no matter how crooked and unreasonable that Margo may be. 
 "The way I figure it, everyone gets a miracle." 
 Q braved the challenge- he took the journey and accepted the would be consequences of it. Little did he know that this journey will not only lead him to Margo, but discover the Margo hiding within too. Thus, making him aware of his own capabilities and weaknesses. Knowing that he will succeed in finding his place in the world someday soon. And maybe, just maybe, he'll find Margo there as well.

 This was kind of a hot mess. There's too much going on here in one book much less one suburban high school. The main couple has 1 dead parent, 1 absentee parent, 1 abusive parent and 1 absentee formerly alcoholic parent. There is bullying, sexual victimization, and cyberbullying. There is underage drinking, drag racing, and violence. Any reasonable action by any type of authority figure whether it be a parent, teacher, principal or police is simply discounted by the author. This world is a parallel universe of adolescent anarchy. 
 The author gives us multiple reasons for the bullying, none of which ring true because of the competing reasons. Either he loves her and is acting out as an adolescent, he wants to protect her from his rapey friends by making her undateworthy, he hates her outright, or he's so damaged from a summer with his abusive father that he's become a sadist. The episodes of bullying are of the type that ascribe to one of these motivations...but it doesn't make sense if he really loved her that he would want her completely friendless. If he hates her, he wouldn't be protecting her from other guys. 
 I love a romance in which strong dislike turns to intense sexual chemistry and eventually love, but it just didn't work for me in this book. It's a YA/NA trope for the virgin heroine to become an instant nympho, and that's what we got...It's even worse in this book because she flipped from being semi-afraid of him to nympho.

Cute and engaging - as is the YouTube channel that inspired it - but to me this book definitely skews on the very young side of YA, if not smack in the middle of middle grade-land. 
 Sunshine moves to a new town with her mom and becomes convinced their house is haunted. Sunshine is awkwardly adorable (sorry, Goodreads blurb, but I reject the word "adorkable") with her quirky thrift shop clothes and her endless frustration with her unruly hair. She makes one friend at her new school-- a guy called Nolan-- and I'm thinking their friendship could definitely turn into a PG-rated romance in later installments. One odd thing about this book is that there aren't a lot of characters at all -- I can think of four total, five if you count a friend back home that Sunshine texts with -- so when the story focused heavily on one seemingly minor person I was certain that this person had something to do with the house's haunting ... and I was right. The book sets up what I assume will be the plan going forward  that Sunshine is some sort of spirit guardian and Nolan is her protector. Like a tween Buffy.  
 For a paranormal book, the creep factor is lo. There was one early scene that made me think this might be a worthy successor to Goosebumps et al, but that didn't continue. I'm kind of a wimp and even I thought this book was pretty tame in the thrills and chills department. 
 I highly recommend this if you're looking for mildly spooky books for readers in the middle grade range. Sunshine is a fun and charming character and the story is just creepy enough for the tween set, plus completely free from YA romantic angst and gratuitous edginess. It reminded me a little of a favorite MG series of mine, Gilda Joyce. 
 But I'm not sure many older teen and adult YA readers are going to find this substantive or compelling enough to satisfy them. 
 PS I'm rarely (never?) nitpicky about ARC errors, but given the fact that Pride and Prejudice was Sunshine's favorite book ever (hooray for that!) I was not happy that my e-ARC misspelled Elizabeth Bennet's name at least four times! I hope this gets fixed in the final copy. 
 PPS. Thanks to the publisher for providing an advance copy for me to read and review.

I've watched every episode of the TV series and read the first two compendiums of the comics and loved them. "Rise of the Governor" is right up there with the other Walking Dead mediums. I thought the writing was pretty excellent, which was surprising to me considering the genre. The landscape, zombies, and killings were described in great, sometimes excruciating, detail. 
 I enjoyed the plot quite a bit too. It was nice to see a little of the backstory of the Governor. It seems like this is the comic Governor, not the television Governor. Kirkman did a nice job keeping the action up. Just when you think the group is going to be safe for a while, it all comes crashing down. 
 I did have two issues that prevent me from giving a five-star review. The first is that the zombie outbreak hasn't fully been explained yet. The comics, show, and books all leave out exactly what caused the outbreak and how it spread so quickly. The other issue was with the Chalmers. I thought their departure from the Chalmers' apartment was poorly done. We know why, but it was all very sudden. And after they leave, the Chalmers are never address again. They are main characters for six chapters (25% of the book) and then never mentioned again. It would have been nice to get an update on them. 
 All-in-all, I really enjoyed this book though. I would recommend it to any fans of the show or the comics. I'm going to get right to reading the second book while anxiously awaiting the release of the third book of the trilogy.

Actual Rating: 3.5 
 I really enjoyed the writing style of this book, of how we were able to see the different perspectives of more than just the main characters but the minor characters as well. It reminds you that even though these characters are minor, that they barely play a role, they still play one and that they are real people with real lives (as real as it can get in a fictional setting, anyways). 
 Natasha's pessimism (or as she says, her realism) is oddly satisfying. I relate to her a lot and I really enjoyed every rebuttal she had for Daniel's hopeless romantic lines, since what she says makes sense to me and I agree with it. 
 I liked these two main character because Natasha is who I connect with in terms of realism and practicality, and Daniel is who I connect with in terms of "my parents want me to do this...but I do this" and the entire racial thing about being Koreans in America, since I'm a second-generation Chinese American. When Charlie didn't want Daniel calling him hyung it really hit close to home, since I used to be embarrassed when my brother called me sister in Chinese in front of my friends. 
 Because the minor characters served as a cause-and-effect situation for Daniel and Natasha to fall in love, the perspectives from their side really helped a lot. I also really liked them because when reading a scene, you judge a character in a certain light, but when you read their backstory, you change your idea about them. For example, when Natasha asked for a fork and the waitress tells Daniel to teacher his girlfriend how to use chopsticks, I was really offended because it's not like you should expect every single person in the world to know how to use chopsticks. But then I read her perspective and she says, "This country can't have everything," which makes me understand her more. 
 I was surprised that Daniel was so forward with Natasha because in the beginning from his perspective, he sounded more shy and I didn't think he would make the first move. Boy was I wrong. 
 I actually really enjoyed Daniel and Natasha's story, despite how insta-love it is. At least, in the beginning, when Daniel was trying to change Natasha's perspective of true love and such. However, after Natasha told him she was getting deported and almost every scene after that Daniel was like "we're meant to be" or "she's the One" I felt like I was constantly rolling my eyes because like. Dude. You've known her for a day. And then Natasha was basically doing the same thing and lost almost all her pessimism, which was something about her I really liked. 
 Okay, I was kind of pissed when Daniel got angry at Natasha for not telling him she was getting deported. I mean like seriously? She was trying to shake you off all day and trying not to fall in love and when he says "you should've said those things" and Natasha said "I did!" I was just so annoyed because Daniel was acting like those men who puts blame completely on women as if he was completely in the right. 
 The coincidences that come after this is like unbelievable. Which is the point, but it had me scoffing a little bit. 
 I was really surprised when the book already got to the post-deportation, since I expected it to be more climatic, like Daniel making some cheesy confession in the middle of the airport before Natasha goes through the security, since that seems like something he would do. Or more dialogue and internal monologue. I liked how Nicola played it out in a detached, omniscient presence though because it wasn't as dramatic or in your face, but more like bam. And over. 
 I really liked how Irene was the one who brought Daniel and Natasha back together in the end because she was the one who technically brought them together in the beginning. 
 Okay, I wish Natasha's dad and Charlie had more closure. It was just kind of an epilogue like have a good life. 
 This book makes me wonder: if every day is this jam packed and intense, what would our lives be like? 
  
 Overall, this book was fantastic and a kind of idealistic but still realistic story that I really related with.

Here's the thing about this book: I'm 100% sure most of the people who will read it will feel betrayed or disappointed or angry or something in between those lines. 
 Why? 
 Because it's not what you expect. Eadlyn doesn't end up with the person most of the people want her to end up with, and in a series that has such a heavy romance, yes, that is going to determine whether or not some people like it. 
 And during all of this I'm just sitting here, giggling like crazy, because I finally felt like Kiera Cass found herself again after that disaster that The Heir was. Also, I got my otp. Let's not forget about that either. 
 So yeah. You can say I'm very happy with this book. 
 Like I said, I felt like Kiera Cass found herself again. Anyone who read my review of The Heir last year know how disappointed I was by the fourth book of the series, and I was honestly questioning what the whole point was to continue a perfectly ended trilogy - it felt like milking the cow and making as much money out of it while there was still interest for it. I questioned how she could have ever think we would root for such annoying, spoiled brat that Eadlyn was and how could we believe that so many people wanted to marry her. I honestly wasn't sure if the whole thing was on purpose or not. 
 Well, it definitely was. Eadlyn made a pretty great character development throughout this last book, and I enjoyed everything about it. The only thing that irred me was that there was no blurr line between the Eadlyn she was in the previous book and the Eadlyn she became in this one. I sort of felt like I was reading about a completely different person - sure, she got quite a lot of slaps in her face at the end of the last book, and you could say that the whole change was the result of that, but still, I would have preferred having a bit less smooth transition with a couple of hickups. 
 The other thing I wanna talk about was who Eadlyn chose in the end. I sat down to read this book expecting it to be Kile. I saw so many people claiming nobody else could be her choice but him and from an outsider's perspective, I could see why others would think that. But somehow I couldn't jump on that ship, I'm sorry. I always thought that would have been wrong. Kile wanted nothing more than to leave the palace since he was a little kid, how forcing him to stay there would have been any good for him on the long run? Sure, they had chemistry, but so did Eadlyn and other boys as well. 
 And while I couldn't really ship Kile with her, I was so down for Eikko and Eadlyn. They were perfect. They slowly got to know each other without any pressure, they let each other close and they were there for each other, and their relationship kept developping through this book as well. It was so nice and beautiful and from the moment I realised they were really happening I could not stop giggling.  
 So yeah. Basically, I was really happy with this book and how the whole series wrapped up. (Hopefully for real this time.) 
 (Seriously, I love this series, but please, let it end instead of dragging it out pointlessly, just for the heck of it.)

A 'cut and shut' is when two cars are welded together to create a vehicle which, while on the outside looks as good as any other used car, actually has the problems of both vehicles. To be fair, the reason most people dislike cut and shuts is that when they buy they're totally unaware it was originally two different motorcars. So perhaps drawing an analogy between this used car dealer's practice and 'Pride and Prejudice and Zombies' is an unfair one, as you could hardly expect to get something other than what's advertised in the title. 
 However this hypergamy of a book is like a cut and shut in that the bringing together just creates its own problems. The wit and sharpness of Austin's prose is blunted, while the excitement of the zombie attacks falls away when we return to Regency romance. By the end I was just mainly concerned with spotting the new bits to the text, and determining how a book works is not the best way to enjoy it. 
 If it had been a short story (or even a television sketch, the Harry Enfield bit where The Terminator is in the cast of 'The Remains of the Day' comes to mind), this may have worked better. But at book length I just felt the conceit was stretched far beyond breaking point.

 1. Will and Layken fall in love

I thought since Layken's father dies, and I didn't know if Will had any parents left, so I figured he must have his dad left, I thought Will's dad and Layken's mom would fall in love with each other.  OMYGOD HE'S A TEACHER 
 HE'S LAYKEN'S TEACHER. 
 Normally I don't like reading about student-teacher relationships, but I just kept thinking "Will's only 21 Will's only 21 and he's hot" 
 Of course they have to stop seeing each other. NOOOOOO.

 Bring on the waterworks.

 I don't know what to say anymore aside from the fact that it's one of the best books I've read this year. The characters were very likeable. I wish Layken's new friends were my friends too.

This book was FANTASTIC. The best Sherlock Holmes retelling I have read and I LOVE Jamie and Charlotte ahhhh. Full review to come closer to the release date! 
 Read this review on my blog: http://tamaraniac.com/2016/02/a-study... 
 Before I even picked up this book I was a little in love with the concept. I love the Sherlock Holmes stories, and I tend to readily jump into modern adaptations of those stories. Sometimes those adaptations work, and sometimes they really, really don't. This was one that worked wonderfully. 
 My favorite part of A Study In Charlotte was how the characters were descendants of the original Holmes and Watson. I have found that adaptations of Sherlock Holmes never seem to truly capture the original duo, so I was glad that this book didn't even try. Instead, in the book's universe both Sherlock and John were very real people, and have families descended from them. Both the Holmes and Watson families are a bit odd and carry certain traits of their ancestors. I just loved that whole concept, with a bunch of Holmeses and Watsons running around and putting themselves in danger, and with the Watson and Holmes of the same age becoming friends and solving crimes. Adorable. 
 I also really enjoyed how it was set at a boarding school. I recently heard Rainbow Rowell speak about Carry On, and she talked about how setting novels about kids at boarding school is a great way to get rid of parents. (without killing them all) I was kind of thinking about that while reading this book, and wow was boarding school a great setting for this book. It really added to the whole mystery - students at the school are dying and it could be anyone on campus who they might be living right next too. 
 A Study In Charlotte did a great job with talking about tough topics. This book deals with some pretty sensitive things such as crime, addiction, sexual assault, and I think it did those topics a great deal of justice. It didn't dumb anything down, and dealt with the victims in the situation kindly while still dealing with that situation as the dark, scary, and harmful thing it is. 
 Charlotte and Jamie were honestly the best Holmesian descendant main characters I could have asked for. They were so perfectly Holmes and Watson but also not at all, because Holmes and Watson are their great-great-great-grandparents and they're their own people of course. Their whole dynamic was fantastic. (I love them so much) I also feel for Jamie quite in a lot of different little ways. He's a very relatable character who has a lot of very relatable problems, along with a few problems that aren't quite so common. (please love him like I do) 
 In conclusion: Great retelling, great characters, gorgeous cover. If you love Sherlock Holmes stories, you won't be disappointed!

Mirror was trapped in a clock by her grandfather and came out as something more than human. She wanders England with her shape-shifting guardian, Goliath. When they encounter the evil Mr. Fingers and his "son" Mr. Loveheart, they must tread carefully, because Mr. Fingers is after Mirror's soul. 
 This book is hard to summarize, because of the threadbare plot and vague, dreamlike (nightmarelike) prose. Had I not been told about this book by a friend and stumbled across it on my own in the bookstore, I'd be lured in by the gorgeous cover art and the seemingly middle-grade premise. The cover and the chapter headers are the best part of this book however. 
 I broke out the page flags again for this beauty. But I couldn't have tabbed all my annoyances because then there would have been more tabs than pages. Warning: Rant Approaching! 
 This book. It's a polished turd. A glimmering bit of fool's gold, shimmering like bright faerie lights. But when you pick it up, the plot and characterization crumble to dust in your hands like burnt moth wings. The weak plot, like a newborn deer tottering on fragile stick legs unravels quickly like so much glittering gold thread, spun by Rumpelstiltskin. The characters are cardboard, dull and grey like storm clouds who've decided not to storm. The story is a fever dream of bad imagery, vile like demon's eyes. The genre is a harlequin mask, shining and deadly. But beneath the middle-grade veneer lies a muddle mess of childlike character names, playful and safe like a dandelion, marred by young adult themes, briefly violent like a car crash you didn't see coming. Marketed as an adult horror novel, but it's a lie, like the faerie feast happened upon in the faerie forest, where the food turns to ash in your mouth. The ash of the aforementioned burnt moth wings. 
 Are you tired yet? Good, me too. That's what it felt like to read this damn book. 
 The writing is so tortured - it reads like the first draft of some bizarre, overwrought nightmare. It's a jumble of vague images, like Bee thought up a bunch of one or two liners that sounded cool to her and then she smashed them together into a "story." I tabbed 6 weird analogies (similes, metaphors, whatever) in the first 4 pages, and those are just the ones that stood out the most. The book includes many "gems" such as: 
 "...Goliath arrives like a star falling and imprinting the surface of the earth. THUD he has landed. A galactic footprint. The moon a stage light for his materialization onto the Liverpool docks." 
 "He deposits us on the docks with a wink and a crooked smile; like a demented midwife, delivers us straight from the sea." 
 "...great splodges of water fall into my eyes and Goliath's beard, disappearing like pearls thrown into a wild forest." 
 "London, city of poisoned water, sour milk, fish stink and shit. Blood bubbles and drips down the thighs of her." This is by far one of the grossest analogies I've heard. 
 Followed by: "He smelled of spermy things." 
 "The smell of hot water bottle fur and his great heart beating lull me asleep." Okay, seriously, what the hell does hot water bottle fur smell like!? 
 "The darkness spreads out before me like a roll of carpet to stuff Cleopatra in." 
 "He smiled, a smile of a thousand cats." 
 "I am a nasty thing and mad as scissors." 
 Mirror describing Loveheart: "You are stuffed with hearts. They burst out of your eyes, fall to your feet like severed heads. Your guts are red ribbons. Your heart is a rose." 
 To add to the ridiculous flow of the story, no color is ever just a color. If it's green, it's frog green. Or gold is fairy (which she also spells faerie) gold, twinkling and shimmery. While this doesn't ordinarily bother me, it's incredibly annoying when used every time a color is mentioned. 
 "The sky is the colour of porridge and the sea, a miserable treacle black." 
 "It had eyes like magic beans, dark and chocolatey..." 
 "....for my eyes were black. The colour of dead things." 
 "It was big and cool and blue like suicide." This one really had me like ?_? 
 When she wasn't busy filling in the gaps with "tick-tock, tickety-tock, clock!" Bee also had some fun dicking around with fonts and word placement; filling a page with the word bitches, or another with weird heart symbols. Meanwhile, the lack of plot ran rampant and left me wondering what the point of the book was. Halfway through, the main timeline is thrown out the window and we're taken back in time, forward in time, dragged around through various new character POVs that were sadly indistinguishable from any previous chapters because every character had the same voice. 
 I was left with many questions, and not in an intriguing manner. Mirror's abilities or non-human attributes are never really discussed, random characters that have no real impact on the story are given chapters that felt completely irrelevant, readers are never enlightened as to why her grandfather shoved her in a magical clock to begin with or what he hoped to achieve by doing so. 
 The genre is just as confusing as the plot. For the most part it reads like a middle grade book, especially with character names like Loveheart, Mr. Fingers, Pomegranate (a terrible reimagining of Persephone), Doctor Cherrytree, Mr. Chimes (a clockmaker of course), and Goliath Honey-Flower. The language is pretty basic, until Bee decides things needed to be spiced up and throws in some swearing, or a few quick scenes of violence. Nothing overly graphic, just Loveheart abruptly shooting someone in the face, or lopping off someone's head with his sword. This would I guess elevate it to a YA book, yet Mirror is only randomly transformed into a 16-year-old halfway through the book (yep) and I don't know that there's anything about her that teens could relate too. I thought perhaps her age was accelerated to facilitate some sort of romance with Loveheart, but even that didn't happen. To top it all off, this book is apparently marketed as adult fiction!? I'm utterly lost... 
 I don't even know why I finished this book. I mean, I read it over two days, so it wasn't a huge timesuck, but really. It's too early to call it, but I would bet money that this ends up in the number one spot of my Worst Reads of 2016 list. 
 If I could give this negative stars, I would.

 Oh boy, where do I start. We will start with the good, because unfortunately there isn't much good to cover. 
 I loved the premise of Infected. This fusion of science and horror was thrilling. As I read, I immediately thought of the movie "The Crazies", though aside from the apparent unprovoked homicidal tendencies, there really is no connection. 
 I was impressed with the level of science in Infected. I am not an authority, and I don't know if any of it was actually accurate, but it made me feel like the author really cared about his book. He did the research. He put in the fancy words. They read a little dry at times, and there was at least one point where they used CDC as an abbreviation, assuming people know the organization (which most people do). And then they backtrack and explain it. In grisly detail. 
 Because Infected was released first via podcast, it has a very conversational narrative which read really easily. Hence the fact it only took me two days to read it, despite the fact that I wasn't the biggest fan of it. 
 And finally, the gore. Some of the gore was kind of "meh", but for the most part it was grisly and horrific... exactly what you want from a horror story. Fair warning... there is a lot of it. 
 With the good covered, we move on to the bad. And the bad was very bad. 
 There were far too many viewpoints, and I hated them all. I didn't like the racist 'Nam survivor CIA agent, and I didn't like the rage-aholic almost-football-star who at 26, still refers to his abusive father as "daddy". There were more minor viewpoints, that of the epidemiologist from the CDC, various other infecteds, etc. I can see this being effective in a podcast, but in print, it was just too scattered. I didn't feel connected at all. 
 While we are on the subject of characters, let us stop at Perry for a moment. He is our main character in all this, and I just didn't like him or believe what he was going through for five seconds. Over the course of the book he lost so much blood, and yet aside from a few blackouts, he doesn't bat an eye. He should have been weak as a kitten by the end, if not dead. But no... he just got up and kept on going. 
 Perry also has an issue with female characters. I was really disgusted with the way he treats the woman he meets near the end of the book. I actually took it really personally, because the author describes this woman almost exactly to my proportions (height and weight) and then proceeds to comment on how fat she is. I know I am not the skinniest person around, but I am far from "fat". Furthermore, women don't have to conform to some set of measurements to be beautiful. This attitude that women are fat after a certain point is so harmful. I am so thankful that this isn't a young adult novel. 
 Infected suffered from repeat-shit-itis, especially where Perry was concerned. And it was very tell-don't-show, which is somewhat understandable considering the book's original medium. But I would have liked to have read less about what a monster Perry was when he played football, and how immortal College students thought they were, and more about the parasites. 
 The ending of Infected wasn't particularly effective. In my humble opinion, they could have cut a few chapters and it would have done much more to draw me in to the rest of the series. 
 Bottom Line: A science-horror crossover that delivers on both fronts. But watch out for the rapidly shifting viewpoints and the characters that you just can't like. I will very likely not be continuing with this series.

Self-Referential 
 I could see someone writing a three-star review of McEwan's latest novel almost as easily as a five-star one. Dropped to four stars on Goodreads because although I can remember a lot of the what of the novel on recollection, I can recall almost none of the why: its theme or focus. Rereading this review has helped me to do so, but for a five-star book I shouldn't have to.  But not I. For the moment the book arrived and I read the first paragraph, I breathed a huge sigh of pleasure, set aside the book I was already on, and set down to enjoy this one. And enjoy it I did, not least because it took me back to my own country and almost my own generation, and the heroine (Serena Frome, to rhyme with "plume," a bishop's daughter, mediocre mathematician, and avid reader) might easily have been the kind of girl I knew at Cambridge. Only luckier in love than I; a fairly active social life culminates in an affair with an older don who grooms her for the security services, and before we know it, she has been accepted as a very junior clerk in MI5. Having recently been disappointed by Simon Mawer's Trapeze, about a similarly sheltered girl recruited as a spy, I was deeply pleased that McEwan seemed to be doing it right. 
 But this is 1970 or so, the waning years of the Cold War, not WW2, and the mission that Serena is eventually given is cultural rather than military. She is to recruit a promising young writer named Tom Healy whose political views may make him a useful ally in the propaganda battle against the Soviets. I am sure one could raise all sorts of objections to this rather flimsy plot, but the moral focus of the novel soon shifts to the personal rather than the political level, as Serena falls in love with Tom, despite her own misgivings about having to lie to him. 
 So we have a political novel (with a painfully accurate portrait of Britain in one of its darkest postwar periods) as an underlay to an somewhat more interesting one about people and their feelings, the roles they play, and the lies they tell. But there is an even more significant layer laid on top of that: this is a novel about writers and the writing process, and in the end this will be the dominant theme. I must admit to some disappointment when I realized this; surely a writer has better subjects than the lint in his own navel? But the subject alone need not spell failure; instead of following the self-centeredness of Howard Jacobson's recent Zoo Time, might McEwan not reach the brilliance of Mario Vargas Llosa's 
 Aunt Julia and the Scriptwriter 
 ? 
 And to a large extent he does. Serena reads several wonderfully inventive stories by Tom Healy which, even in compressed form, are worth the price of the book alone. The writer is clearly a genius, and so even more clearly is the writer behind the writer, McEwan himself. Readers familiar with his other work will note many echoes here of the author's previous novels. For McEwan is writing about the alchemy of writing itself, and the way an author must steal from life and even betray it in order to turn it into art. In the end, he will borrow a device from yet another of his novels, and there will be many who criticize him for it. But I found the ending intriguing and warmly satisfying. I did not mind sacrificing the logic of the spy story, or even the reality of some of the characters, if what I gained was the greater authenticity of a master of his craft exploring the magic of his own mastery.

Embassytown is the god-drug EzRa and I am a helpless Ariekei in thrall to it. China Mieville is a master dealer of an irresistible drug-cocktail depicting alien languages and consciousnesses, galactic politicking, revolutions, personal involvement and loyalty, and a unique world filled with wonder and mystery. 
 I was pretty cautious to read Embassytown after loving Perdido Street Station, admiring The Scar from a distance, and not getting past the halfway-point of Iron Council. None of his books are the same, which works in both good ways and bad. 
 Well, it only took the first couple pages to know this book is a winner. With deft and minimal brush strokes he establishes an alien environment worthy of the term "alien", and proceeds to introduce a species that speaks a unique Language that can only express literal truth. 
 Many others have written far more eloquent reviews of the story (particularly Nataliya, Arielle, and Ben Babcock), so I won't go into details, but suffice to say this book blew me away and reminded my why I love science fiction so much. The sense of wonder and originality here was in full force, in a genre where almost every idea would seem to have been done to death already. And yet there were innumerable moments that recalled The Left Hand of Darkness, Dune, Solaris, and the Miyazaki animated film Nausicaa during the climatic final assault by the Absurd). 
 It's a no-brainer that a story whose central plot revolves about language will quickly engage the imagination of readers if done right, and as the son of a linguist who has heard much about grammar and syntax growing up without understanding it fully, I was thrilled to see a book where similes and metaphors where driving forces in the narrative. 
 In short, this book has restored my faith in the ability of sufficiently-skilled storytellers to pen original works that really take readers for a ride. Thank you, I extend both my fanwings and giftwings in gratitude!

Like many readers, I had mixed feelings about this book (which I read as an audiobook). In fact, I'm pretty sure that those mixed feelings were what Hamilton intended to invoke with her writing. 
 One thing I did like about Hamilton's writing was the way I reacted to and envisioned things from her descriptions: the house she grew up in, her kitchen at Prune, the crumbling Italian villa she stayed in. 
 There are other descriptions of things she's felt or experienced that definitely dragged me along with her emotionally (her account of attending a CIA conference, especially the early morning I left my sleeping child for this?  musings)... 
 She's also, at least in her middle age, an over-thinker of her thoughts and experiences, which I identify with. And again, she drags us along with her, in her emotional choices about relationships with her mother, with her spouse, with her family. She's brutally honest, but she keeps us on the edge of our seats wondering what will happen next. 
 Now, that's a blessing and a curse. I now feel like I know Too Damn Much about Hamilton's inner life. About her opinions and all the things she's a complete bastard about. As a teenager, she made some really dodgy decisions that tripped my [well I came from a screwed up family and I never did that crap] judgy prude circuit in; as an adult, she describes her choices in her major adult relationship in a way that makes me want to scream both "What were you thinking?!" and "O my god you wrote this down and published it, someday your kids will hate you forever!" There's a hell of a lot about that relationship, too, and exactly how and why it's effed up. 
 And you may notice that my review is about emotions, not about cooking. This is no Bourdain memoir, how-I-got-to-be-a-chef. This is a memoir about how-my-fucked-up-relationship-with-cooking-and-cooking-for-others-led-me-to-be-a-chef. I have no doubt she's a good chef; if she wasn't, her restaurant Prune wouldn't still be around. I can go online and read her menus, and read what she says about what she cooks, and be pretty sure I'd like her food. I read her description of working the egg station at brunch and have a visceral notion of what that's like; I can read her description of running a restaurant-while-38-weeks-pregnant and have a much clearer image of that than either BOURDAIN ANTHONY or Heat: An Amateur's Adventures as Kitchen Slave, Line Cook, Pasta-Maker, and Apprentice to a Dante-Quoting Butcher in Tuscany give me. But still, it's mostly about what's in her head. 
 And that made this book fascinating, and also a pain. It wasn't the self-conscious boy-was-I-dumb-then of The Pioneer Woman: Black Heels to Tractor Wheels but I'm not sure I would ever want to sit next to this woman on a train, or be her friend. Sit around on the back stoop of a cooking gig smoking cigarettes and listening to people bullshit-- okay, I could do that. But if I met her in real life, I'd figure she was judging me as inadequate to her own screwed up standards; and if I were her friend, I'd want to punch her half the time. 
 So, yeah. This book drew me in and made me react. And it had lots of good mentions of food, even though there was too much lamb. And I half sympathized/identified with and half judged the author. What else can I say? I didn't fall in love with this memoir. I'm not sure I'll ever re-read it. but I will never, ever forget it, and some of the scenes are now part of the furniture of my mind.

When I found this book I was looking for a book about teenage parents. But what this book gave me was a whole lot more. 
 Corabelle and Gavin went through something that no couple should have to go through: seven days after their son, Finn, was born they had to turn off the ventilator that was keeping him alive. They were seventeen, and it was prom night. Two days later, during the funeral, Gavin walked out and never returned, leaving Corabelle to cope with the loss of their son alone. 4 years later, by chance, Corabelle and Gavin arrive to the same astronomy class and they find that love they long thought was lost is still as strong as ever. 
 However both Gavin and Corabelle hid secrets that could very much hurt the other, and it is because of these secrets that they are unable to move on from their pasts. 
 Corabelle is a shell of her former self, she lost her son and the love of her life so she immerses herself in school, a welcome distraction from all thats missing in her life. Gavin meanwhile has spent the past four years living with the mistake of walking out on his sons funeral. He has no one, and he wants no one, scared of getting close to anyone and having to feel again. 
 The author did a very good job of writing Gavin and Corabelle as equally suffering individuals after losing their son. Corabelle was much more emotional about and definately showed it more, but you can see in Gavin's POV just how much he struggles every single day with the loss, even four years later. 
 With some extremely emotional '4 years earlier' flashbacks which include the birth and death of Finn this is a story full of love and tragedy.
That was an emotional rollercoaster.

 An Ember in the Ashes is a fast paced novel with dual perspectives, and great characters. The book is set in a dystopian world where many are oppressed and enslaved, and the author does not shy away from any of the horrors these people would have suffered. 
 Truthfully, I think Laia should have failed more. As an inexperienced spy, with no background when it comes to stealth or fighting, I didn't expect her to succeed in ways that she did. In my opinion, Laia was a horrible spy: too trusting towards people (revealing her entire story to Cook--Cook threatened her, but Laia didn't even think about fabricating a story or keeping some facts hidden, such as being the daughter of the ex-leaders of the Resistance) and made plans that should've gotten her killed if she wasn't the main protagonist. In the end, she held a knife to Mazen, devised and executed a prison break, and escaped the clutches of the Commandant. A couple feats she could've pulled off as someone with practically no fighting experience, but all of that? Seemed a little unrealistic to me. 
 This wasn't to say that Laia's character was completely unbelievable. I enjoyed the parts where she mourned her weaknesses and lack of courage. Many YA novels have strong, female leads so it was refreshing to see a main character who starts off with no strength but develops them later. 
 I really enjoyed the two perspectives in the book. Since each perspective did not immediately start when one ended, the reader is given a little bit more knowledge of what's going to happen when they start a new chapter. It gives a little bit of suspense and anticipation, especially when I thought Laia was going to get caught as a spy, which was great for the book. I think I liked reading Laia's perspective more, mainly because I liked reading about Izzi and Cook more than the Trials. 
 I don't like love triangles as a general rule, so I wasn't too fond of the love triangle (square?) that existed in the book. From the start, it was predictable: each time a character met their potential love interest(s), there was extra detail to their physical appearance. Personally, I felt like anything that could have been connected to lust sort of was (Elias kept thinking about how beautiful Helene and Laia were, even though he immediately scolded himself for such thoughts afterwards), which I guess that goes to show you what males are always thinking about--another aspect that the author did not shy away from. It was also hard for me to ship anyone since none of the characters were living a sort of lifestyle that gave them freedom to love. 
 I'm a little disappointed that Elias understood his "freedom" after his Fourth Trial, where he refused to kill Laia. I get why his actions in the Third Trial prevented him from learning his freedom and that the Fourth did, but I found it unfair to Elias' classmates and friends. They died, grown up with and known Elias for years, but Elias only understands what true freedom is after he sacrifices his life for a girl he's only known for a short while. 
 I really enjoyed Cook's character, especially when she called Laia out on her inexperience when it came to suffering as a slave. She conveyed the hardships of a slave clearly, something that Laia has underestimated in her several weeks of being one. I have a feeling Cook might have done something to betray the Resistance years ago, but not intentionally, which may have inadvertently caused Laia's parent's deaths, especially her father's. I really want to know what her real name is. 
 The moment when Elias says they should have killed Marcus instead of rendering him unconscious, I literally screamed. I felt like Elias was so dumb for not killing Laia, because Marcus becoming Emperor sounds like the worst thing ever. Of course, this needed to happen for plot, but Marcus as Emperor and Helene his Blood Shrike--at his mercy each second--is something I'm scared of reading in the next book. 
  
 Overall, the Ember in the Ashes is fantastic book with amazing, detailed plot and great character dynamics. I loved the interactions between each character, and the deep past each one carries. I'm curious to learn more about the Augurs--their powers, history, and dreams. Excited to read the next book to find out more about all these characters.

Everyone accused her of expecting nothing but perfection from everyone, but there is no evidence of this in her interactions with her family. None of her questions are intrusive; she is trying to reach out to her children, like they supposedly want, and they reject her time after time. 
 I do get that part of this is about a mother who has made mistakes, because parenting is frigging hard. I did think that the mother needed to understand that she did NOT know her children like she thought she did. She clung to her version of Naomi to a really unhealthy degree. But I don't think I appreciated how hard parenting is until I read this book. Damned if you do, damned if you don't. I don't know though, it just felt really unfair to me. I don't believe for a second that it's the mother's fault little miss princess ran away.  
 Anyway, very deep, moving novel. I love the raw emotion throughout. I love the carrying on of themes throughout. Very well written, very heart-wrenching. Beautifully crafted.
