Wow! This was so absolutely terrible! Why do you always polarise me Gaiman? Sometimes I love what you do and at other times I absolutely hate it. I just have no middle ground with you. 
 Gaiman subverted the standard fairy-tale so much that his ending, one that was clearly meant to be surprising, was so blatantly obvious to the point of actually being mundane. I called this one from the get go. Certainly, some of the changes he makes are, indeed, praiseworthy. We have a gallant hero, one ready to wake the sleeping beauty. So to spice things up a bit Gaiman makes the hero a woman. This was a good move, but nothing overly remarkable. It's been done before, and will be done again. By reversing such things, the story that followed was easy to predict; it was just the opposite of what you'd normally expect to see. I yawned through the entire thing. 
 Now the artwork was undeniably wonderful, but this story doesn't deserve it. . The plot is simple at best, and the final ending just doesn't deliver what it needed to. It relies on its reversal so much. It was disappointing as a story, and not worthy of being in an edition like this by itself. It was weak, so weak. There's no time for anything to develop, and the eventual villain that revealed itself was practically an overdone caricature. There's so little to this. I actually have nothing else to say because there is not much else here to criticise. It's like the bear bones of a story. Gaiman can do so much better than this.

As a reader, this is immensely satisfying even when one is not a fantasy fan. The style is legendesque - you know, like a ballad or beowulf or something - which is not my cup of tea but LeGuin is so deft that it becomes easy to read almost immediately.

Ok, to start, I avoided this series in the beginning. I kept on feeling it was going to be a Harry Potter clone, but with Greek mythology. It wasn't until the movie came out I decided to check it out. Once I saw the movie, I was glad I didn't, as the movie was boring and a bit off. Turns out, the movie was a terrible adaptation, but at time, I had no clue. Then, the second movie came out, and I thoroughly enjoyed it. It was only then, that I gave this book series a real chance. And boy, was I glad I did. Not only are the books better, but they added a lot of humor and awesome mythology, a subject I have always been interested in. After I have finished the first series, I can say with full confidence, this is not a Harry Potter clone and deserves a full 4 out of 5 stars. 
 Disclaimer, it has been a while since I read this series, so forgive me if my memory is not up to par. 
 The Story 
 Percy Jackson is a "troubled child." At least by public school standards. He has ADHD and is dyslexic. Often has difficultly adapting to school life. Turns out, he is this way for a reason. He is a demigod, half Greek God/human. With this discovery, his mom tries to protect him by having him go to a Half-Blood camp. Percy, his best friend and his mom set out for the camp. However, right before he arrives, they are attacked by a Minotaur. His mother, gone. Now, he must learn about this camp and find a way to save his mother. All the while, a war is brewing between the Gods for a missing artifact of Zeus's. It is said, Percy stole it. He, with his new friends, must set out for a quest to find the artifact and prove his innocence before its too late. 
 If there is one thing I can give Rick Riordan high praise for without question, it is his attention and detail within his books to the original Greek Mythologies. He creates this world remaining true to the mythology, yet adding to it to make a believable modern day twist. I love it. The only complaint, compared to later books, this story is a bit slower and there is a lot of new information presented regarding the world, but that is a issue with almost all fantasy novel series. 
 The Characters 
 For personal preface, I like older characters in stories. With the unique sense of humor and voice Percy has, it made up for it. He is written very well and I love to hear everything. The only real issue is once again, the other character play out similar to the story. Starts off a bit slow and difficult to really get attached to during this book. FYI, changes in book 2 and throughout the rest of the series. The highlight in this book is the character building based off of the Greek Mythology and Percy Jackson himself. He is awesome! 
 The Writing 
 Clever and humorous. Makes this a very easy book to read and lose yourself in. Only issue, the slower pacing with the world building, but its excusable. 
 Overall 
 A great start to a great series. I am amazed at how easily I got sucked into this world and how much consistency the world created with reality. It really added to the effect that all this could be happening right now. I love it when books do that as well as this one has. Bravo! 
 Spoilers! 
 My only real complaint is the demigod classification system in the Half-blood camp. Percy was so water based in his powers, why did he need to be claimed to be considered a son of Poseidon? I don't like that part.

 While I think from just reading the summary, most people know they are not walking into a completely black and white, good vs evil, story. You know that it will be somewhere in between, that there is a lot of gray area in this story. And boy was it ever. 
 Brom took this fairytale and crafted such a complex, dark story of two sides who essentially want the same thing, but both going about their own misguided way of doing it, doing what they feel they need to do to survive and win. And while Peter's side is arguably the right side, the other side led by The Captain (and "led" is used loosely here because the Captain actually came to be a likable, competent character who is helpless against greater forces at work) isn't as simple and as evil as you'd think they'd be. 
 Wonderful book. I expected a very dark tale, but I didn't expect to get so emotionally invested in the story of Peter, his Devils (the Lost Boys), Avalon (Neverland), or the flesh-eaters (the Captain and his crew). I shed more than a few tears and laughs with this book. Brom weaved such a wonderful world to explore. I wished the story would've gone and followed them more after their big battle, but then again, I'm glad Brom allowed my imagination to decide what happens next.

Summary: 
 When Will's parents die, he takes over his father's job as an assistant Monstrumologist. A job that entails dark stormy nights, blood, gore, and creatures that are the stuff of myths and legends. When a gravedigger finds evidence that New Jerusalem may have an infestation of monsters, he brings the evidence to the doctor Will serves. What they find will haunt your dreams and lead Will on an adventure that will take him into the bowels of the earth. 
 Review: 
 A friend recommended this book to me, I know she loved it. While I can appreciate the writing, and the gruesome horror of the book, I really had a hard time getting into this book. Maybe it was the topic, maybe I wasn't in the mood, or maybe the book just wasn't for me. I can't be sure, but I will say it wasn't a favorite. 
 I liked Will our young protagonist, but hated the doctor--that is until another character came along who earned my complete animosity and made the doctor look good by comparison. Yancey's characters are very well drawn, and some so deplorable in their moral standards that I felt myself physically disgusted by them. It is a sign of a great writer, when you find yourself really wanting to slap (or in some cases feed them to a monster) the characters of his novel. 
 The settings were well drawn and the book really sets a mood that is reminiscent of classic horror literature. It was dark and stormy and what they were doing was even darker. Yancey, completely pulls you into his world and makes you squirm. He certainly knows how to make gore come alive on the page. 
 The pacing of this novel is pretty quick, but the details can slow you up a bit. Only a short amount of time passes from the beginning of the book to the events in the final chapters, but so much happened in that short amount of time that it felt longer. 
 Audiobook Review: 
 The audiobook for this novel was produced by Recorded Books and read by Steven Boyer who does a fine job with the narration. The CD book is well done, but there is nothing remarkable about it that sets it apart from other audiobooks out there. It is a pleasant way to experience the book. I had trouble starting this novel, so the audio kept me going, I probably wouldn't have finished the book without it. The CD book consists of 10 CDs and while it wasn't the longest book I have read, it felt pretty long to me. 
 Overall: 
 While this book is extremely well written, I didn't find myself really getting into the book until the very end. I don't know if I am curious enough to move on to book two in this series, only time will tell. Overall though, I think readers who like creepy books with lots of gore, and violence will find this book to be very interesting. 
 Cautions for Sensitive Readers: 
 Violence and gore--lots of it.

 I have to thank my friend Corey for giving me the kick in the arse I apparently needed to finally begin THE ABERCROMBIE! I had bought The First Law trilogy boxset three years ago for my birthday & it has sat on my nightstand since then. Readgret, indeed! I owned Half a King also, because I knew Abercrombie was going to be an author I loved. Corey told me how much he loved the Shattered Sea trilogy & that he knew I would fall for Thorn Bathu (I DID), so I moved it up my priority tbr. 
 I ended up devouring it! In saying that, I had a feeling that I was going to like The First Law series even more. 
 This is an epic fantasy. I mean, that gets thrown a lot, doesn't it? Epic fantasy. But this truly is. Abercrombie writes with such complexity, but an engaging one. The plot does take some time. I am a fan of the slow burn, so I didn't find this an issue. Every page cannot just all be kill kill fight sex. The real talent lies in the dialogue, in the plotting of interesting scenes, of setting up something that will affect something else later down the road. Worldbuilding is the most important thing, in my opinion. Abercrombie just.. he fucking gets it. Building an epic universe takes time. 
 However, this isn't just a meandering masterpiece, either. There is bloodshed, betrayal & brutality; subtle, dark humor interspersed throughout; & truly heartwarming, tender moments. Rather than be yet another cliche of the genre, Abercrombie takes something & just runs with the details. He bends the genre to his will. Good things come to those who wait.. & if you weren't already enamored, those last 100 pages are worth the buildup. They are everything. HOT DAMN. 
 Abercrombie knows how to create a new world, but he also knows how to write a damn good character. There are such a wide variety of loathsome assholes within this. And yet.. despite themselves, I found the characters likeable. Damaged, cynical, downright despicable & yet endearing. You can't help but root for them! 
 I cannot wait to see what is in store for FERRO MALJINN, Logen, Glokta (I fucking love his brilliant character), Jezal, Ardee, Bayaz.. they truly make this story. 
 Nine out of ten fingers!

A noticeable improvement over its predecessor, because it's largely a standalone book that tells its own, more personal story, rather than the all-over-the-place madness of Mr. Mercedes. However, it's not entirely standalone - if not for the events of Mr. Mercedes, this book probably wouldn't happen as it does. And it seems that, with the epilogue, we're setting up a third book that'll be more dependent on Book 1 than on Book 2, in a way similar to The Dark Knight Saga. 
 And as for the story in this book - even the dust jacket immediately compares it to Misery, but this one does a much better job. I couldn't stand Misery at all - I barely made it a hundred pages into that one. But this story was much better able to keep me interested in the tale of the crazed fan, especially since he kills his favorite author off right in the prologue, rather than spend an entire book torturing him like in Misery. 
 Pete was a favorite character of mine too, mostly because of the fact that, like me, he intends to major in English and also has an interest in libraries. I'm also the opposite of Pete, though, in that I'm taking the major to bolster my career as a writer, whereas Pete doesn't think he could be a writer himself. 
 I hope the third book manages to ride the high of this one - especially since Mr. King is setting up a possible paranormal spin, based on the epilogue I just finished reading. :)

Good Story #28. Scott finally admits to Julie that he's a digient. Julie knew it all along. 
 ========= 
 I cannot believe I never mentioned this book on Goodreads since it completely blew me away when I read it originally, back when it was being distributed for people to read before Hugo voting. 
 Here's part of a Ted Chiang column I wrote that dealt with this novella.After the zoo she worked at closes, animal specialist Ana Alvarado is hired as a trainer/psychologist to care for a group of "digients," virtual pets designed for a virtual-reality world. These pets have artificial intelligence and the ability to develop personalities and wills as they interact with their owners. Derek Brooks designs the avatars for the digients. Ana and Derek each adopt some digients which--as they grow up--become relevant characters. The story is told in small vignettes spaced several months or a year apart. Thus readers get to see the developmental dynamics of the digients and their owners over time. When the virtual-reality-pet fad fades, Ana and Derek struggle to find ways to keep their digients functioning and growing. 
 The reader can easily extrapolate this to our computer-and-video-game-obsessed culture. What Chiang does, however, is set up parallels between the humans' development and the digients' development. Ana and Derek's efforts are not only about maintaining the virtual environment, but also nurturing their digients' needs as growing, developing life forms. We become aware that the fallible humans in the story also have "software" that is developing. The reader identifies with themes of personal growth, parenthood, and families. Questions about artificial intelligence crossing the line into true life--lived for its own sake--lead to reflection about creation and creator, free will and existing "outside of time," as well as access to the "tree of knowledge." 
 Chiang's latest work may be his most accessible and also may be the entry that tempts readers into his other short stories, all of which are richly rewarding. It is a short work but one that repays the time spent a hundred-fold.FINAL 
 I'm so glad that Scott chose this book and that made me reread it. I remembered the struggles and frustration, but I had forgotten the triumphant celebration of what it means to be humans, to be parents, to love and to want the best for those we love which Chiang included in this book. 
 How does Chiang do this? What a genius!
Fables all about how people are assholes, except that the people are played by animals. Clever but ugly.

It's the book's saving grace and why I'm giving this 2 stars. I just had enough, I guess. I wanted that giddy-in-love feeling. That happy sigh I always get after reading Colleen Hoover books.  I picked this book up because I'd read Westerfeld's amazing Uglies series and was hoping for more. While I didn't get exactly what I was looking for, The Secret Hour was a new and fascinating read. 
 The first half of The Secret Hour is rather slow. The premise of the story and the idea of a twenty-fifth hour definitely had me intrigued, but it wasn't until I reached the middle of the book that I was really captivated. It seemed like everything improved from then on- the characters, the story, the writing, everything. 
 This novel is extremely plot driven and picks up pace as the story progresses. It was a quick read and the ending left me hanging. I'm dying to know what happens next. 
 The thing that bugged me the most about the story was the lack of character development. Westerfeld uses third person and never really expands on any of the main characters. I was never really able to identify with Jessica or her friends. I did see potential, though. I'm hoping that Westerfeld adds more to the characters' personalities in the next two books. I'd also like to see a little more of the romance between Jessica and Jonathon, but that's just me. :) 
 Despite the few things I picked on, I did enjoy this book. Needless to say, I'll be hunting down the rest of the books in the series.

This is by far one of the best books I've read in the New Adult genre so far. I have read quite a few New Adult that took threw two characters together, wrote lots of sex, but forgot all about those pesky storylines that tend to be troublesome when the characters are not having sex. Ms. Aubrey, you have raised the bar for the genre with a perfectly told story. 
 Mia was a great character. I connected immediately. This girl is a blogger and a video game enthusiast. She's also a student, premed, who is struggling to pay for her schooling and to take care of her basic needs (as a ex college student, I know how bad that sucks). The highlight of her week is when her group gets together for game night. She has a best friend who truly cares for her and a mother who is her world. She's doing almost alright. What this girl and I have in common is the inability to ask for help. I felt her struggles as if they were my own. 
 So, the whole selling her virginity online. I had my doubts when I read the book description. Turns out, it was so much better than what I was thinking about. It was more than a story about a girl who wanted to show the world that she was worth more than the price tag they put on her. Mia's desperate attempt at trying to help out those she loves makes her go to extremes. She hides behind this manifesto, one she really does believe in, in order to her family. Mia's love runs deep and I enjoyed seeing it. 
 And the biggest reason to read? Adam Drake. Okay, so the whole who is Adam Drake was a bit predictable, but still charming. This guy! What a hottie! Not only is he hot, he also has the rags to riches story that will tug at the heart strings. He's a rich CEO, but he's more down to earth than Mia realizes at first. I loved the guy. He's a charmer. He charmed me from the very beginning. 
 If you are looking for a good New Adult book without the watered down story covered in sex, this is the book for you.

Here's a tidbit about me: I love AMC's The Walking Dead. I have followed every season through all the horror, group dynamics, and even the boring episodes. I can watch zombies kill and be killed all day long...but when it comes to people violently killing people on the show? OMG my stomach turns. Ahem Negan. 
 Blake Crouch's Run has that same quality about it. People have been "affected" by something that causes them to target the "unaffected". Target meaning kill...brutally. It's not zombie-related or a viral illness, but it's definitely of pandemic, apocalyptic proportions all the same. It's insanity that makes perfect sense to the ones branding the weapons and that psychotic element made this book fit the horror genre to a T. 
 Run is the absolute perfect title for this book. It's fast paced (like can't-catch-your-breath fast) and the suspense is intense. The horror consists of the overall situation obviously but also very graphic and violent scenes of people killing people in a variety of ways. No remorse, no hesitation. Just killing. And one family is on the run, trying their hardest to all stay alive. 
 I ended this book with a few unanswered questions, but they were questions that the main characters never got answers to either so I could accept that. I have to admit that the wife/mother in this family got on my last nerve with her helplessness and putting constant pressure on her husband for everything. Seriously! Get your @ss up, work your brain, and at least help out with some problem solving solutions, but no. However, without spoiling the ending, she did redeem herself in a big way and I was not conflicted at all by her decision. I was standing there, eyebrow cocked, hands on hips, tapping my foot, thinking it's about d@mn time! 
 Blake Crouch told this story through the 3rd-person POV of the male lead character (the father/husband) who was provided a stereotypical, although fairly dated, gender role with the need to protect/provide in order to feel validated and strong. This character element created that much more suspense as you feel the internal pressure he places on himself (not counting the pressure his wife is bombarding him with) as well as everything that is at stake for his family. 
 "There was simply nothing in his experience that even compared with the thrill of killing to protect his family. In this moment, it was the purpose of his existence. He felt, possibly for the first time in his life, like a f@cking man." 
 I was glued to this book. Blake Crouch has his own goodreads shelf on my profile and he has not disappointed me yet. Whether it's Run or one of his others, seriously check him out!!

***ARC received from NetGalley in exchange for an honest review. I'm between 3.75 and 4 stars on this one. I didn't read it and think throughout "OMG I love this" but writing this review I remember the slow burn and slow development of the relationship and how it just worked for me. 
 Ponzi scheme, wife has no clue, wife loses husband, money, job, everything. Cam goes back home to live with her parents and lick her proverbial wounds. Offered a short-term job being the nanny/teacher for a young boy under the temporary care of his uncle, Calvin. 
 Cam makes me laugh. She's angry and bitter (understandable but not over the top miserable) but she's a fighter and won't back down from life or grumpy Calvin. She loves teaching and her interactions with Sam are what a great teacher is. A strong heroine not afraid of life but a little wary yet hopeful of the future. 
 Calvin. What's not to like about a star QB whose sexy and who takes care of his sister's son when she has to go to rehab. Calvin is the proverbial rock for his family since childhood and continues that role. He's also one of the grumpiest heroes you'll read about. If anybody deserved a kick in the ass by a heroine multiple times it was Calvin. Sexy but not a nice guy and a bit of a tool to be honest. 
 Slowly the iceberg that is Calvin starts melting and starts shifting toward Cam (and Sam who he's kept at an emotional distance). No insta love craziness here but a slow development of a tenuous friendship. Slowly start adding in some chemistry and emotional bonding and it's a nice romantic read. I almost forget what a d*ck Calvin was when he first met Cam. It's nice to see the layers peeled back from a hero and watch him slowly fall in love with his family and a woman.

Have you ever watched a movie and wanted to scream at the characters on the screen? That's how I felt reading Dark Matter. Crouch writes a fast paced and gripping story, but I'm not sure if he intentionally wrote his characters to be infuriating or not. For a character that is supposed to be a college professor, Jason Dessen can be pretty dense. 
 Dark Matter deals with what might be unfamiliar concepts, but you don't really need to know anything about quantum physics to enjoy it. The whole superposition of an object nonsense just provides a nice hand-wave explanation for how we get to world jumping. If you spend too much time thinking about what Crouch proposes as serious science, I think you'll get fuming mad and maybe not enjoy the story. So switch off your brain for a bit and just accept it. In fact, accept a lot of the truly ludicrous decisions the main character makes. 
 Crouch has written a very fast-paced thriller that will keep you turning pages. That should be evident from my one-week read time, which is a big improvement from some of the other books I've read this year. This is one of the few sci-fi books that I feel like I can recommend outside of my group of sci-fi reading friends. 
 If you've read the book, expand this spoiler section for more of my thoughts. 
  
 Jason Dessen is an idiot. He takes entirely too long to come around to the idea that he's found himself in an alternate world when this was the work he started his career in. I get that this might not be the first assumption that the average Joe would jump to, but when the cover jacket alludes to world jumping we don't need to wait until page 100 for our protagonist to have his a-ha moment. 
 If that weren't bad enough, his behavior once he starts using cube really cements it. Don't even get met started on the cube, either. It generates a field of non-observation? When a human is in it a drug prevents them from observing, but they can still look out the door? And write notes? And see other people running around inside? Does it require power? How is it just sitting in the middle of nowhere in this apocolyptic universes? Did it just poof into existence as they entered the world? Why not poof into existence to a world on a slightly different orbit and you wind up in space somewhere? 
 Dang, I got started on the cube. What was I saying? Oh, right, Jason is an idiot. When he opens the door to an alternate world that is clearly an apocalypse, what does he choose to do? Shut the door and try again like a sensible person would? No, he chooses to go exploring. For what exactly we don't know. He repeats this again and again. Then we learn they can pilot the cube to a particular world if they just hold in their mind what it would be like. So....why not hold in your mind that you want to go to a world where an alternate world Jason2 has taken over your life? No, that just wouldn't make for a good chase. So instead we have them thinking of the past prior to being abducted. 
 Jason may be insufferable, but the other characters aren't much better. Why was Amanda so motivated to help? It felt like there should have been some better motivation than "these folks are crazy and absolutely anything is better than here". She plays such a passive role. I wish she had figured more prominently rather than simply falling for Jason, then moving on to some other universe. None of the characters have much depth. Charlie, Daniela, Amanda, Ryan....this book is not big on developing characters but instead focuses on the action. 
 I did enjoy the switch of perspective from first-person to third-person after Jason1 is abducted. Any scene with Jason1 remained first-person while scenes with Jason2 were third-person, which was a clever trick to reinforce that we're not dealing with the same character anymore. 
  
 I'd definitely recommend Dark Matter to anyone, but not as a serious sci-fi read. Instead, it's a great, fast-paced thriller that you shouldn't think too much about.

 I started this book last night when I realized most everything I have been reading this week were re-reads of some of my favorite books. Not a bad thing, but I really wanted something new. Nothing new has jumped out at me for awhile but this book has gotten almost ridiculously high ratings and glowing reviews so I figured I'd see what all the hub-bub was about. And yup, I can now see why readers have been enjoying this book. The main characters are likable, even the gruff, kick-'em-from-his-bed-ASAP Luke! The story is simply engaging. A bonus for those wishing for an easy vacation read, the conflict isn't all that intense or heavy, and the angst level is maybe about a five out of ten. If you're looking for an easy read with drama that manages to keep your interest even if it is onlyslightly dramatic this is a perfect choice. 
 My only real complaint is about the characters. If you're looking for unique characters you'll be a bit disappointed. Luke is the Standard Manwhore Romance Hero who starts out wanting only one night (or should I say one hour?) stands, only to fall hard for Dominic, who is the Standard Snarky Romance Hero whose easygoing nature and irreverent humor hide a somewhat insecure nature, all qualities that work to tame Luke. The teens in the book are also sort of Standard Book Teens. Either troubled and acting out while looking for acceptance or well-behaved trying to support their friend while they too look for acceptance. Dominic's parents are stereotypical Staten Island Residents, old-school from the Neighborhood, his Proud Dad's already verbally abusive nature only escalating as business problems become overwhelming. And finally, we round out the cast of characters with Dominic's Everyone Just Needs To Get Along Mom, who his dad wants to treat like glass and she just wants everyone to be happy. 
 Yet regardless of the not-so-original characterizations found here, I didn't care. I liked this book! I have come to realize over the years of reading that books don't always have to be sophisticated or terribly clever to still be thoroughly entertaining. Sometimes recognizable characters aren't boring, but are instead comforting. 
 And honestly? Sometimes, I just need to remember that not every reader has hundreds of books on their Read shelf, and therefore I need to forget about characters or tropes I find to be a tad bit overdone, and instead I need to pay attention to how many times I find myself smiling or laughing out loud while reading the book. 
 Oh, and as for the romance part of this book... 
 Well, their smokin' hot chemistry didn't hurt one bit.

 I feel like this took me a year to finish. 
 I think I'm falling out of love with MacLean's writing. Three books back to back that haven't worked is one too many for me. 
 This was way too melodramatic for me all around. The plot, the ever present overblown 'shameful secret' trope, the hero, the heroine, the writing. It's a 416 page book and it had no reason to be IMO. A good 100 pages could have easily been cut out. I mean I got to the half-way mark which felt more like the conclusion but there were 200 pages left. I think I whimpered at that point, out loud. 200 pages left of what exactly? The hero continuing to lament over and over again how he needs to tell his father the line ends with him (RME) and the heroine constantly having to remind herself that she can't stand the hero. Oy. Give it a rest. 
 I feel like I've been saying this a lot recently but it bears repeating. Dear Authors: The more you drag out a 'shocking reveal'? The bigger you make it, the bigger readers expectations will be. I'm sorry but King acting like a jaded rake for all the world simply because Daddy dearest ran off the milkmaid girl he fell in love with is not shocking or worthwhile IMO. Like...are you kidding me? That's it? He swore off love because of some adolescent misguided love? 
 Come on! Suck it up and grow up dude. I found this so weak and made the hero come off juvenile. And it certainly didn't excuse his arrogant, sad 'woe is me' behavior. 
 "She died inside the damn coach, at my hand." 
 No wonder he hated riding in coaches. "That's why you race the curricles," she said. "You pay your penance. You risk yourself." 
 "I told you that my father killed her. As though he put a pistol to her head." 
 She nodded, not knowing what to say. 
 "It wasn't his hate that put the pistol to her head. It was my love." 
 Shall I pass you your hanky now? 
 MacLean's writing is known for being on the dramatic side, with the constant breaks, the repetition (oh my gawd the REPETITION), and the overly dramatic internal monologues that boarder a 5 hour theater play and you are wondering when it will be over. Here it was twofold because you have a couple who have no chemistry and a plot that is so poorly executed and thin that the author's dramatic tone just screams off the page. 
 Yours. 
 He stayed with her until she returned to earth, to the labyrinth, Ariadne to his Minotaur, somehow able to destroy him with her touch. 
 Yours. 
 He would hear that word, spoken in her voice, for the rest of his life. 
 Yours. 
 Truth and utter lie all at once. 
 She couldn't be his, of course. She couldn't be his, because it would require him to be hers. It would require him to love her the way she deserved. And that would never happen. It was impossible. 
 The number of times we are reminded on every. freaking. page how the hero can't have her and she can never be his is ridiculous. Like....enough. The last 100 pages felt like a year. Because all that was left was regurgitating the same information over and over and over again. There was no rhyme or reason behind it because it added nothing to the plot. You have your main characters just sitting around in different rooms lamenting over which one should leave first and say goodbye, nothing else. For 100 DAMN PAGES. 
 And the dialogue is not smart. You have these two constantly bickering with the heroine counter-arguing & questioning the hero at every turn just to have the final say that she ends up sounding stupid. 
 "You should not bite the hand that feeds you," he said. 
 "Are you calling me a dog?" 
 I mean really? I didn't ask for this. If I wanted ludicrous juvenile sparring I wouldn't be reading Sarah MacLean. So yeah I'm annoyed. I remember that little cameo Lady Sophie made in Never Judge a Lady by Her Cover, the quiet, smart Wallflower who seemed witty and got to dance with the rakish handsome 'Lord E' (which turns out to be King), I was immediately intrigued. But what I got here makes me want to ask for a refund (of my time). 
 "Why not? They shan't be looking for me there." 
 It was likely the truth, but he'd had enough of this woman and the carelessness with which she lived her life. "Because you have a habit of getting shot on mail coaches." 
 "It wasn't on the coach." 
 Yes because that makes a world of difference. SMH. 
 And what's with all the lame monikers?...... 'Royal Rogue' 'Soiled S's' 'Dangerous Daughters'. Really MacLean? Soiled S's? 
 You can do better than that. 
 I honestly was gonna lambast the heroine once I finished this because she drove me insane a good 80% of the story but then things happened and my opinion changed. Only slightly. Sophie Talbot is the kind of bluestocking I abhor, she carries the sniffy 'I'm smarter than everyone' attitude that really gets under my skin. Yes the aristocracy are a bunch of snobbish sexist assholes, but the end of the day, a snob is a snob. I just found her haughty know-it-all judgmental attitude no better. There was just literally nothing at all to make me like this girl or empathize with when she kept acting like an indignant naive brat for a good portion of this. She doesn't like her aristocratic life so she decides to run away, back to her old country life not even thinking her plan through. But when she falls for the hopeless fool hero I started to feel sorry for her. I guess my biggest issue above all my other gripes is that I couldn't buy into the love between the MCs. Everything came off flat and half-approached. The hero King, I struggled to connect with entirely. He's probably the most underdeveloped flat Sarah MacLean hero I've read to date. I just didn't care for him and could not buy into this careless rake falling for the boring 'unfun' Talbot sister. How does one go about not caring at all about a girl, leaving her stranded at an Inn then suddenly rushing to save her and having the shakes over possibly losing her so quickly? This happens by Chapter 5. It just made everything following it weak and insincere. The character development and romance build up was super weak. 
 As for the next book, I'm not even sure I want to give it a try. The Scottish Duke of Werrick didn't rev my engine in here, he's a walking HR stereotype. The whole back thumping, cigar smoking, curricle racing with the chums I find so juvenile. You guys are in your 30s why the hell are you racing up and down London for?! Find a more interesting adult (sexy) hobby please. And the fact that the author felt she had to justify the hero's curricle racing as a 'penance' for his self-induced martyrdom punishment was just cringe-worthy. My eyes couldn't roll any harder. So yeah like I said...not MacLean's best.

4.25 stars. I've had this book on my Kindle for a long time, having downloaded it after so many of the OSRBC members gushed over it. 
 The madness in question is Asperger's. Ian has trouble looking people in the eye; can't tell a lie; has an eidetic memory; has otherworldly mathematical skills; and other issues. It's interesting to speculate how people from the 19th century would have reacted to someone like this. Ms. Ashley is probably accurate that such a person would be found insane. 
 Ian's father, the now-deceased Duke of Kilmorgan, strangled his wife in a rage, and his 12-year-old son Ian witnessed it. (BTW, it sounds like the Duke probably had borderline personality disorder with uncontrolled rages and narcissism.) He had Ian declares insane and committed to an asylum where he was subjected to the "treatments" of the period - such things are considered torture today. 
 When the old Duke died, Ian's oldest brother, Hart, took him out of the asylum. His brothers have taught him how to behave in society and he has learned how to control his rages. 
 Beth Ackerby's father was basically a con man; he married a gentleman's daughter, but when he died early, Beth and her mother went to an East End workhouse. Beth married the parish priest and was very happy and in love. But he died young as well, and Beth became a lady's companion. Fortunately, her employer was a kind woman and very fond of Beth - she left her home and fortune to Beth. 
 Beth becomes engaged to Sir Lyndon Mather, with whom Ian has had dealings. Ian knows he's really a snake after a fortune, so he contrives to meet Beth and warn her. He's immediately attracted to her and proposes. She rejects him, breaks off her engagement and goes to Paris. 
 Ian follows. So does a Scotland Yard Inspector who is convinced Ian is a murderer. Inspector Fellows warns Beth about Ian. 
 So that's the setup. I enjoyed the book SO MUCH! I loved Ian and his brothers - except I got irritated with Hart and his controlling ways. I loved Beth. 
 I'm not going to gush that this is the best romance ever. But it was a compelling love story and an intriguing mystery with fascinating characters and I will definitely read more of the series.

I looked up Apryl Baker's novels after I came across her name on the list of authors due to appear at this year's PennedCon. The book I read prior to this one, while fantastic, was also emotionally heavy resulting in the desperate need for a literary palette cleanser. 
 This novel was exactly that. It was sweet; it was sassy; and just the right amount of trashy. Nikoli is the king of one-night stands, Lily is the bookish modest girl that everyone loves. He can't have her so logically he has to try harder. She's in love with her best friend, Adam, but suffers from a phobia of being touched. They strike a deal - Nikoli will help her overcome her fears to get Adam and in exchange he gets her for a night. The catch is that he can't sleep with anyone for three months or she wins his beloved car. The rules are clear going into the deal - no attachment and they'll go their separate ways. But whoops - turns out they have a lot more in common that they thought and, uh oh, did they accidentally just fall in love? Well, hell, that wasn't how it was supposed to go. 
 This novel has a surprising amount going on for being a romance novel. Family issues, street races, online gaming, and serial killers just to name a few. Most of the subplots are addressed, but a few are left hanging or are unnecessary to include at all. But, at it's heart, this is first and foremost a romance novel, so I could overlook a few loose ends. 
 I truly enjoyed the interaction between Nikoli and Lily from start to finish. The author had a wonderful way of expressing the small things that a couple can do to really show love and appreciation without having sex. Were there sex scenes? Of course, this is labeled New Adult, what did you expect? But they were few with most of the romance happening through everyday interactions. By the end it seemed completely logical that the "manwhore" had reformed his wayward ways and the haphephobic girl was cured (albeit sometimes seeming a bit rushed). Lily was his perfect match - the Robin Scherbatsky to his Barney Stinson if you will (hopefully without the divorce which I still say was just bogus at the end of Season 9). Then again, I'm just a hopeless romantic; everyone should be happy in the end, right?

I will say that there were some truly beautiful passages in the book, which decided me on 3 stars rather than 2. In one scene  Catherine is sitting at lunch with her friend Susan, who suggests that Catherine sue her own mother. Catherine muses to herself, "...Who are you? And who does that make me?" (209).  Thus far, that was probably the most thoughtful and introspective we have seen Catherine be, and marks the beginning of a transformation, from spoiled, selfish, self-centered rich girl to a kinder, more thoughtful, spoiled, and loving rich girl. 
 On page 281, William and Catherine attend a church barbecue. After someone remarks that they are a cute couple "We smiled and held each other's clammy hands, posing for a picture no one was taking." I've been there! I've been in that relationship you are in not because of strong feelings of love or passion, but because that person meets the "check marks" on an unwritten list of qualities and traits a potential mate SHOULD have. Towards the end, after Catherine has evolved into a better person, she remarks that people's lives can be beautiful in the quietest ways, and already are. It seems like people tend to spend so much time trying to be a Catherine, Susan, or a William; we chase the money, power, or influence; our lives will be better after we buy that bag, those shoes, that house. Yet we are left feeling empty. Love and happiness has to come from within ourselves for it to be real, as Catherine is discovering by the end of the book. Take note of the small things, like the sky or a kind deed, in order to find happiness. 
 Glad I read this. I gave it 3 stars though because while Catherine did develop by the end, she still felt a little flat to me. Why, exactly, did  Dan fall in love with her?

I was not sure what to expect with this book as my 'relationship' with Holly Black's books .I really enjoyed her 'Modern Fairie tales' series but didn't like her "Curse workers" series. 
 I did enjoy The Coldest Girl in Coldtown, it was a quick enjoyable read with a dark tone to it. It was not your usually 'vampire teen novel and I was thankful for that. The vampires in this story are not nice, even the 'main' vampire Gavriel is very dark and slightly crazy. 
 The main protagonist of the book is Tana, she didn't have the easiest life but she is brave and honest which make her a good character to follow. 
 Holly does some flashback to explain some elements of the stories. Some of them did make sens and helped understand the characters and their actions better...Some just seems like fillers with no real purpose. 
 I also enjoyed the developing relationship between Tana and Gavriel, it really had its moment but I have to admit one of my main pet peeve is "instant love" between characters and it's exactly what happened here. Gavriel has been alive for about hundred years and yet he falls in love with Tana in like 3 days...I have to admit I did wince at that one. 
 The story is well written and flow nicely, the end managed to take me slightly by surprise but the plot is somehow a little empty...In a sense that, it is not a complicated story it is simplistic and there is nothing for you to 'guess' or try to figure, there is not any big reveal or huge plot lines that surprises you....except for the last little thing. 
 In conclusion: The Coldest Girl in Coldtown is an enjoyable quick read. If you like Vampire Teen fiction with an underlying Dark tone this book is for you, however don't expect to have to think too much because the storyline is quite simplistic and the plot rather sparse.

Will Wheaton was the perfect reader & is actually mentioned by his real name in the story. If you don't know who I'm talking about, then don't bother reading the book or this review. I don't think anyone who isn't into video games or a bit of an SF nerd will get much out of this. It's probably best if you grew up in the 80's, too. Those of us who are a bit older (OK, quite a bit. My kids grew up in the 80's.) but somewhat geeky will also love it. 
 This had it all - a dystopian world of the near future, social issues, a romance, & fantastic adventure, all set to a backdrop of an 80's geekfest. Early video games figure in prominently along with the music & movies of the decade; War Games, Rush, Star Wars, Zork, Joust, and Blade Runner. 
 My biggest complaint with the book was redundancy. Cline was too thorough about explaining everything & if there was any chance the idiot reader might not have grasped it the first time, he told me a second time. Drove me a little crazy at times. C'mon! This was a book for nerds. Anyone who can't remember how Joust works needs to play a game again. There's an online version here: 
 http://www.1980-games.com/us/old-game... 
 Seriously, that's just one of the sites that comes up. Most of these old games are free online, simply google it. 
 The book wasn't perfect. It had some issues with a variety of items & pulled off a few cheap shots in the story line. I didn't care much for the way his big infiltration was handled, for instance. Nor how H traveled around in the RV when the bus required a hit team  or some of the other tech details, but it was a fun romp. I just went with it & enjoyed. I actually kind of got several of the clues, like Captain Crunch, which made it even more fun.

Dark Eyes by William Richter was a solid three-star young adult read. There isn't too much I can say bad about this novel and conversely there isn't too much I can say great either, I am afraid. The Story follow, Wally (Valentina) from her life as an Orphan in Russia to her life on the streets of New York city where she is a runaway, squatting with friends in abandoned buildings. 
 This novel was riddled with typos but it is an ARC so I didn't judge on that at all. The book was well written in a voice that was pleasant and appropriate. This books voice was not at all "dumbed down" for the audience an I really appreciated that. The novel did skip, sporadicly, from one person's limited point of view to another's. I found that to be not only confusing but unnecessary and sometimes, a little boring too. 
 The characters were a bit flat. Especially Wally, who was hard to like. That is probably the number one reason I could so easily set this book down repeatedly and not come back to it for days. Wally is a spoiled rich kid who lives on the streets for seemingly no reason as she doesn't have the emotional scars as her friends. They are the only ones with any, albeit, small depth. I still don't understand Wally's need to run away from home in the first place. She was spoiled rotten and I found it hard to believe that this kid from a rich white family in New York city would suddenly be taken seriously as the leader of a gang of kids who came from violent and destitute situations. 
 There was a lot of mystery in this novel but I felt that everything happened to easily. Wally and her friends continually stumbled upon clues or figured things out just a bit to easily to be believable. Sometimes, the mysteries became so complex that there is not way Wally could have unraveled them so easily. The way some of the people in the story interconnected was just a bit too convenient for me.  For instance some man on Shutter Island just happens so keep a package around packed full of false information and newspaper clippings just in case Wally happened to come through his door? He just happened to know that this would eventually lead Wally to the most valuable stones in the world? Wally's childhood Psychologists had been a teacher at the institute where Wally's mother worker in Russia, really?  
 I also found everything in this novel a bit too predictable. I was disappointed when the big plot twist at the end was what I had assumed since pretty much the start of the novel. There weren't many surprises in this novel to me. Everything was so obvious from the get go that I really didn't have that wonderful moment of surprise not even once.  I Knew it! I knew right away that her mother would be the mother she had grown up with all along. There was too much foreshadowing about her "father" leaving and moving to a different state to start a whole new family. I knew that he probably wasn't the birth father and the wife was the birth mother. What was the sense of having Wally run away from home because she didn't feel loved by her real mother only to find out the one she ran away from was real all along and now that she's dying she's perfect and completed Wally's life. Wait...what???"  
 But the book isn't terrible and it's actually sort of enjoyable. It's just not one of those pick it up and never put it down till you are finished reads.

Start: 5 stars (awesome voice) 
 1/4: 4 stars (questionable content) 
 1/2: 3 stars (more questionable content) 
 3/4: 2 stars (is this going anywhere?) 
 Done: 1 star (fell flat) 
 But I'll up it to 2 because I did enjoy the book there for a little bit. 
 Pros: 
 1. When I started this book, I was excited by the strong, new voice. This author knew his character. You could tell right off the bat, that this kid had a personality and opinions. I loved it. I read quite a bit and you get used to the same kind of voice for characters. It's refreshing to come into something like this. 
 2. An unreliable narrator is always fun to read. It becomes a game of wits between the author and the reader. (Now, I know nothing about the author or even whether he wrote anything else, but that's my opinion in general about unreliable narrators, the game of wits.) I enjoyed reading between the lines, trying to figure out what was really going on. What was wrong with the kid? Why did he say he wasn't in the mood to call the girl when he clearly wanted to? I loved analyzing the character and coming up with my own theories about the reasons for his behaviour. 
 3. The representation of teen angst, inner conflict and confusion was spot-on. 
 BEWARE: if your teen years sucked, you should probably steer clear of this if you don't want to be reminded of all those crappy feelings. 
 4. Your heart bleeds for the kid, since you can tell he is suffering and is stuck in a loop of self-sabotage. 
 Cons: 
 1. Cussing. Lots and lots of cussing. 
 2. Lots of blasphemy. Beware. HATED it. 
 3. No real plot. 
 4. Unfortunately, no character growth. When you give me a character like this, a character with issues, you had better show me how he is learning to overcome them. There wasn't much overcoming, but rather quite a bit of wallowing and immature behaviour. 
 5. Really dark themes. And by 'dark themes' I don't mean cool-enchanted-forest-that-kills-people dark. I'm talking seedy bars, womanizers, hookers, vomit, pedophiles, lies, banal jokes, etc. 
 6. Leaves a bad taste. 
 7. Frustrating. After a while you think: kid, just talk to someone. But the rambling and judgments and irresponsibility just continues forever. 
 8. What an ending.  Here's the book in a nutshell: A teen is troubled and ends up in a psyche ward. A year later he still feels pretty much the same.  
 For the life of me, I cannot see how this was allowed in schools. I would strictly recommend this to 18+, except in special circumstances, where the reader is mature and responsible, otherwise it might mess up a messed up kid more. 
 I can see why some people might relate to this book, but I can't see that it will do them much good to read it, other than to know that they are not alone. It's a negative story with no real lessons learned, sadly.

 I'm not going to spend my review talking about the plot or the story or the characters. There are far too many reviews that will do just that and do it far better than I'd be able to. Given that I ate this up like candy (when I had the chance to actually read it), I didn't do much soul searching throughout it. All I can say for those things is that I really loved the ending and I also thought that King did a great job blending together the mystery/thriller that started this series off with his old hat of telekinesis that started his whole career off through Carrie. 
 Nor am I going to speculate about the future of Stephen King's career with writing. There's other people who do it far better than I ever will. In fact, I'll point you to Edward Lorn's review that really takes a lot into consideration over the possible future. 
 In fact, I just really want to spend my review talking about the theme prominent throughout basically this whole series. Suicide. Cheery, right? But, that's what I want to talk about since it played a role of catalyst in the series, and it was the whole focus for this book. 
 Now, suicide is a major topic these days. There are tons of help lines to call. Help lines for teens, adults, LGBT+ members. On and on the list goes. People know so much about it. Literally, I can count on it being in most of my psych classes for at least a portion of a lecture. The thing is, these days, a suicidal phase is almost expected. Natural. It is normal to feel suicidal for portions of your life. Most teens you talk to -- people in my generation -- will probably say that they've felt that way at least once in their life. I myself have gone through it multiple times. My most serious was the first time I was ever diagnosed with depression (Seasonal Affective Disoder, technically; I just find it utterly ironic that the abbreviation for it is SAD). I felt worthless. I felt like there was no point to me. Rationally, I knew I was wrong with those feelings, but it persisted and I got myself help thanks to my mom picking up on signs and acting. 
 And, I think it's interesting that Stephen King chose to use this in his books. It literally is what ties this whole series together with the first and the third books. While the second book was good, very good, I can't recall there being any real mention of suicide in it. It was a bit of a stand alone compared to these two, which are majorly connected. The reason Brady reached out to Bill was to make him commit suicide, just for a few laughs. Then, our lovely TK Brady decides to make Bill watch as all those he saved commit suicide. 
 Most of the victims of suicide in this book were teenagers. The most susceptible are teens. Whether that's because of the natural teen feeling of "You don't understand me!" and the move to isolate yourself from people who do understand, or if it's because of the internet and globalization being able to spread stories of suicides from across the world, or even if it's something genetic in teens, who knows. I think Stephen King, like usual, picked a topic that resonates with the times we live in. He's reminding adults who feel their teenage years were so far away that teens these days go through, I would argue, so much more than they went through because of the internet and never being able to get away from the bullies. And, also, he's reminding teens that you are not alone. Today, these feelings are natural, but if you have them you need to tell someone no matter how ashamed you feel. (Because, trust me, there's a lot of shame involved with those feelings.) 
 Anyways, all this meditation aside, read this book. It's absolutely absorbing and difficult to put down. It's a perfect ending to the series as a whole, with this ranking first, Mr. Mercedes as second, and, finally, Finders Keepers as third.

 The main storyline which is what the book is supposed to be about is just 10% of the book. I read till page 168/320 before getting completely put off by the writing style...

Audio version - good narration, although the same problem I always have with multiple narrators - the voices for dialogue aren't consistent between different narrators, so the same character will sound really different in different sections of the book. 
 The book itself? Didn't really work for me. Some really nice scenes, even some nice vignettes, but as a novel? It felt self-indulgent, as if the author wanted to include bits because he wanted to include them, not because they served the story. The entire section from Ed's POV was only there, as far as I could tell, to give support for one instance of Holly's supernatural abilities. So an entire novella is included in order to show one scene that could have been easily shown in a paragraph or two from Holly's POV. And the novella from the novelist's POV is similarly unimportant to the overall plot. It felt shoehorned in, to me. 
 Actually, I felt like both of those parts were included as a way for the author to give a political rant about the Middle East and a series of in-jokes/digs at a fellow novelist, respectively. I don't follow novelists as celebrities so the in-jokes mostly went over my head, and the political diatribe (including the environmental message from the last section)? 
 My politics are very closely aligned with the ideas presented in the novel, and I STILL resented the lecturing and hectoring tone. If the political ideas had fit seamlessly into the plot of the story, fine, but they sure didn't. 
 So-some really nice bits of writing, but not a successful novel for me.

 Originally posted on my blog, With Her Head in a Book 
 I received an eARC from Netgalley in exchange for an honest review. 
 Sci-Fi is one of the few genres I don't see read enough; it's got a bad reputation that I can't understand. Every science fiction novel I pick is a grand slam and so is Illuminae. Months later, I'm still hung up on the tearjerker. 
 One of the biggest deciding factors in why I picked up Illuminae is the excessive praise I was hearing from friends and respected reviewers. How does everyone love this book? I had to understand the hype since the description didn't bring out my inner need to riot until I have the book in my hands. Why? To be honest, the biggest feature of Illuminae, the format, originally turned me off. Instead of paragraphs of story telling, the novel is complied of documents, hacked messages, and surveillance videos. This non-traditional style is becoming a new trend in modern lit - something I'm still unsure about despite the success of Illuminae, my first novel like this. I worried about a disconnected plot or worse, a tale that made no sense. If my life story had to be told through my internet history and text messages, I believe it would be the most inaccurate biography ever. Miraculously, the author duo tell a seamless story, though some types of pages don't work well with the entire novel. For example, I wasn't interested in the ship diagrams, the unipedia pages are weird, but the creations of the AI are poetically beautiful. 
 Readers are thrown into the year 2575 - and by "thrown," I almost literally mean thrown. There is no such thing as a "running start" or "handicap mode" to make the journey through time and space a little bit easier. Nuh uh. Before you know it, there are missiles flying. For some of us like Kady, that's no big deal. Others might find this immersive, fast-paced beginning combo'd with the unusual formatting a bit too much and will want to put Illumaine down. I have one word for you: DON'T. Everything will make sense in time. This journey is worth whatever hassle that may come from it and boy, was it a pain for me to read my eARC edition. Bonus: my ebook fibbed so the censored areas were 100% visible. Man, there are a lot of curse words for a Young Adult novel. . .it's WONDERFUL. 
 In my youth, I'd been a heavy gamer and could not help relating Illuminae to the popular games Bioshock and Dead Space. Neither are perfect fits in terms of plot, setting, and time, but are 100% kin in terms of scariness and creepiness. I'm a huge fan of horror, but cannot play the games because of the audio and I've watched every horror movie created on this planet. I loved being able to get through a book that likes to take a walk on the wild side. I was on the edge of my seat with fear and elation; I couldn't turn the pages fast enough. For once, I couldn't tell who would make it to the end or face a horrible death especially with the shocking twists (you really won't see some of them coming). 
 I had my heart broken on multiple occasions and yet as soon as I finished reading the novel, I wanted to immediately begin rereading the series. That's extremely uncommon for me. I don't reread many books. But the well crafted characters and surprises kept pulling me back toward the book. Kady and Ezra are the type of protagonists we all love and hate. They're snarky starcrossed lovers, but also dumb teenagers. Yet they're filled with so much spirit that I couldn't help but root for them. Kady is a typical strong heroine who happens to be great at computers and likes to stick her nose where it doesn't belong. But who is she beyond a kickass girl? I'm not too sure. She's lovesick, homesick, and a bit of a loner. It's as if who she is didn't matter so long as she tries to save the day and says something sassy. My favorite character, though? The AI system AIDEN. He's a mastermind and probably the most poetic villain I've ever read. I won't say much on him, but this here is enough: he alone "made" the book for me. 
 I don't know if this is a book for everyone. I want you all to read this, but I know that the style choices will not work for everyone. Illuminae is GOOD, though. Readers who tough through the beginning pages will more than likely learn to love this novel. My biggest issue is the ending. After everything terrible happening followed by something far, far worse, the conclusion is a little bit too neat and too nice. I could have done without that one tiny surprise at the end. 
 Plot: 4/5 
 Characters: 3/5 
 Writing Style: 4/5 
 All Around Idea: 5/5 
 Total: 4.5/5

I didn't know what I was getting into with The Disreputable History, but it was worth it. While it wasn't my usual kind of book, I enjoyed the main character and the lessons that the book teaches us, both about being a girl in modern society and about finding oneself. 
 Frankie is in a family that doesn't really know who she is. Her father expects her to follow in his footsteps as closely as possible. Everyone calls her 'Bunny Rabbit,' and sometimes she feels like no one respects her. 
 Then she gets involved with the Loyal Order of the Basset Hounds, a secret society of boys at her school. 
 This is a little similar to a growing-up story, in my opinion, because it's kind of a story about Frankie not only finding out who she really is, but about her letting other people know who she really is, no matter what she risks in doing so. 
 I found it enjoyable to get to read Frankie's letter in the very beginning and then throughout the book, learn what each of these strangely named events were. I also thought that the way she tricked everybody into thinking she was Alpha was kind of cool, as well as many of her clever, Basset-y plots. It showed how dedicated she was to the existence of the club, whereas the boys were dedicated to the idea> of the club.  
 I do have a few complaints with this book, though. First of all, I couldn't really relate to Frankie's attraction toward Matthew, Alpha, Callum, etc. She wanted to be a part of their friend-circle, but I just didn't entirely understand why. They were funny, sure, but they didn't always seem polite and came off as kind of immature. In fact, Frankie was actually the only character in the whole book I actually cared about, although Trish was okay. 
 Also, Frankie continued to care about her relationship with Matthew throughout the book, whereas I cared about it very little. In fact, I only cared when they broke up because I felt bad for Frankie.  But on the other hand, it did seem realistic to me, unlike the way many YA romances are portrayed now. 
 Nevertheless, this story had a compelling plot and enjoyable themes, and it never got boring.

It was also distracting that the two major characters have names that are solid cannon from two other very popular and well known story universes.  Zach is on his way to LA and as far away as he can get from London. He only has six more weeks to go, but first, he's asked to edit one more manuscript. The catch is, the novel is an erotica written by Nora Sutherlin. That same novel means more to Nora than anything else she's written and she wants to get it right. She's desperate enough to give Zach total control over it. 
 The blurb promises gruelling, draining, and shockingly arousing writing sessions, which are notably absent from the book. There is writing, there are sessions, there are shredded scenes, and there are excerpts from the book within the book--something I particularly disliked mostly because of the dip in quality--none of which were the reason for my rating. 
 The word I'm stumbling over is the last one in the list--arousing. 
 Once again, I'm the odd man out; I don't get the appeal. 
 Reisz can write well and there were certain things I enjoyed reading. I mostly liked the banter between characters and the characterisations. I liked the fact that none of them were boring or insufferably honourable and good. I liked that they were flawed. 
 I adored Wes. He was used to mirror Nora's relationship with Soren and I kept thinking he was better than that, that he deserved to get away. As good a guy as he was, as vanilla, he never came across as sanctimonious. Quite the opposite, he knew his flaws, just like he recognised Nora's flaws and accepted them. He was honest with himself. 
 Unlike Zach. The Jewish--a very important fact that--Zachary or Zechariah Easton had to quite literally have the truth beaten out of him. That certainly didn't add to his nonexistent appeal, but I'm glad someone found him appealing if it takes him far away from the story. Zach also earned the label too stupid to live for not figuring out or at least suspecting what Nora's day job was. 
 Soren, Nora's old Dom, let's just say that I liked him much more with the robes on than off and that I didn't understand why he'd care for Nora on any level. Although, I wouldn't mind reading more about his flavour of mind-fuckery as long as it was kept out of the dungeon-hell. As a turn on, Soren fails. 
 J.P., Kingsley, and Mary, were among the supporting cast I'd like to know more about, but not as much as I was left wanting layers for the office villain. He was an example of a lazy characterisation and especially disappointing compared to the effort put into the main cast. 
 And then there was Nora Sutherlin, the author and pseudonym for Eleanor Schreiber. The woman, the Switch, who's not afraid of her sexuality or playing the game. In fact, I think that might be the only thing she's not afraid of, the game. Nora only ever came close to being honest with herself and facing her own feelings when she was with Wes. I'd go as far as to call her a coward that's how busy running from herself she was. And all I have for a coward is pity. 
 No, Nora isn't a likeable main character, but being a user and a bitch doesn't make her strong either. It simply makes her interesting and that's where the strength of this novel is--in the characters. 
 But. There's more. 
 Or rather, there isn't. The Siren is an erotica but very unerotic at that. I'm not a fan of pain and I don't particularly get excited by the forbidden aspect of sex--hazards of having been born a Finn with a mother who never shut up about the human reproduction when I was growing up and living in a sauna culture where the most natural state of man is in the nude. The closest I came to finding anything erotic in this book was when Nora was with Wes, Michael, or Sheridan. That's when she let little bit of her armour slip away, emotions trickle out and almost show intimacy. 
 At this point, I feel like I'm repeating myself, because I've written it so often lately. I could list a spoilery list of events--which include hints of blood play, a sex scene with an underaged boy, a f/f BDSM scene, multiple occasions of beatings leading to face injuries, casual dismissal of the law enforcement, a rape, an unrealistic office fight, bringing religion into sexuality, infidelity saving a marriage --and not see a plot in it. But apparently that's okay, because Nora's introduces the reader and Zach to the shocking horrors of BDSM life. I only half-kid. The pure BDSM shocked and horrified me about as much as it aroused me, which is to say very little. 
 To be perfectly honest, I was bored. It didn't take me days to finish reading the book because I was savouring the story; it took me days because reading a sex scene after another became a chore. Neither did the manufactured confrontations or Nora's assumed self-sacrifice help. I only devoured the pages when there was emotional torture or those rare moments honesty for example when Soren was telling Nora off or when was Wes his adorable self. 
 All this left me thinking that this would have been a much better book without the sex and wishing Reisz had written a deliciously twisted character drama centering around something other than kink. As well written as The Siren is, it's not enough to make it a good book. 
 Just to make this clear: Yes, I was trying out a new genre. No, I was not expecting a romance. Yes, I still think the book failed.

Homegoing is a sweeping novel comprised of many connected short stories each covering a generation in a several hundred year family line starting in 1700's Ghana and split in two. The stories follow the line of one sister married to a British slaver and the line of her unknown much younger half sister who is sold into slavery by her unknown elder sister's British husband. 
 This is an example of an outstanding debut novel. The excellence of it stands in Gyasi's short story telling though, as this format doesn't showcase a novel length plot. Through her short stories, Gyasi manages to cover an astounding amount of history and still provide plenty of feeling to go with it. I wonder a little at the possibility of some cliche chapters in there which are hard hitting and all but might be seen as "required" typecasts of African American life by publishers, but if Gyasi did have to pander to that, I appreciated her Ghanaian stories all the more in comparison. I also had some small "I wishes..." at the end, but all in all, I'm very impressed and look forward to more from Yaa Gyasi.

I don't want to give anything away, but I will say that I think things were resolved a little too nicely. This was my neighborhood book club's selection for last summer (2014), and I spent a lot of afternoon reading time on its 500+ pages, enjoying it for the most part. In retrospect, however, it is a mystery story with an unnecessary mystery, and much longer than it needs to be. 
  From the beginning, the question of the circumstances of the narrator's sister's death looms, followed by the conundrums: What is the relation of her best-selling posthumous novel to her own life? Who, in real life, was her lover? More interesting questions come later. 
 Now, I love questions like these, but in a legitimate mystery the answers are withheld because a) the narrator is telling the story chronologically, and didn't know the answers at the time of the events being related, or b) the narrative is in the 3rd person, i.e., not told by a character. In The Blind Assassin, however, the narrator, Iris, knew all the answers at the time these things occurred! Finding this out after 400 pages of torturous suspense, I felt justified in asking, "Why *@?>%W#%&! didn't you tell me at the beginning if you knew?!" Remember, I'm asking this not of Margaret Atwood (I know why she didn't tell me), but of the narrator who, in the context of the story, is writing this as a legacy for her grandchild. 
 She and her creator should have had more consideration for the grandchild's and the reader's time. For myself, I could have read more books last summer.

"I would like to believe this is a story I'm telling. I need to believe it. I must believe it. Those who can believe that such stories are only stories have a better chance." 
 Why did I not read this sooner? How could I possibly have overlooked such a masterpiece, such a thought-provoking dystopian nightmare, filled with simple writing, clear metaphors and deep symbolism? Why did I think that this was not for me, when it clearly was? How could I have been so wrong? 
 The thing is, "The Handmaid's Tale" is one of the most well-crafted dystopian novels that I have ever read. Atwood emphasizes the women's role throughout history as she takes one step back from our modern societies and leaves all women as simple birth-machines, servants and saintly wives, ultimately creating a feminist's worst nightmare. 
 Atwood's writing style is mesmerizing, constantly flowing between the present and the past. The main character is a part of the generation who has to adjust to this new world, and therefore she has a sense of loss. Atwood's dystopian world is not yet fully established when the novel begins; it is still in a phase of transition and exploration. 
 The result is so unlike any other well-known dystopia, the characters are suffering in very different ways than Guy Montag and Winston Smith, because in "The Handmaid's Tale" everybody know what they have lost. There is no rediscovery of a world covered in smoke; Offred has had a man, she has experienced love, born a child and lost a friend. She has been pulled apart from everything that she loved, and she longs for a past which is no longer possible. Her yearning flows through the novel, from beginning to end. 
 The novel is filled with powerful messages about love, identity, freedom and hope. The ending is not an intricate bow, but a loose knot, open for interpretation and discussion. And I can still feel its last words, lingering in the air around me. 
 "What I need is perspective. The illusion of depth, created by a frame, the arrangement of shapes on a flat surface. Perspective is necessary. Otherwise there are only two dimensions. Otherwise you live with your face squashed up against a wall, everything a huge foreground, of details, close-ups, hairs, the weave of the bedsheet, the molecules of the face. Your own skin like a map, a diagram of futility, criscrossed with tiny roads that lead nowhere. Otherwise you live in the moment. Which is not where I want to be."

The second volume of Paper Girls picks up right where the first ended, with Erin encountering her older self in the future. Things don't stay simple (heh) for long, though, as another Erin from further in the future, but looking exactly like Erin from the 1980s, gets involved, and no one is sure exactly who to trust. With KJ missing, though, they have to do something, and since all three Erins are driving the paper girls forward, what else is there to do? 
 The story stagnates a little with this volume, but not because of lack of ambition. Vaughan is driving the story toward a future point he knows well, but he's giving us information only a small piece at a time. We don't get many questions from the first volume answered, and those we do get answered are replaced with more questions as the story grows more complex. I'm a little uncertain by this point, since I was expecting to get something that would ground the story by now, but the potential for where it's going is still great. Vaughan just needs to start bringing it in for a landing sometime soon. 
 A lot of the criticisms I saw regarding the first volume -- that it moves slowly, that it doesn't give us much in the way of the main characters, that the plot is moving at a glacial pace -- still apply, so folks who had those complaints for the first arc won't feel different about the second one. I usually expect a series to lay down the exposition in the first arc, and then start examining the plot in the second, but here it feels like Vaughan still has some exposition to explore. I hope he gets there soon. I'm patient when it comes to graphic novels, but if he doesn't start bringing it together soon, I'm going to lose interest.
