Though not as popular as Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner, "A Thousand Splendid Suns" is an extremely important novel with a huge number of interesting themes which are explored in its rather short amount of pages. In this family saga and moving tale of friendship, hate and love at the same time, Hosseini abbreviates several decades of important history into a fictional story spanning more than thirty years. 
 It's a depressing novel, consisting of a rather dark atmosphere and many chapters which will leave you gasping for breath due to the sheer amount of brutality and inhumanity some characters seem to love carrying out. What I found most intriguing in this novel was the way Hosseini managed to provide a lot of information about the history of Afghanistan, a country which has been dominated by war and destruction for such a long time. At times he came close to sounding like a nonfictional correspondent of the events with his prose, but fortunately it never felt like the author was trying to pour infodump out on his readers. 
 "A Thousand Splendid Suns" is a tough book to review, simply because it deals with so many socially relevant issues that it feels like nitpicking to talk about the writing and the characterization. It's an important book which I can only encourage everyone to read as soon as possible, considering that it offers plenty food for your thoughts and leaves you pondering about themes and questions which you may not have thought about in such detailed precision before. My biggest problem with the novel was mostly about the main characters Laila and Mariam, who - thanks to the rather detached and neutral writing style - felt very difficult to connect or relate to. I started rooting for these characters throughout the course of the novel, though that's rather obvious to say considering the fate these two women had to endure in the course of the plot. 
 As a final note, I think this book - or Hosseini's other books in general - should receive more attention by the public. Nowadays, especially here in Germany, there is a lot of displeasure directed towards foreigners and their cultures, not necessarily people from Afghanistan, but the Middle East and Far East in general. Hosseini manages to introduces his readers who are not familiar with the cultures described in this novel to a different world, a world I personally didn't know as much about before reading "A Thousand Splendid Suns" (and still wouldn't consider myself knowing a lot about). Khaled Hosseini's writing transports the important message that no matter where we come from, we are still all humans. Here in Germany and probably in many other places on our planet as well, people often tend to forget that coming from a different culture does not mean those humans are worth any less than we all are, and I think Hosseini's writing has the strength to remind more people of this fact. We are all human, and everyone deserves to be treated as such - no matter which cultural background you belong to.

Well, it's about time! I have battled with this series from the start, it was just so not what I had expected. I read the first two books out of curiosity and because the Anita Blake series had garnered such high praise, but was left dumbfounded. The third, I even stopped reading halfway through, it just was not doing it for me, but I hate not completing a mission, so I came back to it, after re-reading the entire Cassie Palmer series, and managed to fall a little further into the world created by Hamilton. 
 Book four however, grabbed me by the collar and pulled me in from the get-go and I am so relieved. Finally, I am starting to enjoy this series. 
 This time round we see a lot more of Jean-Claude, and correct me if I'm wrong, but isn't that why read these books, to see the evil/sexy vampire in action? He is still a little leery, has terrible centuries-old dress sense, perverted, powerful and in lust with Anita, but he's also compelling, intriguing and a little funny. 
 Anita's other love interest was an enigma from the start. What did she see in him, Richard seemed so weak and OK sexy, but still, under Jean-Claude's thumb, well, this time it becomes more apparent.  And then there's Anita. I mentioned in my review of book three that I wasn't sure if I even liked Anita, and I'm still not entirely convinced, but she did improve in this one. However, we are made abundantly clear that Anita is not only capable, intelligent and a kick-ass protagonist able to hold her own with the baddies of the night albeit with the most horrible dress sense, but she is also a staunch feminist. I only wish we didn't have this thrust down our throats. A little less don't open the door for me and a little more tenderness and we might just understand what both Jean-Claude and Richard see in her. 
 Finally, what couldn't please me more, is Anita didn't raised too many zombies, well at least none we got to participate in. I have said it before and I'll say it again now, I don't get zombies, never had, never will, and I can't stand the blood and guts Anita wades through to do her day job. But, this time round, we were firmly in vampire territory, hardly a zombie to be seen. Hooray! 
 So, what do I give book four in the Anita Blake series? 
 Finally a Blake book worthy of further pursuit of the series, this one gets an 8/10: " Excellent read, well written, fell right into the fictional world created".

If you don't read this book you are only cheating yourself. I'm not sure I can adequately review this book. I think it may be Sanderson's best so far. How anyone can keep a reader enthralled over almost 1100 pages is a mystery, but he manages it with what appears to be extreme ease of writing. 
 You may want to stop reading at this point because of spoilers. Believe me when I say you do not want to read spoilers on this one. Let the story unfold for you and realize what a master of epic fantasy Sanderson truly is. Actually I've marked anything that truly acts as a spoiler. 
 The good: 
 Sanderson's mastery of writing clear, organized, and consistent English, plot, and character development. 
 You finally get to see all the separate players from Way of Kings come together in what prove to be amusing and plot defining. My personal favorites: 
  
 - Jasnah/Navani engaging the womanizer Adolin to Shallan. 
 - Shallan getting revenge on Jasnah's 'killer' 
 - The sad truth that Kaladin killed Shallan's brother (though she doesn't find out yet. 
 - The first meeting of Kaladin and Shallan was perfect, almost as perfect as their trip together through the chasms after 'miraculously' surviving the 200' fall, each thinking they had somehow saved the other. 
 Amaram's treachery is unmasked! But Kaladin is thrown in jail for challenging a light eyes. 
 We get Shallan's history and a view of Gavilar's murder from Jasnah. 
 Jasnah lives!!!! Seriously I should have seen this coming since she is a Radiant or almost a Radiant, but it took me completely by surprise. 
 Syl's return, after her heartbreaking death. Thank goodness, or all the emotional investment in Kaladin becoming a Radiant would have been wasted. 
 Szeth's redemption??? I guess we'll see. 
  
 The bad: 
 Does everybody have to keep secrets? 
  
 The treachery of the Ghostbloods would probably not be so bad if people would just talk about their concern about it. Come on Shallan. 
 Stormfather's attitude does not bode well for the human race. Luckily he's now bonded as a spren to a Radiant. 
  
 The Ugly: 
 The interludes. Seriously, I know the information is important to the overall story, but!!!! They are like commercials in a show right in the middle of a cliffhanger. And you know you should read them so you can keep up on world events, but honestly I have a hard time tracking the peripheral characters and often spend more time looking up who they were last time. 
 The only exception is the view from Eshonai  a Parshendi general, then Voidbringer, thanks a lot Stormfather, that really brings the whole battle into perspective.  
 The unanswered questions for next time: 
  
 - What is Wit? is he a Radiant? or something that hasn't been truly explained at this time. I mean he knows about the other world and can sense it. 
 - How will people who are not radiants, but can draw on stormlight, be able to use it? 
 - who will the other 4 radiants be? 
 - who gets to be the first Herald? Adolin? 
 - Will Adolin be punished for finally getting rid of that scum Sadeus? 
 - Will they get the rest of the gates open? Actually I know they'll get at least some of them, but what will that mean? 
 - Are Kaladin's parents still alive? and will he find them before the Parshendi/Voidbringer's?

 Rachel Vincent is an auto-buy author for me; so much so that I couldn't resist pre-ordering Shadow Bound a month before its release. Then I got my hands on an ARC five days before the publication date which means that I thankfully didn't have to wait for my mailman to show up. The Unbound world is exactly how I remembered it, pure awesomeness. Vincent has a real gift for storytelling and will have you eating out of the palm of her hand in no time. Even though Kori and Ian's characters didn't quite do it for me and some of their actions aren't always exactly credible; there's still more good than bad to be had in Shadow Bound. 
 This installment focuses on the darker skills, namely shadow-walking and blinding. Right off the bat I felt a connection between Kori and Ian because their gifts are similar in nature and work in tandem. Even though they do manage to resist each other in the beginning it was obvious that they'd become involved sooner rather than later. As a result, there is a certain degree of predictability to the plot that made the story not as enthralling to read as Blood Bound. Although, Rachel does explore the limitations of certain skills and explains how a syndicate contract actually works which I found intriguing and nicely explained. 
 It was impossible not to immediately feel something for poor Kori. When we first hook-up with her she's being released from "the basement" after 6 impossibly long weeks of torture, rape and humiliation. Needless to say, she's not too happy with her boss at the moment and the last thing that she expects to find is love. I enjoyed her spunk, fearlessness and snark. Kori is fiercely defensive of her sister and will never hesitate to protect her at all cost. Ian is smart, determined and loyal; his world gets knocked on its ass when he meets miss Daniels. Together their chemistry wasn't exactly what it could have been but they still manage to have a couple of really great moments. 
 The story took a little too long to take off in my opinion. I found that the character development dragged and the main plot didn't actually kick in until several chapters later. I hate to say it but there was an instance where I was actually a little bored. Vincent also introduces a bunch of new skills without really explaining them which I found disappointing considering she did such a stellar job in the detail department in Blood Bound. 
 Even though Rachel Vincent didn't hit it out of the park with Shadow Bound you can't help but be swept away by her exceptional writing and superior storytelling.

 Beautiful but heartbreaking. If I had to describe In the Shadow of Blackbirds as succinctly as possible, that would be it. So different from pretty much everything out right now and so lovely, both in writing and its story. Cat Winters deftly explores humanity and just how far we will go to survive, even at the expense of others. It's a sad reality to face, but one that's important and not often explored in young adult literature. I don't think I can recommend this book enough. 
 It's 1918 and the United States is deep in the throes of World War I and the Spanish influenza. The American public is in a frenzy. If you're not dying overseas in the war, you're dying from the flu. With death's never-ending presence, people turn to the supernatural to reach their loved ones. Mary Shelley Black, a self-proclaimed girl of science, doesn't believe in the otherworldly. But when she has a close call with death and her deceased first love begins visiting her with unsettling stories, Mary Shelley may just have to rethink her stance, and find out why his spirit is not at rest. 
 I just have to mention that this is definitely a book worth reading in print form. I had an egalley, but won a print copy before I began reading, so I read the physical book. I compared the two, and the digital version just can't hold a candle to the beauty of this book. There are so many details on the pages and the photographs that just look better in the book. I don't think reading a digital version ruins the story, but your experience is definitely enriched. 
 What works best in In the Shadow of Blackbirds is the stark description of the people's state at that time. Mary Shelley visits a Red Cross ward, where soldiers are healing after being injured in the war, and she sees men who've not only lost limbs, but they've lost their spirit. We can't help but wonder at the real cost of our liberty, and who pays that price. Each person, when they leave home, dons a flu mask to prevent germs from getting to them. They chew onion gum and put bags of moth balls around their necks. Fear makes people not human, in a way, and this is shown so well. This all adds to the feel of the book, but it works even better to make it pack a punch to the reader. Also, without this setting, Mary Shelley and Stephen's story would've lacked immediacy and felt like any other book. 
 This is not a feel good, happy kind of romantic book. Yes, Mary Shelley and Stephen have a beautiful, honest, sweet relationship, but if you're looking for a happy ending, don't look here. The dark world presented is not one that gave a lot of happy endings like we've come to expect. But, we can leave with hope, something even better. Even in the darkest and most trying of times, one can always see a ray of hope and take comfort in the wells of strength in characters like Mary Shelley Black.

 God this book is infuriating. Let me lay it out for you, so you can understand why I disliked a book everybody loves. 
 Firstly, I love how Hoover writes. She has a compelling and addictive writing style. I read Ugly love earlier this year and I LOVED it. It's one of my favorite books of the year. 
 This however, not so much. The writing was a bit cliche at times, which I didn't mind all that much, but there it is. I loved Ridge, I think he was a really great character and  I really liked that Hoover decided to make him deaf. It was an interesting perspective and added a lot to the story, and I think she wrote about it very respectfully and did it justice.  Sydney was an okay character, although I don't really like how she treated Bridgette. She put her down, not for the things she should've put her down, but just for her looks, or her Hooters uniform which was stupid. Still, she wasn't that bad. I personally don't think her and Ridge had much of a chemistry. I didn't really feel it. My main issue with the book is the love triangle. I hate them. Truly. I don't understand them and I don't think they are realistic. But hey, let's say they are, just for the sake of it. The problem with this particular one is that the resolution of it was such a cope out.  I hated that Maggie was made sick. I hate it, I hate it. I hate when it's made that people stay with each other because of an illness and I hate that their relationship was built upon him needing to protect her and her wanting to live her life fully.  I just hate it. It such an easy way out of it. And I just don't think he could have ever loved them equally. I don't think he could have loved them both in the first place. But equally??? When Ridge refers to either Sydney or Maggie as "the other half of my heart", that's the moment this book turned sour to me. And I get that in the end it seems as though Sydney really was the one for him, but why  did his relationship with Maggie had to end over her illness??  I don't know, I just felt wrong about the whole thing and I ended up really disliking it. It was good when it started, but bad when I finished it.

 I thought they were a great couple. Devan is a mechanic who was adopted as a baby and comes looking for his birth parents, so he's anxious and tense. Kyle is a lawyer who's had to stop work because he has narcolepsy, which leads him to fall asleep at unpredictable moments (which obvs doesn't go well in court). I never even knew that was a thing, but I can see how it could be treated as a joke, and JL Merrow is sensitive about it. So Kyle is also stressed. So as a couple they are quite tense and emotional. I liked that. 
 I wasn't totally convinced by the amount of slang Kyle used. I thought he could have been a bit more formal to make him more convincing as a lawyer and also to emphasize the differences of class and education between them that are an issue they have to face. Also I didn't much like the ending where they rush off to London to solve the problems of a new character who wasn't really a part of their story.  But overall I enjoyed this very much. 
 Should perhaps mention there's a lot of British slang in it. Also that I had a free review copy.

 Summary of the Story 
 A futuristic retelling of Cinderella involving cyborgs and aliens and the plague. Yes to it all. 
 Cinder is a cyborg mechanic who, along with her android friend Iko, works at a marketplace where she makes money for her evil stepmother. The world they live in is infected with a deadly virus, and they are under constant threat from a race of mean aliens known as Lunars. The Lunar Queen Levana wants to join forces with Earth, but only if Prince Kai marries her so she may rule upon Earth as well. 
 While working at the market, Prince Kai comes to her booth requesting help fixing one of his androids. They get along easily, and eventually, after seeing each other more than once, he asks her to the ball he is holding soon. She knows she can't go because he'll find out she's a cyborg and won't want to have anything to do with her anymore. 
 Cinder's family is preparing for the ball, and although Cinder knows her stepmother will never let her go, she still follows her orders with the false promise of being allowed to accompany them. She, Iko, and her nice step-sister Peony go to the junkyard looking for a part, but Peony gets infected and is taken away. Cinder is given away by her family to be used as a test subject to find a cure for the disease, a procedure that kills all its volunteers. But Cinder's body fights off the virus, and the man in charge of the project, Dr. Erland, tells her that she's immune. Not only that, but she eventually learns it's because she's Lunar. She doesn't remember any of her past up until her stepfather adopted her, so she had no memories of being taken from Lunar and hidden on Earth as a child. 
 As soon as Prince Kai's father dies from the virus, Queen Levana comes to Earth to try getting Kai to finally agree to marry her and have their planets become allies. But the Lunar people have the ability to use magic to glamour themselves and to manipulate people's thoughts. Levana spots Cinder in a crowd of people, and knows she's Lunar. 
 The night of the ball, Cinder receives a message from Kai's fixed android from a Lunar girl who claims to be working for the Queen. Apparently Levana knows that Kai has been looking for Princess Selene, her niece, who escaped from their planet after a failed murder attempt by her aunt herself. Kai wants to find the Princess so that she can overthrow Levana as queen of the Lunar people. The girl reveals that once Kai pledges to marry her, Levana will take the throne and kill him. With this knowledge, Cinder rushes to the ball to tell him. She is seen by the Queen, who tries to immediately kill her. Kai finds out she is Lunar as well as a cyborg, but still bargains for her life. Instead of dying, she gets put in the palace jail. Dr. Erland comes to see her, where he reveals that she is Princess Selene, and he knew it the whole time. He gives her the tools and advice she needs to escape the prison.

Trolls! I know, right? Flashy colorful hair, so-ugly-they're-cute dolls we all had at one point? In Amanda's world, these are all misconceptions. They're called Trylle, and they're beautiful, magical and on the brink of extinction. 
 With an entirely unique lore, Switched is able to stand out from all the other paranormal books available. I was fascinated by the Trylle mythology: How they lived, the monarchy, their custom of switching babies at birth. It was absolutely creative. Into this world comes a collection of commendable characters that are both well developed and easily likeable - even a select few that are fun to hate. Wendy has a big personality. She's had a difficult, traumatic childhood, but that only made her stronger for the wear. She doesn't let anyone manipulate her. She's sympathetic and kind. All of which make her really relatable. I enjoyed going through her dilemmas with her. The stressful demands of becoming a princess overnight, the boy she's falling for- it was all delightful. Almost like a modern day fairy tale. 
 Yes! The wonderful boys! From sweet to sweaty, Wendy has got more than her pick of lovely bachelors to chose from. I absolutely loved how the romance was played out in Switched. It's passionate and heartbreaking. It doesn't fall with the cliches of today's YA novels. It's unexpected - true to life. Truthfully, I devoured it and I can't fathom choosing a team. She can have them all, right? 
 While there is still good story development, I did find some parts of the book were a bit slow. A good portion is dedicated to character and world building, however the book does not completely suffer from "first book syndrome" it does have its own beginning, middle and end, but I think the rest of the trilogy will be much more action packed with powerful plot twists. 
 With this admirable debut, Amanda Hocking has begun a trilogy that has immense potential. Switched is just as beautiful inside as it is on the outside (definite cover lust) and I highly recommend it!

The tone, the language, the plot, the characters... it feels just like reading a classic novel by Austen or one of the Brontes, except there is magic involved. Not just involved - the England of this story has a well-established history of magic with its own literature, legends and reference materials, which Clarke helps the reader to understand by providing helpful footnotes (awesome). In fact, one of the foremost magicians of the previous ages still technically rules all of Northern England, so that the King and Government really only rule Southern England while the rest awaits their ruler's return. Just that idea would have made this book great, but it's so, so much more. 
 Jonathan Strange and Mr Norrell are characters with great depth - both have good and bad qualities; both admirable traits and tendencies that make you want to throttle them. Norrell in particular made me want to scream with his actions (I guess I'm a Strangeite!) but by the end the balance is quite evenly drawn as to who has done right or wrong. 
 I also enjoyed that, really, the most important accomplishment of the book is not really made by the two Foremost Magicians of the Age, but made by the efforts of good-hearted side characters who make choices that warmed my heart. It's sort of the equivalent of the fairy-tale princess saving herself by virtue of her intelligence and goodness. Makes me happy. :) 
 The book works itself up to quite a compelling ending, although my attention never really flagged even in the quieter parts. I did take a long, extended break about halfway through - after reading 400+ pages you feel like you've already read an entire book - but it wasn't for lack of interest. The very end made me cry, and only books with great emotional investment in the characters can do that to me. 
 I can't recommend this one enough.

I wasn't expecting to like this book. It was one of two books up for this month to read for a group I recently joined, and neither one of them sounded that interesting. But I chose this one because I preferred the cover. Yeah, yeah... From the description, I thought it would be preachy and moralistic and ... you know, one of those books with an agenda where the actual story is secondary. 
 But that is totally not the case. This book is very well written and makes excellent use of the dual narrator technique, switching back and forth between Lavinia, who is young, innocent and naive, and Belle, who is older and hasn't been spared the tragedies of the world. To Belle, it is obvious that the biggest difference between the two of them is that Belle is half black and a slave, whereas Lavinia is white and an indentured servant who ended up that way as an orphan. Lavinia doesn't realize that different colors mean anything (having grown up to the ripe old age of 7 in Ireland, she was presumably spared the brainwashing), and she views Belle (and the other slaves) as her family. 
 Lavinia is often spared the truth to save her innocence. When she asks questions about things happening around her, people often reply that she will find out soon enough, and don't explain. But she never does figure it out on her own, and the lack of knowledge leads her to make some decisions that change everyone's lives forever. 
 To be honest, most of the things in this book are caused because people refuse to be honest with each other, or don't push the issue and tell things that need to be told. Belle's true relationship with the captain, for instance, is hidden from his family and no one makes any effort to correct that even after he dies. Likewise, what is going on with the tutor and Marshall -- no one tries nearly hard enough to make it clear to Marshall's parents what is happening. The father of Belle's child - again, had Lavinia been told instead of had the truth hidden from her, many problems later in life could have been avoided. Lavinia probably could have visited the hospital much sooner if she'd made it clear the effect she has on Miss Martha.  There are other cases of this as well, but these are the big plot-important ones. 
 In the end, I found all the characters to be likable at some point during the book (well, except Rankin and the tutor...) and even felt a little bad for Marshall, although I have to admit I am REALLY unclear about his motives for his choice of wife. He had SEEN how she interacted with everyone in the past - did he really expect this to change? 
 Some parts of the book were really, really awful, and brought up strong emotions with me. Lots of violence, often of a sexual nature (but not always). There was an awful lot of death. I'm impressed with the author's research, especially dealing with current events in the time period, and I enjoyed reading the different dialects. Definitely recommend reading this one at least once.

 I enjoyed this book well enough. I only recently put this on my to-read list. I know this is a well-known classic. I just never had a desire to read it. I bought my copy for $0.50 at a book sale. So I figured that even if I didn't like it, I wouldn't have wasted money. 
 I thought the structure was interesting. The book is divided into 3 sections: Mosque, Caves, and Temple. Those section headings center around an important even in each section. Though I would say, for the most part, those actual events don't even take up the bulk of the writing. It seemed more like those aforementioned events inform and shape the rest of the respective sections and develop the plot. Take for instance the cave section. The scenes at the actual caves only take up a quarter (if that) of that section. The rest is filled by the build-up and the following arrest, trial, and immediate after-math of the trial.  
 I was surprised that the main action/incident Adela's alleged assault  happened so far into the book. Much of the beginning of the book is build-up. We get to see, through the world Forster created, British controlled India. We read about the racism and ignorance on the part of the British (most of the British characters - maybe with exception of Fielding) and how the Indians reacted to and dealt with said ignorance and racism. Going into this book, I knew a bit about the history of India and Britain's rule. However this book has furthered my curiosity in the subject and I would love to learn more. 
 Most of the characters were irritating. (Side note: I feel like nearly every review I write some character or another irritates me to the point of no return. I've decided that's because that's how I react to people in real life. That probably doesn't make me sound too great, but hey at least I'm honest.) I really didn't care for Adela at any point of the story. I don't quite understand what happened in the cave, and to be quite honest I don't think she knew either. I found her a weak character who, until the end, had a hard time standing up for herself or at least the truth. I felt similarly about Aziz. Don't get me wrong, I understand his anger toward Adela; I was angry - or at least frustrated with her! . However he was far more conceited (even before the incident) than anyone should be. In short, I did not appreciate or take to his attitude. That being said, I did sympathize with him in regards to wanting India to be free of British rule. For that I understand and agree with him. It was just his general attitude and the way he carried himself that made me dislike him. 
 Forster's writing is beautiful. From beginning to end he creates a believable and enticing scenery. I will say that there are certain sections that dragged a bit and lost me along the way. On occasion I found myself having to go back a reread because I was reading without actually absorbing the content. 
 Do I recommend this one? Yes. If you haven't read this one I'd at least put it on the list. No need, in my opinion, to rush to read this one.

Rachel Watson has spent the last few years stumbling through life in a booze-filled depression ever since her husband left her for another woman. Now she wiles away her days riding the commuter train to and from London, despite having been fired from her job months ago. The train makes a daily stop by her old neighborhood and it is here she spies a couple appearing to be living a perfect life from a beautiful home. She begins to fantasize about the couple, inventing little lives and backstories for them to keep her mind off her own troubles. Rachel witnesses something from the train that upsets her more than it should, and when Megan goes missing, she believes she has key evidence. She goes to the police but the police dismiss her as a drunken, unreliable witness. So she takes things into her own hands.

I loved the first 2/3 of this book, but the last 1/3 was disappointing. I wish the book hadn't focused so much on Maggie, who was definitely the less-interesting of the two main characters. Maggie was selfish, self-righteous, and shockingly un-self-aware for a psychologist. I hate that the book basically agreed with Maggie that Lakshmi was worse than she was. Lakshmi tricked her husband into marrying her for selfless reasons. Her sister was threatening to commit suicide to avoid the wedding, and Lakshmi knew that by tricking everyone the shame would fall to her, not her father or sister, and the groom's family would avoid the shame of canceling a wedding last-minute. She believed the groom would immediately divorce her, and everyone would agree he was the injured party. It was a horrible situation, and the groom was not pristine. He felt entitled to own the beautiful girl he listed after, no matter how she felt, so I can't feel that bad for him that his new property was not as aesthetically pleasing as he anticipated.  Maggie, on the other hand, has an affair for entirely selfish reasons. She's not in love with Peter, her husband Sudhir is wonderful, and she loves and wants to stay with Sudhir. She just lacks self-control. So it was incredibly frustrating to me to have the book spend such a long time agreeing that the divorce  was mostly Lakshmi's fault, and it was wicked of her to put Peter's necklace in Sudhir's night table so he would find out about the affair. It reminds me of how society treats sexual assault victims - "you don't want to ruin his life because of one mistake, do you?" As if the fault lies with the person shining a light on the son, rather than the sinner.  I enjoyed Lakshmi's stories of her village so much that I am rating this book a 3, but really it's more like a 2.5. Too much moralizing with the wrong moral, in my opinion.

4.5 out of 5 stars. 
 I read a Dutch arc of this called 'De horlogemaker van Londen'. 
 'The Watchmaker of Filigree Street' is an incredibly atmospheric novel mostly set in victorian Londen and partly set in historical Japan. The book reads as if you're watching a film. Victorian Londen is one of my favourite settings for historical books to begin with, but with the tiniest touch of magic and steampunk the story really came to life. Mori's amazing inventions not only add colour to the story, but also have real purpose. 
 The characters were very intriguing. It is not often that I care for these types of characters in stories: a slightly boring male klerk and an eccentric Japanese baron, but I cared from the very beginning. Showing that characters don't always need to be relatable to yourself to become important to you. 
 The plot was built up slowly but was easy to follow and kept me wanting to find out more. The changes in time and setting kept the story moving forward and helped us understand the characters better. It is difficult to put this one into a category, it not being just a thriller, historical romance, literary or steampunk story but a mix of all these genres put together. Which I absolutely loved. 
 The only downside to this story was Grace, I wish i would've cared for her more so I would understand the conflict between her and another character better. 
 I would also have liked to find out more about Thaniel's ability to 'see' music.
The end was a bit confusing.

 The Whispering Skull is the second book in the series, set six months after the events that took place in The Screaming Staircase. Picking up the pace from the first one, TWS sees Lockwood & Co. a little busier than they were accustomed to, thanks to the shiny reputation they gained after solving a case in one of England's most haunted houses. 
 If I'm being completely honest, the cast and the dialogue coming from the three main characters (and the skull) are probably the best things about this book. Which isn't to say the rest of it was bad. Yes, the narrative reads like a YA novel thanks to Lucy's vocabulary and manner of speaking (one of the things I love about Stroud's writing) but it's important to remember that this is still a children's book. So the plot's not overly complex, and it kind of lacks the punch that Stroud gave us in the Bartimaeus Sequence, and... it's missing that sense of urgency of danger from his first series as well. And if you're looking for the same wit and snark had us cackling with ol' Barty, then you're going to be disappointed. I mean, the snark's there, just not at the same level as Barty's. 
 But this could just be me nitpicking. It's a good book overall. An enjoyable, if somewhat slow, read. The cast definitely makes up for any of it's shortcomings, and I definitely do recommend it.

I've only read a few of Christopher Golden's books, but I can think of one word that applies thus far: engrossing. 
 Golden is excellent at setting a chilling scene of devastation and survival. His zombie apocalypse focuses on the hungry dead. But this isn't just some contagion turning the living into mindless, ravenous corpses. Instead, Golden brings the supernatural into play and grants his zombies memories, purpose, the ability to reason...these bastards are wily. Having dear departed dad hurl venomous words at you as he tries to bash down the door to chomp your brains is far more terrifying and psychologically damaging than the typical rabid-animal sort of creatures. Time and again, Golden lets us know how connected these revenants are to the living world, how cunning they can be, how ruthless. It's effective. 
 Golden also draws us in by highlighting a variety of characters, hopping around the greater New York area so we can see how the situation spreads and examine how people of disparate backgrounds cope. There's the two college kids, diametrically opposed in their political viewpoints yet thrown together in their need to get to loved ones. There's the Bronx gangbanger (stereotype, but at least his being Korean is unique) on the run who can't quite convince himself not to care about others. There's the teeny bopper singer/actress whose fame should be rendered meaningless in this torn-apart world. And there's the people at the origin point of the phenomenon, flailing in their ignorance of how to put the world to rights. They're all very different - which is what makes their commonalities so striking: the drive to survive; the desire to find those they love; the fierce need to not die alone should it come to that. Hell, even the dead want to be close to their loved ones. (Too bad their version of close means Get In My Belly.) 
 The setting is an added perk for me. Stretching from Manhattan to the Bronx to Westchester, Soulless covers familiar ground. The scenes from the Bronx are 5 minutes from my old neighbourhood - even closer to where I went to high school and college. The Westchester and Manhattan chapters feature stretches of road I've driven a million times, towns and streets where I've spent my weekends. 
 I've never been so keenly aware of how many cemeteries I grew up around... 
 Golden includes fantastic details, both in terms of character and scene development. He slightly changes the POV for each chapter so we can grasp each character's motivation - giving the reader enough to empathise with them without ever pulling us too far from the chaos. He tells and shows what these people are made of. Of the horror surrounding them, there's plenty of gore. But none of it strikes me as gratuitous. The core cast try to maintain a certain remnant of civility in their interactions, their more gruesome acts justified when all things are considered. As for peripheral details, my favourite occurs towards the end as one faction enters Times Square. They witness a huge snow plow barreling down the street, clipping whatever dead it can find. Gory, but so immanently practical. 
 I wonder if they had the salt sprayer going at the back of the truck. (After all, salt is usually good protection when it comes to the supernatural.) 
 It must be said: Let people scoff, but the dedication of the NYC Department of Sanitation in the face of the zombie apocalypse has been duly noted. (How much would I love to hear that driver's story?! And how much time-and-a-half and hazard pay do we think he deserves...) 
 There's a strong message to Soulless and we are beat about the head with it a bit as we come nearer to the close: the human race has become detrimentally detached from reality. We separate ourselves from human connection. We pat ourselves on the back for taming nature to suit our needs. We cause devastation, clean up as best we can, and plod on to wreak havoc another day - lessons un-learned. 
 The characters in Soulless vow to appreciate second chances. But they're just a handful of people. As the risen dead of this tale demonstrate, humans are doomed to revert to what they know, no matter how destructive, how horrific the results. 
 P.S. Lessons un-learned: In light of everything that happened...WHY THE FUCK AREN'T THEY CREMATING ALL THE DEAD FOLK?? ::headdesk:: Maybe some people deserve to be eaten.

 Show of hands. How many of you were worried about Kagawa returning to the Nevernever with a spin-off of an already successful series? *raises hand* I mean, let's think about this for a minute. 
 The Iron Knight 
 concluded and it seemed everything was "happy happy, joy joy," right? But then there were whisperings in the wind of a spin-off and I found myself saying, "What?! NOOO! NO, Julie! I forbid it! Ya hear?!" At the time the saying "Don't beat a dead horse" was running through my head and I was so nervous about this new endeavor. If I'm being honest here, spin-offs usually suck big time. But just like in the case of The Immortal Rules, Julie Kagawa has put me in my place saying, "I got this, YO." And boy, did she ever! The Lost Prince is everything I could want and more. With fresh new characters, cameo appearances and a new evil threatening the Nevernever, how could anyone resist? 
 Before I begin, I need to get something out of my system. 
 PUCK!! I LOVE YOU! 
 *clears throat* 
 What? Don't judge me! 
 Remember the little boy from The Iron King? Meghan's little brother? Did you ever wonder what happened to him and his family once Meghan had gone off for good with her Ice Prince to rule in the Nevernever as a Queen of Faery? That's just what The Lost Prince does. And let me tell you, Ethan Chase is not what I expected. The years of being tormented by the fey and losing his sister to their world has made him a very bitter and angry person. Honestly, I don't blame the guy. He has to constantly look over his shoulder, attempt to pretend They don't exist so as not to draw attention to himself, push people away so they don't catch the eyes of The Good Neighbors. It's a lot of responsibilities for anyone, let alone a teen boy (and yes, he actually sounds like a teen boy). But this is what he has had to endure all his life hopping from school to school due to "bad behavior." Unfortunately for Ethan, the fey just can't seem to stay away from him and he ends up on a quest to save the Nevernever. 
 The plot was brilliantly done. The characters were brilliant. This book was >insert any positive adjective here<!!!! But what did I expect from one of my favorite authors? Exiled fey and half-breeds from the mortal world are disappearing thanks to a new breed of fey. Something even worse then the iron fey?! *gasp* I suspect I know exactly who the Forgotten are if I remember a certain scene from 
 The Iron Knight 
 correctly. But even as someone who has followed this series very closely, I have to admit, I have no idea what direction it could possibly go. 
 The one thing I was worried about most with this spin-off would be comparing the old characters to the new characters. I LOVED the trio in the original series. Meghan, Ash and Puck were the perfect blend of romantic tension, banter and comic relief. And they all do make cameo appearances (Did I mention how much I love Puck?), but this isn't their story. It's Ethan, Kenzie and Kierran's. I really think fans will really enjoy the new trio and it seems like Kagawa has us in for a world of hurt with them too. I mean, I bawled by eyes out so hard with The Iron Queen. Whenever I go back to read that last scene I fall to pieces. But it feels like that could come a lot sooner with The Call of the Forgotten. MY EMOTIONS! Kagawa, stop being so awesome all. the. time! Wait... 
 #DontStop 
 And you know what? Even if you haven't read The Iron Fey - which you'd better go do if you haven't *gives dagger eyes* - you could still follow along easily to this story. For those who have been waiting for a certain Cait Sith (no relation to the cat pictured above, of course) to guide you back through the Nevernever, this will merely feel like a continuation from the original series. And you noobs? There are a few rules you must familiarize yourself with: Never make a contract with Them. Show no fear when dealing with the Fair Folk. Don't draw attention to yourself. And as Grim would say, "Do try and keep up." Welcome to Faery.

1.5 stars. 
 * 
 If you're going to bury the past, bury it deep, girl. Shallow graves always give up their dead. 
 This book has a beautiful and creepy cover, but it was suuuuch a disappointment. 
 I was so excited to start These Shallow Graves. I'd heard so many positive things about it from other people, so I know I'm in the minority when I say this book did not work for me at all. I was expecting something just as creepy and scary as the cover, but unfortunately that wasn't what I got. 
 Actually, the prologue was creepy and scary and really exciting, but what followed was one of the most boring and predictable stories I've read in a while. So much so that I only got to the halfway mark before I skimmed the rest and read only the last few chapters to find out if the twists I predicted happened. They did. 
 My biggest problem was Jo. She was naive to the point of looking incredibly stupid. I understand women, especially young privileged women, being sheltered around that time, but as the book went on it was evident Jo had absolutely no idea what went on in the real world that didn't extend past her circle of equally privileged friends. And that was so disconnected from the Jo we saw in the first chapter when she talked about wanting to be a reporter and even wrote an article about girl laborers. I don't know what happened to that Jo, but to me she was self-centered and unlikable pretty much for the rest of the book. 
 Other problems were: instalove, the predictability of it all, the sloooooow slow pace, flat characters. All of that made These Shallow Graves a torture to read. 
 The one ray of sunshine in this book was Fay. She was badass, fierce, was always prepared for trouble or to cause trouble, and she actually had an interesting backstory! In fact, I might have found this a lot more enjoyable to read if it told Fay's story and not Jo's. 
 * 
 Series: Standalone. 
 POV: Told from Jo's POV. 
 Content Warnings: None.  
 Instalove: Yes.  
 Love Triangle: Jo gets engaged to another guy.  
 Cheating: Not really.  
 Cliffhanger: No. 
 HEA: More open ended than happy.

Scarlet is the sequel to Cinder, and while I sometimes take a breather between books one and two in a series, in this case I jumped right in. Meyer added lots of interesting new facets to her world while still doing a great job of building on the existing ones. Scarlet was still immensely enjoyable, though it did touch on a few of my personal pet peeves. 
 Scarlet is our main character in this retelling of Little Red Riding Hood. Wolf is the love interest and we meet him right away. While I could see some appeal in him, the romantic plotline kind of drove me crazy for two reasons. Scarlet is drawn to Wolf, despite being well aware that she shouldn't trust him. We all have our lapses in judgment, but I thought she was playing a bit too fast and loose on a life or death matter. I also didn't like the fact that it all felt super instalovey. 
 I loved the fact that we still got to see what was going on with Cinder, Prince Kai, and Iko. Seeing how all of their lives were changing is part of what kept me turning the pages of Scarlet so rapidly. I particularly enjoyed meeting Captain Thorne. 
 Even though Scarlet didn't quite live up to Cinder, I still wholly enjoyed reading it. Meyer has created a world that I love to read about. Do we seriously have to wait until 2014 for Cress?

I don't usually read zombie novels, except I'm missing out on an entire group of my beloved post-apocalyptic stories by doing that, so when this showed up on a lot of "Best of 2010" lists for speculative fiction, I earmarked it to give it a try. Then it was offered through NetGalley and I blitzed through it on a few sick days. Oh the irony of reading this book on a cold! 
 The zombies aren't exactly zombies in the traditional sense, or at least they didn't start out that way. The cures for cancer and the common cold morphed into a super virus that turns any mammal of a certain weight into a host. All humans have the virus lying dormant, and it is all a matter of time. 
 But that isn't really the story. A group of political bloggers are invited along the campaign trail of a presidential hopeful, among them adopted brother and sister Shaun and Georgia Mason. The story centers around the campaign, with the background of a country damaged by The Rising, which started around 20 years ago. 
 My only complaint is that the villains are too obvious and that the idea that bloggers being accepted as "real news" being futuristic was a little hard to swallow- that ship has sailed!

This book, this series- was AMAZING! Everyone has pretty much summed up & explained this story and we all agree it is outstanding! All I have left to say is.... BEST. BOOK. BOYFRIEND. EVVVVER!!!! Cole freaking Murphy is the sh*t! :) "To the moon & back!"

Got half way through and I just couldn't finish. This was horrible. 
 I'm good with mystery, and good with gore, I'm very good with horror but this was just depressing. Pages and pages describing in detail the torture (and I stopped reading just before the sexual abuse) of a young girl is just not something I want to spend my time on. Which kind of got me thinking because as a huge fan of horror this was the fist time I've been repelled by a book. Probably because it was too real, too depressing, and that was before I found out it was based on a true story. 
 Horror thrives in the subtleties, in the unsaid and unseen. It's a psychological thrill of the mind that challenges our most primal instincts. This book was not horror. 
 Mystery plays on the puzzle. On trying to understand, succeeding or failing, but in the end getting the answer. This book was not mystery. 
 This book was written for shock value. It was written for the part of us that wants to stare at a train wreck, to know the gory details of what really happened. It was written to drown the reader in sorrow and anguish. I stopped reading before I could find out if there was a way out, an emotional catharsis to release all that pain. I'm not sure there was. 
 If you managed to get through the book and find some kind of insight in what makes us evil, the power of authority and how it's the actions of ordinary people that should really scare us, then good for you. Personally, just reading a short summary about the real case was enough to get that for me. I didn't need the 370 pages of emotional and physical abuse.

3.5 stars. I enjoyed When you were here because I like teen books written from the guy's perspective and I think the author did a good job in capturing that mind set. Even before reading the acknowledgements or even starting to read the book I knew that this was in the vein of or inspired by Gayle Forman's work. And I think readers who enjoyed her books will enjoy this one too. Danny is about to graduate from high school but his life so far has left him pretty much alone except for his faithful dog Sandy Koufax. His mom recently passed away after a long battle with cancer, his dad passed away years ago as well unexpectedly from an accident and the love of his life Holland has broken up with him. Danny takes whatever comfort he can get in prescription drugs, a non-chalant attitude towards parties at his house, casual sex with an older girl and even crashing his car as he parks it one day upon arriving home. From this description you would never guess that Danny is the valedictorian and is set to give a graduation speech - but Danny's mom was supposed to hang on so that she could attend his ceremony and now she is gone. After graduating Danny sets off to Tokyo - a place that him and his family have gone to throughout the years and a place where his mom was seeking one last chance at survival from a so-called miracle doctor. Danny wants to find out why his mom did not hold on for those last two months, but in Tokyo he actually finds out that and much, much more that he did not bargain for. The story was filled with both sadness and loss, but also hope and love. I really enjoyed the bond Danny had with his dog and also his insights into life, death and love. There were heartfelt moments and also some cutesy stuff too and lots of scenery into some aspects of Tokyo life.

The Birds of Azalea Street by Nova Ren Suma- Rating: 4 Stars- I really enjoyed this one, and thought that it was a great start to the book. It took me a couple pages to get into, but this story totally engrossed me. Suma took things that happen in real life, and mixed it with a bit of fantasy. Imagine Law & Order SVU with a sprinkle of Lani Taylor. Suma was able to create a horror that will leave readers wondering if there's someone peaking through their window. 
 In the Forest Dark and Deep by Carrie Ryan- Rating: 3.5 Stars- This was so interesting! I have never read such an interesting (or dark) Alice in Wonderland inspired story. Welcome to Wonderland, but watch out for the White Rabbit, he may or may not be a psychopath. While the story was a bit confusing at first, this one kept me biting my nails until the very last word. 
 Emmeline by Cat Winters- Rating: 2.5 Stars- I think that my main problem with this one was that I tend to not like historical fiction. But I also thought that it just wasn't that scary or thrilling. The characters were also a tad bit annoying. But I did really like the setting, the story, and the overall concept. 
 Verse Chorus Verse by Leigh Bardugo- Rating: DNF- I've had bad luck with Bardugo's stories, and this one was no exception. This story was very boring. It took me three days to read seven pages, and it just didn't seem worth it to continue reading. 
 Hide-And-Seek by Megan Shepherd- Rating: 5 Stars- Now THIS is what I wanted! This was such a fun little novella! I really enjoyed Shepherd's Madman's Daughter trilogy, but I hadn't read anything else by her. I loved how much action was packed into this one. Some of the other stories cold be boring at times, but this one always kept me entertained. I also loved the folklore behind the story. I had never heard of Crow Cullom before, and I'm sure that I won't be forgetting about him anytime soon. Finally, I loved how this book scared me. It's hard to scare me, but this book totally gave me the chills. 
 The Dark, Scary Parts and All by Danielle Paige- Rating: 5 Stars- This was a fabulous story! It didn't have as much action as the previous novella, but I could not put it down! I really enjoyed reading about Marnie. She was a fun character. I thought that it was interesting how she wanted to do the right thing, but she had some evil in her that would be heard. And this story brought up the question, are you willing to love someone, even with their dark, scary parts and all? 
 The Flicker, The Fingers, The Beat, The Sigh by April Genevieve Tucholke- Rating: 1 Star- This wasn't a scary story, this was a sad story. The characters were bland, and I didn't really like any of them (except for Canary, who we really didn't get to meet). There was nothing really interesting about this one, and I was honestly expecting more from the person who put the book together. 
 Fat Girl with a Knife by Jonathan Maberry- Rating: 2 Stars- This was an okay story, but I didn't really like it. I felt for the MC, but I didn't really connect with her. That pretty much ruined the rest of the story for me. I do wish that we had seen more of the zombies, and less of her family. 
 Sleepless by Jay Kristoff- Rating: 3 Stars- This one was super creepy! But I didn't enjoy it as much as some of the other stories. That being said, this was probably the creepiest story I have ever read. This story was the perfect example of the internet going wrong. Told through the POV of a killer, this one will surely give you the creeps. 
 M by Stefan Bachmann- Rating: 2.5 Stars- This was another okay story, I didn't love it, and I didn't hate it. I was super confused at first, and the story started off slow. But it quickly sped up as we were trying to figure out who the murder was. I didn't really like the MC, and that made the novella less enjoyable for me. 
 The Girl without a Face by Marie Lu- Rating: 3 Stars- This was a solid story from Lu! I really enjoyed the mental scares that this one gave. It was interesting to see the MC's guilt form into this monster that followed him. This one could be a little triggering to some readers though, so read with caution. 
 The Girl Who Dreamed of Snow by McCormick Templeman- Rating: 4 Stars- I really liked this one! I thought that it was impressive that Templeman had multiple POVs, and was still able to make each character connectable. I loved the idea of this girl hunting down bad guys for the greater good, and that the "authority figure" was sweet, and not completely heartless. I'm excited to read more of Templeman's work. 
 Stitches by A.G. Howard- Rating: 5 Stars- I loved this story! Howard is the master of creepy stories, and this one did not disappoint. This one had very cool characters, and always kept me guessing. It was gruesome, but that just added to the appeal of the story for me. 
 On the I-5 by Kendare Blake- Rating: 4 Stars- I think that this was a strong ending to the overall novella. I liked the concept of this one, and thought that it made for an interesting and thrilling story. I didn't connect with the MC as much as I wish that I had, but this was still a great story.

You guys! This book was so good! You know those books where you read a page, even just a couple paragraphs, and you know that you are going to love that book? This was totally this book for me. I loved all of the characters, and how diverse they were! This book defiantly surprised me, and I am very glad that I read it! 
 In this book we follow three BFFs, though the book is only told through the perspectives of two of them. There's Charlie, who is a YouTuber and actress who is trying to escape the shadow of her ex boyfriend and costar; there is also Taylor, who has social anxiety, and has feelings for the third BFF, Jamie. The three of them go to a convention, SupaFan, where new relationships are formed, and characters break out of their shells. 
 I loved Charlie in this book! I thought that it was very cool that we got to see her try to distance herself from her old boyfriend, and also form a new relationship with a girl that she really liked. I loved Charlie's relationship with Alyssa, and I thought that they made a really cute couple, but not as cute as Taylor and Jamie. Taylor and Jamie were just the cutest couple! I was rooting for them from chapter one, and I absolutely loved watching them take their first steps in their relationship. 
 Even though it was cool to read about Charlie, especially because we are both bisexual, I found an especially soft spot in my heart for Taylor. It was so empowering to read about her facing her fears, and her meeting people like her. It was also cool because I found parts of myself in her, and I loved what she said about anxiety, and not being able to fit in. 
 So overall I loved this book! This book had a lot of cute, fun, and tear filled moments. With enough movie, video game, and book references to get your inner geek jumping around, this is a highly enjoyable book. 
 ~Anna <3

Stacia Kane didn't hold back with this, the second installment of the Downside Ghosts series. Her characters are just as flawed as ever, just as human as ever. Her ghosts are perhaps even more chilling than ever and after the first installment that took some doing. 
 I found myself seeing some of the corruption of the party line in the Church, but for the most part wanting to forgive the Church for it. It was easy to push it off as a "best for all" understanding of a situation in this book. However, I am still untrusting of this Church overall, if not all those who are a part of it. In terms of wanting to see where Ms. Kane takes this Church, I am completely hooked and can't wait to see if she keeps it merely a framework or if it becames the living, breathing, participating character it seems to want to be. 
 I found myself angry both at and for Chess, our protagonist. I don't usually hold too much of a grudge against folks for an addiction, not if they are highly functional. I respect everyone's right to fight their demons their way, whether I agree or not, whether it is self destructive or not. But I found my tolerance for Chess' addictions beginning to unravel in the book. Truth be told I was a bit frustrated with Ms. Kane, as well. You see, Chess' addictions are about enabling her to stay in denial about pretty much everything. Denial as the personality flaw is a fairly well, indeed overly well, used urban fantasy trope. It's one of the list of things I've become frustrated to see in heroines. So, while I find the use of the drug addiction to add grit, flavor, and new layers to the story, I'm frustrated at the lack of originality for what it's being used for. 
 You thought I was going to say I'm frustrated that the "highly functioning addict" is unraveling and starting to not be as highly functioning, didnt you? Well, yeah, that too. But I can see how it's part of the story. I'm anticipating the unraveling, hoping that it will facilitate some part of Chess' self-actualization. It's effectively pulling me in and making me want to kick her butt. 
 The romance elements in this book were quite frustrating. It was a veritable plethora of "see what kind of cluster fuck you can create when you're too much of a wimp to look at yourself and the situation around you?" From several areas. My heart is aching for Terrible, and at the same time I'm angry with him. I understand why Chess finds Lex easy to spend time with, he's charismatic and attentive, but I still can't trust him entirely. I'm confused by my unwillingness to trust Lex and my total willingness to trust Terrible when neither has done anything worse or better than the other, just different. 
 Yes, Stacia Kane has sucked me in to this gritty world that's I feel a bit more in tune with, and I'm eager to find out what happens with these characters.

So I'm going to do this review in a list form just to keep everything straight since this book was such a clusterfuck compared to the others. I feel like if I don't put down my thoughts in a simple 1, 2, 3, pattern I'll just lose them completely and end up on endless rants. So here are just a few major and minor problems I had with the book. 
 1.	Pacing: Let's start with pacing. It was so hard to get into this book. After the cliff hanger left by Catching Fire I expected this book to start off with something big, some bang that would catch my interest and draw me back into the world of Panem. Instead I get a book that starts with "I stare down at my shoes, watching as a fine layer of ash settles on the worn leather." Honestly I was looking forward to seeing how Katniss would react to the news. Instead I'm thrown into a lifeless world with an equally lifeless Katniss who has seemingly given up all hope right off the bat. 
 Even with the beginning of the book being slow, the rest didn't pick up much either. There were some scenes that I enjoyed reading through but they would be brought to a grinding halt with Katniss' internal monologue that served no point in that scene. She will be in the middle of a battle and start to think of who she should choose, or what the point of it all is? It seems that without the Arena to set the stage Collin's writing has stuttered out and Katniss has lost her fire. 
 2.	Setting: This may be a minor complaint but it's something that bugged me nonetheless. With the monotone writing, the monotone character of Katniss, and the monotone plot, the monotone and banal setting of District 13 doesn't help much. The reader rarely gets a glimpse of the outside world and when they do it's covered in ash, or blood, or gloom. I miss the arenas mostly because of the settings they offered. It was such a dark story to tell in such beautiful places. One of the main reasons that I dislike war movies is because there are always 3 things present in all of them: 1. Someone commits suicide because war is sad, 2. The setting appears in grey, brown, and lifeless colors, 3. The message is always the same. You can argue with me if you like but it won't change my opinions on war movies. Just sayin'. 
 I felt that way with this book. Since its central theme was war the whole tone of the book is set in a dull, grey, monotonous area with no light, no vivid colors, no real look at the outside world. Even when they get sent into the real world it's the grey and brown of buildings, the red of blood, the silver glint of metal, nothing outstanding. Nothing to pull it out of the grim of the plot and characters with a glimpse of something beautiful. 
 3.	Characters: Who are these people? Katniss is meek and uncaring half the time, then a spitfire the next until she gets knocked out and ends up in the hospital at least. But most of the book is her being manipulated, forced into roles she doesn't want, and generally giving up on life. What happened to the girl who held up those berries knowing that the capital wouldn't let them both die? What happened to the girl who played by her own rules? 
 Peeta is not even Peeta anymore, and the real Peeta, the personality I'd come to love, is nowhere to be seen in this book. Even the "brief glimpses" don't feel like Peeta at all. I loved the boy who loved Katniss for who she was, who knew who he was even in the darkest of times, and even though he struggled he always wanted to do the right thing even if it meant dying. 
 Gale feels like the only one who has really remained the same. Don't get me wrong I like Gale as a character but as a love interest for Katniss I just never bought it. Even the best friend thing is hard to buy when he still doesn't even know Katniss. He jumps to anger in a lot of the scenes, uncaring as long as the end result takes down the capital. He can't read Katniss the way Peeta did, and he never tries to coax out the best in her. I just feel like Gale and Katniss should probably have a stronger relationship if they've known each other for so long. As a character though Gale is headstrong, I enjoy that, he knows what he wants and how he feels and will do anything to achieve it. Unless that thing is Katniss, but oh well let's ignore that for now. 
 The rest of the characters all seemed like drugged up versions of themselves, down on their luck and questioning the meaning of life at all turns. And I don't mean philosopher style, I mean "What's the point in being on this planet anymore?" and it just made the whole book feel like this gloom was settling over everything. 
 4.	The Plot: Weak. I hate it because near the end when everything comes together all these images flash before my eyes. The ideas are good. No really they are. But they are so poorly executed it's unbearable! Things just need to happen to get the plot to the end that everything in this book is corrupted, the characters are made to act in ways to move the plot along its path, and a lot of it feels like it was all thrown in last minute because that's when Collins' thought of it. 
 5.	The End What the fuck!? Alright so Katniss never has to choose, everyone in the way is conveniently moved someplace else so that Katniss, by default ends up with Peeta. And the whole conversation that Katniss will choose who she needs to survive instead of who she loves and she gets bitter over it? Remember that? Yeah and then in the end it's all true? It was such a waste, such a stupid pointless waste! Even at the end I'm sure if Gale came back she still wouldn't be able to decide. 
 Another thing which bothers me because 1. I don't want kids either, 2. I've seen this destroy some marriages. Katniss doesn't want kids, her reasons are valid, and yet she decides to have them for Peeta. This can make a person bitter and resentful of their partner for forcing that kind of commitment on them when they made it very clear that isn't what they wanted. Katniss even admits that having the children felt wrong to her and she didn't really like it. That she still struggles with how to bring them up and how to explain the world to them. All she can think of is how she's raising them into a world full of death. Why would someone who loves her like Peeta does force this on her? It just bothered me so much! Probably because I personally don't want kids so it just irks me that much more.  
 Extra: The only time I really felt sad at Prim's loss was when Buttercup walked all that way to find her. The cat broke my heart more than any "human" character did.

A murder and conspiracy mystery set during the reign of Henry VIII, just on the eve of his infamous 'Great Matter'. I was intrigued by the summary, and picked it up from my library. 
 I found the first fifty pages of the story a bit slow, but I kept going and eventually found myself sucked into the tale. 
 Diener creates quite the conspiracy, weaving in the various people and factions of the court of Henry VIII, people like the Duke of Norfolk, William Carey (the first husband of the (in)famous Mary Boleyn), and Nicholas Carew as part of a plot to bring down the king and put one of the Yorkist exiles up in his place. It was quite fascinating, trying to figure out where everyone stood - who was a willing player, who had been sucked in unwillingly, etc. 
 Some parts of the story were a bit jumpy, especially in the beginning when the various attempts on Susanna's life started. It hardly seemed like she and John Parker could have a chance to say five words to each other before they were jumped yet again by men wielding swords/knives/meat cleavers. Also as a result of those constant interruptions, the romance between Susanna and Parker seemed a bit stilted at times. 
 Nonetheless, it was an interesting read. Enough that I'm curious to see more, and thus look forward to seeing the next book in the series.

 I've been gorging on romance novels lately. After reading A Night to Surrender by Tessa Dare, I couldn't wait to read the next full-length novel in the Spindle Cove series. But at the same time, I was nervous, because how could A Week to Be Wicked be as amazing as A Night to Surrender? But, you guys, Tessa Dare created such a wonderful, amazing, book, and I actually liked A Week to Be Wicked even MORE than the first book - which is saying a lot. Basically, Tessa Dare writes my kind of books. 
 In A Week to Be Wicked, we follow Minerva, Spindle Cove's spectacles-wearing geology expert and Colin, Lord Payne, reluctant resident, and lady's man, of Spindle Cove, as they travel to Scotland. I first met Colin and Minerva in A Night to Surrender, so I had an idea of what A Week to Be Wicked would be like, who I thought these two characters where. I was wrong, though. Well, slightly, anyway. Dare brings so much more to Minerva and Colin than I was expecting, but also keeps them like their A Night to Surrender selves. 
 Minerva is a bit geeky, really. She loves to read, she wears glasses, and her passion is geology. She's the middle child, and she has an older sister (Diana) who's beautiful and sweet and kind, and a younger sister who's beautiful and a little wild. Minerva's mother doesn't always have the nicest things to say about her middle daughter, but Minerva weathers it well. I loved that Dare didn't make Minerva a stereotype, though, of that geeky, overlooked girl. Minerva is just Minerva. She loves rocks, and her sisters, and Spindle Cove. 
 I was actually really surprised with how easily Dare made me fall in love with Colin. Ovbiously, I was expecting to like him, but I wasn't sure if I could truly love him as a character. He's a bit reckless, even irresponsible at times, both traits that I don't usually find attractive. But there is so much more to Colin, and Dare showcases it perfectly. Oh my gosh, and can Colin make up stories! Definitely one of my favorite parts of the book was when Colin was inventing all these tales and telling them to the people they met on their way to Scotland. It was hilarious, and I loved him all the more for it. And of course, Colin's refusal to call Minerva her name, always calling her other names that being with M, was adorable. 
 There were no slow parts in A Week to Be Wicked. Honestly, I couldn't put this book down. I started it Sunday, and finished it on Sunday. I loved seeing how dislike and misunderstanding bloomed into like, respect and then love between Colin and Minerva. Really, who can resist a hate-to-love story? It always brings to mind Pride and Prejudice and we all know how perfect that book is. But, seriously, it was the perfect way to spend my Sunday. 
 As much as I love romances, I am not into sappy stuff. I say this because, usually I'm not super into huge, emotional declarations of love. Simple "I love yous" are more my style. But I totally got all swoony with Colin's declaration. It wasn't sappy at all, but he certainly was very clear on elaborating all the reasons he loved Minerva (this totally isn't a spoiler - this is a romance - this is what always happens). I couldn't stop sighing and smiling. Even hours after finishing the book. 
 A Week to Be Wicked is near perfection in my mind, and is one of the few historical romances that I will read again. I loved the characters, the humor, the hate-to-love relationship. Basically, I loved almost everything. I wanted to start the third Spindle Cove novel right after finishing this one, but forced myself to wait a few days. But I only ended up waiting four days, because I just need to read more Tessa Dare!!

Urgh...i know i am going to get a lot of grief for this, but i have to say i didn't like it. Not that it didn't have potential, or a damned good story. It did, in fact it had tonnes. 
 So why oh why couldn't i get into it??? 
 Inconsistencies, and terrible WTF-ery are to blame for drilling so many holes, that eventually sunk this ship... 
 What i thought was truly awesome and original was the world in witch Karou grew up, her art, Brimstone, Kishmish and all the rest. One of my favorites was the living puppet, that scene took the show. The magical portal between two worlds, and the nuances in between were so cleverly designed, that i must say that the first few chapters had me glued to the novel. Karou's innocence in a way, and her very human reaction to the possibility of having a wish within your grasp. The concept of Brimstone, a different being, a wielder of magic, a tooth-fairy like you never seen before. The originality of it all, and the superb execution of it, promised a very fun ride. 
 Sadly it didn't stay that way. 
 The deeper i got into this story the less sense it made. It seemed so elaborate in the beginning, but then it started to slack off, and i found some of the explanations, well, kinda....unbelievable. 
 I know friendships, i know some friends are more understanding then the rest, but for the love of god, i just can't, can't, can't stomach the idea of the mega-super-uber-totes-frosty-beyond-fab-BFF who takes all the supernatural other-worldliness you might throw at them with a simple grin, and a cheesy one-liner. 
 1."I grew up as a Devil's spawn!".... 
 2."Oh my Gaaaawd! That's like, totally awesome, no biggie." 
 1."There's a world you don't know about, right outside your window, and people can get killed or mutilated by forces unknown to man." 
 2."GTFO, are those new highlights? Like, guuuuuurl..." 
 1."This is a supernatural creature, it's an unknown, it's powers are unknown, it has HURT me in the past, some could say it wanted to kill me." 
 2."Uh-huh, did you guys hook up? You totes need to hook up, does he have a brother?" 
 Not just the BFF, but her boyfriend too, nobody here bats a frigging eyelid over the actual existence of angels and demons here. 
 Makes sense??? Nope, to me either, yet it happens, and when authors do that, i simply disconnect. It goes from being an awesome story, to a cheesy TV show with a cheesy predictable ending. My respect for common sense of the storyline diminishes, therefore my respect for the story as a whole suffers. 
 Brimstone made her filthy rich....how? Did she receive a letter from Satan & Son Solicitors, in regards to his Last Will and Testament, to be opened in the case of his otherworldly demise by angelic fire? Or did she simply pull it out of her arse? 
 The blatant disregard for common sense continues with flights throughout a brimming metropolitan city, sitting on a cathedral, fights in the air, all and i mean all with witnesses aplenty, cameras rolling, and only a few cursory questions asked. Her wandering with no actual goal, no actual idea, no actual PLAN is childish. Too childish for me to stay interested. So sorry, this is a 2 star review for me, and nope, i won't read any more of it either.

How embarrassing to have to admit that I simply plowed through this book like an addicted maniac. Not since Twilight have I found myself at once inhaling a book and laughing at myself for doing so. 
 Yikes, where to begin? Fifty Shades of Grey, first off, is not going to win any writing awards. The writing itself is rather on the awful side. How many times must the lead character bite her lip? How many times do we have to be told how unbelievably gorgeous Christian Grey is? Why can't this British writer manage to sort out American word usage? No, we Americans do not have marquees... At the very least, this book could have used a good editor. 
 And yet, I couldn't help myself. I got totally absorbed in this rather trite love story. Can you actually call it a love story? I'm not sure. Innocent, virginal Anastasia Steele falls under the spell of the handsome, enigmatic billionaire Christian Grey, who has a tortured past and a kinky soul. Will he break her, or will she change him? 
 Yes, I know that Fifty Shades supposedly started as Twilight fanfiction, and all the elements are pretty obvious. Meek, self-conscious, clumsy girl who just doesn't realize how special and beautiful she is. Otherworldy good-looking and unobtainable older leading man with a dangerous secret, who has never let anyone get close to him. Warnings from him to her about how she should run away while she still can. Stalker-like behavior, showing up uninvited, taking up every moment of her life, wanting to lavish her with expensive gifts, constantly fearful for her safety. 
 I think I'm making it sound much worse than it is! I can make fun of it no end, but the fact remains that once I started, I really couldn't put this down. The end isn't really an ending, just a stop at a dramatic moment, which means -- damn it! -- that I must immediately acquire book #2. 
 And for those who haven't read all the other hype about this book: Yes, it's graphic. Definitely not for the prudish or faint of heart. Otherwise, have at it, but be warned -- once you start, you probably won't get a whole lot done until you finish.
