There are several borrowings by Western authors of the Russian fairy tale "Vasilisa the Beautiful," particularly involving Koschei, or the mysterious man who represents Death, but this one stood out from the pack for me. Arden's novel contains elements of other Russian fairy tales, most notably "The Frog Princess." 
 I have trouble getting pulled into any fantasy whether the setting is fairy tale or historical in setting, when the fairy tale or historical names seem randomly sprinkled over what is basically another story about a modern American girl with a modern outlook, dressed in costume, as she gains power and agency. There is definitely a feminist subtext here, too, in this tale of Vasya, a wild colt of a girl (she is often referred to as such, especially when men desire her, when she isn't likened to a wild falcon) whose mother died at her birth after claiming that this daughter was for her. But Arden weaves her tale into a rich world, giving the sparkle of life to the stock figures. 
 All the fairy tale elements are there--the antagonistic stepmother, the three brothers, the beautiful stepsister, but Arden tales the time to give each a distinctive personality, with motivations of their own. Even the stepmother at least begins with an interesting dilemma which makes her nominally sympathetic, in that she didn't want to marry at all, and that she has second-sight unlike those around her. She thinks she is alone in seeing demons. 
 Arden chose to set her tale in a specific period of history, when Russians were still sending tribute to the Tatars, and Moscow was mostly a wooden city half-smothered in the soot of constant fires. She evokes the harsh northern seasons, and how life adapted, while weaving in the magical folk figures who seem to be dying off as the people's faith turns to Christianity. 
 We are given two compellingly handsome men of great power, the first, Morozoko, being the Koschei or Death figure--who has appeared in several recent fantasies, ageless and yet beguiled by our teenage heroine. Arden even gives a nod to the trope. 
 The second is a beautiful icon-painting priest with charisma and conviction, who is sent to the north to remove his influence from Moscow. I'm glad to say that Arden mostly avoids the usual treatment of these historical figures (those eeevil Xtian priests versus the noble and environmentally supportive pagans)--mostly. Though she does a great job with evoking the hunger to make art in the icon painter, she manages to leave out the joy, instead telling us that Konstantin is driven by fear instead of faith, without troubling to go into why. 
 His struggle against attraction and his vow of celibacy, and his fall, would have been a lot more interesting if the authorial hand hadn't been quite so heavy in pushing him toward villainy. 
 The stepmother gets the same treatment: at the beginning, we are sympathetic with her desire to become a nun and live in the safety of the convent, ignored by her politically minded family, but then she turns into a screeching, hateful figure, and so becomes less a character than a plot device.)  
 There is nothing new or insightful here: a girl who doesn't fit in discovers her own agency, while the new ways replace the old, but it still made absorbing reading. I appreciated how Vasya, at least at first, did her best to find the old peaceful balance between old ways and new, and the magical razzle-dazzle built to an absorbing climax, even if confusing at times. Suddenly there is a vampire, who recognizes her mother in her. What was that about? Intriguing and yet frustrating as there is no explanation. . 
 Mostly, though, I loved the care with which Arden builds her characters as well as furnishes details of life at that time--the smells, the sights, the foods, the language and what the different nicknames tell us not only about the character being addressed, but the one speaking. 
 By using a specific time, place, and a few actual Russian historical real people, and crafting their world so vividly, Arden gives us the resonance of the real, painted with a magical palimpsest.

 Ever since I started this series, I have been terrified of The Raven King. My love of this world and series is too strong, and series endings so often splat right on their faces, poisoning all that came before. Bless Gansey that this does not happen in The Raven King. Just seriously blessssss. I love my babies, and I love the ending that they've had here. In some ways, The Raven King might be the weakest of the series for me, but it's still fucking brilliant and nigh perfect so who even cares. 
 Squad goals are Henrietta. I mean, there's the 300 Fox Way psychic squad which is down but not out, and, though this book is very much not about the adults, I want to rep them in the background being awesome. I have a lot of Calla feels and Maura feels and Mr. Gray feels and they are all so delightful and found family and MY FEELINGS. Then obviously there's the OT5 of friendship of Gansey, Blue, Ronan, Adam, and Noah. They are so fucking adorable and perfect. 
 I know I talk a lot about banter and how "I love you" doesn't really sell relationships to me as much as sort of being insulting but in a loving fashion. Maggie makes that an artform. When Ronan calls you an asshole, it's basically a declaration of undying love and support and how he will fucking murder anyone who hurts you. He calls all of them assholes a lot basically. And they return the favor. I'm using this as an example of why these relationships kill me so much. Stiefvater doesn't just say "oh hey this is deep abiding love and I'm labeling it"; she shows you in actions and fights and being there for each other that these people love each other and will be friends forever. The romance is stellar but the series is more about the deep, unabiding found family love and friendship between all of these people. All of them find the acceptance and love and caring that they've been searching for all this time. 
 Given how tight-knit the group is, I'm massively impressed that Stiefvater managed to fit someone else into the dynamic without it feeling unreal. So very happy to get more Henry Cheng, to get the real Henry Cheng. Also to find out that he is indeed half-Chinese. I do wish he'd been a wee bit more present in the earlier books, but I still think that he really fits into The Raven King beautifully. I really love when Gansey and Blue bond with him and his friends. All of them can be very clique-ish, and they'd definitely dismissed him as too Aglionby or too different or something, but, once they get to really know him, it turns out he's awesome. There's also a LOT in this series about first impressions versus how someone actually is, from Gansey's ruinous first impression to Blue's tininess. Things and people are not always what they seem on the surface. Like, say GLENDOWER.  
 Emotionally, I am definitely one hundred and six million percent happy with The Raven King. Everything I wanted I got with bonus Henry Cheng. Such a delightful bonus. This ending is so very emotionally satisfying, even if I do still want a million more books about these people because I LOVE THEM SO DAMN MUCH. 
 Intellectually, I do have a few qualms about The Raven King. They don't ruin it for me, but I am left with some thoughts. The Raven King feels somewhat rushed and packed in a way that none of the other books did. Some of those characters clearly brought in briefly early on now need to be justified to the larger plot, it seems. The introduction of Piper's three-headed (sort of) father is awkward and didn't really seem to add much value. 
 What bothers me most, I think, is Glendower. Now, I don't mind that Glendower was actually truly dead the whole time, because I don't mind anticlimactic endings like that really. It's about the journey and sometimes things don't turn out how you think. The victory was theirs, not some deus ex machina where God-dower steps in and fixes everything at the end. It's better this way. At the same time, though, WHO IS THE THIRD SLEEPER???? 
 The death and resurrection of Gansey is something my heart and mind are torn on. I mean, I would not have been happy with dead Gansey at all. And, I mean, I always knew it would be a "Gansey dies but is brought to life" plot, but it also does feel a bit too easy. But then does it? GAH. I am torn as I said. Cabeswater just doesn't really seem an equal sacrifice, especially since Ronan can just dream it back up. But whatever. I choose to be happy because why the fuck not?  
 The Raven Cycle is one of my very favorite things ever. Bless Meg and Gillian for pushing and pushing and pushing until I finally read it. Bless Stiefvater for writing this. Bless the whole crew for being the most wonderful OT6 of friendship and love. I can't believe it's over. I hope Maggie writes spinoffs.

When I first read what this book was about, I got really excited. It sounded so good and I began to have high expectations. When I was asked by the publisher to review this book, I said yes without hesitation. Once I got the book in my hands though, I began to worry. What if it wasn't as good as I had thought? What if it was a big, huge disappointment? I opened this book and began reading the first page...by the next day, I had finished reading this book. 
 Bronwen isn't really Bronwen Oliver. Instead, she's really Phoebe Lilywhite, daughter of Percival and Kitty Lilywhite...or at least Bronwen likes to think she is. Bronwen likes to live in her fantasy where she is switched at birth. She just wants to be with her "real" parents. After all, her brown hair is so much different from her mother's. So when she meets Jared, she's happy to learn that with Jared comes a great, loving family, just like the one she wanted. She can't get enough of the Sondervans and their conversations and their acceptance of Bronwen. Soon, Bronwen finds herself somewhere she never imagined being in the near future: engaged! 
 Erin McCahan's I Now Pronounce You Someone Else was a great read. I loved the dialogue and the short scenes that would have seemed choppy if they hadn't been so well written. There wasn't a place in this book where I was confused. I loved reading about how Bronwen really was Phoebe Lilywhite because of all of her humorous examples! The characters were great and I loved them all, especially Bronwen. I LOVED how she was such a strong girl but she had her moments, when she was sad and scared and needing help. I liked reading about the relationship with her mother and her step father and everyone else and the death of her father. For some reason, I found Bronwen's murky relationship with her step-father...interesting and sweet. At first I couldn't figure out why she acted that way to him, but once everything came out, I felt SO bad for Bronwen. I hated her mother when the truth was revealed and I loved how her step father handled the situation. 
 My one big iffy moment with this book was the fast moving relationship between Bronwen and Jared. I mean, a senior collage guy was ready to commit to a senior in high school? It just moved too fast for my taste. But that's about it. 
 I loved the ending because it left the door open for many possibilities, though I was glad about the decision Bronwen made. It just showed me that she really was a strong willed girl who knew what she wanted, though it took her a while to get there. I Now Pronounce You Someone Else was a great read and I'm in love with it! Erin McCahan's debut is a must read. It's fresh, quirky, charming and has a great heroine!

I feel like it's difficult to write a novella or even a short story about a dystopian/post-apocalyptic world. There's all this world creation you have to do, and not nearly enough time and space to do it in. 
 "Stupid Perfect World" suffered from this lack of space. I didn't get to know enough about the world the characters inhabited or even about the characters themselves. I loved the idea of a "Scarcity" class, where students studied life before whatever it was that suddenly made this world so great. But other aspects were fuzzier. For example: Kieran and Maria choose Scarcity projects like sleeping a little and experiencing teenage hormones/puberty (which, apparently equals writing poetry?). These projects change them, but they aren't life-threatening. But most of their other classmates choose diseases as their Scarcity projects: parasitic worms that cause blindness, cancer, the common cold (doesn't sound that deadly, but the character who chooses it gets a doozy of a cold). All danger of this is counteracted, however, by the fact that apparently they cannot die. They have something called bioframes (never really explained) that prevent them from dying. This does serve to assuage my worry for these high school students safety. I was skeptical of a world that would allow 16 or 18 year olds to threaten their health in such dramatic ways. But it also made me not worry for anyone in the story. No one could die, right? So there was nothing to worry about, no drama. 
 A quick read, and an interesting concept, but more explanation and maybe 50 more pages would have made it better.

Okay. I'm pretty sure I'm not Mr. John Green's target audience anymore. I was past that age even before I started reading his books. But this one still got to me. 
 It's a simple enough story, with some considerate continent developments that can't be ignored. I still enjoyed it a lot, and even shed some tears in the end. 
 Aza was a character that's not often featured in YA books, not your typical I'm troubled by some distinct problem with my family life/my love life pretty girl. She's troubled alright, but even she can't name her fears. Throughout the story, Aza is in turn angry at herself for being sick, angry at the others for not understanding, and angry at herself for troubling the people in her life. It's heartbreaking and sometimes frustrating to read about. But if you want an honest depiction of mental issues, I think this might be as real as a bestselling author can offer. 
 Davies is less unique than Aza(I guess), though I really liked this character. I can't resist a lonely but sensitive and gentle boy character, especially when he's doubting his self-worth when we readers know he's precious. 
 The fanfic references crack me up so often. If you're in the fanfic world, you know what it's like. It's even funnier and more real(in my opinion) than the Fangirl ones. Since this book is not based upon the fanfic world, the references are just here and there, like how it is in real life. 
 I also loved Aza and Daisy's friendship. Daisy is not your typical pretty and rich but kind AF bestie character, either. And I loved that she had a personality and some temper. 
 Regarding the teenagers not talking like real teenagers issue many readers have stated, it doesn't really bother me. I don't read books to learn how American teenagers talk, I read books to enjoy stories and learn stuff. This book offers an interesting and moving story, and educate us about mental issues. That's good enough for me. I really don't need some "real teenage talk" to enjoy the story or get what the book is trying to say. 
 As I've seen other people comment in reviews of this book, I understand why some people don't like John Green's books, but they're by no means trash, they're well crafted. That's my opinion, too. 
 Fun fact, Rick Riordan wrote in one of his Percy Jackson books(can't remember which one), when Dionysus pretended to forget Jason Grace and Annabeth's names, he called them "John Green" and "Annie Bell". And in this book, Davies' ex is called Annie Bell. Coincidence? I don't know. But it's funny as hell for me.

Jack and his wife Patience are just scraping by when they discover that Patience is pregnant. In spite of everything, they're both really excited by the prospect. One night, while Jack is out working, Patience is murdered in their apartment. Jack is devastated. There are no leads; the killer will go unpunished. Flash forward 15 years into the future. Jack still has not recovered from the loss of Patience, but he has discovered that someone has discovered the secret to time travel. Jack decides to go back in time to do a little detective work/timeline tampering. Of course, Jack learns some very important lessons, among them being the notion that tampering with one's own timeline is never as easy as it sounds. 
 Daniel Clowes' newest graphic novel is an intriguing blend of time travel and mystery while still, at heart, a love story. The artwork is classic Clowes - clean lines and lots of color, but with a certain stoic detachment and a dash of pop art sensibility. The story isn't completely unique, but the execution is unexpected nonetheless. Time travel stories always run the risk of being overly complicated, but Clowes manages to keep it simple while making his characters' lives anything but. Fans of Clowes won't be disappointed and new readers will have no trouble jumping right in.

Lyra Belaqua is curious, and brave, and defiant. Bored with her classes at Jordan College, Lyra sneaks into the Board Room and hides in the closet to watch her uncle, Lord Asriel's, presentation where she learns about a strange substance named Dust. 
 Lyra's World 
 Lyra doesn't live in our world. She lives in a parallel universe. According to Lord Asriel, all parallel universes coexist and are connected by the Dust in the Northern Lights (The Golden Compass's original title). 
 And in Lyra's world the totalitarian organization called the Magisterium rules with an iron fist, eradicating any "traitorous" thoughts. 
 Creatures 
 In Lyra's world, people have daemons: animals who represent human souls in an exterior form. Holding a person's daemon affects the human and vice versa. A child's daemon can shapeshift, but starting in puberty, it begins to "settle" into it's adult form, from which it cannot change. 
 There are also panserbjorn or "armored bears" who wear their souls in the armor they make from Sky Iron. On her adventure, Lyra meets one named Iorek Byrnison under strange circumstances. 
 Lyra also encounters the witches of the North on her adventure, including the leader, Serafina Pekkala. Witches, like normal humans have daemons, but they can be separated by large distances unlike humans who can't stray more than a few feet from their daemons. 
 The Alethiometer (Golden Compass) 
 The Alethiometer is a "truth measure" and operates on the mystical Dust. By asking a question in your mind and moving the three red needles to three corresponding images on the rim, the reader will receive an answer when the blue needle points to three other symbols. Very few people can read the se Golden Compasses. 
 Many of the Alethiometers have been destroyed by the Magisterium because they interfered with their rule. Lyra, however, is one of the remaining few who can read one. 
 Style 
 Philip Pullman creates an amazingly rich world populated with majestic creatures and minute details that bring Lyra's world to life. The first few chapters are a little slow and read almost like a textbook that you would find at Lyra's Jordan College, but the action begins very quickly-and once it does, you can't put the book down. 
 Movie 
 The 2007 movie directed by Chris Weitz starring Dakota Blue Richards (Lyra), Daniel Craig, Nicole Kidman, and other does not deserve the bad reputation it's been given. Illustrated and acted very faithfully to the books (in my opinion), I would definitely watch the movie after you've read the book. In the movie, Serafina Pekkala (played by Eva Green) serves as a sort of omniscient narrator.

 It is no secret that I am a fan of Penny Reid and her writing. I know I have said it before, but it bears repeating; Penny writes smart books about and for smart women! She doesn't succumb to using useless drama to fill the pages of her novels. Her character's are REAL (despite what my daughter might think) and deal with real life situations.

 My breathing was understandably heavy when I gasped, "Quinn." 
 He answered my gasp with a growl, kissing then biting my neck, his fingers still hooked in my panties. "Take these off." 
 "Wait, wait, wait -" 
 "Take them off or I'll rip them off." 
 The last thing that happened before I was pulled under, beyond caring or shame, and engaging in a scandalously explicit semi-public display of affection, was my underwear being torn in two by the very happy, very domineering, and very soon to be my husband, Quinn Sullivan. 
 I know right?! HOT, STEAMY AND SEXY writing that encourages you to use your imagination! I don't dislike erotic scenes in books, but sometimes less is more, and Reid knows when to apply this strategy. 
 This series reminds me of another author whose many books I have read and enjoyed, Susan Elizabeth Phillips. I love getting lost in a book and becoming a chuckling, swooning, tearful mess. I mentioned my daughter earlier. While reading this book she texted me from her bedroom (go ahead and do the mom eye-roll at that, I did) here is our conversation: 
 Yea, I was laughing. But how could I not? The situations the Janie and her friends found themselves in was hysterical. Well, every moment they were together was funny actually, but the Spa (BAHAHA! I learned some new things about the "lady garden") and Vegas - I'm laughing as I type this! I am so jealous of their friendship. Each is so loyal and caring. Whether you knit or not you want to become a part of this group! 
 A continuation of Neanderthal Seeks Human, Reid doesn't skip a beat. We are immediately thrust into the story of Janie and Quinn as they are in London where Quinn is finalizing the transfer of some private clients. Those clients were hinted about in NSH and we learn exactly who they are and what is going on. And, why they are a cause of guilt for Quinn. Also, he still holds a lot of guilt for the role he played in his brother's death and these two weigh heavily on him. 
 "I told you, you make me want to be a good guy." 
 "Quinn..." 
 "I'm trying to be a good guy." 
 We are given Quinn's POV and I devoured it. He, *sigh, is such a complex character with all his brooding and sexiness. He is the perfect match for Janie. And he wants her. Now. When he proposes to Janie after only five months of being together, he knows he's going to send her into a panic ridden, robot thinking tailspin. So, he plans the perfect, most beautiful - secluded, proposal. Of course, nothing with Janie is typical and well, let's just say the proposal was "gripping". 
 Janie knew in her heart that she loved him, but the idea of marrying so soon when the only experiences they had with each other were good, caused her to panic. She felt like they needed to experience and learn to deal with bad times before they were married. She decides a big wedding is best as the planning of it would surely cause stress and test their relationship. I laughed so much during this scene that I had tears in my eyes. 
 "...we're having a big wedding so we can be miserable together before we're happy together." 
 I don't want you to get the wrong idea, that this whole book was humorous. Because it wasn't. It was so touching and heartfelt that I had tears from sadness, joy and happiness as well. It was insightful too, which solidified my suspicion that Penny Reid is a genius. Her comparison of a tattoo and marriage was so spot on, I read it multiple times. I think I have it memorized! For the sake of brevity (HA!) I will leave that for you to discover. 
 And please, do discover this series. I recommend it to anyone and everyone who has ever been in love, had friends you cherish and family and tradition you just can't live without!

The literary finesse Mitchell shows with this novel is not his usual flowery prose, but his ability to parse his writing down to clear, precise language that still retains the luster of his more stylized novels (such as number9dream). Despite the story being rather slow and focused mainly on intrigue or unspoken feelings, it entirely hooks you and is a marvelous read. Mitchell is definitely not a one-trick pony (though Cloud Atlas and Ghostwritten were very similar, I found). 
 This novel is the most "realistic" of his that I've read so far, in that there is little focus on fate, destiny, the supernatural, or even daydreaming (there are a few dreams here and there, but even they are far from outlandish), and it is meticulously researched. To be completely honest, novels that impress me the most are ones like these - where it's clear the author takes his job as a writer seriously; how could you not, if you put so much work into making the story historically accurate as well as compelling? It's a shame that a poorly written smut novel is lauded in the media rather than a novel like this, but that's the world we live in, I suppose. Another reason why a post-apocalyptic wasteland is almost preferable... 
 What I really loved about this novel was how realistic the characters' decisions and emotions were. Jacob is torn over his devotion to his fiance that he has a feeling he'll never see again and his attraction to a woman he knows he would likely only be able to be with for so long. Despite the fact he doesn't punch walls or tear at his face in frustration, it's an agonizing decision for him, especially given the social climate he's in and the fact his love for Orito is also a gamble (as he doesn't know if she cares for him at all). But, he is full of 19th century decorum and self-control, which it sometimes his downfall but also is more realistic in terms of behavior. No one runs out into the pouring rain after their lover to beg for them to stay, no one traverses landscapes that would definitely kill them, no one makes impassioned speeches in inappropriate settings that resound in applause, no one is immortal and everyone screws up in some way. It's almost as if you're reading a fictionalized biography, but without the melodrama. I really like the resolution of Jacob and Orito - they may have had crushes on one another, but they were not "in love" as devoted couples are. It makes sense that their attraction might never fade but the depth of their feelings would slough off as life propelled them in different directions. This happens all the time in real life but novels rarely show it, tending instead of make grandiose claims that unrequited love last decades. True, it can, but rarely if the people never see one another.  
 Even the main antagonist is subtle. There is a suggestion that he is supernatural, but I don't believe that's intended to be taken seriously. And there's no big battle scene between hero and bad guy, no denouement really, and the only real "action" scene is based on a real battle (and another major event at the end is based on true events as well). This novel's only spectacular events are derived from reality, not imagination. But imagination gives them life. 
 There were certain parts of the novel that were less interesting than others - my favorite part was the section focused on Orito - but all had their merits and I was quite heavily addicted to this book. I recommend it to anyone - once you get to the 100th page you'll be quite hooked.

Stephenson is a...polarizing writer. He tends to break what are thought of as the rules of writing (show, don't tell; don't use massive, chapter-long infodumps; focus on character; etc.) and produces literature that is a story wrapped around ideas, rather than ideas that tell a story. 
 Of course, I think he does it extremely well and I don't read his books for deep character insights, but for the usually absurdly detailed and complex philosophical problems wrapped in several explosions that make up the storyline. It's a matter of expectations. 
 Anyway, I loved Anathem. I thought the premise was brilliant and I found Erasmas to be a surprisingly compelling character (by Stephenson's standards, of course). But the weirdness of the story and how he weaves in surprisingly complicated Platonic ideals with Derridean take-downs and... 
 Anyway, if you liked Snow Crash, read Cryptonomicon and if you liked Cryptonomicon, read Anathem. It is well worth your time.

Another amazing story... at first I thought Asher was selfish... I mean, he totally was. He expected Daniel to do anything, be anywhere do whatever he wanted him to.... and daniel did it without complaint. I really felt for Daniel, I felt like he just wanted to belong to somebody, wanted someone to love him and need him and although Asher did, he never told him... Then that scene at the club? Are you serious? How did he not knock Nick out??!! I would have!!! I hope he gets his karma eventually in this series, I'd love to see someone put him in his place! 
 Other than that though, I just loved these two together when Asher got his head outta his butt and realized how much he needed Daniel and loved him. 
 Another 5 star for me, can't wait to read the next one!

Simply a hysterical (in a dry wit sort of way) books for kids. It's fun to read aloud, doing voices for each of the characters as the bear searches for his hat. I love the mystery at the end: What happened to the rabbit? Did the bear sit on him or--gasp!--eat him?
I think Rainbow Rowell might be my current favourite author. I can't WAIT for her next book.

Kind of a mixture of Frozen and Divergent and not in a good way. It felt like 60% of the book was about trying to master powers and then when the action finally picked up everything kind of unraveled and made me think we're going to end up with another Game of Thrones for YA knock off. Disappointing.

So so very close to 5 stars. It is technically a 4.8 if you want to get specific. 
 Perks to this wonderful final installation of Fablehaven: 
 1. You have no idea what is going to happen. The foreshadowing or knowledge of the plot ends in the first 100 pages and you have to let your imagination take you to uncharted territories. 
 2. It makes grandparents look at cool as they really are. 
 3. People/creatures are not just good or evil. They are perceived by their choices in life. They can feel regret, learn from mistakes, evolve, ask forgiveness, change their legacy. 
 4. Gender roles are huge for me and this book and series does an incredible job of being generous to both genders. 
 5. This is the most consistently well-written series I've ever encountered. Kudoes to Brandon Mull! I am officially a fan. 
 Can't say enough great things about this book. It is tremendous!

When in 2013???? 
 WHEN IN 2013?????????????????????!!!!!!!!!!!!!!! 
 5/7/13 - Eeehhhh, no. Not loving the cover. Nothing says trying too hard like studded everything. And he's not how I pictured Jet. But I still can't wait to read the book! 
 4/24/14 (the 9 likes are for the above comments, not the review!) 
 4.25 stars. 
 I liked both Jet and Ayden in Rule, though to be honest, while I felt I had a pretty good handle on what Ayden was like, I thought Jet was more serious and bookish for some reason. Not that he's not serious about his business and music, he just came across as more calm in the last book. I have to admit, I like a fired up Jet better than a Zen Jet! 
 In Jet, we learn that both he and Ayden have issues from their past to deal with, and while Jet deals with his on a regular basis, Ayden thought she left hers behind in Kentucky when she moved to Colorado and created a whole new persona for herself. While I figured she must've been a bit of a slut back in the day from the hints that were dropped in the first book and through most of this one, I think the main reason for her some of why she slept around, to get her brother, Asa, out of jams and potentially save his life , was just stupid. No way in hell would I whore myself out like that and get involved in some of the stuff she did to numb what she was feeling about her actions, especially for such a scumbag. It's great that Ayden was able to turn her life around because she really is a good person and though I know she was scared of telling her friends, and especially Jet, about her past life, I think she should've done it way earlier, it would've saved everyone massive amounts of trouble, though of course that would've taken away from the problems that got between Ayden and Jet so it probably would've have been a much shorter book! 
 I really liked how Ayden and Jet were friends for over a year, and got to know each other pretty well, despite leaving out critical details of their family lives, before they started something with each other. Just as with Rule and Shaw, who had known each other for years, their friendship makes the romance that much more believable, rather than the usual, I'm so attracted to you I'll sleep with you the minute after I meet you and get to know you later (usually with insta-love thrown in) garbage. I also liked how Jet finally came to the right decision about how to handle his mother all by himself. What I didn't like was how Ayden looked at Asa's doing one thing right after all the shit he didn't stop her from doing on his behalf (I hope we eventually get more about this story, like if he knew exactly what she was doing and why he either didn't or knew but didn't stop her) when she was younger was such an amazing thing. Yeah, he risked his life for her, but yet again, he created the problem and dragged her into it. I just don't think she should be so forgiving or understanding without really having it out with him. 
 A note about Jet's attire. Blech. Skintight jeans, tons of rings and fingernail polish are things I cannot stand on a guy. Forget that I'm with Ayden on the lack of merits of heavy metal and the fact that piercings below the neck turn me off and/or make me squeamish, I like guys who dress a little more like a guy, not wearing stuff that chicks would wear (not that skinny jeans are okay on anyone, they're not, in my opinion). 
 Something that grinded my gears a bit was, at one point, Jet mentions how he stopped Ayden from having unprotected sex. Unless the words I was reading don't mean what I've always known them to mean, they had unprotected sex, he just didn't finish. And FYI, that doesn't mean you can't get knocked up (I'm not even going to go into how dumb it is regarding STDs), especially since there was never any mention of Ayden being on the pill at the time. 
 One big annoyance in this book was the misuse of words. For example, taunt and taut are not the same thing yet when describing someone's body, taunt was used more often than not (and if the correct word, taut, had been used instead, I'd be complaining about how overused it was) and I have no idea how that got by anyone reading the book before it was published. 
 Finally, for one of the future books, I think I'm going to have to request a diagram of some of the piercings, well, one in particular, because I still can't imagine what it looks like (and don't think I'd want to get up close and personal with one. I really don't know why a guy would put himself through something like that. Just the thought of it being torn out makes my stomach roll, and I'm not even a dude!). 
 I love that we got to see not only Rowdy and Nash but also some of Shaw and Rule (more of them, please! Maybe in Rome's book) and particularly Cora, who I especially like. I'm really looking forward to reading about the rest of the group's stories because they're all not only very loyal but unique and decent guys, despite their whorish behavior and bad boy appearances. I'm not convinced that a certain someone has redeemed himself and I still sort of hate him, but it will be interesting to see what Asa's story holds for him. Since the Kindle prices are so high, I think I may just have to break down and buy the books if I can get a good deal on them, I don't want to have to wait to find out what goes on with Rome and Nash!

Probably my favorite in the series, this is where Harry really starts to develop his wizarding powers and starts to believe in himself. It also sets the stage for many of the story arcs that continue into the remaining books. 
 The book may be labeled as a children's book, but is really one that is enjoyable for all ages, and that's what makes it so great.

Who doesn't love a Cinderella retelling? Even if it will never be as good as the original and might take you awhile to finish because the initial startup is slow. lol. 
 What is it about? 
 Tatum Elsea stars us our Cinderella in this contemporary retelling. After getting into trouble when she is accused of committing a crime, Tatum is put under house arrest by her step-monster and stuck doing community service. She also starts a graphic design business where she meets her prince charming, elusive SK. What started out as a summer that was all levels of suck, turns into one of adventure, romance, and mending fences. Helped by her step-abuela posing as our fairy-godmother, Tatum's summer just might end with a happily ever after. 
 What did I like about it? 
 Tatam isn't your typical damsel in distress. She's more like Rapunzel from Tangled than Cinderella, especially with her strong attitude and willingness to stand up for herself. Reading her correspondence with SK and trying to piece together who he is was also fun, albeit somewhat predictable. It was a sweet story with a cute ending and has all the Cinderella elements that should be there. 
 What did I dislike about it? 
 The beginning was slow and thus what was meant to be a book I could devour in a few hours turned into a week long read. There isn't much to dislike other than the fact that I just wish I was more into the book. 
 What did I take away from it? 
 Letting one mistake ruin your life isn't the way you should go. Take control and continue to forge your way forwards. Waiting around for Prince Charming is also kinda of pointless. Make it happen/let fate intervene. Definitely read this if you need a dose of fairytale in your life. 
 Quotes: 
 "So much that she once said my playing wrecked her." 
 "I'm surprised you didn't find a puddle of me on the ground afterwards."
Another fantastic story. This is one of my favorites.

"'Sneaks, spies, defenders, heroes, masterminds, tenacious bastards-it doesn't matter what you call us. We're the ones who will do whatever it takes to stop those who believe they're entitled to wealth and power at the expense of others.' 
 'The family business,' Yelena said, smiling. 'I like that. Well said, Janco.' 
 Valek squeezed her hand in agreement. For once Janco didn't preen." 
 If I could only point out one thing about this entire series, it would be the character's relationships with each other: 
 Yelena and Valek's quiet, romantic relationship. 
 Janco and Ari's amazing bromace. 
 Ari and Janco's loyalty and friendship with Valek. 
 Valek's loyalty to the Commander. 
 Yelena's relationship with Lief, even though they didn't grow up together. 
 Fisk and the 'little brother' vibe he has with Yelena. 
 And then squishing them all together. 
 For me the secondary characters livened up the first series (Study) to a point in which now Ari and Janco have become just as important as Valek and Yelena. They are fiercely protective, yet they know Yelena can handle herself. I wouldn't mind a run off series including the (mis)adventures of Ari and Janco. 
 Valek and Yelena are not ones to rush into anything. Readers understand that from the years of separation endured while Valek works for the Commander and Yelena works as the liaison. In Night Study, however, you get to see different sides of both of the characters. Sure, we've seen glimpses of a panicked Valek and an overwhelmed Yelena, but for once we get to openly see behind the stoic assassin without the prying of his heart-mate and a Yelena who is having to learn to accept others for support and not work through things on her own. 
 The plot itself is full of twists and mind boggling counter twists. With rogue magicians creating an army against Ixia, it's hard for our crew to distinguish between who's a friend and who's a foe; which are being controlled and which are willingly members of the cartel. That, combined with the Commander becoming extra mysterious and strict with Valek sets off sparks and tension between the counties that have already been near war for years. 
 Overall, Night Study left the reader with more questions then answers, which leaves Dawn Study with even more pressure and anticipation. Start the series, meet the characters, fall in love, grab the complimentary tissues and lock picks on your way in.

 This is SERIOUSLY GOOD. SO GOOD I CAN ONLY EXPRESS MY LOVE IN CAPITALS. LOVE. LOVE. LOVE.

 As far as female lead goes, there's no lead. There's a woman that cries and worries and waits for everyone else to do right by her, but she, herself doesn't do much. Why I felt compelled to buy the third part of this series is simple: hope. Hope that it would return to the entertaining bdsm joyride the first part promised this series to be and that the Girlfriend simply was a failed attempt to give the story of our two lovers some realism. 
 I wasn't rewarded, not really. Again it was more about the whole family drama that seemingly naturally occurs when there is such a huge age difference between the coupe that one of them could be the parent of the other.

 I haven't continued the series so far and I doubt I will.

The difference in the levels of enjoyment i got from this book to it's predecessor is so huge, i can't properly express it! All i can say for the first one is that i'm glad it helped me get a general idea about the Malazan world. 
 Deadhouse Gates has a gripping and intense opening that is indicative of all that comes later on in the book. It's full of characters you empathize with, rage at, and it sometimes surprises you with an unexpected chuckle. 
 While reading Gardens of the Moon, i didn't particularly connect with or like any of the various point-of-views so i was left with a flat feeling when i was done with it. 
 In contrast, right from the start of Deadhouse Gates, i wanted to know everything about Felisin and where she ended up in the main scope of the story. I wasn't disappointed at all, i got what i asked for; it was tragic, frustrating and somehow rewarding. I've seen people who disliked Felisin, all i can say is; she was fourteen, had all that shit happen to her, psychologically i wasn't surprised at how she turned out. I can only hope i get to meet her in the other books. 
 The second interesting pov for me was Mappo and Icarium, complicated friendships and emotional bonds are a sure trap for me, i was destined to get emotionally attached to these two from the outset. It was also good seeing Apsalar (aka Sorry), Crokus (he was more tolerable this time around) and Fiddler again. 
 The next one was The Historian, Duiker and the focus on the war from that angle was interesting to see but it fell short at some points maybe because continuous war plot-lines always bore me. I think the philosophizing he did added something to it that made it more bearable than Kalam's meandering and eventually useless pov, imo. Infact, i would go so far as to say that Fiddler's smaller pov was more enjoyable to Kalam's. 
 All in all though, I think what makes this book such a great read for me (in comparison to the first) was the fact that i actually empathised with the characters, liked the philosophizing that my favourites went into (it didn't feel overly done and actually got me into the mindset they were in) and there was an improvement in the characterisation of the main female characters in this one which was greatly lacking in the first one.

Firstly, I'm not a potterhead, secondly, I have read all the other Harry Potter books. All that said, I really enjoyed this. It had the feel of some classic sci-fi (essentially dealing with the grandfather paradox) but in a Potter/magic style. It was nice to see the gang as adults and seeing the alternative versions of themselves was very entertaining!  
 What I'm trying to say is this was a nice quick read, I'd really like to see it performed! Also, how long do we think it will take before it'll be turned into a movie??

What would happen to us if the Earth suddenly slowed its rotation, as the days grew longer and longer? That's the central question of Walker's beautiful little book, which is as much an exploration of a slightly awkward girlhood as it is a story of the end of days. Walker does a lovely job of capturing a family in chaos and the effects of an unimaginable natural disaster on California and the world at large. Very affecting and well-written, this was a favourite.

So, Eclipse. This was actually one of the better ones. I mean, after New Moon, I didn't now if i should go on. But my Mom read it and she liked it, so, I did. I was pretty happy with it over all. If it was as bad as new moon, there was no way i would read Breaking Dawn. But, honestly, i don't know if it's so much that I liked this book as much as I think I do, but, more that is was strangely addicting. I mean I don't know what it is with twilight. Same thing with the movies (btw, liked the movies more than the books). I liked how Bella killing for Edward was going down some, sort of. It was okay, and i won't lie. But, in the end, i just kind of realize that, again, It wasn't a fantastic book, it was how it was addicting. But, it was definitely not the worst. I still liked it. (But, why would she not pick Jake. TAYLOR LAUTNER!!! Like, he has an 18 pack!)

1.5 rounded up 
 I liked this. Up until about halfway through where backstory starts, we learn everything that happened to lead up to them living in the basement, and at that point-- without going into spoilers-- I found only one ending acceptable. And of course the ending turned out to be the exact opposite. 
 It's well-written, which is why I can't give it only one star, and it kept me sucked into the story, but the ending really just was... unnecessarily gross? Completely the incorrect message you should take away from the novel? I don't know what, but let me just say that, despite the end message of this novel, there are some things you should not/i> do for family, even if it's your own kid.

3.5 stars 
 I enjoyed reading this book. :) It was funny, I liked most of the characters (Mia and Liv were awesome), and I loved the whole thing about the dreams. 
 Overall, there were a few things that bothered me (for example, the romance moved too quickly for my taste), but if you enjoyed Ruby Red, chances are that you'll enjoy Dream a Little Dream as well (though I, personally, prefer Ruby Red).

I liked this one almost as much as the first and am glad that we got to learn more about Jaden. It was great to see glimpses of Ty and Lily in this one but although the continuation of that story is important, that isn't where the focus was for this book and I was ok with it. I would probably put this a 4.5. 
 We know from the first book that Jaden has been through a lot and he doesn't really trust anyone. During the time he was helping Ty and Lily he had a run in with Lyra which didn't necessarily go well (all his fault btw). The book opens up a few months later and a chance run in with Lyra has him thinking about her again. 
 I was glad this one focused on these two and their story. Although I had the mystery figured out pretty early on I still enjoyed the interaction between Lyra and Jaden as well as the development of the story. It was well paced and I found myself, once again, turning the pages and thankful for a 2 hour flight. 
 The characters are engaging from the beginning...to be honest I was interested in learning more about Jaden since he was introduced in the first book and I can't say I was disappointed this book was about him. Dark hair, British accent, tough yet shades of vulnerability...sign me up! Lyra grew on me and I understood why she would decide to leave the pack for a bit as well as why she seemed so defensive around men. Again, the end result of what happened between Lyra and Jaden wasn't necessarily a surprise to me but it didn't take away from the story at all (in my opinion). 
 Overall, another great story by this author and I am curious to see who the next book(s) will be about. I am still keeping my fingers crossed for Damien...just putting that out there.

I was entertained by the story, and couldn't put the book down, but ultimately was disappointed. Bardugo is a great, hooking writer. The cool magical world of Shadow and Bone continued to be unveiled, and new, strong characters were introduced. The pacing was slow, the first part of the book re-hashed the same plot from the prior book, and there was way too much angst with Mal (who isn't the best love interest). The biggest let down was Alina's character. Alina is too passive as a MC. She's captured, saved, and let others make decisions for her instead of being strong and independent.

This is a review of the audio book. Human woman goes to work for a business run by magicians and staffed with exotic (legendary?) creatures. 5 stars for the writing and narration. 
 This is chick lit, guys. Lots of picking out clothes for dates and worrying about appearance, preparing for dates, and post-date discussions. That said, guys will care about the heroine just as the gals have several drool-worthy hunks to choose from, although there is no sex in this book and the romance is just beginning. 
 BUT ... between all that, Ms. Swendson is a word-smith, quip-smith writer whose skills show up in a clever, much smarter than she gives herself credit for, heroine who just managers to use her native human common sense with panache. 
 I give it 5 stars for the writing (and narration) and immediately bought the second book. Which isn't as good, because it relies on the old cliche: Heroine is afraid to tell anyone what is wrong. Guess whether or not that makes things better. The writing is still a delight.

I've read and really enjoyed several of Jennifer Laurens' books. Overprotected won't make my list of favorites but I don't regret reading it. It's a really quick read and since I am a huge fan of "forbidden love" stories I found it worth the time it took to read. 
 The relationship between Ashlyn and Colin never felt as believable as I hoped it would. I kept waiting for some conflict and resolution over their past but never got what I was looking for. While there was definitely a strong attraction between the two of them I never felt like I got the real romance/relationship aspect I hoped for. 
 What I enjoy the most was the family interactions and rebellious nature of Ashlyn in response to her overprotective father. Perhaps because I have my own rebellious streak and don't like being told what to do I could relate to this part of her personality. 
 Rating - 3.5 Stars - Good Book 
 Content: Nothing that I remember

A couple of my friends were disappointed in this installment, so I think I ended up liking it much more than I expected to. I am a fan of books with a lot of scene-setting historical detail, which I know turns a lot of others off. The magic and supernatural elements were really interesting and well-done, I thought. 
 The weak spot for this one is the plot. "Discovery" had the delicious feeling of being pulled along by current into new and amazing situations, but "Shadow" was a little stagnant. Storylines went off into different directions and circled around on one another, not really moving forward much at all. 
 The thing that bugged me the most (minor spoiler) - 
 They got the book. Why on earth didn't they spend every second they had with it trying to find out every last detail about it? Why didn't the author tell us more about it? Gah!  
 I am having a hard time seeing what significant contributions this book made to the narrative arc of the series (other than Diana's magic, I guess), but I will stick around for the third.

It's straddling the line between 4.5 and 5, to be honest. 
 Brief thoughts (review to come later): 
 Great buildup, very cute boys, not sure how I feel about the best friend still, and looking forward to seeing where things will go in the next book.

Go Samantha! I love the growth we get to experience with Samantha in this book. She was forced into a marriage when she got pregnant at 16 and well, this really wasn't the best plan for her. When her daughter goes to college she is sort of at loose ends, her role as Mom isn't really needed now but she never allowed herself to do something for herself. She starts working out and a class in pole dancing really awakens something inside her that she didn't know she was missing. I really never expected Sam to end up working at a gentleman's club but I loved how this job gave her confidence and courage to finally be true to herself. Slate is blown away when he sees "Diamond" dance on the stage, he needs to get to know her. Andrea Smith kept me from that point on. Craziness with her husband Jack, the connection with Slate and how insanely things can intertwine. I don't want to spoil anything so grab it and enjoy!

Giving this a 4-star, mainly because enjoyment-wise, this volume wasn't something I enjoyed all that much compared to the previous volumes despite all the secrets dropped on us. 
 Wow, Kureno. Can I give him a title like "The Person Who Shall Reveal Secrets"? Seriously, this volume's biggest plot twists came from him. I remember the first time I read this and I was like "HOLY SHIT THAT DID NOT HAPPEN!... *a few pages down* OMG THAT DID NOT HAPPEN!... *a few pages later* DAMN IT KURENO HOW MANY PLOT TWISTS ARE THERE?!" 
 First we learn that Kureno has a relationship with Akito that goes beyond the zodiac bond, then we learn that he's no longer bound by the curse, and yet HE REFUSES TO MEET OUR DEAR UO-CHAN, and then WE LEARN THAT AKITO IS A GIRL (!!!), but was raised as a boy thanks to her mother (WTF?).  Wow. Let me pause and let that sink in. *breathes deeply* 
 It's no wonder Tohru reacts the way she did after learning about everything... And then we readers get to know things from Shigure's side (!!!) that Tohru doesn't know (yet?). And WTF Shigure, did you just sleep with the person your love hates the most to spite her for sleeping with another guy ??? This is so messed up, like he points out himself. And yet at the end of the volume Shigure sleeps with Akito. What. The. Actual. Flying fish.  
 Veering away from the Sohma family drama, I love the scene between Tohru, Arisa and Saki. (Does anyone wonder why they call Tohru Tohru, but Tohru calls them by their family names...? So polite, our protagonist.) That is one of my favorite points of this series: that there's many friendships forged. Me love some sisterhood! (Although, poor Uo-chan. *pats* He'll come around, someday.) 
 That scene of Kyo and Tohru just unleashed my inner fangirl. (KYA! KYA! KYAAAAAA!!!!) Kyo, it's SOOOOO obvious you lurve her. Fortunately (or unfortunately?) Tohru's too dense to realize it. That flower scene is just so sweet I feel like I just poured sugar into my mouth, but it's definitely worth it. *goes to fangirl* 
 We also see a development in Yuki and Machi's relationship, and what seems like a budding romance between. A girl running after you just to say hi, when she doesn't seem all that impressed by you just a few volumes ago? Cute. I like how they're slowly discovering each other, seeing each other beyond the facades that they portray consciously or unconsciously to others. Too bad I'm not really all that invested into that relationship. Takaya needs to show more from Machi to really make us readers root for her. 
 All in all, not a bad volume. Not one of my favorites by far, but the huge plot twists and the cute Kyo-Tohru scene make this worth it.

A lot of people here and on tumblr have been talking about Colleen Hoover and how she can do no wrong. 
 But unfortunately I am not loving her books in the same way. There were some good plot points here that usually have me clinging to a book to get to the last page, but this time it didn't. Everything fell a bit flat. 
 I'll probably try a few more of her books though, but this one wasn't a keeper for me.

[This is my first fresh and genuine book review, please don't mind the mess it is in. Thank You] 
 What do I have to say about David and Ev's love story? 
 A LOT. 
 I will start with although there were HEAVY eye-rolling moments I couldn't put the book down. I spent 14 hours reading this book cover to cover. There of course were plenty of unbelievable moments, but how could there not be? The literal plot is waking up in Vegas married to a rock-star who, surprise surprise, is totally entranced by you (I am assuming I am not the only person who reads a book in 1st person as if I am the main character to some degree). 
 So the bizarre-o land setting aside, it was still very enjoyable. There were heavy flirtatious moments to which I am the ultimate sucker for a sexy comeback. 
 My absolute favorite person in the book is Mal! He was without question the BEST character in the novel. 
 (I know the second book is about him and I am too scared to read it right now because often times the reason a character is so intriguing is because they aren't the POV.) 
 I was a girl desperate for more Mal and Ev friend moments. 
 The negative input I have is that towards the end it seemed very rushed and compact. Unfortunately it is too often I pick up a trashy romance novel and settle in for a guilty pleasure of adult and erotic literature to find that after the middle section where everything falls apart and inevitably the main characters leave each other for whichever TYPE A, B, C, Etc reason that the coming together that shortly follows is too congested. 
 Typecast two people that meet and relentlessly fall for one another, even if they are kidding themselves. Follow up with a breakup of some sort because of lies and hidden secrets or ex lovers. Then wrap up in 10 pages or less where they reunite and go from freshly knowing each other and freshly breaking up with each other to hopeless romantics that become married, barefoot and pregnant behind the american white picket fence dream with lots and lots and lots of kinky and spontaneous sex. 
 I just would enjoy a book more if the ending wasn't so rushed into the fairy tale dream. I am all okay with a make up and wild reunion but I hate the rush of kids and buying a house and the whole epitome of novel-marriage-Cinderella crap. 
 Even with my annoyance of David and Ev starting at dinner with her parents rushing in to the barefoot and happy in a new condo talking about children ending, I am still happy I read their story. 
 More so I am saddened knowing that their story is over in the series. Though they will be featured from someone else's POV it still wont be THEIR story. I am disappointed. 
 So there was my first fresh review and I hope it wasn't awful. I tried to keep it spoiler free and open for discussion (as that's the reason I joined GR is to gush over books) I would love some pointers and more importantly I would love it if someone who loved Mal as much as I did could tell me if the second book is worth the sacrifice of his crystal image??? 
 Anyway's, as always, 
 Thanks for the listen

Well I'm not sure what to really say about this book. It was good and I was wavering between 3 stars and 4 stars but just felt like the ending earned it 4. It was a long drawn out story for me, I felt like it dragged and dragged but I still couldn't put the book down. I felt like I had to know what was going to happen and how thing's were going to pan out for Daniel and Luce. Quite simply, this book rocks. 
 I went in expecting a scary, psychological thriller, and was disappointed on that front. It is less of a 'thriller' and far more a psychological delving into absolutely terrible people's minds. Yes, all of the characters are absolutely TERRIBLE people. You will not like ANY of them, all. The primary story-driving character, Rachel, is a horrid drunk whose insights you get about a missing persons case. However, the story that the characters are getting through is interesting enough that you will want to keep flipping through the pages of the book. It gets a bit tedious around the middle when you become absolutely convinced of who dun it, but KEEP GOING. There is 50% of the book left for a reason. 
 SPOILERS FOLLOW... 
 The author's greatest feat was throwing the reader for a loop by making you distrust and dislike Rachel so much towards the middle of the novel. She was a drunk, she couldn't help herself with anything, she was a liar, she took advantage of people, she was a creep towards her ex husband, she needed to stop meddling... and she was abusive towards her ex to boot! All signs point to her being the absolute worst, and I'm sure that every reader is like me and becomes absolutely convinced that Rachel was the murderer all along. The twist seems to be so easy to spot! ...but you are thrown for a loop. 
 I will say that the end was kind of terribly executed. Tom's switch didn't seem altogether believable, and yet I'm totally okay with it. I'm glad Rachel wasn't the one to do it, and I hope she makes it to a month sober. And damn, I hope she gets out of Cathy's place because I feel the most for poor Cath. And FUCK ANNA. She's the worst.

I don't have time to write everything I want, but alas. 
 I was very excited for this installment, though I did have to go back and re-read the first two books because it had been so long and I didn't want to be confused. I'm glad I did, because it picked up right where it left off. 
 First things first, the book splits perspectives between Tris and Tobias. While I was excited for this at first, it kind of bothered me after awhile, only because their voices sounded 
 identical 
 . I would have to go back and look at who's chapter it was sometimes, or wait to see who's name they'd say to figure out who's perspective I was. I liked getting to see more of Tobias' view of things, and hearing his side of the story, but it was hard to keep up with when the reader can't differentiate between the alternating characters. 
 Also, then there's the plot. 
 We find out about the Bureau of Genetics, where they are trying to create the perfect set of genes, or, as we know them, Divergents. But then the gang finds out that the Bureau was the one who supplied Jeanine with the serum to turn Dauntless into mindless killing machines, killing an entire faction - the faction that just happened to have the most Divergents other than the factionless. So, if they were trying to make genetically pure people, or these Divergents, and wanted them to survive to make more, why would they have given the serum to Jeanine? 
 Don't worry, that's never explained. We get a whole new conflict of genetically pure or "GP" vs. the genetically damaged, or "GD"s. How the Bureau thinks that the GD's are what ruins the world, which is why they want GPs. Weirdly enough, GD's aren't too happy with that and start a riot. 
 I'll spare the details, but my last bone to pick is the ending. 
 The entire book I knew either Tobias or Tris would die. I could feel it. But when it was Tris, I was bummed. The entire series, she had sacrificed herself for those she loved, putting herself in danger, and almost dying. Repeatedly. We knew that was part of her character, because we saw it over and over. When Caleb is finally given a turn to redeem himself, Tris throws it away because "he's doing it for guilt." Who the hell cares?? He SHOULD feel guilty. I think it would have said a lot seeing a selfish character become selfless. Hell, even as much as I love Tobias/Four, I think it would have been a deeper message seeing him sacrifice himself as he's never done before. But nope, we see Tris do it yet again. It kind of fell flat for me, and I didn't even really feel that sad about it, even though I know I should. I'm not mad that she died or there wasn't a happily ever after, I just think the message Roth was trying to make could have been clearer if it was a different character. 
 Overall, I liked this series a lot, despite it's flaws. It was a good dystopian, and I felt like I could see and understand the world. I'm excited to see the movies and what else she writes in the future.

I will read anything that Shriver writes. I am completely tuned in to her sensibility. She always picks topics and themes that other authors tend to ignore or who will write about sensationally. Shriver does not shy away from politicizing or making bold statements, but she does so in such a matter-of-fact, specific (yet humanizing) that her books don't feel sensational. That she also takes her stories from her own experiences helps that along. I felt Pandora's revulsion when she picks her brother up from the airport, I felt Pandora's conflict between doing what was right for her brother, at times at great sacrifice to her family and it made perfect sense that the lengths to whcih she went to save her brother both failed and were a total fantasy on her part . The Post-Bithrday World remains my favorite Shriver work, but this pulls a close second.
A tour de force of subtlety. Bravo!

Our journey began in fire... Gideon Cross came into my life like lightning in the darkness-beautiful and brilliant, jagged and white-hot. I was drawn to him as I'd never been to anything or anyone in my life. I craved his touch like a drug, even knowing it would weaken me. I was flawed and damaged, and he opened those cracks in me so easily... Gideon knew. He had demons of his own. And we would become the mirrors that reflected each other's most private wounds... and desires. The bonds of his love transformed me, even as I prayed that the torment of our pasts didn't tear us apart... 
 At first I gave this book 4 stars...dunno why! There have been a lot of comparisons between this book and Fifty Shades of Grey. Christian Grey is a billionaire, is sexy, enigmatic, has a dark past and enjoys sex toward the dark of nature....in my opinion, thats where the similarities cease. Gideon Cross is in a class all by himself, with his dark and brooding demanor and drop-dead sexiness! He's a sex maniac but only with Eva and though he enjoys that sex in a dominating nature he doesn't delve into the inflection of pain as our favorite Dom, 50! Although both of these alphalicious sex Gods come from difficult backgrounds they are vastly different. During the story of Eva and Gideon we get a glimpse into his plethra of issues, he's controlling but in no way as ridiculous as our boy Christian. Gideon realizes that he needs Eva on such a fundamental level and it freaks him the freak out that he's that dependent on someone for his sanity. 
 Eva is a very likable character. She's no damsel, not a virgin...at all and is a well off independent woman in her own right! I loved that about this book. Gideon lavished her with expensive gifts and didn't have to fight with her to take them...like someone we know(Ana)! She has a dark past of her own which makes it difficult for her to trust and having a controlling and mercial man like Gideon is a tough pill to swallow but she learns to love him anyway. Another thing I loved was Cary, Eva's roomate and bi-sexual best friend. He contributed to the light and funny side of Eva's personality and made the whole story more interesting since Cary has his own shit he deals with as well! I don't want to give much away so Ill keep this review short so.... 
 All in all, I absolutely loved it especially on audio! Sylvia Day hit a home run in my book. It was dark, sad and the sex scenes between Eva and Gideon were scortching hot! I recommend this to all the 50 fans and those that are not but love a great erotic romance with depth! I cannot wait to read more about this fantastic couple...they've got a long road to recovery!

So, just as I was finishing up with my review of Beyond Jealousy, I was lucky enough to get this ARC of Beyond Solitude. I devoured it! It takes place at the same time as Beyond Solitude, but could easily be read first. In fact, this one probably stands alone better than any of the stories in the series besides the first one. 
 Derek Ford is a member of the O'Kane gang. Unfortunately a broken leg and old fashioned healing has left him tied to his desk a whole lot more than he likes. One day he's surprised to discover Mia in his office. She's new to the sector and she's not an O'Kane, but she's got ties to Lex, the O'Kane queen. Lex gave Mia a job - she's supposed to help Ford out with his office work. Ford is grumpy and not appreciative of Mia invading his space, but Mia's determined to make things work. 
 I showed the following quote to pretty much everyone in my bookclub trying to convince them to read this series! 
 "I need a job. If you don't want me to mess with your files, fine--" 
 "Okay. Don't mess with my files." 
 She didn't falter, didn't even blink. "Then tell me what to do instead." 
 If I were an asshole... He waved the bottle of whiskey at her. "You could start by letting me drink half of this and jerk off so I can get some sleep." 
 That snapped her teeth together--for about five seconds. "If you're self-conscious about doing that with me in the next room, I could take some work home." 
 "Self-conscious?" He dropped the bottle on his desk and unbuckled his belt. "I'll lay it out right here, buttercup, if you like to watch." 
 Her gaze flicked to his hands, and he got that flash of tongue he'd been waiting for as she wet her lips. "I wouldn't be watching. I'd be working." 
 Filing papers like there was nothing more interesting going on? Fuck that. "Bullshit." Ford tugged open the top button on his jeans. "It may be a little battered these days, like the rest of me, but my ego's not dead. If I start stroking my dick right in front of you, you're damn sure gonna be paying attention. Not just watching--riveted." p.7 
 This is on page SEVEN! And really, the story starts on page 5, so it's really like page 3... It's one hot story. 
 It's also got one of the things I like most about the Beyond series - strong women who support each other. Mia has issues. She's working through them, but it's really important for her to stand on her own. That means falling for her new boss causes her some problems. The real conflict in this story comes when Ford doesn't understand why it's a problem for him to be her boss and lover. The way he makes it up to her is one of the most memorable "I'm sorry" gifts I've ever read, though! 
 This story could probably be read anywhere in the series, as it stands alone really well. It's tamer than most of the other stories, too, as Mia and Ford aren't really interested in the orgies or PDA that the rest of the O'Kanes enjoy so much. So, it might even be a good entry point. I highly recommend it, and even though I got a review copy of this short story, I'm still going to buy the anthology.* For 99c it's hard to turn down! 
 *Note: This novella is part of the Alphas After Dark Anthology. The authors report that the anthology will be on sale for 99c in April and after that the novella will be priced at $2.99

The book starts off with Beatrice Prior, an Abgenation who as we know it is in the selfless faction. The abgenation faction is selflessness, erudite is knowledge, dauntless is courage, amity is peace. 
 At 16, all citizens take a test that will help them determine which faction they are most suited to. She takes the test and her result is that she is Divergent, a combination of all factions. Her final decision faction though is Dauntless. To be accepted as a Dauntless member Beatrice must rank high into each of her trial missions.

I enjoyed reading about the missions very much but I wished the plot started sooner because I wanted to know what the government was up to. And at the very end, I was left with such a cliffhanger that I'm sure I'll be first in line to buy the second novel. Hopefully, all my questions will be answered. 3.75 stars

 I did like this one better overall than Book 1. Especially the hero Reid, who had a little more substance and heart than muscle-headed Knox who only seemed to think with his penis and fists. 
 But there were things that I wasn't crazy about and could have been way better. Sophie Jordan likes to use fast easy loopholes to push her (convoluted) plots along. So you got to suspend all sense of realism & belief big time to read her books. Similar to Knox's story, the whole plot of this was super contrived with a lot of nonsensical things happening for the hero and heroine to get together. From the President's daughter easily sneaking out of her hotel room thinking she won't get recognized and getting kidnapped not even a block away from her hotel (really Jordan???!) and the kidnappers just happened to be on their way to kidnap her (LOL. Plot twist!) to Reid's easy pardon to the couple's nice and tidy HEA. But......I thought the couple were cute. I was skeptical for a good 70% of the story with the constant repetitive arguments to them not really getting anywhere while 'on the run'. I guess that would be my biggest complaint, you have your leads on the run hiding from the police and secret service and the whole damn country and they are sitting ducks for 90% of the story in a cabin in the woods with nothing exciting going on except heated tension, arguments and sex.  Reid doesn't have his one-on-one meeting with the big bad guy until the very end which literally lasts 2 seconds, which took the suspense angle right out of the book.  
 And this is literally the third book I've read by Sophie Jordan where the heroine's character is so inconsistent and misleading from cover blurb to story. How the heroine is packaged on the blurb and the beginning is very inconsistent and drastically changed through the story. I wanna know how "shy awkward" pushover timid Grace transformed into a temperamental raging hellcat within a matter of 2 chapters. Yeah....ok. lol Reid bringing that out of her or not, the context of it made no sense. The development of this character was very fast and loose IMO, it made no sense for her to show that much spine towards her captor and so quickly. Jordan's tendency to have her character's personalities change with a flip of a switch just shows lack of realistic development and depth. 
 But nonsensical bits aside, I thought Reid and Grace were cute and sweet in the end. I loved the epilogue. And the fact that the First family was Latino(?) I found surprising and refreshing. I'm not sure since it was never outright confirmed but there were hints.

5 Rebellion Crew STARS 
 "You can help me pick out a tiara when we`re done saving the world." 
 This is my first 5 stars book of the year!! And it totally deserves the perfect rating because this book was an amazing rollercoaster ride I couldn`t put down. 
 After the silent Lunar attack to Earth that caused thousands of deaths, Emperor Kai is forced to choose the only thing he never wanted to ensure his people's safety: marrying Queen Levana. 
 Now Cinder and the crew are in a mission against time to stop the wedding, exposing Cinder's true identity and getting Levana out of the throne. But for that Cinder will not only need a master plan that works, but to be able to control her Lunar powers as well. 
 And she has two weeks to do that. 
 "Not doing pictures these days?" Jacin mutered as they hurried through the shop. "How very Lunar of you." 
 Cinder glared against the sudden, burning sunlight. "Very wanted criminal of me too." 
 I enjoyed so much the banter between everyone. Wolf and Cinder practicing, Iko being sassy, Thorne being Thorne and Scarlet fierceness. I loved Cress too, I was kinda worried because in the first book we just saw her crying and being kinda desperate, and I thought her character was gonna be weak, but she was not. She was smart, caring and nice, and a badass hacker. Also, the little of what we saw of Jacin and Winter (because my first impression was she was high and hitting on Scarlet)  made me curious for their own POV and backstories. 
 "I mean they`re unpredictable, even under the control of a thaumaturge." He returned his focus to Cinder. "Or any other Lunar. The genethic tampering they undergo to become soldiers affects their brains as much as their bodies. They`re sporadic, wild...dangerous." 
 Thorne leaned against Scarlet`s storage crate, fake-whispering to her, "He does realize that he`s an ex-street fighter who still goes by "Wolf",right?" 
 I do have to give Thorne the award for best quotes in the book, he certainly never disappointed in making me laugh when he opened his mouth. Also, Cress and Thorne stole my heart, I enjoyed their development as characters and relationship with the other while being in lots of dangerous situations. 
 She squirmed, her body was vibrating with nerves. "I know. I`m sorry. I think you might be right, though. Maybe there isn`t such a thing as fate. Maybe it`s just the opportunities we`re given, and what we do with them. I`m beginning to think that maybe great, epic romances don`t just happen. We have to make them ourselves." 
 This installment was more action packed than the previous ones, and the different POV's worked amazingly at having this story in a 360deg perspective, but still keeping the mystery. The romance was nicely done, being present but not overtaking the story. 
 War had begun. 
 "You said yourself that the people of Luna need a revolutionary." She lifted her chin, holding his gaze. "So I`m going to Luna, and I`m going to start a revolution." 
 I could say more things about this book, but I don't feel it`s necessary.This was an addictive multi-layered story, with great characters that you will rally for and that will keep you at the edge of your seat while reading it. 
 To be honest, I couldn't be more in love with this book and the story the author has created. I recommend this one to everyone, you won't regret it.

I can't even, I love this series so much and now it's over.

 Edit: *Here's the "proper review"* 
 4.5 stars 
 So I spent some time thinking and I still consider Cress as my favorite of the series, even though this one was a rollercoaster of emotions (I got teary-eyed three times because I was so happy and emotional  Wolf and Scarlet's reunion, the last scene with Cinder and Kai, and the very last sentence ).
