On the contrary, even though there are times the story is not focused on the initial plot, I don't mind when the author takes time to develop even more the characters or the relationships. Plot-wise, yes, the length could have been reduced, but at this point for me the characters are what I like the most about this series, so I'm happy with the length and the development they got. And so much happened in this book! It was fast-paced and action-packed, and I flew through it. 
 There is one thing that bothered me though: Winter. I like her character, I find her interesting and different, but we don't see her that much. I mean, the book is called after her and I was expecting more elements from the original fairy tale, and I thought they'd happen sooner. Even though some of them were great and I liked how they were incorporated in the story, I still feel like it didn't have as much importance in the plot as the other fairy tales in the previous books; Winter felt more like a secondary character unfortunately. I still enjoyed what we learned about her and her relationship with Jacin, I really liked their chemistry and their scenes together. 
 Overall I'm happy with this conclusion, I really love this series and I'm going to miss it! It was a great series merging futuristic elements with fairy tale retellings, and I'm looking forward to read more of Marissa Meyer's novels.

Bad Romeo is a story about young love, heartbreak and second chances. I did like the story but it was difficult reading the first half of the book. 
 Cassie Taylor and Ethan Holt first meeting at the performing arts college auditions is unforgettable. They instantly clash but there is an intense chemistry between them. Ethan is the dark bad boy who doesn't believe he is worthy of anyone caring for him. Cassie is the naive smalltown girl who is afraid to show her true self because of her fear of disappointing others. As the new school year begins Cassie and Ethan continue to argue but with playful teasing, and underneath it all they are both avoiding the attraction. When they are cast as the lead roles for Romeo and Juliet it becomes apparent to themselves and everyone the intense feelings they have for each other. But just like the characters in the play Cassie and Ethan are destined for doom, just as Ethan warned her. 
 I was captivated with the story of Bad Romeo but I was disappointed in the direction it went. I thought the pace of the story was too slow. Bad Romeo alternates between the present time and flashbacks to their time together in college. I thought the switch between timeframes was good but there were just too many. Just when the story was on the brink of an exciting scene the author would switch to another time. This left me on the edge of my seat but after a while the constant going back and forth was frustrating. By the time I hit 57% of the book I was tempted to stop reading because there wasn't enough of the story for me to connect with the characters. The present time alludes to the major breakup but the build up for it is really slow. But I am glad I stuck with this because by the time I hit 70% of the book everything finally made sense. I'm not going to give any details but this is when I finally understood more about Ethan. From here on the story moves faster and grows even more intense. And the final chapter was so emotional I am so glad I didn't miss this. 
 Despite the slow pace I am looking forward to the next book, Broken Juliet. I recommend Bad Romeo to readers who love young romance that is complicated and filled with drama.

I didn't think I would enjoy this novel, or rather novella. I'm wary of those 160 page books; they often seem so lazy in execution, like something the writer just phoned in. You know, you start and immediately you get, ekhm, the sense of an ending. 
 Additionally, the cover of 'The Spinning Heart' looked dangerously close to Alan Hollinghurst 'The Line of Beauty', so I expected the book to be half-assed and derivative, as well as full of bleakness steeped in alcohol (it being an Irish book). 
 As you can see, I started reading this choice of my book club with my head full of misconceptions. I was so adamant in my prejudice that it wasn't until somewhere halfway through when I finally admitted to myself that 'The Spinning Heart' was. in fact, quite wonderful, although there is a lot of bleakness steeped in alcohol, as it would be unavoidable in a book which takes place in rural Ireland in the wake of the financial crash. I honestly don't know what Irish writers did during their country sudden and short-lived but amazing prosperity. No one wants to hear about that. 
 Every tiny chapter of 'The Spinning Heart' is narrated by a different character who takes the stage to tell their story. All of them have their unique voices and personalities so Ryan's narrative and characterization skills can't be faulted. The plot is interwoven with the stories so seamlessly that the characters never seem like props to push the plot along. They are definitely there to get something of their chests and are completely unaware of the little bits they drop in that let us know where the story is going. 
 The book opens with Bobby's chapter and we immediately paint him in our heads the way he sees himself - a rather average, morally flawed 'culchie'. It's only when we hear about him from other characters he grows in our eyes and eventually becomes a village hero. I absolutely loved putting different glasses on with every chapter and looking at the same community from a different vantage point. As usual, I did feel most for the obvious nutters (coincidentally - Telegraph's reviewer identified three nutters. I only remember two. I missed a nutter?) 
 'The Spinning Heart' might be often bleak but it is also funny, tender and many other things and made me wonder how it was exactly possible for it to be so full and rich while being so short. It reads like a much longer book. And it's cracking! I also think it could be beautifully adapted for stage.

3.5 Stars 
 This was an enjoyable read. The plot was interesting, a different than most historical romance novels. I liked Jeremy and Yvette, they were both interesting characters with solid backstories. 
 One of my big issues was that I felt I was jumping into the middle of a series, when in reality this was the beginning of a series. I think that this is a new series that has jumped off one that came before, and I wish I had known that as I would have started with the previous series. I found that some things were explained but others were not and I was almost left to guess at what happened. 
 I enjoyed that Jeremy was American, which is something you don't see too often in Regency romance. I liked Yvette's hobby of collecting 'dirty' and scandalous words and I would to have liked to seen that taken a slightly bigger role in the story. 
 The actions of the characters didn't stay completely true to the time period and of what may have been considered proper, especially where sex outside of marriage was concerned, but I was able to look past that.

 It didn't work for me. Conspiracy theories, creepy religious sects, historical letters, dead languages - they just don't work for me. And did I mention that the narrator is "the chosen"? I really despise that trope. 
 In short, the novel is okay, but not great. I skipped reading the letters, and the novel itself is far too long. But I read it on NetGalley, so it was free, and at a price like that I can't complain.

Although, if I had lost 20 pounds I would be pretty unhealthy right now, so perhaps its better that that was simply a MASSIVE hyperbole (are massive and hyperbole redundant? I think so...). Before I manage to ramble myself into next year (more hyperbole and some other fancy-sounding technique as well, probably) here is the actual review. 
 There were a few typos. We all have typos. Sometimes typos get missed. It's not the end of the world and it wasn't every page or even every chapter, so I think it gets a pass. 
 I loved the main character's relationship with her brother. I wish my sister liked me that much. Of course, I know she loves me and Cole loved Lily too, but the sheer friendship between them as well as their siblingly (I mean you get 'sisterly' and 'brotherly' why not 'siblingly'....) love is gorgeous and obviously a major thing in this book if you do end up reading it. 
 I will admit that the summary is pretty misleading; I went into it expecting something entirely different than what I got. Whilst this might not necessarily be a bad thing, it was different so much that you might not like the type of book you're getting yourself into based on the summary. However, you are in (somewhat) safe, (somewhat) reliable hands as I will tell you who I would recommend this book to at the end of my review! Just know that although the summary mentions not going in the West Wing, this has zero correlation to Beauty and the Beast. 
 I loved the world. And in a way, the summary did that well. Mysterious enough. An easter egg for those who read it. The world was beautiful and rich, but I wish could have seen more. Likewise with the variety of characters; especially the side characters. That really was a running theme when I was thinking about what to say about this book: I love things, but I needed more of them. I wanted to see more of the side characters, because there were characters I found interesting that I think I could have loved if I had spent more time with them, seen more of their personality. The romance could be incredible if we saw their relationship more. I'm not 100% sure of the timeline of this novel, but I felt like we needed more scenes, especially with how much character development takes place. This is a really short book- only 144 pages- and I feel like it could have benefited from being longer, but, of course, what is there is great! I also kind of wish we got more background about the very first location, as I am still slightly (I have no idea) why that hospital? was it a hospital? was there. Although that might just be me not picking up on details. 
 In conclusion, I really liked this book and gave it 4 stars but I wish I had more. I would recommend this book who like subtle allegories and very bittersweet feelings in their books. I would recommend it to lovers of a more whimsical yet not fantasy (almost magical realism, yet certainly fantastical enough to be fantasy).

Wow....Very rarely does a sequel maintain it's 5 star rating but CP Volume 2 did and if possible, I wish I could give it 10 stars.... 
 Literally I am just blown away right now. AS I stated in my review for Book one, this Genre(Fantasy)is not my type of fiction but I damn sure LOVE this damn trilogy and I am going to be heartbroken when it ends. 
 Let's get on with the review. 
 1. The Plot: 5 out of 5 stars 
 Shortly following up after the end of Book 1, Damen is tasting his first tease of freedom. He is still a slave to Laurent but he is now out of Vere and heading to the boarders to fight alongside his men. Laurent, meanwhile, is ever poised and graceful is beginning to face Challenges not only from his Uncle but from the Captain of his troops. As Laurent begins uncovering twisted truths and revelations about his Uncle, Damen's longing to be free and home quickly becomes challenged by feelings that he is beginning to develop for the beautiful & dangerous Laurent. And when someone discovers his secret, a line between Laurent & Damen will be crossed that will forever change everything...leading to a shocking cliff-hanger. 
 2. The Writing 
 Pacat definitely maintains the SUPERB writing of Book 1, by changing it up. In Book 1, we were mostly restricted to Vere and while that showcased just how corrupted and how much debauchery lay within the nation of Vere, Book 2 showcases life outside of Vere and introduces us to new lands, peoples and just ups the stakes all around. 
 But what makes this book great is that I'd say Book 1 was focal on Damen, and in Book 2 it still is(he is the narrator) but this was more focal on developing Laurent and giving him time to showcase his hidden secrets as well as properly balancing out the secondary cast with some colorful and well-written characters. 
 The pacing once again is excellent and this time, since they are not at Vere, new dangers and schemes are in place that definitely leave you breathless. Never a dull moment. 
 3. Characters: 5 out of 5 
 Damen once again is a strong character! What I love about Damen is, in book 1, you see him utterly despise the people of Vere and for good reason. He has such hatred and resentment in him and he even comes across as a bit low class sometimes. However, Book 2, while the resentment is there, you begin to see that Damianos the Prince & Damen the slave both differ. He realizes that a lot of his beliefs and "truths" he felt towards Vere, came from his father's inability to try and see them as anything but Enemies. His guilt over killing Laurent's Brother, definitely eats away at him, especially when he finds himself developing feelings he never thought he'd feel for Laurent. Damen is such a great guy and he is so sexy to me. 
 Laurent, however, is my favorite character and the star of this book. He was an utter asshole in Book 1, yet you saw tinges of compassion within him. You can say Laurent is twisted and cruel...but I say he is tragic. He has so much hatred in him towards Damen's people and a barely hidden contempt for his uncle and it has molded him into a dark character, who you think you're supposed to hate since he tortured the Protagonist, Damen, but you never really could. Book 2 still has Laurent at his usual manipulative and dangerous self, but it showcases a Vulnerable side to Laurent we had yet to see. Laurent's admissions of doubt & admissions of someone being a better fighter than him, begin to make me fall in love with him more. Laurent has moments in this book where he breaks...Not like a normal man would. He breaks yet still maintains the control and poise that you'd expect. But by the end of the Book, Laurent does what he does best. He surprises not only Damen, the reader...but himself as well. I freaking LOVE Laurent. 
 Secondary Characters are plenty in this book but to name a few standouts....Jord was introduce in Book 1, and we definitely get some amazing development with him and some heartbreak. I like Jord as a character and I love his involvement with the plot. I am hoping to get a bit of him in Book 3. Other standouts include new character, Aimeric, who has a major involvement with the plot as well and who by book end, I was conflicted about. The secondary cast, definitely holds their weight in a book that is lead by the amazing Damen & Laurent. 
 My only disappointment is one of my favorites(Nicaise) from Book 1 was not in this book. But on the flipside, at least I got to meet Aimeric. 
 4. Romance: 5 out of 5 stars 
 Without getting spoilery, the romance is definitely one of the best aspects. There are a couple of romantic plots in this book but Damen is the main focus. 
 You get hints of it in Book 1, but they are still too antagonistic/stand-offish with one another for this to make much impact. Damen showcased an attraction towards Laurent in Book 1, despite himself, and even with everyone ASSUMING they are having sex, he denies it of course but he gradually begins to see that underneath Laurent's ice exterior is a man that few people ever get the luxury to see and he is slowly beginning to feel drawn to Laurent in ways he could never imagine. 
 It makes it all the more heartbreaking because as Damen finds himself drawn towards Laurent, he still has that secret...he is Damianos, the man who killed his brother. 
 Where Laurent stands at...You'll have to read to find out. Do remember, this IS Laurent we are talking about. :) 
 Overall: 5 out of 5 star perfect read 
 I can rave and rave and fanboy for hours about this book. I truly can. The writing is impeccable, the plot is engaging and has enough twists and turns and shockers that leave you hungry for more, Characters that you feel for and you feel like you truly know them and just a fantastic ride. 
 I really have nothing negative to say which is rare because in most books, even if I like or love them, there is always that one BUT....yet there is none here for me. 
 I am Desperately awaiting book 3 and I am so hoping someway, somehow that book 3 is not the end. 
 Especially Chapter 19..Chapter 19 was..Hot lol and that shocking ending was amazing.

BOOK SYNOPSIS 
 Harlan Coben, the master of domestic suspense, returns with a standalone thriller--in the vein of #1 bestsellers Hold Tight, Caught, and Stay Close--that explores the depth and passion of a lost love . . . and the secrets and lies at its heart. 
 Six years have passed since Jake Sanders watched Natalie, the love of his life, marry another man. Six years of hiding a broken heart by throwing himself into his career as a college professor. Six years of keeping his promise to leave Natalie alone, and six years of tortured dreams of her life with her new husband, Todd. 
 But six years haven't come close to extinguishing his feelings, and when Jake comes across Todd's obituary, he can't keep himself away from the funeral. There he gets the glimpse of Todd's wife he's hoping for . . . but she is not Natalie. Whoever the mourning widow is, she's been married to Todd for more than a decade, and with that fact everything Jake thought he knew about the best time of his life--a time he has never gotten over--is turned completely inside out. 
 As Jake searches for the truth, his picture-perfect memories of Natalie begin to unravel. Mutual friends of the couple either can't be found or don't remember Jake. No one has seen Natalie in years. Jake's search for the woman who broke his heart--and who lied to him--soon puts his very life at risk as it dawns on him that the man he has become may be based on carefully constructed fiction. 
 Harlan Coben once again delivers a shocking page-turner that deftly explores the power of past love and the secrets and lies that such love can hide. 
 My Thoughts 
 Six years may not seem to be a long time to some people but for Jake Sanders six years is a lifetime without the woman he loves, when he unexpectedly comes across the obituary of the man that Natalie married instead of him Jake takes it as a reason to break the promise to stay away made those long years ago. In doing so he then makes a discovery that starts him on a quest to find Natalie, a quest that has Jake facing some hard questions whose answers he is not really prepared to face! 
 Filled with secrets, lies, betrayals and murder this thriller is one that will just about make your heart stop as you experience right along with Jake every step he takes to find the truth even as that truth almost costs him his life. 
 Having read and enjoyed the work of author 
 Harlan Coben 
 for years I have come to expect to be amazed at his intricate plot twists that lead the reader in one direction with the expectation that things are going to work out a certain way, only to quickly find out that those expectations were way off base as things work out totally different than what you would have them to! 
 This makes the reader keep on their toes as you never know what is going to happen next, once all the characters are introduced and the story takes off that is when the real fun begins. In the case of Jake Sanders his awakening to the fact that for six years he has been laboring under false assumptions as to what is the truth makes for a very eye opening reading experience, especially once all the secrets that Jake uncovers lead him to the truth that may or may not actually be more than he bargained for! 
 Like every other book that I have enjoyed by the author once again the twists and turns that he builds for the story slowly and delicately on the way to the finish line just have me in awe of just how he manages to pull it all together for his reader at the end. No other mystery suspense thriller author even comes close for me to this ones ability to set up such interesting and unpredictable plot lines over and over!

 Facing the inevitable loss of her young daughter, Hazel Hunter is a woman with a dark and lonely past, and an uncertain future. Drawn to a man for reasons she can't understand, Hazel becomes enthralled with Obsidian Fox, the reclusive owner of an exclusive underground fighting club. Fox is brutal, complex and dominating. He feels a pull to Hazel that he has never felt for another woman, and struggles to understand his own feelings. While this sounds like a cliche of a plot, there was nothing about this story that was typical. 
 Fox is actually more of an anti-hero than a romantic figure, but I couldn't help but care for him. He has a past that is both heartbreaking and terrifying, and as it is exposed to the reader little by little throughout the book, you gain a better understanding of what makes up this utterly flawed, confused and destroyed man. 
 The emotions between Fox and Hazel were raw and intense, and while I found myself thinking "Why doesn't she walk away??", I also wanted her to understand Fox and stay with him and help him heal. This book was hard to read, but for all of its darkness, this was a fantastic story, and I could not put it down or get it out of my head until long after I finished it. It was so different than anything I had read before, and I found myself drawn into the dark madness that made up Fox's world. I found myself crying and wanting Hazel and Fox to find a way to work everything out, despite the fact that I could not see how that would ever be possible. I felt pity for both Fox and Hazel, while also cheering them on to find redemption. 
 It is difficult to describe too much of the story here without giving away anything about Fox's history that is best read as it slowly unfolds in the book. All I can say is that this was an amazing novel that was dark, heart-wrenching and ultimately satisfying.

Year of Wonders has all the elements to be a really great novel. As I recall, it was the first novel Geraldine Brooks wrote, and it's quite good for a first effort, really stellar, in fact. The problem is, there's both too much and not enough going on with the plot for it to ever really take off and suck you in. 
 I think it's that the main antagonist is a disease (the black plague), and it's hard to demonize a disease. The other conflict is man vs God, which. Religion in general was a theme in this book, but since Brooks is writing accurate historical fiction, God doesn't become a character, and there's no real drama there, especially since the conflict isn't really with Anna and God, but with Mr. Mompellion. And there are various man vs man conflicts throughout, but nothing that really drives the plot with any force. 
 That said, it was quality writing, and I appreciated the close attention to historical details.

First, let me say I didn't go into this with expectations of anything like the Harry Potter series. Those were, yes, children's books. This is a book intended for adults. Still, I had hoped the writing talents exhibited in those earlier works would be translated to the new audience and genre. 
 Sadly, this was not the case. This is a slow-paced book I had to force myself to finish, hoping at some point I would start to connect with it. It has flashes of drama, comedy, and sympathetic characters. But in the end it is about the "message" it has to convey about British society, class, and the issues faced in a modern world. 
 It's that emphasis on message that both elevates and weighs this book down simultaneously. For tackling weighty issues, I give JKR a lot of credit. She could have just cashed in with more wizarding tales or otherwise continue in the light, enjoyable reading vein. Using her popularity to get readers who might otherwise not sit through a lecture on the ills of British society to think about them is to be commended. 
 But did she have to do it in such a godawful boring way? 
 No one in this book is ever even mostly likeable. They may have stray moments of likeability or sympathy, but that is quickly followed by behavior that makes you want to throw the book across the room. Perfect characters are boring and flawed ones more realistic, but when flawed reaches the point of unlikeable (in, to my recollection, every instance) then you've gone too far. 
 I appreciate that JKR doesn't try to sugarcoat these issues with a "happy ending" and simplistic solutions. Still, from a story, I expect a satisfying resolution and a certain amount of closure. While I may have been left with a new appreciation and sympathy for the issues, I was left ambivalent about the characters.

 With this book comes to end to a series I've adored for almost 2 years. I've anticipated each installment eagerly and devoured them rather quickly and it breaks my heart a little to finally have to let go but at the same time I can genuinely say that I am satisfied. Estep did NOT disappoint with the finale. Perhaps there could have been a little less cheese but in the end the conclusion was well done. 
 The beginning had me a little vary. Logan and Gwen were not back to normal and there was still a certain distance to them. Logan was still heartbroken about what had happened back in Crimson Frost and I was a little worried at this point. I thought Midnight Frost would have ironed out some of the bumps but it hadn't. With the kidnapping of her grandmother things became even worse and well.. I was worried I'd have to spend the whole book like I did Midnight Frost but there was nothing to worry about because that was sorted out easily. 
 Gwen is a very likeable female lead. She always makes a point to understand people's points of views even if they don't line up with her own. She may not agree, hey no one asked her to, but she respects other people's opinions. Especially when it came to the situation with her Grandma. She HATED Linus for not trading the candle but at the same time she realizes she would have made the same choice had she been in his position because there is too much at stake. Gwen isn't a hero. Yes she is Nike's champion, yes it's up to her to end the war but she isn't a savior. She very much needs help from other people. She isn't some lone wolf who can take care of everything on her own. She also takes responsibility for her actions and is loyal to a fault. She loves her family and is willing to do anything for her grandma and this just adds up to make Gwen a relateable and very down to earth female lead. 
 This series also has some of the most adorable relationships ever. From the one she shares with her friends, to the one with Logan, her family and Nickamedes. I love how her friends are ACTUALLY GOOD FRIENDS. They see through her bullshit with an ease that only true friends can. They support her and back her up and are willing to help her no matter the cost. Logan was also the sweetest guy ever. You probably wouldn't have expected it in book one but he isn't a bad boy cliche. He is ADORABLE. The two are the cutest couple too. Gwen doesn't want to drag him into her mess not because she doesn't trust him or couldn't use help but because she doesn't want to make him choose between her and his father and you can tell Logan is glad for that, later, even when he doesn't say it and even when he actually HELPED. I love Grandma Frost and her relationship with her Grandma is adorable. It always makes me want to give mine a huge squeeze (accept that I am an awkward hugger). My favorite relationship in this series it the one between Nickamedes and Gwen; they've come such long ways since the beginning of the series, from barely containing their animosity to truly caring for each other. AND THEY FINALLY HUGGED. 
 All of that aside, I AM SO EFFING HAPPY ABOUT THE BATTLE SCENE. Holy crap Estep wrote an amazing battle scene. One that did my proud. The scenes before the battle were perfect. Dripping in tension, you could feel the emotions rolling off the pages. I was nervous, scared, frightened and really hoping that everything went well. When the battle commenced, I kid you not, there was music playing in my head. IT WAS PERFECT. The battle was VERY WELL DONE. I don't think I can emphasize that enough (even with all my caps locks) because well it's the thing we've been looking forward to since the beginning of this series. The show down. The end of it all. The fate of the series, whether I would like it or not, was all dependent on that one bit. The battle. And it didn't let down. Emotions ran high, things were tense, and everyone was on the edge (including me). 
 My biggest qualm about this book was the aftermath of the battle. I was running on a high from the wonderful battle scenes and the high was ruined by an overload of cheese. I didn't like how Nickamedes and Metis ended up together. I don't know why it bothers me so much but it did. I HATED IT.  
 One of the biggest plus points of this series is that the gods are actually kind of cool. They aren't some kind of joke. They are serious beings with a shit load of power. 
 I still cannot quite wrap my head around the fact that this series is over. Admittedly, it isn't a favorite or even an out of my mind experience, but I had a certain attachment to this series. Gwen was a great female lead and her adventures will be missed. To those who haven't started the series, I'd definitely recommend this to you if you're looking for a cute/fun series to latch on to.

Need is one of those books that I've had my eye on for awhile, it was on my wish list, I looked out for it at book shops and I looked out for it at the library, where I found a copy. I must mention that the libraries in my area have been getting some fantastic, wish list-ey books in ;) Seriously, I could've taken out about twenty but I'm only allowed to take out seven...:( 
 Anyway, when I saw Need sitting on the shelf I may have let out a little shriek of excitement, gaining strange looks from others sitting in the library. I took the book off the shelf (Along with six others), checked it out and had it on my blue, wooden chair in my bedroom (where I keep my library books)waiting to be read. Then yesterday (September 20th 2012), I decided to start Need. I'd been looking forward to it for a while (Had to read the other three books first) and now I could sit down, open it up and immerse myself in the story. I did just that, I did have a couple of issues with Need, but it was a book that I just simply couldn't put down, I would recommend it to Twilight/Stephanie Meyer fans. 
 The beginning had me hooked. I love how the chapters are named after an interesting phobia relating to that specific chapter. The first page immediately drew me in, I was curious about what she was saying. Why did she "collect fears, like people collect stamps"? Why had her dad died? There were already intriguing questions flitting about on page one and I knew I just had to read the rest of the book to find out the answers to these questions. Need kept me hooked throughout the book, there were some riveting parts where my heart was racing and I my eyes were flying over the pages, as I read on. However, there were sometimes a couple of pages where my mind wandered and I had to put the book down and do something else,that lasted for a very short time though and it shortly redeemed itself. 
 The plot was pretty well structured. There were quite a few twists that had me quite surprised but most of the time I could guess what was happening. The author left clues leading up to the surprise, but unfortunately some of the clues were so apparent that I knew exactly what was about to happen, which disappointed me, as I love to be surprised by a book (D.I.V.E.R.G.E.N.T!!!) . I did feel that the author could've maybe planned her plot a bit better. I felt like her idea wasn't consistent. Sometimes it was like she said this was happening but then a couple of pages later, she was backtracking on the idea she had just introduced. Parts of the book didn't flow together that well together, it was like they were quite randomly written. I can't say more as to avoid spoilers. :) 
 I liked the characters. I didn't love them. Zara could be quite whiny and clingy. All I wanted for her was to stop clinging to Nick and kick some pixie butt! But she didn't. She even needed to be rescued by Nick when she slipped on the ice O_O. She also moped about quite a bit, I think the author was aiming for her to do that in the beginning as she was depressed with her father passing away but I do think she could've had more depth to her. That's another issue I had with Need, I didn't feel like we really got an insight on the characters' lives. It was like we just watched them do these actions, not always knowing why. I hope the next book in the series will give the characters more personality and depth. The author also didn't tell us how the character looked, at all. The pixies, Nick and a few others were described, but Zara? I wasn't told what colour hair she had, what colour eyes, nothing about her physical appearance. I love getting a description of the main character's physical appearance as then I can really picture my own individual image of the character. 
 Nick was sweet. He reminded me of Jacob, from Twilight and I <3 Jacob. I did get a bit annoyed with him at times, I like it when the love interest is protective over the girl, but at times it can get a bit much. This was one of those cases. I was shouting at Nick to just leave Zara alone for a minute, so that she can learn to fight for herself and not having to constantly lean on him. He didn't listen though. Boys *eyeroll* 
 The other thing that bugged me was that the first day Zara started at her new school, in a new town, two boys already had this stand-off against her and she already made two best friends. Which bugged me. Because I mean, really, how often is it that the moment you walk into the school's car park two boys are having a stand-off against you? And you make two best friends? From personal school experience, that hasn't happened to me or anybody that I know. I do think the author could've toned it down a bit. 
 There were a lot of cheesy moments in this book. Not like the sweet,"Awww" moments in books, but those awkward moments that don't suit the genre. Its a paranormal fantasy and I don't think the way the characters spoke and acted were suited to the paranormal fantasy genre. Zara spoke like the stereotypical teenagers from American chick-flicks, which really got on my nerves. You must either go Paranormal Fantasy or Contemporary, for me, those two don't go well together if written in the same book. 
 Need also seemed like a rip-off of Twilight. Werewolves and Pixies (Twilight had Vampires). A character who continually needs to be saved. The creepy, dull atmosphere. I think Need is a lot like Twilight but I do think the Twilight saga was written a lot better. Twilight really sets the scene, describes the characters and has an unpredictable plot. I hope that the other books in the series will be written better and have more depth to it. 
 Overall, Need was an interesting book that I couldn't put down. There were some riveting parts that had my heart racing and my palms sweating. A new paranormal creature was involved in this book that I hadn't seen before, which was a refreshing change. I would recommend this to all PF and Twilight lovers. With a unique twist, an interesting plot and some deadly secrets, Need will have you craving more.

The world building and character development in this story were phenomenal. The author's writing style was smooth and rhythmic so that I could sink into the movie playing in my head and forget I was reading a book. And the sex? WOW! Yeah, good stuff. 
 Only one thing messed with my movie, and even that wasn't enough to lower my rating. 
  For a movie to work, I need to see the characters. Some might be blurry, but the main characters need to be more finished than the secondary ones. In the first scene where we meet Darius, he is described as having 'dark skin'. That can mean so many different things, especially for a man who spends his time marching from place to place every day. I read a bit further and found no other hints to help me, so I considered writing the author because I found my movie now had a blank spot where Darius was supposed to be. 
 While considering emailing Ms. Gormley, I noticed a review with a picture uploaded. It included what I figure was the readers representation of Darius, and he was a white guy. 
 Let me stop here to just say what I feel doesn't need to be said...but will anyway. Being black is different from being white. The difference didn't affect my attraction to Darius, but not knowing did. So, under the assumption that the review was made by someone who finished the book and felt Darius was white, I decided against writing the author and continued on. My movie now featured a well muscled grizzly white man with salt and pepper hair, a hard jaw, and squinty eyes. 
 On into the book, Jacob calls Darius a slur that makes it clear that Darius is most likely black. I had to set the book down at that point. My entire movie had been wrong. Now I had to reconsider the man I was very much attracted to in this story. I had to re-see all the prior scenes with another Darius. 
 When I picked the book up again the next day, I couldn't help but think of the old soap operas my grandmother watched, with the whispered voice announcing, "The part of Darius will now be played by Terry Crews." 
 The story was still amazing. 
 Now to a little bit of soap box. This is not aimed at this book but much more. 
 Ignoring race is not any better than making it an issue. Most of us want to handle prickly issues correctly, but without really knowing the right way, we decide to completely remove any mention of it. :-/

Loved, loved Justin, well, and Nathaniel too. And all the rest of the cast. But it's Mark who has me captivated and can't wait for his story! 
 This is the second book in the Sins of the Cities series and it continues the mystery/suspense plot from the first book as the background of a rather unexpected romance. 
 Justine Lazarus, the Seer of London, a fake psychic making money by deceiving gullible rich people who turn to him is very much at the heart of this story. And he is such a special character, he is so unapologetically bad you can't help cheer for his HEA. Justine is a shameless crook, who has no regrets and second thoughts about what he does for a living. Yet, we gradually see another side of him - he is smart and observant and crafty and resourceful and ultimately, someone with a moral code of his own, someone who cares about his people, wants to do better, live a better life. 
 He is not an easily likable character, especially at the beginning, but I had no trouble understanding him, relating to him, accepting as legitimate the reasons that made him act the way he did. Deep down he is a good person, caring in his own way, and what makes him even more special is that despite the difficulties he had been through , him acting like a cold-hearted cynic is all more or less a mask, a role he plays to perfection in order to survive. And still, he has dreams, and hopes, is able to love and show compassion and care. 
 Nathaniel was a bit harder for me to pin down as a character - strong and stoic, recovering from the loss of his lover. He was a sort of a justice warrior, guided by strong moral principles. While I'm sympathetic to his struggles to come to terms with his attraction to someone like Lazarus, he acted too superior and judgmental for my liking. His privilege was showing in his insistence for Justin to change his ways. Even though in the end he accepted him the way he was, I didn't like his attitude for most of the story. 
 They are an unlikely pair, which started with an irresistible sexual chemistry in a enemies-to-lovers scenario. I felt the attraction was a bit instantaneous and while I see it as fitting Lazarus, it felt forced with Nathaniel. He's been mourning his partner for a long time and suddenly his attraction awakes, just like that, out of nowhere and it draws him to the unlikeliest of love interest 
 The mystery/suspense part of the story was full of plot twists and turns that kept me on my toes the whole time while reading. It was exciting and unexpected and intense and moving without ever going into melodrama and really enjoyed it. 
 The writing is we have come to expect by KJ Charles flawless, engaging, full of nuanced detail, creating a rich sense of place and time. 
 As the solving of the overarching mystery of the series progresses, not it's time for Mark to get his story told and I can't wait to read it later this year.

I fell in love with him instantly too, what a sweet, mature, and by the sounds of it, HOT specimen of a guy. I'm really looking forward to the sequel. 
 This is another young love story/ college-school students/ sweet virgin-hot guy/ style story. But it's a good one!

As other reviewers have correctly stated; it was a fast-paced page-turner. But I am not so impressed by that. Personally to me I find it rather alarming how short attention spans have dropped and how this aspect is reflected in literature, books, movies etc, so much so that fast paced is somewhat over appreciated. The sci-fi subject matter of this is somewhat in question and I didn't find it very convincing -but I'm somewhat of a skeptic. Nevertheless it was entertaining but not scientifically believable and I, therefore, couldn't begin to call it a hard sci-fi, of which I appreciate much more in general in the sci-fi genre unless the drama, cultural parallels or philosophy of a sci-fi is particularly noteworthy as such in Dune. But then again, that's more or less a fantasy. 
 On a more positive note, I did liked the action and a bit of the unique twist toward the latter portion of the book. Unfortunately it comes with a hole in the plot that you can drive a truck through.  I have read and watched several different movies and TV shows with the same theme of multiple dimensions but this one had a unique spin of it realized towards the end where multiple versions of the protagonist are found to come back spilling into his original reality. But the very thing that make it interesting is also the thing therein that lies the hole in the story.... 
 We have to ask ourselves; Are we to just assume that the Jason-2, who created the multi-dimensional box, didn't visit other worlds? Wouldn't at least other versions of Jason-2 have visited other worlds? So why don't we see multiple Jason-2's as well as Jason-1's? Also, why weren't there some versions of Amanda's with the multiple Jason 1's? How about Amanda's who were separated, like original the Jason 1, but Amanda stumbled into Jason's original world. Wouldn't there be other worlds that discovered the multiverse and wouldn't they then see a phenomena of several different people spilling out into the world wreaking havoc?  Logically, there should be an exception where this only applies to the protagonist, or in other words, the author can't have his cake and eat it to. 
 Overall, I'd say the book was entertaining and a fun read but as far as sci-fi's go, it certainly wasn't in my personal top 20 or even 50. I'd give it 2.5 to be honest.

The book was a wonderful page turner from beginning to end. I wasn't particularly surprised to find out who the thief was, but it was enjoyable getting to that point. I'm also pleased to see a book written for the early to mid teen crowd, full of adventure, danger and ghosts, that features a strong female in a central role.

I thought this was really great, and it feels right now like excellent writing about a timely issue (I am hugely curious to see how this ages). And I confess when I first saw the announcements about it, I was a little ... I guess hesitant because it struck me as something that could be so heavy and ponderous that was going to be a real commitment. But for its subject matter, it's absolutely charming. It's about real characters who have a wide range of experiences and opinions and there's this genuine affection that you get as a reader and in many ways it's a joyful book. 
 My only extremely minor note on this is that there were parts that felt a little overly explainy, some of which were involving the "good" white person character, where the tone and voice felt a little like a departure from the rest of the book. Two or more people are suddenly having a conversation about historical and social context that is chronological and accurate as if they're giving a lecture. My first reaction was "is this truly necessary?" but after some reflection, I recalled that no one ever went broke overestimating the cluelessness, sometimes intentional, of white people, so sure. 
 Edited to add: Okay, I HAD TO come back and add some more, because even when I read it myself, it sounded so awful, like I was saying "well gosh, I only want to read books about happy black people." My initial hesitation was more about emotional preparedness, like when you know you are going to read a book about the Holocaust and so you have to ready yourself a bit so that you can process what you are reading while concurrently being emotionally overwhelmed. And what is happening to black people, especially young black men, during interactions with law enforcement is that kind of horrific. None of this is to say that the events described in this book are handled lightly -- they are serious and they are heartbreaking. It's more that they are presented in a narrative context that makes room for reflection and affirmation.

when i first saw this on goodreads, my first thought was that it sounded like sharp objects. like, kind of exactly like it. dead body in the woods, reporter unexpectedly put on the case in a small town, brings back trauma... 
 however, this book goes to show how different two books can be with similar premises. where they found her achieves a lot in its relatively short form. almost an epistolary novel, it introduces us to five separate storylines that all tie in together at the end: the journalist; her psychiatric transcripts; a doting mother; a teenage girl; and a diary. each is equally intriguing and combines with the others to form a solid second novel, even more solid than mccreight's first. 
 a baby's dead body is discovered at the start of this engrossing tale. soon, questions arise: who is the mother? who is the father? how did the baby die? why was it buried where it was? journalist molly sanderson is put on the scene, assigned to the case, taking the place of an out-of-town colleague. as molly attempts to solve the case alongside the police, she discovers a bounty of other secrets. 
 where they found her is a wonderful thriller, with tight writing and a well-constructed plot.

 I started Texas Destiny last night before I went to bed, finished it this morning. A quick read with likable characters, each with their own grim pasts. 
 Houston and Amelia meet for the first time at the train station in Fort Worth. Dallas, Houston's brother and Amelia's intended, broke his leg the day before he was supposed to leave to meet her. Leaving Houston to travel a three week journey to collect Amelia in his stead. 
 Their travels are strewn with mishaps, as Amelia called them, doubling the time it should take and allowing the characters time to get to know each other, and become quite close. I thought that I would dislike reading about the journey because I expected it to drag, but I actually wouldn't have minded a few more days written in. 
 They arrive at Dallas' property, Houston sends up smoke signs from their camp fire, signaling his brother, and what he intends to be the end of thier time alone together. His brothers and a couple ranch hands ride out to meet them, and they continue onto the ranch. 
 Amelia continues to send looks his way every time Houtson is near and constantly brings up things that they talked about during the trip, which Dallas notices. I mean, the girl did just spend almost two months with him. She's asked him so many questions along the way that she's probably already talked about any and everything with Houston. 
 I didn't expect for Amelia to actually marry Dallas, but it happens and only when he's about to die does Houston finally tell her he loves her.

Despite outward appearances, this isn't a comic: it's illustrated prose. The text is self-sufficient, but it's interspersed with lots of paintings. A lot of people seem to really like the artwork, and I guess it's ok if you like that sort of thing. Personally, I don't, so this was an expensive/bulky way to read a short story. As for the prose, there's nothing wrong with it but it's not particularly memorable. Maybe I'm missing the implications here, of the lessons that all the characters learnt. Anyway, my advice is to borrow this before you buy a copy.

Look, I know I'm probably supposed to give this 4 or 5 stars because it's a Booker Prize winner, but guess what? I didn't like it. The characters grated my nerves, with the exception of Tony's ex-wife; she may be the only character with a level head. While the novel isn't lengthy, there's a whole lot of Not Much Happening for most of the story. Honestly, I feel like Barnes took 163 pages to say something that could have been summarized in 5 sentences. 
 Now, having said all that--the writing style is very beautiful and elegant, which is why I'm rating this 3 stars (even though I'd much rather rate it 2 for plot and general tone). I do love books that tackle the subjects of time, memory, and loss; I thought this would be something I'd love. Unfortunately, that didn't happen.

I love fairy tale retellings, and especially those that blend elements of multiple fairy tales together (hence I'm a huge fan of Once Upon a Time, no matter how twisted it gets; honestly, the more twisted, the better). But for some reason this book never really struck me as a must-read. I guess Cinderella as a cyborg mechanic didn't appeal to me much. But I'd heard great things from people whose opinions I trust about this novel and the series as a whole. And with reviews of WINTER coming in, I thought it was probably time I gave this a try. 
 I'm glad I did. It was a very enjoyable book. Obviously departs quite drastically from the classic Cinderella, but it is incredibly creative and there are really great references to the source material (such as Cinder's car being orange...you know, like a pumpkin?). 
 It's sci-fi, but what I like to call "light" sci-fi. I found this book kind of shallow, in that the world building wasn't that thorough. I just think Meyer was light on some of the details about this futuristic world. This critique is not wholly an insult, however: I really like this world she created but I wanted to know more! 
 The story was pretty predictable. Believe me, I NEVER see plot twists coming. Ever. I'm a terrible guesser. But even I was able to guess at Cinder's identity early on. 
 From reading reviews it sounds like the series gets stronger as it progresses which makes sense. This was Meyer's debut novel and given that, it's very strong. I'm glad she has three more novels to flesh out this world and these characters. 
 I like that Cinder is such a stronger character than her classic counterpart. And this seems like a theme that will continue throughout the series. I also really liked Iko! Makes me want an android with a personality. 
 While I'm here I'm going to go ahead and predict that Dr. Erland's "Crescent Moon" is Cress aka the namesake of book 3 aka the girl Cinder spoke to via the direct comm. Admittedly I have an advantage in making this prediction since Cress has already been published and I've been able to read its blurb. But like I said, I'm a terrible guesser. So if I'm right, just let me have this small victory. If I'm wrong, just don't tell me.

I finally finished it! I say 'finally' because I took a months-long hiatus from this book--it was too intense for me at the time, so I set it aside, returned to it much later, and finished it within days. Go figure. 
 I won't rehash the plot--who hasn't heard of The Shining or seen the movie? I'm glad to have read the book because it's SO MUCH BETTER than the Kubrick adaptation. Seriously. There are numerous elements in the book that were changed for the movie and not necessarily for the better. While the movie is great, the book (as always) is superior. 
 The thing that stands out the most, for me, is that Book Jack Torrance is far more terrifying than Movie Jack. I felt that Movie Jack was basically insane from the beginning, whereas Book Jack escalates as the story goes on and it's not solely that he's 'crazy,' it's that his alcoholism causes a true downward spiral that we get to witness. There's also something inside Book Jack that shows, deep down, he does love his son and I didn't feel that from the movie version. 
 Also, Book Wendy is SO MUCH BETTER than Movie Wendy. Seriously. Book Wendy is strong and protective of her son, whereas Movie Wendy...ugh, don't even get me started. Movie Wendy is so weak and incapable. 
 And! Hallorann! How dare Kubrick kill him off in the movie because Book Hallorann is SUCH AN AWESOME CHARACTER who lives at the end of the book! He was okay in the movie, but I loved him in the book. He helps Danny understand what shining is and they're such kindred spirits. It warmed my heart a little.  
 My only complaint is that the middle part of the book lagged a bit for me. But I'm glad I stuck with it because the final third of the book is incredibly suspenseful--I stayed up late and had to finish. 
 My lingering thought about The Shining is that it's not necessarily a typical horror novel; there are no vampires, werewolves, or witches here. Rather, it's about the darkest parts of who we are as human beings. Sometimes the best horror isn't about ghouls or creatures, but the monsters that we become when we succumb to our inner demons. 
 There's something very triumphant about the end of this book. I'm kind of hesitant about the sequel, but I'm sure I'll read it anyway.

The book is marvelously written. Throws you into an interesting universe with little or no signboards. As you tread through the chapters, you encounter significant events with little or no imagination. I'm not sure if it does, but if the book has a following, it has to be one with a lot of fodder. Philip ensures that the ride is very interesting but leaves a lot demanding. 
 The fact that he doesn't shy away from complex philosophical, theological, and political arguments and monologues, significantly adds to the experience.

Wow... that was so beautiful and so bleak all at the same time. The 5th Wave series has always been rather dark considering it involves child soldiers fighting off an alien invasion that has already obliterated 99% of the planet's population. So to say this book is bleak is really saying something. The thing that really makes this book so amazing is how lyrically poetic the tragedy is portrayed. It makes you find the beauty of all this chaos and pain. Which is the exact thing the book is trying to get across. There can be no joy without pain. There can be no hate without love. Humanity is what makes us human and a human without humanity is something Other. The sum of one thing is the sum of all things. 
 So there you go. You can love the good in us and hate the bad, but the bad is in us, too. Without it, we wouldn't be us. 
 Sam: He had a couple of chapters from his perspective (IE Chapter 38. Which is the best damn chapter of this whole book!!!) and it was so unique. He's 6 and a trained soldier. He can't remember his alphabet but he knows how to make bombs. The way his mind processes things is just so utterly fascinating. 
 In the instant before he pulled the trigger, he remembered his mother's face, the face they had given her, and the bullet that tore down the barrel held his rage, bore his grief, contained the sum of all he had lost. It connected them as if by a silver cord. When her face blew apart, they became one, victim and perpetrator, predator and prey. ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ 
 Ringer: I love Ringer. I find her to be a much more complex heroine than Cassie. However I do appreciate the fact that both of the girls are very different and fully realized people.  That scene with Ben, where she's debating drinking a capfull of antifreeze because she thinks the 12th system will protect her and it will abort her baby. O man. That was a heart breaking scene. Bleak but beautiful due to Ben's trust and devotion to her.  
 Cassie and Evan: Meh. I didn't really care much for their scenes in this book. I loved them in The 5th Wave and The Infinite Sea but I just didn't like them so much here. Cassie was just getting on my nerves. Evan was barely there. So Cassie dies in the end to blow up the mother ship! That was such a beautifully bleak moment as well. It was symbolic of humanity enduring but still... I hate it when the main character gets killed off. :(  
 Ben: I really liked Ben through out the entire series but in The Last Star he serves a very important purpose. I think he is the last glimmer of hope. If humanity ever has a chance to recover, it will be because of people like Ben Parish. 
 That ending: It ended. That's the best way to describe it. Was everything back to normal in the end? HELL TO THE NO! But it felt like a real ending. Like in The 5th Wave and The Infinite Sea our protagonists are going to to the best they can for as long as they can. That's really the best anyone can hope for.

3.5 stars 
 Now, I have very mixed opinions about this book. Everyone I know really loved it and I did like it a lot but I don't think it was really that wonderful. 
 The book follows the life of Patroclus - Achilles' 'best friend' in the mythology and follows the theory that  Achilles and Patroclus are lovers . This idea for the plot is the main thing that I fell unsure about - I'm interested in Greek mythology and I liked it as a book but it's not like she's had an original idea - she's just re-written a story that already existed in her own way. I do like it and I think it was well done but, if you know anything about Achilles or the Trojan war, it's going to be at least a little bit spoilt for you and so I feel that the very idea lacked the potential to produce a masterpiece. 
 I quite liked Achilles as a character - he was somehow simultaneously perfect (as he should be) and imperfect - being too trusting but also rather uninterested in most people. He has a human complexity but is also believably something more than human. I think this was very well done. 
 I was not so keen on Patroclus - he wasn't terrible but I did find him kind of annoying. I did like the relationship between Achilles and Patroclus. 
 Something else that I feel a bit mixed about is my emotional response to the book. I was fairly attached to the characters and I did care about them to some extent but I had no strong emotions, even when events occurred that should have been very emotional. I don't know if perhaps this is because of how they were written or because I knew what was going to happen but I wish that I had felt more. 
 The Song of Achilles is enjoyable but perhaps not memorable, nothing special. I know plenty do disagree with me though so who knows?

I came into this book with very high expectations, and whenever that happens, I almost always am let down. Good Omens was well-written, clever, imaginative...but it just didn't do it for me. 
 Neil Gaiman is pretty hit or miss for me in general. His plots often feel disorganized and lack a clear arc. It's funny, though, because after reading the Author Q&A section at the end, I learned that Gaiman was responsible for the scenes between the demon Crowley and the angel Aziraphale, and he was also responsible for the four horseman scenes. These were actually the scenes that I liked most - though I certainly appreciate the humor that Terry Pratchett brought to the table. 
 It just felt like new characters were constantly being introduced, and despite the handy list of characters at the beginning of the book, I could not keep them, or their story lines totally straight. It wasn't til the end that I think I got the hang of it, but by then, I wasn't invested in any of them fully. I felt like when Shadwell was introduced, I just lost patience. I feel like this would be a good movie or mini-series, though! I think it would translate really well to the screen. 
 Overall, the book was stuffed with characters, many of whom did little to further the plot, and it was much longer than it had to be. They could have easily have made it shorter by about 100-150 pages. So three stars, because regardless of my complaints, it is an entertaining, clever read, and is a cult classic for a reason.

3.5 F***ing Fairy Stars 
 This book captured and held my attention from the very start. There were a few grammatical and punctuational errors, but honestly, they didn't take away from the book, which is really saying something coming from me, because I am like the Head Grammar Nazi. But I digress. 
 The story line in this book was very original and put a new twist on all things Fairy and Fae. I completely loved the way the author spun the story to be about a modern day world where Fae, Vampires, and Witches all lived together, not exactly in harmony, but not in war either. The Guild was a great concept to me. I absolutely love the thought of a "school" type system that teaches witches everything they need to know about spells and magic and fighting. The author got really creative with her world here, and it shows in the book. 
 The plot follows Synthia, a witch  Who was really not a witch. I totally called the fact that she was a fairy! Called it!!!  who is a completely badass, take-no-shit-from-anyone kinda girl. She is terrified of all Fae because they brutally raped and murdered her parents when she was five years old, while she watched. She lives with her coven of three, including herself, Larissa, and Adam. They are the smallest coven, but they are more than that, they are family. But then Syn gets drafted to work for Ryder, the Dark Prince, who she can't stand at first. SHe even has to sign a contract with him- basically signing her soul to him- to make sure she upholds her end of the bargain. But the more time she spends around Ryder and his men, working with him and arguing- lots and lots of arguing- with him, she starts to rethink all the feelings she has for Fae. Ryder makes her feel safe for the first time. And while their romance is budding (actually it's more like raging) they have to find out who is murdering innocent Fae and witches and taking their body parts. The outcome will surprise you. But that ending! It will leave your mouth hanging open, and you will be dying to know what happens next! 
 There were only a few things I didn't like about this book. I already mentioned the grammatical errors, which weren't that bad. In typical epic fantasy style, Through Wolf's Eyes is both long and filled to the brim with characters to remember. There are lots of battles and backstabbings, too. Additionally, there is a hint of magic, not the spell kind, but a subtler magic, talents certain people have for gardening or healing or working with animals. The world building here is excellent and I liked the idea of the girl raised by wolves and of the Greater animals. (There are Great wolves, the kind who raised Firekeeper, who are smarter and larger than regular wolves; the same is true of other animals, like falcons.) 
 The cast of characters, too, is quite likable, although I did not get too especially attached to most of them. Firekeeper is interesting, but not yet really a fitting heroine. She is too much wolf yet to have any romantic entanglements with her own kind or to involve herself too deeply. Derian, who becomes responsible for her training, is a good guy, who I think could become quite a good fellow later on. My favorite character by far is Doc, Jared; he's just such an intelligent sweetie pie. I actually quite liked King Tedric, as well. Lady Elise started out as a bit of an airhead, but grows into a much better character. Lady Sapphire is a bit tetchy and whiny, but kicks serious ass. 
 For those who do not read epic fantasy, I should warn that with this novel especially, but also the genre generally, the plot often moves kind of slowly. There will be exciting battles here and there, but there is a lot of necessary back story and plot development to get through, so there will almost always be some parts that drag and some completely irritating characters you have to follow along with. Through Wolf's Eyes definitely has slow parts and has less action than most, focusing primarily on the search for an heir to Hawk Haven, although I promise there are battles and such later on. 
 So far this is a good read, if a bit slow, and I look forward to reading the next, which is good, because I'm planning to read through the whole series.

As many people are aware, the 'Wool' saga began with an eponymous, self-contained short story. 
 The subsequent four sections in 'Wool' are not so self-contained. They're all longer, and they're all really 'chapters' rather than independent stories. Chronologically, they follow the events of the first section, and follow a growing conflict within the silo between the Mechanical group and the IT group. As with any story that deals with hidden knowledge and old secrets, there's a gradual reveal which precludes giving away too many plot points. But rest assured that the whole book maintains a great tension, features engaging characters, and is both thoughtful and fun (in a dark way.) At times, the 'feel' of the book reminded me a lot of 'Metropolis.' Highly recommended for all fans of dystopic and post-apocalyptic literature. 
 I'll definitely be reading the next installment, and I've also picked up a couple of the stories written in Howey's world by other authors.

Ira Levin specializes in disturbing tales of enormous vision. As such, Rosemary's Baby is a quintessential tale of terror, standing beside giants like Frankenstein and Dracula, because it creates a new, oft-imitated horror form. The book is essentially a psychological conflict set in New York CIty, the capital of the modern sophisticated world, where a young newlywed couple, composed of an ambitious self-centered actor and his made-in-Omaha housewife, is drawn into a world of Satanists for the express purpose of forging (with Rosemary's reluctant assistance) Satan Incarnate. The book is set in 1966, "Year One" of the new era, a year of tremendous conflict and change, and this plays a role in the book's setting and also figures in the plot, part of Rosemary's reaction is in response to the cover of Time that says "Is God Dead?"  
 I've read it three times now and I've reacted differently each time. The first time I was quite young and thoroughly shocked (it was the late 70s) and absolutely riveted. I saw the movie immediately after and was mesmerized with its elegant terror. I have heard it said that the movie - being so faithful to the book in its adaptation - is an adequate replacement for reading Levin's novel, but I'd argue that Rosemary's internal dialog (it's written from her POV) is valuable, especially as we see her movement back and forth between trusting Guy and their neighbors, how guilt is used against her, and how her internal compass gets decalibrated. 
 The second time I read it (late 80s) for pure pleasure and was surprised that it no longer seemed as frightening compared to its new competition. In truth, Levin's avoidance of the grotesque, always choosing the type of subcutaneous chill that most ignites psychological horror, creates tension without the weight of relentless violence we see in films like Friday the 13th and books like Headhunter. What happened in my case is that this terror incubates, never leaving, so that the mere thought of Rosemary's conflict with the coven is enough to invite shivers. There are few books that I've read (It by Stephen King is another - every time I pass a storm drain, I swear I look for clowns) that so perturb that the fear never really leaves. 
 Thus, now I read it, almost studying it, because of its craftsmanship, and I see it entirely different, perhaps because of my age. I mean, I'm much closer to Roman Castavet's age than Rosemary's, right? What do I see different? Well, first of all, I appreciate the utter simplicity of their time. If 1966 was a complicated time, at a crossroads so to speak, 2015 is a high-speed interchange. A cover that says "Is God Dead?" wouldn't even spark surprise today. Their world of Manhattan seems almost quaint, but the power of the novel survives. The characters (the ambitious actor, the innocent housewife, the malignant Satanists, the Dr. Kildare obstetrician, the junkie project) all seem to be tropisms, and it's hard to believe they were ever original, but nothing is really lost there either. The dialog is as witty as ever (Levin is really good) and the scene of Satanic seeding is as tasteful and delicious as ever (though the use of Kennedy and Jackie O may have lost some symbolic power . Almost everything still works actually. In fact, a book that seeming required to be set in the great period of flux is actually timeless. What an astounding success! 
 I think it's because Ira Levin taps into eternal themes: Guy's ambition, Rosemary's guilt and alienation from her family. There is also the theme of Satanists, which could indeed be any occult obsession. The Devil of Levin isn't necessarily Lucifer, but the quest for the third rail of religion. On top of that, there is also an essential message about the elemental power of motherhood and its substantial power, which I glossed over in earlier reads, but (probably because I'm older now) I see as a counterweight to the masculine obsession with raw power. 
 Rosemary's diet though... 
 tl/dr: A finely crafted tale of psychological terror with a Satanic/witchcraft theme. Highly recommended! Five stars.

 I am completely enamored. Maggie Stiefvater has wowed me. Consider me dazzled. The Raven Boys by Maggie Stiefvater is a fantastic book about friendship, adventure, family, and pretty much all the things I love in a good book. 
 Characters 
 : Blue and the Raven Boys are extremely well written. Right off the bat, each character had their own distinct personality. Even minor(ish) characters like Whelk and the 300 Fox Way women are interesting, entertaining, and they have their own motives and hidden agendas. The multiple POVs didn't even bother me because each POV clearly had a purpose that drove the plot forward and revealed new things about the other characters. 
 Blue is such a special little adventurer. She's kind of weird and likes to make odd fashion choices. She feels like no one gets her at school, which she's okay with because she's never really experienced being understood by other people. She doesn't want to be normal and then she meets these guys who are on the surface pretty much everything she's against but they're on this extraordinary quest. I loved that she fit in with them so well so quickly. It just reminded me of that instant first connection you get with people who end up being your closest best friends, and I wanted that so badly for Blue. That magic of new friendship between these characters was everything I could hope for. Also, Blue is so sassy and snarky and it's pretty much the best thing. 
 On to Gansey: I personally never saw Gansey as condescending but I definitely could see why Blue or Adam might see some of his behavior that way. He just always seemed like a little mother hen checking that his little birds were okay.  We keep being told Gansey and Blue are gonna end up together because Gansey has to die before the year ends and Blue is gonna kill her true love with her kiss. And while she is currently with Adam (but are they even really together??), I can clearly see why Gansey and Blue would be good together. They're made up of the same stuff. They're both searching for something bigger than themselves and they can see the beauty in the search for it.  We don't know too much about Gansey but I'm looking forward to hopefully knowing more about him and peeling back all these different versions of himself that he presents to the public. 
 As for the other Raven boys:  I was completely shocked that Noah was dead the entire time. I actually went back and re-read the bit where they revealed this because I thought I'd read something incorrectly. There were clues all over the place hinting at him being a ghost but I missed them all. I did not see that plot twist coming.  I really liked that Noah got along so well with Blue because they both seemed like because she's so spunky and he's very loyal and soft-spoken. Adam was probably the second character I decided I liked after Blue. He just seems like a really good person and you can tell he cares so much about his education and friends. He's that hardworking A+ student that juggles a million different things at once, but does everything in a really efficient manner. While his pride issues annoyed me at times, Maggie writes him so well that I understood the reasons behind his behavior.  And my heart broke every time they alluded to his father beating him. I'm still a little bit confused as to what exactly his Cabeswater sacrifice entailed. I was really hoping the gang would get there in time to stop him but I guess we'll have to deal with the repercussions of his actions in the next book. Ronan was probably the last Raven Boy to really grow on me because he has a tough exterior and says things that can be misconstrued as rude.  So many hints were dropped about him doing weird dream stuff and I am super proud of myself for catching them because Stiefvater is a master at subtlety. Once the scenes with Chainsaw and Ronan started popping up I began to like him waaayyy more. Not to say that I dislike him because I do love him, but I'm just hoping a softer side of him is revealed in the next book. And of course I'm looking forward to learning more about how exactly he takes things out of his dreams. My new answer to the "if you could have any superpower what would it be" question asked in interviews is gonna be the power to create and take things out of my dreams because it just sounds amazing and so magical.  
 The 
 writing style and the plot 
 ! GAHH! It's just so perfect and I honestly don't know how Maggie does it. That magical, mysterious, creepiness mixed with the feeling of endless possibilities is absolute perfection. It's fantastical and there's a bunch of mythology thrown in there, which is always what I want and need. I never felt like I was reading filler. Even when the plot was slow, I was enjoying myself. I felt like every word and sentence was carefully chosen to craft this wonderful book. Nothing was predictable and it was so unique. There search for Glendower was like something right out of one of my Celtic and Welsh mythology classes. It was extremely interesting to me and I loved how enthusiastic Gansey is about it. I also liked that they alluded to how he knows all these really cool professors and important people in that field. It's nice to see that he is clearly taken seriously by professionals and not treated like some dumb, impulsive teenager. I started reading this like a week or two after I finished watching Stranger Things which is probably why I was able to get into the magical paranormal vibe really quickly. But even then, this book is completely unlike anything I've read or watched before. 
 Overall, this will definitely be in my top faves of the year (and just life in general), and there is a very high chance I will recommend this to everyone I know.

This sequel to INSIDE OUT continues to follow Trella's adventures. Previously, she had uncovered secrets about Inside and Outside, but now she's discovering that there's even more to that. And despite the rebellion, not everything's perfect. People still don't get along, and there are some who say the new conditions are even worse than the old ones. There are some who think this is Trella's fault and want to persecute her. Just as everything looked like it was getting better, it all slips downhill again, except this time, there's even more at stake. 
 I've never really been much for action and adventure, so it's mostly been the mysteries, plot twists, and character development that carried me through the first book and made me start OUTSIDE IN. I'd really hoped to find out more about the secrets of Inside and Outside, but there weren't as many twists revealed as I wanted. So many questions remain unanswered, chief among them being the reason for why they're hurtling through space in the first place. 
 It was interesting to watch Trella grow as a character. Much like in the first book, she's obstinate and distrusting, and often that was frustrating for me to watch. However, as other characters justifiably call her out on that, she starts to grow more, learning that sometimes it's okay to depend on other people. I feel like the main focus isn't so much on the characters but the exciting, suspenseful tensions of the plot, and that worked here. 
 I wasn't as impressed by this one as I was by the first book. Trella could sometimes be a bit on the irritating side and I wanted to know more about the backstory than was provided. If I come across the third, I might still pick it up if only to find out who the Outsiders are and why there exists an Inside in the first place. If you were a big fan of the first book and you like action and adventure, then OUTSIDE IN is for you.
