 Story: 
 The story sounded really interesting when I started reading it. However the plot progresses a bit slow. There's a lot of action happening but that's not really what I want. I want the character to ask important questions, do the first things first but he doesn't do them. For ex.  When two people try to kidnap him in college one of them hits Barry. Clearly Barry must have seen that guy. So later on when they're discussing about how there's no trace of those two people the most sensible thing would be to meet up with Barry, ask him whether he saw those two people, is he okay, what's his verion of the story. But instead the main character ignores him completely.  
 Then there are weird character personas. For ex the FBI turned teacher friend he has. What happens is  she agrees to trace Natalie for him. Then later meets him and her update is that she found nothing. But instead of telling it to him like a normal person she starts asking him lots of personal questions. I found that really weird. It doesn't fit in with a character. If you had no info for someone what would you do? You would just tell them that you have no info. But instead if you were asking them detailed qs it meant that you had some kind of hypothesis in your head that you were trying to work out. It's just a weird character. And then both of them don't communicate with each other which was again a weird thing. Are they normal people or do they have some kind of trust disorder?  
 Overall: 
 It sucked. Bad characters. Lot of action but no noticeable progress in plot. Lots of - yeah, yeah, uh-huh, but little concrete conversation. People around acting weird for no reason. Sucked! I'm glad I'm able to drop books without any guilt. There are millions of books coming out every year and I would much rather spend time reading something that I connect with.

 I was super excited when I first discovered this novel because I've been meaning to give Kristen Painter's writing a try, and although I've heard great things about her HOUSE OF COMARRE series, I have a more difficult time playing catch-up than I do jumping on the bandwagon at book 1. HOUSE OF THE RISING SUN has a lot going for it including captivating characters, detailed world-building, and a strong plot. Overall, I thought it was a good first installment, and a great introduction to Painter's new CRESCENT CITY universe. However, I did have a major issue with Harlow; I found her to be very self-absorbed and I couldn't sympathize with her daddy issues. She does get better as the story progresses, and I'm all for character growth, but her brattiness was just too extreme that it was difficult to see past it. 
 I really loved the world-building in this first installment--I wish there had been more of it! The CRESCENT CITY universe is so rich and diverse that I was hoping for a background chapter or maybe a glossary to help fill-in some of the blanks. Now, it's my understanding that Augustine's a secondary character from this author's first series, so I'm assuming I would have probably benefited from starting with HOUSE OF COMARRE. But, already I find myself fascinated by all of the different types of fae. What sets the Shadeux apart from the Smokesinger and the Raptor? Vampires, shifters, witches, and voodoo further complete the picture, and help ensure that all paranormal readers will be able to enjoy this book no matter their preferred poison. 
 Harlow. Where do I begin? She and I did not get off to a good start. I found her bratty and very self-absorbed, and my opinion of her didn't change until well past the mid-way point. I struggled to understand why she chose to alienate herself from her mother because of a man (her dad) she never met. Her attitude towards her inheritance on the tail end of her mother's death was distasteful, and her prejudice against the fae was unjustified, especially given her genetics. Harlow does eventually begin to grow, and I found myself liking the character she might one day become if she continues down her new path. Unfortunately, the author made her heroine a little too hateful to the point that Harlow's behaviour actually overshadowed some of this novel's other merits. 
 Augustine is a phenomenal character, and I can definitely understand why he earned his own spin-off series. I liked how his dark and light sides battle each other; he wants to do right by Olivia, his mom and Harlow, but it's so hard to please everyone, and revenge has a way of twisting even the best of intentions. I enjoyed the diversity and scope of Painter's secondary characters; Dulcinea, Fenton and Lally were insta-favourites, and I look forward to learning more about their backgrounds and seeing what roles they will play as this series progresses. It's also worth mentioning that the villain is especially heinous, and I'm optimistic that the hunt is going to be almost as satisfying as the eventual final showdown. 
 New Orleans is a great setting for this story, and the author makes good use of her location. I enjoyed the beginnings of Kristen Painter's main plot arc, and see a lot of potential for future installments. HOUSE OF THE RISING SUN has one major downfall, but otherwise delivers on all fronts. I have high hopes for CITY OF ETERNAL NIGHT.

 is book four in the Black Knights Inc. series by Julia Ann Walker. This one can be read as a stand alone. We get action, suspense, and romance. 
 These books in this series fascinate, impress, and transfix me with the situations, storyline and predicaments these guys and gals find themselves in. 
 Rock Babineaux is an "enigma wrapped in a riddle and surrounded by bearded stubble". Yep, that describes him perfectly. I loved Rock. Dame he was hot, sexy, and protective. Vanessa Cordova, hired as a communication specialist for the Black Knights. I liked her. She is strong, determined, and pushes herself past her limited experiences to bring back Rock. These two work well together. The sexual tension was just oozing off the pages. The action and suspense kept me transfixed and glued to the pages. I love the additional side characters and of course the previous characters. It all adds a great dynamic to the book, especially when you add in the banter and humor they have. It shows you how close everyone is. How the Black Knights have become a family. 
 I love the Black Knights Inc. series. The characters and situations are always entreating. Thrill Ride delivers an action packed adventure! If you have not picked up this series yet, I highly recommend you do.

"In Cassiel's name, I protect and serve" 
 Many have reservations about this book. There is certainly a fair amount of erotica, but don't let that fool you. The intricacy of this book's plot provokes emotions that make people look at me strange if I'm reading it in a public place. 
 The first part of the book is your basic "how the character was raised" fantasy introduction. But the feelings come in waves once Joscelin Verreuil enters the story. And it builds and builds as they go through a terrible journey together. So I've provided my emotional reaction to a specific scene in the book. I've hidden the details as spoilers, and left the emotions readily available for your reading pleasure. 
 At the battle of Troyes-le-Mont , Phedre no Delauney picked her way across the enemy encampment, as they held siege, in order to deliver a message to her queen. I see this in my mind over and over again. I see her dangerously delivering her message to the guards in the fortress. I see Waldemir Selig catch her and drag her to her knees. I hear him yelling at the fortress, telling the queen to watch how he pleases spies. I see him rip off her dress and bring the knife to her flesh and start to skin her alive. And then  I hear her scream. Gods how I hear her scream, so loud that it reaches into the heart of the fortress and the heart of my soul. It rings over and over in my mind. I see the red haze of pain and hear the beating of Kushiel's wings. I see Joscelin ride up, madness in his eyes, and I hear him challenge Selig to the Holmgang and then, after, in order to save the woman he's oathsworn to protect. I see him take his daggers out, one poised to throw into Phedre's heart and the other ready to slit his own throat,  and then I hear it. "In Cassiel's name, I protect and serve." And I cry. I go back and reread the passage and I put the book down and replay it over and over in my head for years. And when the memory starts to fade, I pick the book up again. No passage in any book has ever touched me the way the beginning of the battle of Troyes-le-Mont has.

Summertime is the prefect time for fast paced thrillers, and this new one got rave reviews, so took it out for a spin. I've had this author on my TBR for a while, but this is the first book of his I've read. Color me disappointed. After about 200 pages, so about halfway through, I decided to stop wasting my time and DNF it. 
 I heard Helen Mirren say that the thing all humans have in common is our interest/fascination with sex and violence. TV, movies and best selling books seem to bear this out, but in my opinion there is a difference between violence that serves a purpose in story telling and gratuitous violence. This story seems to showcase the latter, but to give credit where credit is due, the violence is against both women and men. Equal opportunity violence. 
 The plot revolves around a young boy, a troubled female dectective, a cop recently released from prison, and a serial killer. It's set in a small town, so I'll suspend disbelief, and go along with the premise that they are all connected in the manner that unfolds. The problem is that the plot needs the violence to move it along, as there is no other anchor point into this story. The characters are not well fleshed out, their motivations are murky at best, and in a couple of instances simply mind boggling. The point of view changes from character to character, all in the third person, which does little to pull you into the story. The writing was not good enough to pull me along either, and I was bored. The reason I even got this far in the book is that it is a quick read, and I was at the halfway point in a couple of sittings. However, I could care less about these people and where they are headed, even though I think I have a pretty good idea of the grand reveal. 
 This was labeled as a literary thriller. I found it to be neither, but based on all the 5 star reviews, it might just be me.
So, controversial... I've decided to order this anyway and read it for myself... :)

Spoilers throughout- be warned!  
 I wrote in my review of Divergent that the trains represent the book itself: evocative, vivid, continuous fast-paced action, making up for an irrational premise (trains that never charge a fare and never stop running and never stop at a station? Who pays for the fuel, and why don't the other factions insist that the trains stop at stations so they can be a public service usable by factions other than the Dauntless?) 
 Insurgent loses that fast-paced flow of action, so there's less distraction from the irrationalities of the story. The book opens with Tris having just been shot. Losing a great deal of blood apparently has no effect on her ability to function, because being tough means that physiology is only for other people. 
 When people are shot and and bleed profusely, besides watching the murder of their parents, in addition to killing their own close friend, amidst the slaughter of nearly all their childhood friends at the hands of their new friends due to mass deployment of a mind control serum by an enemy faction, in an event which signals a catastrophic breakdown of the five-faction society they have always known and may well render them factionless in the wake of a regime change within their own faction, they will go into shock. That is what will happen to the body after the adrenaline crashes. If it does not happen and the character functions pretty normally, jumping on and off of trains and following the proceedings of a journey and a group discussion with interest and connectedness, it is not a sign of toughness. It is a sign that what you are struggling to read is not very authentic. 
 Going back to my earlier train analogy, the train does not shoot on an exciting ride through a vivid cityscape in this book. It putters to a halt and sits and thinks about its boyfriend for ages, then fights with the boyfriend, demands the truth from the boyfriend, and lies to the boyfriend. They make up and make out, and the train sporadically starts chugging again until it peters out for the next go-round. 
 This has stopped being about a girl fighting for her place in the world and for her friends' safety and for the greater good of their society, who also has a special romance on the side. It started being about a girl who loves her boyfriend and is mad at him and wants the truth but tells a lie and loves him soooo much, plus there's other stuff going on. 
 I hoped that some of the plot problems would be skillfully explained in Insurgent. Actually the big explanation turned out to be even less internally consistent or rational. An eyerolling cliffhanger ending that was intended to be shocking revealed that the faction system was very recently thought up and then implemented through some kind of brainwashing. No word on why they think you cannot be both clever and brave, but it seems that they predicted that if you make up a nonsensical faction system of non-mutually exclusive personality traits and truly believe that they are mutually exclusive, then people with special brains would "evolve" and save humanity. No word on how the saving would happen, but it's important to cause the factions to think that the ones who can save us are a dangerous threat who should be eliminated. 
  
 My vote: don't bother to read Insurgent unless you feel addicted to Divergent. The fast-paced action is gone, and the characters are different and somehow less compelling.

I wanted this to be amazing for me. I really, really did. I did all the "right" things: I stayed away from reviews, didn't know what to expect, didn't even read the blurb!  What I liked: The writing was really unique and lovely. The setting is of course, gorgeous, and easy to picture. There is mystery, and intrigue, and all kinds of ridiculous family drama/first-world problems. It is a quick book that is definitely easy to read. 
 What I didn't: I guessed the twist early on, at one point in the story that perhaps others would overlook, but immediately, I read one particular sentence and knew at least part of the big plot point. So maybe that's on me, but it does dampen the excitement for the book. Also, every time I read "Cady", all I heard in my head was Tim Meadows saying "Cady Heron" ala Mean Girls. Again, that one is probably on me too. And I didn't really connect with Cady a ton either, which probably made it less enjoyable. Ultimately, the ending just didn't live up to the hype, and I was left kind of feeling a bit let down. 
 What confused me: I still don't have the faintest clue why they've always been called The Liars. Seriously, someone going to fill me in? Did I miss something? 
 Bottom Line: 
 It wasn't a bad book by any means, it just didn't "wow" me in the way I was expecting. Perhaps I went in with too many expectations. Either way, I still think is definitely a book worth reading. Obviously, you're going to want to form your opinions on this one, and it really is quite well written and a quick read.

The premise of "The Ones Who Walk Away From Omelas" is a time-honored one: is the happiness of an entire civilization worth the suffering of just one person? The question has been posed in many forms over the years, but Ursula K. Le Guin poses it again in this short story about a seemingly utopian society that ends up being more like a well-hidden dystopia, with its dark secret tucked away in a cellar somewhere. Except the thing is that it's not a secret: everyone knows the sacrifice the town of Omelas has given so everyone else can have happiness, the simple yet not-so-simple form they all wish to achieve. Le Guin's story is a description of the town and its shortcomings, an interesting read, especially thinking about the what-ifs and all the questions that are raised about how such a society came to be and why people still believe what they do to maintain their way of life. Is it worth it to turn a blind eye to suffering and continue to live in isolation and denial? Is it better to escape Omelas, to accept reality and to realize that life is nuanced and has as many good and bad aspects as their are grains of sand on this earth? This is not my favorite short story by any means, but certainly one worth reading. The link to read it online is here.

I think Mary Calmes is a guilty pleasure. I read her books and can point out the flaws, of which there are many, yet there is an engaging voice and sheer outrageousness to the characters and actions that delivers an entertaining and fun read regardless. Calmes is the kind of reader that fans love even if the story has issues and I can appreciate that because there is something about the characters that draws you in. I easily read Trusted Bond in one sitting and although it sets up the same situation over and over again - Jin in trouble, again as everyone wants him - the story remains entertaining. 
 In this sequel to Change of Heart, Jin and his mate Logan are back. Jin is the star of this story as his special status makes him a repeated target. I'd suggest you read the first book before tackling the sequel or re-read the first book if you want to understand it all. You can pick this one up for the sheer guilty pleasure and not care about the various interconnecting storylines and then it won't matter. I'd read CoH over a year ago and while I could remember some details, Trusted Bond throws out tons of names, details, positions, and situations that seem foreign without any context. I was pretty lost in how the majority of these people and their jobs/positions connected to Jin and his family but after a while I just gave up and didn't care. 
 The world building feeds into this confusion since it's so haphazard. The rules and theories of the werepanther world change to meet whatever tension and drama is needed. This is what happened in the first book and continues here with rules mentioned and then ignored later with no consequences. It keeps the tension high as the overly political were packs have tons of rules, regulations, laws, and protocol that all work to keep Jin from Logan, or so it seems. So the reader is never quite sure what will happen since really anything can. It's a very sloppy way of creating tension with messy world building at best. Additionally, many of the characters offer information via dialogue that makes no sense. The information is important for the reader but the characters would already know it, so their saying it is a clumsy way of conveying that information to the reader. 
 The action tends to be very frantic and exaggerated with the characters even more so. Jin is once again the special were panther with abilities never seen in one like him before. He's the super special flower, the only one in existence that's like him and well if you've read Calmes books before you know how exaggerated and perfect her characters tend to be. Jin is no better but he has warmth and charm that makes you want to forgive his obvious characterization and root for him anyway. His chemistry with Logan is smoking hot and their sex scenes are delightful, sexy, and plentiful. He is too perfect though and he only becomes more so in this book with even more power, even more special abilities, and even more people vying to save or kill him. 
 The frantic action keeps the story hopping though as Jin manages to be beaten, kidnapped, and/or both no less than three times in a row. There is some relationship drama with Logan as Logan's gay for you love freaks Jin out. Jin comes to put more trust and faith in Logan and their love by the end of the story and the two have a special, one of a kind connection. Their relationship works even though Logan never really gets out of his rather flat, two dimensional box. The story is all about Jin though so that's ok. I wish Domin and Koren would get their own book because that's a couple that nearly steals all the attention when they're on page. 
 Really the engaging writing and easy to read entertainment make this a fun guilty pleasure. It has a lot of problems though so for those readers that are bothered by messy world building, clumsy information dumps, perfect characters, and obvious scenarios may have problems with this. It's not perfect at all and will appeal more to those readers that can ignore the faults because they enjoy the writing anyway. If you're that reader - you'll likely adore this. If you're not, I wouldn't recommend this.

There are some books that are good. There are some books that are great and every once in a while there's a book that's phenomenal. The Beginning of Everything was phenomenal. This book is just about as brutally honest as coming of age stories go. The Beginning of Everything represents life, teenage angst, first loves, and first heartbreaks. It represents what it means to find yourself in the most unlikely of times and around the most unlikeliest of people. The book represents what it means to grow up and face shattered dreams and later a hopeful future. The Beginning of Everything was a clear representation of what it means to be a teenager today. 
 I feel like reading this book was a privilege in itself. It's rare to find a YA contemporary that truly speaks to you, that you connect with a hundred percent and the book itself feels like an extension of your own body, especially told from an honest male's POV. But that's just what The Beginning of Everything was; it was honest and rare, raw and funny. It tore my heart out into a million pieces and threaded it back together by the end. Our injured protagonist, Ezra is one of my favorite characters of all time. He was intelligent and funny, his constant witty remarks had me smiling and laughing out loud. There were moments I had to close the book, tip my head back and have a nice giggle at the things he thought. Ezra really grows into himself in the book, he matures and realizes just how vain and selfish he used to be and not only realizes it but he even gets disgusted by it. We see how the events after the accident really put things in perspective for Ezra and how he comes to accept his past and look into the future with open arms. Ezra even went out of his way to make sure he'd never be the old vain and childish self he once was, he was repulsed by how he used to be and knew he didn't want to go there again. 
 The romance in this book I also found to be really enjoyable. It was slow building, not perfect and exactly the way teenage romance really is. The relationship between Cassidy and Ezra wasn't without its faults, they weren't perfect and that's just what made them all the more memorable. They had their fair share of bumps in the road and nothing was ever really simple with the two. This book is Ezra's story about finding himself and his belief that Cassidy was the catalyst to his new life, to him changing his ways all the while Ezra may not have been Cassidy's. I love how Robyn Schneider left things with Ezra and Cassidy in the book, it went along with my own beliefs that sometimes a person can change your life, but that doesn't mean you're the one to change theirs. 
 "I still think that everyone's life, no matter how unremarkable, has a singular tragic encounter after which everything that really matters will happen. That moment is the catalyst--the first step in the equation. But knowing the first step will get you nowhere--it's what comes after that determines the result. -- Robyn Schneider, The Beginning of Everything 
 The Beginning of Everything deals with the belief of tragedy, and how one's true honest self is born from tragedy. The book explores how one only truly accepts life and learns the meaning of living it to the fullest after tragedy strikes. This belief is what really struck a chord in me and I was able to connect with it from the start. I have yet to go through my own personal tragedy, and in all honesty I'm scared to death too. But this theory Ezra has is one I've had myself for years, years and years of watching drama movies and drama reading books have left me with the idea that maybe I won't know how to fully live life until after I've nearly lost it. 
 "Life is the tragedy,' she said bitterly. 'You know how they categorize Shakespeare's plays, right? If it ends with a wedding, it's a comedy. And if it ends with a funeral, it's a tragedy. So we're all living tragedies, because we all end the same way, and it isn't with a goddamn wedding." 
 -- Robyn Schneider, The Beginning of Everything 
 From beginning to end I was completely sucked into the book and Ezra's thoughts. I feel like if there's an adult out there who understands what it's like to be a teenager this day and age it's Robyn Schneider. I said before in this review that reading this book in itself felt like a privilege, and I still think that. I think through Ezra, Robyn perfectly captured the funny/angst/scariness of being a teen. And through Ezra, Cassidy and Toby, Robyn captured parts of herself. She gave us readers a brief glimpse of what it's like to be inside her head. And for that I feel privileged. All I ask now is that Robyn Schneider NEVER stop writing.

Whimsically fun, but there's far more spoof than substance here--which was likely the intent in the first place. As a spoof, it works rather well. The sci-fi world owes an immeasurable debt to the Star Trek television franchise, and this entire novel is a gentle ribbing at the shortcomings of the series (like why the bridge always has to explode in sparks during battle scenes when it's the farthest point from the actual damage). As a novel, though, it felt far too self-aware for me to lose myself in the story, with enough winks and nods interspersed throughout the story to continually remind the reader that this is all a lark. 
 What threw me for a loop is that the codas made a sudden transition to seriousness, and I wasn't sure what to do with it.  That divergence also made the novel seem much less cohesive, as though too many things were being attempted without enough narrative glue to hold it together. Everything works independently, but packaging the material in one novel seems forced and even a bit contrived. The incessant use of "he said" also started to drive me batty, especially in lengthy scenes of back-and-forth dialogue where those words closed every single line of speech. It made the whole experience feel more like a rough draft rather than a final copy.

3.5 Stars 
 I have been anticipating the start of this series for YEARS. Since the moment we first met Dane in the Sinners on Tour series, I've been dying to know more about his band. And of course about him! I completely understand why we are not starting this series with his book, much as I like to grumble about it. It wouldn't make sense. 
 This is about the base player Logan. He's the type of hero with a playful attitude and a lot of confidence. He doesn't take himself very seriously but you have to suspect that there's something deeper that drives him to act the way he does. To hide the scars he carries inside. 
 Toni on the other hand is the opposite. She hasn't had a lot of life experience. She's self sacrificed most of her life to the care of her sister with special needs. She's still a virgin, still sheltered by her mother, and going on tour with Exodus End might just be the platform to proof to everyone and herself that she has what it takes to succeed in life standing on her own two feet. She's there to write an interactive biography about the band, a position that she got because her mom is the owner of the publishing house hired to do the job. 
 I've seen this trope done before in rock star books and I have to admit it's not my favorite. At times I really liked Toni because deep down she's such a good person. She has bursts of coming out of her shell that come out of nowhere and made things a bit unrealistic for me based on her background, but the tenderness of her personality shines through in the end and I ended up being ok with her. However, she's a bit too naive and immature to be the type of heroine I gravitate to. Just my personal opinion on that, though. 
 Logan is older than her and has lived the party like a rock star lifestyle for a long time. He realizes that there's gotta be more than that and has a huge case of insta-lust and insta-love? in a way with Toni. I found him completely endearing in all his possessiveness! 
 INSIDER is a great intro to the Exodus End band! We get the perfect amount of glimpses about every member of the band, including a good dose of Dane. What we learned in this book is making me itch to get to Dane AND Max's books! For Sinners fans, there's plenty of sightings of our favorite characters and some even are struggling with some issues. Like Reagan, Trey and Ethan who will be dealing with their issues in a second book about them in the next book in this series, OUTSIDER. So looking forward to that! 
 As always, Olivia Cunning cements herself as one of my go to authors when it comes to rock star romance. Just keep them coming!

 Logan glanced at Toni and found her gazing at him with adulation. Awesome. Keep talking me up, guys. He was all about getting noticed. Always had been.

This is the second in the Armand Gamache series, and I think it's safe to say that I am hooked. I enjoy the omniscient third person point of view that is a little less jarring now that I am used to it, and you have to give credit to an author who can make living in Canada in the winter sound appealing. 
 Though I've rated it the same, I probably liked this installment slightly less than the first. It is difficult to wish to see a murder solved with quite the same intensity when the deceased is one that everyone hates and her murderer is obvious from the beginning. There was a slight swerve that almost threw me at the end, but not quite. 
 Like many other reviewers, I have to say that I was disappointed with the author's treatment of CC's depressed and verbally abused daughter, Cri. Penny does a wonderful job of creating varied characters, but the most negative feature she seems to be able to give someone is obesity. Poor 14 year old Cri is in turn teased and ignored simply because she is fat. We are told that she is intelligent and has a beautiful singing voice, but that simply cannot make up for the fact that she is not much (or perhaps too much) to look at. Even her teachers call her Brie. How cruel. 
 I enjoyed the description of the 'three Graces' and their life long relationship. Life of Pi by Yann Martel (2001) 
 I can see why there is such a range in opinions regarding this book. Reading others' reviews, I see how much some people despise it while others are completely moved by it. I fall into the latter group - for me, something resonated deeply. 
 I could probably spend 227 days replying to other people's reviews, especially those that didn't enjoy it; but I think what it comes down to is that you have to read this book as a philosophical, spiritual, and/or religious journey. It IS about religion; or perhaps, more accurately, God. It says so in the Author's Note "Then the elderly man said, 'I have a story that will make you believe in God.'" 
 So, if you are not prepared to examine this story as an allegory from that perspective, then I suppose you won't really enjoy the book. If I was to speculate as to a couple of reasons why someone would NOT enjoy this book, I would say that Part 1 is slow-moving. There is a really BIG set-up in this book and the set-up is extremely important in understanding the rest of the book. In particular, descriptions of zoo life, including the temperament and care of the zoo animals is important; as is Pi's devotion to God and practice of three different religions (i.e., Hindu, Muslim, and Christianity). 
 For anyone thinking of reading this book or who has started and is having trouble moving forward...be patient. Every piece of information from these early chapters contributes to the understanding of Parts 2 and 3. If you are a person that likes to skip over parts, or likes to skip to the end, seriously...don't bother picking up this book. It's totally not for you. This book is about the journey. I've read reviews saying that Parts 1, 2 and 3 are disjointed - I couldn't disagree more; in fact, I would argue that they are three necessary parts to the whole. 
 Another reason I think some people would NOT like this book is the ambiguous ending. The story told in Part 2 is absolutely riveting. Martel is a brilliant story-teller. I could envision myself in Pi's shoes and followed with the ups and downs in his psyche as he experienced them being shipwrecked. It would have been a really great story if the end had been Pi's (and Richard Parker's) rescue. In fact, I bet that for those that didn't like the book, they would have given a higher rating if it had ended like that. (Just guessing). But, instead Martel offers an alternative account of Pi's experience (stripped down and much more horrific). The ending thus can leave the reader puzzled, frustrated, or perhaps even angry (based on reading others' reviews). 
 Most people tend to like nice tight and neat endings after investing so much time, emotion, and energy to reading a book. Martel's story leaves us hanging and allows the reader to choose the ending they believe. I still get goosebumps reading the text that brings it all together (from Chapter 99, p. 317): 
 "'So tell me, since it makes no factual difference to you and you can't prove the question either way, which story do you prefer? Which is the better story, the story with animals or the story without animals?' Mr. Okamoto: 'That's an interesting question?' Mr. Chiba: 'The story with animals.' Mr. Okamoto: 'Yes. The story with animals is the better story.' Pi Patel: 'Thank you. And so it goes with God.'" 
 Brilliant!! This is the text that brings together all three parts of the book. I love the way a few little sentences can pull together a whole story. Love it! This passage brings to mind the stories from the Old Testament, Daniel and the Lion's Den, Noah's Ark, the Tower of Babel, etc. Those were some good stories, weren't they?  
 Ok, so at the end of the day, Martel's writing is superb, the story is absolutely riveting, and the ending is thought-provoking. I can see myself reading this book in a few years with a fresh perspective and re-interpreting the story. It is THAT kind of book.

When I read Shades of Milk and Honey, I wasn't that impressed -- even when I reread it. But I quite liked Glamour in Glass. Probably partly out of sheer bloodymindedness; I looked at some reviews and oh how they whined about Jane's attitude to pregnancy in this book. And I thought, wait: that's actually interesting. Yes, let's address how dangerous pregnancy could be at that time. Let's address how "confinement" literally imprisoned women. Yes! Let's discuss the aftermath of the Austen and Heyer novels and their neat marriages: the babies, the risks to the women, how those women were limited. 
 Someone called it anti-pregnancy, and I don't think it's that. It just turns to something that went unspoken in that period, and scrutinises it a little, and articulates a fear and dread of the constraints pregnancy placed upon women (shown even more clearly in this world because a woman can't work any glamour while pregnant). It's still a fairly light read, despite that theme; I read it in an hour and a half, so if you're a fan of the first book, don't think that it's suddenly changed entirely in style and subject. 
 This is less frothy than the first book, seriously examining the relationship between Vincent and Jane, their equality and finding a balance between them. I anticipated the political plot ahead of time (perhaps because I'm fresh from Voyage of the Basilisk); it feels a bit rushed, honestly, particularly toward the end, but I appreciated seeing Jane and Vincent facing down these issues, and his growing regard for and trust in her.

 Lachlan Crow is a potential heir to the throne of the Irish mafia in Boston. He's described as quiet and reserved, but make no mistake-he's calculating, menacing...definitely not a man to be fucked with. After the recent untimely death of his grand-da, he's out for revenge, but it must be done delicately and diplomatically, so as not to soil a pending alliance with the Russians.

 Mackenzie "Mack" Wilder is a tough girl from Southie with a dark past and a single mission on her mind: to find her best friend, Talia, who has been missing for almost a year. Mack knows that nothing good can possibly have befallen her troubled friend, who was last seen working a new job at Slainte, a bar/strip club and front for the Irish mafia. Finding the Feds incredibly unhelpful and apathetic to her cause, she boldly decides to take on her own undercover mission. 
 Mack's method of making herself known and remembered in front of the Irish is bold and borderline insane. And it works. She immediately catches the attention of Lachlan and from there, there's no shaking it. Not that she wants to. A man in his position possesses peak potential for gathering the information she needs. Doesn't hurt that he's a sexy Irish mob boss with tats, abs, and a penchant for boxing. Did I mention the dirty talk?

On Mack's end, we see the internal struggle she has as she battles a deep-seeded guilt for not protecting her friend in her time of need, and subsequently "sleeping with the enemy" (as she sees it). As her feelings continue to grow for Lachlan, it becomes increasingly problematic and at odds with her mission to spy on him and uncover more information. 
 On Lachlan's end, we get to see a similar internal battle. His job comes with several obligations that make his obsession with Mack a dangerous distraction that puts them both at risk.

I received this book for free in exchange for an honest review. This does not affect my opinion of the book or the content of my review. 
 Claire is on her fourth fiance when her "curse" strikes again but Lord Alexander Pembrooke miraculously shows up and wants to be her fifth. 
 Years of planning have finally put Alex in position to destroy his old friend Lord Paul, gaining the beautiful Claire is simply a bonus. 
 Old hurts and lies by omission will work to keep Alex and Claire apart if they can't figure out how to open their hearts to one another. 
 "Our marriage is based upon hate and revenge." 
 First in the Cavensham Heiresses series, The Bad Luck Bride is Janna MacGregor's debut book. The prologue was intense, dark, and intriguing as we get introduced to our hero Alexander and his two friends, Lord Somerton and Lord Paul. There's betrayal, pain, anger, and hurt, all set in a swirling snow storm; I was instantly hooked. As the story went on though, the author had a tendency to overwrite (a bit too descriptive at times for my tastes), the cast of characters became a bit overwhelming, the story started to drag with repetitiveness, and the focus on the lead's chemistry faded away. 
 Alex misinterpreted a suicide note left by his sister and blamed his friend Lord Paul for her death. This is the catalyst for the story as he works to destroy Paul and leads Alex to marrying Claire. If we would have just had this one misunderstanding, I would have went with it but Alex is a rush to judgment guy and the repeating of him getting angry and then saying oops (not the best apology man) was a bit frustrating. 
 I liked Claire in the beginning as she seemed unfairly saddled with the "curse" talk but we lose her as the story goes on. The curse was brought up so much, I almost thought I was reading a medieval and it was a big deal because people wanted to burn the witch at the stake. I wish it would have been handled more as a bullying tactic the ton was using instead of the awkward heavier weight it was given, especially since it isn't fully explained until the very end. 
 When our leads first meet, I loved the chemistry they had, their discourse had some great by-play but as the story went on, due to the overload of the curse talk, overly handful of secondary characters, and forced angst, Alex and Claire seemed to be kept apart more than they were together. Their fights and flushing out of feelings was less interactions and more in their own heads, I prefer the characters to interact more. 
 I wish the editor had been heavier handed as trimming up side tangents that become repetitive or simply didn't add much to the story, could have made this stronger as more scenes and the focus would have been more on what worked, the chemistry between the leads. There's also some series baiting characters, I'll be interested to see if the author plans on trying to redeem Lord Paul as he seems to have gotten a raw deal but also had a tendency to tell some lies that make him pretty hard to like. 
 As a debut though, I can see the hints of promise this author has and will be interested in trying her again.
Sweet and fun read - I'm very much looking forward to the rest of this series.

What we did agree on was that it was hot and it was dark. It was a deep, sweat-drenched night sometime in the worst stink of summer when the locks came open. None of us could argue over that. 
 I've been rushing to read as many 2016 Printz contenders as I can before the awards are announced, but since I finished The Walls Around Us two days ago, I haven't wanted to pick up a new book. I didn't have this experience with Bone Gap, which I read right before this and is, from what I'm seeing online, most people's pick for the win. I liked Bone Gap, but I loved The Walls Around Us. 
 This novel is narrated by two girls, Amber (incarcerated in Aurora Hills Juvenile Detention Center) and Violet (about to leave home to attend Julliard in New York City). They are connected by Orianna, Violet's former best friend, who is now locked up with Amber at Aurora Hills for violently murdering two fellow ballerinas. Violet tells the story of her friendship with Orianna, ending with the incident that resulted in Orianna's arrest, and Amber describes life at Aurora Hills from the inside. Typically when I read a book with more than one POV, I find myself looking forward to one narrator's chapters over another, but that wasn't the case here. Both narrators have compelling stories to tell. As Violet's story unfolded I found myself wanting to fling the book away - she is that creepy. And Amber functions as the voice for all of the prisoners at Aurora Hills, often using second person plural to explain what it's like to be one of its forty-two residents: 
 Some of us knew for sure it was a Saturday, the first one of August. Some of us kept track of days... Then there were those of us who didn't want to keep track, whose sentences ran as long as a set of train tracks to all the places we'd never been. We pretended weeks were days, and years were weeks. That we still got to live our lives out in the sunshine. 
 In a way, The Walls Around Us reminded me of a Gillian Flynn novel, in that it has a female character so depraved, so completely off-the-charts insane, that I was chilled to the bone. It's the kind of story that makes you wary of everyone around you, even - especially - your closest friends. This book is, as so many reviewers have said before me, extremely disturbing. It's also the best YA novel I've read this year. Beautifully written, as I'm finding is typical for Nova Ren Suma, but also very controlled. The paranormal elements are handled well and the ending, while a little crazy, is satisfying. The Walls Around Us gripped me much harder than Bone Gap did, and overall, I think this book just worked better. Its voice was stronger. I don't think it's likely to win the Printz award over Bone Gap or Challenger Deep, but I hope it gets an honor. It has my vote, anyway.

Of course, I loved this book. With shades of Piers Anthony's Incarnations of Immortality series, a 17-year-old anorexic girl is tapped to become Famine, one of the Four Horsemen (Horsepeople?) of the Apocalypse. It is interesting to see how anorexia rules her entire life and fractures her personal relationships, and the reader wants to smack Lisa upside the head so often -- except it is clear that it isn't really *her* that is making these choices. She is compelled by the Thin voice in her head, who tells her repeatedly how fat and worthless and pathetic and disgusting she is. Being a teen is hard enough for people without these voices; I can't even imagine how difficult it must be from someone suffering from an eating disorder. 
 At any rate, I loved this book with my whole heart. The writing was fast-paced, and I devoured this book in an afternoon. I just couldn't put the dang thing down. It also amused me highly that Death appeared to Lisa as an incarnation of Kurt Cobain. 
 Highly recommended. Well done, Ms Kessler.

Fail-Zoned: A Rant About Unfortunate Reading Events 
 Before I start this review, go watch this video. If you think the Maldita Lisiada is the worst scene ever, Friend-Zoned comes to prove you wrong. 
 A while ago, I found this book. The title and the cover themselves made me want to read it. I mean, it's a story about the oh-so-terrible friendzone--it must be fun, right? 
 Well, flash news... It ain't fun at all. This book has been a great disappointment, one that ultimately pissed me off. A lot. 
 The writing 
 I'll put it simple--it's atrocious. My English isn't the best, of that I know. But a) it's not even my mother language, and b) I'm not charging money for you to read what I write. 
 It is not only juvenile, but way too simplistic. I felt like reading a fanfic, a really bad one. Plus, there are a lot of mistakes. As in, too many mistakes that are unacceptable. If I was able to notice them, anyone proofreading this book should've noticed them too. Which leads me to think this has no proofread whatsoever. 
 "[...]me and Nat on one side of the mattress, Lola and Meems on the other with Bear accepting cuddles and pats from all sides smack dab in the middle." 
 "Only when I was her huge smiling face did I begin to relax." 
 Excuse me? You were what? 
 "This pistol is my baby. My dad gave it to me when I fifteen." 
 "I'm can't believe we beat him up." 
 "He must the worry in my eyes." 
 "I haven't noticed Nik stiffen and but I have notice his arms tighten around me." 
 "[...] and I will start the sisterhood of Nik's Anonymous for women who are having trouble getting over Nik then we'll have to hire a church and make sandwiches and punch for the thousands of women who come!" 
 If you read that paragraph without having a stroke, congratulations! 
 "Nat told me my going on a date the day after his birthday will really cut Nik deep." 
 "Max stood up taller looked at her with brows bunched and uttered, [...]" 
 "This guy could be dangerous for, Christ sake!" 
 "I take my cell phone out of the bag look at the display fake frowning." 
 "Even with heels on the man is ridiculously tall." 
 Now, you have a serious problem with commas, missy. 
 "I kiss his lips hard and say whisper, "Oh my god!" Cry-Laugh." 
 "Two thirty comes and I arrive at the warehouse the Sixes own better known as the factory." 
 "We are over people trying to bring us down and Mimi told me that if I had any more problems with anyone this week to flip em the bird and say some really nasty words which made me giggle and blush." 
 I'm really starting to think I've read a whole different book. How on Earth this thing has a 4-star rating average? Those quotes above are just a few of the ones I highlighted on my Kindle. There are a ton more, including mistaking "we're" for "were", "him" for "his", "passed" for "past", and "your" for "you're". More than once. 
 Overall, the writing is bad, the editing is beyond terrible and even the formatting sucks. 
 The Characters 
 Are we sure they're adults? Because they act like five year old kids, after eating about a ton of sugar. They're just immature, take terrible decisions and don't act accordingly the characterization they're given. 
 Let's meet Tina, the dumbest character I've ever read about. Yes, it's even worse than Anastasia Steele. 
 "His arms are amazing! They're muscular and have veins running up them." 
 No way! Veins?! Unbelievable. 
 "[...] But I did get the choc chip cookie for him instead of his preferred white choc almond. Yeah, I'm badass." 
 "Her sweet, tear streaked face looks down at my somewhat deflated cock and she whispers brokenly "It- It- It -It's not going to fit!" She finishes on a soft wail." 
 She's 28, and already had a baby. 
 "[...]I don't blame him. I never told him I had my birth control device taken out." 
 This happens right after Nik finds out she's pregnant. Now, she didn't even bother to tell him that unprotected sex would lead to pregnancy, while some time ago she made it clear that she was using one and didn't want to have babies. Isn't that the kind of stuff you should tell your partner? Well, fuck being responsible! :D  
 She's childish, and puts herself in risk by doing stupid things NO ONE with a functioning brain would do. And don't get me started with slut shaming. Just don't. 
 What about Nik? He's no better. His reactions are plain unbelievable (but at least not as ridiculous as Tina's... No, wait. Maybe they are), and he doesn't sound like a man. In fact, he reads exactly like any other female character, but with a penis. 
 "Second, he comes on to my girl. ...not that she knows she's my girl. But, anyway..." 
 "Then hurricane Tina tore through my life and my heart. I built her up so much. I was sure she was perfect. Now, she's not quite perfect anymore." 
 You know why he thinks that? Because Tina told him she didn't want to have children. Wonderful. A woman that doesn't want to be a mother can't be perfect at all, duh! 
 Before Tina, he treated women like a use-and-ditch object. But, of course, our female lead had to change him... 
 "He looked like a crappy casual sex partner but I can already see that he treats me different than girls like Sissy." 
 Because, you know, women that are into casual sex aren't worth a thing. 
 "I hope I haven't overstepped a line here. I would hate for things to become awkward between us." He clears his throat. "I like having you around." 
 I beam on the inside and assure, "No, not at all. It probably would've been weird if I found out some other way but you came right out and told me." 
 He had her investigated, and that's her reaction. Like, how would she be mad? It's perfectly normal to have your friend/boyfriend hiring a private investigator to find out anything and everything about you. No biggie. 
 All in all, the characterization is laughable at its best. As in the type of laughter that comes when you're about to have a mental breakdown. 
 The plot 
 I have the feeling the author didn't know what to do after the 50-60% mark... So she just threw a bunch of random side storylines to "make things more interesting". It started as a (supposedly) cute and funny romance book, and then I was in the middle of gang wars, with mafia guys, psychopaths, and kidnappings included. And let's not forget about crying! We could do a drinking game out of this. Drink every time someone cries--I assure you you'll be not only drunk but intoxicated before you reach the end of the book. And no, I'm not exaggerating. They cry at least once in each chapter. 
 In the end, nothing made sense! It was like a terrible mexican tv show (aka telenovela). No, no--it was far worse. 
 Inconsistent, repetitive, full of cliches and unnecessary descriptions that added nothing to the story--it dragged on for what seemed to be an eternity. 
 As a side note, this book taught me that all you need to get a 700k dolars deal are cupcakes, so I may start baking right about now.

 --Lose brain cells; 
 --Be bored to death; 
 --Feel the pain I feel. 
 However, I suggest you to take a look at this review.

 Why I Read this Book: Ever since I read 
 Hush, Hush 
 last year (which I really enjoyed), I've been dying to read Crescendo. A year seemed like too long of a wait but the time has arrived! And let me just state for the record, I re-read Hush, Hush (in 24 hours nonetheless!) before cracking open Crescendo. That is so unlike me to re-read a book! But I don't think I would have been able to make it through Crescendo without doing so. It was a nice refresher because I had really forgotten a lot of what happened in Hush, Hush since I read it a year ago. 
 The spooky thing about this all: I read Hush, Hush (the first time) and re-read it on the exact same day, one year apart. I didn't realize this until after I had finished reading it the second time. I had started reading it on 10/17 and finished on 10/18, both times. Freaky! 
 What I Liked: The writing is good. The author took me through a range of emotions, good and bad. There was many a time where I wanted to throw this book at the wall because of either Nora's emotions or her actions. 
 The suspense was killing me! Crescendo is definitely a page turner. I was glued to the book trying to find out what was going on. 
 Another thing I was pleased to find out in Crescendo: Patch's real name. 
 What I Didn't Like: Nora and Patch frustrated me to no end, mostly Nora with her being so naive. There are many situations and circumstances that I will not go into because they will give part of the story away. But I will say that her emotions completely took over her sense of reasoning. She acted irresponsibly and erratically throughout most of Crescendo. I'm kind of upset with the way things left off between Nora and Patch in regards to their relationship. The author evoked such strong, unfavorable emotions from me towards these two characters. 
 Patch's reasoning at the end of the book did not justify his actions, especially his involvement with Marcie. Patch caused Nora so much grief, so much pain. This was another cause of frustration for me. 
 Overall Impression: I liked Crescendo; I just didn't enjoy it as much as I enjoyed Hush, Hush. Becca Fitzpatrick throws in a killer cliffhanger ending which has me anxiously awaiting Tempest Silence, the third book in this series. I was also left with quite a few questions that were left unanswered. Questions I hope will be answered in the next book, which I will definitely be reading.

 4 stars! Melted my heart! 
 This is such a highly compulsive read. I fell IN LOVE with the characters that Stephanie Perkins created with Lola and the Boy Next Door. Truthfully, this is a light and fun book. It will never be a literary classic so if that's what you're looking for, go elsewhere. But if you want something that is warm-hearted, deliciously unputdownable and just plain old high school crushin' fun? I'd check this little gem out. 
 Lola is the girl who stands out in a crowd, literally. She dresses eccentrically and makes no apologies for her love of costume. Her life is very well on it's way to being perfect. If only she could get her dads to approve of her sex god rocker boyfriend, Max. Life, however, has it's own plans for Lola when the infamous Bell twins move back in next door to her. Lola thought she was long over her days of pining over Cricket Bell. His re-emergence into her life now has her in a tailspin. What will Lola do about this unexpected turn in her story? 
 I think this book stuck out to me more than Anna and the French Kiss because I genuinely connected with Lola more than I did with Anna. I've seen the negative reviews stating her as absurd, not-realistic, too wacky, selfish and what have you. And while I saw those things as well, I also remembered being self-centered and melodramatic at 17 and still sometimes find myself as such at 23. I remember doing outlandish things to set myself apart from the crowd. I adore Lola because of her flaws. And like Lola, I make no apologies for it. 
 And I will say it openly, I am in love with a fictional 18 year old named Cricket Bell! So sue me. He is so damn likeable and so damn cute and awkward and GAHHHHHHH!!!! 
 My only criticisms for this book are as follows: 
 (1) The names are ridiculous. I found it endearing but I can see how that could throw someone off. 
 (2) Why'd you have to make Max a douche? I was already rooting for Cricket. Yeah, I want for there to be tension. But I want to feel like its a struggle to choose between two love interests. I did feel like some of it was believable but some parts were just not. And that didn't work for me. Which is what held this book back from being a 4.5 or 5 star rating.  
 However, those were minor points in the grand scheme. The truth is that I tore through this book. Now I'm genuinely distraught that I'll never read this book for the first time ever again. I don't know what to do with my life. 
 If you don't mind, I'm going to weep into my raw cookie dough and long to live in San Fran with these ridiculously-named, lovable hooligans.

READ THIS BOOK ONLY SO YOU CAN READ THE NEXT ONE, BECAUSE HOLY HERA ACOMAF IS !!!!! 
 Maas's "A Court of Thorns and Roses" is at its best mediocre. It will make you mad- very mad- but ultimately it is worth reading. The second ACOTAR book is 500% better, and I give you my word. Despite how little I enjoyed the first book, I'm really impressed by Maas's character development ability and how much she grows as a writer from book to book. She understands that women aren't perfect, so it's impossible to write perfect women. That's not to say that our hero Feyre is dumb and helpless, it's to say that she's human. In ACOTAR #2, A Court of Mist and Fury, Feyre realizes her strength and how she held herself back and how she let others hold her back. This is a very human crisis that Maas writes beautifully. Plus, if you think Tamlin is dreamy in ACOTAR, just WAIT until Rhysand in ACOMAF... Dear Lord. 
 Good things about ACOTAR #1: 
 Great world building. Maas is very, very skilled at world building without describing every tiny detail, sort of like Tolkien. ACOTAR is sort of like "Prithian: A History" and that's all that's really important about it. Like the Silmarillion but sexier. 
 Characterization is outstanding. It's very rare that I grow attached to characters in just one book, but Maas has a talent for making characters you absolutely love and absolutely hate. In ACOTAR #1, her strongest characters in terms of development and depth are Feyre, Tamlin, and Lucien. The ending is weak, so her weakest characters in ACOTAR are Amarantha and, ironically, Rhysand. 
 Sorta Poor Qualities of ACOTAR #1: 
 Not much action, just world building essentially and sexual tension. The main focus is on Feyre and Tamlin, so the rest of the story is pretty weak and underdeveloped. But boy, oh boy, does that change in ACOMAF. Please read ACOMAF. 
 Only lovable character is Feyre, which can turn off readers and not make them want to read the next book. BUT PLEASE, I BEG YOU, READ ACOMAF. You will fall in love with like seven faeries I promise. 
 Another big thing that bothers me, especially in YA fantasy, is that most characters are white and straight. This may not seem like a big deal to some, but for many it is, especially if you're not actually white and straight. It's 2017. YA writers (and they're mostly white) need to realize this. 
 It's overall just kinda a weak book. Weak beginning, weak rising action (if there really is any... Things just kinda... Happen.) and weak ending, although the ending is the strongest out of the book. Maas does a good job of setting up the next book subtly, but it's still weak and doesn't really leave you craving the next book... I only read ACOMAF because my friend begged me to and because I'd spoiled a bit of it for myself on Tumblr... So don't go on Tumblr before you read ACOMAF because those suckers will RUIN the book for you because ACOMAF is so dang good!!!! 
 *** 
 So I hoped this helped you decide whether or not to read ACOTAR #1... I was really skeptical at first because I really, really hate YA fiction... Before ACOTAR the last YA novel I'd read was "The Winner's Curse," and wow what kinda racist trash. I was appalled. And although ACOTAR's characters are pretty much all white and all straight, it avoids cliches and is kinda a breath of fresh air. But again, it's ACOMAF that really got me.
There's absolutely nothing wrong with this book - I suspect it is a very good book. It's just not the book I want to read right now.

 Listening to the end, though, I realised how much I actually loved this book. It was more than just fun (though it certainly was that), it was gripping and well thought out and I was very much emotionally invested. After some of my recent listens (Champion series, Empire of Storms, even the last few Vampire Academy books), I though maybe romances just didn't work as well on audiobook, but no. I really liked Izzy and Dex. And I absolutely love the friendship between Izzy and Romy. It just seemed so normal. Aside from the ghost stuff, that is. Obviously.  The end was strong both plot-wise and emotionally. I can see where the rest of the originally planned series would have gone, and while I would have loved to read that, I'm pretty happy with where we left everything. Not awesome, not terrible. I admit while reading it I had to keep making myself read it, and went between it and several other books before finally deciding to just finish it and I did so quickly because I have to finish any book I start (its a weird thing I always do, even if I hate it). That isn't to say I hated it but I knew it wasn't going to be a favorite of mine. It is one of Stephen Kings less talked about novels and it feels like he wrote it with that in mind almost. 
 The protagonists are old.... really old, which is sort of.. meh, because you don't care too terribly much about their well-being when you have the feeling that they will die in a few years any how. 
 It did pull me into the story but it got sort of... ridiculous and absolutely nuts. And not in the good way. In the way where you think the only way the author can tie it all together is by coming up with something so nuts and crazy. I'd say this book isn't as plot drive as it is ... umm what's the term I'm looking for... well.. Basically it uses the crazy nature of characters and the plot to use for its message and theme. It's about abortion and I think the message here was, people who are all balls to the wall for a certain cause (ie abortion) will do literally anything for their cause no matter how nuts or crazy or ridiculous. This book is a practical satire of those said people and the lengths they will go to in order to fight a battle without end that has no winners or losers. 
 I personally liked that part, since people who argue about abortion are really arguing over something that is already legal. They can't change it, they won't change it, they're just people who are obsessed with arguing over a dead topic. They do crazy things to gain recognition by the people on their side; to basically become heroes. Oh look what Ed did, chucking dolls full of blood at the abortion clinic and got arrested! He sure does care for our cause, we need more people like him on our side! When in reality all it does is show how strongly he feels about it, while being completely unproductive. I know I just rambled but I'm stating what I believe King was trying to say in this novel. The book ends sort of tragically, but it is a bittersweet tragedy. 
 Part of the thing I mentioned earlier about  having old characters in the novel, and I mean like REAL old. That part makes you care less about the well-being of the characters, when Ralph dies you really aren't heartbroken because of his age, and also because he is exchanging his life for someone else's life.  That part sort of annoyed me, and is likely why there aren't geriatric characters in books such as these. 
 It's wort a read, but is quite long, and if you aren't really drawn in by the premise or uber curious about it, I don't know if you could sit in for the entire novel.

A Discovery of Witches has been on my radar since shortly after it came out. I'd seen glowing reviews and heard great things from friends, so I figured I should give it a shot. I received this book for Christmas last year, and finally got a chance to pick it up about a week ago. Honestly, I'm not really sure what I think. 
 Here are the basics: 
 Our main character, Diana Bishop, is a historian and non-practicing witch descended from the famous Bridget Bishop (of Salem Witch Trials fame). Not wanting to be accused of getting ahead by using her magic, Diana refuses to use it for anything aside from necessities. When the book begins, Diana is at Oxford, researching alchemy for her next project. She puts in a request for the well-known Ashmole 782, and given her credentials, it's readily provided to her. Suddenly, it seems that every supernatural creature in all of Europe has flocked to the library to watch what happens, because little did Diana know, but Ashmole 782 has been something of a mystery for hundreds of years. This super-special, super-enchanted manuscript has baffled even the most powerful witches, but Diana opens it by simply laying her hands on it. She knows there's something special about it, but given the fact that she's denying her magical heritage, she just gets what she needs and sends it back to the stacks. That's when all hell breaks loose and she requires the assistance of a very old, very mysterious, very handsome vampire to keep her safe. 
 I'm not going to lie. I really struggled through the first half of this book. At one point, I made it about five pages before falling asleep. In the middle of the day. (That is not something I do, ever.) The first half of the book is dedicated to ridiculous, painstaking, overly-detailed descriptions of what Diana is reading, what Matthew is drinking, and what everything smells like. It's like Harkness hadn't quite found her plot yet, but wanted to keep filling pages while she thought about it. The pacing does improve about halfway in, but not enough to compensate for the first half. With the improved pacing comes a fairly predictable plot: 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 * Diana is put in harm's way. Can Matthew save her? (Of course he can.) 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 * Diana is put in harm's way. Matthew can't save her this time, but can she save herself? (Obviously, there's two more books.) 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 * Diana is put in harm's way. Can she figure out how to use her magic in order to save herself? 
 * Diana and Matthew passionately kiss. Diana wants to sleep with Matthew, but he turns her down. 
 I took issue with a few things in the book that made it really hard to like the main characters: 
 * Matthew thinks it's perfectly fine to break into Diana's rooms himself -- before he even knows her. But he flies into a rage when he finds out that someone else did the same. 
 * Matthew convinces Diana to flee to France with him because of the supposed danger she's in at Oxford. But once they're there, he abandons her (probably because he loves her so much, or something) and she literally cries enough to fill a room with water. 
 * What am I even supposed to think about this marriage nonsense? Diana and Matthew kiss in front of Matthew's vampire mother, then declare their love for each other. (This is after they've known each other for approximately two weeks.) "Just so you know, we're married now," Matthew says. "Oh, okay," says Diana, as she begins referring to his children as her own. WHAT? THAT'S NOT HOW MARRIAGE HAPPENS, GUYS.  
 This book is basically just Twilight for adults, and I really wish someone would have told me that before I started, because this is not what I signed up for. 
 A Discovery of Witches is much too long, and much too detailed. A decent editor could have cut out at least 100 pages of unnecessary descriptions and backstories. A good editor could have probably taken this book down to half its length. 
 I'm not sure whether I'll pick up the next two books in the series. Harkness seems to think that by having Matthew repeatedly say, "You don't need to know about this right now, I'll tell you later," I'll be compelled to keep reading. Honestly, I don't think it's worth the effort. I was frustrated with the slow-moving plot and pages upon pages of unnecessary description. I wasn't impressed by A Discovery of Witches, but it's also not the worst book I've ever read. 
 I'll give it a generous two and a half stars for drawing me in at the very end.

This imaginative novel has a host of characters, but there are three main characters: Aomame is a sports/physical therapy trainer, and Tengo, a writer/mathematician. The third key character is Fuka-Eri, a 17-year-old girl who grew up in a religious cult, and escaped at the age of 10. Fuka-Eri wrote an imaginative novel, and Tengo is persuaded by his editor to be a ghost-writer, to rework the novel so that it is more literary. 
 When I first started reading this novel, I was just sucked into the story. For some reason--it pulled me in. Each chapter alternates between the points of view of the main characters. After reading the first two chapters, I thought that the book was a collection of short stories. There was simply no connection between them. It takes quite a while before the connection becomes clear. And there are surprises--I thought I understood Aomame by the end of the first chapter--boy, was I wrong! 
 Although I have classified this book as "fantasy"--it really is not fantasy. It is not moralistic and would be better classified as "supernatural". The characters slip from the real world of 1984 into a parallel world of 1Q84. In this world, there are little people who walk out of the mouths of dead animals and people, and two moons. Otherwise, the story is based on reality with occasional inexplicable happenings. 
 This is also a romance; Aomame and Tengo last saw each other 20 years ago while in grade school. They both would like to see each other again, but Aomame admits that she is not willing to go out of her way to find Tengo. She prefers to leave such a meeting to fate. 
 All that said, I found the book starting to become tedious after a while. It is far too long--it could easily be cut in half without missing crucial components. The flavor became repetitive, and at a certain point the surprises petered out, and the plot became somewhat predictable. 
 However, this book was translated from Japanese to English by Jay Rubin and Philip Gabriel--and the translation is masterful. The novel reads as if it were originally written in English. Kudos to the translators!

Greene's narrator, a supercilious correspondent who invites you to despise him on every page, is a strong character - in fact the only complex character in the book.  I waited until I'd read the book before I turned back to Robert Stone's introduction, which surprised me by its caustic assessment of Greene.His rendering of all the American characters as pathetic straightmen, helpless before irony, blinking in the pure light of the British characters' ordinary, instinctive decency and wholesome common sense has a darkly familiar tone. In this modern coming-of-age novel, we learn about Charlie and his experiences through the letters he is writing to an anonymous friend. I usually do not like this style of writing, but it worked for me in this novel. One of the first events that Charlie reports is the suicide of his friend Michael. Next we learn a little bit about his immediate family and his Aunt Helen. Aunt Helen is deceased but she has played a crucial role in Charlie's life. Even though Charlie has experienced a tragedy and lost important relationships, his life improves when he meets Sam and Patrick. They are seniors and sort of adopt Charlie like a pet of theirs. Sam is a girl and Charlie immediately forms a crush on her. Patrick, her stepbrother is gay. He becomes a close friend to Charlie. Throughout the novel Charlie experiences a lot of intense experiences-drugs, sex, and the Rocky Horror Picture Show. 
 The Pitfalls of Being A Wallflower 
 Charlie is quiet and introspective. His English teacher remark that "...sometimes people use thought to not participate in life." Charlie is a passive person-he just sort of lets things happen to him without exerting much free agency. Like the time when he allows a couple to invade the room he is in to have sex-in front of him-without objecting. When he later realizes that the sex was really a date rape, instead of reporting it to the police or confronting the guy during the crime, he slashes his tires to get back at him. In another instance he allows Patrick to kiss him because Patrick's heartbroken even though he isn't gay. 
 Charlie 
 The events in the novel along with Charlie's feelings and actions throughout seem unbelievable. For instance, he cries a lot in front of his peers. He also asks for advice about sex from Sam, specifically how to tell his girlfriend he isn't ready. His friends Sam and Patrick don't seem to mind his idiosyncrasies, but most of the other kids at school think he is a freak. I thought he was strange too, but once I found out what is haunting him I came to understand why he is the way he is. 
 Quotes Teens Like  
 "...sometimes people use thought to not participate in life." 
 "Charlie, we accept the love we think we deserve." 
 "And in that moment, I swear we were infinite." 
 !!!!Spoiler Alert!!!! 
 Charlie is a victim of sexual abuse by his aunt. He has repressed the memory but a sexual experience triggers it. I congratulate the author for addressing this topic. While our society no longer denies that sexual abuse occurs we still often picture the perp as a stranger when it is most often a relative or close family friend. All victims feel ashamed, but the sexual abuse experienced by a male child and perpetrated by a female is the most shameful secret of all. Kudos to Chbosky for treating this topic with Perks.

I could not wait to read Hero when I first heard that Samantha Young was writing this standalone story, and I was not disappointed at all! This book was everything that I have loved from Samantha Young in the past, and was also so much more. It was captivating and interesting, and I absolutely couldn't put it down. This book sucked me in right from the start, and ended with me staying up way past my bed time because I had to finish. 
 After finding out some awful things about her father, Alexa Holland has worked hard to turn her life into one that she can be proud of. She works hard and is determined to be nothing like her father. When she meets Caine Carraway, she knows that she needs to apologize for the horrible things that her father did to his family. But Caine wants nothing to do with her, and doesn't care that she is trying to find some redemption. But when Alexa gets fired from her job due to Caine, he offers her a job working for him. Caine decides to make things as hard as possible for Alexa in the hopes that he will push her too far and she will walk away for good. But Alexa isn't going anywhere easily and is determined to show Caine that she is nothing like her father. The more time they spend together, the more the tension between them increases until it finally explodes. Alexa wants Caine and is convinced that they can find happiness together, but Caine knows that he is not the white knight that Alexa wants him to be. 
 I really liked Caine. He was sexy and confident, to the point of being cocky and arrogant at times. He had his moments where he was a jerk and tended to say some horrible things, but I found myself loving him anyways. He had so much pain from his past, that it was clear to see he had never really dealt with anything. As soon as he would say something awful, he seemed to genuinely feel bad about it which made me think that he wasn't as horrible as he tried to come off as. He and Alexa brought out so many emotions and feelings from one another, that things were very intense between them. It was clear to see that the passion between them would explode one way or another, and sometimes they ended up hurting one another when they didn't mean to. Alexa had just as many issues as Caine did, and I think that she really understood him. She was strong and relentless, and I loved that she never gave up on Caine. She was so dedicated to showing him what they could have, and I really liked that about her. No matter how many times he hurt her or pushed her away, she saw it for what it really was. Though sometimes a character like hers can come off as weak or a doormat, Alexa didn't to me. She wasn't weak, but rather stronger than anyone knew. She was exactly what Caine needed and I loved seeing her help him grow and heal. These two had so much chemistry between them, and they were super hot together. But I really enjoyed seeing them get to know one another and form an emotional bond as well. 
 Overall, this book was so good and I really cannot recommend it enough. I loved the characters and how complex they were. Caine had so much beneath his surface and it was clear that we didn't know everything through most of the story. He had battled through so many hard times, and I knew that when his past was finally revealed that he felt awful about how he had become the man he was. He did what he had to do to survive and make something of himself, and I really felt for him because he wasn't proud of how he had achieved that. But I was glad that Alexa was able to show him that none of that mattered to her and that she loved him for the man he was and not what had been his past. If you are a fan of Samantha Young's you will really enjoy this book, and if you are new to her this is a great place to start. I really loved Caine and Alexa's story, and I cannot wait to read more from Samantha Young in the future.
