This is a review that compares the actual play onstage in London with the script in book form (with thoughts on the general story as well). Spoilers are hidden. 
 I watched the play in London on 4 August (Part One) and 5 August (Part Two) and finished the book a few days later - so I had everything from the play fresh in mind. 
 Firstly I want to say that the play was beautifully done. All the illusions and effects used to achieve magic was ingenious, to say the least. The audience was wow'ed over and over again and we all gasped and 'oh!'ed and clapped in unison when something particularly brilliant was pulled off. This is obviously something the script lacks; as it is not a novel, there are no in-depth descriptions of how a spell works or how something magical happens. This means that your imagination is working over-time, relying on everything it has learned earlier from the books and films to fill out the gaps. My guess is that this is easier for some people than others. 
 Something else which I've seen in several reviews already; the fanfiction vibe this script has. It is true, it does. But in the theatre, this is not obvious at all. This script was made for the stage, and theatre is a very different form of entertainment from screen and books - it relies heavily on its audience and the ability to constantly keep up the pace and the wow-factor. Thus an overload of jokes and over-the-top plot points have been incorporated, making it seem a little far-fetched, at least on paper. I can tell those of you who haven't seen the play that this all works rather well onstage; it keeps the audience going and we all laughed along with the jokes (especially Scorpius') and sat on the edge of our seats when something exciting was happening. 
 In book form all this falls a little flat - again we miss out on the effects onstage that supports many of the plot points that seem far-fetched on paper. The jokes seem one too many. The characters seem like ghosts of themselves, because we lack descriptions of their tone, their facial expressions, their gestures. All that we get onstage, and though some characters didn't seem like the perfect casting, most of them did a brilliant job - especially Harry was absolutely perfect and sounded and acted exactly how I would imagine 'our' Harry as an adult would. 
 Plot discussion time: again addressing the fanfiction vibe. 
 I have one part of the plot that I cannot cope with and I will not accept it as being true: Delphi being Voldemort's daugther by Bellatrix. With a character like Voldemort who is so possessed by power and who cannot love, and who is indifferent to others' desires and devotion, it just doesn't add up. I could have accepted if they made her a child of Bellatrix' who had inherited her mother's obsession with the Dark Lord. My boyfriend argued that Voldemort might want an heir, but I don't believe that either, because Voldemort wants to live forever and thus there is no reason for an heir . I stand by this and my claim that this would never have happened in a novel by JK. Therefore I have decided to pretend it didn't happen. Sorry. 
 The Time-Turner  plot has also received some hits from fans. Claims of inconsistencies and the likes. I agree that this is an example of plot points that seem far-fetched and over-the-top, but I also believe that JK could have worked wonders with this in an actual novel and I am still and of course bummed that this will not happen. However, theatre doesn't have much time and space to work with and this is already a 5 hour play in two parts! 
 Albus and Scorpius are the stars of this script/play and are both beautifully written and acted. The play itself was brilliant and entertaining and quite well done. The script falls a little flat without the actors, sets and effects to support it. Personally I don't think it should exist in book form, mainly because it will ruin this new story for many fans. But I also realise that those who cannot see the play would want to experience it in another form, and I would probably feel the same way if I hadn't been able to see it either. The play would get 5 stars from me, and the book gets 3. 
 All in all I have difficulties viewing it as a continuation of the books. To me it's more of an addition to the universe, much like Fantastic Beasts is going to be. 
 If you read all this, thank you! I realise it is quite long ;)

 actual rating : 4.5, because of the ending. 
 I admit, reading this from the start, I knew it was not going to end well, I just kept my hopes high, and it only ruined me more, because a tiny part of me believed that Will would change his mind after Lou. Yet, he always, right from the start, implied that he absolutely hated not having a choice regarding anything in his life. 
 reading about Will's condition made me reevaluate my life. now I am more aware of all the blessings that I take for granted. 
 that being able to prop myself up from my bed in the morning without needing help is such a big thing. 
 Will's reasons for the way he wanted his life to go (or end) was completely justified, it was bound to the readers to accept it or not. On his defense, he did live as a quad for two years, and he could not bear it. a Man who lived his life to the fullest could not go through another day of those tortures. 
 although I refuse to accept the assisted suicide, and the fact that he never changed his mind even after Lou. He could have given her six months the way he has given his parents. But maybe the fact that she came into his life only made him more determined to go through with it. 
 He loved her and he wanted her to live. not to be bound to him, watching him and taking care of him 24/7. 
 was that selfish of him? yes. 
 I am sure at some point he tried therapy and support groups. and if this life suited someone else, it was not going to suit him. he couldn't just be a stander-by and watch everyone else live as he was a burden, an obstacle to the people he loved, especially Lou. 
 and if he wanted to die, I would have accepted his death, but not this way. 
 There is a thing where awfully sick people could sign a document where they no longer accept medical treatment, so next time he has an acute infection, no one can do anything about it other than watching him die. 
 and on the rate that he got sick in, it was bound to happen a few months later than 13/Aug. 
 I loved the characters and I got really attached to them. Lou and Treena and Will and Nathan and both the family. IT was so real and reliable. 
 that being said, I am still angry about Will's death. He owed Lou giving her a change, to expand his horizons in a new life just the same way he wanted her to expand hers.

 Why Cadence freaks me out: Summer 15, an accident happened that screwed with Cadence's mind. Now she has migraines and swirly thoughts. Her mother tells her to act normal quite frequently while Cadence tends to 'melt' or have something over dramatic and scary happen to her in her head.  the other characters: Honestly didn't care about them. There was a scene that was supposed to be incredibly sad, the author was really going for the waterworks, but I couldn't find it in me to care. Bad sign.  
 The writing style was new, the premise was interesting, and the foreshadowing and emphasis on the mysterious accident kept me reading, especially because I heard that this book has a twist ending. I might have guessed it, but read the ending a third of the way into the book :( wish I had surprised myself. 
 Would I recommend it? Yes! Though this book was not a true stand-out for me, it was interesting and a new concept. Just don't expect the beautiful Sinclair family to be truly beautiful.

Despite the serious topic, the research that obviously went into this and the nice, easily readable writing, this book felt very cheesy to me. I admit, that I do not enjoy romance stories very much in general, so the novel had this working against it from the start. 
 In particular, however, I'm very skeptical when it comes to romanticization of severe illness and the tragedy of a death threat hanging over a loved one, since in reality, such strokes of fate leave little to no room for anything romantic. 
 The book was still funny enough to be entertaining for most parts, but as the story unfolded, I found that I did not like the plot and the characters very much. 
 Louisa is indeed rather boring and quite immature. At 26, she has apparently never really thought about anything at all. I still liked her narration, but her family is borderline abusive to her, apparently telling her since childhood how stupid she is instead of encouraging her to do something with her life, and rewarding her selfish sister for being irresponsible. The thing with her and Patrick was dragged out way too long and Louisa's youth trauma added to Will's situation was just a bit too much tragedy for one book. 
 Also, the ending felt very forced to me, as in "forcing the tragic ending". How can "the best 6 months of your life" still not make said life worth living? Makes no sense, unless you're aiming for tears. . 
 Without the cheesy and over-dramatic parts, the book would probably have been a 3-stars-read for me, but I realize that it probably would not have been nearly as successful either. As comparison, I enjoyed The Intouchables more, which deals with the same topic without the romance.

Originally posted at The Book Nympho 
 The setup 
 Figure skater Matty Marcus is struggling to not only recover from a back injury but also his failure to medal at the last Olympic Games. A benefactor reaches out and offers him an opportunity to earn some serious money while continuing to heal and get back into competitive shape. He moves to Montana to house sit a home that has the handsome rancher, Rob Lovely, as a neighbor. 
 The issues 
 With Rob, the flamboyant Matty finds strength, courage and confidence to do what's necessary to prepare for the upcoming Olympics. He also learns how to be submissive in the bedroom, being able to relinquish control without losing himself. Even though their feelings are deepening towards each other, Matty's eventual departure looms over them as they struggle to come to terms with the probable end date for their relationship. And, Rob has a 12-year old son who shows promise as a skater with Matty's help, complicating an already tough dilemma. Winning an 
 Olympic medal and doing everything he can to reach that goal is Matty's primary goal. 
 What worked for me 
 Matty forced me out of my comfort zone with respect to m/m romances. He's effeminate, dresses outrageously and wears makeup, leaving no question as to his sexual orientation. I was unsure if I could connect with him and here was the power of the story. Matty had to not only excel in his skating but also overcome the judges (and others) stereotypical thinking about his style. I loved that he never felt compelled to change any aspect of his identity, with full awareness of what it might cost him and the reactions of those around him. Rob's embrace of all that was Matty and his patience with him made him so appealing. Their romance was at times sweet and always sensual. I loved their relationship, even when Matty made it difficult. He got under my skin and I ended up adoring him. 
 What was a challenge for me 
 Be forewarned that the sex is graphic, which doesn't really bother me normally but there were some dom/sub scenes that pushed me beyond my limits. I actually found myself skimming over some of the encounters as I found them confusing to the story. 
 The bottom line 
 I loved the story, the romance and the sometimes bratty Matty. It's my understanding that the author was channeling the Olympic skater Johnny Weir and this book helped me develop a new level of respect and appreciation for him. My perceptions were completely altered and that's pretty powerful. I'm thrilled that the author created Matty and wrapped this wonderful story around him.

[FROM THE PREFACE:] 
 The Discworld is not a coherent fantasy world. Its geography is fuzzy, its chronology unreliable. A small traveling circle of firelight in a chilly infinity has turned out to be the home of defiant jokes and last chances. 
 There are no maps. You can't map a sense of humor. Anyway, what is a fantasy map but a space beyond which There Be Dragons? On the Discworld we know that There Be Dragons Everywhere. They might not all have scales and forked tongues, but they Be Here all right, grinning and jostling and trying to sell you souvenirs. 
 Enjoy. 
 Thus begins my Grand Discworld Reread, which will likely wreck my really great author gender ratio this year, although I'm not planning on reading them all in one fell swoop. This series is really near and dear to my heart -- I read every single book and grew up on them, devouring them from our school library, and I spent so many hours in Discworld MUD. I love this world so much. 
 However, this book is really not the best. I tell every new reader not to start with The Colour of Magic, and to pick up something like Guards! Guards! or Equal Rites instead -- partially because I overall prefer the Watch and the witches sub-series, but also because it takes Pratchett a little while to find his stride, his voice, his style. In this very earliest book, you can really see the nuts & bolts of him first figuring out how this lifelong series will work. 
 Still, though, I'm going to be stubborn and go through all 41 books in publication order, because I'm interested to follow a) the social and technological development within the Discworld itself, and b) the evolution of Pterry's writing as he goes. 
 The good: Ankh-Morpork is already fantastic. The best parts of this book imo are the first half within the city itself; it already has a living breathing identity of its own, and the comedy of Twoflower's oblivious arrival was great. 
 I really like the themes of technology vs. magic: part of the joy in this series is seeing how they replicate modern technological inventions but with magic. Rincewind, on the other hand, expresses his despair that he lives in such an absolutely bonkers world where science doesn't stand a chance. 
 Rincewind, Twoflower, and the Luggage (shush, it totally counts) are a good set of characters. They're classic, although Rincewind does more interesting things later; again, this book is testing the waters. But 'the first-ever tourist' as a plot is a fantastic conceit for showing off the Disc, and Twoflower is endearingly naive and cheerful as he waltzes his way from mortal peril to mortal peril, trailed by the cowering fake wizard. Also his ruminations about going everywhere & seeing everything just made me go yes, considering my love of seeing new places and how I wish I had all the money to just travel. 
 This book mainly spoofs things like Hercules/Conan-esque barbarian fantasy, magic swords, and Lovecraftian horrors. 
 For an old-time reader, the signs that Pterry has still not quite worked out his formula: 
 This is more like a collection of short stories assembled into the vague shape of a novel, just episodic adventures, rather than a single coherent story. Plotlines and characters are picked up and dropped in order to get on to the next sight, the next shenanigans. 
 The Patrician is unnamed, and not quite as cool as he becomes later, though you can see glimpses of it. 
 Death is really, really out-of-character for what I remember of him. Every time he expressed delight in random killing or lost his temperI was like :( :( considering my memories of the sympathetic, philosophical, sort-of-hero we grow to love later. 
 There aren't any named characters from the Watch yet. 
 There are like no female characters; the only one is a barely sketched-out outline of a stereotype, unlike his later strong female characters who bust out of their tropes. 
 There's only one footnote!! This especially caught me off-guard, considering Discworld is known for being rife with footnote humour. 
 That modern-day AU sequence is bizarre. I had completely forgotten about it. I was not a fan. 
 In conclusion tho: If you're a new reader, I still stick by my original advice: this is not the place to begin Discworld. The Colour of Magic is more interesting as an artefact of its time, as an archaeological fossil to this legendary series. If you are a stubborn completionist like me, just be prepared for the fact that this one is sloppy and messy and a little mediocre (around 2.5-3 stars from me)... but the series gets better (so, so so so so much better) later, and you should absolutely stick with it. This one is an interesting ride that briefly introduces you to this zany world, but nothing much of significance happens.

After finishing book three of the Vampire Diaries, and liking it considerably more than the first two installments, I noticed the irony of the titles and how I felt about each book. 
 The Awakening - I never woke up for it. 
 The Struggle - I struggled to get through it. 
 The Fury - I was gonna be really irritated if this book wasn't moderately better than the first two. 
 Thank you! It was better! (Moderately.) 
 Even though I admire people who can put books down when they don't like them, I find that I learn things about what I want and need from books when I read them through. Apparently, I am fairly dependent upon action to get me through a story. 
 The action finally picks up in The Fury. I noticed that the immaturity of the characters that I complained about in the first two installments didn't bother me here, although I will admit that it's probably because I was so thankful for the action that I didn't notice it anymore. (I remember a few eye rolls, so it was still there.) 
 I was bothered by the "white light and rainbows" feelings towards vampires however. They are obviously dark entities, and there are considerable debates over the state of their souls and the evil/goodness of their natures. But they are painted as saviors in The Fury, and too easily suppress their dark natures to help the humans. I was also disturbed by the fact that they cried, had beating hearts, and lots of compassionate feelings. Ew. 
 But the story was better; I liked how it turned out (and hated it, too) which means I was finally becoming attached to the town and its characters. I liked the elevated role that secondary characters from the first books were given. 
 I still recommend this only for younger audiences. Adults may find the plot juvenile.

"Newark was left behind and the post-chaise-and-four entered on a stretch of flat country which offered little to attract the eye, or occasion remark." 
 Georgette Heyer was a wonderful writer. A beloved writer, in fact, known for her regency romances in particular. Her books are rich in detail--but not in a burdening, cumbersome way. And her characters are always nicely drawn from human nature--flaws abound, but that's always a good thing. Vices and temptations abound in her works--drinking, gambling (be it at the gaming table or in a sporting arena), keeping bad company, and fashion to name just a few examples. (How is fashion a vice? Well, if you're too vain or selfish and spend too much time primping in front of a mirror, then chances are you're in for a comeuppance. Also, spending too much money on fashion--clothes, hats, gloves, jewelry, etc.--is just one way it can be a vice.) 
 In Regency Buck, we've got the story of a brother and sister newly arrived in London. Peregrine Tavener, the brother, and his older sister, Judith Tavener. They are coming to set up house, and perhaps even more importantly to meet their guardian. (Both of their parents have died. And the father's will left them under the care of Lord Worth.) They are expecting an older gentleman. A man that would have been the contemporary of their father. Someone with gout presumably. What they find is that Lord Worth is a young man--just a handful of years older. He isn't particularly pleased with this added responsibility, and he's not shy admitting this to his wards. But for one year at least--until Judith's birthday--Lord Worth is their official guardian. 
 The Taveners do set up their own house. Mrs. Scattergood, a relation (cousin???) of Lord Worth, is Judith's companion. Needed during that time to protect young women and provide them with counsel on how to behave in society. An older woman to act as chaperone. Of course, Peregrine, offers protection to his sister as well. But who's protecting him? Peregrine being prone to gambling and partying. When Peregrine becomes engaged to a young woman, Harriet, then a few strange coicidences occur to threaten his life which convinces Worth that someone is out to kill his ward. 
 The two stand to inherit much money when they come of age. And for this reason, suitors abound for Judith's hand. One of her most persistent suitors is her cousin, Bernard Tavener. But Lord Worth turns them all away. Saying that no man will marry her while he is still her guardian. Something that both repulses and pleases her. She's known some of the men are completely unsuitable--some as old as her father, all looking for a wealthy wife--but the idea of being controlled by a man irritates her at the same time. 
 Worth (Julian) and Judith (whom he persists in calling Clorinda) are always bickering. The banter flows easily between these two. While both tend to be a bit cranky around the other, the reader knows without any doubts that these two secretly feel very differently about each other. 
 I love Worth and Judith. I love the rich-layers of Regency Buck as well. For example, Judith's reading of Sense and Sensibility. And the presence of Lord Byron and the discussion of his poetry. There are a dozen or so other things I could point out, but those are just two examples of bits that made me smile.

Oh god. I'm going to say a lot of things because I just finished this and I don't know if any of them will be coherent. I think, I think this is somewhere between 3.5 and 3.75 stars. But maybe I'll save it at three, because there is just... there is so much. And I don't know what or how to think. 
 My short review is: This is the best novel Handler has written (as Handler) since The Basic Eight. I love Adverbs, but I don't quite count that as a novel; if you know me, you'll know that I was NOT ENAMOURED with Why We Broke Up and I DNF the incest book that I pretend doesn't exist (because god, why, why, why was that written. why did that need to be written). The prose remains Handlerian--Handler is a stylist, I get it, he has a huge crush on Nabokov (and why shouldn't he)--but at the same time, it's toned down. One of the reasons I couldn't stand WWBU was because of how pretentious it felt, except for the giant paragraph at the end where Min says everything she isn't. I know him well enough to spot the hallmarks of his style ("I thought," he said, "that I said that"; not a direct quote but he does have a habit of putting his dialogue tags in strange places in the dialogue, so you've got to wait for it), but at the same time, they weren't overwhelming. They didn't distract from the story. 
 I've gotta say one thing on language, though. Let's talk about race, Daniel. Let's talk about some of the weird stuff you have in here that, frankly, I don't know how it made it in. Especially after the National Book Awards. You made a good apology, you put your money where your mouth was, and you didn't phrase it as "sorry if you were offended"--it was legitimately "sorry I said a racist thing." But? But? A woman "screamed the way the appearance of a black man makes everything suddenly scary." What the actual christ, Daniel. Yes, Manny is black, yes, he shows up, yes, the woman screams because of piracy, but just... dear lord. I hate that sentence. There are a few others, a strange comment about (black) police officers working "twice as hard, due to injustice,"one about a "knocking, clasping ritual believed at the time to be favoured by black people," and there's one other. The first sentence I've mentioned is absolutely not okay, and it bothered me throughout. The others were just... strange. They felt unnecessary. Unneeded. Why did you put those in there, Daniel? Why? 
 Okay. Now to the actual plot of the book: 
 The basic plot is there's a dad who's in radio and he's floundering in life. His infinitely more interesting daughter, Gwen, has been caught stealing. As punishment, she's has to go to an old folks home and talk to old people there. Suddenly, piracy happens. And we watch that unfold. 
 Interesting plot. I found this a really gripping story, and I had to keep reading to find out what would happen next. 
 Character-building was weird. I didn't like Phil a whole lot; he's kind of a sleazebucket and I never quite trusted him. Yet he shares equal screen-time with his daughter, Gwen. I found myself less interested in Phil's parts, partially because I had a hard time following what was happening, but also because he reads as a terrible person. I don't quite know if he's supposed to be sympathetic. Part of me doesn't think he is, mainly because of the way he treats Levine and ignores Marina, HIS WIFE, and is a bit of a snooper. See also: him reading Levine's personal file on her computer, where she's writing an erotic note, and he Gets Ideas . On the other hand, he's billed first on the book blurb, so he's clearly one of the protagonists. No doubt he's flawed, and I really don't mind flawed protagonists, but on the whole he turned out kind of bleh. 
 Gwen, though. Gwen's intriguing. Fourteen-year-old who's frustrated with everything, alter-ego who commits crimes, suddenly swept up in ideas of piracy? Yes, that's more like it. To be honest, I found myself wishing this were more overtly her story, rather than flipping back and forth between the two. I felt bad for Phil once or twice (when Gwen goes missing, but that was more regarding the horror of a missing child ) but Gwen I sympathized more with. This isn't because I read a lot of YA, although maybe it is--she was just more interesting overall. 
 As for other characters: they didn't feel as defined. In some, that's okay. In some, that's not. I wanted more Marina, Phil's wife, Gwen's mum--she intrigued me more than her husband did. The Glassermans were occasionally sketchy, although I was okay with that. Amber was fascinating, perhaps a little thin but nonetheless amusing. I also thought this was going to be a tale of reconciliation between Gwen and Naomi, and I never quite got why Gwen broke off her friendship with Naomi. Oh well. Can't win 'em all.  
 As for the actual piracy: Okay. I should've seen bloodshed coming, but I was absolutely shocked that Gwen was prepared to kill. That's such a drastic action, especially for a fourteen-year-old. Yes, I've read TBE, I know Handler writes this grand tradition of teenage murderesses, but also, that's... that's so big... and it didn't ring true, not quite, not for me. I also didn't get Gwen's sudden PIRACY!!! obsession. It happens as soon as she meets Errol, but I really would've loved to watch it expand. It felt, eh, not quite shoe-horned in, but dealt with too quickly. There was a lot that worked, a lot that didn't. Eh.  
 Oh, and there's a twist at the end that makes you want to re-read the book. I guess I should've seen it coming that Gwen and Errol were related, that Errol was grandfather, that he would die, but I didn't. Don't know how I felt about it, although I didn't feel like it was a cheapo plot device. So that's good.  
 Aaaaaand one last thing that I loved: I shipped Gwen/Amber all the way through and then they KISS on the BOAT and it's described as ROMANTIC and it was actually pretty glorious. SO THAT WAS REALLY NICE.  
 OVERALL: I don't regret reading this, I had a lot of fun with it, although it's less of a fun romp than I would've liked. Be prepared for strangeness and terror and feelings.

So when I'm choosing a book to read, I have to be honest, I get the book that has a cover that attracts me. The cover for this isn't the worst, but it's not something I'd normally go for. I gave this book a chance because K.A. Applegate and I had loved her Animorphs series.I'm glad I did. 
 The font type and spacing made this extremely easy to read but I found the broken sentences distracting. The POV changes a lot and I can see what the author was trying to do but I found that the voices blended together too much and she would head- hop even within a scene so there was more confusion over who was owning a scene than there should have been. So, the novel: 
 It's 2011 and it's the end of the world in just a few short days- there's an asteroid on its way, one large enough to destroy everything. There's a ship, a small one, that can take 80 people and potentially save their lives. 
 Sh*t gets real fast. Although the narrative is written for maybe a grade six level, I think the contents are more appropriate for an older age group. 
 It's bleak, it's hopeless, and I loved that for this novel. It should be depressing- the entire world is ending and so many people are going to die. The only survivors are going to be eighty people from the US, which is problematic for so many reasons that I can't even get into it. 
 I hate how the character of Essence is treated and even Cordelia. Please, people. Women are people too, I promise. The Yago guy is creepy and I'd be happy not to see him again. Of course, that probably means that he's going to live for ever. 
 I disliked the sheer number of foolish names in this novel- what is wrong with the name you were born with? They all give themselves nicknames because they obviously don't understand that it doesn't work like that. 
 This novel is way over populated by white blond(e) people, but that's pretty much par for the course in media today. The only people of colour are either 'disfigured' or are the creepy serial killer to be: Yago. 
 The plot moves along at a nice pace and the destruction of the Earth was nice- I kept thinking, nice, K.A. actually did it. 
  
 All that said, I'm going to be reading the next book in the series.

Review for Alpha by Jasinda Wilder 
 Wow. 
 Just wow. 
 No, really, that's all I've got. 
 Alpha by Jasinda Wilder is by far the HOTTEST book I have read so far in 2014. It is going to take an act of God or some other monumental occurrence for anyone to top it. This is the first book of the year that I have read and the moment I finished it I wanted to skip right back to the beginning and start again. I rarely, if ever, reread a book. I just don't have time and frankly there are just so many out there that I find myself moving on quickly. Alpha is going to be joining my short list of go-to books when I'm in a book slump. 
 If you haven't ever read a book by Jasinda Wilder before, well, you need to pick this one up. I can't even find the right words to explain how completely amazing this book is. Not just the storyline, which wasn't exactly what I expected, I LOVE when an author can blow through my expectations and leave me on the other side slack-jawed, but the characters in this book -- so fully developed I swear somewhere in the world there just HAS to live a Kyrie and Roth. That's how much those two got into my head. 
 Okay, into the story we go (no spoilers as always whores)... 
 Kyrie is having a bad time. Her boss is a douche canoe. Her job was just made obsolete. Her mother is crazy. Her bills are stacked up beyond anything she can ever get out from under and then she gets a check. Not just any check. It's ten grand... should she cash it? The choice is simple... cash it and avoid becoming homeless. The checks kept coming. Every month, for a year... and then it's time to repay her debt. 
 Roth is a mystery. He's private and reclusive. Sex on a freakin' stick. Kyrie describes him best... 
 "He was totally dominant, powerful and confident, skilled and passionate and attentive." 
 I've read dozens of the dominant millionaire meets poor girl books. The men are almost always overbearing, overprotective, jackholes... they can be sweet and sexy, but overall in reality if anyone were to treat a woman like that we would run... run far and fast and not look back. Roth... oh man... Roth is THE KING of all millionaire (or billionaire) alpha men. He's bossy, but with purpose. He is protective, but not smothering. He is courteous and would do absolutely anything for those he cares for. Oh and sexy... can't forget sexy. Wait, did I mention his dirty mouth? Wow. 
 "That's my girl... I love the way you take my cockadoodledoo, Kyrie. You take it all, and you always want more. Sofa king hot."

 Move over Christian, Jesse, and Gideon... Roth is taking no prisoners and making you all look like bumbling teenagers. 
 FIVE PLUS STARS for an amazing storyline and FIVE PLUS drenched, torn, and stuffed in a pocket panties for the best smut of 2014. Absolute MUST READ NOW.

I thought this was the best Laundry book yet, and judging by average Goodreads reviews, the public agrees with me. So let's see if I can justify my opinion. 
 I think a good portion of it is finding a way to incorporate vampire myths into a Cthulhu cosmology, which not even Call of Cthulhu has ever really done well. It's not a curse or a virus or anything--it's a symbiote that's attracted to ritual magic, and it provides its host with superior physical abilities; an immunity to K Syndrome, thus allowing them to use magic without inevitably killing themselves; immortality; and mind control. Sure, they need to drink blood and burn in the sun, but, well, there's no such thing as a free lunch. 
 As it turns out, it's not just ritual magic, it's a specific frame of mind that can often come about through ritual magic, and when a group of quantitative analysts end up investigating a new means of market prediction that ends up attracting the parasites (vampires-as-bankers is obvious, but I still appreciated it), it's up for the Laundry to deal with the problem. Bureaucratically, of course. 
 That was probably my favorite part of the novel, actually. When Bob went on a mission to the bank, I was fully expecting the vampires to capture him, to rant at him for a while, and then for the cavalry to come in and plot to get resolved, because that's how the previous Laundry books have tended to go. Essentially, I was expecting the spy thriller part of the book to win out. But what actually happened was that the plodding bureaucracy part won out, and that's when I paused, noticed how much of the book was left, and wondered where the plot was going next. 
 I also liked The Rhesus Chart's version of vampire society--namely, that there isn't one. Most vampires who survive any length of time are sociopaths who are willing to go to nearly any length to avoid being discovered, since burning to death in sunlight is obviously an easy weakness to exploit. Every other vampire is a threat to their own existence because it increases the chances of discovery. As such, the ideal number of vampires in any given area is one and existing vampires enforce this with extreme prejudice. 
 The biggest problem with The Rhesus Chart is the increasing density of memes. I get that self-awareness is a part of the Laundry, and part of the reason the vampire bankers were interesting early on is that their first reaction was immediately: "How does this work? Sunlight? Stakes? Garlic? Blood? Consecrated ground? What are we dealing with here?" but when you're literally quoting "If I fits, I sits," it does a lot more to take me out of the novel than to ground me in Bob's character. I get it. He's the nerdy IT consultant dealing with Lovecraftian horrors. That is, in fact, the basis for the whole series, and I don't need it constantly in my face to remember it. 
 Well, or maybe it's the tendency of Howard to interject himself into the narrative to exposition-dump. I do love worldbuilding and normally this wouldn't bother me, but it's mostly in the form of bureaucratic reports, and dry memos are dry even in a fictional context. 
 Oh, and the mention that the CASE NIGHTMARE GREEN awareness campaign could be:Disguised as background material for a role-playing game if it leaks early and we need plausible deniability.I see what you did there, Stross 
 The resolution bothered me as well: Namely, the fact that Basil was the mole. I figured it out as soon as he showed up in the meeting, since he was clearly trying too hard to be the out-of-touch pensioner who's completely harmless and who everyone can safely ignore. I can't actually complain about this, because it's the most reasonable course of action for a vampire hiding at the heart of an organization explicitly tasked to deal with that sort of threat. But I knew it was going to happen, and after the way hiring on the Scrum threw me, it was a bit of a letdown.  
 I went into The Rhesus Chart a bit disappointed the Stross wasn't pulling the trigger on CASE NIGHTMARE GREEN, but after the way it turned out, I can forgive him. Hopefully future Laundry books are more like this one and less like the previous books in the series.

This book is one I've been waiting for! Excellent and beautiful storytelling. This novel reminds me of the throne of Glass series and I love that series. Can't wait to read the next one!

"It was just one day and it's been just one year. But maybe one day is enough. Maybe one hour is enough. Maybe time has nothing at all to do with it". - Willem" 
 I loved it! I loved getting to know Willem's character! Seeing things from his POV, seeing his journey on finding out who he wanted to be and what he wanted out of life. 
 Though I could have done without  him sleeping with all the women!  I wanted more of Allyson/Lulu and Willem! I missed her SO much in this story! But I think that is part of the beauty of Forman's writing, you could still feel her presence in the story and I could feel Willem's ache for her throughout the whole thing! 
 I do have to say though, that I need need need NEED a sequel!!!! Please Ms. Forman!! Give us a book #3 or even a novella, anything! I need more of Willem and Allyson/Lulu!!! PLEASE!

Forsaken is the first of a new series written by Jana Oliver about Demon Trappers. Forsaken starts off with main character Riley Blackthorne the only girl demon trapper within the group, all the men included think she shouldn't be doing this profession including her father Master Trapper Paul Blackthorne but she won't back down and feels this is in her blood to do. Riley tries to catch a demon in the school library but when something doesn't feel right and it all goes wrong she's left humliated. Switching to Beck's point of view Paul's apprentice it follow them both on a hunt but when things take a tragic turn and Paul Blackthorne is killed, it's left to Beck to break the new to Riley. Devestated Riley is now all on her own, fending for herself which pushes her more into Trapping to make some money, the rest of the book follows her journey of dealing with her fathers death, trying to be a demon trapper and falling in love for the first time... 
 I will be honest, I was quite dissapointed with Forsaken, 
 I picked up the book thinking, "Yes, let's move on from Vampires and Angels for a while and try some Demon Trappers" 
 So I sit down and start to read and it's starts off good, some action, a back story so I know who all the characters are but as it moves on, especially after Paul's death the book goes way down, gone are they demons and the book becomes more about Riley dealing with having no parents and trying to look after herself, there were a few incidents which brings the book more entertainment but it goes sour too quickly for me. 
 Only at the end did it start to pick up again with a major fight between Trappers and Demons and to be honest I didn't think the ending was all that great either. 
 I was torn between giving the book 2 or 3 stars, in the end I decided 3 because I liked Riley and the action that eventually appeared in the book. 
 I won't rush to read Forbidden but I would like to give it a try and hope that it's better and to continue on with the story.

 I loved this prequel to Scarlet, where I'm guessing Ze'ev will be The Big Bad Wolf. This novella was amazing! Seriously, I enjoyed these 20 pages more than the entirety of Cinder. This story breathed fresh air into this hyped series, and has given me the motivation to continue on with it! 
 We learn in Cinder that the Lunar Queen is building a very strong army to conquer Earth. This story shows you exactly what kind of army she is building; which is a pack of werewolves! 
 Ze'ev proves at the end that his pack is the strongest. It's impossible not to love him and develop empathy for him. He was taken from his family at a mere twelve-years-old, surgically "enhanced", to then having no friends or loved one for five whole years Until his brother is, too, taken into this military program; who then wants nothing to do with Ze'ev . As much as I enjoy the Percy Jackson series, this new series featuring brother and sister Carter and Sadie is even richer and more edge-of-your-seat. The shifting point of view between the two siblings (and their snarky sibling-esque asides to each other) work beautifully, and Riordan breathes life into the well-known and little-known Egyptian gods in a way that he never quite achieves with the Olympians. A captivating and multi-layered story... can't wait to see what he does with the sequel.

Picked up Trinity War on a recommendation after posting an interest in Forever Evil. I can see why this is probably required reading for anybody interested in trying on John's next big book. This does come off a little like an extended prologue to Geoff's Forever Evil. Have a few friends (Anne's review , Mike's review) with dramatically different opinions about this one and I sort of fall in the middle I guess. 
 I wasn't sold on Pandora. She is a central figure in this one and I just never bought into her or her curse. I feel like Johns, Lemire, and Fawkes could have put this together somehow without needing to introduce a new character. The "magic" thing has just never really done it for me. A little here and there is just fine, but it's really a big part of this collection. Probably why this version of the Question bugged me too. Not enough Rorshach and too much Harry Potter in his back story. Could have done without the trip to Heaven or purgatory or whatever. Again with the magic, spirits, and angels. I like Constantine. Just not mixed with my Batman. This is why I never had an interest in the Justice League Dark title. I was also a little unclear as to why everybody wanted to kick each other's ass at the end. I was never really sure if it was me or that the time line between the different titles collected was disjointed and didn't flow smoothly. 
 I did like seeing Superman lose it. The back and forth between Waller's League and the original League amused. For some reason this collection reminded me of Identity Crisis (which I liked) at times. Maybe because of the mystery angle or the big reveal at the end  the tiny woman did it . Despite not being a "magic" fan, it was fun seeing Shazam and Constantine hanging out together at a bar. Diana and Steve's awkward " we're ex's" exchange. This one definitely had a couple of moments I enjoyed. I also liked most of the artwork in this one too. Ivan Reis and Doug Mahnke put together some good stuff here. 
 Awkward. 
 I have to say it pulled together for me at the very end and left me excited to check out Forever Evil.  Bring on the Crime Syndicate!  I really think that this was the intent from the beginning of this story. I just think they could have done this without this mammoth crossover, confusing story, and the Trinity of Sin stuff. This is a case where less probably would have been more for me.

The first of Block's books I didn't fall into and float around wrapped in bliss. This is a collection of re-told fairy tales, and the only one I really liked was "Wolf". That story had everything I adore about Block's writing- the perfect adolescent girl voice, the atmospheric prose, the hint of danger and dispair- but the others left me cold.

Holden Caulfield is one of those characters that lives in the immagination of a lot of people. A young man unsure of his place in the world, not really trying to fit in and struggling with his feelings of being rootless and aimless. This is a snapshot of a few days in his life, the people he interacts with and his attitude to them. He is a sorry character, but I could see reflections of my own life in his. 
 I would probably have enjoyed this more as a teenager but I really disliked those years so a revisit is a bit torturous.
Good use of a format I normally find stale: letters. The characters are wonderfully written, brilliant people who aren't normal in the slightest. The plot is unreal and not ordinary. Fun to read.

This long book is worth the investment. There are endearing characters who are developed well, and a realistic plot that progresses slowly over time. The setting of this book isn't one I normally take interest in, but I'm glad all the hype surrounding this a few years back caused me to finally pick it up.

This may just be y favorite book out of the slew of fiction I've read this year. It's a juxtaposed tale of a Harvard grad student in the midst of her dissertation research set against the events surrounding the Salem witch trials in 1692. As you might expect, the two stories end up intertwining, but that is by no means a criticism. 
 This is a warm, beautifully crafted story, and the texture of Connie's world is very believable to me in a way that dreamy, detail-oriented narratives are to sentimentalists and dreamers. It's a story about a lot of things including the power of women, the hysteria of crowds, the place of people within a natural order, and most of all, family and all that entails.
A very good book with some disturbing themes. Both compelling and uncomfortable.

A magical anthology with some real gems; perfect for younger audiences and those wishing for less horrible things than is found in more contemporary collections. Gabriel-Ernest by Saki and Come Lady Death by Peter S. Beagle may have been my favorites. The title pages feature delightful illustrations, which is a nice bonus.
Then cliffhangers though...

Not for me..... I rarely gravitate towards Romances but a friend insisted I give this a try but nope, still not a fan of romance books and I don't think I ever will. 
 PS Just to clarify I like romance in my books but I find that books centered around the romance not my cup of tea.

** spoiler alert ** 
 Wow. The only thing I'm a bit torn about is the back story thing. Does it take or add to this particular telling? Certainly one of the most terrifying aspects about this character is the uncertainty behind "his" back story. Nevertheless, I think the way it was told, and the comment at the end about how the story changes every time, might be enough to suggest this is ONE OF THE MANY. I prefer to think it as that, and keep the chilling and thrilling emotions this masterpiece brought to the table. By the way, the new coloring must be the impression you get of this if you're reading it for the first time anywhere after 2008. Then you can go back to read the original, but this coloring just adds too much to it.

The synopsis pretty much sums up this book, and indeed, Saving Cee Cee Honeycutt is a heartwarming, entertaining story about a neglected little girl who found love in places and people she could never imagine. 
 I warmed up to the character Cecelia Rose Honeycutt from the very begging. Being merely twelve years old, she is burdened with the task of taking care of her mentally-ill mother who dreams of a glorious life which has long-passed. Her father is always running away from harsh realities of life by using his job as an excuse, and Mrs. Odell is her only refuge. 
 After her mother's sudden death, Cee Cee moves in to stay with her great aunt Tootie. The first person she gets to know besides her aunt is none other than Aunt Tootie's personal cook, Oletta Jones. At the beginning, Oletta is cold towards Cee Cee, but after knowing her past, she sympathizes Cee Cee's plight and offers the child her support. 
 Cee Cee quickly learns that the women in the neighbourhood are kind, though each of them have different personalities. Aunt Tootie is always optimistic, Oletta Jones has a warm heart beneath her cool behaviour, Miz Goodpepper is nice but somewhat quirky, and Miz Hobbs' presence always makes her uneasy. 
 Jam-packed with wit, humour and charm - spiced up by the presence of two quirky, eccentric, always-at-each-other's-throats neighbours - Miz Goodpepper and Miz Hobbs, Saving Cee Cee Honeycutt will definitely make its way into your heart.
I loved this book, and thought it was a really fun read. One of the better young adult books I've read this year!

ARRGGHHHHHH!!! This book is incredible! It was such a beautiful story, and it was so well written, and the characters were great... I could go on and on about this book (And I am about to do just that!) I don't think that this review will do the book justice, and I don't even know if it will be cohesive enough to make sense, but I loved this book so much and highly recommend it! 
 The story is written in short, punchy chapters that makes it a quick easy read (in contrast to the content being handled). Some parts of the story are beautiful and poetic, whilst others are gruesome and tragic. The different themes and moods are well balanced, and the story is very well written. 
 The story alternated between four characters' points of view, all written in first person. At first I was wary of this style, but I thought that it really added to the story and helped it to flow. The different characters all have different backgrounds and experiences which change the way they experience events. It was fascinating to learn about how different people viewed the events, and there is such a brilliantly wide range of characters that made the story so much better! 
 Joana: "Guilt is a hunter" 
 Joana is the first character introduced to the story. She is a Lithuanian nurse with a big heart to hep other people. She is my favourite of the main characters; her resilience and determination really stand out and she soldiers on regardless of the difficult circumstances. She has a caring, loving nature which, when coupled with her courage, makes her a really great character. 
 Florian: "Fate is a hunter" 
 Florian is the next character introduced, and he is probably the most complex. A young Prussian hiding secrets, he can be prickly and grumpy at times. However, once you get to know him better he can be quite compassionate and it is fascinating to read from his perspective and get to better understand his views on what is happening. There are times when he is selfish, but also times when he is so selfless that he seems almost like a different person. Just when you think you have Florian figured out, you'll have a new piece of information sprung on you and be fascinated by him all over again. 
 Emilia: "Shame is a hunter" 
 Emilia is a Polish girl, only fifteen years old. Joana is my favourite main character, but Emilia is my favourite perspective to read from. Despite her youth, she understands much of what is going on around her, although there are times when it really stands out that she is only just still a young girl. She puts on a brave face and keeps going on, despite everything that is going on around her, and it was definitely a unique perspective on the events. 
 Alfred: "Fear is a hunter" 
 Alfred. Where to start. Every review I've read about this book said that Alfred was the worst thing that happened in the story and that they hated him. Whilst I also immensely disliked him, I am glad that his perspective was included because it gives significant insight into the situation. When you look past the initial dislike, I think the next thing you feel for Alfred is pity. If only he would open his eyes and look at the people around him! It doesn't excuse the things he did, but nonetheless I think that more than anything I feel sorry for Alfred, and his lack of understanding about what he was doing and the real motives of the people around him. 
 Klaus: 
 Klaus was not a main character, but he definitely deserves a mention. He is small and innocent, yet has some unexpected insight. He knows enough to go along with the stories which the others have created to keep them safe, and I am very glad that he was included. 
 Ingrid: 
 Ingrid was not a major character, but she deserves a mention. I love her so much! She is brave, bold, determined, kind, and doesn't let her blindness stop her. 
 Shoe Poet: 
 Look, I think you can tell just how much I love this book by the fact that I'm obsessing over the shoe poet Heinz. But please bear with me, he was my most favourite character in the whole book! He is extremely wise, he is loving and caring (particularly towards Klaus, and also Emilia) and he is also honest. Also known as Opi, the shoe poet has endured hardship and sets his eyes on the future. He is brilliant. Alhfg;hldfg;mhuns; I love him so much I can't even!!! 
 Um, so yeah the characters were brilliant. But also, the messages which were conveyed through the book were meaningful, important and included into the story fantastically. The way the characters endure hardship, the sacrifices they make for each other, the way that they show kindness and love even in the dark times. Despite the underlying tragedy and horrifying circumstances it is a really beautiful story. 
 This review was not intended to be this long, but I loved so many things about it that I just had to go into details about all of them. I don't feel my review really encapsulates the novel or does it justice, but it is a great story and I highly recommend it!

A book about a girl who keeps dying and then reliving her life over again. Usually I like plots like that, but I never got a good grasp for "the rules" of the setup. Sometimes she remembers parts of her life, sometimes she doesn't? The book was too slow moving for me. I liked the sections in which she dies repeatedly over the course of multiple short chapters while she attempts to overcome a particular deadly obstacle. The long periods of her life bored me because I didn't really feel invested in any of the characters. I put the book down at about 70% complete and I just struggled to pick it back up again (but eventually did just to say I finished it).

I'll admit that I picked up this book to read because Stephen Colbert recommended it. It was well-written, with interesting characters. But the plot rambled on a bit and the story seemed incomplete. 
 The US had gone downhill. The rich are holed up in private communities. Dangerous gangs roam about. So Cal and Frida head off into the woods. 
 The story unfolds, slowly revealing their past and moving them forward. But the danger and mystery seem incomplete. I had higher hopes for how the story would go.

Ultimately I had to give this book 3 stars. Mainly because it felt like I was reading two different books here. One where Sarah was struggling with her sexuality, and the other with battle sequences. 
 I typically avoid urban fantasy, because the love interests tend to be a little bit rapey. I thought with a lesbian protagonist I'd avoid that trope. And while the love interest is fine, there's a sequence in the middle of the book that bothered me, involving the heroine and two men that didn't ring true. Of course, it was all downhill from there. 
 So while I finished and did mostly enjoy this book, I won't be continuing in the series.

I liked the ideas in it and I always like reading about new concepts about "magic" in the fantasy world. It got slow around the end I found and it would pick up again in parts before going on a memory tangent. Still I'm enjoying the series so far so fingers crossed that I enjoy the rest.

I was struggling to decide whether to give this 4 or 5 stars, but ultimately I decided on 5. I know if I had read this closer to the time read the previous books there would have been no question. I wasn't so attached to the characters anymore because it's been forever since I read the first two book and I think that is understandable. I'm still pretty much basing the rating on enjoyment (as if I didn't always do that) and even though there were things I didn't like in this book I still really enjoyed it. 
 This book had so many elements that I like: great main characters, action, science fiction, mystery, romance etc. It was great to see Amy and Elder discussing and making decisions together and collecting pieces to see what's really going on. I loved learning more and more and figuring it all out even though it was pretty easy to guess who the real enemy is. *Haymitch voice* This once again showed how ruthless and careless humans can be. And the sad thing? It didn't surprise me at all.  
 The one thing that irritated me was Amy's dad (and maybe some other "Earthborns"). That attitude! First he didn't like Elder. He didn't like the "shipborns" and he treated them like he and the Earthborns were better than them. Then all he wanted was blood. To kill all the aliens. Basically every human thought of Centauri-Earth as their planet and thought they could do anything without consequences. But no, it's not their world, it's already inhabited. 
 Yes, I do like conflict. Otherwise I couldn't give this five stars! :D But I really liked how everything turned out in the end, I think it was a good way to end this trilogy.

I love William Herondale more than possibly any other character and it was the fact that he was in this story that I read it. 
 I didn't really understand the point of the story and the only reason I even gave it 3 stars was because of Will, Tessa, and James. Otherwise I felt like the characters didn't really act like themselves and everything was forced. The dialogue didn't seem realistic to Will and Tessa's characters. However it did kind of make me excited to see how James's story pans out!

This is probably a familiar story to many. I had meticulously planned an order in which to whittle down my 'To-Read' pile, including books from my 'must-reads' challenge. However, I work in a school and recently our library ordered a whole bunch of new books. Good new books. Not just ones that some stuffy old man has suggested is good reading for secondary school kids. Amongst these was Moira Young's Blood Red Road which has been on my list ever since I attended a talk with her and Michael Grant. With that in mind, Blood Red Road shoved every over book out of the line to stand smugly at the front. 
 To briefly summarise what to expect, think Mad Max with a young, female protagonist and a severe lack of cars. This is a dystopian, but felt quite refreshing after reading so many city-based, political dystopias over the last few years. The world is all heat and sand, with only a few idyllic, green areas surviving. People scavenge for parts to repair their homes and sandships and they survive by using the resources left behind by the ancestors they refer to as Wreckers. 
 Saba lives on the dried up lakebed of Silverlake with her Papa, twin brother Lugh and little sister Emmi. Their home, a tin hut held together by scraps, protects them from the harsh heat of the sun and the red dust storms which sweep across the desert. During one such storm, Saba and Lugh are caught in the middle of it, throwing themselves facedown in the sand to protect themselves. But four men arrive on horseback, grabbing Lugh, and galloping away as quickly as the storm arrived. 
 Saba's Papa dies as he attempts to retrieve Lugh, and she is left with the little sister she blames for their mother's death years before. The twins have never been apart before, and Saba promises that she'll do anything to get him back. She sets off for Hopetown seeking revenge and the brother she cannot live without. 
 In recent years there has been a real push for strong, female leads, and therefore, Saba's journey should feel refreshing. I quite liked that it was she, the quiet sibling who liked to remain in her brother's shadow, who was the one to set out and save her brother. However, there have been so many YA stories that have switched the 'damsel in distress' roles, that I didn't experience the same levels of anxiety as a result. 
 There's a point in the plot where Saba is forced to entertain the residents of Hopetown in a gladiator-style arena. Opponents fight each other until one is unable to continue, and when one fighter has lost three matches, they must run for freedom in the hope that the spectators will not kill them first. Saba is good, and quickly becomes famous. Her moniker as the 'Angel of Death' gains a lot of attention and sells many tickets. Yet, none of it felt real. Before the first match, I didn't feel we were given a real indication that Saba was capable of defending herself that well. Nothing from her history suggests she would make a good combat fighter, and it's almost like she's good only because the plot requires it of her. I needed a bit more realism here.  
 There were a few exciting twists and turns along the way, and the introduction of some fantastic characters. Some sequences of events were particularly clever - The escape from the slave pit was well executed and thought through  and as the story's events continued, I relaxed into it. It began a little coincidental, and a lot of things which should have had reasoning, didn't. For example, Saba's unique natural ability in close combat despite having no real explanation as to why. 
 Saba made for an interesting protagonist. At first, she is presented as the shadow to Lugh's light. It gives the impression that she is shy, doubts herself and that she looks to her brother for support. When he is taken, it's as if she has lost a limb. But, this severance also unleashes someone who is the complete opposite of the Saba in the first few pages. She is fierce, determined and is an excessively angry individual. And that is what characterises her throughout the whole novel; her anger. 
 Yes, she's been taught from a young age to distrust people but her immediate defence is to be angry and rude. This often leads her to treat her friends the same and, for the majority of the time, tends to cloud her judgment. Those people who are genuinely helpful are pushed away consistently, and it's a wonder how they never give up and leave. She is also incredibly guarded, taking the conscious effort to keep up her walls even when she is presented with powerful reasons to relax. 
 I also found her particularly masculine. Unfortunately, I felt as if Saba had fallen into the "strong, independent, YA female protagonist' trap where she came across masculine in order to appear strong. Most of her triumphs were successful as a result of violence or aggression, and at times, these particular decisions resulted in more trouble for her and her friends. 
 Her saving grace is that at times, she could be quite humorous. She has a particularly sharp-tongued, witty form of response, especially when she has her guard up. She's also fiercely loyal and this extends to people beyond her brother as the novel progresses. 
 Jack is the first friendly male we meet after Lugh's capture, and this takes place a considerable time after Saba's initial decision to leave Silverlake. He's also presented as a mystery which needs to be solved, so he feels important, yet remains distant while some of the plot progresses. At about a third of the way through, we finally have our first conversation with him, but Saba is on edge, with her defences up, so we don't get to meet all of him at once. However, for me, I found that was enough to make me want to see more of him. He met Saba's sturdy walls with a wry humour - the same that Saba is capable of and often returned in kind. 
 I did like Jack. True to his name, he does have a rather 'Jack-the-lad' attitude about him which was infectious. He does things with an optimism and a smile which contrasts greatly with the bleak existence of the wasteland. His cheek and sarcasm meets Saba's stony attitude perfectly and is probably the only thing that effectively brings her back to ground level. I felt the pace and tone picked up once Jack had more of a presence. 
 At first, I was drawn in by the premise of the narrative. What kept me was the presentation of the story. This is a first person narrative written by Saba. As a result, the spelling and syntax reflects Saba's voice and tone. I love books that do this. While at first it was a bit jarring as I tripped over the deliberate misspellings, it became the one thing that absorbed me into the world Young was depicting. Here's a bit of an example: 
 "Lugh's bin sayin it fer a while now. Pa's gitten worse. Mind you, he ain't bin right fer a long time." 
 It sounds so much more like a conversation between you and Saba that you as the reader are able to connect with her on some form of level, despite the way she hides herself away and keeps herself to herself. She doesn't open up to any of the characters, but this style of writing shows that she will open herself up to the reader. You can start to understand why she is so guarded, even if you might wish she wasn't. 
 Last Thoughts 
 This is a good start to the trilogy and was enough to allow me to invest something into each character. I have left wanting to revisit this world and catch up with its inhabitants. I hope that we get to see a softer side to Saba and have the opportunity to see the other characters receive some further development. The novel ended quite openly, so I have no idea what to expect from the next instalment. I am very much looking forward to it. 
 Reading Recommendation: Read it! 
 TL;DR 
 Think Mad Max with a young, female protagonists and without all of the cars. Horsemen capture Saba's brother and she'll do anything to get him back. Cue a very angry journey to get him back.

<<Overview>> 
 Flawlessly paced. Volumes 1 and 2 seemed to pass in the blink of an eye, and while Volume 3 was still a fast read, it felt like a complete arc. It also, unsurprisingly, left me desperate for more. 
 Take your copy of Volume 3. Flip it over. Take a minute to just appreciate how effing hot Alana and Marko are. 
 ALL THE FEELS. All of them were felt in this volume, from laughter, to suspense, to happy tears, to heartbreak. 
 <<Plot>> 
 The story does a tiny rewind and backs up to a few days before Volume 2 ended. A couple of new characters are introduced, and our happy family arrives on the planet Quietus. After Alana proves herself to totally be the most badass mom ever (wielding a mace against a bone monster, all with baby Hazel safely in her arms), we get a very unimpressive introduction to D. Oswald Heist. As the story says, "But no one makes worse first impressions than writers." They all join him in his lovely lighthouse home, and all seems well until the inevitable arrives, something we know is coming: Prince Robot IV. 
 The Will, Gwendolyn, and Slave Girl are stranded on a lush, exotic planet. While waiting to get the ship fixed, The Will renames Slave Girl as Sophie, and also starts hallucinating about The Stalk in a very Battlestar Galatica way (was I the only one picturing Gaius and Six while he was having a conversation with both Gwendolyn and his hallucination?). After being wishy-washy about wanting to continue his pursuit of Alana, Marko, Hazel, and IV, a rather momentous event occurs that causes Gwendolyn to seek out Marko's help, rather than his head on a stick. 
 Also, the page solely between Sophie and Lying Cat. It will simultaneously melt and break your heart all at once. I had chin wibbles. You'll know it when you see it. 
 We also meet two new characters, Upshet and Doff, a couple of journalists (and the first gay couple we're officially introduced to as characters) in pursuit of the story of a lifetime. The story of Alana and Marko and their darling lovechild is one neither side wants to let out, and it makes them some serious enemies straight out of the gate. Even with their tongues tired, I doubt this will be the last we see of this duo. 
 Oh, and all the Robots are assholes. Not a surprise. 
 Annnd...spoilers! 
  Sophie stabbing The Will! Nooo! I really don't want The Will's character out of play for long, especially with Gwendolyn's admission to love at the end. 
 Gale was totally lying about Alana, right? Right?! He just said that to throw Upshet and Doff off the scent. He wouldn't just spill such a big secret to two nobody reporters, right...? 
 Heist's death was awful. I don't think I've ever had such a reaction to a character death in a graphic novel before. His bond with Klara, and the family, and just...ugh. They already took Barr from us, why did they have to take Heist too?  
 <<Cast>> 
 Some of this could get spoiler-y, so read at your own caution. 
 D. Oswald Heist makes yet another fabulous character introduction: totally drunk, wearing nothing bug a robe and slippers, and promptly puking all over baby Hazel. But, of course, that's only our first impression. Heist is a very kind, generous, and intelligent man. He immediately bonds with Klara over the loss of their loved ones. (The sentiment they share over the pain of losing your partner being worse than losing your child. Ungh. It killed me.) He takes to the family, and becomes an unbeatable schemer with Klara in planting ideas into the happy couple's head about their future. I was so very sad that we don't have him in the story anymore. 
 I do love Klara, as well. She's so snarky, but it's obvious she cares about her granddaughter. While she obviously struggles with Alana's race moreso than her late husband, you can tell she's coming around, and that she plans to protect and help her family, no matter what. She can be abrasive, but she has the young family's best interests at heart. I love having her acidity around to tamper down the sweetness of Alana and Marko. There's mutual respect building between Alana and Klara as well, like how Alana wouldn't throw an arm-wrestling match to her new mother-in-law just because she's wounded and grieving. They're beginning to respect one another's strength. 
 Gwendolyn is developed more in this volume as well, and I'm impressed. She catches on to the hallucinogenic food like a lightning bolt. She also proves that she's not just all about revenge when she seeks out Marko's help for The Will, putting aside her need for revenge in the face of losing someone she only recently admits to loving. 
 Alana's little booknerd moments nearly killed me. When she actually said "bookgasm" out loud, and freaked out over spoilers to Heist's next book. Gah! Not to mention, we learn how Hazel got her name. The couple named her after the librarian that first introduced Alana to Heist's books. How freaking adorable is that? 
 Upshet and Doff don't get too much actual character development this time around, besides being journalists and being a couple on a planet that severely frowns on homosexuality. I hope to see more of them because, yay diversity! 
 We also get a glimpse at The Will's sister, The Brand. The Brand has a ridiculously animal companion, an evil Saint Bernard that can shoot darts out of its nose. I kind of want one. Also, it was lovely to see some vulnerability and emotion when it comes to the bounty hunters. The scene with her in the hospital with The Will, calling him by his real name and getting teary? Just wonderful. How sweet is it that The Will named Slave Girl after his sister, too? 
 <<Art>> 
 I'm slowly becoming convinced that there is no comic book artist that can compare to Fiona Staples. From neon sky sharks, to naked unicorn ladies, she tackles it all and it makes perfect sense. She can convey a lot of emotion in her characters' faces, her world-building is jaw-dropping, and her color palette just makes you want to sink right into the pages. Everything is lush and vibrant and unique. 
 I also don't know if this is just the benefit of having a female artist that doesn't have to follow any rules (because Saga obviously has none), but the diversity of body imagery is refreshing. I know there are a lot of issues in the comic world with how women are portrayed, and I feel Saga really tackles that. Alana's stepmother, Even, is short and pear-shaped, with an obvious tummy-pooch, even though she's young. Gwendolyn is tall and lanky, athletic with very little curve. The Brand is almost entirely androgynous. Alana is beautiful and fit, but remains almost completely covered up most of the time. There's no weird sexy poses for action sequences, just lots of badassery. 
 My favorite comic book art ever. I think I can safely say that now.

 Another great read from Colleen Hoover. The first chapter of Hopeless was fantastic and set the tone for the rest of the book. It pulled me in and I knew I'd been set up - I wasn't putting this one down until I was finished. 
 /// 
 Sky has lead a sheltered life. Adopted as a toddler, she's survived until now with no television, telephones or internet. Now, it's her senior year and she's managed to convince her mother to attend public school. Being home schooled her entire life hasn't hindered Sky's extracurricular activities though, and with some help from her neighbor and best friend, Sky's already got a reputation. Making it worse, her friend is doing a semester abroad, leaving Sky to fend for herself. 
 Dean's been gone for last year. If you believe the rumors, that year was spent in juvie. Now he's back in town and on a collision course with Sky. The first time they meet is an intense experience, leaving Sky feeling shaken. Use to feeling numb, the emotions Dean makes Sky feel after only a few moments rattle her. Sky knows she should stay away from him, but he's not going to make it easier. 
 As Sky and Dean spend time together, she realizes that he might not be who he claims. He's hiding something, something big. When the truth is revealed, Sky will learn that there are worse things than feeling numb. Some things are just hopeless. 
 /// 
 [ Spoilered Review ] 
 While I really liked this story, it wasn't without a few weaknesses. 
 Hoover gives us another emotional, intense read and a great cast of characters with Hopeless. I love her character building. She's able to create unique personalities, each with distinctive voices. She's also so good at developing characters through the challenges they face. The book also held a good pace through most of the story. It had the right mix of romance, drama and mystery. The flashback chapters were well placed, giving enough enough away to help the reader try to piece it together and think they've got it all figure out - which makes the true "holy shit" moment far more unexpected and shocking. 
 My issue with the pace of the book comes with the scene involving Sky's confrontation with her father. It was too short, too undeveloped and not that well placed within the story. It caused the rest of the story to really drag. They argue, a gun is drawn and he blows his damn head off. And then...that's it. Sky and Holder drive off to the hotel and that's the end of it. No consequences, nothing more is really said about the incident afterwards. To me, that should have been one of the the big moments of the book. Sky confronts the catalyst for her entire life, the reason for her broken memories and stolen life and the entire thing was so...lackluster and blah. The rest of the book was still good, but by then it just felt like a lot of fluff. 
 All in all, this is another solid addition to my bookshelf. Hoover has become an "I will read anything you write" author for me, and this book is no exception. 4/5 stars for this one.

Overall it was a good book. In some regards it is dated. The counter to that is the details seem more plausible than a normal espionage book. Le Carre is a former member of Her Majesty's Secret Service. 
 Leamas is a 50-year old English spy. He headed up the Berlin network. The story begins with his chief turncoat being gunned down at the Berlin Wall. Ready for retirement after this disaster and the effective end of the network, Leamus retreats back home. There he is presented with one last job. The balance of the book is that job. 
 We learn about a spy's commitment to the job. It's not about the money as we find Leamus living a horrifically sparse life that finds him jailed. It's all part of the con. He falls for a Communist. Liz seems to be his downfall, but again, it has all been thought out. 
 The plot marches along fairly predictably until the end. It is then that some twists are offered. It is also there that the book falters some for me. The double-twist at the Communist trial is not explained well enough for me. Did Leamus know Mundt was in it all along? If not, then how did it come that Mundt helped with the escape? It would seem rather forced at that point. 
 Liz was shot dead climbing the Berlin Wall. I think a better ending for her would have been to have refused to climb. Staying behind the wall to show her allegiance to the Party seems far more fitting. And did Leamus make it? It is unclear. I suppose that is done purposely. I don't care for it. 
 Le Carre's writing agrees with me. Perhaps it is because the book is 47 years old and is how books I grew up with were written. Perhaps it is just Le Carre's style. I noted he used lain perfectly. Given my struggles conjugating that verb, it is always nice to see the work used.
