Super shy and nerdy scientist Angie is pursued by super hot and sexy rockstar architect Mat. 
 The Good 
 -Kindle Unlimited 
 -Funny: I enjoyed the snark between the characters alot and I thought there were several classic funny lines throughout the story that I'd use in real life lol. 
 -Character driven story: Genuine conversations between Mat and Angie helped to display their attraction and chemistry. 
 -Strong hero: Mat's a strong hero who has no problems with his feelings for Angie, which I enjoyed. His protectiveness and attraction for Angie was attractive. This is split first person POV with Mat and Angie, and I felt his feelings and actions were the stronger of the two and easier to read/connect with. 
 -Solid relationships: By far, I think the strength of this story lies within the relationships between Angie's friends, her father and Mat's family. I'm Latina, so I loved the little things, like calling his mother mami, or when Danny teased Mat by calling him Biggie or Lurch, like real family does. Their banter and affection for each other was something I found easily relatable, and I enjoyed their scenes throughout. 
 -Standalone story: Though it works on its own, I would re-visit this little 'verse. I think Les or Danny have a solid presence that could carry a first person story. 
 The Bad and Everything in Between 
 -Angie's self esteem issues: My biggest obstacle to loving this story. I understand when a character starts off with these issues, and it truly *is* a fine line to ride, but I would have liked to have seen her outgrow it as the story went on. Even as far as 80% in, her inner dialogue was so negative that it was hard to believe in her ability to have an equal relationship with Mat. Angie was a bit too emotionally fragile a heroine for me - Mat and her father had to take care of her, the inevitable crying jags just made her weaker as a heroine. 
 -Cartoon-ish mother/villain: there was little character development with Angie's mother. She gave some insight as to why Angie is so insecure, but there was nothing even remotely redeemable about her, which made her pretty one-dimensional. 
 -Speaking of offputting: The first "close encounter" in the tent threw me for a bit of a loop because while I think having Mat's sister in the tent is meant to be played for laughs, it took me out of what could have been a sexy hot moment and made me cringe a bit.  
 -Grammar/punctuation/spelling errors: I know to expect some from a self-pub, but there were several peppered throughout the text that distracted me and just took me out of the moment. It's something that can be corrected with a good editor. 
 The Bottom Line 
 Despite my issues with Angie as a heroine, the story was engaging and there's alot I did like about it. I think this a promising start from a new author. I would recommend for those who don't mind a weepy heroine, and looking for a light, funny read. I would check out more by Ms. Vianna in the future.

 For me this is a remarkable reading experience. I always fall in love with a book that stirs my emotions. So much. This did it. This was a knee weakening, gut twisting, kind of book for me. WOW! 
 That was quite a ride. 
 I was more than a little hesitant to read this book, I read enemies of the state and was blown away by it and I thought there is no way a second book with the same characters is going to live up to it. 
 I was wrong, in fact this book was even better than book 1. 
 This book had so many twists and turns it was impossible to predict where anything is going. Just when you would settle into a new reality, the author would whoosh you to a different one and before you could catch your breath you are being thrown into yet another one. Everyone and everything is suspicious and you can't rule out betrayal from people you want very much to trust. 
 Tal Bauer has an amazing talent of putting together things that would be otherwise boring to someone like me, I don't usually want a lot of details in military actions, machinery, technology, government bureaucracy, geography etc. He takes these things and makes them so much part of the personalities in the story such that you want every little detail as mundane as it might be to understand the whys and hows of it. 
 The fact that he can combine all that macho, political and military content with an exceptional display of emotions is what made it such a delicious story. 
 I mean, he can write heartbreak in such a way that you yourself want to Ethan to pass that bottle of whiskey to you so that you can be miserable together.  even the health tests before Ethan and Jack could commit to doing away with condoms had me on the edge wondering if they were going to be interfered with or if they would turn out bad, I was completely feeling Ethan's apprehension and the reality of what ifs, it was so real.  
 I have no idea how much of the stuff on this story is reality and how much is creative license but this reads like a well researched and appropriately portrayed book. 
 I have one or two complaints about the probability of certain things occurring as commonly and as often as they do but they don't take away from the magnificence of this book. 
 I can't wait for book three.

Talk about a misleading synopsis. The cover image and the blurb make it sounds as though this book is about a girl, possibly a teen. 
 It's not. It's about a grown woman, probably mid-twenties -- and if the age were the only issue that annoyed me, we'd be in much better shape here. 
 The premise of this book is actually fascinating. Hope cannot be remembered. People who see her day after day react each time as though they're meeting a stranger. Hope is so unmemorable that she seems to create holes that the subconscious works to fill. Someone who had a delicious dinner with Hope will remember being at the restaurant -- for a meal that they ate alone. She can disappear in any crowd, because as soon as she's out of sight, she's literally out of mind. 
 The parts of the book that work best are about Hope's inner life and how it is to be in the world so utterly alone, absolutely free of any restrictions or responsibilities, yet with no connections that last longer than a few hours. It makes sense that ultimately Hope would become a gifted thief. You can't exactly hold down a steady job when each day your boss thinks you're someone completely new... and it's easy to get away with crimes when eyewitnesses never remember seeing you. 
 The plot of the book centers around a creepy app called Perfection, encouraging people to become "perfect" through an endless cycle of feedback on their habits, choices, purchases, and more. Hope becomes obsessed with tracking down the people who profit from Perfection and hurting them, and ends up involved in international espionage as part of a very long manhunt. Unfortunately, much of Hope's journey has to do with her vendetta against Perfection, and it's confusing and distracting and really, very disjointed. 
 It bothered me that Hope's brain-damaged sister Grace was the only one who could always remember and recognize Hope. This is never explained. Can other people with brain injuries remember her as well? Is her condition something in her own brain, as we're led to believe? If so, why would Grace be immune from the memory impairment? You'd think Hope would want to explore this question, if she's truly interested in understanding her condition and finding a treatment, but she never even thinks about it, as far as we can see.  
 Frankly, this book was a slog to get through. Like I said, the concept of Hope's inability to be remembered is pretty mind-warping stuff -- but the plot ends up in a pointless, long drawn-out crime caper, and the writing seems to consist mainly of strings of phrases with a noticeable lack of verbs. 
 I might have enjoyed this book more if it were about 100 pages shorter, but even so, the entire crime story left me cold. Terrific concept, weak execution. I didn't hate the book, but I can't say I particularly enjoyed it either.

'I find I think of myself not as a writer so much as someone who provides a gateway, a tangenital route for readers to reach the circus. To visit the circus again, if only in their minds, when they are unable to attend it physically. I relay it through printed words on crumpled newsprint, words that they can read again and again, returning to the circus whenever they wish, regardless of time of day or physical location. Transporting them at will. 
 When put that way, it sounds rather like magic doesn't it?' 
 The Night Circus had been flirting with me for a long time, catching my eye every time I walked into a bookshop, drawing me in with its glimmering stars, suave characters and promises of its spell. When I finally bought it, it was because I longed for something magical, pairing it with A New York Winter's Tale. The latter did not go well, but this fulfilled every promise made on the cover. 
 It was truly a magical experience. 
 The best way I can think of to describe it, is like the film The Prestige, pulled that just bit further past the realm of possibility (and with a lot less cynicism). And this works; illusions and conjurings and manipulations are natural in the distorted world of the circus. This is where Mogenstern is to be truly complimented for such wonderful evocation of atmosphere, so nothing feels out of place within the world. Ice sculptures, boats of paper on seas of ink, a forest composed of sonnets, ballrooms exploding with colour, and circuses of black and white. 
 The reason though, it is only four stars are slight issues with the story itself; the climax seemed rushed and didn't make as much sense as the rest of the novel. More importantly though is the Challenge itself, the game that is the anchor for the tale. For two-thirds of the book it is vague, without much consequence. I can see why this is; Morgenstern is simply putting us in the shoes of the Opponents, the two protagonists, who themselves are never clear on the rules. But the inevitable result is that the reader doesn't grasp what is at stake, aimless where there is little clear direction. 
 I'm also debating with myself on the character of Marco, who seems a bit of a non-entity, with little personality to match the beautifully depicted cast of characters by whom he is surrounded. The question is whether this is deliberate, part of his illusion, or just the latest in a line of heroes upon whom readers can project their own fantasies. 
 But for these flaws, the book still gripped me, enveloped me and enchanted me. And for that, I can forgive a lot.

When I was younger, I believed librarians were superheroes in their own realm: the library, surrounded by books. And according to Genevieve Cogman, I wasn't far off from the truth. Granted, these Librarians aren't the traditional sort of hero with capes and sidekicks running about saving people. Instead their goal is simple: preserve unique literature across alternate universes and through time. 
 Sounds like a superhero to me. 
 I couldn't believe I'd never heard of The Invisible Library before. It came into my reading sphere by pure accident, in fact, but I can't say I'm unhappy with that particular course of events. Cogman has created not one but multiple worlds centered around the mysterious Invisible Library. And in this particular story, the Librarian Irene is off to an alternate London (though nothing like the Londons of V.E. Schwab's books) 
 I want to be a Librarian. 
 These people don't just maintain a collection of books. They steal them. They travel to alternate universes to steal books. They're time-traveling literary pirates! Damn right I want to join them. 
 The particular world for this book is a London full of werewolves, fairies, vampires, and other beings of chaos. Though the whole bit about chaos is only described in brief and in a somewhat vague manner, I wasn't bothered by the lack of information. Dragons act as the balance against chaos, though Irene isn't entirely sure herself how that works. But dragons! Give me ALL the dragon books! We get a glimpse of these great and powerful creatures in The Invisible Library but shhh...spoilers. You'll have to read it. 
 I loved Irene. She's jumped up on my list of favorite fantasy heroines. Not only is she determined and passionate about her work, but she doesn't let anything get in her way even if it involves a bumpy airship ride across the city or a submerged carriage. Her loyalty to the Library is beyond reproach (though might get her in trouble someday). Irene is definitely flawed with not only her loyalty-unto-death mindset but also she has a thing for private investigators. It's absolutely adorable, and when she gets to meet one in the flesh she fangirls as much as a woman in the time period can. 
 Clearly, Irene is a true reader. 
 Her trainee, Kai, has a lot of question marks floating around him. He has a habit of adapting to whatever situation he's placed in despite is so-called street background, and while I had my guesses about him early on I was pleasantly surprised during the big reveal. He definitely grew on me and I need to know more about him. The aforementioned detective, Vale, is just as interesting but in a different sort of manner. He's an ode to Sherlock, specifically reminding me of the movies starring Robert Downey Jr. -- unexpected warrior and observational genius. Now I need see some hints of a potential triangle between these two intriguing gentlemen and Irene, but even if that does happen, I don't think she'd draw it out. 
 The only aspect of The Invisible Library that could've been better is some of the writing. I loved the style but at times the descriptions bogged down the story and moved things more slowly that I would've liked (to be fair, I devoured this book in one sitting so clearly is wasn't a big problem). 
 So will you like this book? Do you like fantasy? Do you like steampunk tech? Do you want to be a Librarian? Of course you do! And hey, if none of that sold you, there are dragons. I bet that seals the deal. Snag a copy of your own and keep an eye out for the sequel, The Masked City. You can bet I will be.

This is a fascinating look at what happens to us after we die, from medical experimentation to embalming and burial to more experimental methods of disposing of corpses. Roach incorporates histories of various practices, scientific details, and a clear and humorous narrative voice into her book. 
 I was worried that I would be too grossed out by the nitty gritty details of, say, decomposition and dissection to be able to read the book, but as it turns out, although there are a lot of details on such subjects, they are dealt with frankly but lightly. Roach's personal voice helps in these moments. I can see how her style, which features her own responses to the research she is doing and the things she is faced with, might not be for everyone, but I definitely enjoyed it. When I start to feel overwhelmed by a description of maggots eating a decaying corpse, Roach is right there with me, recognizing the difficulty of seeing such things but refusing to deny its reality. 
 The portions of the book I really had trouble with actually had nothing to do with human corpses but dealt with experiments conducted on animals (instead of on human corpses or living humans). Some experiments that involved dog head transplants almost forced me to set the book aside. Fortunately, however, animal cruelty and experimentation is not a significant element of the book. 
 Overall, I would recommend this book. It reads quickly, is highly entertaining (in a perhaps rather morbid way), and left me feeling far more informed than I was when I began it. Plus, it makes a pretty strong argument for the validity of donating one's body to science or pursuing an alternative, more ecologically sound way of disposing of one's remains, both of which are ideas I support.

This is another one of those books with a cover so intriguing that I always pick it up whenever I see it, only to put it back down after reading the description on the back cover and finding it not to my liking, then immediately forget that I was ever interested in the book at all, until the next time I see it, when I do it all over again. And so it goes, until finally I cave, due either to a sudden interest in the topic or to my suddenly realizing that I picked this book up literally hundreds of times and must therefore read it so I can move on with my life. 
 As it was a sudden interest in the topic that precipitated my finally reading Carter Beats the Devil, I must admit that I was sorely disappointed by the book. It's hard to say precisely where the book goes wrong; my first inclination is to say that there is too much at play in the book, that the author tries to cram in too many plot twists to form a cohesive story. However, since I learned from the author's note, as well as a blurb from the back cover, that Carter the Great is an actual historic personage, and so many of these things must have actually happened, I think the problem actually is that, in the novel, the author lacks grace in his attempt to weave together the disparate elements of Carter's life. The inception of television, for example, may have played a large role in Carter's act, but its introduction in the story is clumsy and, as with many other elements of the book, drawn out far longer than it should have been, well past the point of suspense and into the vast desert of boredom. There was enough presented in the novel to make me curious about the actual history of Carter the Great (most especially to find out how much of the story of Mysterioso is true, the resolution of which in the novel was entirely unsatisfying), but would not impel me to read anything else by Glen David Gold.

This is going to sound weird but I read the first two books in Rachel Van Dyken's Consequence series out-of-order ON PURPOSE and I have no regrets! It most likely changed the mood and tone of each story for me. But I have to say that after reading the first book, I'm so glad I got to know Max in his book first and then got to know Colton and Milo in their book afterwards. It probably won't make sense unless you've already read the books. I'll try to explain, though. 
 "The Consequence of Loving Colton" is told in mostly Milo and Colton's point of views. Milo has been in love with Colton, her older brother's best friend, since they were kids. But Milo was always "Jason's sister" (ain't that the way it always is?). After four years away at college, Milo is dreading coming home for her brother's wedding and seeing Colton after so long. Can she handle it? Not without casualties. 
 Hi-jinks start immediately in chapter one as Milo discusses the intense dilemma of getting out of her car once she arrives home with her best friend Max over the phone. Be prepared for mundane tasks made hilariously huge and catastrophic. There is a plot behind the story of Colton and Milo getting together. It's a doozy of a wedding weekend planned at Jason and Milo's childhood home. I kind of thought the over-the-top antics slightly overshadowed the love story at times. But there is a love story there, woven in between some wedding intrigue, lies, crazy old ladies, drinking, and unrequited love. 
 Don't get me wrong, I really enjoyed this story and it was mostly because of the banter between the characters. They were constantly having to solve problems and get out of messes and their conversations were laugh out loud hysterical. I was a sucker for anytime Max graced the pages, though. He is one smart cookie, that one! Granted, he carries around narcotics to knock people out but hey, you never know when you might need them! 
 I recommend this book for anyone who wants a quick, romantic, not-at-all-serious read; people who take life too seriously need not apply (errrr, enjoy).

The answer is 42. But what is the question? 
 Douglas Adams' take on the Universe and everything in it is that, really, it's just a bit of a joke. There isn't a grand meaning, as decades of science looks to discover. It is, in fact, bumbling along like we are. 
 Take Earth's last resident, unknowingly hitchhiking off of earth in its final seconds. He is quintessentially British. He grumbles, he rationalises, he seeks tea. Or Marvin, the robot who is sick of all the uppity, positive computer systems surrounding him and is by all accounts depressed. Spend a moment with him and you'll feel a little sad too. 
 Ford ended up stranded on Earth for 15 years too long, Trillian discovers her pet mice are actually more intelligent and powerful beings than her, and Zaphod masterminded one of the greatest thefts of the age and he doesn't even know why. They just kind of bumble along, and that's why it's good. 
 It's funny, and instead of having a round of protagonists demanding a reason for their existence, they just kind of blindly go on with what they're doing, whatever that is, and whether or not they actually know why. 
 Can someone tell me why I didn't read this until now?

There was no doubt that I was going to enjoy this third installment in the series but I didn't count on caring so very much about Cormoran and Robin's relationship. I cared in the last two books but now I REALLY care. The investigation of who has sent Robin a severed leg involves three men from Corm's past, all human detritus. As such we get a lot more information on Cormoran's past, from his youth living rough with Leda and his last step-father to his time in SID. It all helps to explain more about him and his motivations. It also served to blind him fairly well to what he needed to see to solve the case. The tough ones are always the personal ones. 
 Robin, who was already fairly awesome, upped her awesome game here and we're treated to more about her background. Her past holds a crime committed against her and gives a wider scope to her personality. One thing was resoundingly clear, she really doesn't need to marry Matthew, I don't care if we're breathing on the culmination of all the plans we've been reading about since book one. Much of my time was spent restricting myself from jumping to the end to see if she does or doesn't. I'm not saying. I will say that Matthew continues to be a real jerk. There's a nice flip of a coin shown between the personalities of Cormoran and Matthew. When Robin and Matthew are on the outs, Cormoran refrains from running Matthew down in any way and simply listens to Robin. Later, when Robin and Cormoran are on the outs, Matthew takes the opportunity to basically list for Robin all things flawed about Cormoran.  It was very telling about both men and how they see Robin and I really enjoyed that. I'm just waiting on her to see. 
 Can I also say that there was no Charlotte sighting here and I'm half glad but honestly was hoping she'd turn up as a murder victim. Her full on crazy was not missed but I'm still annoyed with her from past books. I also was wishing for Matthew to be dispatched since he was an obstacle to the killer who had targeted Robin. Alas, no joy there either. I've resigned myself to Matthew continuing on with us but I'm going to take that to mean that when Robin gets rid of him, it'll be epic. 
 And I can't forget to say that the newest "addition" to Team Strike is awesome! Shanker, you can stay! I loved his backstory that explained how he and Cormoran came to know one another and I like that they've kept in touch all these years. Also, he totally had Cormoran's back when things got real there at the end. 
 A few stray observations before I wrap this up: 
 *I'm starting to expect these books to be like watching an episode of Luther where I learn about all manner of murderous deviance. Like, seriously there's abuse of corpse and then there's these killers. This one didn't top The Silkworm in ick factor but there was plenty that made me cringe. 
 *I found myself actually worried about Cormoran's financial situation. I need him to be more solidly liquid because it's wearing on my peace of mind. More than two paying customers at a time, please! 
 *I honestly didn't know if I was supposed to care that Elin was around or not but I do know that I'm not a fan of the random heart stopping, drop dead gorg, woman MM character is sleeping with that he doesn't really like just to have something to do in every book. 
 So 4 stars for this one & I highly recommend it. It's still early enough in the series to get in if you haven't yet. I'll be impatiently awaiting the next book.

The title of the novel is a quotation from the poem Lycidas by Paradise Lost author John Milton: 
 The hungry sheep look up, and are not fed, 
 But swollen with wind and the rank mist they draw, 
 Rot inwardly, and foul contagion spread ... 
 This is an important book, with a capital "I". It is a shame everyone doesn't read it, and even more of a shame that many who would read it would dismiss it as silly liberal propaganda as they have dismissed all discussions on climate change. Because it was written in 1972, before some of the gains of the sexual revolution and civil rights had been realized and when the population of the United States was about 100 million less, some of the words and attitudes seem a bit out of date, i.e. use of fuzz or pig for police; the remarks Peg, as a female reporter, has to endure just because she is good-looking; what is considered wealthy, the price of things and the scale of the economy, etc. Kind of like Dr. Evil in the Austin Powers movies who, because he is transported to the future from the 60s, puts a pinky to his mouth and demands a ransom of One Million Dollars! to save the world from destruction (and everyone giggles). 
 The events that take place, though, don't seem out of place at all with current times. They seem eerily prescient. Any one of the increasingly common news items and disasters in the story could happen, and do, happen every day now in 2012.....pollution, boil water notices, accidental poisonings, acid rain, ruined rivers, streams and oceans, birth defects linked to medications, antibiotic-resistant diseases, endless wars, riots, crop disasters, increasing rate of earthquakes, deforestation, extinction of species, rise of corporate controlled government and total collapse of the environment. The whole world is rotting and the core of that rot is the United States with its population of proud, polluting, entitled, careless, clueless millions with their attitudes of we are the best, our way is the only right way, everything was put on this earth just for us, etc. Or so says the author. 
 The book is written in chapters of varying length, some just a few words, a poem, a sign or a press release. A little disconcerting at first but it all adds up to a concise picture and the inevitable conclusion from Austin Train and others that the only way to cure the Earth's ills is  to get rid of its worst offenders....a housewife in Ireland smells smoke, and says to a visiting doctor: "We ought to call the fire brigade, is it a hayrick?" to which the doctor replies, "The brigade would have a long way to go. It's from America. The wind is blowing [from] that way." . Great book.

I am a sucker for a good first contact novel, and this is probably the best I've ever read. The main character, Caine Riordan, uncovers a conspiracy of some sort and gets turned into an ice cube for a long period of time. When he is revived, his memory is fiddled with so that he is missing 100 hours. Those responsible use those 100 hours as a carrot to draw Riordan into reluctantly doing their bidding. 
 As a polymath, he has an unusually quick mind which gets him into all sorts of trouble with the mysterious agents who are trying to kill him at every turn. This book is part science fiction action movie, part covert spy novel. 
 The first contact scene, which takes up the latter third of the book is a wonderful dance of diplomacy, and features aliens that are truly alien. 
 The writing had a few quirks which were sort of awkward, IMO, but did not detract from the story. It is fast paced and accessible while being fairly meaty at the same time. A very enjoyable read.

Oh god, where to start with this one. I am so torn. First of all I was given this book in exchange for an honest review. I wanted to like this book so much. But it turned me off from the beginning. I'll admit I'm a little biased though. I absolutley adored the animated series Avatar: The Last Airbender. I could not get into the beginning of this book because this was WAY to reminiscient of that. The four realms, the fire realm being the egomanical power hungry bad guys, the kid prrotectors, there were too many similarities for me. I also HATED Roxy. Every time we switched to her point of view I wanted to pull my hair out. The small minded, petty views she expressed, her self-centered spoiled child attitude, way too much for me. Jazz I liked a lot more. Still, on her side, come on, your best friend whom you tell everything too, comes home and you can't open up and express your fears. She's so oblivious to her own stuff. I kept waiting for her to open up and share with someone, anyone. The pacing of this book was so slow. Way too much talking about the things they were going to do and nothing really happened. I kept picking it up, reading a chapter, and putting it down. And I never do that with a book. I was forcing myself through the first 2/3 of the book. It was so frustrating. 
 Then it happened. Jazz finally decides to listen to her dreams and we're off. Roxy and Brae were talking. Things were happening. From there on out I was with the story. As our little dynamic group was trying to figure out what Jazz's dreams meant, and what the fire realm was plotting, I was cheering for them. Suddenly I felt like the story was happening; the characters were interesting. But because it took sooooooo long to get there I feel a little disapointed that there wasn't more time to explore things. I felt Roxy's transition was rushed. And I would have loved to have watched everyone sneaking around trying to figure out the plot for longer. Still that final 1/3 gave me enough I'd be interested in reading the next book and seeing where it goes. It was a good cliff hanger and there is a lot of potential with where they left things.

This is Allison's Story. She lives in a world ruled by vampires, and the humans are basically walking food supply. She has chosen to be an unregistered outsider living on the fringes staying on the brink of starvation with her "gang", she collects book and other small tokens of the world before. Unlike the others Alli can read, though books and literacy have been banned. The book takes a turn when Allie goes outside the "secure area" in search for food - b/c the supplies have dwindled to nothing! 
 WELL- the vamps are not the only thing she has to fear! Rabids (Monsters created by a plague) are blood-hungry beasts who's bite causes the bitten to become what they fear! 
 Without giving too much away she is attacked & She is given the choice by Kanin (who I personally loved even with his supposed cold nature) to become a vamp or die. 
 She chooses to live, and the story circles around Allie trying to accept the life she has chosen. Understanding she can never go back to the life she once had and trying to decide how to continue on without becoming the monster that the humans believe all vamps to be. 
 I REALLY enjoyed this book. The only things that could have been better is if it would have circulated around Kanin. 
 *Swoon.. Also, I didn't love Z as much as Kagawa wanted me too.. Maybe the next book he will hold my heart... WE SHALL SEE!

** spoiler alert ** 
 I groaned and grunted my way through the first few chapters because guess what, Robert Langdon just found himself in the middle of a manhunt. Again To think Langdon should have been able to handle being hunted by now without some chick saving his smart ass time and time again. 
 I quickly got over that, though, because this time the stakes are higher and the characters are so much harder to spell. Especially the revelation about Sienna Brooks being FS-something. I knew there was something about her but that absolutely surprised me. Regarding her, no theory of mine was correct. 
 Still, the conclusion is quite upsetting. I did not appreciate so diplomatic an ending. After all that talk of a plague having been created to strike half the Earth's population, more so when I got to the part where they found out it's been a week since the virus has been released to the Earth's atmosphere, I just expected there'd be more collateral. 
 Bertrand Zobrist was waging war against humanity no matter how good his intentions are for the whole. At least that's how Dan Brown made it look like. And war is supposed to be intensely emotional and tragic. When Sienna Brooks almost escaped but decided to give Langdon the explanation she owed him, she admitted she knew about the virus, she tried to stop it, and it was actually more dangerous than what they initially thought. 
 I was already filled with trepidation knowing nothing will ever be the same again for all humanity. I braced myself for the horrors about to come. I was ready for them. 
 Imagine how I felt when I figured out the virus doesn't cause death nor even the slightest sickness to whoever it affects, but just renders them infertile. Moreover, the virus was genetically randomized to affect only a certain number of people such that in the long run the Earth's population is moderated and maintained at a certain number. NOW WHAT THE HELL IS SO DANGEROUS ABOUT THIS??! 
 It's not a plague after all, but a compromise. The fanatic for an enemy who jumped to his death, pursued by the World Health Organization, even the CDC, was not at all an enemy but some genius risk-taker who actually had humanity's best interest at heart. In the end as well, the WHO secretary accepted it as the solution they've been waiting for. 
 So who was the antagonist in the end? Zobrist? Sienna for not confiding in the authorities? The WHO secretary for not listening? ANG SAKIT PO SA ULO. 
 It would've been nice to have someone to blame and in the end defeat. 
 It would've been nice as well if an actual plague broke out then Sienna, being the smartest person in the book (based on what IQ test they used), found a way to save the world. But nooooo. 
 Plenty resources had to be wasted just to put Langdon in some kind of Truman show. The WHO and CDC had to chase off a brilliant geneticist to his death when he could've led scientists to more advancements in genetic engineering. Not to mention the deaths of that spike-haired woman and Robert's friend Il duomino. 
 *Deep breathing* 
 Okay, rant done. Obviously I have my opinions. 
 That being said, I still loved the book. It was like I toured Florence, Venice, and Istanbul's museums and temples with Dan Brown as a docent. Great fragments of history are displayed in the pages and I always slowed down to admire them despite the exhausting chase. And despite my disagreements with Dan Brown's decisions for the story's ending, I admit it also had its intrigue. I particularly enjoyed thinking about the ethical and moral implications of the virus's release. There are plenty of interesting points to note. 
 All in all, Inferno is brilliant. An intellectual treat as well as an intellectual torment.

 This is a Good Read. It's a mix of a detective story and Medieval church politics, theology, and philosophy. The way that the two aspects of the book intermix is perfect, never feels contrived, and the pacing back and forth between action and intellectual discussion is great. Just when you're getting bored, say, hearing some old stodge ranting about the indecencies of humor and laughter, or detailing the particularities of heretical sects, the blood starts pouring and the action begins again. 
 The insurgent peasantry acts from behind the curtain, shaping the events of the story, but is never directly seen. Heretical movements force the hands of the Church, abbey, and the reformers. The monks of the abbey aren't so historically frozen as it may seen, they each have their own desires. Even from the perspective of the status quo, the Name of the Rose makes the story of the heretics feel all the more intense with their absence. The power of the heretical insurrections is felt in the frantic meetings between reformers & Inquisition. 
 I'd love to read a story about Fra Dolcino or other radical heretics. Or, I'd love for Adso to have taken revenge for his lover and assassinate Bernard Gui. Or, a triumphant heretical horde to burn the abbey to the ground. Regardless, the abbey is burnt in the end even if others have to burn as well.
